Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Paramatthadīpanī

The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning

Saṅgaha mahāṭīkā pāṭha

The Text of the Great Sub-commentary on the Compendium

Ganthārabbhakathā

Discourse on the Commencement of the Treatise

[Ka]

[Ka]

Udayā [M 0.0001] yassa ekassa, saddhammaraṃsi jālino;

Pabujjhiṃsu janambujā, jātikkhette mahāsare.

By the arising of that unique one, possessing a blaze of rays of the True Dhamma, the lotus-like people awakened in the great lake of the field of birth.

[Kha]

[Kha]

Vandāmi taṃ mahāsūraṃ, mahāmoha tamonudaṃ;

Sañjātaṃ so hadaye mayhaṃ, tamokhandhaṃ panūdataṃ.

I pay homage to that great hero, the dispeller of the great darkness of delusion; having arisen in my heart, may he dispel the mass of darkness.

[Ga]

[Ga]

Porāṇakehi viññūhi, vaṇṇitā vaṇṇanā bahū;

Dissanti idha lokamhi, abhidhammatthasaṅgahe.

By the wise ones of old, many expositions have been composed on the Compendium of Abhidhamma Meanings; they are seen here in this world.

[Gha]

[Gha]

Na tāhi tuṭṭhiṃ vindanti, ye sāratthā bhimānino;

Te maṃ saṅgamma yācanti, paramatthassa dīpanaṃ.

Those who esteem the essential meaning do not find satisfaction in those (expositions); they approach me and request an elucidation of the ultimate meaning.

[Ṅa]

[Ṅa]

Mahaṇṇave ratanāni, uddharitvā dipavāsinaṃ;

Yathicchakaṃpi dajjeyyuṃ, na vattabbāva ūnatā.

Having drawn jewels from the great ocean for the island-dwellers, even if they were to give as they wish, no deficiency should be spoken of.

[Ca]

[Ca]

Tathevettha [M 0.0002] vipulatthā, aṇṇave ratanūpamā;

Satakkhattuṃpi vaṇṇeyyuṃ, pariyādinnā na hessare.

Even so here, the vast meanings, like jewels in the ocean; even if they were to be expounded a hundred times, they would not be exhausted.

[Cha]

[Cha]

Tasmā tāsu vaṇṇanāsu, sāramādāya vaṇṇanaṃ;

Nānāsārattha sampuṇṇaṃ, uttāna padabyañjanaṃ.

Therefore, taking the essence from those expositions, an exposition complete with various essential meanings, with clear words and phrases.

[Ja]

[Ja]

Nātisaṅkhepa vitthāraṃ, mandabuddhippabodhanaṃ;

Karissaṃ taṃ paramatthesu, suṇantu pāṭavatthinoti.

Not too concise, nor too extensive, for awakening those of dull intellect; I shall compose it on the ultimate truths. Let those who are skilled in the text listen.

Pathamagāthā-paramatthadīpanī

The First Verse: The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning

1. Abhidhammatthasaṅgahaṃ kattukāmo anuruddhatthero saṅgahārabbhe tāva sappayojane pañcapiṇḍatthe dassento ādigātha māha. Pañcapiṇḍatthānāma ratanattayavandanā, ganthābhidheyyo, ganthappakāro, ganthābhidhānaṃ, ganthappayojanaṃ. Tattha tīsu ratanesu nippaccakārakaraṇaṃ ratanattayavandanānāma. Sā sammāsambuddhamatulaṃ sasaddhammagaṇuttamaṃ abhivādiyāti etehi padehi dassitā. Sakalena ganthena abhihitā padhānatthabhūtā cattāro abhidhammatthā ganthābhidheyyo. So abhidhammatthasaṅgahantipade abhidhammattha saddena dassito.

1. The Venerable Anuruddha, wishing to compose the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, first spoke the introductory verse at the commencement of the compendium, showing the five summary meanings with their purpose. The five summary meanings are: homage to the Triple Gem, the subject matter of the treatise, the mode of the treatise, the title of the treatise, and the purpose of the treatise. Among these, homage to the Triple Gem means performing an act of reverence without expectation of return. That is shown by these words: 'Having paid homage to the matchless Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, together with the excellent True Dhamma and the supreme Community.' The subject matter of the treatise is the four principal Abhidhamma meanings, which are expressed by the entire treatise. That is indicated by the word 'Abhidhammattha' in the phrase 'Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha'.

[1] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[1] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

Saṅgahitabhāvopi abhidheyyoyevāti katvā abhidheyyo abhidhammatthasaṅgahapadena dassitotivuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It has been stated that, having considered that the state of being compiled is also the subject matter, the subject matter is indicated by the term 'Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha'. That is not proper.

Na hi so appadhānatthabhūto saṅgahitabhāvo imasmiṃ piṇḍatthadassane abhidheyyo nāma bhavituṃ yuttoti. Ito paṭṭhāyaca ṭīkāyanti vutte imassa saṅgahassa dvīsu sīhaḷaṭīkāsu pathamāṭīkā daṭṭhabbā. Vibhāvaniyanti vutte etarahi pākaṭā dutīyā. Ṭīkāsūti vutte dvepi. Mahāṭīkāyanti vutte visuddhimagge mahāṭīkā daṭṭhabbā. Yañca vacanaṃ vibhāvaniyaṃpi āgataṃ, aññatthāpi āgataṃ, taṃpi idha vibhāvaniyaṃtveva vuccati āsannattāti. Sabhāgadhammasaṅgahavasena ganthavidhānākāro ganthappakāro. So pana saṅgaha saddena dassito.

For it is not fitting that this state of being compiled, which is not a principal meaning, should be called the subject matter in this exposition of summary meanings. From this point onward, when 'in the ṭīkā' is said, the first ṭīkā among the two Sinhalese ṭīkās on this compendium should be understood. When 'Vibhāvanī' is said, the second, now well-known, is meant. When 'in the ṭīkās' is said, both are intended. When 'in the Mahāṭīkā' is said, the Mahāṭīkā on the Visuddhimagga should be understood. And any statement that has come in the Vibhāvanī, or has come elsewhere, is also called 'Vibhāvanī' here due to its proximity. The mode of the treatise is the way of structuring the treatise by way of a compilation of homogeneous phenomena. And that is indicated by the word 'saṅgaha' (compendium).

[2] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[2] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

Abhidhammatthasaṅgahapadenāti [M 0.0003] vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It has been said by the term 'Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha'. That is not proper.

Na hi abhidhammatthasaddo ganthavidhānākāraṃ dīpetīti. Atthā nugatā ganthasamaññā vanthābhidhānaṃ. Taṃ abhidhammattha saṅgahapadena dassitaṃ. Saṅgahaganthe kate sati taduggahaparipucchādivasena anāyāsato laddhabbaṃ dhammānaṃ sarūpāvabodhādikaṃ anupādāparinibbānantaṃ ganthassa phalānuphalaṃ ganthappayojanaṃ taṃpi abhidhammatthasaṅgahapadeneva sāmatthiyato dassitaṃ.

For the word 'Abhidhammattha' does not indicate the mode of structuring the treatise. The title of the treatise is the designation of the treatise that follows the meanings. That is indicated by the term 'Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha'. When the compendium treatise has been made, the purpose of the treatise is the fruit and secondary fruit of the treatise, which is the understanding of the nature of phenomena, easily obtained through learning, questioning, and so forth, up to Nibbāna without residue. That too is indicated by the term 'Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha' by its implication.

[3] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[3] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

Saṅgahasaddenāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It has been said by the word 'saṅgaha'. That is not proper.

Na hi abhidhammatthasaddena vinā anāyāsato saṃsiddhimattadīpakena saṅgahasaddamattena tādiso anupādāparinibbānanto payo janaviseso sakkā viññātuṃ, asaddhamma saṅgahānaṃpi loke sandissanatoti.

For without the word 'Abhidhammattha', and merely by the word 'saṅgaha', which effortlessly indicates mere accomplishment, such a specific purpose ending in Nibbāna without residue of clinging cannot be known, since even compilations of false doctrine are seen in the world.

2. Tattha ratanattayavandanā tāva asaṅkheyyaappameyyappayojanā hoti. Yathāha –

2. Therein, the homage to the Triple Gem is indeed of incalculable and immeasurable benefit. As it is said:

Te tādise pūjayato, nibbute akuto bhaye;

Na sakkā puññaṃ saṅkhātuṃ, yamettha mapi kenacīti.

For one honoring such ones, who are extinguished, fearless from any quarter; it is not possible for anyone to reckon the merit here.

Ya metthamapītiettha yenakenaci api manussenavā devenavā brahmunāvā saṅkhātuṃ na sakkāti yojanā. Ṭīkākārāpi taṃ payojanaṃ tattha tattha bahudhā papañcenti. Saṅgahakārā pana antarāyanīvāraṇameva visesato paccāsīsanti. Saṅgahakārā tica buddhaghosattherādayo aṭṭhakathācariyā vuccanti.

The explanation of 'yam ettham api' is that it cannot be reckoned by any human, deva, or brahmā. The sub-commentators also elaborate on that purpose in various ways here and there. The compilers, however, particularly expect only the warding off of obstacles. And by 'compilers' are meant the commentators, such as the Elder Buddhaghosa and others.

Nippaccakārassetassa,

Katassa ratanattaye;

Ānubhāvena sosetvā,

Antarāye asesatoti hi vuttaṃ.

For it was said: 'By the power of this act, done towards the Triple Gem without expectation of return, having dried up all obstacles without remainder.'

3. Kathañca [M 0.0004] ratanattayavandanāya antarāyanīvāraṇaṃ hotīti. Vuccate-ratanattayavandanā hi nāma vandanākiriyābhinipphādako sattakkhattuṃ sattakkhattuṃ anekakoṭisatasahassavāre pavattamāno mahanto puññābhisando puññappavāho. So ca anuttaresu buddhādīsu puññakkhettesu saṃvaḍḍhitattā therassa ca uḷāracchandasaddhābuddhiguṇehi paribhāvitattā mahājutiko mahapphalo mahānisaṃso ca puññātisayo hoti. So sayaṃ payogasampattibhāve ṭhatvā bahiddhā vipattipaccaye apanetvā sampattipaccaye upanetvā atipaṇītautucittāhāra samuṭṭhitānaṃ sarīraṭṭhakadhātūnaṃ upabrūhanaṃ katvā paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya laddho kāsassa janakakammassa anubalaṃ deti. Aladdhokāsassa ca puññantarassa okāsalābhaṃ karoti. Atha laddhānubalena laddho kāsena ca tadubhayena puññena nibbattā rūpārūpasantatiyo therasantāne yamakamahānadiyo viya balavabalavanti yo hutvā pavattanti. Tadā tasmiṃ iṭṭhaphalaghanaparipūrite therasantāne aniṭṭhaphalabhūtānaṃ rogādi antarāyānaṃ uppattiyā okāso nāma natthīti iṭṭhaphalasantānavibādhakāni aniṭṭhaphalasantānajanakāni ca apuññakammāni dūrato apanītāneva honti. Na hi kammānināma puññāni apuññāni ca attano vipākuppattiyā okāse asati vipaccantīti. Tato tasmiṃ santāne āyuvaṇṇā dayo iṭṭhaphaladhammā yāva ganthaniṭṭhānā yāva āyukappapariyo sānāpi vā vaḍḍhanapakkhe ṭhatvā pavattanti. Yathāha –

3. And how does the homage to the Triple Gem become a warding off of obstacles? It is said: The homage to the Triple Gem is indeed a great outpouring of merit, a stream of merit, which brings about the act of homage and occurs for countless hundreds of thousands of crores of times. And because it is developed in the unsurpassed fields of merit—the Buddha and others—and because it is cultivated by the Elder’s lofty aspiration, faith, and qualities of wisdom, it becomes a supreme abundance of merit that is greatly radiant, immensely fruitful, and of great benefit. Standing in a state of successful application, it removes external conditions for failure and brings near conditions for success. Having nourished the eight bodily elements arisen from extremely fine climate, mind, and food, it gives supportive strength to the generative kamma that has found its opportunity from rebirth-linking onwards. And for other merit that has not found its opportunity, it creates the gaining of an opportunity. Then, by the strength gained and the opportunity obtained, by that twofold merit, the continuities of matter and non-matter produced in the Elder’s continuum proceed, having become very powerful, like great twin rivers. At that time, in that continuum of the Elder, which is filled with a mass of desirable results, there is no opportunity whatsoever for the arising of obstacles such as disease, which are undesirable results. Thus, the unwholesome kammas that obstruct the continuity of desirable results and generate the continuity of undesirable results are kept far away. For kammas, whether meritorious or demeritorious, do not ripen if there is no opportunity for their result to arise. Therefore, in that continuum, desirable resultant states such as longevity, beauty, and others proceed, remaining in the phase of increase, until the completion of the treatise, or even until the end of the life-span. As it is said:

Abhi vādanasīlissa, niccaṃ vuḍḍhāpacāyino;

Cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhanti, āyuvaṇṇo sukhaṃ balanti.

For one who habitually pays homage, who constantly respects the venerable ones, four things increase: longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength.

Evaṃ tāya vandanāya antarāyanīvāraṇaṃ hotīti. Tasmā saṅgahārabbhe ratanattayavandanākaraṇaṃ therassa attanā ārabbha mānasaṅgahassa anantarāyena parisamāpanutthaṃ. Na kevalañca therasseva, sotūnañca saṅgahaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ ādimhiyeva ratanattaya vandanā siddhito anantarāyena gahaṇa kiccasampajjanatthanti.

Thus, by that homage, the warding off of obstacles occurs. Therefore, the Elder's act of homage to the Triple Gem at the commencement of the compendium is for the purpose of completing the compendium, which he himself had begun, without hindrance. And not only for the Elder, but also for the listeners who are taking up the compendium, since the homage to the Triple Gem is accomplished at the very beginning, it is for the purpose of the successful completion of the task of grasping it without obstruction.

[4] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[4] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

Sattasu [M 0.0005] javanesu pathamajavana vaseneva vandanā payojanaṃ vibhāvitaṃ viya dissati. “Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyabhūtā”ti hi tattha vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

Among the seven impetuses, the purpose of homage appears to be explained as being by way of the first impetus alone. For it is said there: 'Being experienceable in this very life.' That is not proper.

Upatthambhanakiccasseva idha adhippetattā. Tassa ca sattasupi javanesu upaladdhattāti. Yathā hi āhārarūpassa dvīsu kiccesu ojaṭṭhamakarūpajananakiccaṃ parittakaṃ appamattakaṃ hoti. Catussanta tirūpupatthambhanakiccameva mahantaṃ adhimattaṃ. Tathāhi paṭṭhānepi tadupatthambhanakiccameva gahetvā kabaḷīkāro āhāro imassa kāyassa āhārapaccayena paccayoti vibhaṅgavāro vibhatto. Evamevaṃ idhapi pathamajavanassa avunāva vipākajananakiccaṃ parittakaṃ appamattakaṃ hoti. Ahetukavipākamattaṃ janetīti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Kammantarupatthambhanakiccameva mahantaṃ adhimattaṃ. Tañca sattasupi javanesu upalabbhati yevāti. Yasmā pana ganthābhidheyye ganthappakāre ganthappayojane ca ādito vivitesati sotu janānaṃ ganthassavane ussāho jāyati. Tasmā tesaṃ ganthā bhidheyyādīnaṃ dassanaṃ ganthe ussāhajananatthaṃ. Ganthābhidhānadassanaṃ vohārasukhatthanti. Idamettha piṇḍatthadassanaṃ.

For the function of support is what is intended here, as it is found in all seven impulsions. Just as for matter derived from nutriment, among its two functions, the function of generating the octad with nutritive essence is minor and insignificant, while the function of supporting the four continuities of matter is major and predominant. For even in the Paṭṭhāna, taking only that supporting function, the Vibhaṅgavāra is analyzed thus: 'Edible food is a condition for this body by way of nutriment condition.' Similarly, here too, the function of the first impulsion in generating a resultant in this very life is minor and insignificant. The commentaries state that it generates only a rootless resultant. The function of supporting other kamma is major and predominant, and that is indeed found in all seven impulsions. Moreover, since enthusiasm for hearing the text arises in listeners when its subject matter, type, and purpose are revealed from the outset, the exposition of the text's subject matter and the like serves to generate enthusiasm for the text, and the exposition of the text's title is for ease of discourse. This is the presentation of the condensed meaning here.

4. Ayaṃ pana padattho. Sammāca bujjhi sāmañca bujjhīti sammā sambuddho. Ettha ca sammāsaddo aviparītatthe nipāto. So bujjhitabbesu ñeyyadhammesu bujjhanakriyāya asesabyāvibhāvaṃ dīpeti. Tathāhi padesañāṇe ṭhitā paccekabuddhādayo attano visaye eva aviparītaṃ bujjhanti. Avisaye pana andhakāre paviṭṭhāviya hontīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Visayo ca tesaṃ appamattakova sabbaññuvisayaṃ upādāya yathā hattha puṭe ākāso appamattakova ajaṭākāsaṃ upādāyāti. Te hi phassādīsu dhammesu ekadhammampi sabbākārato bujjhituṃ nasakkontīti. Sabbaññubuddhānaṃ pana avisayo nāma natthi, yattha te viparītaṃ bujjheyyuṃ. Te hi anamatagge saṃsāre anantāsu ca [M 0.0006] lokadhātūsu tiyaddhagate addhamuttake ca dhamme hatthamaṇike viya samasame katvā bujjhanti. Sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāta māgacchantīti hi vuttaṃ. Tattha ñāṇamukheti sabbaññuṃmahābhavaṅgaṃ sandhāyāha. Tattha hi te dhammā bodhimaṇḍe sabbaṃ abhidhammaṃ sammasanato paṭṭhāya niccakālaṃ upaṭṭhahantīti. Sabbaññubuddhā pana yattake dhamme vicāretuṃ icchanti. Tattake dhamme āvajjanāya visuṃ katvā āvajjitvā vicārentīti. Nanu dhammā mahantā bhavaṅgaṃ parittakanti na codetabbametaṃ. Arūpadhammānañhi paramukkaṃsapattānaṃ esa ānubhāvoti. Saṃsaddo pana sāmanti etassa atthe upasaggo. So bhagavato paṭivedhadhammesu anācariyakataṃ dīpeti. Na me ācariyo atthīti hi vuttaṃ. Nanu bhagavato tatīyacatutthāruppa samāpattiyo āḷārudakamūlikāti. Saccaṃ. Tā pana analaṅkaritvā laddhamattāva hutvā chaḍḍitattā pacchā bujjhanakriyāya pādakamattāpi nahonti. Kuto paṭivedhadhammāti. Tasmā tā bhagavato buddhabhāve sācariyakataṃ na sādhentīti. Ayamettha pāḷi anugato attho. Yathāha –

4. This is the meaning of the word. He understood rightly and he understood by himself, thus he is Perfectly Self-Enlightened. Here, the word 'sammā' is a particle in the sense of 'not perverted'. It signifies the complete and thorough understanding of all knowable phenomena without remainder. For instance, Paccekabuddhas and others, established in partial knowledge, comprehend only within their limited sphere without error. Outside their sphere, they are as if plunged into darkness, as stated in the commentary. And their sphere is indeed minor compared to the sphere of the All-knowing One, just as the space in a cupped hand is negligible compared to boundless space. They are incapable of fully comprehending even a single phenomenon, such as contact, in all its aspects. But for the All-knowing Buddhas, there is no sphere where they would understand perversely. Throughout beginningless saṃsāra and across infinite world-systems, they comprehend all phenomena—past, present, future, and the unconditioned—as clearly as if holding a myrobalan fruit in their hand. It is said that all phenomena in every aspect come into the range of the knowledge-door of the Blessed One, the Buddha. Here, 'knowledge-door' refers to the great omniscient life-continuum (bhavaṅga). From the time of comprehensively considering the entire Abhidhamma at the seat of enlightenment, all phenomena constantly present themselves to them. When the All-knowing Buddhas wish to investigate certain phenomena, they separate out those phenomena by way of advertence and examine them. One should not object that phenomena are vast while the life-continuum is limited, for this is the power of immaterial phenomena that have attained the highest excellence. The prefix 'saṃ', however, is a preposition in the sense of 'by oneself' (sāmaṃ). It signifies that the Blessed One's realization of the Dhamma was without a teacher. As it is said, "I have no teacher." But one might argue, "Did not the Blessed One attain the third and fourth formless attainments under Āḷāra and Uddaka?" True, but those attainments, being merely acquired and then discarded without being refined, did not even serve as a basis for his later enlightenment. How then could they be the dhammas of realization? Therefore, those attainments do not establish that the Blessed One's state of Buddhahood was dependent on a teacher. This is the meaning here that follows the Pāli, as it is said:

Tattha katamo ca puggalo sammāsambuddho. Idhekacco puggalo pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi. Tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇāti. Balesu ca vasibhāvaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo sammāsambuddhoti.

Here, what sort of person is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One? Here, a certain person, with regard to things unheard before, fully awakens to the truths by himself. And in regard to that, he attains omniscience and mastery over the ten powers. This person is called a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Tatthāti nimitte bhummaṃ. Balesūti dasabala ñāṇesu. Vasibhāvanti issarabhāvaṃ. Etthaca pubbe. La. Sāmantietena saṃsaddassa atthaṃ dasseti. Tatthātiādinā [sammāsaddassaatthanti. Sammāsambuddhapadaṃ]

'Therein' (Tattha) is the locative of specification. 'In powers' (Balesu) refers to the ten powers of knowledge. 'Mastery' (Vasibhāvaṃ) means sovereignty. And here, by 'by oneself' (sāmaṃ) in the preceding passage, the meaning of the prefix 'saṃ' is shown. By 'Therein' and so on, [the meaning of the word 'sammā' is explained, regarding] the term 'Sammāsambuddha'.

5. Idāni thero attano vandanaṃ suṭṭhubalavaṃ karonto atulanti āha. Anekaguṇapadavisayā hi vandanā suṭṭhutaraṃ balavatī hotīti. Nanu ekaguṇapadavisayāpi vandanā antarā yanīvāraṇesamatthā siyāti kiṃ dutīyenāti. Na na samatthā. Viññujātikā pana satthuguṇatthomane mattakārino nāma na honti[M 0.0007]. Thero ca tesaṃ aññataro. Tvaṃ pana aviññujātiko. Tasmā mattaṃ karonto codesīti. Apica. Na kevalaṃ antarā yanīvāraṇameva vandanāya icchitabbaṃ hoti. Athakho paññāpāṭavādiatthopi icchitabboyeva. Sopi hi anāyāsena gantha niṭṭhānassa ganthapārisuddhiyā ca paccayo hotīti. Anussatiṭṭhānesu hi cittabhāvanā cittasamādhānāvahā hoti. Citta samādhāne ca sati paññātikkhāsūrā hutvā pahati. Samāhito bhikkhave yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā tadatthāyapi attano vandanā suṭṭhu balavatī kātabbāyevāti.

5. Now the elder, making his own salutation exceedingly strong, said 'incomparable.' For a salutation that encompasses numerous qualities is indeed very powerful. But could not a salutation focused on even a single quality be capable of preventing obstacles? Why a second one? No, it would not be capable. But those of wise nature do not act in moderation in praising the Teacher’s qualities. And the elder was one of those. But you are of unwise nature. Therefore, acting in moderation, you object. Moreover, not only should the prevention of obstacles be desired through salutation, but also skill in wisdom and other benefits should indeed be desired. For that too, without difficulty, becomes a condition for the completion of the text and the purification of the text. For, regarding the objects of recollection, the cultivation of the mind brings about mental concentration. And when the mind is concentrated, wisdom becomes sharp and quick, and it strikes down defilements. For it is said: 'O bhikkhus, one who is concentrated understands things as they really are.' Therefore, for that purpose too, one’s own salutation should indeed be made very strong.

[5] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[5] But it is to be elucidated:

“Yathāvuttavacanattha yogepi sammāsambuddhasaddassa bhagavati samaññāvasena pavattattā atulanti iminā vise setī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said, 'Even though the meaning of the words as stated is connected, because the word 'Sammāsambuddha' is used as a designation for the Blessed One, it is distinguished by 'incomparable'.' That is not well said.

Mahantañhi satthuguṇapadānaṃ majjhe etaṃ sammāsambuddhapadaṃ, cando viya tārakānaṃ majjhe. Tasmā taṃ sabhāvaniruttiṃ jānantānaṃsantike bhāvatthasuññaṃ satthusamaññāmattaṃ bhavituṃ nārahati. Aññesaṃ pana padasahassaṃ vuccamānaṃpi satthu samaññāmattameva sampajjatīti. Tulayitabbo aññena saha pamitabboti tulo. Na tulo atulo, natthitulo sadiso etassāti vā atulo. Bhagavā. Na hi atthi bhagavato attanā sadiso koci lokasminti. Yathāha –

Great indeed among the terms for the Teacher's qualities is this term 'Sammāsambuddha', like the moon among the stars. Therefore, for those who understand its true etymology, it is not fitting that it be merely a conventional designation for the Teacher, empty of real meaning. For others, however, even if a thousand words are spoken, they amount only to a mere designation of the Teacher. 'Tula' is that which can be weighed or measured against another. 'Atula' is that which is not 'tula'; or, 'atula' means 'there is no one equal to him'. The Blessed One. For there is indeed no one in the world equal to the Blessed One. As it is said—

Na me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati;

Sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, natthi me paṭipuggaloti.

I have no teacher, one like me exists not; In the world with its gods, no counterpart to me exists.

Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ buddhabhūtassa atulattaṃ. Sampatijātassapi panassa atulatā paññāyati. Tadā hi mahāpuriso sampatijātova samāno puratthimadisābhimukho aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ disā bhāge anantāni cakkavāḷāni ekaṅgaṇāni ahesuṃ. Tesu ṭhitā devabrahmāno mahāpurisa idha tumhehi sadiso natthi. Kuto uttaritaroti [M 0.0008] paramāya pujāya pūjesuṃ. Evaṃ sesadisāsupi. Tadā mahāpuriso attano sabbalokaggabhāvaṃ ñatvā aggohamasmi lokassa, seṭṭhohamasmilokassa, jeṭṭhohamasmilokassa ayamanti mājāti, natthi dāni punabbhavoti evaṃ achambhivācaṃ nicchāresīti. Idaṃpi anacchariyaṃ, yaṃ pacchimabhavaṃ pattassa atulattaṃ. Yadā pana so sumedhabhūto dīpaṅkarabuddhassa santike niyatabyākaraṇaṃ gaṇhi. Tadāpi thapetvā dīpaṅkarasammāsambuddhaṃ pāramitāguṇehi tena sadiso koci nattheva. Natthibhāvocassa tadā pavatte hi dasasahassilokadhātukampanādīhi asādhāraṇapāṭihāriyehi dīpetabbo. Tāni hi paccekabodhisattānaṃ satasahassaṃpi pavattetuṃ na sakkhissatiyeva. Kuto sāvakabodhi sattānanti. Teneva hi tadā pavattipāramipavicayaññāṇaṃ attano visaye sabbaññuthaññāṇagatikanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sāvakabodhisattāpi hi yato paṭṭhāya attano bodhiyā anurūpe sambhāradhamme sayameva jānituṃ sakkonti. Tato paṭṭhāya anivattidhammā hutvā vattānusārimahāputhujjanabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā bodhisattabhūmiṃ okkantā honti. Ekena pariyāyena niyatā sambodhiparāyanā ca nāma honti. Tadā eva buddhānaṃ sammukhibhāve sati niyatabyākaraṇaṃ labhanti. Sabbaññu bodhisatta paccekabodhisattesu vattabbameva natthīti.

And it is not astonishing that he, having become a Buddha, is peerless. Moreover, his peerlessness is evident even at the moment of his birth. For then, the Great Being, immediately upon being born, stood facing the eastern direction. In that direction, countless world-systems appeared as one unified expanse. The gods and Brahmās standing there honored the Great Being, saying, 'Great Being, there is none like you here; how much less one superior!' They paid him the highest homage. The same occurred in the other directions as well. Then, the Great Being, knowing his supremacy over all the world, declared without hesitation, 'I am the highest in the world, the foremost in the world, the eldest in the world. This is my last birth—there is now no more rebirth for me.' This too is not astonishing—the peerlessness of one who has reached his final existence. When he was the ascetic Sumedha and received the definite prediction in the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, even then, apart from Dīpaṅkara the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, there was none equal to him in the virtues of the perfections. Indeed, his peerlessness at that time is to be shown by the extraordinary miracles that occurred, such as the shaking of the ten-thousand-world-system—miracles that even a hundred thousand Paccekabodhisattas would not be able to perform, how much less disciple-bodhisattas! Therefore, it is stated in the commentary that at that time, his knowledge of investigating the perfections as they occurred had the range of omniscience. For even disciple-bodhisattas, from the time they are able to know for themselves the qualities that are the requisites for their own enlightenment, from that time onwards, they become irreversible, transcend the state of a great worldling who follows the round of existence, and enter the stage of a bodhisattva. In one sense, they are called 'those who are certain and have supreme enlightenment as their final goal.' It is then, when in the presence of the Buddhas, that they receive the definite prediction. As for the omniscient bodhisattas and paccekabodhisattas, there is nothing that needs to be said.

[6] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[6] But it is to be elucidated:

Samitatthe yyakārassa akārassa vā vasena etaṃ siddhanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said that this is established by means of the letter 'yya' or the letter 'a' in the sense of 'samita'. That is not sound.

Na hi tulasaddo dhātusiddho kammasādhano ca bhavituṃ na yutto. Tulayituṃ asakkuṇeyyoti atulo. Appame yyoti hi ṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Etena tulasaddo kammasādhanoti dipeti. Evañca sati kammasādhaneneva tadatthasiddhito kiṃ tato samitatthe yyakārassaakārassa vā cintāyāti. Vatticchānugato saddappayogoti katvā etaṃ vuttanti ce. Na. Yathā [M 0.0009] sutaṃ yuttaṃ vajjetvā assutassa parikappanāya payo janābhāvatoti. [Atula padaṃ]

For it is not unsuitable for the word 'tula' to be derived from a root and to have an objective sense. 'Atula' means 'that which cannot be weighed.' For in the sub-commentary it is said, 'immeasurable.' By this, it is shown that the word 'tula' has an objective sense. And this being so, since its meaning is established by the objective derivation itself, what need is there then for consideration of the letter 'yya' or 'a' in the sense of 'equal'? If it is said that this is stated because 'the usage of words follows the intention of the speaker,' [we say,] 'No.' For there is no purpose in speculating about what is unheard, having rejected what is suitable according to what is heard. [The word 'atula']

6. Imehi pana dvīhi padehi satthu tisso sampadā vibhā vitā honti. Hetusampadā phalasampadā sattupakārasampadācāti. Tattha satthu mahākaruṇā samaṅgitā bodhisambhārasambharaṇañca hetusampadānāma. Bodhimaṇḍe pavattitā catuvīsati koṭisabhasahassasaṅkhā mahāvajiraññāṇasaṅkhātā sabbaññumahā vipassanāpi ettheva saṅgahitā. Sā hi mahābodhiyā padaṭṭhāna bhūtāti. Pahāna sampadāyameva vā sā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Phalasampadā catubbidhā pahānasampadā ñāṇasampadā ānubhāvasampadā rūpakāyasampadā cāti. Tattha saha vāsanāya kilesappahānaṃ pahānasampadā nāma. Pahānassa sabbapāripūritāti attho. Atthato pana ariyamaggo, aggamaggaññāṇameva vā. Sabbaññuta ññāṇa dasabalaññāṇādīni ñāṇasampadā.

6. By these two terms, the Teacher's three perfections are explained: namely, the perfection of cause, the perfection of fruit, and the perfection of benefiting beings. Herein, the Teacher's being endowed with great compassion and his accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment are called the perfection of cause. The great insight of omniscience, known as the great diamond knowledge, reckoned as twenty-four hundred thousand crores, which arose at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, is also included here, for that is the proximate cause of the great enlightenment. Alternatively, it should be understood that it is included in the perfection of abandonment. The perfection of fruit is fourfold: the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of spiritual power, and the perfection of the form-body. Herein, the abandonment of defilements together with their latent tendencies is called the perfection of abandonment; it means the complete fulfillment of abandonment. In essence, it is the noble path, or indeed the knowledge of the supreme path. The knowledge of omniscience, the knowledge of the ten powers, and so on, constitute the perfection of knowledge.

[7] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[7] But what is to be clarified

Etāsu dvīsu sampadāsu ñāṇasampadā pathamaṃ vuttā, tato pahānasampadā. Pahānasampadāyeva pana pathamaṃ vattabbā. Sā hi ñāṇasampadāyapubbaṅgamabhūtā paccayabhūtā ca. Mahāṭīkāyañca sāyeva pathamaṃ vuttāti.

Among these two perfections, the perfection of knowledge was mentioned first, then the perfection of abandonment. However, the perfection of abandonment should indeed be stated first, for it is the forerunner and the condition for the perfection of knowledge. And in the Great Sub-commentary, it is this very one that is mentioned first.

[8] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

[8] And what is to be clarified

“Sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ aggamaggaññāṇa”nti ñāṇasampadāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yujjati.

'The knowledge of the supreme path is the proximate cause of the knowledge of omniscience,' is said concerning the perfection of knowledge. That too is not fitting.

Aggamaggaññāṇañhi pahānasampadā eva bhavituṃ arahati. Na hi maggaññāṇato aññā pahānasampadānāma atthīti. Yañca koci vadeyya maggaññāṇaṃ ñāṇañca hoti pahānañca. Tasmā ubhayattha vattuṃ yuttanti. Taṃpi na yujjati. Evañhi sati sampadāsaṅkaro hotīti.

For the knowledge of the supreme path is indeed worthy to be the perfection of abandonment, as there is no other perfection of abandonment apart from path-knowledge. And if someone should say that path-knowledge is both knowledge and abandonment, and therefore it is fitting to speak of it in both places, even that is not fitting, for in that case there would be a confusion of perfections.

[9] Tathā vibhāvaniyaṃ

[9] Similarly, what is to be clarified

Ñāṇasampadāyaṃ [M 0.0010] sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sabbapathamaṃ vattabbaṃpi na vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

In the perfection of knowledge, although the knowledge of omniscience should be mentioned first of all, it was not mentioned. That too is not sound.

Nanu “tammūlakāni ca dasabalādi ññāṇānī”ti ettha ādisaddena sabbaññutaññāṇaṃpi gahitanti ce. Taṃpi na yujjati.

If it is said: 'But is it not so that in the phrase, "and the knowledges such as the ten powers are rooted in that," the knowledge of omniscience is also included by the word 'ādi' (etc.)?'—that too is not fitting.

Na hi appadhānaṃ sarūpato niddisitvā padhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ ādisaddena gahitanti ñāyāgataṃ hotīti. Acinteyyānubhāvehi sīlā diguṇehi iddhi dhammehi ca sampadā ānubhāvasampadā. Lakkhaṇā nubyañjanappaṭimaṇḍitassa rūpakāyassa sampatti rūpakāyasampadā. Sattupakāroduvidho āsayasampadā, payogasampadā ca. Ajjhāsayassa uḷāratā kāyavacīpayogassa ca parisuddhatāti attho. Tattha devadattādīsu virodhisattesupi niccaṃ hitajjhāsayatā āsaya sampadā. Loke abhiññātānaṃ rājūnaṃ rājamahāmattānaṃ seṭṭhi gahapatīnaṃ devarājūnampi dhammaṃ desentassa lābhasakkārādi nirapekkhatāvasena desanāpayogasuddhi payogasampadā. Tattha dve pahānañāṇasampadā sammāsambuddhapadena vibhāvitā. Dvīhi ānu bhāvarūpakāyasampadāhi saha dve sattupakārasampadā atulapadena. Hetusampadā pana dvīhipi padehi sāmatthiyato vibhāvitā. Na hi tādisiyā hetusampadāya vinā itarāsaṃ pavatti atthīti. [Sampadā]

For it is not logical that, after indicating the non-principal in its own form, the manifest principal is understood as included by the word 'ādi' (etc.). The perfection of spiritual power is the perfection through inconceivable powers, virtues such as morality, and psychic powers. The perfection of the form-body is the accomplishment of the form-body adorned with the major and minor characteristics. The benefit to beings is twofold: the perfection of aspiration and the perfection of application. The meaning is: the nobility of aspiration and the purity of bodily and verbal application. Herein, constant aspiration for the welfare of even hostile beings like Devadatta and others is the perfection of aspiration. The purity of the application of teaching, free from expectation of gain, honor, and so on, when teaching the Dhamma to kings, royal ministers, wealthy householders, and even divine kings renowned in the world, is the perfection of application. Herein, the two perfections of abandonment and knowledge are explained by the term 'Sammāsambuddha'. Along with the two perfections of spiritual power and the form-body, the two perfections of benefiting beings are explained by the term 'atula'. The perfection of cause, however, is explained by the capacity of both terms, for without such a perfection of cause, the occurrence of the others is not possible. [Perfections]

7. Punapi thero attano vandanaṃ balavataraṃ karonto sasaddhammagaṇuttamanti āha. Etena dhammasaṅghānaṃpi vandanā katā hoti. Dūratohaṃ namassissaṃ, sasaṅghaṃ lokanāyakanti hi vutte saṅghassapi namanakriyāpatti sahasaddena viññāyati. Eva midaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha namassissanti namassiṃ.

7. Furthermore, the elder, making his own veneration stronger, said, 'together with the True Dhamma and the excellent Sangha.' By this, veneration is also made to the Dhamma and the Sangha. For when it is said, 'From afar I will pay homage to the world-leader together with the Sangha,' the application of the act of homage to the Sangha is also understood by the word 'saha' (together). Thus this should be understood. Herein, 'namassissaṃ' means 'I paid homage'.

[10] Yampana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[10] But what is to be clarified

“Guṇībhūtānaṃpi hi dhammasaṅghānaṃ abhivādetabba bhāvo sahayogena viññāyatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha abhivādetabba bhāvoti navattabbaṃ. Abhivāditabhāvoti pana abhivādananti [M 0.0011] vā vattabbaṃ. Evañhi sati idha adhippetassa kriyā samavāyassa siddhattā dhammasaṅghānaṃpi therassa vandanā kriyāpatti siddhā hotīti. Itarathā tabbapaccayassa arahatthadīpanato abhivādanā rahatā saṅkhāta guṇasamavāyo vutto siyā. Soca idha nādhippeto. Attano nidassanena ca saha na sameti saputtadāro āgatoti.

For it is said: 'The state of being worthy of veneration of even the Dhamma and Sangha, which have become secondary, is understood by the connection with `saha`.' Herein, `abhivādetabbabhāvo` should not be said. Rather, `abhivāditabhāvo` or `abhivādanaṃ` should be said. For this being so, since the intended combination of action here is established, the application of the elder's act of veneration to the Dhamma and Sangha is also established. Otherwise, because the `-tabba` suffix indicates the meaning of 'worthy,' a combination of qualities called 'worthiness of veneration' would be stated. And that is not intended here. And it does not accord with the given example, such as 'he came with his wife and children'.

Apica thero imaṃ ganthaṃ racayissāmīti pubbabhāgeyeva tīṇi ratanāni vandi, atha taṃ attano vandanaṃ ganthappaṭiññāya saha ghaṭetvā dassento imaṃ gāthaṃ racayītipi na na sakkā vattunti. Tathāhi abhivādiyāti vuttaṃ. Na abhivādiyāmīti. Esanayo aññatthapi. Tattha saddhammena ca gaṇuttamena ca attanā nimmitena sakalalokassa saraṇabhūtena saha vattatīti sasaddhamma gaṇuttamo. Sammāsambuddho. Na hi paranimmitena saddhammena gaṇuttamena ca sahitā sāvakā sasaddhammāti ca sagaṇuttamāti ca vuccanti. Na ca attanoeva saraṇabhūtena saddhammena sabrahmacārigaṇuttamena ca sahitā paccekabuddhā tathā thomanaṃ arahantīti, tasmā idaṃpi satthu asādhāraṇaguṇapadameva hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Moreover, it is also possible to say that the elder, intending to compose this treatise, first paid homage to the Three Jewels in the introductory section, and then, connecting his own veneration with the declaration of the treatise, composed this verse. For `abhivādiya` (having paid homage) is said, not `abhivādiyāmi` (I pay homage). This method applies elsewhere as well. Herein, `sasaddhammagaṇuttamo` means 'he who exists together with the True Dhamma and the excellent Sangha, created by himself and become a refuge for the entire world.' This refers to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. For disciples, associated with a True Dhamma and an excellent Sangha created by another, are not called `sasaddhamma` or `sagaṇuttama`. Nor do Paccekabuddhas, who are associated with the True Dhamma and the excellent Sangha of their fellow practitioners which has become a refuge for themselves only, deserve such praise. Therefore, this too should be understood as a term for a quality unique to the Teacher.

Tattha dhāretīti dhammo. Ke dhāreti, attānaṃ dhārente. Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacārinti hi vuttaṃ. Kathañca dhāreti, catūsu apāyesu vaṭṭadukkhesuca apatamāne karonto. Kiñca dhāraṇaṃnāma, yesaṃ vasena sattā apāyesuvā vaṭṭadukkhesuvā patanti, tesaṃ kilesānaṃ ekadesenavā sabbasovā samucchindanaṃ. Imasmiṃ atthe cattāro ariyamaggā nibbānañca nippariyāyato dhammonāma. Ariyamaggā hi kilese samucchindantā nibbānena saheva hutvā samucchindanti. Na vināti, tasmā teyeva pañca ekantato dhammonāmāti. Pariyattidhammo pana dhāraṇupāyoyeva hoti. Cattāri sāmaññaphalānica dhāraṇaphalāniyeva honti, kilesānaṃ paṭippassambhanavasena pavattattā dhāraṇānukūlappavattāni ca. Tasmā ete pañca pariyāyadhammāyevāti. Athavā[M 0.0012], dhārīyatīti dhammo. Dhāraṇārahoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo hi dhārentaṃ ekantena dukkhato moceti. Aggasukheca patiṭṭhāpeti. Soyeva dhāraṇārahattā idha dhammonāmāti. Kopana soti, yathā puttadhammāyeva. Tehi keci bhāvanā vasena keci sacchikiriyavasena keci diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāravasena keci uggaha dhāraṇavasena dhārīyanti. Te ca evaṃ dhārīyamānā dhārentaṃ yathārahaṃ apāyadukkhato vaṭṭadukkhatoca mocenti, aggeca phalasukhevā nibbānasukhevā patiṭṭhāpentīti. Dhārentivā sappurisājanā apāyesu vaṭṭadukkhesuca attānaṃ apata mānaṃ vahanti etenāti dhammo. Dharantivā ettha dhammadīpā dhammappaṭisaraṇā janā laddhappatiṭṭhā hontīti dhammotipi yujjatiyeva. Kasmā panettha dhammo dasavidhova vutto. Nanu paṭipattidhammena saha ekādasavidhova vattabboti. Saccaṃ. Sopana paṭipattidhammo maggassa pubbabhāgappaṭipadāeva hotīti pubbacetanā viya dāne magge eva so saṅgahito. Tasmā dhammo dasavidhova sabbattha vuttoti daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, 'dhāretīti' (it upholds) means the Dhamma. Whom does it uphold? Those who uphold themselves. For it is said, 'The Dhamma indeed protects one who practices the Dhamma.' And how does it uphold? By preventing one from falling into the four states of misery and the suffering of the cycle of existence. And what is this upholding? It is the partial or complete eradication of those defilements by which beings fall into states of misery or the suffering of the cycle. In this sense, the four noble paths and Nibbāna are, in an absolute sense, called the Dhamma. For the noble paths, in eradicating defilements, eradicate them together with Nibbāna, not without it. Therefore, these five alone are, in the ultimate sense, called the Dhamma. The scriptural Dhamma, however, is merely a means of upholding. And the four fruits of recluseship are also the fruits of upholding, as they arise through the calming of defilements and are conducive to upholding. Thus, these are called the Dhamma in a figurative sense. Alternatively, 'dhārīyatīti' (it is upheld) means the Dhamma. This means it is worthy of being upheld. For that which completely liberates the upholder from suffering and establishes them in the highest bliss is, because of its worthiness to be upheld, here called the Dhamma. And what is that? It is like the duties of a son. By these qualities, some are upheld through meditation, some through realization, some through dwelling in the bliss of the present Dhamma, and some through learning and retention. And being thus upheld, they liberate the upholder, as is appropriate, from the suffering of miserable states and the suffering of the cycle of existence, and establish them in the supreme bliss of the fruits or the bliss of Nibbāna. Or, virtuous people, not falling into miserable states and the suffering of the cycle, carry themselves by means of it—thus, it is called the Dhamma. Or, it is also fitting that here people, having the Dhamma as their island and the Dhamma as their refuge, gain a firm footing—thus, it is the Dhamma. But why is the Dhamma here spoken of as tenfold? Should it not be elevenfold, including the Dhamma of practice? True. But that Dhamma of practice is the preliminary practice for the path, and is thus included in the path itself, just as prior intention is in the act of giving. Therefore, it should be understood that the Dhamma is everywhere spoken of as tenfold.

Apica, yadaggena pariyattidhammo idha dhammasmiṃ saṅgahito. Tadaggena pariyattidhārakopi saṅghe vandaneyye saṅgahitoti yutto. Yadaggenaca puthujjanakalyāṇako saṅghe sekkhesu saṅgahito. Tadaggena tassa kalyāṇahetubhūto paṭipatti dhammopi dhamme vandaneyye saṅgahitoti daṭṭhabbo. So hi puthujjanabhūtopi yehi dhammehi samannāgatattā sekhe sotāpatti phalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanne saṅgahito. Te pana dhammā sekkhe sotāpattimagge asaṅgahitāti nasakkā vattunti. Ettāvatā ye vadanti saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti, ettha puthujjana kalyāṇako saṅghe asaṅgahito. Na hi taṃsaraṇaṃ gacchantassa saraṇagamanaṃ sampajjatīti. Tesaṃ taṃ paṭikkhittaṃ hoti. Evaṃ pana vattabbo, yo vo ānanda mayā dhammoca vinayoca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthāti evaṃ satthuṭhāne thapetvā bhagavatā saṃvaṇṇito pariyattidhammo dhammasaraṇe saṅgahitoti [M 0.0013] yutto, taṃ dhārentopana kalyāṇappaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitopi atthi. Aṭṭhitopi atthi. Yo aṭṭhito, so attanopi saraṇaṃ nahoti. Kuto parassa. Satthārā ca anekesu suttasahassesu so garahito. Tasmā so saṅghasaraṇe asaṅgahito. Itarova saṅgahitoti yuttoti.

Moreover, to the extent that the scriptural Dhamma is included here in the Dhamma, to that extent the bearer of the scriptural Dhamma is also rightly included in the venerable Sangha. And to the extent that a virtuous ordinary person is included in the Sangha among the trainees, to that extent the Dhamma of practice that is the cause of their virtue should be seen as included in the venerable Dhamma. For although they are an ordinary person, because they are endowed with those qualities, they are included among the trainees who have entered upon the way to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. And it cannot be said that those qualities are not included in the trainee's path of stream-entry. By this, the view of those who say, 'The virtuous ordinary person is not included in the Sangha to which one goes for refuge, for the going for refuge of one who resorts to them is not successful,' is refuted. But it should be said thus: 'Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Discipline that I have taught and laid down for you, that shall be your teacher after my passing.' The scriptural Dhamma, praised by the Blessed One and placed in the position of the Teacher, is thus rightly included in the refuge of the Dhamma. However, one who bears it may be established in virtuous practice, or may not be. One who is not established is no refuge even for themselves—how much less for others? Such a person is censured by the Teacher in many thousands of discourses. Therefore, they are not included in the refuge of the Sangha. Only the other is rightly included.

Santānaṃ dhammoti saddhammo. Samitakilesānaṃ tatoyeva pasatthānaṃ pūjitānaṃ sappurisānaṃ paṇḍitānañca dhammoti attho. Yoca santānaṃ dhammo, sopi ekantena santoyeva hotīti santo dhammotipi saddhammo. Pasattho pūjito dhammoti attho. Sacco vā. Ayañhi aññatitthiyadhammo viya dhārentaṃ navisaṃvādeti. So hi ayaṃ me hitoti dhārentassa ahitoyeva sampajjati. Ayaṃ pana tathādhārentassa hitoyeva sampajjatīti. [Saddhammapadaṃ]. Gaṇuttamapade loke samāna diṭṭhisīlānaṃ sahadhammikānaṃ samūho gaṇoti vuccati. Idha pana uttamehi sīlādiguṇehi yutto bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho uttamoca so gaṇocāti atthena uttamagaṇonāma. Soyeva idha gaṇuttamoti vuccati yathā muniseṭṭho munivaroti.

The Dhamma of the peaceful is the True Dhamma (Saddhamma). This means it is the Dhamma of the good and wise persons who have calmed their defilements and are, for that very reason, praised and honored. And since the Dhamma of the peaceful ones is also entirely peaceful, the peaceful Dhamma is also the True Dhamma. This means the praised and honored Dhamma. Or, it is true (sacca). For, unlike the doctrines of other sects, it does not deceive one who upholds it. For another doctrine, when upheld by one thinking, 'This is for my benefit,' results only in harm. But this Dhamma, when upheld in that way, results only in benefit. [On the term Saddhamma]. In the world, a multitude of co-religionists sharing the same view and moral conduct is called a 'group' (gaṇa). But here, the Blessed One’s community of disciples, endowed with the highest qualities such as morality, is called 'the supreme group' (uttamagaṇa) in the sense that it is both a supreme and a group. That very community is here called 'the supreme among groups' (gaṇuttama), just as the foremost sage (muniseṭṭha) is called 'the excellent sage' (munivara).

[11] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[11] But it should be explained:

“Gaṇānaṃ gaṇesuvā devamanussādisamūhesu uttamo gaṇuttamo”ti ca vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It has also been said: "The supreme among groups (gaṇānaṃ uttamo), or among the assemblies of devas, humans, and so forth (gaṇesu... uttamo), is the 'supreme among groups' (gaṇuttamo)." That is not a good explanation.

Etasmiñhi atthe sati uttamasaddo padhānabhūto hoti. Soca guṇamhiyeva pavattatīti tena idha ariyasaṅgho vuttoti nasijjhatīti. Etthaca gaṇoti saṅghoyeva vuccati. Soca saṅgho duvidho sammutisaṅgho, dakkhiṇeyyasaṅghoti. Tattha samaggena saṅghena kataṃ upasampadākammaṃ sammutināma. Tāya sammutiyā upasampannabhūmiṃ patvā ṭhito bhikkhusaṅgho sammutisaṅghonāma. So vinayakammesu pasiddho. Dakkhiṇeyyasaṅgho nāma aṭṭha ariyapuggalasamūho. Sopana kiñcāpi sammutisaṅghepi antogadhoyeva hoti. Tathāpi saraṇagamana vandanā māna [M 0.0014] pūjāsakkārānussatiṭṭhānesu anuttara puññakkhetta vise sapariggahatthaṃ bhagavatā tathā tathā saṃvaṇṇetvā so visuṃ vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Puthujjanasaṅghohi puññakkhettaṃ samānopi anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ nahoti. Kasmā. Sālikkhette tiṇānaṃ viya khettaduṭṭhānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchānusayānaṃ sabbhāvāti. Puññakkhettabhāvo panassa purime saddhammapade vuttanayena veditabboti. [Sasaddhammagaṇuttamapadaṃ]

For if this were the meaning, the word 'supreme' would be the primary element. And since that word refers only to a quality, it would not follow that the Noble Sangha is meant here. Furthermore, here 'group' (gaṇa) refers to the Sangha. And that Sangha is twofold: the conventional Sangha and the Sangha worthy of offerings. Therein, the formal act of ordination performed by a complete Sangha is called a 'convention' (sammuti). The community of monks that stands on the level of the ordained through that convention is called the 'conventional Sangha.' It is prominent in the procedures of the Vinaya. The 'Sangha worthy of offerings' is the assembly of the eight noble individuals. Although it is included within the conventional Sangha, it should be understood that the Blessed One has described it separately in various ways in contexts of going for refuge, veneration, reverence, offerings, honor, and recollection, in order to designate it as a special, unsurpassed field of merit. For although the assembly of ordinary people is a field of merit, it is not an unsurpassed field of merit. Why? Because, like weeds in a rice field, there is the presence of identity view, doubt, and underlying tendencies, which corrupt the field. However, its being a field of merit should be understood according to the method stated earlier in the section on the True Dhamma. [On the term Sasaddhammagaṇuttama].

8. Abhivādiyāti visesato vanditvā. Ettha ca ayaṃ loke sīlādiguṇayutto seṭṭho vandaneyyoti evaṃ seṭṭha cittaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā vandanto visesato vandatīti vuccati. Vandanā pana tividhā kāyavandanādivasena. Yathāha –

8. 'Abhivādiya' means having especially venerated. Here, one who venerates by establishing the thought, 'This person, endowed with such qualities as morality, is the best in the world and worthy of veneration,' is said to venerate especially. Veneration, however, is threefold, beginning with veneration by the body. As it is said:

Tisso imā bhikkhave vandanā, katamā tisso. Kāyena vandati, vācāya vandati, manasā vandatīti.

Monks, there are these three kinds of veneration. What three? One venerates with the body, one venerates with speech, and one venerates with the mind.

Tattha seṭṭhacittaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā jāṇudvaya kapparadvaya nalāṭa saṅkhātāni pañca aṅgāni bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā vandaneyyānaṃ abhimukhaṃ nippajjanto kāyena vandatināma. Yaṃ sandhāya pañcappatiṭṭhitena vanditvāti tattha tattha vuttaṃ. Yāyaca avandiyaṭṭhānesu vandantassa āpatti hotīti. Guṇapadāni vācāya pavattento vācāya vandatināma. Namo buddhassa, namatthu buddhassa, namo vimuttiyā, namo vimuttānaṃ, vipassissa namatthūti evamādīsupi vācā vandanāyeva. Guṇapadāni anugantvā guṇe anussaranto manasā vandatināmāti.

There, having established a superior mental state, placing the five limbs—namely the two knees, the two elbows, and the forehead—on the ground, prostrating while facing those worthy of veneration is called bodily veneration. Regarding this, it is said in various places, "having venerated with the five-point prostration." And there is an offense for one who venerates in places that are not fit for veneration. Uttering words of virtue is called verbal veneration. Expressions such as "Homage to the Buddha," "Homage to the Buddha," "Homage to liberation," "Homage to the liberated," "Homage to Vipassi"—these and others are indeed verbal veneration. Following the words of virtue and recollecting the virtues is called mental veneration.

9. Bhāsissanti kathessāmi. Kāmañca thero imaṃ saṅgahaṃ racayanto potthakāruḷhaṃ katvāva racayissati. Ganthakammaṃ nāma vācākammesu pasiddhanti katvā bhāsissanti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

9. 'They will speak' (bhāsissanti) means 'I will tell' (kathessāmi). Although the elder, while composing this compilation, will indeed compose it by having it written in a book, it should be understood that since the act of composing a book is well-known among verbal actions, it is therefore said, 'they will speak'.

10. Abhidhammatthasaṅgahanti pade abhidhamme vuttā atthā abhidhammatthā. Te saṅgayhanti ettha etenātivā abhidhammatthasaṅgaho. Saṅgayhantitica therena saṃkhipitvā gayhanti kathīyantīti attho. Abhidhammeti cettha abhiatireko abhivise soca dhammo abhidhammo. Dhammoti ca vinayapāḷito aññaṃpāḷi dvayaṃ [M 0.0015] vuccati. Yo vo ānanda mayā dhammoca vinayoca desito paññattoti hi vuttaṃ. Tañca pāḷidvayaṃ āṇāvidhānasaṅkhātaṃ vinayana kiccaṃ vajjetvā kusalādike yathāpavatte paramatthadhamme eva dīpetīti. Evaṃ dīpentesuca tesu dvīsu dhammesu yo itarato atirekoca hoti visesoca. Ayameva abhidhammo nāma. Itaropana dhammoyeva. Evañca katvā dhammo abhidhammo vinayo abhivinayoti idaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha dhammonāma suttantapiṭakaṃ. Abhidhammonāma yattapakaraṇāni. Vinayonāma ubhato vibhaṅgo, abhivinayonāma khandhakaparivārāti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Atirekavisesatā cettha kusalādi vasena khandhādivasena saṅgahādivasena tathā tathā desetabbappakārānaṃ anavasesavibhattivasenavā suddhadhammādhiṭṭhāna desanāpavattivasenavā veditabbā. Yato sabbaññubuddhā imaṃ abhidhammadesanaṃ devesueva desenti. Na hi manussā evarūpaṃ tayo māse nirantaraṃ pavattanayogyaṃ kathāmaggaṃ ekena iriyāpathena ādito paṭṭhāya pariyosānaṃ pāpetvā paṭiggahetuṃ sakkonti, naca eva rūpo ekamātikānubandho kathāmaggo nānākhaṇesu nānājanānaṃ desetuṃ sakkuṇeyyo hotīti. Kecipana vinayapāḷitopi abhirekavisesataṃ tassa vaṇṇenti. Taṃ aṭṭhasāliniyā na sameti. Tattha hi dhammanāmikānaṃ dvinnaṃ pāḷīnaṃ majjheeva ayaṃ atirekavisesatā vicāritā. Naca yujjati vinayena saha tathā vicāretuṃ asamānakiccavisayattā. Vinayo hi kāyavācānaṃ vinayanakicco, ajjhācāravisayoca. Dhammo pana dhammavibhāgakicco dhammappavatti visayocāti. Kecipana vadanti evaṃ santepi vinayo eva sabbajeṭṭhako siyā. Vinayaṃ vivaṇṇentassa hi pācittiyāpatti hoti. Dhammaṃ vivaṇṇentassa dukkaṭāpattimattāti, taṃ nayujjati. Vinayo hi āṇācakkaṃ. Dhammoca dhammacakkaṃ. Tattha vinayaṃ vivaṇṇento satthu āṇācakke pahāraṃ deti. Satthari agāravo mahanto hoti. Yassaca satthari agāravo, tassa dhammasaṅghesu tīsu sikkhāsuca agāravo siddho hoti. Tasmā vinaya vivaṇṇane [M 0.0016] āpatti mahantī hoti. Na sabbajeṭṭhakattāti. Apica, vinayonāma sāsanassa mūlaṃ. Vinaye aṭṭhite sāsanaṃ natiṭṭhati. Tasmā sāsanassa ciraṭṭhitatthaṃpi vinayavivaṇṇane mahatī āpatti paññattāti.

10. In the term 'Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,' the meanings stated in the Abhidhamma are 'abhidhammatthā.' They are compiled herein or by this means; hence, it is the 'Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.' And 'saṅgayhanti' means that they are summarized, grasped, and related by the Elder. Here, in 'Abhidhamma,' 'abhi' signifies 'exceeding' and 'special'; thus, Abhidhamma is the exceeding and special Dhamma. And 'Dhamma' refers to the two collections of texts other than the Vinaya Piṭaka. For it is said: 'Ānanda, that which has been taught and laid down by me as the Dhamma and the Vinaya.' And those two collections of texts, setting aside the function of the Vinaya, which consists of command and regulation, elucidate only the ultimate realities as they actually occur, such as the wholesome. Among these two Dhammas thus elucidated, that which is more exceeding and special than the other is called 'Abhidhamma,' while the other is simply 'Dhamma.' And so, this fourfold division should be understood: Dhamma, Abhidhamma, Vinaya, and Abhivinaya. Therein, 'Dhamma' is the Suttanta Piṭaka. 'Abhidhamma' is the seven treatises. 'Vinaya' is the two Vibhaṅgas. 'Abhivinaya' is the Khandhakas and Parivāra, as stated in the commentaries. The exceeding and special nature here should be understood in terms of the wholesome, etc., in terms of the aggregates, etc., in terms of the compilations, etc., or in terms of the complete division of the various ways things are to be taught, or in terms of the exposition proceeding from a foundation of pure phenomena. For the Omniscient Buddhas deliver this Abhidhamma teaching only among the gods. Humans are not able to receive such a discourse, proceeding continuously for three months in a single posture from beginning to end; nor could such a path of discourse, bound by a single matrix, be taught to various people at various times. Some, however, praise its exceeding and special nature even in comparison to the Vinaya Piṭaka. This does not accord with the Aṭṭhasālinī. For there, this exceeding and special nature is examined only between the two collections of texts called 'Dhamma.' Nor is it proper to compare it with the Vinaya in this way, as their function and domain are not similar. For the Vinaya's function is the disciplining of body and speech, and its domain is transgression. The Dhamma's function, however, is the analysis of phenomena, and its domain is the process of phenomena. Some say that even so, the Vinaya must be the most senior of all, for one who disparages the Vinaya incurs a pācittiya offense, while one who disparages the Dhamma incurs only a dukkaṭa offense. This is not correct. For the Vinaya is the wheel of authority, and the Dhamma is the wheel of Dhamma. Therein, one who disparages the Vinaya strikes at the Teacher’s wheel of authority; the disrespect for the Teacher is great. And for one who has disrespect for the Teacher, disrespect for the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the three trainings is established. Therefore, the offense for disparaging the Vinaya is grave, but not because it is the most senior. Moreover, the Vinaya is the root of the Dispensation. If the Vinaya is not established, the Dispensation does not stand. Therefore, for the long-term stability of the Dispensation, a grave offense is prescribed for disparaging the Vinaya.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyā nāma abhidhammattha saṅgahassa

Thus, in the Paramatthadīpanī, of the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,

Catutthavaṇṇanāya pathamagāthāya

of the commentary on the fourth chapter, of the first verse.

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The Paramatthadīpanā is finished.

Dutīyagāthā-paramatthadīpanī

The Paramatthadīpanī on the Second Verse

11. Evaṃ ādigāthāyataṃtaṃ payojana sahite pañca atthe dassetvā idāni te abhidhammatthe uddesato dassento dutīyagāthamāha. Tattha tatthāti bhāsissaṃ abhidhammattha saṅgahanti vutte tasmiṃ abhidhammatthasaṅgahapade mayā vuttā abhidhammatthā sabbathāparamatthato catudhā hontīti yojanā. Etthaca -

11. Thus, having shown in the introductory verse the five meanings together with their respective purposes, now, showing those Abhidhamma meanings in summary, he speaks the second verse. Therein, the connection is as follows: when it is said, 'Therein... I will speak the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,' this means that in that term 'Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,' the Abhidhamma-meanings spoken by me are, from an ultimate standpoint, fourfold in every way. And here—

[12] Ṭīkāyaṃ tāva

Firstly, in the sub-commentary,

Tattha tasmiṃ abhidhammatthasaṅgahapakaraṇetivā abhidhammattha padetivā abhidhammetivā tasaddattho niddiṭṭho. Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana tasmiṃ abhidhammeti. Sabbaṃ nasundaraṃ.

There, the meaning of the word 'ta' is indicated as 'in that treatise, the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,' or 'in that term, abhidhammattha,' or 'in the Abhidhamma.' In the Vibhāvanī, however, it is 'in that Abhidhamma.' All of this is not sound.

Na hi abhidhammattha saṅgahapakaraṇe mayā vuttā abhidhammatthāti yujjati. Pakaraṇaṃpi hi upari vuccamānameva hoti. Natu vuttaṃ. Kuto abhidhammatthāti. Na ca saṃvaṇṇanāpakaraṇesu ādimhiyeva tāva tasaddo appadhānapadāni paccāmasatīti atthi. Tasmā aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ ādimhi tattha kena ṭṭhena abhidhammoti vākyeviya idha tasaddattho veditabboti. Evañhi sati –

For it is not fitting to say, 'the Abhidhamma-meanings stated by me in the treatise Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.' Indeed, the treatise itself is only now being spoken of; it has not yet been stated. From where, then, are the Abhidhamma-meanings? Nor is it the case that in the introductory sections of explanatory treatises the word 'ta' immediately refers back to subordinate terms. Therefore, the meaning of the word 'ta' here should be understood as in the Aṭṭhasālinī at the beginning, in the sentence, 'Therein, for what reason is it Abhidhamma?' For when this is so—

[13] Ṭīkāsu

In the sub-commentaries,

Sabbathā vuttāti yojanāpi paṭikkhittā hoti.

the explanation 'stated in every way' is also rejected.

Sā hi vakkhamānehi sabbayāpi dvādasa, sabbathāpi aṭṭhārasātiādīhi nasametīti. Tatta sabbathāti dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ vuttena kusalādinā [M 0.0017] sabbappakārenapi catudhāva honti, vibhaṅge vibhatte na khandhādinā sabbappakārenapi catudhāva hontīti attho. Dhātu kathāyaṃ vuttenātiādināpi vattabbaṃ.

For that explanation does not accord with what will be stated later, such as 'twelvefold in every way,' and 'eighteenfold in every way.' There, 'in every way' means that in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, by every method, such as the wholesome, etc., as stated, they are just fourfold; and in the Vibhaṅga, when analyzed by every method, such as by the aggregates, etc., they are just fourfold. The same should be stated regarding what is mentioned in the Dhātukathā, and so on.

12. Paramatthatoti paramattha saccato. Dve hi saccāni sammutisaccaṃ, paramatthasaccanti, tattha satta puggala atta jīvādikā paññattiatthā sabhāvato avijjamānāyeva honti. Dhammavavatthānaññāṇarahitānaṃpana mahājanānaṃ citte mahantamahantāpi hutvā vijjamānāviya paññāyanti, teca mahājanā samaggā hutvā tesaṃ ekantena atthibhāvaṃ gahetvā tathā tathā voharanti ceva sampaṭicchantica. Tasmā te mahājanehi samaggehi sammatattātatoyevaca vacīsaccaviratisaccānaṃ vatthubhūtattāsammuti saccanti vuccanti. Tasmiṃ sammutisacce ṭhatvā sammā paṭipajjantā sabba lokiyasampattiyoca sabbabodhisambhāra dhammeca ārādhenti. Micchāpaṭipajjantā apāyapūrakā honti. Evaṃ mahantañhi sammuti saccanti. Paramatthasaccaṃ pana patvā taṃ saccameva nahoti. Tañhi sayaṃ avijjamānaṃyeva samānaṃ mahājane vijjamānantveva gaṇhāpeti. Sakkāyadiṭṭhi dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhi tividhamicchādiṭṭhīnaṃ vatthu hutvā bālajanānaṃ vaṭṭadukkhato niyyātuṃ nadeti. Evaṃ viparītañhi sammutisaccaṃ. Evaṃ mahāsāvajjañcāti. Paramatthasaccaṃpana duvidhaṃ sabhāvasaccaṃ ariyasaccanti. Tattha dhammasaṅgaṇiādīsu sattasu pakaraṇesu vibhattā kusalādayo dhammā sabhāvasaccaṃnāma. Te hi sayaṃ sabhāvato vijjamānattā kusalānāma dhammā atthi sukhānāma vedanā atthīti gaṇhantena visaṃvādentīti. Taṃ pana ariyasaccaṃ patvā kiñci asaccaṃpi hotiyeva. Tathāhi anubhavanabhedamattaṃ upādāyeva vedanā sukhā dukkhā adukkhamasukhāti vuttā. Na sabbākārato sukhabhūtattā. Sabbehi pana aniccatā saṅkhatatādīhi anekasatehi ākārehi sabbāpi vedanā dukkhāeva. Tathā anavajjasukhavipākaṭṭhena kusalabhāvopi akusalaṃ upādāyeva vutto. Sabbepi hi tebhūmakā kusalasammatā dhammā sāsavatā saṃkilesikatā oghaniya yoganiya upādāniyatā [M 0.0018] saṅkhātehi vajjehi sāvajjāeva honti. Dukkhasaccabhūtānañca vipākānaṃ jananaṭṭhena ekantena dukkhavipākāeva honti. Ajjhattattikañca sabbalokiyasammataṃ upādāya vuttaṃ. Sabbepi hi catubbhū makadhammā ekantena attāpināma natthi. Kuto ajjhattānāma. Bahiddhāeva honti. Saṅkhāre parato passāti hi vuttanti. Ayaṃ nayo sesattika dukadhammesupi yathārahaṃ netabbo. Ariya saccaṃnāma sabbesaṃ tebhūmakadhammānaṃ ekanta dukkhabhāvo taṇhāya ekanta dukkhasamudaya bhāvo nibbānasseva dukkhanirodha bhāvo aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggasseva dukkhanirodhamaggabhāvocāti. Idhameva hi parisuddhabuddhīnaṃ ariyānaṃ ñāṇe acalamānaṃ sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ nippariyāyasaccaṃ hotīti. Tesu idha sammutisaccaṃ nivattento paramatthatoti ida māha. Tena vuttaṃ paramatthatoti paramatthasaccatoti. Tattha attho duvidho sabhāvasiddhoca parikappasiddhoca. Tattha yo vinā aññāpadesena kevalaṃ visuṃ visuṃ attano lakkhaṇena vijjamāno hutvā siddho. So cittādiko attho sabhāvasiddhonāma. Yopana attano lakkhaṇena vijjamānoyeva nahoti. Vijjamānassapana atthassa nānā pavattiākāre upādāya cittena parikappetvā saviggahaṃ katvā gahito cittamayo cittanimmito hutvā citteeva upalabbhamāno hoti. So sattapuggalādiko attho parikappasiddho nāma. Tesu sabhāvasiddhoyeva paramatthonāma. So hi santi bhavanti buddhisaddā etthāti attho. Ekantavijjamānaṭṭhena itarato paramo ukkaṃsagato atthoti paramattho. Api ca, ye ayaṃ atthi ayaṃ upalabbhatīti gahetvā tassa abhiññeyyassa abhiññatthāya, pariññeyyassa pariññatthāya, pahātabbassa pahānatthāya, sacchikātabbassa sacchikaraṇatthāya, bhāvetabbassa bhāvanatthāya paṭipajjanti. Tesaṃ tadatthasādhane avisaṃvādakaṭṭhena paramo uttamo atthoti paramattho. Itaropana avijjamānattā tassa abhiññādiatthāya paṭipajjantānaṃ tadatthasādhane [M 0.0019] visaṃvādakoyeva bhavissati. Napana tadatthaṃ sādhessa tīti paramatthoti vattuṃ nārahatīti.

12. By 'ultimate reality' is meant ultimate truth. There are indeed two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth. In this context, beings, persons, souls, life-principles, and so forth, are merely conceptual designations that do not exist by way of intrinsic nature. However, in the minds of the great multitude who lack the knowledge that discerns phenomena, these appear as though they exist in a grand and substantial way. And when these people collectively agree upon their absolute existence, they speak and accept them as such. Therefore, because they are agreed upon by the masses, and because they are the basis for the truth of speech and the truth of abstention, they are called conventional truth. By relying on this conventional truth and practicing rightly, people achieve all worldly attainments and all the requisites for awakening. But those who practice wrongly become fillers of the lower realms. Thus, conventional truth is indeed of great importance. However, from the standpoint of ultimate truth, that conventional truth is not truth at all. For what does not exist by itself is taken by the masses as existing. It becomes the basis for personality view, the sixty-two kinds of wrong views, and the three kinds of wrong views, preventing foolish beings from escaping the suffering of the cycle of existence. Thus, conventional truth is misleading and highly blameworthy. Ultimate truth, however, is twofold: truth of intrinsic nature and Noble Truth. Among these, the wholesome and other phenomena analyzed in the seven treatises, such as the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, are called the truth of intrinsic nature. Since they exist by their own nature, one who asserts, 'There are wholesome states; there are pleasant feelings,' does not speak falsely. However, from the standpoint of the Noble Truth, this is also in a sense untrue. For example, feelings are described as pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant only based on the distinction of experiential modes, not because they are entirely pleasant in every way. In reality, all feelings are suffering due to their impermanence, conditioned nature, and hundreds of other aspects. Likewise, their wholesome nature is spoken of based on their faultless and pleasant result, but only in relation to unwholesome states. All these phenomena regarded as wholesome within the three realms are nevertheless flawed because they are associated with taints, defilements, floods, yokes, and clinging. And because they generate results that are included in the truth of suffering, they are exclusively of painful result. Even the internal triad is spoken of conventionally, using what is accepted by all the world. For all phenomena of the four planes ultimately do not have a self; so how much more so the so-called 'internal'? They are merely external. As it is said, 'One sees formations as other.' This principle should be applied accordingly to the remaining triads and dyads of phenomena. The Noble Truth is the absolute suffering of all phenomena of the three realms, the absolute origin of suffering in craving, the cessation of suffering in Nibbāna alone, and the path to the cessation of suffering in the Noble Eightfold Path. For this alone, in the knowledge of the noble ones with purified intellect, becomes the unshaken, fully complete, and unequivocal truth. Here, setting aside conventional truth, one speaks of 'ultimate reality.' Therefore, it is said: 'By ultimate reality is meant ultimate truth.' In this context, meaning is twofold: established by intrinsic nature and established by conceptualization. That which exists distinctly by its own characteristic, without dependence on anything else—such as consciousness—is called meaning established by intrinsic nature. But that which does not exist by its own characteristic, yet is taken as existing in various modes of occurrence through mental construction, elaborately formed, and existing only as a mental creation—such as beings and persons—is called meaning established by conceptualization. Among these, only meaning established by intrinsic nature is called ultimate reality. For it is the meaning wherein the terms 'exists,' 'becomes,' and 'is understood' apply. Because it exists absolutely, it is supreme and exalted above the other, hence 'ultimate reality.' Moreover, those who practice for the purpose of directly knowing what should be known, fully understanding what should be understood, abandoning what should be abandoned, realizing what should be realized, and developing what should be developed—for them, this meaning serves as an unfailing means to achieve that goal. Therefore, it is the highest, supreme meaning—ultimate reality. The other, being nonexistent, would only deceive those who practice for such purposes and fail to accomplish the goal. Thus, it does not deserve to be called ultimate reality.

[14] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[14] Now, what is to be elucidated:

“Paramassavā uttamassa ñāṇassa attho gocaroti paramattho”tipi vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is also said: 'Ultimate reality (paramattha) is the meaning or object of supreme knowledge.' That is not well-stated.

Na hi paramasaddoñāṇe vattamāno dissati. Naca atthasaddo gocareti. Yañca anuṭīkāyaṃ saccameva saccikaṃ. So eva attho aviparītassa ñāṇassa visayabhāvaṭṭhenāti saccikaṭṭhoti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi aviparītena ñāṇena araṇīyato upagantabba to atthoti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Naparamasaddassa atthanti. [Paramatthapadaṃ]

For the word 'parama' is not found used in the sense of knowledge, nor does the word 'attha' mean object. And in the subcommentary it is said: 'What is true is indeed real.' That very meaning, because it is the object of unperverted knowledge, is said to be 'saccikaṭṭha' (the meaning of the real). That too shows this meaning: that it is the meaning to be gone to and approached by unperverted knowledge. It is not the meaning of the word 'parama'. [The word 'paramattha']

13. Cittanti ettha cintetīti cittaṃ. Etthaca cintanakriyā nāma niccaṃ ārammaṇāpekkhā hoti. Na hi sā ārammaṇena vinā labbhatīti. Tasmā ārammaṇaggahaṇa ārammaṇupaladdhiyeva idha cintanāti daṭṭhabbāti. Evañhi sati bhavaṅgasamaya visaññisamayesu cittaṃ ārammaṇena vināpi pavattatīti evaṃ vādīnaṃ vādo paṭikkhitto hoti. Santesupica nissaya samanantarādīsu tassa paccayesu tehi nāmaṃ alabhitvā ārammaṇapaccayavasenevassa nāmaṃ siddhanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cintenti sampayuttakā dhammā etenāti cittaṃ. Tañhi ārammaṇaggahaṇakicce pubbaṅgamabhūtanti taṃ sampayuttadhammāpi ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhantā tassa vaseneva gaṇhantīti. Cintanamattaṃvā cittaṃ. Sabbepi hi dhammā taṃtaṃ kriyāmattāva honti. Na tesu dabbaṃvā saṇṭhānaṃ vā viggahovā upalabbhati. Paccayāyatta vuttino ca honti. Na te attano thāmenavā balenavā vasenavā sattiyāvā uppajjituṃpi sakkonti. Pageva cintetuṃvā phusetuṃvāti. Khaṇamattaṭṭhāyinoca honti, na kadāci kassaci vase vattituṃ sakkontīti. Tasmā tesu idaṃ dabbaṃ, ayaṃ satti, aya kriyāti evaṃ vibhāgo nalabbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañca katvā sabbesu paramatthapadesu ekaṃ bhāvasādhanameva padhānato labbhati. Tadañña sādhanānipana [M 0.0020] pariyāyatova labbhantīti veditabbaṃ. Ettha ca dabbādivasena abhedassa cintanassa atthavisesañāpanatthaṃ vibhāga kappanāvasena bhedakaraṇaṃ pariyāyakathāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā silā puttakassasarīranti, tathā karaṇañca taṃ taṃ kriyāsaṅkhāta dhammavimuttassa paraparikappitassa kārakabhūtassa atta jīva satta puggalassa sabbaso abhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Sati hi attādimhi kiṃ abhedassa bhedakappanāyāti.

13. Here, 'citta' (mind) is so called because it thinks (cinteti). And here, the act of thinking is always dependent on an object, for it cannot be obtained without an object. Therefore, the grasping of an object, the apprehension of an object, should be understood here as thinking. This being so, the view of those who claim that the mind arises even without an object during moments of bhavaṅga or in states of non-perception is refuted. Moreover, even when its conditions such as dependence (nissaya), contiguity (samanantara), etc., are present, it must be understood that its name is not derived from them but is established solely through the condition of the object. Associated mental factors (sampayuttakā dhammā) think by means of it, hence it is 'citta'. For since the mind is the forerunner in the function of grasping an object, its associated states also grasp the object only through its influence. Or, 'citta' is simply the act of thinking. Indeed, all phenomena are merely their respective functions. In them, no substance, shape, or form can be found. They occur in dependence on conditions. They cannot arise by their own stability, power, influence, or capacity—let alone think or make contact. They endure only for a moment and cannot persist subject to anyone's will. Therefore, it should be understood that no distinction can be made among them, such as 'this is substance,' 'this is capacity,' or 'this is action.' And so it is that in all statements of ultimate reality, only one derivation—in the sense of the state of being (bhāvasādhana)—is primarily obtained. It should be known that other derivations are obtained only figuratively. And here, it should be understood that making a distinction by conceiving a division of undifferentiated thinking into substance and so on, for the purpose of indicating a specific meaning, is a figurative explanation. Just as one might say, 'the body of a stone doll,' so too, the use of the instrumental case (karaṇa) is for the purpose of demonstrating the complete non-existence of a self, a life-principle, a being, or a person conceived by others as being an agent (kāraka), which is in reality free from those phenomena designated as action. For if there were a self and so on, what purpose would there be in conceiving a division of that which is undifferentiated?

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

However, it should be elucidated.

Sasavisāṇaṃ viya abhūtassa bhūta kappanā vuttā viya dissati. Ayamassādhippāyo-dhammesu kattāvā kāre tāvā koci natthi. Lokepana attappadhāno kriyā nipphādako kattānāma siddho. Tasmā cintanakicce attappadhānatā dīpanatthaṃ taṃ kattubhāvaṃ citte āropetvā cintetīti cittanti vuttaṃ.

It appears as if a conceptualization of the unreal as real, like a hare's horn, has been stated. This is its intention: in phenomena, there is no agent or doer whatsoever. But in the world, an agent, the accomplisher of actions for whom the self is primary, is established. Therefore, to show the primacy of the self in the activity of thinking, that state of agency is superimposed on the mind, and thus it is said, 'it thinks, hence it is citta'.

Cittassaca balena taṃsampayuttānaṃpi tasmiṃ kicce tadanukūlappavattidīpanatthaṃ punakaraṇabhāvaṃ citte kattubhāvañca tesu āropetvā cintenti sampayuttakā dhammā etenāti cittanti vuttanti. Api cettha cittasaddo vicitratthavācako daṭṭhabbo. Vuttañhe taṃ saṃyuttake –

And to show the favorable functioning of its associated states in that activity due to the mind's power, by further superimposing the state of being an instrument on the mind and the state of being a doer on them, it is thus said: 'The associated mental factors think through it, hence it is citta.' Moreover, here the word 'citta' should be understood as conveying the meaning 'variegated'. For it is said in the Saṃyutta:

Diṭṭhaṃ vo bhikkhave caraṇaṃnāma cittanti. Evaṃ bhante. Tampi kho bhikkhave caraṇaṃ cittaṃ citteneva cintitanti. Tenāpi kho bhikkhave caraṇena cittena cittaññeva cittataranti, nā haṃ bhikkhave aññaṃ ekanikāyaṃpi samanupassāmi yaṃ evaṃ cittaṃ. Yathayidaṃ bhikkhave tiracchānagatā pāṇā. Tepi kho bhikkhave tiracchānagatā pāṇā citteneva cittikatā. Tehipi kho bhikkhave tiracchāna gatehi pāṇehi cittaññeva cittataranti.

“Have you seen, monks, the painting called ‘The Wanderer’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Monks, that painting ‘The Wanderer’ was devised by the mind. Yet, monks, the mind is even more variegated than that painting ‘The Wanderer’. Monks, I do not see any other single class of beings so variegated as these animals. Monks, those animals are made variegated by the mind. Yet, monks, the mind is even more variegated than those animals.”

Tattha caraṇaṃnāma cittanti yatthavicitrāni dibbavimānādīni cittakammāni katvā idañcidañca puññaṃ karontā idhacidhaca nibbattāti dassento vicaranti[M 0.0021]. Tassa paṭakoṭṭhakassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Cittenāti nissakke karaṇavacanaṃ. Yathayidanti yathā ime. Cittikatāti vicitrā katā. Etthaca cittavicittakāya saññāvicittā. Saññāvicittatāya taṇhāvicittā. Taṇhāvicittatāya kammāni vicittāni. Kammavicitta tāya yoniyo vicittā. Yonivicittatāya tesaṃ tiracchā nagatānaṃ vicittatā veditabbā. [Vacanattho]

Herein, ‘the painting called The Wanderer’ (caraṇaṃ nāma cittaṃ) is a painted chamber depicting beings who wander about, showing that by creating various painted works such as divine mansions and performing this and that merit, they are reborn here and there. This is the name for that painted chamber. ‘By the mind’ (cittena) is the instrumental case in the sense of the agent. ‘As these’ (yathayidaṃ) means ‘like these’. ‘Made variegated’ (cittikatā) means ‘made diverse’. And here, because the mind is variegated, perception is variegated. Because perception is variegated, craving is variegated. Because craving is variegated, actions are variegated. Because actions are variegated, wombs are variegated. Because wombs are variegated, the variegation of those animals should be understood. [Meaning of the words.]

Taṃ taṃ sabhāvo lakkhaṇaṃ, kiccasampattiyo raso;

Gayhākāro phalaṃvāpi, paccupaṭṭhāna saññitaṃ.

Āsannakāraṇaṃ yaṃ taṃ, padaṭṭhānanti taṃ mataṃ;

Dhammānaṃ vavatthānāya, alaṃ ete vibuddhino.

The respective intrinsic nature is the characteristic; the accomplishment of function is the essence. The mode of being grasped, or its result, is termed its manifestation. Whatever is its proximate cause, that is considered its foundation. These are sufficient for the wise to determine phenomena.

Ārammaṇavijānanalakkhaṇaṃ cittaṃ, pubbaṅgamarasaṃ, sandhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānaṃ. [Cittaṃ]

The mind has the characteristic of cognizing an object, the function of being a forerunner, the manifestation of connecting, and name-and-form as its proximate cause. [Citta]

14. Cetasikanti ettha cetasi bhavaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti cetasikaṃ. Phassādi dhammajātaṃ. Etthaca tadāyattavuttitā nāma ekuppādatādīhi lakkhaṇehi cittena saha ekī bhūtassa viya pavatti. Etena yā cittassa jāti. Sāeva phassādīnaṃ.
