Yā cittassa jarā, yaṃ cittassa maraṇaṃ, yaṃ cittassa ārammaṇaṃ, yaṃ cittassa vatthu, tadeva phassādīnanti evaṃ ekapuppha mañjariyaṃ ekavaṇṭupanibbandhāni pupphāni viya cittena saha ekajātiyādi upanibbandhā phassādayo dhammā idha cetasikaṃnāmāti siddhā honti. Evañca sati cittaṃpi tehi phassādīhi saha tatheva āyattaṃ pavattatīti taṃpi phassikaṃ vedanikantiādinā vattabbanti ce. Na. Cittasseva jeṭṭhakattā. Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā, manoseṭṭhā manomayāti hi vuttaṃ. Etthaca manomayāti manasāeva pakatā nimmitā cittakriyā bhūtāti attho. Etena te phassādayo dhammā cittena vinā nupalabbhantīti dasseti. Cittaṃpana tehi kehici vināpi pavattatiyeva. Pañcaviññāṇa cittañhitehi kehici vitakkādīhi vinā uppajjatīti. Tasmā tesaññeva tadāyatta vuttitā vattabbā na cittassāti.

14. Here, ‘cetasika’ means that which arises in the mind, due to its dependent functioning on it. It is the collection of phenomena beginning with contact (phassa). In this context, ‘dependent functioning’ means functioning as if unified with the mind through characteristics such as co-arising. By this, the birth of the mind is also the birth of contact and other phenomena; the aging of the mind, the death of the mind, the object of the mind, and the base of the mind—these are likewise the same for contact and other phenomena. Thus, just as flowers in a cluster bound to a single stalk are connected to one stem, so too are the phenomena beginning with contact established here as ‘cetasika,’ bound to the mind through shared birth and other characteristics. Even so, if it is said that the mind also functions dependently with these phenomena—contact, feeling, etc.—and therefore should also be called ‘characterized by contact,’ ‘characterized by feeling,’ and so on, [we say] no. Because the mind is the chief. For it is said: “Phenomena are preceded by mind, have mind as their chief, and are made of mind.” And here, ‘made of mind’ means created, produced, or brought into being by the activity of the mind. This shows that phenomena like contact cannot be found apart from the mind. The mind, however, can function even without some of them. For the five sense-consciousnesses arise without certain factors like initial application (vitakka). Therefore, it is these phenomena that should be described as having dependent functioning on the mind, not the mind on them.

[15] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[15] However, it should be clarified.

Ekālambaṇatā [M 0.0022] mattena tesaṃ tadāyattavuttitaṃ cetasi kattañca vibhāveti. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

Merely by their having a single object, he explains their dependent functioning on it and agency in the mind. That is not sound.

Na hi ekālambaṇatāmattena cetasikaṃnāma jātanti. Ettha ca loke nānāvaṇṇadhātuyo udake ghaṃsitvā vatthumhi nānā cittakammāni karonti, tattha vatthumhi pharaṇaṃ bandhanañca udakasseva kiccaṃ, na vaṇṇadhātūnaṃ. Nānārūpa dassanaṃ vaṇṇadhātūnameva kiccaṃ, na udakassa. Tattha vatthuviya ārammaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Udakaṃviya cittaṃ. Nānā vaṇṇadhātuyoviya cetasikadhammāti. [Cetasikaṃ]

For a mental factor does not come to be merely by having a single object. And here in the world, various colored pigments, having been ground in water, create diverse paintings on a canvas. In this case, the spreading and binding on the canvas are the functions of the water, not of the pigments. The appearance of diverse forms is the function of the pigments, not of the water. In this analogy, the object should be seen as the canvas, the mind as the water, and the mental factors as the various colored pigments. [Cetasika]

15. Rūpanti ettha ruppatīti rūpaṃ. Sītuṇhādīhi virodhi paccayehi visama pavatti vasena vikāraṃ āpajjati, tehi vā vikāraṃ āpādīyatīti attho. Yathāha –

15. Here, ‘rūpa’ is so called because it is afflicted (ruppati). It undergoes modification due to opposing conditions such as cold and heat by way of its unstable occurrence, or it is caused to undergo modification by them—this is the meaning. As it is said:

Ruppatīti kho bhikkhave tasmā rūpanti vuccati. Kena ruppati. Sitenapi ruppati. Uṇhenapi ruppati. Jighacchāyapi ruppati. Vipāsāyapi ruppati. Ḍaṃsa makasa vātātapa sariṃ sapa sapphassehipi ruppatīti. Ruppatītica ruppati, kuppati, ghaṭṭīyati, piḷī yati, bhijjatīti.

“Because it is afflicted, bhikkhus, it is therefore called form. By what is it afflicted? It is afflicted by cold, it is afflicted by heat, it is afflicted by hunger, it is afflicted by thirst, it is afflicted by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. And ‘it is afflicted’ means: it is afflicted, disturbed, struck, oppressed, and broken.”

Mahāniddese vuttaṃ. Ayamettha piṇḍattho, ye dhammā ciraṭṭhitikāca honti sappaṭighasabhāvāca. Tesaññeva ṭhitikkhaṇesu virodhipaccayehi samāgamonāma hoti. Napanaññesaṃ parittakkhaṇānaṃ appaṭighasabhāvānanti. Tesañhi appaṭighasabhāvānaṃ sukhuma rūpānaṃpi bahiddhā sītādīhi samāgamonāma natthi. Kuto parittakkhaṇānaṃ appaṭighasabhāvānañca arūpadhammānanti. Yadievaṃ sukhumarūpānaṃ arūpatāpatti siyāti. Nasiyā. Oḷārikarūpehi samānagati kattā. Tānihi oḷārikesu ruppamānesu ruppantiyevāti. Samāgamoca nāma idha thapetvā āpātagamanaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇañca aññamaññaviruddhānaṃ ṭhitipattānaṃ oḷārikarūpānaṃ mahābhūtānamevavā aññamaññābhighaṭṭanaṃ [M 0.0023] vuccati, ruppati ghaṭṭīyati pīḷīyatīti hi vuttaṃ. Ruppanañcanāma parasenāyuddhena raṭṭhakhobhoviya kalāpantaragatadhātūnaṃ kuppanaṃ bhijjanaṃca vuccati. Kuppati bhijjatīti hi vuttaṃ. Etthaca kuppatīti khobhati cañcalati, bhijjatīti vikāraṃ āpajjati. Yasmiṃ khaṇe virodhipaccayasamāgamaṃ labhanti. Tato paṭṭhāya sayaṃpi vikārapattā honti. Omattādhimattarūpasantatīnaṃ uppattiyā paccayabhāvaṃ pattā hontīti attho. Apicettha ruppanaṃ duvidhaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ, hāyanañca. Tadubhayaṃpi kappavuṭṭhāne kappasaṇṭhāne nānāāyukappa saṃvacchara utu māsa ratti divādīnaṃ parivattaneca pākaṭaṃ hotīti. Kasmā pana rūpanti nāmaṃ ghaṭṭanavasena ruppanadhammānameva siddhanti. Tesameva saviggahattā. Rūpadhammā hi samūhasaṇṭhānādi bhāvapattiyā saviggahā honti. Tasmā tesameva ruppanaṃ paccakkhatopi lokassa pākaṭanti tesveva rūpanti nāmaṃ siddhanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Arūpadhammā pana aviggahāti na tesaṃ vikāro paccakkhato lokassa pākaṭo hoti. Taṃ taṃ rūpavikāraṃ disvāvā sutvā vā pucchitvāyeva vā so lokena jānitabbo aññatra paracittavidūhi. Tasmā tesaṃ rūpatāpatti natthīti.

It is stated in the Mahāniddesa. Here is the summary: those phenomena that are long-lasting and have a resistant nature. For them alone, the coming together with opposing conditions occurs in their moments of stability, but not for other phenomena that are momentary and have a non-resistant nature. For those with a non-resistant nature, even for subtle forms, there is no external coming together with cold and so on. How much less for momentary, non-resistant phenomena and for formless states? If it were so, the state of formlessness would apply even to subtle forms. But it does not, because they follow the same course as gross forms. For when the gross forms are afflicted, they too are afflicted. And ‘coming together’ here, excluding direct approach and the making of an object, refers to the mutual collision of gross forms that have attained stability and are mutually opposed, or of the great elements themselves; for it is said, ‘it is afflicted, struck, and oppressed.’ And ‘affliction’ is said to be the agitation and fragmentation of elements within a group, like the turmoil of a kingdom from an enemy army; for it is said, ‘it is disturbed and broken.’ And here, ‘disturbed’ means agitated and unsteady, and ‘broken’ means undergoing change. At the moment they encounter opposing conditions, from that point onward, they themselves undergo change. This means they become conditions for the arising of continuities of inferior and superior forms. Moreover, affliction here is twofold: increase and decrease. Both are evident in the evolution and dissolution of an eon, and in the cycles of various eons, years, seasons, months, nights, and days. But why is the name ‘form’ established only for those phenomena that are subject to affliction through impact? Because they alone have corporeal characteristics. For form phenomena, by attaining the state of being an aggregate, shape, and so on, possess corporeal characteristics. Therefore, their affliction is directly evident to the world, and so it should be understood that the name ‘form’ is established for them alone. Formless phenomena, however, lack corporeal characteristics, so their changes are not directly evident to the world. Such change is to be known by the world only by seeing, hearing, or inquiring about this or that change in form, except by those who know the minds of others. Therefore, the state of being form does not apply to them.

[16] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[16] Now, this is to be clarified:

Tesaṃ rūpatāpattippasaṅgo sītādiggahaṇa sāmatthiyena nivattito. Yasmā pana vohāronāma lokopacārena vinā nasijjhati. Lokopacāroca pākaṭanimittavase neva pavatto. Tasmā idha sītādiggahaṇena vināpi tappasaṅganivatti lokatova siddhāti daṭṭhabbā.

The implication of their attaining the state of form is averted by the capacity for grasping cold and so on. Because, however, a designation is not established without worldly convention, and worldly convention proceeds only by way of prominent signs, therefore it should be understood that here, even without the grasping of cold and so on, the aversion of that implication is established from the world itself.

Yasmā ca brahmaloke brahmānaṃ kāyavikāra vacīvikārā ca iddhivikuppanāvasappavattā nānārūpavikārāca dissantiyeva. Teca ekena pariyāyena ruppanākārāeva nāma honti, tasmā tesaṃ vasena tattha rūpānaṃ rūpatāsiddhi hotīti veditabbaṃ. Rūpayati vā attano sabhāvena pakāsatīti rūpaṃ. Arūpadhammā hi na attano sabhāvena pākaṭā honti. Rūpasannissayeneva gahetabbā[M 0.0024]. Idaṃ pana attano sabhāveneva pākaṭaṃ pañcaviññāṇehipi gahetabbanti. Imasmiṃ atthe sati brahmaloke rūpānaṃpi uju katova rūpatāsiddhi hotīti.

And because in the Brahma-world, transformations of the Brahmās’ bodies and speech, and various transformations of form occurring by way of the manifestation of psychic power, are indeed seen. And these, in one sense, are indeed modes of affliction. Therefore, it should be known that by their means, the establishment of form-ness for forms occurs there. Or, it is ‘form’ (rūpa) because it manifests (rūpayati) or reveals its own nature. For formless phenomena are not apparent by their own nature; they are to be apprehended only in dependence on form. This, however, is apparent by its very own nature and is to be apprehended even by the five consciousnesses. This meaning being the case, even in the Brahma-world, the establishment of form-ness for forms is rightly made.

[17] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[17] Now, this is to be clarified:

Anuggāhakānaṃ sītādīnaṃ vasena taṃ sabhāvā nātivattana vasenaca tattha rūpatāsiddhi vibhāvitā. Yasmāpana sīte nāpi uṇhenāpītiādivacanaṃ nidassanamattaṃ hoti. Kamma cittāhārānaṃpi vasena ruppanassa sambhavato, tathāhi saññā viññāṇānipi rūpārammaṇarasārammaṇehi eva pāḷiyaṃ niddiṭṭhāni. Na hi saññā rūpaṃeva sañjānāti. Na ca viññāṇaṃ rasa meva vijānāti. Nidassanamattena desanā hotīti viññāyatīti. Tasmā sītādiggahaṇaṃ amuñcitvāva tattha rūpatāsiddhivibhāvanena payojana natthīti. [Rūpaṃ]

The establishment of form-ness there is explained by way of the supporting factors such as cold, etc., and by way of its nature not being transgressed. Because statements such as ‘by cold, also by heat’ are merely illustrative. For affliction is also possible by way of kamma, mind, and nutriment; just as perception and consciousness are pointed out in the Pāli canon only with form as object and taste as object respectively. For perception does not perceive only form, nor does consciousness cognize only taste. It is to be understood that the teaching is by way of example only. Therefore, without letting go of the grasping of cold and so on, there is no purpose in explaining the establishment of form-ness there. [Form]

16. Nibbānanti ettha nibbāyanti sabbe vaṭṭadukkhasantāpā etasminti nibbānaṃ. Nibbāyantīti ye kilesāvā khandhāvā abhāvitamaggassa āyatiṃ uppajjanārahapakkhe ṭhitā honti. Teyeva bhāvitamaggassa anuppajjanārahapakkhaṃ pāpuṇantīti attho. Na hi khaṇattayaṃ patvā niruddhā atītadhammā nibbāyanti nāma. Paccuppannesu āyatiṃ avassaṃ uppajjamānesuca dhammesu vattabbameva natthīti. Vaṭṭadukkhasantāpāti kilesavaṭṭa kammavaṭṭa vipākavaṭṭa dukkhasantāpā. Na hi tividha vaṭṭadukkhasantāparahitānaṃ rukkhādīnaṃ anuppādanirodho nibbānaṃnāma hotīti. Etasminti visaye bhummaṃ. Yathā ākāse sakuṇā pakkhantīti. Yehi te nibbāyanti. Tesaṃ tabbinimuttaṃ aññaṃ nibbutiṭṭhānaṃnāma kiñci natthīti. Nibbāyanti vā ariyajanā etasminti nibbānaṃ. Nibbanti dhīrā yathayaṃ padīpoti hi vuttaṃ. Nibbāyantīti taṃ taṃ kilesānaṃvā khandhānaṃvā puna appaṭisandhikabhāvaṃ pāpuṇantīti attho. Ekasminti visayeeva bhummaṃ, etasmiṃ adhi gatetipi yojenti. Ṭīkāsupana bhavābhavaṃ vinanato saṃsibbana to vānaṃ vuccati taṇhā. Tato nikkhantanti nibbānanti vuttaṃ.

16. Nibbāna: Herein, all the sufferings and distresses of the cycle cease in this; therefore, it is Nibbāna. ‘Cease’ means this: those defilements or aggregates which, for one who has not developed the path, stand in the category of being liable to arise in the future, for one who has developed the path, they reach the category of being not liable to arise again. For past phenomena that have ceased after reaching the three moments are not what is called ‘ceasing’. As for present phenomena and those that will certainly arise in the future, there is nothing to be said. ‘Sufferings and distresses of the cycle’ means the sufferings and distresses of the cycle of defilements, the cycle of kamma, and the cycle of results. For the non-arising and cessation of things devoid of the threefold suffering and distress of the cycle, such as trees, is not called Nibbāna. ‘In this’ is a locative of sphere, as in ‘birds fly in the sky.’ For those things that cease, there is no other place of cessation apart from that. Or, noble persons cease in this; therefore, it is Nibbāna. For it is said: ‘The wise are extinguished, like this lamp.’ ‘Cease’ means that they attain a state of no future relinking of those respective defilements or aggregates. The locative is in the sense of a single sphere; some also construe it as ‘when this is attained.’ But in the subcommentaries, craving is called ‘vāna’ from weaving or sewing together existence and non-existence. It is said that Nibbāna is that which has ‘departed from that.’

[18] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[18] Now, this is to be clarified:

“Nibbābhivā [M 0.0025] etena rāgaggiādikoti nibbāna”ntipi vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is also said: ‘By this the fire of lust and so on is extinguished; therefore, it is Nibbāna.’ That is not well-said.

Na hi maggeviya nibbāne katthaci karaṇasādhanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, naca nibbānaṃ nibbūti kriyāsādhane rāgādikassa kattuno saha kāripaccayo hotīti. [Nibbānaṃ]

For an instrumental derivation is nowhere seen for Nibbāna as it is for the path. Nor, in the accomplishment of the action of extinguishing, is Nibbāna a cooperative condition for the agent, which is lust and so on. [Nibbāna]

Dutīyagāthāya paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the ultimate meaning of the second verse is concluded.

Cittasaṅgaha-paramatthadīpanī

Cittasaṅgaha-paramatthadīpanī

17. Idāni uddesakkamena cittaṃ tāva niddisanto tattha cittantiādimāha. Tatthāti tesu catūsu abhidhammatthesu. Tāva pathamaṃ. Cattāro vidhā pakārā yassa taṃ catubbidhaṃ.

17. Now, first, indicating consciousness according to the order of the summary, he says, ‘Therein, consciousness…’ and so on. ‘Therein’ means: among those four ultimate realities of Abhidhamma. First of all. That which has four kinds or modes is fourfold.

18. Kāmāvacaranti ettha kāmīyatīti kāmo. Kāmentivā ettha sattā avikkhambhitakāmarāgattā kāmaratiyāeva ramanti. Na uparibhūmīsu viya jhānaratiyāti kāmo. Ekādasavidhā kāmabhūmi. Nanu cettha jhānalābhinopi santīti. Na na santi. Tepana kadāci devāti natthettha doso. Avīcinirayādayo kathaṃ kāmīyanti. Kathañca tattha sattā kāmaratiyā ramantīti. Nimittassādavasenavā bhavanikantivasenavāti. Maraṇakāle hi upaṭṭhitā nirayaggijālā suvaṇṇavaṇṇāviya khāyanti. Eko kira micchādiṭṭhiko brāhmaṇo maraṇamañce nippanno hoti. Tassa ācariyabrāhmaṇā samīpe ṭhatvā brahmalokaṃ bho gacchāti vadanti. Tassapana avīciniraye aggijālā upaṭṭhahanti. Tadā so bho ācariyā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā paññāyantīti āha. Esa bho brahmaloko. Tattha gacchāti vadanti. So kālaṅkatvā avīcimhi uppajji. Evaṃ nimittassādavasena te kāmīyanti. Tattha uppannānaṃpi bhavanikantināma hotīti. Apica, tattha uppannā avikkhambhitakāmarāgāeva honti, okāse sati kāmaratiyā ramissanti yevāti. Tasmiṃ kāme avacaratīti kāmāvacaraṃ. [M 0.0026] Etthaca avacaratīti padassa uppajjatīti attho na gahetabbo. So hi attho pāḷiyāca nasameti. Nānādosayuttoca hotīti. Yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannāti hi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yadi cettha so attho adhippeto siyā. Evaṃ sabhi etthāvacarā etthuppannāti vuttaṃ siyā. Napana vuttaṃ. Naca pariyāpannasaddo uppannasaddena saha samānatthoti sakkā vattuṃ. Na hi lokuttaracittāni tīsu bhavesu uppannā nipi tatra pariyāpannāniyeva hontīti. Evaṃ tāva pāḷiyā nasametīti.

18. The sense-sphere (kāmāvacara): Here, it is called 'kāma' because it is desired (kāmīyati). Or, beings here, not having suppressed sensual passion, delight solely in sensual enjoyment, not in the joy of jhāna as in higher realms; therefore, it is kāma. The sense-sphere is elevenfold. But are there not beings here who attain jhāna? Indeed, there are. But they are sometimes devas; thus, there is no fault in this. How are Avīci hell and other such realms desired (kāmīyanti)? And how do beings there take pleasure in sensual enjoyment? It is due to the allurement of the sign or the attraction for existence (bhavanikanti). For at the time of death, the flames of hell that appear seem to be of a golden color. It is said that a certain brahmin of wrong view was lying on his deathbed. His brahmin teachers, standing nearby, said, 'Go, good sir, to the Brahma-world!' But to him, the flames of Avīci hell appeared. Then he said, 'Good sirs, they appear golden in color!' They said, 'That is the Brahma-world, go there!' He died and was reborn in Avīci. Thus, through the allurement of the sign, these realms are desired. For those born there, there is also what is called attraction for existence. Furthermore, those born there have unsubdued sensual passion, and if given the opportunity, they will indulge in sensual enjoyment. It is called the 'sense-sphere' (kāmāvacara) because one wanders (avacarati) in that kāma. Here, the meaning of 'avacarati' should not be taken as 'arises,' for that interpretation does not accord with the Pāli texts and is fraught with various faults. For in the Pāli texts it is said, 'Those who wander in this, those included in this.' If that meaning were intended, it would have been stated as, 'Those who wander in this, those born in this.' But it is not so stated. Nor can the term 'included' (pariyāpanna) be said to have the same meaning as 'born' (uppanna). For supramundane consciousnesses, although arising in the three realms of existence, are not included therein. Thus, it does not accord with the Pāli text.

Yadica so attho gahito siyā. Evañca sati tasmiṃ kāme ye mahaggata lokuttaradhammā uppajjanti. Tesaṃpi kāmā vacaratāpattidoso rūpāvacaratādi muttidosoca āpajjati. Yeca kāmāvacaradhammā rūpārūpabhūmīsu uppajjanti. Tesañca rūpārūpā vacaratā pattidoso kāmāvacaratā muttidosoca āpajjatīti. Nanu yebhuyyavuttivasenapi kesañci nāmalābho hoti. Yathā vanacarako saṅgāmāvacaroti. Tasmā idhapi tesaṃ dhammānaṃ attano attano bhummīsu uppannabahulattā kāmāvacarādi nāmalābhe sati na koci dosoti.Na. Evañhi sati lokuttara dhammānaṃ kāmāvacaratādi muccanatthaṃ yebhuyyena uppannabhūmi visuṃ vattabbā siyā. Na ca sā nāmabhūmi atthi. Yattha te yebhuyyena uppajjantīti. Tehi uppajjantā tīsu bhavesu eva uppajjanti. Tasmā tesaṃ kāma rūpārūpāvacaratāpattidoso dunnivāro siyāti. Evaṃ nānādosayutto hotīti. Tasmāssa tathā atthaṃ aggahetvā etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannāti bhagavatā saṃvaṇṇitena pāḷinayenevassa attho gahetabboti. Ayañhettha attho. Kāme avacarati pariyāpannabhāvena tasmiṃ ajjhogāhetvā carati pavattatīti kāmāvacaranti. Pariyāpannabhāvocanāma attano ādhārabhūtena tena kāmena saha samānajātigottanāmatā saṅkhātehi paritobhāgehi tasmiṃ kāme āpannabhāvo anuppaviṭṭha bhāvo. Antogadhabhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti. Soca tathā [M 0.0027] pariyāpannabhāvo pariggāhiniyā kāmataṇhāya katoti daṭṭhabbo. Ettāvatā yedhammā rūpārūpasattasantānabhūtāpi mayhaṃ eteti kāma taṇhāya pariggahitā kāme pariyāpannāva honti. Te kāmāvacarānāmāti siddhā honti. Rūpārūpā vacaresupi ayaṃ nayo netabbo. Tesupana rūpataṇhā arūpataṇhāca pariggāhinī taṇhā daṭṭhabbā.

If that meaning were grasped, then for those sublime and supramundane states that arise in the sense-sphere, the fault of belonging to the sense-sphere and the fault of being released from the form-sphere, etc., would arise. And for those sense-sphere phenomena that arise in the form and formless spheres, the fault of belonging to the form and formless spheres and the fault of being released from the sense-sphere would arise. Is it not so that some things get a name by way of general usage, like 'forest-dweller' or 'battlefield-dweller'? Therefore, here too, because those phenomena arise in abundance in their own spheres, there is no fault when they obtain the designation of sense-sphere, etc. No. For if that were so, then for supramundane phenomena to be released from belonging to the sense-sphere, etc., the sphere in which they predominantly arise would have to be stated separately. But there is no such sphere by name where they predominantly arise. They arise only in the three realms of existence. Therefore, the fault of their belonging to the sense, form, or formless spheres would be difficult to avoid. Thus, it would be fraught with various faults. Therefore, without grasping the meaning in that way, the meaning should be understood according to the method of the Pāli texts as declared by the Blessed One: 'Those who wander here are included here.' And here is the meaning: 'Sense-sphere' (kāmāvacara) means that which wanders (avacarati) in the sense-sphere (kāma); it moves and proceeds by having plunged into it with a state of inclusion. And 'the state of being included' means a state of having entered, a state of having penetrated, a state of being contained within that sense-sphere, which is its own support, along with its surrounding aspects known as having the same birth, lineage, and name. And that state of being so included should be understood as caused by grasping sensual craving. To this extent, even those phenomena that are in the mental continuum of form and formless beings, when grasped by sensual craving as 'mine,' are indeed included in the sense-sphere. Thus, they are established as being of the sense-sphere. This same principle should be applied to the form and formless spheres. However, there, form-craving and formless-craving should be understood as the grasping craving.

Yepana dhammā tiṇṇaṃ taṇhānaṃ pariggahavimuttā honti. Te tīsu bhavesu uppannāpi tatra apariyāpannāeva hontīti lokuttarā nāma jātāti veditabbā. Etthaca paṭṭhāne āruppe kāmacchandaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ paṭicca uddhaccanīvaraṇantiādinā arūpasattasantānepi kāmacchandasaṅkhātāya kāmataṇhāya uppatti vuttā. Tasmā rūpārūpa bhūmīsu uppannānaṃ kāmadhammānaṃ pariggāhinītaṇhā rūpārūpasattasantāna gatāpi daṭṭhabbā. Pāḷiyaṃ kāmacchandanīvaraṇanti idaṃ nīvaraṇajātikattā vuttaṃ. Na hi jhānabhūmīsu ekantanīvaraṇakiccāni nīvaraṇāni sakkā laddhunti. Atra kāmabhedo vattabbo. Dvekāmā kile sakāmoca, vatthukāmocāti. Tattha thapetvā rūpārūparāge añño sabbopi lobho imasmiṃ catubbhūmiparicchede kile sakāmonāma. Thapetvāca rūpārūpāvacaradhamme aññe sabbepi tīsu bhūmīsu uppannā kāmāvacaradhammā vatthukāmonāmāti. Yaṃpana aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ sabbepi tebhūmakā dhammā vatthukāmoti vuttaṃ. Taṃ mahāniddese niddiṭṭhena suttantikapariyāyena vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Na hi rūpārūpāvacaradhammā abhidhamme kāmanāmena vuttā atthīti. [Kāmāvacarapadaṃ]

But those phenomena that are free from the grasp of the three cravings, even when they arise in the three realms of existence, are not included therein; they should be understood as belonging to the supramundane class. And here, in the Paṭṭhāna, with the words 'in dependence on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of restlessness arises,' etc., the arising of sensual craving, known as sensual desire, is spoken of even in the mental continuum of a formless being. Therefore, the grasping craving for sense-sphere phenomena that have arisen in the form and formless spheres should be understood as also being present in the mental continuum of form and formless beings. In the Pāli, 'the hindrance of sensual desire' is stated because it belongs to the class of hindrances. For in the jhāna spheres, it is not possible for hindrances to perform exclusively the function of a hindrance. Here, the distinction of kāma should be stated. There are two kāmas: defilement-kāma and object-kāma. Therein, setting aside lust for form and the formless, all other greed in this division of the four spheres is called 'defilement-kāma.' And setting aside form-sphere and formless-sphere phenomena, all other sense-sphere phenomena arisen in the three spheres are called 'object-kāma.' As for what is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī, that all phenomena of the three spheres are 'object-kāma,' that should be taken as spoken according to the Suttanta method pointed out in the Mahāniddesa. For in the Abhidhamma, there are no form-sphere or formless-sphere phenomena called by the name 'kāma.' [The term 'kāmāvacara']

19. Rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaranti ettha rūpārūpasaddā tāsu bhūmīsu niruḷhāti daṭṭhabbā. Apica dve bhūmiyo rūpabhūmi, arūpabhūmīti. Tattha ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ yattha natthi, sā catubbidhā bhummi arūpabhūmināma. Sesā sattavīsatividhā bhummi rūpabhūmināma. Tatthaca heṭṭhā ekādasavidhā bhummi oḷārikena kāmena visesetvā kāma bhūmīti vuttā. Upari soḷasavidhā bhummi rūpabhūmiicceva vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Yatthapana taṇhāvā jhānānivā rūpārūpasaddehi vuttāni. Tattha [M 0.0028] nissayassanāmaṃ nissite āropanavasena nissayopacāro veditabbo. Yatthaca kāmāvacarādisaddehi bhūmieva vuttā. Tattha nissitassa nāmaṃ nissaye āropanavasena nissito pacāroti. Yamettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ kāmāvacarapade vuttanayamevāti. Ayamettha tebhūmaka paricchede pāḷianugatā paramatthadīpanā. Yathāha –

19. Here, regarding 'of the form sphere' and 'of the formless sphere,' it should be understood that the words 'form' and 'formless' are established terms for those spheres. Moreover, there are two spheres: the form sphere and the formless sphere. Therein, the fourfold sphere where there is no form characterized by 'being crushed' (ruppana) is called the formless sphere. The remaining twenty-sevenfold sphere is called the form sphere. And among these, the lower elevenfold sphere, being distinguished by gross sensuality, is called the sense-sphere. It should be understood that the upper sixteenfold sphere is called simply the form sphere. But where craving or jhānas are spoken of by the words 'form' and 'formless,' there it should be known as a metaphor of the support, by way of attributing the name of the support (nissaya) to that which is supported (nissita). And where the spheres themselves are spoken of by words such as 'of the sense-sphere,' there it is a metaphor of the supported, by way of attributing the name of that which is supported (nissita) to the support (nissaya). Whatever is to be said here is by the same method as was stated in the section on the sense-sphere. This, herein, is the 'Illumination of the Ultimate Meaning' in accordance with the Pāli in the section on the three spheres. As it is said:

Katame dhammā kāmāvacarā. Heṭṭhato avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito paranimmitavasavattīdeve anto karitvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā khandhadhātuāyatanā rūpā vedanā saññā saṅkhārā viññāṇaṃ. Imedhammā kāmāvacarā. Katame dhammā rūpāvacarā. Heṭṭhato brahmalokaṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito akaniṭṭhe deve anto karitvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare etthāvacarā ettha pariyāpannā samāpannassavā upapannassavā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissavā cittacetasikā dhammā, ime dhammā rūpāvacarā. Katame dhammā arūpāvacarā. Heṭṭhato ākāsānañcāyatanupage deve pariyantaṃ karitvā uparito nevasaññā nāsaññā yatanupage deve anto karitvā yaṃ etasmiṃ antare. La. Ime dhammā arūpāvacarāti.

What are the phenomena of the sense-sphere? Below, taking Avīci hell as the lower limit, and above, including the Paranimmitavasavattī gods as the upper limit—whatever aggregates, elements, and sense bases are within this interval, belonging here, included here: form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. These phenomena are of the sense-sphere. What are the phenomena of the form-sphere? Below, taking the Brahmā world as the lower limit, and above, including the Akaniṭṭha gods as the upper limit—whatever mental states and mental factors are within this interval, belonging here, included here, of one who has attained jhāna, or is reborn in that realm, or dwells happily in the present life. These phenomena are of the form-sphere. What are the phenomena of the formless-sphere? Below, taking the gods abiding in the base of the infinity of space as the lower limit, and above, including the gods abiding in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the upper limit—whatever phenomena are within this interval. Thus, these phenomena are of the formless-sphere.

[19] Ṭīkāsu pana

In the subcommentaries, however,

Yathāvuttaṃ suvisadaṃ pāḷinayaṃ aggahetvā aññathā vacanatthāca vinicchayāca ettha vuttā. Sabbe te sārato na paccetabbāti.

Without grasping the clearly stated Pāli method, other interpretations, meanings, and judgments are mentioned here. All of them should not be accepted in essence.

Nanu aṭṭhasāliniyameva teca aññeca atthā vuttāti. Saccaṃ. Bhūtaṃpana suvisadaṃ pāḷianugataṃ atthaṃ ñatvā kiṃvikkhepenāti.

Is it not that in the Aṭṭhasālinī itself those and other meanings are stated? True. But having understood the meaning that is truly clear and conforms to the Pāli, what is the purpose of confusion?

20. Lokuttaranti ettha lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko vuccati yathāvutto tebhūmakadhammo. Yathāha lujjati palujjatīti kho bhikkhave tasmā lokoti vuccatīti. Evaṃ sante lokuttaradhammānaṃpi nibbānavajjānaṃ lokatāpatti siyā. Kasmā, tesaṃpi [M 0.0029] lujjanapalujjanadhammattāti. Nasiyā. Yattha hi nicco dhuvo sassatoti mahājanassa micchāgāho nivisati. Tattheva tassa nivāraṇatthaṃ ayaṃ lokasamaññā niyamīyati. Tasmā sabbaso micchāgāhavimuttānaṃ tesaṃ lokatāpatti natthīti vadanti. Yesaṃvā lujjanaṃpalujjanañca mahājanassa pākaṭaṃ. Tesaññeva lokatāsiddhīti natthi lokuttarānaṃ lokattappasaṅgoti. Lokato uttaratīti lokuttaraṃ. Maggacittaṃ. Tato uttiṇṇanti lokuttaraṃ. Phalacittaṃ. Nibbānaṃpana idha nalabbhatīti. Uttaraṇañcettha taṇhāttayaggāha vimuttiyā tīsu lokesu apariyāpannabhāvoyeva. Soca apariyāpannabhāvo kesaṃ dhammānaṃ adhiṭṭhāna bhūtoviya gayhatīti visuṃ ekā catutthī avatthābhūmināmāti.

20. Here, regarding 'lokuttara' (supramundane): the 'world' (loka) is so called in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating, referring to the phenomena of the three realms as previously described. As it is said: 'It crumbles, it disintegrates, monks, therefore it is called the world.' If this is so, even the supramundane phenomena, with the exception of Nibbāna, might fall into the category of the world. Why? Because they too have the nature of crumbling and disintegrating. But this is not the case. For wherever the wrong view of permanence, stability, and eternity takes hold among the masses, there alone is this designation 'world' applied to dispel that misconception. Therefore, they say that for those states which are entirely free from such wrong views, there is no falling into the category of the world. Alternatively, the designation 'world' applies only to those states whose crumbling and disintegration are evident to ordinary people. Thus, there is no occasion for the supramundane states to be considered part of the world. 'Lokuttara' means 'it rises above the world'—this refers to the path-consciousness. 'It has transcended it' refers to the fruition-consciousness. However, Nibbāna is not included here. The transcendence here is precisely the state of non-inclusion in the three worlds through liberation from craving and the grasp of self. And that state of non-inclusion is taken as if it were the basis for certain phenomena, hence it is called a distinct fourth stage or plane.

Catubbhūmivibhāgassa paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The illumination of the ultimate meaning of the division of the four planes is completed.

21. Evaṃ cittaṃ bhūmibhedena hīnapaṇītā nukkamato catudhā niddisitvā idāni tadeva catubbidhaṃ cittaṃ yathāniddiṭṭhakkamena vibhajanto pathamaṃ kāmāvacaracittaṃ. Tatthaca hīnaṃ asobhaṇacittaṃ. Tatthaca sabbahīnaṃ akusalacittaṃ tāva dassetuṃ somanassasaha gatantiādimāha. Etthaca kāmāvacaracittassapi akusalāhetuka sahetukānukkamo hīna paṇītānukkamavasena vuttoti daṭṭhabbo.

21. Thus, having designated consciousness as fourfold according to the sequence of inferior and superior based on the division of planes, now, dividing that same fourfold consciousness according to the designated sequence, the text first deals with sense-sphere consciousness. And within this, the inferior is the unbeautiful consciousness. And within this, to show first the unwholesome consciousness, which is the most inferior of all, the text states 'accompanied by joy,' and so on. And here, it should be understood that even within the sense-sphere consciousness, the sequence of unwholesome, rootless, and rooted states is stated according to the sequence of inferior and superior.

[20] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[20] However, in the Vibhāvanī:

Upari vuccamānānaṃ bahūnaṃ cittānaṃ sobhaṇasaññākaraṇasukhatthaṃ appake pāpāhetukeyeva pathamaṃ dassentoti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is stated that for the sake of easily making the 'beautiful' designation for the many types of consciousness to be mentioned later, only the few unwholesome and rootless states are presented first. That is not well-stated.

Tadattho hi yathāvuttahīnādikkameneva siddhoti.

For that meaning is indeed accomplished by the aforementioned sequence of inferior and so forth alone.

[21] Yañca tattha

[21] And what is stated there:

Tesu tesuca bhavesu gahitappaṭisandhikassa sattassa ādito vīthicittavasena lobhasahagata cittuppādāna meva sambhavato teyeva pathamanti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi nayujjati.

It is stated that in those various existences, for a being who has taken rebirth-linking, only greed-accompanied consciousness-arisings occur first by way of the cognitive process, and therefore these are stated first. But that too is not fitting.

Ādito [M 0.0030] vīthicittavasena manodvārā vajjanasseva sabbapathamaṃ uppajjanatoti. Akusalesu pana lobhamūla cittaṃ bahukañca hoti. Dvīhi vaṭṭamūlehi yuttattā padhānaṃ pākaṭañca hotīti tadeva pathamaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For from the very beginning, by way of the cognitive process, it is the mind-door adverting consciousness alone that arises first of all. Among the unwholesome states, however, the greed-rooted consciousness is both abundant and, being connected to the two roots of the round of existence, prominent and manifest. It should be understood that it is for this reason that it is stated first.

22. Tattha sundaraṃ manoti sumano. Siniddhacittaṃ. Na hi anavajjaṭṭhena sundaratā idha yuttāti. Sundaraṃ mano etassābhivā sumano. Siniddhacittasamaṅgī puggalo. Sumanassa bhāvo somanassa. Mānasikasukhavedanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Etthaca sumanassa bhāvoti tasmiṃ citte puggalevā sumanābhidhānassavā ayaṃ so sumanoti sumanabuddhiyāvā pavattinimittanti attho. Bhāvoti hi abhidhānabuddhīnaṃ pavattinimittaṃ vuccati. Bhavanti pavattanti abhidhānabuddhiyo etasminti katvā. Etasminti ca nimitte bhummaṃ. Yathā nāgo dantesu haññateti. Yathā hi tattha attano dantanimittaṃ dantayutte nāge hananappavatti hoti, evamidhapi taṃ vedanānimittaṃ vedanāyutte manasmiṃ puggalevā abhidhānabuddhiyo pavattantīti. Bhavanti buddhisaddā etenāti bhāvotica vadanti. Etasmāti ca apare. Somanassena saha ekato gataṃ pavattanti somanassasahagataṃ. Somanassavedanāsampayuttanti attho. Dassanaṃ diṭṭhi. Sā pana sammādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhivasena duvidhā. Idha micchādiṭṭhiyuttā. Akusalādhikārattā. Diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigataṃ. Yathā gūthagataṃ muttagatanti. Diṭṭhigatena samaṃ pakārehi yuttanti diṭṭhigata sampayuttaṃ. Diṭṭhigatena ekuppādatādīhi pakārehi samaṃ ekībhūta miva yuttaṃ saṃsaṭṭhanti attho. Asaṅkhārikamekaṃ sasaṅkhārikamekanti ettha saṅkhāroti pubbātisaṅkhāro. Soca duvidho payogo, upāyocāti. Tattha āṇattiyāvā ajjhesanāyavā tajjetvā vā idaṃ karohīti parehi kato kāyavacīpayogo payogonāma. Āṇattādināpana vināva kammassa karaṇatthaṃ taṃ taṃ upāyaṃ pare ācikkhanti. Akaraṇe ādīnavaṃ karaṇeca ānisaṃsaṃ dassenti, katikaṃvā karonti, daṇḍaṃvā thapenti, sayameva vā taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ anussarati, paccavekkhati. Evamādinā nayena [M 0.0031] upāyo anekavidho. So duvidhopi idha saṅkhāro nāma. Saṅkharoti attano pakatiyā kātuṃ anicchamānaṃ citta santānaṃ akātuṃ adatvā karaṇatthāya saṃvidahati tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kamme payojetīti katvā. Yopana paccayagaṇo tena saṅkhārena virahito hoti. So asaṅkhāro. Yopana tenasahito hoti. So sasaṅkhāroti. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

22. Here, 'sundaraṃ mano' means 'sumano' (a pleasant mind), a serene mind. For here, beauty in the sense of being blameless is not appropriate. Or, 'sumano' is one whose mind is pleasant, a person endowed with a serene mind. The state of being 'sumano' is 'somanassa' (joy). This is a name for mentally pleasant feeling. And here, 'the state of being sumano' means the cause for the arising of the designation 'sumana' or of the thought 'this is sumana' with regard to that mind or person. For 'bhāvo' (state) is called the cause for the arising of designations and thoughts, because designations and thoughts arise and occur from it. And 'etasminti' is the locative case indicating the cause. Just as it is said, 'The elephant is killed for its tusks.' For just as there, the act of killing an elephant that possesses tusks occurs because of its tusks, so here too, designations and thoughts arise with regard to the mind or person endowed with that feeling, because of that feeling. And they also say 'bhāvo' because 'buddhi-saddā' (thoughts and terms) arise by means of it. And others say 'etasmā' (from this). Occurring together with joy, it is 'somanassasahagataṃ' (accompanied by joy). The meaning is 'associated with the feeling of joy.' 'Dassanaṃ' is view (diṭṭhi). That, however, is twofold: right view and wrong view. Here, it is associated with wrong view because the context is unwholesome. View itself is 'diṭṭhigataṃ' (gone to view), just as 'gūthagataṃ' (gone to feces) or 'muttagataṃ' (gone to urine). Associated with wrong view in various ways is 'diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ' (associated with wrong view). The meaning is 'united as if one, connected with wrong view by ways such as simultaneous arising.' Regarding 'one is unprompted, one is prompted' (asaṅkhārikaṃ ekaṃ, sasaṅkhārikaṃ ekaṃ), here 'saṅkhāro' means prior instigation. And that is twofold: exertion and means. Among these, exertion (payoga) is the bodily or verbal effort made by others through command, request, or threat, saying 'Do this!' However, without command, etc., others suggest various means for performing the action. They point out the danger in not doing it and the benefit in doing it, or they make an agreement, or they impose a penalty, or one oneself recalls and reflects on the reason. In this way, the means are manifold. Both types are called 'saṅkhāro' here. It is called 'saṅkhāro' because it disposes the mind-continuum, which is by nature unwilling to act, not allowing it to not act, and arranges it for action, engaging it in that particular task. That group of conditions which is devoid of such instigation is 'unprompted' (asaṅkhāro). That which is accompanied by it is 'prompted' (sasaṅkhāro). This is stated in the commentary:—

Saha saṅkhārenāti sasaṅkhāro. Tena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena saupāyena paccayagaṇenāti atthoti.

'Sasaṅkhāro' means 'with instigation.' The meaning is: with that group of conditions which is prompted, possessing exertion and means.

Etthaca paccayagaṇoti ārammaṇādiko sādhāraṇo paccaya gaṇo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto. Asādhāraṇopana kusalakammesu sappurisupanissayādiko akusalakammesu asappurisupanissayādiko paccayagaṇo visesetvā yojetuṃ yutto. Sopana yadā duvidhena saṅkhārena vinā sayameva cittaṃ asaṃsīdamānaṃ katvā uṭṭhāpeti samuṭṭhāpeti, tadā soasaṅkhāronāma. Yadāpana tena vinā sayameva cittaṃ uṭṭhāpetuṃ samuṭṭhāpetuṃ nasakkoti, saṅkhāraṃ sahāyaṃ labhitvāva sakkoti, tadā so sasaṅkhāronāma. Iti asaṅkhāro sasaṅkhārotica idaṃ paccaya gaṇasseva nāmaṃ. Na cittassa. Cittaṃpana asaṅkhārena suddhena paccayagaṇena uppannaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ. Sasaṅkhārena paccayagaṇena uppannaṃ sasaṅkhārikaṃ, uppannatthe hi ayaṃ ikapaccayoti. Yasmiṃ samaye akusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ diṭṭhigatasampayuttaṃ sasaṅkhārenāti hi pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti. Etthaca sasaṅkhārena paccayagaṇena uppannaṃ hotīti yojetabbanti. Ayamettha asaṅkhārikasasaṅkhārikapadesu paramatthadīpanā.

Herein, 'group of conditions' means the common group of conditions such as object, etc., as stated in the commentary. But the uncommon group of conditions, such as reliance on good persons in wholesome actions and reliance on bad persons in unwholesome actions, should be applied specifically. When one, without a prompting, having made the mind not sink, arouses and instigates it by oneself, then that is called 'unprompted.' But when one is unable to arouse and instigate the mind by oneself without a prompting, and can do so only by obtaining the support of a prompting, then that is called 'prompted.' Thus, 'unprompted' and 'prompted' are names for the group of conditions itself, not for the consciousness. The consciousness, however, that has arisen through a mere unprompted group of conditions is called 'unprompted.' One that has arisen through a prompted group of conditions is called 'prompted,' for the suffix '-ika' here is in the sense of 'arisen.' As it is said in the Pāli text: 'At the time when an unwholesome consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, with a prompting…' Here, it should be construed as 'has arisen through a prompted group of conditions.' This is the exposition of the ultimate meaning regarding the terms 'unprompted' and 'prompted'.

[22] Ṭīkāsu pana

In the subcommentaries, however,

Imamatthaṃ asallakkhetvā cittameva asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāranti ca gahetvā yaṃ vuttaṃ, “natthi saṅkhāro assāti asaṅkhāraṃ. Tadeva asaṅkhārikaṃ. Saha saṅkhārena vattatīti sasaṅkhāraṃ. Sasaṅkhārameva [M 0.0032] sasaṅkhārikanti ca. So yassa natthi. Taṃ asaṅkhāraṃ. Tadeva asaṅkhārikaṃ. Saṅkhārena sahitaṃ sasaṅkhāri kanti ca”. Sabbametaṃ na yujjatiyeva.

Not discerning this meaning, and taking the consciousness itself to be unprompted and prompted, what was said—namely: 'There is no prompting for it, thus it is unprompted; that itself is unprompted (asaṅkhārika). It proceeds together with a prompting, thus it is prompted; the prompted itself is sasaṅkhārika. That for which there is no prompting, that is unprompted; that itself is asaṅkhārika. And what is together with a prompting is sasaṅkhārika.'—all this is indeed not tenable.

[23] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

And in the Vibhāvanī:

Saṅkharoti cittaṃ tikkhabhāvasaṅkhātamaṇḍanavisesena sajjeti. Saṅkharīyativā taṃ etena yathāvuttanayena sajjīyatīti saṅkhāroti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

It was said: 'It prompts the consciousness, that is, it adorns it with the special ornament called sharpness. Or, it is prompted, that is, it is adorned by this in the aforesaid manner; therefore it is called a prompting.' This too is not a good explanation.

Evañhi sati sasaṅkhārikapi cittaṃ tikkhaṃnāma siyāti.

For if this were so, even a prompted consciousness would be called sharp.

[24] Yañca tattha

And what is said therein:

“So pana attano pubbabhāgappavatte cittasantāneceva parasantāneca pavattatīti taṃ nibbattito cittassa tikkhabhāva saṅkhāto visesova idha saṅkhāroti” vuttaṃ. Taṃpi asaṅkhārika sasaṅkhārikapadānaṃ vacanatthesu virajjhitvā tadanu rūpassa saṅkhārassa parikappanāvasena vuttattā nayuttameva.

It was said: 'But since that occurs in one's own preceding mental continuum and in the mental continuum of others, the distinction produced by it, called sharpness of mind, is here the "prompting".' That too, being contrary to the literal meanings of the terms 'unprompted' and 'prompted' and having been stated by way of a conception of a corresponding prompting, is indeed not proper.

[25] Etena

By this,

Pubbappayogasambhūto, viseso cittasambhapī;

Saṅkhāro taṃ vasenettha, hotyāsaṅkhārikāditāti.

The distinction born of prior effort, and the mind's agitation, is the prompting; by its power here, there comes to be the state of being unprompted, etc.

Sādhakagāthāpi paṭikkhittā hotīti.

the illustrative verse is also rejected.

[26] Yañca tattha

And what is said therein:

“Athavā, sasaṅkhārikaṃ asaṅkhārikanti ce taṃ kevalaṃsaṅkhārassa bhāvābhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Natassa sahapavattisabbhā vā bhāvatoti. Bhinnasantānappavattinopi saṅkhārassa idhamatthitāya taṃ vasena nibbattaṃ cittaṃ saṅkhāro assa atthīti sasaṅkhārikaṃ. Salomako sapakkhakotyādīsuviya saha saddassa vijjamānatthaparidīpanato. Tabbiparītampana tadabhāvato vuttanayena asaṅkhārika”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi pāḷiaṭṭhakathāsiddhaṃ [M 0.0033] ujuṃ visadaṃ atthaṃ muñcitvā attano parikappanā vasena vuttattā na gahetabbameva.

It was said: 'Or, if it is said that "prompted" and "unprompted" are stated with reference merely to the presence or absence of a prompting, it is not because of its co-occurrence or existence. Even when a prompting occurs in a different continuum, because of its existence here, the consciousness produced by its power is "prompted" in the sense "a prompting exists for it," just as in "hairy," "winged," etc., because the word "with" (saha) indicates the meaning of "existence." Its opposite, "unprompted," is so called because of its absence, in the way stated.' This too, having abandoned the direct, clear meaning established in the Pāli and the commentaries and being stated by way of one's own speculation, should certainly not be accepted.

Etthaca attano icchāya vinā paresaṃ āṇattiyāvā ajjhe sanāyavā yācanāyavā pavattitaṃ cittaṃ payogasamuṭṭhitaṃ nāma. Tathā attano icchāya vinā paresaṃ bhayenavā lajjāyavā gāravenavā kathikāyavā daṇḍabhayenavā pavattitaṃ upāyasamuṭṭhitaṃ nāma. Sayamevavā attano līnaṃ cittaṃ ñatvā tena tena upāyena attānaṃ ovaditvāvā taṃ taṃ upāyaṃ anussaritvāvā pavattitaṃ cittaṃ upāyasamuṭṭhitaṃ nāma. Idañca nayadassanamevāti. Diṭṭhigatena vippayuttaṃ diṭṭhigatavippayuttaṃ. Udāsinabhāvena pekkhati anubhavanākārena ārammaṇaṃ passatīti upekkhā. Upapattito yuttito ikkhati passatītivā upekkhā. Yathāhi somanassa domanassāni ārammaṇaṃ adhimattato passanti. Yato somanassito puggalo tena ārammaṇena viyoge vikārapatto hoti. Domanassitoca tena ārammaṇena saṃyoge vikārapatto hoti. Na tathā ayaṃ, ayaṃ pana yuttitova passati na ārammaṇasaṃyoga viyogahetu puggalaṃ vikāraṃ pāpetīti. Kecipana upapattito yuttito ikkhatīti idaṃ idha nasambhavati. Na hi akusalaṃ yuttarūpaṃ nāma hotīti vadanti. Upekkhāya sahagatanti samāso.

Herein, a consciousness that arises not by one's own wish but by another's command, request, or solicitation is called 'arisen from an instigation.' Similarly, a consciousness that arises not by one's own wish but through fear of others, shame, respect, talk, or fear of punishment is called 'arisen from a means.' Or, having known one's own sluggish mind, a consciousness that arises after one has admonished oneself by some means or has recollected some means is also called 'arisen from a means.' This is just an indication of the method. Dissociated from wrong view is 'dissociated from wrong view.' It looks on with an attitude of neutrality, experiencing the object; this is equanimity. Or, it sees, it perceives, from the standpoint of what is suitable and proper; this is equanimity. For just as joy and displeasure see the object excessively—whence a person feeling joy becomes distressed by separation from that object, and a person feeling displeasure becomes distressed by union with that object—this is not so. This one sees only from the standpoint of what is proper and does not cause a person to become distressed on account of union with or separation from the object. But some say: 'This "it sees from the standpoint of what is suitable and proper" is not possible here, for the unwholesome is not what is called proper.' 'Accompanied by equanimity' is a compound.

23. Etthaca kiñcāpi phassādayo vitakkādayo mohādayoca dhammā iminā sakalena aṭṭhavidhena cittena saha gatā sampayuttāca honti, na pana te vedanāviya sayaṃpi bhedavantā honti. Naca diṭṭhisaṅkhārānaṃ viyatesaṃ imasmiṃ citte katthaci honti katthacinahontīti ayaṃ vikappo atthi. Tasmāte imassacittassa bhedakarā nahontīti idha nagahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Lobhopana aññehi imassa aṭṭhavidhassa bhedakaro hoti. Vedanādiṭṭhi saṅkhārāca imassa aññamaññassa bhedakarā hontīti teeva idha gahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Nanu pīti māna thinamiddhānipi bhedakarāni hontīti tānipi idha sapītikaṃ apītikanti mānasampayuttaṃ mānavippayuttanti [M 0.0034] thinamiddhasampayuttaṃ thinamiddhavippayuttanti ca gahetabbā nīti. Na. Tesu hi somanasse gahite pīti gahitāva hoti. Itarānica tīṇi aniyatayogīnica honti, yevāpana kānicāti nagahitānīti.

23. Herein, although factors such as contact, initial application, and delusion are accompanied by and associated with this entire eightfold consciousness, they are not themselves variable like feeling. Nor, like view and prompting, is there the alternative that they are sometimes present in this consciousness and sometimes not. Therefore, it should be understood that since they are not differentiators of this consciousness, they are not taken up here. But greed is a differentiator of this eightfold consciousness from others. And it should be understood that since feeling, view, and prompting are differentiators of this consciousness from one another, they alone are taken up here. But are not rapture, conceit, and sloth-and-torpor also differentiators? Therefore they too should be taken up here as 'with rapture' and 'without rapture,' 'associated with conceit' and 'dissociated from conceit,' and 'associated with sloth-and-torpor' and 'dissociated from sloth-and-torpor.' No. For among them, when joy is taken, rapture is also taken. And the other three are occasional factors; therefore, even when they are present, they are not taken up.

[27] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī:

Phassādivitakkādimohādidhammā ito aññehipi citte hi yuttā hontīti nate aññehi imassa visesaṃ karonti. Tasmā te idha na gahitāti iminā adhippāyena yaṃ vuttaṃ “kasmā panettha aññesupi phassādīsu sampayuttadhammesu vijjamānesu somanassasahagatādibhāvova vuttoti. Somanassādīnameva asādhāraṇa bhāvatoti. Phassādayohi keci sabbacitta sādhāraṇā keci kusalādi sādhāraṇā. Mohādayoca sabbā kusalasādhāraṇāti na tehi sakkā cittaṃ visesetu”nti. Taṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

With the intention that 'Since factors such as contact, initial application, and delusion are associated with other consciousnesses apart from this one, they do not create a distinction for this one from others; therefore they are not taken up here,' it was said: 'Why, when other associated factors such as contact are also present here, is only the state of being accompanied by joy, etc., mentioned? Because joy and the like are uncommon. For some factors like contact are common to all consciousnesses, some are common to wholesome states, etc. And factors like delusion are common to all unwholesome states. Thus it is not possible to distinguish the consciousness by them.' This should be investigated.

Evañhi sati somanassupekkhā saṅkhārāpi aññesu dissantīti tepi aññehi imassa visesaṃ nakaronti. Tasmā tepi idha nagahetabbā siyunti.

For if this were so, since joy, equanimity, and prompting are also seen in other consciousnesses, they too do not create a distinction for this one from others. Therefore, they too should not be taken up here.

24. Etthaca somanassappaṭisandhikatā, agambhīrappakatitā, iṭṭhārammaṇasamāyogo, byasanamuttica somanassassa kāraṇaṃ. Somanassappaṭisandhikohi sadā bhavaṅgasomanassena paribhāvita santāno hotīti tassa cittaṃ uppajjamānaṃ yebhuyyena somanassasahagataṃ uppajjatīti. Agambhīrappakatikoca hīnajjhāsayo appakaṃpi mahantaṃ maññati. Hīnaṃpi paṇītaṃ maññati. Tasmā tassapi cittaṃ uppajjamānaṃ yebhuyyena somanassasahagataṃ hotīti. Iṭṭhārammaṇasamāyogoti attanā icchitena hīnenavā paṇītenavā ārammaṇena samāyogo. Byasanamuttīti ñātibyasanādito mutti. Upekkhāpaṭisandhikatā, gambhīrappakatitā, majjhattārammaṇasamāyogo, [M 0.0035] byasanamuttica upekkhāya kāraṇaṃ. Etthaca gambhīrappakabhitānāma mahajjhāsayatā. Tādiso hi puggalo mahantaṃpi appakaṃ maññati, paṇītaṃpi hīnaṃ maññatīti. Diṭṭhajjhāsayatā, diṭṭhivipannapuggalasevanā, saddhammavimukhatā, micchāvitakkabahulatā, ayoniso ummujjanañca diṭṭhiyā kāraṇaṃ. Tattha diṭṭhajjhāsayatāti kāṇāriṭṭhassaviya sunakkhattassaviyaca purimabhave diṭṭhi gatikabhāvena āgatattā imasmiṃ bhavepi sassatucchedāsaya bhāvo. Saddhammavimukhatāti ciraṃpi kālaṃ saddhammena vinā āgatatā. Micchāvitakkabahulatāti attano avisayesu sabbaññuvisayesu ṭhānesu attano pamāṇaṃ ajānitvā cintāpasutavasena micchāvitakkabahulabhāvo. Ayoniso ummujjananti attanādiṭṭhakāraṇameva sārato saccato ummujjanaṃ. Tabbiparītena diṭṭhivippayuttakāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Asaṅkhārikakammajanitappaṭisandhi katā, kallakāya cittatā, khanti bahulatā, purisakāresu diṭṭhānisaṃsatā, kammappasutatā, utubhojanādi sappāya lābhoti idaṃ asaṅkhārikakāraṇaṃ. Tattha khantibahulatāti sītuṇhādīnaṃ khamanabahulatā. Purisakāresūti purisehi kattabbesu kammesu. Kammappasutabhāti kammesu ciṇṇavasitā. Tabbiparī tena sasaṅkhārikakāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Imesaṃpana cittānaṃ uppatti vidhānaṃ visuddhimagge gahetabbaṃ. Aṭṭhapīti pisaddena nesaṃ labbhamānakammapathabhedato kāla santānā rammaṇādi bhedatoca anekavidhattaṃ sampiṇḍetīti.

24. Here, rebirth-linking with joy, a shallow nature, association with desirable objects, and release from misfortune are causes for joy. For one with a joyful rebirth-linking, whose mental continuum is always imbued with joy in the life-continuum, the mind that arises, arises for the most part accompanied by joy. One of a shallow nature is a person with inferior inclinations who considers a little to be much and the inferior to be excellent. Therefore, for such a person too, the mind that arises, arises for the most part accompanied by joy. Association with desirable objects is association with an object, whether inferior or excellent, that one desires. Release from misfortune is freedom from the loss of relatives and so on. Rebirth-linking with equanimity, a profound nature, association with neutral objects, and release from misfortune are causes for equanimity. Here, a profound nature means having great inclinations. Such a person considers much to be little and the excellent to be inferior. An inclination for views, associating with persons whose view is defective, aversion to the good Dhamma, abundance of wrong thoughts, and unwise emergence are causes for view. Here, an inclination for views means that, as with Kāṇāriṭṭha and Sunakkhatta, because view had become their destiny in a previous existence, in this existence too there is an inclination to eternalism and annihilationism. Aversion to the good Dhamma means having been without the good Dhamma for a long time. Abundance of wrong thoughts means being frequently engaged in wrong thoughts by being intent on one's own thinking, not knowing one's own measure in matters that are beyond one's scope, matters within the scope of the All-Knowing One. Unwise emergence is emerging into a conclusion that a reason seen by oneself is the essence, is the truth. The cause for being dissociated from view should be understood as the opposite of this. Rebirth-linking generated by unprompted kamma, a sound body and mind, abundance of patience, seeing the benefits in human endeavor, being intent on action, and obtaining suitable conditions such as climate and food—this is the cause for the unprompted. Here, abundance of patience is great endurance of cold, heat, and so on. In human endeavor means in actions to be done by humans. Being intent on action is mastery over actions through practice. The cause for the prompted should be understood as the opposite of this. The mode of arising of these consciousnesses should be grasped from the Visuddhimagga. The particle 'pi' together with 'eight' serves to summarize their manifoldness, which is due to differences in their obtainable paths of kamma, and differences of time, continuity, object, and so on.

Lobhamūlacittassa paramatthadipanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the exposition of the ultimate meaning of consciousness rooted in greed.

25. Dosamūlacitte duṭṭhumanobhi dummano. Virūpaṃ cittaṃ. Duṭṭhumano etassātivā dummano. Virūpacittasamaṅgīpuggalo. Dummanassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Mānasikadukkhavedanāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sā hi attanā sahagate cittevā taṃ samaṅgīpuggalevā dummanā bhidhānassavā ayaṃ so dummanoti dummanabuddhiyāvā pavattinimittaṃ hotīti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Domanassena saha gatanti samāso. Paṭihaññatīti paṭigho. Doso. Sohi uppajjamāno [M 0.0036] sampayuttadhammepi paṭihanati. Lūkhe santatte karoti. Attano vatthumpi paṭihanati. Hadayappadesaṃ dahati. Taṃ puggalaṃ dummukhaṃ karoti, attano ārammaṇaṃpi paṭihanati. Taṃ bādhaya māno gaṇhāti. Tasmā paṭighoti vuccatīti.

25. In the analysis of consciousness rooted in hatred: one with a corrupted mind is sad-minded (`dummano`). The consciousness is distorted. One who has a bad mind is `dummano`; this is a person endowed with a distorted consciousness. The state of being sad-minded is displeasure (`domanassaṃ`). This is a designation for mental painful feeling. For that feeling becomes a condition for the arising of the mind associated with it, for the person endowed with it, for the designation 'sad-minded,' or for the notion 'this is a sad-minded person.' The rest is as was stated above. 'Accompanied by displeasure' is a compound. 'It strikes against,' thus it is 'aversion' (`paṭigho`). This is hatred (`doso`). For when it arises, it strikes against even the associated states, making them coarse and burning. It also strikes against its own physical base; it burns the heart region. It makes that person grim-faced. It also strikes against its own object, grasping it while causing affliction. Therefore it is called 'aversion.'

26. Ettha siyā. Saṅkhāro tāva imassa cittassa bheda karoti tassa idha gahaṇaṃ yuttaṃ. Vedanā paṭighāpana bhedakarā na hontīti te idha na gahetabbāti. Vuccate, domanassaggahaṇaṃ tāva imassa cittassa kadāci aññavedanāyogatā pasaṅganivattanatthanti. Yadāhi rājāno hasamānāyeva coravadhaṃ pesenti. Yadāca janā attano verīnaṃ maraṇe tuṭṭhiṃ pavedenti. Maraṇaṃ abhinandanti. Yadāca bālajanā hasamānāva migapakkhino mārenti. Tadā idaṃ nukho somanassena yuttanti attheva pasaṅgo. Upekkhāyogepana vattabbameva natthi. Tappasaṅganivattanatthaṃ domanassaggahaṇanti. Paṭighaggahaṇaṃpi aññadhammasampayuttatā pasaṅganivattanatthaṃ. Tathāhi ye natthikāhetukā kiriyamicchā diṭṭhikā pāṇavadhe apuññaṃnāma natthīti gaṇhanti. Yeca manussapāṇa vadheeva apuññaṃ hoti, tiracchānagatapāṇavadhe apuññaṃ natthīti gaṇhanti. Yeca pāṇavadhaṃ katvā yaññaṃ yajantānaṃ mahantaṃ puññaṃ hoti, dibbasaṃvattanikanti gaṇhanti. Te sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā vissaṭṭhā pāṇavadhaṃ sayaṃvā karonti. Aññevā pesenti. Tadā idaṃ diṭṭhiyāpi sampayuttaṃ siyāti pasaṅgo hotiyeva. Yepana sammādiṭṭhikesu bālā abyattā, te kadāci tesaṃ micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ laddhiṃ gahetvā pāṇaṃ vadhantā ādito vematikajātāva honti. Tadātesaṃ idaṃ vicikicchāyapi yuttaṃ siyāti pasaṅgo hoti. Tappasaṅga nivattanatthaṃ paṭighaggahaṇanti. Itarathā purima cittassa lobhasahagatabhāvoviya imassa paṭighasampayuttabhāvo cūḷanigameneva siddhoti tesaṃ gahaṇaṃ niratthakaṃ siyāti. Etthaca issāmacchariyakukkuccānaṃ thinamiddhassaca aggahaṇaṃ purimacitte mānathinamiddhanayena veditabbaṃ. Ayamettha paramatthadīpanā.

26. Here it might be said: 'Volitional formation makes a distinction in this consciousness, so its inclusion here is proper. But feeling and aversion do not make a distinction, so they should not be included here.' To this it is said: The inclusion of 'displeasure' is for the purpose of warding off the unwanted consequence that this consciousness might sometimes be connected with another feeling. For when kings order the execution of thieves while laughing, and when people express delight at the death of their enemies and rejoice in their death, and when foolish people kill beasts and birds while laughing, the unwanted consequence arises that this consciousness might be conjoined with joy. Regarding its connection with equanimity, there is nothing to be said. The inclusion of 'displeasure' is to ward off that unwanted consequence. The inclusion of 'aversion' is also for the purpose of warding off the unwanted consequence of its being associated with other mental states. For those who hold the nihilist view, the view of causelessness, or the view of non-action maintain that there is no demerit in killing living beings. And some maintain that there is demerit only in killing human beings, but no demerit in killing animals. And some maintain that for those who perform a sacrifice after killing a living being, there is great merit, which leads to a heavenly existence. Released from restraint by identity view, they kill living beings themselves or have others do so. Then the unwanted consequence arises that this consciousness might be associated with view. Further, among those with right view, there are foolish and incompetent people who sometimes adopt the doctrine of those with wrong view and kill a living being, being doubtful from the start. Then the unwanted consequence arises that for them this consciousness might be conjoined with doubt. The inclusion of 'aversion' is to ward off that unwanted consequence. Otherwise, just as the previous consciousness's state of being accompanied by greed is established by the minor corollary, so this consciousness's state of being associated with aversion would be established. Thus their inclusion would be meaningless. Here, the non-inclusion of envy, stinginess, and remorse, and of sloth and torpor, should be understood in the same way as the non-inclusion of conceit and sloth and torpor in the previous consciousness. This is the exposition of the ultimate meaning here.

[28] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana mahāṭīkāyañca

[28] But in the Vibhāvanī and in the Great Subcommentary,

“Asādhāraṇa [M 0.0037] dhammavasena cittassa upalakkhaṇatthaṃ domanassaggahaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha asādhāraṇadhammavasenāti idaṃ tāva nayujjati.

it is said: 'The inclusion of displeasure is for the purpose of characterizing the consciousness by way of its unique quality.' Therein, the phrase 'by way of its unique quality' is not appropriate.

[29] Satipi imassa somanassupekkhāsahagatabhāve anaññasādhāraṇeneva domanassena imassa upalakkhaṇatthanti atthassa āpajjanato. Yathātaṃ satipi purimassa imassaca cittassa mohasahagatabhāve anaññasādhāraṇeneva lobhena paṭighenaca upalakkhaṇatthaṃ lobhasahagatapaṭigha sampayuttaggahaṇanti. Upalakkhaṇatthanti ca na vattabbaṃ.

[29] For the meaning that would follow is: 'Even though this consciousness is sometimes accompanied by joy and equanimity, it is for the purpose of characterizing it by displeasure, which is not shared with any other.' This is just as, even though the previous consciousness and this one are accompanied by delusion, the inclusion of 'accompanied by greed' and 'associated with aversion' is for the purpose of characterizing them by greed and aversion respectively, which are not shared with any other. And it should not be said that it is 'for the purpose of characterizing.'

Evañhi sati pākaṭena domanassena apākaṭānaṃ aññavedanā naṃpi idha laddhabhāvaṃ upalakkhetīti āpajjati. Yathā laddhātapatto rājakumāroti.

For if this were so, it would follow that by the manifest displeasure, one also characterizes the state of obtainment here of other, unmanifest feelings. It is like 'the prince who has obtained the umbrella.'

[30] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

[30] And as to what is said in the Vibhāvanī:

“Paṭighasampayuttabhāvopana ubhinnaṃ ekanta sahacāritā dassanatthaṃ vutto”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

'The state of being associated with aversion, however, is stated to show the invariable concomitance of both.' This too is not good.

Imassa cūḷanigameneva tadatthasiddhitoti.

For that meaning is established for this consciousness by the minor corollary alone.

27. Etthaca dosajjhāsayatā, agambhīrappakatitā, appassukatā, āghātavatthusamāyogovā, aniṭṭhārammaṇasamāyo govā domanassassa paṭighassaca kāraṇaṃ. Tattha dosa bahula bhāvato āgatavasena dosajjhāsayatā daṭṭhabbā. Agambhīrappakatitā hīnajjhāsayatā. Appassutassaca aniṭṭha loka dhammehiphuṭṭhassa taṃkutetthalabbhāti paccavekkhanā natthīti. Imesampi dvinnaṃ uppattividhānaṃ visuddhimagge gahetabbaṃ. Pisaddassa atthopi vuttanayoevāti.

27. Here, an inclination to hatred, a shallow nature, being unlearned, and association with grounds for hatred or with a disagreeable object are causes for displeasure and aversion. Therein, an inclination to hatred should be seen as coming from a predominance of hatred. A shallow nature is an inferior disposition. For an unlearned person, when affected by undesirable worldly conditions, there is no reflection such as: 'How could that be obtained here?' The mode of arising for these two should also be grasped from the Visuddhimagga. The meaning of the word 'pi' is also as has been stated.

Dosamūlacittassa paramatthadipanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the ultimate meaning of consciousness rooted in aversion is concluded.

28. Mohamūlacitte vicikicchuddhaccānaṃ padattho upari āgamissati. Yasmāpana idaṃ cittaṃ mūlantaravirahena laddhokāsena suṭṭhubalavantena mohenaceva saṃsappamānavikkhipamānehi vicikicchuddhaccehi [M 0.0038] ca yuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā idha vedanāpi ārammaṇaṃ adhimattato anubhavituṃ na sakkotīti upekkhāvedanāva yuttā hoti. Evaṃ santepi idaṃ cittaṃ somanassa domanassa sahagatānaṃpi anantare uppajjati. Tasmā tadubhayavedanāhipi idaṃ yuttaṃ siyāti pasaṅgo hotīti tappasaṅganivattanatthaṃ idha upekkhāgahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Anaññacittasādhāraṇena dhammena cittassa niyamanatthaṃ vicikicchāgahaṇaṃ. Uddhaccaṃ pana sabbākusalesu yuttaṃpi idha laddhokāsaṃ hutvā suṭṭhu balavaṃ hotīti dassanatthaṃ idheva gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevahi dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ dhammuddesavāre uddhaccaṃ aññesu pāpacittesu sarūpato anuddharitvā yevāpanakabhāveneva vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ antimacitteeva sarūpato uddhaṭanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmāca idaṃcittadvayaṃ sattānaṃ pakatisabhāvabhūtanti payogena vā upāyena vā kenaci uppādetabbaṃ nāma natthi. Sabbakālampi bhavaṅgacittaṃviya anosakkamānaṃ asaṃsīdamānaṃ akicchena akasirena pavattati. Tasmā ekantena asaṅkhārikameva hotīti katvā idha saṅkhārabhedo na gahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevaca pāḷiyaṃpi purimacittesuviya idha sasaṅkhārenāti dutīyacittavāro navuttoti. Ayamettha paramatthadīpanā.

28. The explanation of the terms 'doubt' and 'restlessness' in the consciousness rooted in delusion will come later. For this consciousness, being without other roots, gains an opportunity and is associated with delusion, which is very powerful, and with doubt and restlessness, which creep and scatter. Therefore, here the feeling is unable to experience the object intensely, so equanimous feeling is appropriate. Even so, this consciousness arises immediately after states accompanied by joy or displeasure. Thus, the contingency arises that it might be associated with both those feelings; to prevent this contingency, equanimity is mentioned here. Doubt is mentioned to define the consciousness by a factor not common to other consciousnesses. But restlessness, though associated with all unwholesome states, is mentioned here to show that, having gained an opportunity, it becomes very powerful here. For that very reason, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in the section on the enumeration of dhammas, restlessness is not extracted in its own right from other evil consciousnesses but is mentioned only by way of inclusion. It should be understood that only in this last consciousness is it extracted in its own right. And since these two types of consciousness are the natural state of beings, they are not something to be produced by any effort, means, or device. Like the life-continuum consciousness, they proceed at all times without receding, without sinking, without trouble, without difficulty. Therefore, it should be understood that because they are exclusively unprompted, the distinction of being prompted is not made here. For that reason, in the Pāli Canon too, unlike in the case of the preceding consciousnesses, a second type of consciousness with the words 'with prompting' is not mentioned here. This is the explanation of the ultimate meaning here.

[31] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[31] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Imāni dve cittāni atisammuḷhatāya aticañcalatāya ca sabbatthapi rajjanadussanarahitāni honti. Tasmā upekkhā sahagatāneva pavattantīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

These two consciousnesses, due to being utterly deluded and excessively fickle, are in every way devoid of lust and aversion. Therefore, it is said that they proceed only accompanied by equanimity. That is not correct.

Rajjana sahitānaṃpi lobhamūla cittānaṃ upekkhā yogassa diṭṭhattāti.

Because a connection with equanimity is seen even in consciousnesses rooted in greed that are accompanied by lust.

[32] Yañca tattha mahāṭīkāyañca

[32] And in the Great Subcommentary:

“Tatoyevaca sabhāvatikkhatāya ussāhetabbatāyaca abhāvato saṅkhārabhedopi nesaṃ natthī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha sabhāvatikkhatāya abhāvatoti iminā imassa asaṅkhārikabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Ussāhetabbatāya abhāvatoti iminā sasaṅkhārikabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Tadubhaye pana [M 0.0039] idaṃ cittadvayaṃ sabbaso saṅkhāravimuttaṃ hotīti dasseti. Taṃ aṭṭhakathāyapi tāva na sameti.

It is said: 'And because of the absence of both natural keenness and the need to be instigated, for them there is no distinction of prompting.' Herein, with 'because of the absence of natural keenness,' he rejects its unprompted nature. With 'because of the absence of the need to be instigated,' he rejects its prompted nature. By both, he shows that these two consciousnesses are entirely free from prompting. This, however, does not agree with the Commentary.

Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅgaaṭṭhakathāyañhi saṅkhārabhedena avijjāya duvidhabhāvova vutto. Yadica idaṃdvayaṃ saṅkhāramuttaṃ siyā. Evaṃ sati idha mohopi saṅkhāramutto siyā. Soca avijjāyevāti tividhabhāvova avijjāya tattha vattabbo. Naca vuttoti. Evaṃ tāva aṭṭhakathāya nasameti.

For in the Commentary on the Analysis of Dependent Origination, a twofold nature of ignorance is stated based on the distinction of prompting. And if this pair were free from prompting, this being so, then delusion here would also be free from prompting. And since that delusion is just ignorance, a threefold nature of ignorance should have been stated there. But it is not stated. Thus, it does not agree with the Commentary.

[33] Yasmāca idha tikkhabhāvonāma vinā saṅkhārena kevalaṃ pakati paccaya gaṇa vaseneva pavattanasamatthatā vuccati. Idañca cittaṃ tatheva pavattati. Tasmā idaṃ sabhāvatikkhaṃ na hotīti na sakkā vattunti.

[33] Because here, 'keenness' is said to be the ability to proceed solely by the power of the set of natural conditions, without prompting. And this consciousness proceeds in just that way. Therefore, it cannot be said that this is not naturally keen.

Laddhokāsena mohena suṭṭhu muyhantīti mohamūhānīti vattabbe niruttanayena momūhānīti vuttaṃ.

Because they are thoroughly bewildered by delusion that has gained an opportunity, they should be called `mohamūhāni`; but by way of etymological method, they are called `momūhāni`.

29. Iccevantiādi mahānigamanaṃ. Tattha iccevanti iti evaṃ. Nipātasamudāyo hesa. Pacchimovā evaṃ saddo purimassa itisaddassa atthavacano. Iccevantivā visuṃ eko nipāto. Sabbathāpi iminā somanassasahagatantiādinā vuttappakāre nāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Idañca dvādasāti ettha visesanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sabbathāpīti dhammasaṅgaṇīyaṃ vuttena pakārenāpi dvādaseva. Vibhaṅge vibhattena pakārenāpi dvādaseva. Dhātukathādīsu vuttena pakārenāpi dvādaseva. Tesu tesu suttantesu vuttena pakārenāpi dvādaseva. Kāladesa santānādi bhedabhinnena pakārenāpi dvādaseva. Kathaṃ dvādasevāti. Iccevaṃ dvādasevāti yojetabbaṃ.

29. `Iccevanti`, etc., is the great conclusion. Herein, `iccevanti` is `iti evaṃ`. This is a collection of particles. Or the latter word `evaṃ` expresses the meaning of the former word `iti`. Or `iccevanti` is a single, separate particle. In any case, the meaning should be understood as 'in the way stated, such as "accompanied by joy," etc.' And this should be understood here as qualifying 'twelve'. In all ways: even in the manner stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, there are just twelve. Even in the manner explained in the Vibhaṅga, there are just twelve. Even in the manner mentioned in the Dhātukathā and so on, there are just twelve. Even in the manner stated in those various Suttas, there are just twelve. Even when distinguished by differences of time, place, personal continuity, etc., there are just twelve. How are there just twelve? It should be connected as: 'Thus, there are just twelve.'

[34] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[34] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Heṭṭhā vutto sampayogādi ākārova vibhāvito. Sopana iccevanti imināva siddhoti.

The mode of association, etc., stated below has been clarified. But that is established just by this word `iccevanti`.

Akusalacittānīti kusalapaṭiviruddhasabhāvattā evaṃ laddhanā māni cittāni. Etthaca ekantena saddhādayoeva kusalānāma. Mohādayoeva akusalā nāma. Cittaṃpana phassādayo viya aññasamānameva [M 0.0040] hoti, na hi ārammaṇa vijānanaṃvā ekantena muyhanādiviya sāvajjaṃvā hoti. Saddahanādiviya anavajjaṃvāti. Taṃpana akusalehi yuttaṃ akusalanti vuccati. Kusalehi yuttaṃ kusalanti. Saddhādīnaṃpana mohādīnañca paṭiviruddhabhāvo yathākkamaṃ pahāyakapahātabbabhāvena veditabbo. Akusaladhammāhi dubbalā honti. Suvaṇṇappaṭirūpakāviya pheggubhūtā abhāvanārahā punappunaṃ āsevīyamānāpi cañcalantiyeva vikkirantiyeva. Niyāmaṃ okkamantāpi ekasmiṃbhave eva apāyabhāgitāya okkamanti. Napana kusalamūlāni sabbaso pacchinditvā satte vaṭṭasotaniyate kātuṃ sakkonti. Kusaladhammāpana balavantā honti. Jātisuvaṇṇāviya sārabhūtā bhāvanārahā punappunaṃ āsevīyamānā thiratarapattā lokiyesu yāva iddhividhānā lokuttaresuca yāva arahattamaggā vuddhiviruḷhīdhammā honti. Niyāmaṃ okkamantā apāyasotaṃvā vaṭṭaso taṃvā sabbaso samucchinditvā anupādisesanibbānabhāgitāya okkamanti. Tasmā kusala dhammāeva pahāyakānāma. Itarepana pahātabbāeva nāmāti veditabbā. Apica kusaladhammānāma antamaso ālopabhikkhā dānamattāpi lokebhesajjavidhānāniviyaakusalappahānāya eva paṇḍitehipaññapīyanti karīyanti ca, tasmā teeva pahāyakā. Akusaladhammāpana loke nānārogajātiyoviya sakalalokassa pakatisabhāvabhūtāeva hontīti te pahātabbāevāti. Samantato anavasesato ādiyiṃsu gaṇhiyiṃsūti samattāni. Apica samattānīti niṭṭhitāni paripuṇṇānivā. Aṭṭhadhātiādisaṅgahagāthā. Lobhomūlaṃ etesanti samāso. Dvādasā kusalā siyunti ettha siyunti nipātapadaṃ idha daṭṭhabbaṃ. Akusala cittāni dvādasa bhavantīti attho.

Unwholesome consciousnesses: These consciousnesses have acquired this name because their nature is opposed to the wholesome. Herein, faith and so on are exclusively wholesome; delusion and so on are exclusively unwholesome. Consciousness, however, like contact and so on, is common to both. For the cognizing of an object is not, like delusion and so on, exclusively blameworthy, nor, like faith and so on, exclusively blameless. But when associated with unwholesome factors it is called 'unwholesome'; when associated with wholesome factors, 'wholesome'. The opposition between faith, etc., and delusion, etc., should be understood respectively in terms of what abandons and what is to be abandoned. Unwholesome states are indeed weak. Like counterfeit gold, they are insubstantial, unworthy of development; even when repeatedly cultivated, they are unstable and scattered. Even when they enter a fixed course, they do so only for a single life with a share in the plane of misery. But they are unable to make beings subject to the stream of the round by completely cutting off the wholesome roots. Wholesome states, however, are powerful. Like pure gold, they are substantial, worthy of development; when repeatedly cultivated, they become very firm. In the mundane sphere, they are states that grow and increase up to the attainment of psychic powers; and in the supramundane, up to the path of Arahantship. When they enter a fixed course, they do so with a share in Nibbāna with no residue remaining by completely cutting off the stream to the plane of misery or the stream of the round. Therefore, wholesome states are what abandon; the others should be known as what are to be abandoned. Moreover, wholesome states, even if only the giving of a morsel of alms, are prescribed and performed by the wise for the abandoning of the unwholesome, like medicines in the world; therefore, they are what abandon. Unwholesome states, however, like the various kinds of diseases in the world, are the natural state of the entire world; thus they are what are to be abandoned. Samattāni: they are concluded, completely taken up without remainder. Or samattāni means finished, completed. The summary verse beginning 'Eightfold, etc.' Lobhamūlaṃ etesanti is a compound. In 'Twelve unwholesome there might be' (Dvādasākusala siyuṃ ti), siyuṃ should be seen here as a particle. The meaning is: 'There are twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.'

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus in the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,

Catutthavaṇṇanāya akusalacittassa

in the fourth chapter's explanation of unwholesome consciousness,

Paramatthadipanā niṭṭhitā.

the Explanation of the Ultimate Meaning is concluded.

31. Evaṃ [M 0.0041] sabbanihīnaṃ akusalaṃ saṅgahetvā idāni ahetukaṃ saṅgaṇhanto tatthaca sabbanihīnaṃ akusalavipākaṃ tāva dassetuṃ upekkhāsahagatantiādimāha.

31. Having thus summarized the unwholesome, which is altogether base, now, summarizing the rootless, and therein, in order to show first the unwholesome resultant consciousness, which is altogether base, he said, 'accompanied by equanimity,' etc.

[35] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[35] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Taṃ akusala vipākattāyeva akusalānantaraṃ pathamaṃ dassitanti adhippāyena yaṃ vuttaṃ “tesaṃ akusalavipākā divasena tividhabhāvepi akusalānantaraṃ akusalavipākeyeva vibhajitu”nti. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

What was said with the intention that 'it is shown first immediately after the unwholesome precisely because it is an unwholesome resultant'—namely, 'Although their unwholesome resultants are threefold by way of division, they should be analyzed as unwholesome resultants immediately after the unwholesome'—that is not correct.

Evañhi sati kusalavipākānipi kusalā nantareeva vattabbāni siyunti.

For if this were so, the wholesome resultants too would have to be stated immediately after the wholesome.

31. Cakkhusotādīnaṃ padattho upari āgamissati. Vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ. Yathāha-vijānāti vijānātīti kho bhikkhave tasmāviññāṇanti vuccatīti. Cakkhuṃ nissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Cakkhunāvā paccayabhūtena janitaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Kammenavā cakkhussa upanītaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Cakkhutovā jātaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ.
