Cakkhussavā indriyabhāvena sāmi bhūtassa viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Cakkhusmiṃvā uppannaṃviññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Esanayo sotaviññāṇādīsupi. Pāḷiyaṃpana mahā taṇhāsaṅkhayasutte –

31. The explanation of the terms 'eye,' 'ear,' etc., will come later. 'It cognizes' (vijānāti), therefore it is consciousness (viññāṇa). As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, it cognizes, it cognizes, therefore it is called consciousness.' Consciousness that depends on the eye is eye-consciousness. Or, consciousness generated by the eye as its condition is eye-consciousness. Or, consciousness led to the eye by kamma is eye-consciousness. Or, consciousness born from the eye is eye-consciousness. Or, consciousness of the eye, which is master in the sense of a faculty, is eye-consciousness. Or, consciousness arisen in the eye is eye-consciousness. This same method applies to ear-consciousness, etc. But in the Pāli Canon, in the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayasutta—

Seyyathāpi bhikkhave kaṭṭhañca paṭicca aggi jalati. Kaṭṭhaggītveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Sakalikañca paṭicca aggi jalati. Sakali kaggītveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tiṇañca paṭicca aggi jalati. Tiṇaggī tveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Gomayañca paṭicca aggi jalati. Gomayaggītveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Thusañca paṭicca aggi jalati. Thusaggītveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Saṅkārañca paṭicca aggi jalati. Saṅkāraggītveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Evamevakho bhikkhave cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpeca uppajjati viññāṇaṃ. Cakkhuviññāṇanteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Sotañca paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati viññāṇaṃ. Sotaviññāṇanteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Ghānañca paṭicca gandheca uppajjati viññāṇaṃ. [M 0.0042] Ghānaviññāṇanteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Jivhañca paṭicca raseca uppajjati viññāṇaṃ. Jivhāviññāṇanteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbeca uppajjati viññāṇaṃ. Kāyaviññāṇanteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Manañca paṭicca dhammeca uppajjati viññāṇaṃ. Mano viññāṇanteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti vuttaṃ.

Bhikkhus, just as a fire burns in dependence on wood, it is reckoned as a wood-fire; when it burns in dependence on splinters, it is reckoned as a splinter-fire; when it burns in dependence on grass, it is reckoned as a grass-fire; when it burns in dependence on cow-dung, it is reckoned as a cow-dung-fire; when it burns in dependence on chaff, it is reckoned as a chaff-fire; when it burns in dependence on rubbish, it is reckoned as a rubbish-fire. So too, bhikkhus, when consciousness arises in dependence on the eye and forms, it is reckoned as eye-consciousness; when consciousness arises in dependence on the ear and sounds, it is reckoned as ear-consciousness; when consciousness arises in dependence on the nose and odors, it is reckoned as nose-consciousness; when consciousness arises in dependence on the tongue and flavors, it is reckoned as tongue-consciousness; when consciousness arises in dependence on the body and tangibles, it is reckoned as body-consciousness; when consciousness arises in dependence on the mind and mind-objects, it is reckoned as mind-consciousness. Thus it is said.

Tathāti iminā upekkhāsahagatanti padaṃ ākaḍḍhati. Dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ. Sampayuttadhamme taṃ samaṅgipuggalaṃvā bādhati hiṃsatīti attho. Duṭṭhuvā khanati kāyikasukhanti dukkhaṃ. Dukkarenavā khamitabbanti dukkhaṃ. Dukkaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etassātivā dukkhaṃ. Kāyikadukkhavedanāyeva nāmaṃ. Suṭṭhu paṭimukhañca icchatīti sampaṭicchanaṃ. Suṭṭhūti amuñcamānaṃ. Paṭimukhanti anaññāpekkhaṃ. Icchatīti kāmeti abhinandati paṭiggaṇhati. Tenevahi bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti ettha sampaṭicchiṃ sūti vaṇṇayiṃsu. Suṭṭhu tīreti tuleti vicāretīti santīraṇaṃ. Ṭīkāyaṃ tīreti niṭṭhāpetīti vuttaṃ. Vibhāvaniyaṃ tīreti vīmaṃsatīti vuttaṃ.

By 'thus,' this draws in the phrase 'accompanied by equanimity.' 'It causes suffering,' thus it is suffering (dukkha). The meaning is that it afflicts or harms the associated states or the person endowed with them. Or, 'it digs out badly' bodily pleasure, thus it is suffering. Or, 'it is endured with difficulty,' thus it is suffering. Or, 'the giving of an opportunity for it is difficult,' thus it is suffering. This is a name for bodily painful feeling itself. 'It desires it well and directly,' thus it is acceptance (sampaṭicchana). 'Well' means not letting go. 'Directly' means without regard for anything else. 'Desires' means longs for, delights in, accepts. Therefore it was said, 'they delighted in it,' which they explained here as 'they accepted it.' 'It investigates well, weighs, considers,' thus it is investigation (santīraṇa). In the Ṭīkā it is said, 'investigates' means 'brings to a conclusion.' In the Vibhāvanī it is said, 'investigates' means 'scrutinizes.'

32. Etthaca cakkhussa asambhinnatā, āloka sannissayappaṭilābho, rūpānaṃ āpātāgamanaṃ, manasikāroti cattāro paccayā cakkhuviññāṇassa uppattikāraṇāni. Sotassa asambhinnatā ākāsasannissayappaṭilābho, saddānaṃ āpātāgamanaṃ manasikāroti sotaviññāṇassa. Ghānassa asambhinnatā, vāsusannissayappaṭilābho, gandhānaṃ āpātāgamanaṃ manasikāroti ghānaviññāṇassa. Jivhāya asambhinnatā āposannissayappaṭilābho. Rasānaṃ āpātāgamanaṃ, manasikāroti jivhāviññāṇassa. Kāyassa asambhinnatā, pathavisannissayappaṭilābho, tiṇṇaṃ phoṭṭhabbānaṃ aññatarassa āpātāgamanaṃ, manasikāroti kāyaviññāṇassāti. Etthaca āloka ākāsādīnaṃ sannissayānaṃ gahaṇaṃ tehi vinā rūpādīnaṃ pasādesu āpātāgamanasseva abhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ, na hi āloke sati rūpāni sannihitānipi cakkhumhi āpātamāgacchanti. Esanayo sesesupīti. Yaṃpana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ -

32. And here, the four conditions that are causes for the arising of eye-consciousness are: the unimpairedness of the eye, the obtaining of the support of light, the arrival of forms in the focal range, and attention. For ear-consciousness: the unimpairedness of the ear, the obtaining of the support of space, the arrival of sounds in the focal range, and attention. For nose-consciousness: the unimpairedness of the nose, the obtaining of the support of air, the arrival of odors in the focal range, and attention. For tongue-consciousness: the unimpairedness of the tongue, the obtaining of the support of the water element, the arrival of flavors in the focal range, and attention. For body-consciousness: the unimpairedness of the body, the obtaining of the support of the earth element, the arrival of one of the three kinds of tangibles in the focal range, and attention. And here it should be understood that the inclusion of the supports of light, space, etc., is because without them there is no arrival of forms, etc., at the sense faculties. For when there is no light, forms, even though present, do not come into the focal range of the eye. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. But as to what is stated in the commentary—

Cakkhusmiṃpana [M 0.0043] asambhinnepi bahiddhārūpārammaṇe āpātaṃ anā gacchante cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nuppajjati. Tasmiṃ pana āpātaṃ āgacchantepi ālokasannissaye asati nuppajjatīti vuttaṃ.

But even when the eye is unimpaired, if an external form-object does not come into the focal range, eye-consciousness does not arise. And even when it does come into the focal range, it is said that if there is no support of light, it does not arise.

Taṃ vinā ālokena viññāṇuppattiyā abhāvadassanaparaṃ. Napana āpākāgamanaṃnāma āloke asatipi sambhavatīti dassanaparanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Itarathā rattandhakārepi rūpāni cakkhumhi āpātaṃ āgacchantīti āpajjatīti. Akusalassa vipākāni akusala vipākāni.

This is meant to show the absence of the arising of consciousness without light. But it should be understood that this is not meant to show that what is called 'arrival at the focal range' can occur even in the absence of light. Otherwise, it would follow that even in the pitch darkness of night, forms come into the focal range of the eye. The results of the unwholesome are unwholesome results.

33. Etthā kenaṭṭhena vipākaṃnāmāti. Vipaccanaṭṭhena. Kiñca vipaccananti. Yathā loke ambaphalādīnaṃ taruṇabhāvaṃ atikkamma pariṇatabhāvappattivipaccananti vuccati. Evamevaṃ idhapi vipaccanaṃ veditabbanti. Ayañca attho catūhi samaṅgītāhi dīpetabbo. Catassohi samaṅgītānāma cetanāsamaṅgitā, kammasamaṅgitā, upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā, vipākasamaṅgitāti. Tattha pubbe taṃ taṃ kammāyūhanakāleyā kusalākusalacetanāya khaṇattayasamaṅgitā. Ayaṃ cetanāsamaṅgītānāma. Sāpana cetanā nirujjhamānā sabbaso abhāvaṃ patvā nanirujjhati. Āyatiṃpana vipākapātubhāvāya attano sabbākāraparipūraṃ kriyāvisesaṃ tasmiṃ cittasantāne nidahitvāva nirujjhati. Soca kriyāviseso yāva okāsaṃ nalabhati. Tāva kappasaṃtasahassaṃpi taṃsantānaṃ anugatoyeva hoti. Yaṃ sandhāya dhammapade –

33. Here, in what sense is it called 'result' (vipāka)? In the sense of ripening. And what is ripening? Just as in the world, the attainment of a mature state by mango fruits and the like, having passed beyond their immature state, is called ripening, so too here should ripening be understood. And this meaning should be explained by way of four endowments. These four endowments are: endowment with volition (cetanā), endowment with kamma, endowment with support (upaṭṭhāna), and endowment with result (vipāka). Therein, formerly, at the time of accumulating this or that kamma, there is the endowment for three moments with wholesome or unwholesome volition. This is called the endowment with volition. But that volition, in ceasing, does not cease by reaching complete non-existence. Rather, it ceases only after having deposited in that mind-continuum a special potency, completely perfected in all aspects, for the future manifestation of the result. And that special potency, for as long as it does not obtain an opportunity, follows that continuum even for a hundred thousand eons. With reference to this, it is said in the Dhammapada:

Na hi pāpaṃ kataṃ kammaṃ, sajjukhīraṃva muccati;

Dahantaṃ bālamanveti, bhasmā channova pāvakoti vuttaṃ.

An evil deed that has been done does not, like fresh milk, curdle at once; smoldering, it follows the fool, like a fire covered by ashes. Thus it is said.

Sopana visuṃ eko paramatthadhammotipi saṅkhyaṃ nagacchati, anusayadhātuyoviyāti. Ayaṃ kammasamaṅgitānāma. Sopana yadā attano anurūpe paccaye labhati. Tadā vipaccanatthāya okāsaṃ karoti. Kathaṃ karotīti. So āsannamaraṇassa sattassa attānaṃvā paccupaṭṭhāpeti. Attano nimittaṃvā paccupaṭṭhāpeti. Gatinimittaṃvā paccupaṭṭhāpeti. Soca satto taṃ amuñcamāno yadi gaṇhāti. [M 0.0044] Tadā okāsaṃ labhati. Ayaṃ upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitānāma. Taṃ amuñcitvā cutassapana cutianantarameva so kammasaṅkhāto kriyā viseso visuṃ eko sasampayutto paramatthadhammarāsi hutvā ekaṃ bhavaṃ pūrayamāno vipaccati, ekaṃ bhavaṃ pūrayamānotica yāva tāyukaṃ bhavaṅgakiccaṃ chasu dvāresu taṃ taṃ dvārikavipākakiccāni pariyosāne cutikiccañca sādhayamānoti attho. Tattha purimā tisso samaṅgītā taruṇā vatthānāma honti. Pacchimā vipākasamaṅgītā pariṇatāvatthānāmāti veditabbā. Iti vipaccantīti vipākāni mudutaruṇāvatthaṃ atikkamitvā pariṇakāvatthasaṅkhātaṃ vipakkabhāvaṃ āpajjantīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Evañca katvā pāḷiyaṃ kusalākusalakammasamuṭṭhānānaṃpi kaṭattārūpānaṃ vipākapade aggahaṇaṃ hotīti. Tānihi kammasantānato visuṃ siddhattā visuṃ kammato jātāniyeva nāma honti, navipakkāni nāmāti. Aññaṃhi arūpadhammānaṃ santānaṃ. Aññaṃ rūpadhammānanti. Ayamettha vipākapade paramatthadīpanā.

And this potency is not reckoned as a separate, single ultimate reality, just like the underlying tendencies. This is called the endowment with kamma. And when this potency obtains suitable conditions, it creates an opportunity for ripening. How does it do so? It presents the kamma itself to a being nearing death, or it presents a sign of the kamma, or it presents a sign of the destination. If that being, not letting go, grasps it, then it gains the opportunity. This is called the endowment with support. For one who has died without letting go of that, immediately after death that special potency called kamma ripens, becoming a distinct, single mass of associated ultimate realities, fulfilling one existence. 'Fulfilling one existence' means accomplishing the function of the life-continuum for the duration of that life-span, the functions of the respective door-resultants at the six doors, and at the end, the function of death. Herein, the first three endowments are called the immature stage; the last, the endowment with result, should be known as the mature stage. Thus, 'they ripen' means the results, having transcended the tender, immature stage, attain the state called ripened, the mature stage; this is the meaning to be understood here. And for this reason, in the Pāli, kamma-born material phenomena are not included under the term 'result.' For these, being established separately from the kamma-continuum, are called 'born from kamma' but not 'ripened.' For the continuum of immaterial phenomena is one thing, and the continuum of material phenomena is another. This is the explanation of the ultimate meaning of the term 'result' here.

Yepana arūpabhāvena sārammaṇabhāvenaca kammena sadisa tāmattaṃ gahetvā arūpadhammānameva vipākattaṃ sādhenti. Tesaṃ vipākasaddo arūpadhammesu ruḷhīvasena pavattoti āpajjatīti. Yañca tattha sālibījanibbattesu nāḷapattapupphaphalesu bījasadisānaṃ phalānameva sāliphalasālipakkanāmaṃ siddhaṃ viyāti upamaṃ dassenti, sāpi nasameti. Na hi phalānipi taruṇakāle pākanāmaṃ labhanti. Naca nāḷapattapupphānipi pariṇatakāle pākanāmaṃ nalabhantīti. Tāni pihi tadā nāḷaṃ pakkaṃ, pattaṃ pakkaṃ, pupphaṃ pakkanti na navuccantīti. Sukhayatīti sukhaṃ, sampayuttadhamme taṃsamaṅgīpuggalaṃvā laddhasātaṃ karotīti attho.

But as for those who, taking just the similarity to kamma in being immaterial and having an object, maintain that only immaterial phenomena are results, for them it would follow that the word 'result' applies to immaterial phenomena only by convention. And the simile they adduce—that among the stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits produced from a rice seed, only the fruits, which are similar to the seed, are established by the names 'rice-fruit' and 'ripened rice'—that too is not fitting. For fruits do not get the name 'ripe' when they are young. And it is not that stalks, leaves, and flowers do not get the name 'ripe' when they are mature. For at that time, are they not called: 'the stalk is ripe,' 'the leaf is ripe,' 'the flower is ripe'? 'It gives happiness,' thus it is happiness (sukha); the meaning is that it makes the associated states or the person endowed with them experience pleasure.

34. Suṭṭhuvā khanati kāyikadukkhaṃ. Sukhenaca khamitabbaṃ. Sukaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etassātivā sukhaṃ. Kusalassa vipākāni sampayutta hetuvirahato ahetukānicāti kusalavipākā hetuka cittāni.

34. Or, it digs out bodily suffering well. And it is to be endured with ease. Or, the giving of an opportunity for it is easy, thus it is happiness. The results of the wholesome are rootless due to the absence of associated roots; thus there are wholesome resultant rootless consciousnesses.

[36] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[36] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Pubbakammasahajātena [M 0.0045] nibbattakahetunāpi idha vipākassa sahetukatāpasaṅgokato. So na sundaro.

Here, the result's state of having a root would be entailed even by the generating cause that is conascent with the previous kamma. That argument is not sound.

Na hi abhidhamme katthaci pubbakammasahajātena nibbattakahetunā vipākassa sahetukāhetukatā sambhavonāma atthi. Asatica sambhave byabhicārassapi abhāvato so pasaṅgo niratthakovāti. Tattha byabhicārassāti pasaṅgassa iccevattho. Etthaca akusalavipākānaṃ sayaṃ abyākatadhammattā lobhādīhi akusalahetūhica sayaṃ akusalavipākattā alobhādīhi anavajjahetūhica sahetukatā sambhavo natthi. Asati ca taṃ sambhave tesaṃ ahetukabhāvo abyabhicāroyeva hotīti tattha ahetukaggahaṇaṃ na kataṃ. Kusalavipākānaṃ pana sayaṃ kusalavipākattāyeva alobhādīhi kusalā byākatayogīhi anavajjahetūhi sahetukatā sambhavo atthiyeva. Satica tasmiṃ sambhave tesaṃ ahetukabhāvo byabhicārasahito hotīti tattheva ahetukaggahaṇaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For nowhere in the Abhidhamma is there any possibility of a resultant being rooted or rootless on account of a productive cause co-nascent with past kamma. Since this is impossible, and there is thus no deviation, that objection is meaningless. Here, 'of the deviation' has the same meaning as 'of the objection.' Furthermore, because unwholesome resultants are themselves indeterminate phenomena and are unwholesome resultants, there is no possibility of their being rooted, either by unwholesome roots such as greed, or by blameless roots such as non-greed. Since this is impossible, their state of being rootless is invariable; therefore, the term 'rootless' is not used there. In the case of wholesome resultants, however, because they are themselves wholesome resultants, there is indeed a possibility of their being rooted by blameless roots such as non-greed, which are wholesome and associated with the indeterminate. Since this is possible, their state of being rootless is subject to deviation; therefore, the term 'rootless' is used precisely there. This should be understood.

35. Cakkhādike pañcadvāre uppannaṃ āvajjanaṃ pañcadvārāvajjanaṃ, tañhi pañcadvāre ghaṭṭitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā āvajjanaṃ uppajjatīti. Bhavaṅgasaṅkhāte manodvāre uppannaṃ āvajjanaṃ manodvārāvajjanaṃ. Tañhi tasmiṃ āpātaṃ āgacchantaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā āvajjantaṃ pavattatīti. Etthaca manodvāranti sakalaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

35. The adverting that arises at the five sense doors, such as the eye, is called five-door-adverting. For it arises by taking as its object that which has impinged upon the five sense doors. The adverting that arises at the mind-door, which is designated as the life-continuum, is called mind-door-adverting. For it occurs by taking as its object that which has come into range and adverting to it. And here, 'mind-door' should be understood as the entire life-continuum consciousness.

[37] Yaṃpana ṭīkāyaṃ

[37] But what is in the sub-commentary:

Tāva “manodvāranti ettha āvajjanassa anantara paccayabhūtaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ manoti vuccati. Tadeva dvāraṃ āvajjanajavanādi thicitta pavattiyā mukhattā”ti vuttaṃ.

It is said: 'Here, in the phrase "mind-door," the life-continuum consciousness that is the proximity condition for adverting is called "mind." That itself is the door, because it is the entrance for the occurrence of process consciousnesses such as adverting and impulsion.'

Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

And in the Vibhāvinī:

“Āvajjanassa anantara paccayabhūtaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ manodvāraṃ, pīthicittānaṃ pavattimukhabhāvato”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃpi na yujjatiyeva.

It is said: 'The life-continuum consciousness, which is the proximity condition for adverting, is the mind-door, because it is the entrance for the occurrence of process consciousnesses.' All of that is indeed incorrect.

Yadihi [M 0.0046] yassa bhavaṅgassa anantaraṃ vīthicittāni pavattanti. Tadeva ekantena tesaṃ pavattimukhattā manodvāraṃnāma hoti. Na tato purimānīti ayamattho siyā. Evañcasati yesu cakkhādīsu rūpā dīnaṃ ghaṭṭitattā āvajjanādīni vīthicittāni pavattanti. Tāneva ekantena tesaṃ pavattimukhattā dvārānināma honti. Na tato aññānīti ayamattho āpajjati. Naca tāni cakkhādīni nāma atthi. Yāni cakkhādīni dvārarūpānināma na hontīti. Sabbametaṃ upari dvāra saṅgahe āvibhavissatīti. Hasanaṃ hasitaṃ. Mukhassa pahaṭṭhākārappavatti. Taṃ uppādeti janetīti hasituppādo. Taṃvā uppādenti khīṇāsavā etenāti hasibhuppādo. Taṃvā uppajjati etenāti hasituppādo. Soeva cittanti samāso. Khīṇāsavānaṃ anoḷārikesu ārammaṇesu yena cittena sitaṃ pātukaronti, tassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Na hi khīṇāsavā lokiya mahā janāviya rajjanīyādi bhāvena oḷārikesu hasaniya vatthūsu hasantīti. Ṭīkāsu pana cittaṃ apekkhitvā hasituppādanti niddiṭṭhaṃ siyāti. Vuttanayena ahetukānica tāni vipaccana vipākuppādana kiccarahitattā taṃ taṃ kriyāmattabhūtāni cittānicāti ahetukakriyacittāni. Etthaca vīthimuttacittāni kiccadubbalattā pañcaviññāṇāni vatthudubbalattā sampaṭicchanādīnica kiccaṭṭhānadubbalattā attano ussāhena vinā kevalaṃ vipaccanamattena pavattantīti tāni sabbāni vipākānieva honti. Yānipana balavakiccattā attano ussāhena pavattanti. Āyatiṃca vipākuppādanatthaṃ ussāhasahitāni honti. Tāni kusalākusalānināma honti. Yāni pana cittāni vipaccanamattaṃ atikkamma attano ussāheneva pavattanti. Tesu āvajjanadvayaṃ vipākasantānato laddhapaccayattā thokaṃ dubbalabhāvato itarānica nirānusayasantāne pavattattā sabbaso vipākuppādanatthaṃ ussāharahitānieva hontīti tāni sabbāni kriyānināma jātānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For if it were the case that only that life-continuum consciousness immediately after which process consciousnesses arise is called the mind-door because it is the entrance for their occurrence, then it would mean that those preceding it are not. And if this were so, it would follow that only those sense faculties, such as the eye, upon which visible forms and so on have impinged, are called doors because they are the entrance for the occurrence of process consciousnesses like adverting, and not others. But there are no such things as 'eye, etc.' that are not also called 'door-materiality.' All this will become clear later in the section on the doors. Laughter (`hasanaṃ`) is smiling (`hasitaṃ`), the occurrence of a pleased expression on the face. That which produces or generates it is the smile-producing consciousness (`hasituppāda`). Or, the Arahants produce it by means of this, thus it is the smile-producing consciousness. Or, it is produced by means of this, thus it is the smile-producing consciousness. This is a compound for 'that very consciousness.' This is the name for that consciousness by which Arahants manifest a smile in regard to subtle objects. For Arahants do not laugh at gross, laughable things in the manner of worldly people, with a state of lust, etc. But in the sub-commentaries, it might be designated as 'smile-producing' with reference to the consciousness. In the way stated, they are rootless and, being devoid of the function of ripening and producing a result, are mere functional states of consciousness; thus they are 'rootless functional consciousnesses.' Here, since process-free consciousnesses are weak in function, the five sense-consciousnesses are weak in base, and the receiving consciousness, etc., are weak in function and station, they arise without their own effort, merely by way of ripening. Thus they are all resultants. But those that arise with their own effort due to strong function, and are accompanied by effort for the purpose of producing a future result, are called wholesome and unwholesome. As for those consciousnesses that, transcending mere ripening, arise only by their own effort: among them, the two advertings, because they have obtained their condition from the resultant continuum, are somewhat weak; and the others (i.e., the functional impulsion of Arahants), because they arise in a continuum free from underlying tendencies, are entirely without the effort to produce a future result. Therefore, they have all become functional. This should be understood.

36. Idāni ādito paṭṭhāya vedanāvicāraṇā vuccati. Tathāhi cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ tāva vatthūnica ārammaṇānica upādārūpāneva [M 0.0047] honti, upādārūpānañca vicupiṇḍakānaṃviya aññamaññasaṅghaṭṭanaṃ dubbalamevāti tāni iṭṭhe aniṭṭheca ārammaṇe upekkhā sahagatāneva hontīti. Kāyaviññāṇassapana ārammaṇāni mahābhūtāni hontīti yathā adhikaraṇimatthake thapitaṃ picupiṇḍakaṃ ayokūṭena paharantānaṃ ayokūṭassa picupiṇḍakaṃ atikkamma akhikaraṇighaṭṭanaṃ balavataraṃ hoti. Tathā tesaṃ ārammabhūtānaṃ kāyavatthuṃ atikkamma kāyanissaya bhūtesu saṅghaṭṭanaṃ balavataraṃ. Tasmā kāyaviññāṇaṃ iṭṭhe sukhasahagataṃ aniṭṭhe dukhasahagataṃ hotīti. Sampaṭicchanacittaṃpana sabbadubbalānaṃ pañcaviññāṇānaṃ anantaraṃ uppajjatīti niccaṃ dubbalaṃ hutvā sabbattha upekkhāsahagatamevāti. Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana asamānanissaye hi tehi laddhapaccayatāvasena ayamattho vibhāvito, santīraṇaṃpana sayaṃpi balavavatthuṃ nissāya pavattati. Tādisenaca balavavatthunissayena purimacittena laddhapaccayaṃ hotīti thokaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ kusalavipākaṃ iṭṭhe upekkhāsahagataṃ abhiiṭṭhe somanassasahagataṃ hoti. Akusalavipākaṃpana aniṭṭhepi abhianiṭṭhepi upekkhāsahagatameva hoti. Kasmā itice. Yadihi taṃ atianiṭṭhārammaṇavasena vedanā bhedayuttaṃ siyā. Dukkhenavā domanassenavā yuttaṃ siyā. Tattha dukkhena tāva na yujjati, kasmā, ekantakāyikattā dukkhassāti. Domanassenapi na yujjati. Kasmā, paṭighena paṭihaññattāeva domanassabhāvaṃ pattā domanassavedanā paṭighena vinā nappavattatīti. Ekantākusalabhūtena paṭighena niccayogino domanassassa abyākatesu asambhavatoti. Āvajjanadvayaṃpana santīraṇatopi thokaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Vipākānañhi pavattituṃpi attano ussāhabalaṃnāma natthi. Balavantehipana kammādipaccayehi jātāni balavantānināma honti. Dubbalehi jātāni dubbalāni nāmāti. Evaṃ santepi taṃ āvajjanadvayaṃ kammānubhāvatoca muccitvā vipākasantānatoca paccayaṃ gahetvā uṭṭhitattā dubbalameva hotīti sadāpi upekkhāsahagatamevāti.

36. Now the investigation of feeling is stated from the beginning. Indeed, the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and so on are merely derived materiality, and the mutual impact of derived materiality is very weak, like that of cotton clumps. Therefore, they are accompanied only by equanimity with both desirable and undesirable objects. But the objects of body-consciousness are the great elements. Just as when one strikes a lump of cotton placed on an anvil with an iron hammer, the impact on the anvil, passing through the cotton, is stronger, so too, the impact of those objects (the great elements) on the elements that are the support for the body-base, passing through the body-base, is stronger. Therefore, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure with a desirable object and by pain with an undesirable one. The receiving consciousness, arising immediately after the five very weak sense-consciousnesses, is always weak and thus is everywhere accompanied only by equanimity. But in the Vibhāvinī this meaning is explained thus: because it has obtained its conditionality from those (sense-consciousnesses) which have a dissimilar support. The investigating consciousness, however, arises depending on a strong base. Because it is conditioned by a preceding consciousness with such a strong base, it is somewhat strong. Therefore, when it is a wholesome resultant, it is accompanied by equanimity with a desirable object and by gladness with a highly desirable one. But when it is an unwholesome resultant, it is accompanied only by equanimity with both undesirable and highly undesirable objects. Why? If it were to be conjoined with a different feeling on account of a highly undesirable object, it would have to be conjoined with either pain or displeasure. It cannot be conjoined with pain, for pain is exclusively bodily. Nor can it be conjoined with displeasure, for the feeling of displeasure, having attained its state by being struck by repugnance, does not arise without repugnance; and since displeasure is invariably conjoined with repugnance, which is exclusively unwholesome, it is impossible in indeterminate states. The two advertings are somewhat stronger than the investigating consciousness. For resultants have no power of their own effort to arise; those born of strong conditions such as kamma are strong, while those born of weak ones are weak. Even so, those two advertings, being free from the influence of kamma and having arisen by taking their condition from the resultant continuum, are weak and thus are always accompanied only by equanimity.

[38] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[38] But in the Vibhāvinī:

Pañcadvārāvajjanaṃ [M 0.0048] pubbe kenaci aggahite ārammaṇe ekavā rameva pavattattā manodvārāvajjanañca visadisacittasantānaparāvattanavasena byāpārantarasāpekkhattā ārammaṇarasaṃ adhimattato anubhavituṃ nasakkotīti sabbatthapi majjhatta vedanāyuttamevāti vuttaṃ. Tattha byāpārantarasāpekkhattāti idaṃ na yujjati.

It is said that because five-door-adverting occurs only once on an object not previously grasped by anything, and because mind-door-adverting, being dependent on another operation—the turning around of a dissimilar continuum of consciousness—cannot experience the flavor of the object intensely, in all cases it is conjoined only with neutral feeling. Here, the phrase 'being dependent on another operation' is incorrect.

Na hi cittānaṃ balavadubbalatāvisesoattanopacchā pavattassa cittassa vasena sakkā vattuṃ. Attanopana paccayehieva so sakkā vattunti. Itarathā santīraṇassapi byāpārantarasāpekkhatā siyā. Taṃpi hi visadisacittasantānaṃ attanāparaṃ vatteti yevāti.

For the specific strength or weakness of a consciousness cannot be explained by way of the consciousness that occurs after it. Rather, it can be explained only by its own conditions. Otherwise, even the investigating consciousness would be dependent on another operation, for it too causes a dissimilar continuum of consciousness to proceed after itself.

37. Imāni cittāni attano pakati paccayagaṇasamāyoge sati nuppajjantīti natthi. Tasmā asaṅkhārikānevāti vadanti. Mūlaṭīkāyaṃ pana vipākuddhāre –

37. It is not the case that these consciousnesses fail to arise when their own natural set of conditions is present. Therefore, they are called 'unprompted.' But in the Mūlaṭīkā, in the exposition on resultants:

Ahetukavipākānaṃ aparibyattakiccattā sasaṅkhārika kamma viruddho asaṅkhārikabhāvopi natthi. Asaṅkhārikakammaviruddho sasaṅkhārikakāvopi natthi. Tasmā tesaṃ ubhayakammenapi uppatti therena anuññātāti vuttaṃ.

Because rootless resultants have an indefinite function, there is no state of being unprompted that is opposed to prompted kamma, nor is there a state of being prompted that is opposed to unprompted kamma. Therefore, it is said that their arising from both kinds of kamma has been allowed by the Elder.

Etena tiṇṇaṃ kriyacittānaṃpi tadubhayabhāvābhāvo vutto hoti. Tānipihi aparibyattakiccāniyevāti. Athavā. Rūpadassa na saddassavanādīni sattā kadāci attano icchāya karonti. Kadāci parehi ussāhitā karontīti paccakkhatova siddhametaṃ. Tattha yadā attano icchāya karonti. Tadā pañcadvārāvajjanādīni sabbāni vīthicittāni asaṅkhārikānināma honti. Yadā parehi ussāhitā karonti. Tadā sasaṅkhārikānināma honti. Dvāra vimuttesupana dvīsu upekkhāsantīraṇesu aṭṭhamahāvipākesuviya vattabbo. Iti sabbāni ahetukacittāni tena pariyāyena saṅkhārabhedena [M 0.0049] paccekaṃ bhinnānieva honti. Evaṃ santepi apari byattakiccattāyeva tesaṃ saṅkhārabhedo pāḷiyaṃ navuttoti veditabbo.

By this, the absence of both states—prompted and unprompted—is also stated for the three functional cittas, for their function is indeed indefinite. Alternatively, that beings sometimes perform actions such as seeing a form and hearing a sound by their own wish, and sometimes perform them when prompted by others, is established by direct experience. Therein, when they act by their own wish, all the process-cittas beginning with five-door adverting are called unprompted. When they act when prompted by others, they are called prompted. But in the case of the two investigating cittas with equanimity, when they are free from the doors, the explanation is like that for the eight great resultant cittas. Thus, all rootless cittas are indeed individually distinct by that method, through the distinction of prompting. Even so, it should be understood that this distinction of prompting for them is not mentioned in the Pāli texts precisely because their function is indefinite.

38. Yasmāpana hetuyonāma mahantadhammā honti. Tasmā te dubbalakammanibbattesu dubbalavatthukiccaṭṭhānesuca imesu cittesu nuppajjanti. Tattha sabbaṃ pāpakammaṃ vikkhepayuttaṃ sayaṃpi cañcalati dubbalaṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ kappaṭṭhitikaṃpi samānaṃ kālantare hetuyuttaṃ vipākaṃ janetuṃ nasakkoti. Tihetukakammaṃpi samānaṃ dubbalesu cakkhādivatthūsuca dassanādīsu kiccaṭṭhānesuca hetuyuttaṃ vipākaṃ janetuṃ nasakkoti. Āvajjanahasanakiccā nica dubbalakiccānieva honti. Tasmā imāni sabbāni sampayuttaheturahitāni jātānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

38. Because roots are indeed great factors, they do not arise in these cittas, which are produced by weak kamma and have their functional basis in weak bases. Herein, all evil kamma is connected with distraction and is itself unsteady and weak. Therefore, even though it may last for an eon, it is unable to produce a result connected with roots at a later time. Even a kamma with three roots is unable to produce a result connected with roots in weak bases such as the eye, etc., and in functional sites such as seeing, etc. The functions of adverting and smiling are indeed weak functions. Therefore, it should be understood that all these have arisen devoid of associated roots.

39. Sabbathāpīti padassa attho heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

39. The meaning of the word 'sabbathāpi' should be understood according to the method explained previously.

[39] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[39] But in the Vibhāvinī:

Sabbathāpīti akusalavipāka kusalavipāka kriyabhede nāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: 'Sabbathāpi' refers to the divisions of unwholesome-resultant, wholesome-resultant, and functional. That is not correct.

Sohi bhedo iccevanti imināva gahitoti. Saṅgahagāthāyaṃ akusalavipākāni vatthukiccabhedena satta, puññapākāni vatthukiccavedanābhedena aṭṭhadhā, kriyacittāni kiccadvārabhedena tīṇīti ahetukacittāni aṭṭhārasa hontīti yojanā. Etthaca puññapākesu vedanābhedopi vattabbo. Itarathā santīraṇassa abhedo siyā. Tathā kriyāsu dvārabhedopi vattabbo. Aññathā āvajjanassa abhedo siyāti. Ṭīkāsupana so na vuttoti.

For that division is already included by the words 'just so.' The connection in the summary verse is as follows: the unwholesome-resultant cittas are seven by division of base and function; the wholesome-resultant cittas are eightfold by division of base, function, and feeling; and the functional cittas are three by division of function and door. Thus there are eighteen rootless cittas. Here, in the case of wholesome-resultants, the division by feeling should also be stated; otherwise, the investigating citta would not be divided. Similarly, in the case of functional cittas, the division by door should also be stated; otherwise, the adverting citta would not be divided. But in the subcommentaries, this is not stated.

Ahetukacittassa paramatthadīpanā.

Exposition of the Ultimate Meaning of the Rootless Cittas.

40. Idāni heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ cittānaṃ asobhaṇanāmaṃ upari vuccamānānañca sobhaṇanāmaṃ thapento gāthamāha. Upari vuccamānānañhi [M 0.0050] sobhaṇatte vutte heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ asobhaṇatā avuttāpi siddhā hotīti. Tattha pāpāhetukamuttānīti pāpehi ahetukehica muttāni ekūnasaṭṭhicittāni. Athavā. Ekanavuticittānipi sobhaṇānīti vuccare vuccantīti yojanā. Tattha pāpehīti akusalehi. Akusalānihi attasamaṅgino satte anicchanteyeva apāyaṃ pāpenti. Tasmā pāpānīti vuccanti. Etena puññānaṃpi sugatipāpanaṭṭhena pāpatā pasaṅgo nivattito hoti. Na hi icchantānaṃ pāpane pāpanabyāpāro pākaṭo hotīti. Lāmakaṭṭhenavā tāniyeva pāpānīti vuccantīti. Sobhaṇehi saddhādiguṇadhammehi yuttiyā tatoyeva ca sayaṃpi sobhaggapattiyā sobhaṇānīti.

40. Now, to establish the name 'unbeautiful' for the cittas mentioned previously and the name 'beautiful' for those to be mentioned later, he states a verse. For when the beautiful nature of those to be mentioned later is stated, the unbeautiful nature of those mentioned previously is established even though unstated. Herein, 'freed from the evil and the rootless' refers to the fifty-nine cittas that are freed from the evil and the rootless. Alternatively, the connection is that the ninety-one cittas are also called 'beautiful.' Here, 'evil' refers to the unwholesome. Unwholesome states lead beings who possess them to the plane of misery even against their wish; therefore they are called 'evil.' By this, the implication that wholesome deeds are also 'evil' because they lead to a happy destination is refuted, for in leading those who wish for it, the act of leading is not manifest. Or, they are called 'evil' simply because of their inferior nature. They are called 'beautiful' because of their association with wholesome qualities such as faith, and because for that very reason they themselves attain a state of beauty.

41. Idāni tāni sobhaṇāni hīna paṇītā nukkamena dassento somanassasahagatantiādimāha. Tattha jānātīti ñāṇaṃ, yāthāvato paṭivijjhatīti attho. Ñāṇena sampayuttaṃ vippayuttanti samāso. Natthi saṅkhāro assāti asaṅkhāro. Saṃvijjati saṅkhāro assāti sasaṅkhāro. Sappurisupanissa yādiko kusaluppattiyā pakatipaccayagaṇo. Sohi yadā duvidhena saṅkhārena vinā kevalaṃ attano balena kusalacittaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tadā asaṅkhāronāma. Soyeva yadā attano balena kusalacittaṃ samuṭṭhāpetuṃ na sakkoti. Saṅkhārasahāyaṃ labhitvāva taṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tadā sasaṅkhāronāma. Asaṅkhārena uppannaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ. Sasaṅkhārena uppannaṃ sasaṅkhārikanti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Etthaca somanassādīnaṃ uppattikāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Apica saddhāsampatti dassanasampatti deyyadhamma paṭiggāhaka sampattīti evamādi somanassakāraṇaṃ, tabbiparītaṃ upekkhākāraṇaṃ. Yānica pītisambojjhaṅgassa upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassaca kāraṇāniaṭṭhakathāsu vuttāni. Tānipi imasmiṃ ṭhāne vattabbānīti. Paññā saṃvattanika kammupanissayatā, abyāpajjalokupapattitā indriyaparipākatā, kilesadūratāca ñāṇuppattiyā kāraṇaṃ. Tihetukapaṭisandhikatā, amohajjhāsayatā, paññavantapuggalasevanā. Sutacintāpasutātipivattuṃ [M 0.0051] yujjati. Yānicadhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa kāraṇāni aṭṭhakathāsu vuttāni. Tānipi idha vattabbāni. Tabbiparītaṃ ñāṇavippayuttakāraṇaṃ. Saṅkhārakāraṇaṃpi pubbe vuttameva. Yānica vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa passaddhisambojjhaṅgassaca kāraṇāni aṭṭhakathāsu vuttāni. Tānipi idha vattabbānīti. Imesaṃpi uppatti vidhānaṃ visuddhimagge gahetabbanti.

41. Now, showing those beautiful states in ascending order from inferior to superior, he begins with 'accompanied by joy,' and so on. Herein, 'it knows,' thus it is knowledge (ñāṇa); the meaning is 'it penetrates in accordance with reality.' 'Associated with knowledge' and 'dissociated from knowledge' is a compound. 'There is no prompting for it,' thus it is unprompted (asaṅkhāra). 'There is prompting for it,' thus it is prompted (sasaṅkhāra). This refers to the natural set of conditions for the arising of a wholesome citta, such as dependence on a good person. When this set of conditions gives rise to a wholesome citta by its own strength alone, without the two kinds of prompting, it is called unprompted. When it cannot give rise to a wholesome citta by its own strength but does so only after obtaining the help of a prompting, it is called prompted. What arises from the unprompted is unprompted (asaṅkhārika); what arises from the prompted is prompted (sasaṅkhārika)—all this has been explained previously. And here, the causes for the arising of joy and so on have also been explained previously. Furthermore, accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in view, and accomplishment in the gift and the recipient—these and similar things are causes for joy; their opposites are causes for equanimity. And the causes for the enlightenment factors of rapture and equanimity stated in the commentaries should also be mentioned in this place. The support of kamma conducive to wisdom, rebirth in a world free from ill will, maturity of the faculties, and distance from the defilements are causes for the arising of wisdom. It is also fit to say: having a three-rooted rebirth-linking, a disposition free from delusion, association with wise persons, and being devoted to learning and reflection. The causes for the enlightenment factor of investigation-of-states stated in the commentaries should also be mentioned here. The opposite of these is the cause for dissociation from knowledge. The cause of prompting has also been stated before. And the causes for the enlightenment factors of energy and tranquility stated in the commentaries should also be mentioned here. The method of their arising should be understood as taken from the Visuddhimagga.

42. Aṭṭhapīti ettha pisaddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena imesaṃ idha vuttappakārato aññehi pakārehi anekavidhataṃ sampiṇḍeti. Tatrāyaṃ nayo. Imāni aṭṭhacittāni dasahi puññakriyāvatthūhi guṇitāni asīti honti. Puna tāni chahi ārammaṇehi guṇitāni cattārisatāniceva asīti ca honti. Puna tāni tīhi kammehi guṇitāni sahassaṃ cattāri satāni cattālīsaṃca honti. Puna tāni tīhi hīnamajjhimapaṇītehi guṇitāni cattāri sahassāni tīṇi satāni vīsatica honti. Tāni imāni suddhikānīti katvā dvīsu ṭhānesu thapetabbāni. Tato ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ gahetvā dvidhā karontassa ñāṇasampayuttāni dvesahassāni sataṃ saṭṭhica honti. Tathā ñāṇavippayuttānīti. Puna tattha ñāṇasampayuttāni catūhi adhipatīhi guṇitāni aṭṭhasahassāni chasatāni cattālīsaṃca honti. Ñāṇavippayuttānipana vīmaṃsāvajjitehi tīhi adhipatīhi guṇitāni chasahassāni cattārisatāni asītica honti. Puna tadubhayāni sampiṇḍitāni dasasahassaṃ pañcasahassāni sataṃ vīsatica honti. Puna tāni pubbe visuṃ thapitehi suddhikehi sampiṇḍitāni dasasahassaṃ navasahassāni cattāri satāni cattālīsañca hontīti. Yaṃpana ṭīkāyaṃ idha vuttanayena suddhikānica ñāṇavippayuttāni ca visuṃ akatvā sabbāni puññakriyādīhi samaṃ guṇitāni sattarasa sahassāni dve satāni asītica hontīti vuttaṃ.

42. Here, in 'aṭṭhapi,' the particle 'pi' has the sense of inclusion. By it, he includes their manifoldness in ways other than the way stated here. The method is as follows: These eight cittas, multiplied by the ten bases of meritorious action, become eighty. Then, multiplied by the six objects, they become four hundred and eighty. Next, multiplied by the three kinds of kamma, they become one thousand four hundred and forty. Further, multiplied by the three grades—inferior, medium, and superior—they become four thousand three hundred and twenty. These are to be taken as 'pure' ones and set aside in two portions. Then, taking one portion and dividing it in two, the ones associated with knowledge become two thousand one hundred and sixty; likewise for the ones dissociated from knowledge. Again, among them, the ones associated with knowledge, multiplied by the four dominants, become eight thousand six hundred and forty. But the ones dissociated from knowledge, multiplied by the three dominants excluding investigation, become six thousand four hundred and eighty. Then, combining both becomes fifteen thousand one hundred and twenty. Further, combining these with the 'pure' ones previously set aside becomes nineteen thousand four hundred and forty. However, it is stated in the subcommentary that without separating the 'pure' ones and the ones dissociated from knowledge, and multiplying all equally by the bases of meritorious action, etc., they become seventeen thousand two hundred and eighty.

[40] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

[40] And the point for clarification:

Suddhikāni [M 0.0052] visuṃ akatvā ñāṇavippayuttānieva visuṃ katvā tathā guṇitāni vīsa satādhika pannarasa sahassāni hontīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ na yuttaṃ.

It is stated that without separating the 'pure' ones, but separating only those dissociated from knowledge, and thus multiplying them, they become fifteen thousand two hundred. All that is not correct.

Evañhi sati imāni kāmāvacarakusalāni niccaṃ sādhipatikāni hutvā niyatādhipatikānināma bhaveyyuṃ. Naca imāni upari mahaggata kusalāni viya lokuttarāni viya ca niyatā dhipatikāni hontīti. Ṭīkānayenapana ñāṇavippayuttānipi vīmaṃsāsahagatānīti āpajjatīti. Yathāvā kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena kusalātiettha ñāṇavippayuttānipi kosallena nānāvajjanavīthiyaṃ pavattena upanissayañāṇena sambhūtattā kusalāni eva nāma honti. Evamidhapi tāni teneva vīmaṃsādhipatibhūtena sambhūtattā vīmaṃsādhipateyyānipi nāma hontīti na nasakkā vattunti iminā adhippāyena tāni visuṃ akatāni siyunti. Evaṃsantepi kāmakusalānināma adhipativimuttāni eva bahutarāni honti. Tasmā nasakkā sabbāni kāmakusalāni vīmaṃsādhipatimūlikāni bhavitunti.

For if this were so, these sense-sphere wholesome states would always have a predominant influence and would be called 'invariably predominated.' But these are not invariably predominated like the lofty wholesome states above or the supramundane states. According to the method of the subcommentary, however, it would follow that even states dissociated from knowledge are accompanied by investigation. Just as, in the sense of 'arisen from skill,' even states dissociated from knowledge are called wholesome because they have arisen from skill—that is, from the support-knowledge that occurs in the various cognitive processes of adverting—so too here, because they have arisen from that very investigation which has become a predominant influence, they might also be called 'predominated by investigation.' It is not possible to say this is not so. It may be that with this intention they were not treated separately. Even so, most sense-sphere wholesome states are actually free from predominance. Therefore, it is not possible for all sense-sphere wholesome states to be rooted in investigation as a predominant factor.

43. Kāmāvacarānica tāni kusalāni cittānicāti viggaho. Tattha kenaṭṭhena kusalānīti. Ārogyaṭṭhena, sundaraṭṭhena, chekaṭṭhena, anavajjaṭṭena, sukhavipākaṭṭhenacāti. Rāgādayohi dhammā cittasantānassa rujjanaṭṭhena rogānāma. Ahitaṭṭhena asundarā nāma. Anipuṇaṭṭhena achekānāma. Gārayhaṭṭhena vajjānāma. Aniṭṭha vipākaṭṭhena dukkhavipākānāma honti. Imānipana tehi vuṭṭhitattā kusalānināma arogāni nāmāti attho. Tappaṭipakkhattāca sundarāni chekāni anavajjāni sukhavipākāni ca nāma hontīti. Kucchite pāpadhamme salayanti cālenti kampenti viddhaṃsentīti kusalāni. Kucchitenavā ākārena sattasantāne senti anusentīti kusā. Rāgādayo. Te lunanti chindantīti kusalāni. Kusaṃvā vuccati ñāṇaṃ kucchitānaṃ sānaṭṭhena tanukaraṇaṭṭhena antakaraṇaṭṭhenavā. Kusena lātabbānīti kusalāni. Kusāviya [M 0.0053] hatthappadesaṃ saṃkilesapakkhaṃ lunantītivā kusalāni. Apica, kucchite pāpadhamme saranti hiṃsantīti kusalāni. Rakārassa lakāro. Kosallasambhūtaṭṭhenavā kusalānīti.

43. The analysis is: 'They are sense-sphere and they are wholesome consciousnesses.' Herein, in what sense are they wholesome? In the sense of health, beauty, skillfulness, blamelessness, and yielding a pleasant result. For states such as lust are called 'diseases' in the sense that they cause affliction to the mental continuity; 'ugly' in the sense that they are unbeneficial; 'unskillful' in the sense that they are not clever; 'blameworthy' in the sense that they are reprehensible; and 'yielding painful results' in the sense that they have undesirable results. But since these have arisen beyond them, they are called wholesome, meaning they are called 'healthy.' And because they are their opposites, they are called beautiful, skillful, blameless, and yielding pleasant results. They shake, stir, agitate, and demolish vile, evil states, thus they are 'wholesome' (kusalāni). Or, 'kusā' are those things that lie and lie dormant in the continuity of beings in a vile manner—lust and so on. These states 'cut' (lunanti) them, thus they are 'wholesome' (kusalāni). Or, knowledge is called 'kusa' because it makes vile things fall away, or because it attenuates and destroys them. They are to be obtained by that 'kusa' (knowledge), thus they are 'wholesome' (kusalāni). Or, like kusa grass, they cut the part of defilements that is within reach of the hand, thus they are 'wholesome' (kusalāni). Moreover, they go against and destroy vile, evil states, thus they are 'wholesome' (kusalāni); the 'r' (in saranti) becomes 'l'. Or, they are 'wholesome' in the sense of being arisen from skill.

44. Mahāvipākesu padatthato vattabbaṃ natthi. Vedanābhedo ārammaṇavasena vattabbo. Tānihi atiiṭṭhe iṭṭhamajjhatte ca ārammaṇe yathākkamaṃ somanassena upekkhāya ca yuttānīti. Sampayogabhedo kammavasena javanavasenaca vattabbo. Tānihi balavakammena janitāni ñāṇasampayuttāni honti. Dubbalakammena janitāni ñāṇavippayuttāni. Kadācipana tadārammaṇavasena pavattikāle yebhuyyena tihetukajavanānubandhāni ñāṇasampayuttāni honti. Itarajavanānubandhāni ñāṇavippayuttānīti. Saṅkhārabhedopi kehici ācariyehi kammavaseneva kathito. Asaṅkhārikakammajanitāni asaṅkhārikāni. Sasaṅkhārikakammajanitāni sasaṅkhārikānīti. Saṅgahakārenapana sannihitapaccayavasena vutto. Tānihi paṭisandhiyaṃ purimabhave maraṇāsannakāle ñātakādīhi tena tena payogena upaṭṭhāpitāni kammādīni ārammaṇāni gahetvā pavattāni sasaṅkhārikānināma honti. Tādisena payogena vinā sayameva kammabalena upaṭṭhitāni gahetvā pavattāni asaṅkhārikānināma honti. Tadārammaṇa kālepana asaṅkhārikajavanānubandhāni asaṅkhārikānināma. Sasaṅkhārika javanānubandhāni sasaṅkhārikāni nāmāti. Etthapi sampiṇḍanattho visaddo. Tena ārammaṇachakka hīnattikavaseneva kāladesa santānādivasenaca tesaṃ anekabhedattaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Yasmā panetāni dānādivasena kāyakammādivasena chandādīni dhuraṃ katvā ca na pavattanti. Tasmā tāni puññakriyāvatthūnaṃ kammādhipatīnañca vasena vaḍḍhanaṃ nalabhantīti.

44. Regarding the great resultants, there is nothing to be said from the standpoint of the term's meaning. The distinction of feeling should be explained by way of the object. For when the object is extremely desirable or moderately desirable, they are respectively associated with joy and equanimity. The distinction of association should be explained by way of kamma and by way of impulsion. For those generated by strong kamma are associated with knowledge, while those generated by weak kamma are dissociated from knowledge. But sometimes, at the time of their occurrence by way of retention, they are for the most part associated with knowledge when they follow a three-rooted impulsion; when they follow other impulsions, they are dissociated from knowledge. The distinction of prompting has also been explained by some teachers solely by way of kamma: those generated by unprompted kamma are unprompted; those generated by prompted kamma are prompted. The author of the Compendium, however, has explained it by way of the proximate condition. For at the time of rebirth-linking, those that occurred at the death-proximate moment in the previous existence, having taken as object kamma, etc., presented by relatives and others through some kind of effort, are called 'prompted.' Those that occurred having taken as object what was presented by the power of kamma itself, without such an effort, are called 'unprompted.' At the time of retention, those that follow an unprompted impulsion are called 'unprompted'; those that follow a prompted impulsion are called 'prompted.' Here too, the word 'vi' has the sense of summarizing, by which he groups their many distinctions by way of the sixfold classification of objects, the inferior triad, and the divisions of time, place, continuity, etc. But since these do not occur by way of giving, etc., by way of bodily action, etc., nor by making zeal, etc., the main factor, they therefore do not obtain increase by way of the grounds of meritorious action and the predominance of kamma.

[41] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[41] But the point for clarification is:

Imāni viññattisamuṭṭhāpanābhāvato kammadvāra vasena na pavattanti. Avipākasabhāvatoca kammavasena napavattantīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

Because they do not give rise to intimation, they do not occur through the doors of kamma. And it is said that because of their non-result-producing nature, they do not occur as kamma. This should be investigated.

Heṭṭhāhi kusalesu kammattikavaseneva vaḍḍhanaṃ vuttaṃ. Napana visuṃ kammadvāravasena. Kammattikañcanāma tividha kammadvāra vaseneva siddhanti. Nanu aṭṭhakathāyaṃ yohi kāmāvacarakusalesu kammadvāra kammapatha puññakriyāvatthubhedo vutto. So idha natthi. Kasmā. Aviññattijanakato avipāka dhammato tathā appavattiyācāti vuttanti. Saccaṃ. Tattha pana aviññattijanakato kammadvāra bhedo idha natthīti etena kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammanti evaṃ bhedassa abhāvaṃ vadati. Avipākadhammato kammapathabhedo idha natthīti etena dasavidhassa kammapathabhedassa abhāvaṃ vadati. Idhapana kusalesupi kammapathabhedaṃ aggahetvā tividhakammadvāra bhedabhinnaṃ kammattikameva gahitaṃ. Tañca viññatti samuṭṭhāpanā bhāvato tividhakammadvāravasena napavattantīti imināva siddhaṃ. Yadica heṭṭhā kusalesupi dasavidhakammapathabhedavasena visuṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ vuttaṃ siyā. Evaṃsati idhapi avipākasabhāvato kammapathavasena napavattantīti idaṃ vattabbamevāti.

For below, in the section on wholesome states, the elaboration was stated only by way of the triad of kamma, not separately by way of the doors of kamma. And the triad of kamma is established precisely by way of the threefold door of kamma. But is it not so that in the commentary, in the case of sense-sphere wholesome states, the division into doors of kamma, courses of kamma, and grounds of meritorious action was stated? That is not found here. Why? Because it is said that this is due to their not generating intimation, their being non-resultant phenomena, and their not occurring in that manner. True. But here, when it is said, 'the division by doors of kamma is not found here because they do not generate intimation,' this speaks of the absence of the division into bodily kamma, verbal kamma, and mental kamma. When it is said, 'the division by courses of kamma is not found here because they are non-resultant phenomena,' this speaks of the absence of the tenfold division of the courses of kamma. Here, however, even in the wholesome states, without taking the division of the courses of kamma, only the triad of kamma, distinguished by the threefold division of the doors of kamma, was taken. And that they do not occur by way of the threefold doors of kamma because they do not give rise to intimation is established by this very fact. And if below, even in the wholesome states, the elaboration had been stated separately by way of the tenfold division of the courses of kamma, then in that case, here too it should indeed be said that they do not occur by way of the courses of kamma because they have the nature of non-resultants.

45. Mahākriyacittesupi mahāvipākesuviya ārammaṇa vaseneva vedenābhedo upari sayameva vakkhati. Ñāṇasampayutta, vippayutta, asaṅkhārika, sasaṅkhārikabhedopana yathārahaṃ kusalesu vuttanayena veditabbo.

45. In the great functional consciousnesses, too, just as in the great resultants, the distinction of feeling is solely by way of the object, as will be explained below. But the divisions into associated with knowledge, dissociated from knowledge, unprompted, and prompted should be understood as appropriate according to the method stated for the wholesome states.

[42] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[42] But it should be explained:

Tathā avicāretvā kriyacittānaṃpi kusale vuttanayena yathārahaṃ somanassa sahagatāditā veditabbāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

It has been said that, without investigating thus, the states 'accompanied by joy,' etc., of the functional consciousnesses should also be understood as appropriate according to the method stated for the wholesome. That is not correct.

Iccevaṃ sabbathāpīti padānaṃ attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Sahetuka kāmāvacara kusala vipāka kriya cittānīti ettha sahetu kaggahaṇaṃ kusala sadda sambandhe bhūtakathana visesanaṃ. Tenevahi taṃ kusalacittānaṃ cūḷanigamena gahitaṃ. Vipāka kriya saddasambandhepana byavacchedakavisesanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The meaning of the words 'Thus in every way' has already been stated below. In the phrase 'rooted sense-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses,' the inclusion of 'rooted' is a descriptive qualifier in connection with the word 'wholesome.' For that reason it was included in the minor conclusion on wholesome consciousnesses. But in connection with the words 'resultant' and 'functional,' it should be seen as a restrictive qualifier.

[43] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[43] But it should be clarified:

Sakkharakathalikaṃpi [M 0.0055] macchagumbaṃpi tiṭṭhantaṃpi carantaṃpi passatīti suttapade viya idha yathālābha yojanāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sameti. Tatthahi sakkharakathalikaṃnāma nacaratīti yuttaṃ. Idhapana kusalaṃ sahetukaṃ nahotīti nayuttametanti.

It has been said that here, as in the Sutta passage, 'He sees a heap of gravel or a school of fish, whether stationary or moving,' the application should be made as is available. That does not fit. For there, it is fitting that a heap of gravel does not move. But here, it is not fitting that a wholesome state is not rooted.

46. Saṅgahagāthāyaṃ vedanā ñāṇa saṅkhāra bhedenāti vedanābhedena, ñāṇabhedena, saṅkhārabhedenaca. Tattha vedanā bhedenāti vedanābhedasiddhena cittabhedena, ñāṇabhedenāti ñāṇayogā yogasiddhenacittabhedena. Saṅkhārabhedenāti saṅkhārena vinā sahaca pavattapaccayagaṇabhedasiddhena cittabhedenāti attho. Idañhi samāsapadānaṃ sāmatthiyaṃ, yadidaṃ suviññātānaṃ nānāppakārānaṃ padatthānaṃ appakena byañjanena dīpanasamatthatāti.

46. In the summary verse, 'by the division of feeling, knowledge, and prompting' means by the division of feeling, by the division of knowledge, and by the division of prompting. Herein, 'by the division of feeling' means by the division of consciousness established through the division of feeling. 'By the division of knowledge' means by the division of consciousness established through the presence or absence of knowledge. 'By the division of prompting' means by the division of consciousness established through the division of the group of conditioning factors that occur either with or without prompting—this is the meaning. For this is the power of compound words: the ability to illuminate, with few syllables, the various kinds of word-meanings for those who understand them well.

[44] Etena vibhāvaniyaṃ

[44] By this it is to be clarified:

Sayaṃ abhinnānaṃ ñāṇasaṅkhārānaṃ bhedavacane cittassa bhedakara bhāve ca codanāya anokāsatā sādhitā hotīti.

Thus is demonstrated the lack of opportunity for an objection regarding the statement of the division of knowledge and prompting, which are themselves not distinct, and regarding their being dividers of consciousness.

Tatrāyaṃ yojanā. Sahetu kāmāvacara puññapākakriyā vedanāñāṇasaṅkhārabhedena yathākkamaṃ chaca dvādasaca catuvīsati ca matāti. Etthaca –

Herein, this is the application: Rooted sense-sphere meritorious, resultant, and functional consciousnesses are reckoned as six, twelve, and twenty-four respectively, according to the distinctions of feeling, knowledge, and prompting, in due order. And herein—

Vedanāñāṇasaṅkhāra, bhedenetāni aṭṭhadhā;

Puññapākakriyābhedā, catuvīsatividhā makā tipi.

By the division of feeling, knowledge, and prompting,

these are eightfold;

By the division of meritorious, resultant, and functional,

they are reckoned as twenty-four kinds.

Vattabbā. Evañhi sati atthagatica visadā hoti. Upari vakkha, mānāhica saṅgahagāthāhi saddhiṃ sametīti.

This should be stated. For when this is so, the course of the meaning becomes clear, and it accords with the summary verses to be spoken of below.

47. Kāmetiādi sabbesaṃ kāmacittānaṃ saṅgahagāthā. Tattha kāme kāmabhūmiyaṃ pākāni sahetukāhetukavasena sabbāni vipākacittāni tevīsa. Puññāpuññāni kusalākusalacittānica vīsati. Kriyāca sahetukāhetukavasena sabbāni kriyacittāni [M 0.0056] pana ekādasa honti. Iccevaṃ sabbathāpi catuppaññāsa hontīti yojanā. Sabbathāti cettha visaddo lutta niddiṭṭho. Dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ vuttena sabbappakārenapi catuppaññāsaeva. Vibhaṅge vibhattena sabbappakārenapi catuppaññāsa evātiādinā tassa attho heṭṭhā vuttoyevāti.

47. “In the sense sphere,” etc., is the summary verse for all sense-sphere consciousnesses. Here, `kāme` means in the sense-sphere plane. The resultants (`pākāni`), divided into those with roots and those without roots, are all twenty-three resultant consciousnesses. The meritorious and demeritorious, that is, the wholesome and unwholesome consciousnesses, are twenty. And the functional consciousnesses, divided into those with roots and those without roots, are eleven. Thus, in every way, they are fifty-four: this is the connection. Herein, in the word `sabbathā`, the syllable `vi` is indicated as elided. As stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, in every way they are indeed fifty-four. As analyzed in the Vibhaṅga, in every way they are indeed fifty-four, etc. Its meaning has already been stated below.

[45] Etena vibhāvaniyaṃ

[45] By this it is to be explained:

Idha vuttānaṃ kusalādīnaṃ antogadhabhedavasena tassa atthavibhāvanā paṭisiddhā hoti.

Here, the explanation of the meaning of the wholesome, etc., stated here, by way of divisions included within them, is prohibited.

[46] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

[46] And what is to be explained:

Kāme bhaveti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi vicāretabbaṃ.

“In the sense sphere” and “in existence” are stated. That too should be investigated.

Bhavasaddo hi kusalākusalakammesu kammanibbattesuca vipāka kaṭattārūpesu vattamāno abhidhamme diṭṭho. Na tadaññesu nāmarūpadhammesūthi. Bhūmipariyāyoca idha kāmasaddo. Bhūmītica sahokāso indriyā nindriyabaddhadhammasamūho vuccatīti kāme kāmabhūmiyanti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo. Bhavotivā bhūmieva vuccati suttantapariyāyena bhavanti ettha sattā saṅkhārācāti katvā. Esanayo paratthapīti.

The term 'existence' (`bhava`) is seen in the Abhidhamma as pertaining to wholesome and unwholesome kammas, and to the resultant consciousness and kamma-produced matter born of kamma. It is not seen applied to other phenomena of mentality-materiality. Here, the term 'sense sphere' (`kāma`) is a synonym for 'plane' (`bhūmi`). And 'plane' is said to be the collection of phenomena bound to faculties and not bound to faculties, together with its location. Thus, the meaning of `kāme` as 'in the sense-sphere plane' should be understood. Or, according to the Suttanta method, 'existence' (`bhava`) itself is called 'plane' (`bhūmi`) because beings and formations 'exist' (`bhavanti`) here. This principle applies elsewhere too.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus in the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,

Catutthavaṇṇanāya kāmacittassa

the fourth explanation concerning sense-sphere consciousness,

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

the Paramatthadīpanā is concluded.

48. Evaṃ kāmacittasaṅgahaṃ dassetvā idāni yathānuppattaṃ rūpacittasaṅgahaṃ dassento vitakkavicārapītisukhekaggatāsahitantiādimāha. Vitakkoca vicāroca pītica sukhañca ekaggatācāti dvando. Tāhi sahitanti samāso. Vitakkavicārapītisukhe kaggatā saṅkhātenasamuditenapathamajjhānena sampayuttaṃkusalacittaṃ pathamajjhānakusalacittaṃ. Tattha kenaṭṭhenapathamaṃ, kenaṭṭhenaca jhānanti. Ādito paṭipajjitabbattā pathamaṃ. Kasiṇādikassa ārammaṇassa aniccādilakkhaṇassaca upanijjhāyanato paccanīkadhammānañca jhāpanato dayhanato [M 0.0057] jhānaṃ. Imesu dvīsu atthesu ekaggatāeva sāti sayayuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Sāhi ekattārammaṇasaṅkhāto eko aggokoṭikoṭṭhāsovā assāti atthena ekaggasaṅkhātassa cittassa tathāpavattane ādhipaccaguṇayogena ekaggatāti ca vuccati. Sāyeva cittaṃ nānārammaṇesu vikkhipituṃ adatvā ekasmiṃ yevārammaṇe paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ dūrībhāvena sammāca ādhiyati thapeti. Indriyānañca samabhāvaṃ katvā tattheva līnuddhaccābhāvāpādanena samañca ādhiyati thapetīti atthena samādhītica vuccati. Sāyevaca pāḷiyaṃ avikkhepo avisāhāro saṇṭhiti avaṭṭhitīti niddiṭṭhāti. Vitakkādayopi pana tassā sātisayaṃ upakārakattā jhānanteva vuttā. Tathā hi vitakko tāva cittaṃ thinamiddhavasena osakkituṃ adatvā daḷhaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhameva karoti. Ārammaṇābhiniropana lakkhaṇohi vitakko. Thina middhanīvaraṇassaca ujuppaṭipakkhoti. Vicāroca naṃ vicikicchāvasena saṃsappituṃ adatvā daḷhaṃ ārammaṇānubandhameva karoti. Ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo hi vicāro paññāpakatiko. Vicikicchānīvaraṇassaca ujuppaṭipakkhoti. Pītica cittaṃ byāpādavasena ukkaṇṭhituṃ adatvā ārammaṇe parituṭṭhameva karoti. Ārammaṇasaṃpi yāyanalakkhaṇā hi pīti. Byāpādanīvaraṇassaca ujuppaṭipakkhāti. Tathā sukhañca naṃ uddhacca kukkuccavasena avūpasamituṃ adatvā ārammaṇe laddhasātaṃ upabrūhitaṃ karoti. Sākalakkhaṇañhi sukhaṃ, uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇassaca ujuppaṭipakkhanti.

48. Having thus explained the compendium of sense-sphere consciousness, now, in order to explain the compendium of fine-material sphere consciousness as it comes in sequence, he begins with the words, “accompanied by initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness.” “Initial application and sustained application and joy and happiness and one-pointedness” is a dvandva compound. “Accompanied by these” is a samāsa compound. The wholesome consciousness associated with the first jhāna, which is designated by the collection of initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness, is the first-jhāna wholesome consciousness. Herein, in what sense is it “first,” and in what sense is it “jhāna”? It is “first” because it is to be attained at the beginning. It is “jhāna” because of closely meditating on an object such as a kasiṇa and on characteristics such as impermanence, and because of burning up and consuming the opposing states. In these two meanings, one-pointedness should be seen as especially appropriate. For it is called “one-pointedness” (ekaggatā) because of its quality of predominance in the functioning of the mind that is called “one-pointed” (ekagga), in the sense that it has one (eka) supreme (agga) point (koṭi) or part (koṭṭhāsa), namely, a single object. It is that which, not allowing the mind to be scattered among various objects, properly places and establishes it on a single object by the removal of opposing states. And it is called “concentration” (samādhi) in the sense that, having brought the faculties to a state of balance, it places and establishes them evenly by producing an absence of sinking and restlessness. In the Pāli canon, it is designated as non-distraction, non-wandering, stability, and steadiness. Moreover, initial application and the others are also called “jhāna” because they are especially helpful to it. For initial application, by not allowing the mind to shrink away through sloth and torpor, directs it firmly towards the object. For the characteristic of initial application is the applying of the mind to the object, and it is the direct opposite of the hindrance of sloth and torpor. Sustained application, by not allowing the mind to waver through doubt, keeps it firmly connected with the object. For the characteristic of sustained application is the sustained examination of the object; it is of the nature of wisdom and is the direct opposite of the hindrance of doubt. Joy, by not allowing the mind to become discontented through ill will, makes it thoroughly satisfied with the object. For the characteristic of joy is delighting in the object, and it is the direct opposite of the hindrance of ill will. And happiness, by not allowing the mind to be unsettled through restlessness and worry, enhances its satisfaction with the object, having obtained pleasure. For the characteristic of happiness is gratification, and it is the direct opposite of the hindrance of restlessness and worry.

Upekkhāca santasabhāvattā sukheeva saṅgahitāti. Evaṃ karontāca te dhammā tasmiṃ ārammaṇe tassa cittassa suṭṭhu ekaggabhāvatthāyaca honti. Ekaggabhāvotica ekaggatāyeva. Sāca ekaggatā tehi dhammehi tathā anuggahitā suṭṭhu balavatī hutvā sayaṃ kāmacchandavasena nānārammaṇesu cittavidhāvanaṃ nīvāretvā kasiṇanimittādike tasmiṃ ārammaṇe niccalaṃ ṭhatvā taṃārammaṇaṃ upagantvā nijjhāyati oloketi. Tasmā te sabbepi dhammā upanijjhāyanaṭṭhenapi jhānanti vuttāti. Tesuca tathā pavattamānesu [M 0.0058] tappaccanīkā nīvaraṇadhammā okāsaṃ alabhitvā manasmiṃpi pariyuṭṭhituṃ nasakkonti. Jhāpitānāma honti. Tasmā te paccanīkajjhāpanaṭṭhenapi jhānanti vuttāti. Evaṃ santepi yasmā jhāna magga sambodhisaṅkhātesu tīsu ṭhānesu dhammasāmaggī padhānaṃ hoti. Aṅgānaṃ samaggabhāveeva appanāpattivasena upanijjhāya nādi kiccasaṃsiddhito. Yasmāca ete dhammā vuttanayena visuṃvisuṃ attano kiccaṃ karontāpi cittassa ārammaṇe niccalappavatti saṅkhātaṃ ekameva upanijjhānakiccaṃ sādhenti. Tasmā rathaṅgānaṃ samudāyeeva rathavohāroviya tesaṃ samudāyeeva jhāna vohāro siddhoti veditabbo. Aparepana pañcannaṃpi tesaṃ ārammaṇābhiniropanādīni yathāsakaṃ kiccāniyeva visuṃ visuṃ upanijjhānakiccānināma hontīti paṭṭhāne jhānapaccayaṃ patvā sabbepete visuṃ visuṃ jhānapaccayaṃ sādhentiyeva. Tasmā te visuṃ visuṃpi jhānāniyeva hontīti sakkā vattuṃ. Yathāca pañcaṅgikaṃ sīlaṃ dasaṅgikaṃ sīlanti ettha pañcasamuditādīni tesaṃ sīlānaṃ pañcaṅgikā dināmalābhasseva kāraṇāni honti. Na sīlabhāvassa. Na hi pāṇātipātā veramaṇādikaṃ ekaṃpi samānaṃ sīlaṃnāma na hotīti. Evamevaṃ idhapi pañcasamuditādīni pañcaṅgikādi bhāvasseva pathamajjhānādi bhāvassevaca kāraṇāni. Napana jhānabhāvassāti nasakkā viññātuṃ. Itarathā jhānapaccaye jhānaṅgāni paccaniyāniyeva siyuntipi vadanti. Ettāvatā satipi imassa cittassa phassādīhipi sahitabhāve tesaṃ tathāvidhakiccavisesābhāvā idha aggahaṇantipi siddhaṃ nahotīti. Vicārapītisukhekaggatā saṅkhātena dutīyajjhānena sampayuttaṃ kusalacittaṃ dutīyajjhāna kusalacittaṃ, evaṃ sesesupi.

And equanimity, because of its peaceful nature, is included under happiness. Thus, when these states function in this way, they are for the sake of the thorough one-pointedness of that mind on that object. The state of one-pointedness is simply one-pointedness. And that one-pointedness, being thus supported by those states and having become very powerful, itself prevents the mind from running about to various objects due to sensual desire; and remaining motionless on that object, such as a kasiṇa sign, it approaches, contemplates, and observes that object. Therefore, all those states are also called 'jhāna' in the sense of close meditation. And when they are functioning in such a way, their opposing hindrances, finding no opportunity, are unable to obsess the mind. They are said to be 'burnt up.' Therefore, they are also called 'jhāna' in the sense of burning up the opposition. Even so, because the harmony of states is primary in the three instances designated as jhāna, path, and enlightenment—since the function of close meditation, etc., is accomplished only when the factors are in harmony, by way of reaching absorption—and because these states, though performing their own respective functions in the way described, accomplish the single function of close meditation, which is designated as the motionless proceeding of the mind on the object, therefore, it should be understood that just as the term 'chariot' applies only to the collection of chariot parts, so the term 'jhāna' is established only for their collection. But others say that for all five of them, their respective functions of applying the mind to the object, etc., are individually the function of close meditation. Having reached the jhāna condition in the Paṭṭhāna, they all individually accomplish the jhāna condition. Therefore, it can be said that they are individually jhānas. And just as in the case of 'five-factored virtue' and 'ten-factored virtue,' the collection of five, etc., are the reasons for those virtues obtaining the names 'five-factored,' etc., but not for their being virtue—for it is not that abstinence from killing living beings, etc., is not called virtue even when it is single—so too here, it cannot be understood that the collection of five, etc., are the reasons for the state of being 'five-factored,' etc., and for the state of being the first jhāna, etc., but not for the state of being jhāna. Otherwise, they say, in the jhāna condition, the jhāna factors would be hostile conditions. By this it is established that, although this consciousness is accompanied by contact and other factors, they are not included here because they lack such a special function. The wholesome consciousness associated with the second jhāna, which is designated by sustained application, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness, is the second-jhāna wholesome consciousness. So too for the remaining ones.

49. Ettha siyā. Kenapana imesaṃ jhānānaṃ aṅgabhedo katoti. Puggalajjhāsayena katoti. Yohi vitakkasahāyo hutvā pañcaṅgikaṃ pathamajjhānaṃ uppādetvā tattha vasībhāvaṃ katvā punavitakke nibbindati. Tassa vitakkaṃ samatikkamitvā avitakkaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ adhigantuṃ ajjhāsayo saṇṭhāti. Tadā so [M 0.0059] tameva pathamajjhānaṃ pādakabhāvatthāya daḷhaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tena ajjhāsayena saheva punabhāvanaṃ anuyuñjanto avitakkaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ adhigacchati. Tattha sā bhāvanāsayaṃ vitakkayuttāpi tena ajjhāsayena paribhāvitattā vitakkavirāga bhāvanānāma hoti. Tassā bhāvanāya. Balena taṃ jhānaṃ uppajja mānaṃ avitakkaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ uppajjati. Sesajjhānādhigamesupi esevanayoti. Evaṃ puggalajjhāsayena tesaṃ jhānānaṃ aṅgabhedo katoti veditabbo. Etthaca uttaruttarajjhānā dhigamane pādakabhāvatthāya purimapurimajjhānassa samāpajjanaṃ avassaṃ icchitabbaṃ. Heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ paguṇajjhānaṃ uparimassa uparimassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hotīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ajjhāsayabalenapana uttarajjhānaṃ uppajjamānaṃ pādakajjhānasadisaṃ nahoti. Pādakajjhānatohi puggalajjhāsayova balavataro. Tenāha bhagavā ijjhati bhikkhave sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattāti. Ayañca attho upari lokuttaracittaṃ patvā āvi bhavissatīti.

49. Here, it might be asked: How is the distinction of factors among these jhānas made? It is made based on the individual’s inclination. For one who is accustomed to initial application first attains the five-factored first jhāna, gains mastery in it, and then grows disenchanted with initial application. His inclination then settles on transcending initial application and attaining the four-factored jhāna without it. At that time, he firmly enters that very first jhāna as a foundation and, upon emerging, applies himself to further development with that inclination, thereby attaining the four-factored jhāna without initial application. There, even though that development is associated with initial application, because it is cultivated by that inclination, it is called 'development of dispassion for initial application.' Through the power of that development, the jhāna, when arising, arises as the four-factored jhāna without initial application. This same method applies to the attainment of the remaining jhānas. Thus, it should be understood that the distinction of factors among these jhānas is made based on the individual’s inclination. Here, when attaining successively higher jhānas, one must necessarily resolve to enter the immediately preceding jhāna as a foundation. As it is said in the commentary: 'Each lower jhāna, when well-mastered, serves as a proximate cause for the next higher one.' However, by the power of inclination, when a higher jhāna arises, it is not similar to the foundational jhāna, for the individual’s inclination is stronger than the foundational jhāna. Hence the Blessed One said: 'Monks, the mental aspiration of a virtuous one succeeds on account of its purity.' This meaning will become manifest later when we come to the supramundane consciousness.

50. Ettha siyā. Kasmā idha saṅkhārabhedo navuttoti. Pāḷiyameva avuttattā. Kasmāca so pāḷiyaṃ avuttoti. Paṭipadā bhedavacaneneva siddhattāti. Tathāhi sabbesaṃpi lokiya lokuttarajjhānānaṃ sukhappaṭipadabhāve siddhe asaṅkhārikabhāvo siddhoyeva hoti. Dukkhappaṭipadabhāveca siddhe tesaṃ sasaṅkhārikabhāvo siddhoyeva hotīti. Kathaṃ viññāyatīti ce. Aṭṭhakathādassanato. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ -

50. Here, it might be asked: Why is the distinction of promptings not mentioned here? Because it is not mentioned in the Pāḷi text itself. And why is it not mentioned in the Pāḷi text? Because it is established by the statement of the distinction of practice. For when the state of easy practice is established for all mundane and supramundane jhānas, the unprompted state is thereby established; and when the state of difficult practice is established, their prompted state is thereby established. How is this to be understood? From the commentary. For it is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī:

Yo ādito kilese vikkhambhento dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilamanto vikkhambheti. Tassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti. Yo kilese vikkhambhento sukhena akilamanto vikkhambheti. Tassa sukhāpaṭipadā hotīti.

“Whoever from the beginning suppresses the defilements with difficulty, with prompting, with exertion, while toiling—for him the practice is difficult. Whoever suppresses the defilements with ease, without toiling—for him the practice is easy.”

Tathā sammohavinodanī visuddhimaggesupīti. Etthaca pubbavākye dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogenāti diṭṭhattā paravākyepi sukhe na asaṅkhārena appayogenāti diṭṭhameva hoti. Tattha sasaṅkhārena [M 0.0060] sappayogenāti saṅkhārappayogasahitena kāmādīnavadassanādinā paccayagaṇenāti attho. Etena sabbesaṃ dukkhappaṭipadajjhānānaṃ sasaṅkhārikabhāvo vutto hoti. Asaṅkhārena appayogenāti saṅkhārappayogarahitena teneva paccayagaṇena. Etena sabbesaṃ sukhappaṭipadajjhānānaṃ asaṅkhārikabhāvo vutto hotīti. Khippābhiññajjhānānaṃpihi dukkhappaṭipadabhāve sati sasaṅkhārikatāva viññāyati. Dandhabhiññajjhānānaṃpi sukhappaṭipadabhāve sati asaṅkhārikatāva viññāyatīti. Yadievaṃ paṭipadārahitānaṃ magga siddhaupapattisiddhajjhānānaṃ kathaṃ saṅkhārabhedo siddhoti. Tesaṃpi vaḷañjanakāle samāpattippaṭibandhakānaṃ paccayānaṃ sannihitā sannihitavasena dukkhasukhappaṭipadabhāvasambhavo hotiyevāti. Tattha maggasiddhajjhānaṃnāma suddhavipassanāyānikānaṃ maggappaṭilābhena saheva siddhajjhānaṃ. Taṃ duvidhaṃ heṭṭhimamaggasiddhaṃ, arahattamaggasiddhanti. Tattha mahāsamayasutte āgatānaṃ pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ jhānaṃ heṭṭhima maggasiddhaṃ. Ānandattherassa jhānaṃ arahattamaggasiddhaṃ. Yaṃpi anāgāmīnaṃ ajānantānaññeva satthena hanitvā sahasā marantānaṃ uppannaṃ. Taṃpi maggasiddhagatikaṃ. Yopana aṭṭhasamāpattiyo bhāvetvā aññatarasmiṃ rūpi brahmaloke nibbatti. Tassa tā samāpatti yo tattha pākatikāeva honti. Idaṃ upapattisiddhanti. Ekasmiṃ bhavepi hi laddhajjhānāni vaḷañjanakāle sannihitapaccayavasena nānāpaṭipadāyuttāni hontīti. Jhānuppattippaṭipadā rahitattāvā asaṅkhārikajjhānesu tesaṃ saṅgaho yutto siyāti. Apica, nettipāḷiyaṃ sabbesaṃ lokiya lokuttarasamādhīnaṃ saṅkhārabhedo sarūpatova niddiṭṭho. Yathāha-dve samādhayo sasaṅkhāro samādhi asaṅkhāro samādhīti. Aṭṭhakathāyañca sukhappaṭipadā pubbakānaṃ dvinnaṃ dandhābhiññakhippābhiññasamādhīnaṃ asaṅkhārabhāvo dukkhappaṭipadā pubbakānaṃ dvinnaṃ sasaṅkhārabhāvoca vuttoti. Ettāvatā sabbesaṃ mahaggatalokuttarajjhānacittānaṃ asaṅkhārika sasaṅkhārikavasena visuṃ visuṃ duvidhabhāvo siddho hoti. Yasmāpana ayaṃ saṅkhāravohāro akusalānaṃpi sādhāraṇo. Paṭipadāvohāropana [M 0.0061] visesena paṭipattidhammesveva pākaṭo. Mahaggata lokuttaradhammāca ekantaṃ paṭipattidhammāeva. Tasmā tesaṃ bhedaṃ saṅkhāravasena avatvā paṭipadāvaseneva dhammasaṅgaṇi pāḷiyaṃpi vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Ayamettha paramatthadīpanā.

So too in the Sammohavinodanī and the Visuddhimagga. And here, since in the former sentence ‘with difficulty, with prompting, with exertion’ is seen, in the latter sentence too ‘with ease, without prompting, without exertion’ is indeed seen. Therein, ‘with prompting, with exertion’ means with the set of conditions, such as seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, etc., that is accompanied by prompting and exertion. By this is stated the prompted nature of all jhānas of difficult practice. ‘Without prompting, without exertion’ means with that same set of conditions but devoid of prompting and exertion. By this is stated the unprompted nature of all jhānas of easy practice. For even in the case of jhānas with quick intuition, when they are of difficult practice, their prompted nature is understood. And in the case of jhānas with slow intuition, when they are of easy practice, their unprompted nature is understood. If so, how is the distinction of promptings established for jhānas attained by the path or by rebirth, which are devoid of a path of practice? For them too, at the time of use, the possibility of a state of difficult or easy practice arises according to the presence or absence of obstructive conditions for the attainment. Here, ‘jhāna attained by the path’ means the jhāna attained together with the path by those who have pure insight as their vehicle. It is of two kinds: attained by a lower path, and attained by the path of arahantship. Here, the jhāna of the five hundred bhikkhus mentioned in the Mahāsamaya Sutta was attained by a lower path. The jhāna of the Venerable Ānanda was attained by the path of arahantship. The jhāna that arises in non-returners who are suddenly killed by a weapon without their knowing it is also included in the category of that attained by the path.
