Again, one who has developed the eight attainments is reborn in some Rūpa Brahma-world. For him, those attainments are natural there. This is ‘attained by rebirth.’ For even within a single existence, jhānas that have been obtained can be connected with different paths at the time of use, depending on the presence of conditions. Or, since they are devoid of a path for the arising of jhāna, their inclusion among the unprompted jhānas would be proper. Moreover, in the Nettippakaraṇa, the distinction of promptings for all mundane and supramundane concentrations is pointed out in its own right, as when it says: ‘Two concentrations: prompted concentration and unprompted concentration.’ And in the commentary it is said that the two concentrations with slow and quick intuition preceded by easy practice are unprompted, and the two preceded by difficult practice are prompted. By this much, the twofold division of all sublime and supramundane jhāna-cittas into prompted and unprompted is established. However, since this term ‘prompting’ is common even to unwholesome states, while the term ‘practice’ is especially evident in states of the path, and since the sublime and supramundane states are exclusively states of the path, their distinction is stated in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī-Pāḷi not by way of prompting but by way of practice. This is the elucidation of the ultimate meaning here.

51. [47] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

51. [47] Now, concerning what is said in the Vibhāvinī:

“Sabbassapi jhānassa parikammasaṅkhātapubbābhisaṅkhārena vinā kevalaṃ adhikāravasena anuppajjanato asaṅkhārikantipi. Adhikārenaca vinā kevalaṃ parikammābhisaṅkāravaseneva anuppajjanato sasaṅkhārikantipi nasakkā vattu”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha parikammasaṅkhāta.La. Asaṅkhārikantipi nasakkā vattunti idaṃ tāva nayujjati.

It is stated therein: “It is not possible to say of any jhāna that it is unprompted on the grounds that it does not arise simply by the power of aptitude without the preliminary volition called preparation; nor that it is prompted on the grounds that it does not arise simply by the power of the volition of preparation without aptitude.” Therein, the statement, “It is not possible to say that it is unprompted,” is, in the first place, incorrect.

Na hi parikammasaṅkhāta pubbābhisaṅkhāro imasmiṃ saṅkhārabhede saṅkhāro evanāma hoti. Kasmā, jhānuppattiyā pakatipaccaya bhūtattā, tathāhi loke sāsaneca sabbaṃpi kusalākusala kammaṃ attano anurūpena parikammasaṅkhāta pubbābhisaṅkhārena vinā uppannaṃnāma natthi. Antamaso ālopabhikkhādānamattaṃpīti. Yañca cittaṃ yena attano anurūpena parikammasaṅkhātapubbā bhisaṅkhārena vinā na uppajjati. So tassa cittassa pakatipaccayagaṇeevaanto gadho hoti. Jhānānica lokiya lokuttara bhūtāni sabbāni attano anurūpena parikammasaṅkhāta pubbabhāgabhāvanā bhisaṅkhārena vinā uppannānināma natthīti so tesaṃ pakatipaccayagaṇesueva antogadho hotīti. Itarathā sabbaṃpi kusalākusala kammaṃ asaṅkhārikaṃ nāmanatthīti āpajjatīti.

For the preliminary volition called ‘preparation’ is not what is termed ‘prompting’ in this distinction of promptings. Why? Because it is a natural condition for the arising of jhāna. For in the world and in the Dispensation, no wholesome or unwholesome kamma whatsoever arises without its corresponding preliminary volition called preparation, not even the mere giving of a mouthful of almsfood. And any consciousness that does not arise without its corresponding preliminary volition called preparation, that volition is included right within the set of that consciousness’s natural conditions. And since all jhānas, mundane and supramundane, do not arise without their corresponding preliminary volition of preliminary-part development, that volition is included right within their set of natural conditions. Otherwise, it would follow that there is no such thing as unprompted wholesome or unwholesome kamma.

[48] Yañca tattha

[48] And as to the other statement there:

Adhikārenaca vinā kevalaṃ.La. Sasaṅkhārikantipi nasakkā vattunti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yujjatiyeva.

The statement, “…nor that it is prompted on the grounds that it does not arise simply by the power of the volition of preparation without aptitude,” is also incorrect.

Na hi lokiyajjhānānināma adhikārena vinā nuppajjantīti atthi. Kevalaṃpana pubbe samathakammesu katādhikārassa sukhappaṭipadajjhānaṃ uppajjati. Akatādhikārassapana dukkhappaṭipadajjhānanti evameva aṭṭhakathāsu [M 0.0062] āgataṃ. Vuttañhi tattha yoca samathe akatādhikāro. Tassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti. Katādhikārassasukhāti. Apica, purimabhave siddhaṃ adhikāraṃ gahetvā idha saṅkhārabhedavicāraṇāpi nayuttāeva. Kusalakriyajjhānesu hi sanni hitapaccayavaseneva tabbicāraṇā yuttāti.

For it is not the case that mundane jhānas do not arise without aptitude. It is just that for one who has formerly developed aptitude in the serenity exercises, a jhāna of easy practice arises; but for one who has not developed aptitude, a jhāna of difficult practice arises—so it has come down in the commentaries. For it is said there: “For one who has not developed aptitude in serenity, the practice is difficult; for one who has developed aptitude, it is easy.” Moreover, it is not proper to consider the distinction of promptings here by taking into account an aptitude accomplished in a previous existence. For in the case of wholesome functional jhānas, that consideration is proper only on the basis of conditions present here and now.

[49] Ettāvatā

[49] By this much,

Athavātiādiko pacchima vikappopi paṭikkhitto eva hotīti.

the latter alternative beginning ‘Or…’, is also refuted.

52. Ettha jhānaṃ anuyuñjantassa nimittuppādato pubbaṃ paṭipadāya khettaṃ, pacchā abhiññāya khettaṃ. Tattha pubbe viruddhapaccayānaṃ sannihitena kilamantassa sato paṭipajjantassa bhāvanā paṭipadā dukkhānāma hoti. Akilamantassa sukhā. Pacchāca dandhaṃ appanaṃ pattassa bhāvanābhiññā dandhābhiññānāma hoti. Khippaṃ pattassa khippābhiññānāma. Tattha pubbe dukkhā paṭipadā pacchā dandhaṃvā khippaṃvā uppannaṃ jhānaṃ dukkhappaṭipadaṃnāma karoti. Sukhāpana sukhappaṭipadaṃnāma karotīti. Dutīyajjhānādīsupana purimajjhāne nikanti vikkhambhanassa dukkhasukhatāvasena paṭipadābhedo veditabbo. Yopana etarahi gahaṭṭhovā pabbajitovā pubbabhave akatādhikāropi antarāyikadhammamutto kalyāṇapaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhito chinnapalibodho pahitatto jhānaṃ bhāveti. Tassa jhānabhāvanā nasampajjatīti natthīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbanti. [Kusalajjhānaṃ]

52. Here, for one devoted to jhāna, before the arising of the sign is the field of the path, and after is the field of direct knowledge. In this regard, for one who, being mindful, practices while becoming fatigued due to the presence of adverse conditions, the path of development is called painful. For one who does not become fatigued, it is pleasant. And afterwards, for one who attains absorption slowly, the direct knowledge of development is called slow direct knowledge; for one who attains it quickly, it is called quick direct knowledge. Here, if the earlier path was painful, the jhāna that arises later, whether slowly or quickly, makes the path painful. If it was pleasant, it makes the path pleasant. In the second jhāna and so on, the distinction in the path should be understood by way of the painfulness or pleasantness of suppressing delight in the preceding jhāna. Moreover, if at the present time a householder or one gone forth, though one who has not made the necessary preparations in a previous existence, is free from obstructive states, established in good practice, has cut off impediments, and is resolute in mind, develops jhāna—that his development of jhāna would not succeed is impossible; this is the conclusion to be reached here. [Wholesome Jhāna]

53. Vipākajjhāne kāmakusalaṃ appanaṃ apattaṃ mudubhūtaṃ dubbalaṃ hoti. Parittesu nānākiccaṭṭhānesuca hīnesupi attabhāvesuca vipaccati. Tasmā taṃ attanā asadisaṃpi vipākaṃ janeti. Mahaggatakusalaṃpana appanāpattaṃ tikkhaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Uḷāre brahmattabhāve bhavaṅgaṭṭhānesuyeva vipaccati. Tasmā taṃ sadāpi attanā sadisameva vipākaṃ janeti. Teneva vitakkavicārapīti sukhekaggatā sahitantiādinā vipākaṃpi sabbaso kusala sadisameva dasseti.

53. In the context of resultant jhāna, sense-sphere wholesome kamma that has not reached absorption is soft and weak. It ripens in minor and various functional states and in inferior existences. Therefore, it produces a result that can be dissimilar to itself. But sublime wholesome kamma that has reached absorption is sharp and strong. It ripens only in lofty brahma-existences and in the state of bhavaṅga. Therefore, it always produces a result similar to itself. For that very reason, it is shown that the result, too—endowed with initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness, and so on—is in all respects similar to the wholesome.

[50] Anantarabhaveyeva [M 0.0063] phaladānattā taṃ attanā sadisameva vipākaṃ janetītica vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ.

[50] Some say that because it gives its fruit in the very next existence, it produces a result similar to itself. This is not a good explanation.

Evañhi sati kāmakusalaṃpi sattamajavanaṃ attanā sadisavipāka meva janeyyāti. Yasmāca kusalameva niranusayasantāne pavattaṃ kriyajjhānaṃ nāma hoti. Tasmā kriyacittaṃpi kusala sadisameva dasseti.

For if that were so, even the seventh impulsion of sense-sphere wholesome kamma would produce a result similar to itself. And because it is wholesome jhāna occurring in a continuity free from underlying tendencies that is called functional jhāna, therefore functional consciousness, too, is shown to be similar to the wholesome.

54. Pañcadhātiādisaṅgahagāthā. Tattha jhānabhedenāti pathamajjhānādīhi pañcahi jhānehi sampayogabhedena. Rūpāvacaramānasaṃ jhānabhedena pañcadhā hoti. Pathamajjhānikaṃ, dutīyajjhānikaṃ, tatīyajjhānikaṃ, catutthajjhānikaṃ, pañcamajjhānikanti evaṃ pañcavidhaṃ hotīti attho. Tameva puññapākakriyābhedena pañcadasadhā bhaveti yojanā.

54. The summary verse beginning 'Fivefold.' Here, 'by distinction of jhāna' means by distinction of association with the five jhānas beginning with the first. The fine-material sphere mind becomes fivefold by distinction of jhāna. That is, pertaining to the first jhāna, second jhāna, third jhāna, fourth jhāna, and fifth jhāna—thus it is fivefold; this is the meaning. The connection is: that same mind, by the distinction of meritorious, resultant, and functional, becomes fifteenfold.

[51] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[51] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Jhānabhedenāti jhānaṅgehi sampayogabhedenāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: '"By distinction of jhāna" means by distinction of association with the jhāna factors.' That is not a good explanation.

Añño hi jhānabhedo. Añño jhānaṅgabhedo. Tattha pathamaṃ jhānaṃ dutīyaṃ jhānantiādijhānabhedo. Pathamajjhāne pañca aṅgāni. Dutīyajjhāne cattārītiādi jhānaṅgabhedo. Tesu idha jhānabhedova adhippeto. Na jhānaṅgabhedo. Cittañhi jhānabhede neva pañcavidhaṃ hoti. Najhānaṅgabhedena. Jhānameva pana jhānaṅgabhedena pañcavidhanti.

For the distinction of jhāna is one thing, and the distinction of jhāna factors is another. Therein, the distinction of jhāna is: first jhāna, second jhāna, and so on. The distinction of jhāna factors is: in the first jhāna there are five factors; in the second jhāna, four, and so on. Of these, it is the distinction of jhāna that is intended here, not the distinction of jhāna factors. For the mind becomes fivefold only by the distinction of jhāna, not by the distinction of jhāna factors. It is jhāna itself, however, that is fivefold by the distinction of its factors.

[52] Yañca tattha

[52] And as to what is said therein:

“Pañcadhāti pañcaṅgikaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ tivaṅgikaṃ duvaṅgikaṃ puna duvaṅgikanti pañcavidhaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

It is said: '"Fivefold" means five-factored, four-factored, three-factored, two-factored, and again two-factored—thus it is fivefold.' This too is not a good explanation.

Jhānameva hi pañcaṅgikādi hoti. Na cittanti.

For it is jhāna itself that is five-factored and so on, not the mind.

Rūpāvacara cittassa paramatthadhīpanā.

Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning of the Fine-Material Sphere Consciousness.

55. Idāni yathānuppattaṃ arūpacittaṃ niddisanto ākāsānañcā yatanakusalacittantiādi māha. Tattha bhuso kāsati dibbatīti [M 0.0064] ākāso. So hi sayaṃ sarūpato anupalabbhamānopi candasūriyobhāsādīnaṃ vasena ativijjotamānoviya khāyatīti. Nakassati chedana bhedana vasena na vilekhīyatīti akāso. Akāsoeva ākāso tipi vadanti. So pana ajaṭākāso paricchinnākāso kasiṇugghāṭimākāso rūpakalāpaparicchedākāsoti catubbidho hoti. Tattha idha kasiṇugghāṭimākāso adhippeto. So hi anantena ajaṭākāsena saha ekībhūtoviya hoti. Yogināca anantabhāvena pharīyati. Tasmā ananto ākāsoti ākāsānanto. Nāssa uppādantovā vayantovā paññāyatīti anantotipi vuttaṃ. Soyeva ākāsānañcaṃ. Sakatthe yakārena saha siddhattā. Yathā pana devānaṃ adhiṭṭhānavatthu devāyatananti vuccati. Tathā idhapi tasmiṃ appanāpattassa sasampayuttassa jhānassa adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena tadeva āyatanantipi vuccati. Iti ākāsānañcaṃ āyatanamassāti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Cittacetasikarāsi.

55. Now, indicating the immaterial consciousness in due order, he said: 'The wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space,' and so on. Herein, ākāsa is so called because 'it shines brightly, it is divine.' For though its own nature is not perceived, it appears as if it shines exceedingly by means of the light of the moon, sun, and so on. It is akāsa because 'it is not scratched by way of cutting and splitting.' Some also say that akāsa is simply ākāsa. It is of four kinds: unentangled space, limited space, space opened up by the kasiṇa, and space as the delimiter of material groups. Here, it is the space opened up by the kasiṇa that is intended. For it appears as if it has become one with the infinite, unentangled space. And it is pervaded by the yogī as infinite. Therefore, 'infinite space,' thus 'infinity of space.' It is also called 'infinite' because its beginning and end are not discerned. That itself is ākāsānañca, formed with the suffix -ya in its own meaning. Just as the devas' resort is called a 'deva-base,' so here too, since it is the base for the jhāna, together with its concomitants, that has reached absorption in it, that itself is also called a 'base.' Thus, 'base of the infinity of space' is that which has the infinity of space as its base; it is the aggregate of consciousness and mental factors.

Ākāsānañcā yatananti ākāsānañcā yatanaṃ samāpannassavā upapannassavā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissavā citta ceta sikādhammāti hi vibhaṅge vuttaṃ.

'The base of the infinity of space' means the states of consciousness and mental factors of one who has attained the base of the infinity of space, or of one who has been reborn there, or of one who is dwelling happily in this very life—so it is said in the Vibhaṅga.

Ākāsānañcāyatane pavattaṃ kusalacittanti ākāsānañcāyatanakusalacittaṃ. Viññāṇañcāyatananti ettha viññāṇaṃnāma ākāsānañcāyatanacittameva. Taṃpana sayaṃ uppādādi antavantaṃpi anantasaññite ākāse pavattanato anantanti vuccati. Koṭṭhāsatthovā antasaddo. Attano uppādādīsu koṭṭhāsesu ekadese aṭṭhatvā sakalassa pharaṇavasena tadārammaṇāya bhāvanāya pavattanato anantanti vuccati. Anantasaññitevā ākāse pavattanato anantanti evaṃ tadārammaṇāya bhāvanāya pavattattā anantanti vuccati. Anantasaññitevā ākāse attano pharaṇākāra vasenapi anantanti vattuṃ yujjatiyeva. Anantaṃ viññāṇanti [M 0.0065] viññāṇānantaṃ. Tameva viññāṇañcaṃ niruttinayena, viññāṇañcaṃ āyatanaṃ assāti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ. Viññāṇañcāyatana saṅkhāte cittacetasikarāsimhi pavattaṃ kusalacittantisamāso.

Wholesome consciousness occurring in the base of the infinity of space is 'wholesome consciousness of the base of the infinity of space.' Regarding 'the base of the infinity of consciousness,' here 'consciousness' is just the consciousness of the base of the infinity of space. Though it itself has a beginning, etc., and thus an end, it is called 'infinite' because it occurs in space that is perceived as infinite. Or the word 'anta' (end) has the meaning of 'part.' It is called 'infinite' because, having established itself in one part among the parts of its own arising, etc., it proceeds by way of pervading the whole through the development that has that as its object. It is called 'infinite' because it occurs in space perceived as infinite; thus it is called 'infinite' because it occurs through the development that has that as its object. Indeed, it is also fitting to call it 'infinite' on account of its mode of pervading in space perceived as infinite. 'Infinite consciousness,' thus 'infinity of consciousness.' By way of etymology, that itself is viññāṇañca. 'The base of the infinity of consciousness' is that which has the infinity of consciousness as its base. The compound means: wholesome consciousness occurring in the aggregate of consciousness and mental factors designated as 'the base of the infinity of consciousness'.

Viññāṇañcāyatananti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassavā upapannassavādiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissavācittacetasikādhammātihi vibhaṅge vuttaṃ.

'The base of the infinity of consciousness' means the states of consciousness and mental factors of one who has attained the base of the infinity of consciousness, or of one who has been reborn there, or of one who is dwelling happily in this very life—so it is said in the Vibhaṅga.

[53] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana mahāṭīkāyañca

[53] But in the Vibhāvanī and also in the Mahāṭīkā:

“Dutīyā ruppa viññāṇena añcitabbaṃ pāpuṇitabbanti viññāṇañca”ntipi vuttaṃ. Taṃ pāḷiyā na sameti.

It is also said: 'Viññāṇañca is so called because it is to be honored and attained by the second immaterial consciousness.' But that does not agree with the Pāli.

Anantaṃ viññāṇanti tadeva viññāṇaṃ ñāṇena phuṭṭhaṃ manasikaroti, anantaṃ pharati. Tena vuccati anantaṃ viññāṇantītihi vuttaṃ. Etena ca taṃviññāṇaṃ ekantena anantavisesanayuttaṃ hotīti viññāyatīti. Tameva ākāsantipi pāṭho. Ākiñcaññāyatananti ettha kiñci kiñcananti atthato ekaṃ appamattakassa nāmaṃ. Natthi kiñcanaṃ appamattakaṃ antamaso bhaṅgamattaṃpi avasiṭṭhaṃ assa pathamā ruppaviññāṇassāti akiñcanaṃ. Akiñcanassa bhāvo ākiñcaññaṃ. Pathamāruppaviññāṇābhāvo. So hi natthi kiñcīti manasikāra vasena taṃnāmaṃ labhatīti. Ākiñcaññaṃ āyatanamassātiādi vuttanayameva. Nevasaññā nāsaññāyatananti ettha oḷārika saññaṃ sandhāya nevatthi saññā assāti nevasaññaṃ. Sukhumasaññaṃ sandhāya naca natthi saññā assāti nāsaññaṃ, nevasaññañca taṃ nāsaññañcāti nevasaññā nāsaññaṃ majjhe dīghaṃ katvā, citta cetasikarāsieva. Tameva yogino sukhavisesānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatananti nevasaññā nāsaññāyatanaṃ. Tasmiṃ pavattaṃ kusala cittanti samāso. Athavā. Saññāyeva paṭusaññākiccassa abhāvato nevasaññāca hoti. Saṅkhārāvasesa sukhumabhāvena vijjamānattā asaññāca nahotīti katvā nevasaññānā saññānāma, sāyeva āyatanaṃ, tenaca sampayuttaṃ kusala cittanti samāso. Etthaca yasmā ādito paṭṭhāya oḷārike nīvaraṇadhamme [M 0.0066] vitakkādikeca pajahitvā sesadhammeca bhāvanā balena uparupari sukhumabhāvaṃ pāpetvā anukkamena paṭipajjantā sukhumaṭṭhena lokiyadhammesu muddhabhūtaṃ imaṃ samāpattiṃ pāpuṇanti. Tasmā idha cittaṃpi nevacittanācittameva hoti. Phassopi neva phassanāphassoeva hoti, tathā vedanādayopīti. Tasmā idhasaññāggahaṇaṃ desanāsīsamattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vipākesu viññāṇañcāyatananti ettha viññāṇanti pathamāruppakusala viññāṇameva. Tañca atītānantarabhave pavattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Akiñcana bhāvoca tasseva natthi bhāvoti. Kriyacittesu pana viññāṇaṃ nāma kusalabhūtaṃ kriyabhūtañca duvidhaṃ pathamāruppaviññāṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Akiñcanabhāvoca tasseva duvidhassa viññāṇassa abhāvo yevāti.

‘Consciousness is infinite’: one attends to that very consciousness as touched by knowledge and pervading infinitely. Therefore it is said, ‘Consciousness is infinite.’ And by this it is understood that this consciousness is entirely endowed with the quality of infinity. There is also the reading ‘infinite space’ for this. Regarding ‘the base of nothingness,’ here ‘anything whatsoever’ (kiñcana) is, in meaning, a name for even the slightest thing. Because there is not anything, not the slightest thing, not even a moment of dissolution remaining of the first formless consciousness, it is ‘nothing’ (akiñcana). The state of being nothing is nothingness (ākiñcaññaṃ), that is, the absence of the first formless consciousness. For it obtains that name by way of the attention, ‘There is nothing.’ ‘The base of nothingness,’ etc., is to be understood in the way already stated. Regarding ‘the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,’ here, with reference to gross perception, because ‘there is no perception in it,’ it is ‘neither-perception’ (nevasañña). With reference to subtle perception, because ‘perception is not absent from it,’ it is ‘non-non-perception’ (nāsañña). ‘Neither-perception’ and ‘non-non-perception’ becomes ‘neither-perception-nor-non-perception’ (nevasaññānāsaññaṃ) by lengthening the middle vowel; it is just the aggregate of mind and mental factors. For a yogi, that itself is the base (āyatana) in the sense of a foundation for special kinds of bliss; hence ‘the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ The wholesome consciousness occurring in it: this is a compound. Alternatively, because of the absence of the function of sharp perception, perception itself is ‘neither-perception’; and because it exists in a subtle state as a remainder of formations, it is not non-perception. Thus it is named ‘neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’ That itself is the base, and the wholesome consciousness associated with it: this is a compound. Here, because from the beginning, having abandoned the gross hindrances, thought-conception, and so on, and having progressively refined the remaining states through the power of meditation, practitioners gradually attain this attainment, which is the peak among mundane states. Therefore, here the mind is neither mind nor non-mind; contact is neither contact nor non-contact; and so too are feeling and the rest. Therefore, the mention of perception here should be seen as merely a heading for the exposition. In the resultants, regarding ‘the base of infinite consciousness,’ here ‘consciousness’ is only the wholesome consciousness of the first formless attainment. And that should be seen as having occurred in the immediately preceding existence. And the state of nothingness is the state of absence of that very consciousness. In the functional consciousnesses, however, ‘consciousness’ should be understood as the twofold first formless consciousness, that which is wholesome and that which is functional. And the state of nothingness is just the absence of that twofold consciousness.

56. Saṅgahagāthāyaṃ ārammaṇappabhedenāti ālambi tabbānaṃ kasiṇugghāṭimākāsādīnaṃ catunnaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ pabhedena. Duvidhaṃhi idha ārammaṇacatukkaṃ, atimikkatabba catukkaṃ, ālambi tabba catukkañca. Tattha pathamāruppe rūpapañcamajjhānassa ārammaṇa bhūtaṃ. Kasiṇanimittaṃ atikkami tabbaṃnāma. Taṃ ugghāṭetvā laddhaṃ ākāsaṃ ālambitabbaṃ nāma. Dutīyāruppe pathamāruppassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ ākāsaṃ atikkamitabbaṃnāma. Pathamāruppaviññāṇaṃ ālambi tabbaṃnāma. Tatīyāruppe taṃpathamāruppaviññāṇaṃ atikkamitabbaṃnāma. Tassa natthibhāvo ālambitabbaṃnāma. Catutthāruppe so natthi bhāvo atikkamitabbaṃ nāma. Tatīyāruppaviññāṇaṃ ālambi tabbaṃ nāmāti. Tattha kiñcāpi imaṃ āruppamānasaṃ catunnaṃ atikkami tabbānaṃpi bhedena catubbidhaṃ hoti, tathāpi ākāsānañcāya tanantiādinā idha ālambitabbānaññeva sarūpato gahitattā tesaṃ bhedena imassa bhedo pākaṭoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Āruppamānasaṃ ālambaṇappabhedena catudhā ṭhitaṃ. Tadeva puññapāka kriyabhedena dvādasadhā ṭhitanti yojanā.

56. In the summary verse, ‘by the division of the object’ means by the division of the four objects to be taken as object, namely, the space from the removal of the kasiṇa, and so on. Here there is a twofold tetrad of objects: the tetrad to be surpassed and the tetrad to be taken as object. Therein, in the first formless attainment, the kasiṇa sign that was the object of the fifth form jhāna is the thing to be surpassed. The space obtained by having removed that is the thing to be taken as object. In the second formless attainment, the space that was the object of the first formless attainment is the thing to be surpassed. The consciousness of the first formless attainment is the thing to be taken as object. In the third formless attainment, that consciousness of the first formless attainment is the thing to be surpassed. Its non-existence is the thing to be taken as object. In the fourth formless attainment, that non-existence is the thing to be surpassed. The consciousness of the third formless attainment is the thing to be taken as object. Therein, although this formless consciousness is fourfold by the division of the four things to be surpassed, still, since here only the things to be taken as object are mentioned by their own nature with such terms as ‘the base of infinite space,’ it should be seen that the division of this consciousness is made clear by the division of those objects. The formless consciousness stands as fourfold by the division of the object. That same consciousness stands as twelvefold by the division into wholesome, resultant, and functional. This is the connection.

Arūpacittassa paramatthadīpanā.

The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning of Formless Consciousness.

57. Idāni [M 0.0067] yathānuppattaṃ lokuttara cittaṃ dassento sotāpattimaggacittantiādimāha. Tattha savati sandati anivattagamanavasena pavattatīti soto, gaṅgādīsu jalappavāho. Sohi pabhavato paṭṭhāya yāvamahāsamuddā antarā anivatta māno savati sandati pavattatīti. Sotoviyāti soto. Aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyamaggo, yathāha-yokho āvuso ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi. La. Sammāsamādhi. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso sototi. Ayaṃpihi yadā uppajjati. Tato paṭṭhāya ānubhāvapharaṇavasena yāvaanupādisesanibbānadhātuyā antarā anivattamānoyeva hutvā savati sandati pavattatīti. Yathāha -

57. Now, showing the supramundane consciousness in due order, he says, ‘The consciousness of the path of stream-entry,’ etc. Herein, it flows (savati), it proceeds (sandati), it goes on by way of non-returning: this is a stream (soto), like the current of water in the Ganges and other rivers. For that flows, proceeds, and goes on from its source up to the great ocean without turning back in between. Like a stream is the stream: the Noble Eightfold Path. As it is said: ‘Friend, this Noble Eightfold Path is the stream. That is: right view... right concentration. This, friend, is called the stream.’ For when this path arises, from then on, by way of the pervasion of its power, it flows, proceeds, and goes on without turning back until the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. As it is said:

Seyyathāpi bhikkhave yākāci mahānadiyo. Seyyathidaṃ. Gaṅgā, yamunā, aciravatī, sarabhū, mahī. Sabbā tā samuddaninnā honti samuddapoṇā samuddapabbhārā. Evameva kho bhikkhave bhikkhu ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvento bahulikaronto nibbānaninno hoti nibbānapoṇo nibbāna pabbhāroti.

‘Just as, bhikkhus, whatever great rivers there are—such as the Ganges, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—all verge towards the ocean, slope towards the ocean, incline towards the ocean; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who develops and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path verges towards Nibbāna, slopes towards Nibbāna, inclines towards Nibbāna.’

Etthaca tena tena maggena pahīnānaṃ kilesānaṃ puna anupagamana vasena saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ anukkamena paripākagamanavasenaca anivattagamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathāha -

And here, the non-returning should be seen by way of the non-re-arising of the defilements abandoned by the respective paths, and by way of the gradual maturing of the faculties such as faith. As it is said:

Seyyathāpi bhikkhave ghaṭo nikkujjo vamateva udakaṃ. Nopaccāvamati. Evamevakho bhikkhave ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvento bahulikaronto vamateva pāpake akusale dhamme. Nopaccāvamatīti. Yathācāha-sotāpatti maggaññāṇena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese napuneti napacceti napaccāgacchatītiādi.

‘Just as, bhikkhus, an overturned pot vomits out the water and does not take it back in, so too, bhikkhus, one who develops and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path vomits out evil, unwholesome states and does not take them back in.’ And as it is said: ‘Those defilements that have been abandoned by the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, he does not go back to those defilements, does not return to them, does not come back to them,’ and so on.

Yathāca puthujjanā pahīnepi kilese puna upagacchanti. Tihe tukabhūtāpi puna dvihetukāhetukabhāvaṃ gacchanti. Yato te uparibhavagge [M 0.0068] nibbattāpi puna apāyesu sandissanti. Sīlavantāpi puna dussīlā honti. Samāhitāpi puna ummattakāvā khittacittāvā honti. Paññavāpi puna duppaññā eḷamūgā honti. Natathā ariyā. Tepana tena tena maggena pahīne kilese puna naupagacchanti. Puthujjanabhāvaṃvā heṭṭhimāriya bhāvaṃvā na gacchanti. Anukkamena saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ paripakkabhāvameva upagacchantīti. Sabbañcetaṃ ariyamaggasseva ānubhāvena siddhanti sototināmaṃ mūlappabhavabhūte tasmiṃ maggeeva niruḷhanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tassa sotassa ādito pajjanaṃ pāpuṇanaṃ sotāpatti. Sotāpattiyā adhigamamāno maggo sotāpattimaggo. Athavā, dhammasota samāpanno ariyoti pavuccatīti vuttattā sabbe ariyasantānagatā lokiya lokuttarabhūtā bodhipakkhiyadhammā upari sambodhiparā yanatāvasena anupādisesanibbāna parāyanatāvasenaca anivatta gatiyā pavattamānā yathāvuttena atthena sototi vuccanti. Taṃ sotaṃ ādito pajjanti pāpuṇanti etāya paṭipadāyāti sotāpatti. Sotāpattica sā maggocāti sotāpattimaggo, pathamamaggasaṅkhātāya sotāpattiyā aṅganti sotāpatti yaṅgantihi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, maggotica patho upāyo. Nibbānaṃ maggeti, nibbānatthikehi maggīyati, kilese mārento gacchatīti maggotica vadanti.

For worldlings, even when they have abandoned defilements, approach them again. Even those with three roots revert to a two-rooted or rootless state. Hence, though reborn at the peak of existence, they are seen again in the planes of misery. The virtuous become immoral again. The concentrated become deranged or distracted again. The wise become foolish or stupid again. It is not so with the noble ones. They do not again approach the defilements abandoned by the respective paths. They do not revert to the state of a worldling or to a lower noble state. They proceed only to the progressive maturing of the faculties such as faith. All this is accomplished by the power of the noble path. It should be seen that the name ‘stream’ is established in that very path, which is its root source. The entering upon, the attainment of, that stream from the beginning is stream-entry (sotāpatti). The path by which one attains stream-entry is the path of stream-entry. Alternatively, since it is said, ‘One who has entered the stream of the Dhamma is called a noble one,’ all the mundane and supramundane states conducive to enlightenment that have entered the continuity of a noble one—because they are bound for supreme enlightenment above and for the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining—are called ‘the stream’ in the aforesaid sense, as they proceed with an irreversible motion. They enter upon, they attain, that stream from the beginning by this practice; thus it is stream-entry. That is stream-entry and it is the path; thus it is the path of stream-entry. In the commentary it is said: ‘a factor of stream-entry, which is reckoned as the first path.’ And ‘path’ (maggo) means a way, a means. They also say it is a path because it leads to Nibbāna, because it is sought by those who seek Nibbāna, and because it goes along destroying the defilements.

[54] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[54] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Ariyamaggasotassa ādito pajjanaṃ etassāti sotāpatti. Puggaloti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

‘The entering from the beginning upon the stream of the noble path is his; thus he is a stream-enterer (sotāpatti).’ It is said to be the person. That is not correct.

Na hi puggale pavatto sotāpattisaddo katthaci diṭṭhoti.

For the word ‘sotāpatti’ is nowhere seen used for a person.

[55] Etena tassa maggo sotāpattimaggoti idaṃpi paṭikkhittaṃ hoti.

[55] By this, the statement ‘his path is the path of stream-entry’ is also rejected.

Sotāpattimaggena sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ sotāpattimaggacittaṃ.

The consciousness associated with the path of stream-entry is the consciousness of the path of stream-entry.

[56] Ṭīkāsu pana

[56] But in the subcommentaries,

Sotāpattiyā [M 0.0069] laddhaṃ maggacittaṃ sotāpatti maggacittanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: ‘The path consciousness obtained by means of stream-entry is the consciousness of the path of stream-entry.’ That is not correct.

Na hi cittasaddasambandho sotāpattisaddo katthaci pāḷiyaṃ diṭṭhoti.

For the word ‘sotāpatti’ is nowhere seen in the Pāli canon in connection with the word ‘citta’.

58. Paṭisandhivasena sakiṃ imaṃlokaṃ āgacchati sīlenāti sakadāgāmī. Dutīyaphalaṭṭho. So hi asamucchinnakāma rāgānusayattā kāmalokāgamana kilesasabbhāvena taṃ sabhāvānāti vattanato upari bhavagge ṭhitopi paṭisandhivasena puna imaṃ kāmadhātuṃ āgamanappakatikoeva hotīti. Vuttañhetaṃ catukkanipāte -

58. He is a once-returner (sakadāgāmī) because it is his nature to come to this world once by way of rebirth-linking. He is one established in the second fruit. For, since the underlying tendency to sensual lust has not been eradicated, due to the existence of defilements that cause arrival in the sense-sphere world and because it is his nature to be subject to them, even if he is established in the peak of existence above, he is by nature one who returns again to this sense-sphere world by way of rebirth-linking. For it is said in the Book of the Fours:

Idha sāriputta ekaccassa puggalassa orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni appahīnāni honti, so diṭṭhevadhamme nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. So aparihīno kālaṃ kurumāno nesaññānāsaññā yatanupagānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjati. So tato cuto āgāmī hoti āgantvā itthattaṃ. Idha pana sāriputta ekaccassa puggalassa orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni pahīnāni honti, so diṭṭheva.La. So tato cuto anāgāmī hoti anāgantvā itthattanti.

Here, Sāriputta, in the case of a certain person, the lower fetters are unabandoned. In this very life he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Without having fallen away from it, when he makes an end, he is reborn in the company of the devas who have gone to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having passed away from there, he is a returner, one who comes back to this state of being. But here, Sāriputta, in the case of a certain person, the lower fetters are abandoned. In this very life he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.... Having passed away from there, he is a non-returner, one who does not come back to this state of being.

Aṭṭhakathāyañca itthattanti imaṃ kāmāvacara pañcakkhandha bhāvanti vuttaṃ. Ayañca attho kilesagativasena vutto. Na puggala gativasena. Na hi brahmabhūtā sotāpanna sakadā gāmino paṭipaṭisandhivasena heṭṭhimaṃpi brahmalokaṃ āgacchanti. Kuto kāma lokaṃ. Kathaṃ viññāyatīti ce. Anusayayamake –

And in the commentary it is said: '"This state of being" (itthatta) means this state of the five aggregates belonging to the sense sphere.' This meaning is stated in terms of the destination of the defilements, not in terms of the destination of the person. For stream-enterers and once-returners who have become Brahmas do not return even to a lower Brahma world by way of rebirth-linking, still less to the sense-sphere world. If it is asked, 'How is this known?' In the Anusayayamaka it is said:

Kāmadhātuyā cutassa rūpadhātuṃ arūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa kassaci sattaanusayā anusenti, kassaci pañcaanusayā anusenti, kassaci tayo anusayā anusentīti vatvā [M 0.0070] rūpa dhātuyā arūpadhātuyā cutassa kāmadhātuṃ upapajjantassa satteva anusayā anusentīti.

Having said: 'For one who has passed away from the sense-sphere world and is being reborn in the form world or the formless world, in some the seven underlying tendencies lie latent, in some five underlying tendencies lie latent, and in some three underlying tendencies lie latent,' it is then said: 'For one who has passed away from the form world or the formless world and is being reborn in the sense-sphere world, seven underlying tendencies and no others lie latent.'

Vuttattā viññāyati. Tattha purimavākye puthujjanassa vasena satta. Dvinnaṃ sotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃ vasena pañca. Anāgāmissa vasena kayoti vuttaṃ, pacchimavākyepana brahmabhūtānaṃ sotā pannasakadāgāmianāgāmīnaṃ paṭisandhivasena kāmalokaṃ gamanassa natthitāya kevalaṃ puthujjanasseva vasena sattevāti vuttaṃ. Dhammahadaya vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyañca –

This is known because it has been stated. There, in the former sentence, 'seven' is stated with respect to a worldling; 'five' is stated with respect to the two, the stream-enterer and the once-returner; and 'three' is stated with respect to the non-returner. But in the latter sentence, since for stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners who have become Brahmas there is no going to the sense-sphere world by way of rebirth-linking, 'seven and no others' is stated with respect only to a worldling. And in the commentary on the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga it is said:

“Rūpāvacare nibbattā sotāpannasakadāgāmino napuna idhā gacchanti, tattheva parinibbāyanti. Etehi jhānaanāgāmino nāmā”ti ca. “Navasu brahmalokesu nibbattaariya sāvakānaṃ tatrupa pattipi hoti uparūpapattipi. Naheṭṭhu papatti. Puthujjanānaṃpana tatrupapattipi hoti uparūpapatti heṭṭhupapattipī”ti ca.

“Stream-enterers and once-returners reborn in the form sphere do not come here again; they attain final Nibbāna right there. These are called ‘non-returners by jhāna.’” And: “For noble disciples reborn in the nine Brahma worlds, there is rebirth in that same plane and rebirth in a higher plane, but not rebirth in a lower one. But for worldlings, there is rebirth in that same plane, rebirth in a higher plane, and rebirth in a lower plane.”

Vuttaṃ. Tañcakho anāgamanaṃ maggasahāyena jhānānubhāveneva siddhaṃ. Namaggānubhāvenāti. Etthaca imaṃ lokanti padassa imaṃ manussalokanti vā imaṃ kāmāvacaralokantivā dvidhāpi attho aṭṭhakathāsu vutto. Tattha purimasmiṃ atthe sati āgacchatīti etassa devalokato āgacchatīti attho. Pacchimasmiṃ pana brahmalokatopi ca āgacchatīti. Pāḷiyaṃpana pacchimatthova vuttoviya dissati. Vuttañhetaṃ puggalapaññattiyaṃ anāgantvā itthattaṃ anāgāmī tena daṭṭhabbo. Āgantvā itthattaṃ sotāpannasakadā gāmino tena daṭṭhabbāti. Etthaca anāgantvā itthattanti iminā imaṃ kāmāvacaralokaṃ na āgacchatīti anāgāmīti atthaṃ dasseti. Āgantvā itthattanti imināpana dvepi sotāpannasakadāgāmino sakiṃ puna imaṃ kāmāvacaralokaṃ āgacchantīti sakadāgāminoti atthaṃ dasseti. Kasmā, nirantaravākyesu ṭhitānaṃ dvinnaṃitthatta saddānaṃ nānātthā sambhavato. Majjhimapaṇṇāseca kaṇṇakattha sutte -

It is said. And that non-returning is accomplished only by the power of jhāna assisted by the path, not by the power of the path alone. Here, for the phrase 'this world,' a twofold meaning is given in the commentaries: either 'this human world' or 'this sense-sphere world.' When the former meaning is taken, 'he comes' means 'he comes from the deva world.' But in the latter, it means 'he comes even from the Brahma world.' In the Pāḷi text, however, it seems that only the latter meaning is stated. For it is said in the Puggalapaññatti: 'The non-returner should be known as a non-returner because he does not come back to this state of being. The stream-enterer and the once-returner should be known as such because they come back to this state of being.' Here, by 'not coming back to this state of being,' it shows the meaning: 'He is a non-returner because he does not come to this sense-sphere world.' But by 'coming back to this state of being,' it shows the meaning: 'He is a once-returner because both the stream-enterer and the once-returner come again once to this sense-sphere world.' Why? Because it is impossible for the two instances of the word 'itthatta' standing in consecutive sentences to have different meanings. And in the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta in the Middle Fifty:

Yo [M 0.0071] so mahārāja brahmā sabyāpajjho, so brahmā āgantā itthattaṃ. Yoso brahmā abyāpajjho, so brahmā anāgantā itthattanti.

That Brahma, great king, who is subject to affliction, is one who will come back to this state of being. That Brahma who is free from affliction is one who will not come back to this state of being.

Bhagavatā vuttaṃ. Tattha sabyāpajjhoti etena puthujjanena saha sotāpannasakadāgāmibhūtā brahmāno gahitā honti. Tehi paṭighānusayassa appahīnattā cetasikadukkhasaṅkhātaṃ byāpajjhaṃpi apahīnamevāti sabyāpajjhānāma. Āgantā itthattanti imaṃ kāmalokaṃ paṭisandhivasena puna āgamanasīlo āgamanappakatikoti attho. Tabbiparītena pacchimassa vākyassa attho veditabbo. Tesupana dvīsu sakadāgāmīsu purimassa anaññasā dhāraṇeneva sabbapathamaṃ ariya magga sotādhi gamana guṇena sotāpanno tveva nāmaṃ siddhanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Puggalagativasena panettha brahmaloke ṭhitānaṃ sattakkhattuparamatādibhāvoviya sakadāgāmibhāvopi natthi. Pathamadutīyaphalaṭṭhāpihi tattha anāgāmisaṅkhyameva gacchanti. Tasmā sakadāgāmīti idaṃ kāmajātikā naṃeva dutīyaphalaṭṭhānaṃ siddhaṃ nāmanti katvā tesaṃ kāmaloke eva heṭṭhuparupapatti vasena sakiṃ āgamanaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañca katvā pāḷiyaṃpi pañcannaṃ idha niṭṭhā sattakkhattuparamassa kolaṃkolassa ekabījissa sakadāgāmissa yoca diṭṭheva dhamme arahāti vuttanti. Sopana chabbidho hoti. Idhapatvā idhaparinibbāyī, tattha patvā tattha parinibbāyī, idhapatvā tattha parinibbāyī, tattha patvā idha parinibbāyī, idhapatvā tatthanibbattitvā idha parinibbāyī. Tatthapatvā idhanibbattitvā tatthaparinibbāyīti. Tattha idha patvā idha parinibbāyīti idha manussabhave sakadāgāmimaggaṃ patvā idhamanussa bhaveyeva arahattamaggaṃ labhitvā parinibbāyanadhammo. Tattha patvā tattha parinibbāyīti tasmiṃdevaloke sakadāgāmimaggaṃ patvā tasmiṃ devalokeyeva arahattamaggaṃ labhitvā parinibbāyanadhammo. Nibbattitvāti paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena uppajjitvā. Yesaṃ pana imaṃ lokanti padassa imaṃ manussalokanti attho. Tesaṃ so pañcavidhoyeva vutto, na chaṭṭho puggalo.

It was said by the Blessed One. Here, by 'subject to affliction,' Brahmas who are worldlings are included along with those who are stream-enterers and once-returners. Because the underlying tendency to aversion has not been abandoned by them, the affliction described as mental suffering is also unabandoned; thus they are called 'subject to affliction.' 'One who will come back to this state of being' means one who is by nature disposed to come back again to this sense-sphere world by way of rebirth-linking. The meaning of the latter sentence should be understood in the opposite way. But among these two—the stream-enterer and the once-returner—it should be understood that the name 'stream-enterer' is established for the first of them simply on account of the unique quality of having first attained the stream of the noble path. From the perspective of the person's destination, for those abiding in the Brahma world, there is no state of being a once-returner, just as there is no state of being a seven-times-at-most and so on. For even those established in the first and second fruits are counted there only as non-returners. Therefore, having considered that the term 'once-returner' is established as the name for those established in the second fruit who are of sense-sphere birth, it should be understood that their single return to the sense-sphere world by way of rebirth in a lower or higher plane is spoken of in the commentaries. And thus, it is also said in the Pāḷi that five attain finality here: the seven-times-at-most, the clan-to-clan, the one-seeder, the once-returner, and the one who is an arahant in this very life. But he (the once-returner) is sixfold: (1) one who attains here and attains final Nibbāna here; (2) one who attains there and attains final Nibbāna there; (3) one who attains here and attains final Nibbāna there; (4) one who attains there and attains final Nibbāna here; (5) one who attains here, is reborn there, and attains final Nibbāna here; (6) one who attains there, is reborn here, and attains final Nibbāna there. Here, 'one who attains here and attains final Nibbāna here' is one who, having attained the once-returner’s path in this human existence, attains the path of arahantship in this very human existence and is thus of a nature to attain final Nibbāna. 'One who attains there and attains final Nibbāna there' is one who, having attained the once-returner’s path in that deva world, attains the path of arahantship in that very deva world and is thus of a nature to attain final Nibbāna. 'Having been reborn' means having arisen by taking a rebirth-linking. But for those for whom the phrase 'this world' means 'this human world,' he is said to be of only five types; there is no sixth person.

Vibhāvaniyañca

And to be clarified.

“Pañcasu [M 0.0072] sakadāgāmīsu pañcamakova idhādhippeto, so hi ito gantvā puna sakiṃ idha āgacchatī”ti vuttaṃ.

“Among the five kinds of once-returners, the fifth is meant here; for, having gone from here, he comes back here only once more,” it is said.

Mahāparinibbāna suttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mahāvagga saṃyuttaṭṭhakathā yañca sopi chaṭṭho puggalo sakiṃ āgamanaṭṭhena āgatoyeva. Yasmāca sabbaññubuddhāpi yāva uparimaggo nāgacchati. Tāva pathamaphalaṭṭhabhūtā sattakkhattu paramatāyaṃviya dutīyaphalaṭṭhabhūtā sakiṃ āgamanappakatiyaṃ saṇṭhitāyeva honti. Tasmā idha koci dutīyaphalaṭṭho sakiṃ āgamanaṭṭhena nippariyāyena sakadā gāmīnāma na nahotīti sabbopi so chabbidho puggalo idha nippariyāyena sakadāgāmiyevanāma hotīti daṭṭhabbo. Sakadā gāmissa maggo sakadāgāmimaggo. So hi sayaṃ janakabhūto sakadāgāmīnaṃ janetabbaṃ janetīti idha janetabba janakasambandhena visesana visesitabbatā ñāyāgatā eva hoti. Yathā tissamātā phussamātāti.

But in the Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta and the Commentary on the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, that sixth person, too, is included by virtue of returning once. For, so long as the higher path has not been attained, even the All-Knowing Buddhas remain established in the state of one who has attained the first fruit, like one who is at most a seven-times-returner, and in the nature of one who has attained the second fruit, as a once-returner. Therefore, here, no one who has attained the second fruit is not, in the unqualified sense, called a once-returner by virtue of returning once. Thus it should be understood that all six types of persons here are unequivocally called once-returners. The path of a once-returner is the once-returner path. For it, being the generator, generates what is to be generated as a once-returner. Here, the relationship between the generated and the generator is understood as that between the qualified and the qualifier, as in ‘Tissa’s mother, Phussa’s mother.’

[57] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[57] But to be clarified:

Sāñāyāgatāeva nahoti. Payojanaṃ pana kiñci atthi. Payojanavasena aviruddhā hotīti iminā adhippāyenayaṃ vuttaṃ “kiñcāpi maggasamaṅgino tathāgamanāsambhavato phalaṭṭhoyeva sakadāgāmīnāma. Tassapana kāraṇabhūto purimuppanno maggo maggantarāvacchedanatthaṃ phalaṭṭhena visesetvā vuccati sakadāgāmimaggoti. Evaṃ anāgāmimaggo”ti. Taṃ na yujjati.

That principle is not accepted. However, there is some purpose. It is with the intention that ‘it is not inconsistent in terms of purpose’ that this was said: “Although for one endowed with the path, because it is impossible to come again in such a way, it is the one standing in the fruit who is called a ‘once-returner.’ But the previously arisen path, which is its cause, is specified by the one standing in the fruit for the purpose of demarcating it from other paths, and is called ‘the once-returner path.’ Similarly, ‘the non-returner path.’” That is not tenable.

Sakadāgāmimaggena sampayuttaṃ cittanti samāso.

‘The consciousness associated with the once-returner path’: this is the compound.

59. Orabbhāgiyasaṃyojanānaṃ sabbaso samucchinnattā paṭisandhivasena puna imaṃ kāmalokaṃ na āgacchatīti anāgāmī. Ekantena brahmalokaparāyanoeva hotīti attho. Idañca kevalaṃ imassa maggassa ānubhāvavaseneva vuttaṃ. Uparimagga vipassanāya [M 0.0073] pana āgatāya so tasmiṃ ṭhāneyeva arahatta maggaparāyanopi hotiyeva. Anāgāmissa tatīyaphalaṭṭhassamaggo. Tena sampayuttaṃ cittanti viggaho.

59. Because the lower fetters have been completely cut off, one does not come back again to this sense-sphere world by way of rebirth-linking; thus one is a non-returner (anāgāmī). The meaning is that one is exclusively destined for the brahmā world. And this is said solely by the power of this path. However, when insight into the higher path has arisen, in that very state one may indeed be destined for the path of arahantship. The path of the non-returner, who is one standing in the third fruit. ‘The consciousness associated with that’: this is the analysis (viggaho).

60. Mahapphalakāritāguṇayogena pūjāvisesaṃ arahatīti arahā. Khīṇāsavo catutthaphalaṭṭho. Arahato bhāvo arahattaṃ, catutthaphalaṃ. Tassa maggo. Tena sampayuttacittanti nibbacanaṃ. Pisaddena pāḷiyaṃ vibhatte maggacittappabhede sampiṇḍeti. Tattha dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ tāva pathamamagge jhānanāmena vuttesu pañcasu vāresu pathame suddhikapaṭipadāvāredvinnaṃ catukkapañcakanayānaṃ vasena navacittāni honti. Tathā suddhikasuññatāya suññatappaṭipadāya suddhikappaṇihite appaṇihitappaṭipadāyacāti pañcasu vāresu dasannaṃ nayānaṃ vasena pañcacattālīsacittāni honti. Tathā maggasatipaṭṭhānādīhi ekūnavīsatiyā nāmehi vuttesu paccekaṃ pañcasu vāresūti vīsatiyā nāmehi vutte vārasate dvinnaṃ nayasatānaṃ vasena navacittasatāni honti. Puna catūhi adhipatīhi yojetvā vuttesu catūsu vārasatesu aṭṭhannaṃ nayasatānaṃ vasena tīṇi sahassāni chasatānica hontīti. Evaṃ pathamamagge naya sahassavasena cattāricittasahassāni pañcacitta satānica honti. Tathā sesamaggesupīti evaṃ catūsu maggesu catunnaṃ naya sahassānaṃ vasena aṭṭhārasa magga citta sahassāni honti. Saccasatipaṭṭhāna vibhaṅgesu pana vīsatinaya sahassānaṃ vasena navutimaggacittasahassāni. Maggavibhaṅge aṭṭhavīsatiyā naya sahassānaṃ vasena satasahassaṃ chabbīsatisahassāni ca maggacittāni hontīti. Aṭṭhakathāsupana nayabhedāeva vuttā. Nacitta bhedāti.

60. One is an ‘arahant’ because one is worthy of special veneration on account of the quality of bringing about a great fruit. One is a destroyer of the taints, one standing in the fourth fruit. The state of an arahant is arahantship, the fourth fruit. The path to that. ‘The consciousness associated with that’—this is the derivation. By the word ‘also’ (pi), it summarizes the divisions of path-consciousness distinguished in the Pāli text. Therein, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, with regard to the first path, in the five sections spoken of by the name of jhāna, in the first section on the pure practice-path, there are nine consciousnesses by way of the two methods, the fourfold and the fivefold. Similarly, in the five sections—the pure voidness, the voidness practice-path, the pure signless, and the signless practice-path—there are forty-five consciousnesses by way of ten methods. Likewise, when spoken of under nineteen names such as the path’s foundations of mindfulness, etc.—that is, when spoken of under twenty names—in one hundred sections, there are nine hundred consciousnesses by way of two hundred methods. Further, when combined with the four dominants, in four hundred sections, there are three thousand six hundred consciousnesses by way of eight hundred methods. Thus, in the first path, there are four thousand five hundred consciousnesses by way of one thousand methods. Similarly in the remaining paths. Thus, in the four paths, there are eighteen thousand path-consciousnesses by way of four thousand methods. But in the Vibhaṅga of the Truths and the Vibhaṅga of the Foundations of Mindfulness, there are ninety thousand path-consciousnesses by way of twenty thousand methods. In the Vibhaṅga of the Path, there are one hundred and twenty-six thousand path-consciousnesses by way of twenty-eight thousand methods. In the commentaries, however, only the divisions of the methods are stated, not the divisions of consciousness.

[58] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[58] But what is to be clarified:

Pisaddena saccavibhaṅge āgataṃ saṭṭhisahassabhedaṃ nayaṃ saṅgaṇhātīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ imasmiṃ kusalanigame na vattabbaṃ.

It is said that by the word ‘also’ (pi), it includes the sixty-thousand-fold method found in the Saccavibhaṅga. That should not be stated in this conclusion on the wholesome.

Sohi saṭṭhisahassabhedo nayo vipākaṭṭhāneeva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatoti.

For that sixty-thousand-fold method is found in the commentary only in the section on result.

[59] Yañca tattha

[59] And as to what is said there:

Paṭipadābhedaṃ [M 0.0074] anāmasitvā kevalaṃ suññato appaṇihi toti dvidhā vibhattoti vuttaṃ. Taṃ nayujjati.

It is said that, without touching upon the division of the practice-path, it is divided in two ways, merely as voidness and the signless. That is not tenable.

Pāḷiyañhi paṭipadābhedo ādimhiyeva āgatoti. Naca ādimhi suññato appaṇihitoti dvidhā vibhatto nirantaravāro atthīti.

For in the Pāli text, the division of the practice-path is found right at the beginning. And there is no continuous section at the beginning that is divided in two as voidness and the signless.

[60] Yañca tattha

[60] And as to what is said there:

Suññato eko nayo, appaṇihito eko, paṭipadā visiṭṭhā suññatā cattāro, appaṇihitā cattāroti katvā dasanayā hontīti adhippāyena evaṃ jhāna nāmena dasadhā vibhattoti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yujjatiyeva.

It is said that it is divided tenfold by the name of jhāna with the intention that there are ten methods, taking it as: voidness is one method, the desireless is one, voidness specified by the path of practice are four, and the desireless specified by the path of practice are four. That too is certainly not tenable.

Na hi suññatādayo idha nayānāma honti. Tesu pana eke kasmiṃ dve dve catukkapañcakanayāeva idha nayānāmāti. Etena tathā maggasatipaṭṭhāniccādikaṃpi sabbaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ hotīti. [Maggacittaṃ]

For voidness and so on are not what are called ‘methods’ here. Rather, in each of them, the two methods—the fourfold and the fivefold—are what are called ‘methods’ here. By this, all such things as the path, the foundations of mindfulness, impermanence, etc., are also refuted. [Path-Consciousness]

61. Phalacitte phalanti vipākabhūto aṭṭhaṅgika maggo. Sampayuttadhammasamūhovā. Sotāpattiyā adhigataṃ phalaṃ. Tena sampayuttaṃ, tatthavā pariyāpannaṃ cittanti sotāpatti phala cittaṃ. Esanayo dutīyatatīyesupi. Arahattañca taṃ phalañcāti arahattaphalaṃ. Tena sampayuttaṃ, tasmiṃvā pariyāpannaṃ cittanti nirutti.

61. In fruition-consciousness, ‘fruit’ (phala) is the resultant Eightfold Path, or the collection of associated states. The fruit attained through stream-entry. ‘The consciousness associated with that, or included therein,’ is the stream-entry fruition-consciousness. This is the method for the second and third as well. Arahantship and that fruit is the fruit of arahantship. ‘The consciousness associated with that, or included therein,’ is the definition.

62. Saṅgahagāthāyaṃ catumaggappabhedenāti catukkhattuṃ pattabbattā catubbidhānaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikamaggānaṃ pabhedena. Kasmāpana te catukkhattuṃ pattabbāti. Vuccate. Sotāpattimagge tāva saddhādīni indriyāni mudūni honti, tasmā so diṭṭhivicikicchāeva samucchindituṃ sakkoti. Aññepana kāmarāgabyāpādepi tanubhūtepi kātuṃ nasakkoti. Dutīyamagge tāni thokaṃ paṭūni honti. Tasmā so kāmarāgabyāpāde tanubhūte kātuṃ sakkoti. Samucchindituṃ pana nasakkohiyeva. Tatīyamagge tāni paṭutarāni honti. Tasmā so kāmarāgabyāpāde samucchindituṃ sakkoti. Rūpārūpa rāgamānuddhaccāvijjāyopana [M 0.0075] samucchindituṃ nasakkotiyeva. Catuttha maggepana tāni indriyāni paṭutamāni honti. Tasmā so tāca aññeca sabbepi pāpadhamme samucchindituṃ sakkoti. Evaṃ catukkhattuṃ pavattamānāeva pariniṭṭhitakiccattā te maggā catukkhattuṃ pattabbā hontīti. Kusalaṃ cittaṃ catumaggappabhedena catudhā mataṃ. Pākaṃpi tassa catubbidhassa kusalassa phalattā tathā catudhāmataṃ. Iti anuttaraṃ cittaṃ aṭṭhadhā matanti yojanā. Natthi attano uttaraṃ adhikaṃ etassāti anuttaraṃ.

62. In the summary verse, ‘by the fourfold division of the path’ means by the division of the four kinds of Noble Eightfold Path, because they are to be attained four times. But why are they to be attained four times? It is said: In the path of stream-entry, the faculties such as faith are tender; therefore, it can cut off only wrong view and doubt. But it cannot even attenuate sensual lust and ill will. In the second path, those faculties are somewhat keen; thus, it can attenuate sensual lust and ill will, but it certainly cannot cut them off. In the third path, they are keener; therefore, it can cut off sensual lust and ill will, but it certainly cannot cut off lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. But in the fourth path, those faculties are keenest; therefore, it can cut off those and all other evil states. Thus, because their function is completed only by occurring four times, these paths are to be attained four times. The construction is: ‘Wholesome consciousness is considered fourfold by the fourfold division of the path. Its resultant, too, being the fruit of that fourfold wholesome consciousness, is likewise considered fourfold. Thus the supramundane consciousness is considered eightfold.’ ‘There is nothing higher or superior to it’; thus it is ‘supramundane’ (anuttaraṃ).

63. Kasmā panettha kriyacittaṃnāmana gahitanti, kriyānuttarassa abhāvāti, kasmā panassa abhāvoti. Maggacittassa ekacittakkhaṇikattāti. Yadi hi taṃ lokiyakusalaṃviya nānākkhaṇesu pavatteyya. Tadā niranusayasantānepi pavattitvā kriyā nuttaraṃnāma siyāti. Kasmāpana taṃ ekacittakkhaṇikameva hotīti. Maggassa mahānubhāvattāti. Kathañca mahānubhāvoti. Vuccate. Ariyamaggohi nāma sakiṃ pavattamānoyeva attanā pahātabbe kilese puna anuppādadhammataṃ āpādetvā pajahati. Ayamassa eko ānubhāvo. Vipākañca kusalakriyajavanaṃviya javanakicca yuttaṃ yadā kadāci samāpajjanakkhamañca katvā attano anantarato paṭṭhāya janeti. Ayamassa dutīyo ānubhāvo. Tasmā tassa kilesappahānatthāyapi puna uppādetabbakiccaṃnāma natthi. Tathā samāpatti atthāyapīti. Sacepi hi koci ahaṃ phalaṃ samāpajjituṃ na icchāmi. Pubbe laddhaṃ maggameva samāpajjissāmīti parikammaṃ kareyya. Tadā pubbe sakiṃ uppajjitvā niruddhamaggacetanānubhāvena phalacittameva pavatteyya. Na maggacittaṃ. Kasmā, appaṭibāhi yānubhāvattā maggassa. Ayañhi maggānubhāvonāma kenaci chandena vā vasenavā ajjhāsayenavā parikammenavā paṭibāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyoyeva hotīti.

63. But why is functional consciousness not taken here? Because there is no supramundane functional consciousness. But why is there none? Because path-consciousness is of a single mind-moment. For if it were to occur over various moments like a mundane wholesome consciousness, then it could arise even in a continuity free from underlying tendencies and would be called a supramundane functional consciousness. But why is it of only a single mind-moment? Because of the great power of the path. And how is it of great power? It is said: The noble path, arising just once, abandons the defilements to be abandoned by it, having rendered them of a nature not to arise again. This is one of its powers. And starting from the moment immediately after itself, it generates its fruit, which is fit for the function of impulsion like a wholesome or functional impulsion and is capable of being entered upon at any time. This is its second power. Therefore, there is no need for it to be generated again for the purpose of abandoning defilements, nor for the purpose of attainment. For even if someone were to make the preliminary effort, thinking, 'I do not wish to enter upon fruition, I will enter upon the very path I previously attained,' then by the power of the path-volition that arose once before and ceased, only fruition-consciousness would arise, not path-consciousness. Why? Because of the unhindered power of the path. For this power of the path cannot be obstructed by any will, control, disposition, or preliminary effort.

64. Dvādasākusalānevantiādi sabbesaṃ catubbhūmaka cittānaṃ jātivasena saṅgaho. Evaṃ iminā vuttappakārena akusa lāni [M 0.0076] dvādasevahonti. Kusalāni ekavīsatieva. Vipākānichattiṃ seva. Kriyacittāni vīsatievāti ṭīkāyaṃ yojīyati. Kecipana kusalānaṃ vipākānañca uparivaḍḍhamānattāevasaddaṃ ādiantapadesveva yojesuṃ. Catupaññāsadhātiādi bhūmivasena saṅgaho. Kāmepariyā pannāni cittāni catupaññāsadhā īraye katheyya. Rūpe pannarasa. Arūpe dvādasa. Tathā anuttare pariyāpannāni cittāni aṭṭhadhā īrayeti yojanā. Etthaca anuttareti lokuttara bhūmiyaṃ. Sā pana duvidhā saṅkhatabhūmi, asaṅkhatabhūmīti. Saṅkhatāpi catubbidhā. Yathāha –

64. ‘The twelve unwholesome states,’ etc., is a summary of all consciousnesses of the four planes by way of their class. Thus, in the manner stated, it is construed in the subcommentary that the unwholesome states are just twelve, the wholesome states just twenty-one, the resultant states just thirty-six, and the functional states just twenty. Some, however, because the wholesome and resultant states increase further on, applied the word ‘just’ only to the terms at the beginning and the end. ‘Fifty-fourfold,’ etc., is a summary by way of planes. The construction is: one should speak of the consciousnesses included in the sense-sphere plane as fifty-fourfold; in the fine-material sphere, fifteen; in the immaterial sphere, twelve. Similarly, one should speak of the consciousnesses included in the supramundane plane as eightfold. Here, ‘supramundane’ refers to the supramundane plane. This, however, is twofold: the conditioned plane and the unconditioned plane. The conditioned is also fourfold, as it is said:

Yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti pathamāya bhūmiyā pattiyā.La. Dutīyāya.La. Tatīyāya.La. Catutthāya bhūmiyā pattiyāti.

At the time when one develops supramundane jhāna for the attainment of the first plane; … for the second; … for the third; … for the attainment of the fourth plane.

Tattha bhūmīti sāmaññaphalaṃ adhippetanti vuttaṃ. Pathamamaggaphalayu gaḷaṃvā pathamabhūmi.La. Catuttha maggaphala yugaḷaṃ catutthabhūmīti evaṃpi yujjatiyeva. Atthatopana rāgattayapariggahavimuttiyā tebhūmakadhammesu apariyāpannatā saṅkhātena avatthā visesena yutto dhammaviseso. Soca kilesappahāna visesena catubbidho jātoti.

Here, it is said that ‘plane’ is intended to mean the fruit of recluseship. The pair of the first path and fruit is the first plane… the pair of the fourth path and fruit is the fourth plane; this too is fitting. In terms of meaning, however, it is a special Dhamma endowed with the special state designated as non-inclusion in the dhammas of the three planes—through release from the grasp of the threefold lust—and it becomes fourfold by way of the distinction in abandoning defilements.

[61] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[61] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Itarabhūmiyoviya lokuttarabhūmināma visuṃ natthi. Nava vidhadhammasamūhoeva tesaṃ bhūmipariyāyoti katvā yaṃ vuttaṃ. “Katthaci apariyāpannāni navavidhalokuttara dhammasamūhekadesabhūtāni rukkhe sākhā tyādīsu viya anuttare cittānīti vuttānī”ti. Taṃ nayujjati.

The statement that was made, taking it that, unlike other planes, there is no separate plane called the supramundane plane, but that the ninefold collection of Dhammas itself is their designation as a plane—namely: ‘The supramundane consciousnesses, being a part of the ninefold collection of unincluded supramundane Dhammas, are like branches on a tree, etc.’—that is not appropriate.

Duvidhāhi bhūmi avatthābhūmi, okāsabhūmīti. Tattha avatthā bhūmieva nippariyāyabhūmi. Na itarā. Sā hi okāsabhūmināma dhammānaṃ taṃ taṃ avatthāvisesavaseneva siddhāti. Taṃ taṃ avatthā visesotica [M 0.0077] heṭṭhā vuttanayena kāmāvacaratādi avatthā viseso daṭṭhabbo. Apica ekattiṃsabhūmiyopi kusalākusaladhammānaṃ hīnapaṇītaoḷārikasukhumatā saṅkhātehi avatthāvisesehieva sijjhantīti.

Planes are twofold: state-planes (avatthābhūmi) and location-planes (okāsabhūmi). Of these, the state-plane alone is the plane in the primary sense, not the other. For the location-plane is established only by virtue of the particular state of the respective dhammas. And that particular state should be seen as the state of being sense-sphere, etc., in the way stated below. Moreover, even the thirty-one planes are established by virtue of the particular states of wholesome and unwholesome dhammas, designated as inferior and superior, gross and subtle.

65. Evaṃ catubbhūmaka cittāni saṅkhepato niddisitvā idāni puna vitthārato niddisanto itthantiādigāthamāha. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā. Athavāpana itthaṃ yathāvuttappakārena ekunanavutippabhedaṃ mānasaṃ cittaṃ ekavīsasataṃ katvā vicakkhaṇā paṇḍitā vibhajantīti.

65. Having thus briefly indicated the consciousnesses of the four planes, now, indicating them again in detail, he utters the verse beginning ‘Itthaṃ.’ Herein, this is the construction: Or again, the discerning wise divide the mind, which has eighty-nine distinctions as stated, making it one hundred and twenty-one.

[62] Ṭīkāsu pana

[62] But in the subcommentaries:

Gāthāya pubbaddhaṃ purimagāthānaṃ nigamanaṃ katvā aparaddhameva ārabbhantaraṃ katvā yojenti. Taṃ kathamekūna navutividhaṃ cittaṃ ekavīsasataṃ hotīti iminā nasametīti.

They construe the verse by taking the first half as a conclusion to the preceding verses and taking only the second half as the start of a new section. That does not accord with the question: ‘How does the eighty-ninefold consciousness become one hundred and twenty-one?’

Idāni taṃ ekavīsasatavibhāgaṃ dassento kathaṃ.La. Hotīti pucchitvā vitakkavicārapīti sukhekaggatā sahitantiādimāha. Tattha pathamajjhāna sotāpattimaggacittanti ettha pañcaṅgikena pathamajjhānena yutto sotāpattimaggo pathamajjhānasotāpattimaggo. Tena sampayuttaṃ cittanti samāso.

Now, showing that division into one hundred and twenty-one, having asked, 'How does it become...?' he speaks the passage beginning, 'Accompanied by initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness.' Here, in the phrase 'the first-jhāna stream-entry path-consciousness,' the compound is as follows: the stream-entry path conjoined with the five-factored first jhāna is the 'first-jhāna stream-entry path'; the consciousness associated with that.

[63] Ṭīkāsu pana

[63] But in the subcommentaries:

“Pathamajjhānañca taṃ sotāpattimaggacittañcā”ti yojenti. Taṃ na yuttaṃ.

They construe it as: 'the first jhāna and that stream-entry path-consciousness.' This is not correct.

Na hi jhānaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Naca cittaṃ jhānaṃ. Aññañhi jhānaṃ, aññaṃ cittanti.

For jhāna is not consciousness, nor is consciousness jhāna. Jhāna is one thing, consciousness another.

[64] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

[64] And in the Vibhāvanī:

“Jhānaṅgavasena pathamajjhāna sadisattā pathamajjhānañcā”ti vuttaṃ. Tampi na yuttaṃ.

It is said: 'And it is the first jhāna because of its similarity to the first jhāna with respect to the jhāna factors.' That too is not correct.

Na hi pañcaṅgikaṃ lokuttarajjhānaṃ pathamajjhānasadisaṭṭhena pathamajjhānasaññaṃ labhatīti sakkā vattuṃ. Tañhi sayameva attano pañcaṅgikabhāvena [M 0.0078] nippariyāyato pathamajjhānaṃnāma hotīti. Idañhi jhānaṃnāma lokiyaṃvā hotu lokuttaraṃvā. Yaṃ pañcaṅgikaṃ hoti. Taṃ sayameva pathamajjhānanti siddhaṃ. Yaṃ caturaṅgikaṃ. Tiyaṅgikaṃ. Duvaṅgikaṃ. Puna duvaṅgikaṃ. Taṃ sayameva pañcamajjhānanti siddhanti. Lokuttarevā dutīyādibhāvassa uppattikkamavasena asiddhattā evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For it cannot be said that the five-factored supramundane jhāna obtains the designation 'first jhāna' on account of its similarity to the first jhāna. For by its very own five-factored nature, it is, in the primary sense, the first jhāna. Indeed, any jhāna, whether mundane or supramundane, that is five-factored, is thereby established as the first jhāna. That which is four-factored, three-factored, two-factored, and again two-factored, are thereby established as the subsequent jhānas up to the fifth. It should be understood that this is said because, in the supramundane sphere, the state of being second, third, etc., is not established by way of an order of attainment.

[65] Yañca tattha

[65] And what is said therein:

Sadisabhāveneva lokuttare tesaṃ pañcaṅgikādīnaṃ jhāna vohārasiddhatādīpanatthaṃ. “Pādakajjhāna sammasitajjhāna puggalajjhāsayesu hi aññataravasena taṃ taṃ jhānasadisattā vitakkādiaṅgapātubhāvena cattāropi maggā pathamajjhānādi vohāraṃ labhantā paccekaṃ pañcadhā vibhajantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tampi nayujjatiyeva.

And what was said therein to show that in the supramundane sphere the establishment of the designation 'jhāna' for those five-factored states, etc., is only by way of similarity—namely: 'For the four paths obtain the designations "first jhāna," etc., and are each divided fivefold, through the appearance of the factors such as initial application, due to their similarity to this or that jhāna in one or another way, that is, by way of the basic jhāna, the comprehended jhāna, or the individual’s disposition'—that too is indeed not appropriate.

Na hi maggā pathamajjhānādi vohāraṃ labhanti. Añño hi maggo, aññaṃ jhānanti. Apica, yadi upanijjhāyanaṭṭhena paccanīkajjhāpanaṭṭhenaca jhānaṃnāma siyā. Tadā lokuttarajjhānānieva sātisayato jhānānināma siyuṃ. Na itarāni. Tāni hi kasiṇādinimittamattaṃ upecca nijjhāyanti. Paccanīkadhammeca vikkhambhanamattena jhāpenti. Lokuttarāniyevapana atigambhīraṃ abhiduddasaṃ nibbānaṃ upecca nijjhāyanti. Paccanīkadhammeca samūle sānusaye sabbaso samucchindanavasena jhāpentīti. Etthaca appanājhānānaṃ pañcaṅgikabhāvonāma pakatiyā eva siddho hotīti na pathamajjhānikesu maggaphalesu pādakajjhā nādinā paccayavisesena kiccaṃ atthi. Caturaṅgikādi bhāvo pana tena paccayavisesena vinā na sijjhati. Asatihi tasmiṃ sabbaṃpi jhānaṃ pañcaṅgikameva bhavissatīti. Tattha yathā lokiyajjhānesu ādikammikakāle tassa tassa dutīyādikassa jhānassa upacārabhūtā bhāvanā sayaṃ vitakkādiyuttā samānāpi vitakkādīsu ādīnavadassanaññāṇenaceva idāni avitakkaṃ jhānaṃ uppādessāmi, idāni avicāraṃ jhānaṃ uppādessāmīti evamādinā pavattena ajjhāsaya [M 0.0079] visesenaca yuttattā kāci vitakkavirāgabhāvanānāma hoti. Kāci vicāra virāgabhāvanā nāma. Kāci pītivirāgabhāvanā nāma. Kāci sukhavirāgabhāvanānāma. Kācī rūpavirāgabhāvanānāma. Asaññigāmīnaṃ pana saññāvirāgabhāvanānāma hoti. Sā attano attano jhānaṃ avitakkaṃvā avicāraṃvā appītikaṃvā upekkhāsaha gataṃvā kātuṃ sakkoti. Jhānesu vasībhūtakālepana ādīnavadassanaññāṇena vinā kevalaṃ ajjhāsayamattena yaṃyaṃ jhānaṃ icchati. Taṃ taṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjatiyeva. Evamevaṃ idhapi tassa tassa maggassa upacārabhūtā vuṭṭhānagāmini vipassanāsaṅkhātā bhāvanā sayaṃ vitakkādiyuttā samānāpi nānāsattiyuttā hoti. Kāci vitakkavirāgabhāvanānāma. Kāci vitakkavicāravirāgabhāvanā nāma. Kāci vitakkavicārapīti virāgabhāvanānāma. Kāci vitakkavi cārapītisukhavirāgabhāvanānāma. Tattha yā vitakkaṃ virājetuṃ atikkāmetuṃ sakkoti. Sā vitakkavirāgabhāvanānāma. Esa nayo sesāsupīti.

For the paths do not obtain the designation 'first jhāna,' and so forth. For the path is one thing, and jhāna is another. Moreover, if jhāna were so called by the meaning of close meditation and the burning up of opposing states, then only the supramundane jhānas would pre-eminently be called 'jhānas,' not the others. For those others meditate closely only on a sign such as a kasiṇa, and they burn up opposing states only by way of suppression. But the supramundane jhānas meditate closely on Nibbāna, which is extremely profound and very difficult to see, and they burn up the opposing states with their root and underlying tendencies completely by way of eradication. Here, the five-factored nature of the absorption jhānas is naturally established, so for the first-jhāna path and fruition, there is no need for a special condition such as a base jhāna. However, the four-factored state and so on are not accomplished without that special condition. For in its absence, every jhāna would be only five-factored. In this regard, just as in the mundane jhānas, at the time of the initial practitioner, the development that is the access to the second jhāna and so on, though itself endowed with initial application and other factors, is called 'the development of dispassion toward initial application' because it is endowed with the knowledge of seeing the danger in initial application, etc., and with the special disposition that proceeds thus: 'Now I will arouse a jhāna free from initial application,' 'Now I will arouse a jhāna free from sustained application,' and so on. Similarly, there is 'the development of dispassion toward sustained application,' 'the development of dispassion toward rapture,' 'the development of dispassion toward happiness,' and 'the development of dispassion toward form.' For those going to the non-percipient realm, there is 'the development of dispassion toward perception.' Each of these can make its respective jhāna free from initial application, free from sustained application, without rapture, or accompanied by equanimity. When one has mastery over the jhānas, one can enter any desired jhāna merely by disposition, without needing the knowledge of seeing the danger. In the same way, here too, the development that is the access to each path—known as 'insight leading to emergence'—though itself endowed with initial application and other factors, is connected with various powers. Some is called 'the development of dispassion toward initial application'; some, 'the development of dispassion toward initial and sustained application'; some, 'the development of dispassion toward initial application, sustained application, and rapture'; and some, 'the development of dispassion toward initial application, sustained application, rapture, and happiness.' Among these, that which is capable of causing dispassion towards and transcending initial application is called 'the development of dispassion toward initial application.' This same principle applies to the rest.

66. Kassapana balena sā vipassanā nānāsatti yuttā hotīti. Vuccate, pādakajjhānabalenāti eko theravādo. Sammasitajjhāna balenāti eko. Puggalajjhāsaya balenāti eko. Tattha yaṃ yaṃ jhānaṃ tassā vipassanāya pādakatthāya āsanne samāpajjīyati. Taṃtaṃ pādakajjhānaṃnāma. Taṃce pathamajjhānaṃ hoti. Vipassanā pākatikāeva. Sace dutīyajjhānaṃ hoti. Vipassanā vitakkavirāgasattiyuttā hoti. Magge avitakkaṃ jhānaṃ niyāmetuṃ sakkoti. Esanayo sesesupi pādakajjhānesūti ayaṃ pādakavādo. Pādakajjhāne sati taṃsadisameva magge jhānaṃ hoti. Asatipana magge pathamajjhānameva hoti. Sammasi tajjhānaṃvā puggalajjhāsayovā magge jhānaṅgaṃ niyametuṃ nasakkotīti adhippāyoti. Pādakajjhāne sati taṃvā aññaṃvā yaṃyaṃ jhānaṃ sammasīyati. Taṃce pathamajjhānaṃ hoti. Vipassanā pākati kāeva. Sace dutīyajjhānaṃ hoti. Vipassanā vitakkavirāgasatti [M 0.0080] yuttā hoti. Magge avitakkaṃ jhānaṃ niyāmetuṃ sakkoti. Esanayo sesesupi sammasitajjhānesūti ayaṃ sammasitavādo. Vipassanāya ārammaṇabhāvena saha caritattā sammasitajjhānameva pādakajjhānato ajjhāsayatoca balavataranti adhippāyoti.

66. By what power, it may be asked, is that insight endowed with various powers? It is said: 'By the power of the base jhāna'—this is one school of the elders. 'By the power of the jhāna that is comprehended'—this is another. 'By the power of the individual's disposition'—this is another. Therein, whatever jhāna is attained nearby for the purpose of being a basis for that insight, that is called the base jhāna. If that is the first jhāna, the insight is natural. If it is the second jhāna, the insight is endowed with the power of dispassion toward initial application; it is able to determine that the jhāna on the path is without initial application. This is the method for the remaining base jhānas as well. This is the doctrine of the base jhāna. When there is a base jhāna, the jhāna on the path is similar to it. But when there is none, the jhāna on the path is only the first jhāna. The meaning is that neither the jhāna that is comprehended nor the individual's disposition is able to determine the jhāna factors on the path. When there is a base jhāna, whatever jhāna—that one or another—is comprehended, if it is the first jhāna, the insight is natural. If it is the second jhāna, the insight is endowed with the power of dispassion toward initial application; it is able to determine that the jhāna on the path is without initial application. This is the method for the remaining comprehended jhānas as well. This is the doctrine of the comprehended jhāna. The meaning is that because it occurs together with being an object for insight, the jhāna that is comprehended is more powerful than the base jhāna and the disposition.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But it should be clarified:

Vipassanāpādakaṃ kiñcijhānaṃ natthīti imasmiṃ vāde vuttaṃ. Taṃ aṭṭhakathāya na sameti.

'There is no jhāna that is a basis for insight,' this is said in this doctrine. That does not agree with the commentary.

Pādakajjhāne sati taṃvā aññaṃvā magge yaṃyaṃjhānaṃ icchati. Taṃtaṃ jhānaṃ ijjhati. Vipassanāpi icchānurūpaṃ vitakkavirāgādibhāvaṃ pattā hotīti puggalajjhāsayavādo. Yathā lokiyajjhānesu āsanne vuṭṭhitajjhānaṃ uparijjhānupacāra bhāvanāya upatthambhakamattaṃ hoti. Na pana uparijjhāne jhānaṃ attasadisaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti. Ajjhāsayoeva uparijjhāne jhānaṅgaṃ niyāmeti. Evamevaṃ idhapi pādakajjhānaṃ vipassanāya tikkha visadabhāvatthāya balavupanissa yo hoti. Ajjhāsayoeva vipassanaṃ vitakkavirāgādibhāvaṃ pāpetvā magge jhānaṅgaṃ niyāmetīti adhippāyoti. Yo panettha vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāeva magge jhānaṅgaṃ niyāmetīti mahāṭṭhakathā vādo. Tatthapi puggalajjhāsayavisesabalena vitakkavirāgādisatti visesayuttā vuṭṭhānagāmini vipassanāevāti attho veditabbo. Kāmañcettha aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ theravādānaṃ aññamaññaṃ avirodho vuttoviya dissati. Imepana vādā aññamaññaṃ saṃsanditvā pavattā nahonti. Paccekaṃ sabbaṃ lokuttarajjhānaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā pavattā. Tasmā nasakkā tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ virodho pariharitunti. Etthaca jhānalābhīnaṃ vipassanākamme pādakajjhānasamā pajjanaṃnāma bhagavatāeva suṭṭhuvihitaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ cūḷasuññatasutte –

This is the doctrine of individual disposition: When there is a base jhāna, whichever jhāna one wishes for on the path—that one or another—that jhāna is accomplished. Insight, too, attains a state of dispassion toward initial application, etc., in accordance with one’s wish. Just as in the mundane jhānas, the jhāna one has recently emerged from is merely a support for the development that is the access to a higher jhāna; it cannot make the jhāna in the higher jhāna similar to itself. Disposition alone determines the jhāna factors in the higher jhāna. Exactly so here, the base jhāna is a strong decisive support for the sharpness and clarity of insight. The meaning is that disposition alone, having led insight to a state of dispassion toward initial application, etc., determines the jhāna factors on the path. Herein, the doctrine of the Great Commentary is that insight leading to emergence itself determines the jhāna factors on the path. In that case, the meaning should be understood thus: by the power of a special individual disposition, the insight leading to emergence is itself endowed with special powers such as dispassion toward initial application. And although in the Aṭṭhasālinī it seems as if the non-contradiction of these three schools of the elders is stated, these doctrines do not proceed having been compared with one another. Each proceeds having individually perfected all the supramundane jhānas. Therefore, it is not possible to resolve their mutual contradiction. Here, for those who have obtained jhāna, the attainment of the base jhāna in the practice of insight has been well laid down by the Blessed One himself. And this was stated in the Cūḷasuññata Sutta:
