Idhānanda bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi pathamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Dutīyaṃ jhānaṃ. Tatīyaṃ jhānaṃ. Catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So ajjhattaṃ suññataṃ manasikaroti. Tassaceajjhattaṃsuññatāya cittaṃ [M 0.0081] napakkhandati. Napasīdati. Tena bhikkhunā tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ santhape tabbaṃ, sannisādetabbaṃ, ekodi kātabbaṃ, samādahātabbantiādi.

Here, Ānanda, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. He gives attention to internal emptiness. If his mind does not leap up at, does not grow confident in, does not settle upon, and is not liberated in internal emptiness, then that monk should steady his mind right on that former sign of concentration, settle it, unify it, and concentrate it.

Tattha suññataṃ manasikarotīti vipassanākammaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitteti pādakajjhānasamādhi nimitte. Navanipāteca –

Therein, 'he gives attention to emptiness' refers to the work of insight. 'On that very same former sign of concentration' means on the sign of the concentration that is the base jhāna. And in the Book of the Nines:

Pathamaṃ pāhaṃ bhikkhavejhānaṃ nissāya āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi.La. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ pāhaṃ bhikkhave jhānaṃ nissāya āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmīti vuttaṃ.

'Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who is dependent on the first jhāna.... Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who is dependent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' it is said.

67. Imesupana tīsuvādesu puggalajjhāsayavādo balavataroviya khāyati. Lokiyajjhānesupi hi pādakajjhānaṃnāma icchitabbameva. Tañca uparijjhānassa upacārabhāvanāya tikkhavisada bhāvatthāyaeva hoti. Ajjhāsayoevapana upacāra bhāvanāya vitakkavirāgādibhāvaṃ sādheti. Upacārabhāvanāeva uparijjhāne jhānaṅgaṃ niyāmeti. Evamevaṃ idhapi pādakajjhānabalena tikkhavisada bhāvapattā vuṭṭhānagāmini vipassanāeva ajjhāsayavisesabalena vitakkavirāgādisattivisesayuttā hutvā magge nānājhānāni sādheti. Asati pana ajjhāsayavisese taṃtaṃ pādakajjhānānurūpaṃ ajjhāsayasāmaññaṃsaṇṭhāti. Tasmā ajjhāsayavisese asati pādakajjhānameva pamāṇaṃ hoti. Satipana tasmiṃ soeva pamāṇanti yuttaṃ. Icchi ticchita lokiyajjhāna samāpajjana sadisañhi sabbajjhānesu ciṇṇavasībhūtānaṃ maggesu icchitajjhāna nibbattananti. Yo panettha pādakajjhānādivasena pavatto viseso. So sabbopi vipassanā visesatthāya eva hoti. Vipassanā visesoeva magge jhānaṅgaṃ niyāmetīti katvā aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ visuddhi maggeca vipassanāva pamāṇaṃ katvāvuttā. So sabbopi viseso pādakajjhānena vinā nasijjhatīti katvā maggavibhaṅgamaggasaṃyuttaṭṭha kathāsu pādakajjhānaṃ eva pamāṇaṃ katvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Yasmā pana pāḷiyaṃ –

67. But among these three doctrines, the doctrine of individual disposition appears to be the strongest. For even in the mundane jhānas, the base jhāna is indeed desirable. And that is for the sake of the sharpness and clarity of the access development for the higher jhāna. But disposition itself accomplishes the state of dispassion toward initial application, etc., for the access development. The access development itself determines the jhāna factors in the higher jhāna. Exactly so here, insight leading to emergence—having attained sharpness and clarity by the power of the base jhāna—endowed with special powers such as dispassion toward initial application by the power of a special disposition, accomplishes the various jhānas on the path. But in the absence of a special disposition, a general disposition corresponding to the respective base jhāna is established. Therefore, in the absence of a special disposition, the base jhāna itself is the standard. But when that special disposition exists, it alone is the proper standard. For the production of a desired jhāna on the paths for those who have practiced and gained mastery in all jhānas is like the attainment of any wished-for mundane jhāna. Whatever distinction has occurred here on account of the base jhāna, etc., all that is only for the sake of distinction in insight. Because the distinction in insight itself determines the jhāna factors on the path, in the Aṭṭhasālinī and the Visuddhimagga insight is stated as the standard. Because all that distinction is not accomplished without a base jhāna, it should be understood that in the commentaries on the Maggavibhaṅga and the Maggasaṃyutta, the base jhāna is stated as the standard. But since in the Pāḷi:

Idha [M 0.0082] gahapati bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi. La. Pathamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati. Idaṃpi kho pathamajjhānaṃ abhisaṅkhataṃ abhisañcehayitaṃ yaṃkhopana kiñci abhisaṅkhataṃ abhisañcetayitaṃ. Tadaniccaṃ. Taṃ nirodhadhammanti pajānāti so tattha ṭhito āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pāpuṇāti. La. Dutīyaṃ jhānaṃ, tatīyaṃ jhānaṃ, catutthaṃ jhānaṃ, mettā cetovimuttiṃ. Karuṇā, muditā, upekkhāceto vimuttiṃ, ākāsānañcā yatanaṃ.La. Ākiñcaññā yatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati. Ayaṃpikho ākiñcaññā yatanasamāpatti abhisaṅkhatā abhisañcetayitā. Yaṃ khopana kiñci abhisaṅkhataṃ.La. Khayaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

Here, householder, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, attains and dwells in the first jhāna. He reflects thus: 'This first jhāna is conditioned and volitionally produced; and whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.' Understanding this, he abides there and attains the destruction of the taints. He attains and dwells in the second jhāna, the third jhāna, the fourth jhāna, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, the liberation of mind through compassion, the liberation of mind through appreciative joy, and the liberation of mind through equanimity, the base of infinite space, the base of nothingness. He attains and dwells in the base of nothingness. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of nothingness is also conditioned and volitionally produced; and whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is subject to cessation.' He attains the destruction of the taints.

Evaṃekādasanipāte –

Thus in the Book of the Elevens:

Idhānanda bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ pathamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. So yadeva tattha hoti rūpagataṃ vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ, te dhamme aniccato dukkhato anattato samanupassati. So tattha ṭhito āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pāpuṇāti. No ce āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pāpuṇāti. Teneva dhammarāgena tāya dhammanandiyā pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā upapātiko hoti. Tattha parinibbāyī anāvattidhammo tasmā lokāti.

Here, Ānanda, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He regards whatever phenomena there that are connected with form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent, as suffering, as not-self. Standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very delight in the Dhamma, that joy in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who arises spontaneously. There he attains final Nibbāna, not liable to return from that world.

Ādinā mālukyaputtasutta anupadasuttādīsuca anekesu suttantesu aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu ekekāya samāpattiyā vuṭṭhāya vuṭṭhitasamāpattidhammasammasanameva āgataṃ. Napana aññajjhāna sammasanaṃ. Tasmā satipi yogīnaṃ icchāvasena pādakajjhānato aññajjhānasammasane pādakajjhānameva pamāṇanti sakkā viññātunti. Ettāvatā sammasitavādo sabbadubbaloti siddho hotīti. Yepana aṭṭhasamāpattilābhinopi jhānaṃ pādakaṃ akatvāva maggaṃ uppādenti. Pathamajjhānamevavā pādakaṃ katvā ajjhāsayavisesaṃ akatvā [M 0.0083] maggaṃ uppādenti. Pathamajjhānamattalābhinovā hutvā tameva pādakaṃ katvā maggaṃ uppādenti. Yeca sukkhavipassakā hutvā maggaṃ uppādenti. Tesaṃ pathamajjhānikova maggo hotīti veditabbo. Apica ye pakatiyāva aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu ciṇṇavasībhūtā honti. Te vināpi āsannapādakena yaṃyaṃjhānaṃ icchanti. Taṃtaṃ jhānaṃ tesaṃ maggesu nasamijjhatīti navattabbaṃ.

In the Mālukyaputta Sutta, the Anupada Sutta, and many other discourses, it is stated that upon emerging from each of the eight attainments, one reflects only on the phenomena of the attainment just left. There is no reflection on other jhānas. Therefore, even if meditators wish to reflect on other jhānas apart from the base jhāna, the base jhāna itself should be taken as the standard. This can be understood thus. At this point, the claim that one must reflect is entirely weak and thus refuted. Furthermore, even those who attain the eight attainments may generate the path without making any jhāna the foundation, or they may make only the first jhāna the foundation, without any special inclination, and generate the path. Or they may attain only the first jhāna and make that alone the foundation to generate the path. And those who practice dry insight and generate the path—their path should be understood as based solely on the first jhāna. Moreover, those who are naturally skilled and have mastered the eight attainments—even without a proximate foundation, it should not be said that whichever jhāna they wish for will not succeed in their path.

66. [66] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

66. [66] Whatever is to be clarified.

“Sacepana puggalassa tathāvidho ajjhāsayo natthi. Heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānato vuṭṭhāya uparuparijjhānadhamme sammasitvā uppāditamaggo pādakajjhānaṃ anapekkhitvā sammasitajjhānasadiso hotīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

If, however, a person does not have such an inclination, having emerged from progressively lower jhānas and contemplating the progressively higher jhāna states, the path produced is said to be similar to the contemplated jhāna without relying on the foundational jhāna. This should be examined.

Na hi ārammaṇamattabhūtaṃ sammasitajjhānaṃ uparimaṃpi samānaṃ āsanne vuṭṭhitajjhānato balavataraṃ bhavituṃ arahati. Āsanne vuṭṭhitasseva cittasantānaṃ visesetuṃ samatthabhāvato. Tato yevahi so sammasitavādo sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu kecivādapakkhe eva thapitoti. Nanu puggalajjhāsayavādopi tathāthapitoevāti. Saccaṃ, sopana lokiyajjhānānaṃ uppattividhānena saha saṃsandikattā yuttataroeva hotīti.

For a contemplated jhāna, existing only as an object, cannot be stronger than the jhāna one has just emerged from, even if it is a higher one, because only that from which one has just emerged is capable of bringing distinction to the mental continuum. Therefore, in all the commentaries, that doctrine of contemplation is placed only on the side of the 'some say' view. Is it not so that the doctrine of personal disposition is also placed in the same way? True, but that doctrine is more justified, as it corresponds with the method of arising of the mundane jhānas.

[67] Etena yaṃ tattha vuttaṃ.

[67] By this, what was stated there:

“Uparuparijjhānato pana vuṭṭhāya heṭṭhima heṭṭhimajjhāna dhamme sammasitvā uppāditamaggo sammasitajjhānaṃ anapekkhitvā pāda kajjhānasadiso hoti. Heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānatohi uparu parijjhānaṃ balavatara”nti. Taṃpi paṭikkhittaṃ hoti.

“But having emerged from progressively higher jhānas and contemplated the progressively lower jhāna factors, the path produced is similar to the foundational jhāna, without relying on the contemplated jhāna. For the progressively higher jhānas are stronger than the progressively lower jhānas.” This too is refuted.

Na hi pādakajjhānaṃ uparima bhūtattāyeva balavataraṃ hoti. Pādakabhūtattāyeva pana balavataraṃ hotīti.

For the foundational jhāna is not stronger merely because it is higher. Rather, it is stronger precisely because it serves as the foundation.

[68] Yañca tattha

[68] And as for what is stated there:

Magge vedanāniyamopana pādakajjhānādīnaṃ vasena nasiddho. Aññathā vipassanā yāyakāyacivedanāya yuttā hutvā tehi [M 0.0084] niyamitāya ekekāya maggavedanāya saddhiṃ ghaṭi yeyyāti iminā adhippāyena “vedanāniyamopana sabbatthapi vuṭṭhānagāmini vipassanāniyamena hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tampi na yujjati.

The determination of feeling on the path, however, is not established by way of the foundational jhānas, etc. Otherwise, insight, being associated with whatever feeling, would be connected with each path-feeling regulated by them. With this intention, it was said, "The determination of feeling in all cases occurs through the regulation of insight leading to emergence." This, too, is not fitting.

Pādakajjhānādīnaṃ vaseneva vipassanāya saha vedanāniyamassa siddhattā. Tathāhi taṃtaṃ pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya vipassantassa vipassanā ādito kadāci somanassasahagatāvā hoti. Kadāci upekkhāsahagatāvā. Maggavuṭṭhānakālepana yadipādakajjhānaṃ somanassajjhānaṃ hoti. Vipassanā ekantena somassasaha gatāva hutvā maggena saddhiṃ ghaṭiyatīti. Vuttañhetaṃ saḷāyatana vibhaṅgasutte –

For the determination of feeling together with insight is established precisely by way of the foundational jhānas, etc. Thus, for one who emerges from a particular foundational jhāna and practices insight, the insight is from the outset sometimes accompanied by joy and sometimes by equanimity. But at the time of the path's arising, if the foundational jhāna is a joy-associated jhāna, the insight, being exclusively accompanied by joy, combines with the path. As this was stated in the Saḷāyatana Vibhaṅga Sutta:

Tatra bhikkhave yā cha nekkhammassitā upekkhā. Tā nissāya tā āgamma yāni cha nekkhammassitāni somanassāni. Tāni pajahatha. Tāni samatikkamatha. Evametesaṃ pahānaṃ hoti. Evametesaṃ samatikkamo hotīti.

“Here, monks, relying on and depending on the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation, you should abandon, you should transcend the six kinds of joy based on renunciation. Thus is their abandonment; thus is their transcendence.”

Aṭṭhakathāyañca aṭṭhasu samāpattīsu pathamādinica tīṇijhānāni suddhasaṅkhāreca pādake katvā vipassanaṃ āraddhānaṃ catunnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pubbabhāga vipassanā somanassasahagatā vā hoti. Upekkhāsaha gatāvāvuṭṭhānagāminīpana somanassasahagatāva hoti. Catutthajjhānādīni pādakānikatvā vipassanaṃ āraddhānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pubbabhāgavipassanā purima sadisāva. Vuṭṭhānagāminīpana upekkhāsahagatāva hoti. Idaṃ sandhāyayā chanekkhammassitā.La. Pajahathāti vuttaṃ. Ajjhāsayavisesena saha maggavuṭṭhānepi esevanayo. Balavavipassanākāle hi vipassanāratināma suṭṭhu paṇītatarā hoti. Sakalasarīraṃ pharamānā ajjhottharamānā pavattati. Yathāha –

And in the commentary it is said: For the four monks who, having made the first three jhānas and the pure formations among the eight attainments their foundation, begin insight, their preliminary insight is accompanied by joy or by equanimity. But the insight leading to emergence is exclusively accompanied by joy. For the five monks who, having made the fourth jhāna and so on their foundation, begin insight, their preliminary insight is just like the former, but the insight leading to emergence is exclusively accompanied by equanimity. It was with reference to this that 'the six... based on renunciation... abandon' was said. This same principle applies also to the arising of the path, along with a difference in inclination. For at the time of strong insight, the delight in insight is exceedingly refined; it proceeds pervading and suffusing the entire body. As it is said:

Suññāgāre paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī rati hoti, sammadhammaṃ vipassatoti.

“For a monk who has entered a solitary abode, whose mind is calmed, a non-human delight arises when he rightly contemplates the Dhamma.”

Tasmā [M 0.0085] tadā pādakajjhānavisesenavā ajjhāsayavisesena vā vinā vipassanā upekkhāsahagatā na hoti. Ekantena somanassasahagatāva hotīti. Etthapana sabbajjhānesu vasībhūtassa yaṃkiñci ekaṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā taṃ pā aññaṃvā maggeyaṃyaṃ jhānaṃ icchati. Maggavuṭṭhānakāle ajjhāsayabalena taṃtaṃjhānānurūpaṃ vipassanāyaca maggeca vedanā pariṇāmo veditabbo. Napana vedanāniyāmonāma visuṃ vattabboti.

Therefore, at that time, without a distinction of foundational jhāna or a distinction of inclination, insight accompanied by equanimity does not occur; it occurs exclusively accompanied by joy. But here, for one who has mastered all the jhānas, having made any jhāna whatsoever the basis, and desiring whichever jhāna for the path—be it that one or another—at the time of the path's arising, the transformation of feeling in insight and in the path should be understood as being in accordance with that particular jhāna, through the power of inclination. However, a determination of feeling should not be stated separately.

67. Saṅgahagāthāyaṃ anuttaraṃ aṭṭhavidhaṃ cittaṃ jhānaṅgayogabhedena ekekaṃ pañcadhā katvā cattālīsavidhanti ca vuccatīti yojanā. Idāni sabbāni mahaggatā nuttaracittāni pañcavidhe jhāna koṭṭhāse saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ yathāca rūpāvacarantiādimāha. Yathā rūpāvacaraṃ cittaṃ pathamādijjhānabhede gayhati. Jhāna bhedasiddhe pathamajjhānikacittādike pañcavidhe cittabhede saṅgayhati, tathā anuttarañca cittaṃ pathamādijjhānabhede saṅgayhati. Āruppañcacittaṃ upakkhekaggatā saṅkhātena pañcamajjhānena yuttattā pañcame jhāne pañcamajjhānikacittabhede saṅgayhati. Tasmā ekekaṃ patamādikaṃ pathamajjhānikacittādikaṃ jhānaṃ jhānacittaṃ ekādasa vidhaṃ hoti. Antetu antimabhūte pañcamajjhānikacittabhedepana jhānaṃ cittaṃ tevīsatividhaṃ bhaveti yojanā. Etthaca jhānasaddena taṃsampayuttaṃ cittameva vuccati. Na hi jhānaṃ ekādasavidhaṃvā tevīsatividhaṃvā hotīti.

67. In the summary verse, the construction is that the eightfold supramundane consciousness is said to be fortyfold, by making each one fivefold according to the division of its connection with the jhāna factors. Now, to show how all sublime and supramundane consciousnesses are included in the fivefold jhāna categories, it is said, “just as the form-sphere,” etc. Just as form-sphere consciousness is included in the divisions of the first jhāna and so on, and when the divisions of jhāna are established, is included in the fivefold divisions of consciousness such as the first-jhānic consciousness, so too is the supramundane consciousness included in the divisions of the first jhāna and so on. And formless consciousness, being associated with equanimity and one-pointedness, which are characteristics of the fifth jhāna, is included in the fifth jhāna, in the division of fifth-jhānic consciousness. Therefore, each of the first jhānas and so on, that is, the first-jhānic consciousness and so on, as jhāna-consciousness, is of eleven kinds. But finally, in the ultimate division of fifth-jhānic consciousness, the jhāna-consciousness becomes twenty-threefold. And here, by the word “jhāna,” only the consciousness associated with it is meant. For jhāna itself is not elevenfold or twenty-threefold.

[69] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[69] But as for what is in the Vibhāvanī:

“Rūpāvacaracittaṃ pathamajjhānantiādinā vuccatītica āruppañcāpi pañcamajjhānavohāraṃ labhatī”ti ca vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

“It has been said that form-sphere consciousness is spoken of as the first jhāna and so on, and also that formless consciousness obtains the designation of the fifth jhāna.” This is not fitting.

Na hi cittaṃ pathamajjhānaṃ hoti. Naca pañcamajjhānavohāraṃ labhatīti.

For consciousness is not the first jhāna, nor does it obtain the designation 'fifth jhāna'.

[70] Yāca imissāgāthāyaṃ aparāpi yojanā vuttā. Sāpi na yuttāeva.

[70] And the other explanation that is given for this verse is also unsuitable.

Tathā saddassa pathamādijjhānabhedeti padassa purato paṭhitattāti. Evaṃ yathā vibhajitabbe ekadese vibhatte sabbaṃ ekūnanavutividhaṃ cittaṃ ekavīsasataṃ katvā vibhattaṃnāma hoti. Tathā vibhajitvā idāni taṃsaṅgahaṃ dassento antimagāthamāha. Puññaṃ sattatiṃsavidhaṃ hoti. Tathā pākaṃ dvipaññāsavidhaṃ hoti. Iti ekūnanavutividhāni cittāni ekavīsasataṃ katvā budhā paṇḍitā āhu kathesuṃ. Kathentivā vibhajanti vicakkhaṇāti vuttaṃ hotīti.

Because the word 'thus' is read before the phrase 'the distinctions of the first jhāna, etc.' Thus, when one part that should be divided has been divided, all the eighty-nine kinds of consciousness are said to be divided as one hundred and twenty-one. Having divided them thus, now, to show that summary, he states the final verse: Meritorious consciousness is of thirty-seven kinds; similarly, resultant consciousness is of fifty-two kinds. Thus the wise and learned have stated the eighty-nine kinds of consciousness, having made them one hundred and twenty-one. Or, it is said: 'The discerning ones declare and analyze'.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus, of the commentary on the Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha named the Paramatthadīpanī,

Catutthavaṇṇanāya cittasaṅgahassa

of the fourth explanation, the Compendium of Consciousness,

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

the Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning is concluded.

Cetasikasaṅgaha paramatthadīpanī

The Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning on the Compendium of Mental Factors

68. Evaṃ [M 0.0087] cittaṅgahaṃ dassetvā idāni anupattaṃ cetasika saṅgahaṃ dassento catūhi sampayogalakkhaṇehi saha vacanatthañca sarūpatthañca tāva dassetuṃ ādi gāthamāha. Tattha ekuppādanirodhācaekālambaṇavatthukāti catussampayogalakkhaṇadassanaṃ. Ceto yuttāti vacanatthadassanaṃ. Cetasiyuttā cetasāvā yuttā cetasikāti dassanato. Dvipaññāsadhammāti sarūpadassanaṃ. Cetasikāti pana siddhapada dassanaṃ. Tattha dhammānaṃ anāgatabhāvasaṅkhātā pubbantato uddhaṃ pajjanaṃ gamanaṃ sarūpato pātubhavanaṃ uppādo. Jātīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbepihi saṅkhata dhammā anāgatabhāvapubbā eva honti. Tato paccayasāmaggiṃ labhitvā paccuppannabhāvaṃ gacchanti. Tato nirujjhitvā atītabhāvaṃ gacchantīti. Nirujjhanaṃ nirodho. Sarūpavināso bhaṅgo aniccatā maraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yā cittassa jāti, sāyeva phassādīnaṃ. Yā cittassa jarā, yaṃ cittassa maraṇaṃ, yaṃ cittassa ārammaṇaṃ vatthu. Tadeva phassādīnantiādinā heṭṭhā vuttanayena eko uppādo etesanti ekuppādā. Eko nirodho etesanti ekanirodhā. Ekuppādāca te ekanirodhācāti ekuppādanirodhā. Uttarapade ekasaddassa lopo. Evaṃ paratthapi. Ekaṃ ālambaṇaṃ etesanti ekālambaṇā. Ekaṃ vatthu etesanti ekavatthukā. Ekālambaṇāca te ekavatthukācāti ekālambaṇavatthukā. Ālambaṇaṃ panettha ekacittassapi bahudeva hoti. Ekattaṃpana upanetvā ekaṃ ālambaṇanti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

68. Having thus shown the Compendium of Consciousness, now, to show the Compendium of Mental Factors in its turn, he first states the initial verse to show the verbal meaning and the essential meaning along with the four characteristics of association. Therein, 'arising and ceasing together, having a single object and basis' is the demonstration of the four characteristics of association. 'Associated with consciousness' is the demonstration of the verbal meaning. The derivation of the term is: 'conjoined in consciousness' or 'conjoined with consciousness,' hence 'mental factors' (cetasikā). 'Fifty-two states' is the demonstration of their nature. 'Mental factors,' however, is the demonstration of the established term. Herein, for states, arising is their emergence from the prior state designated as the future state, their manifestation in their own nature. This is called birth. For all conditioned states first exist in a future state. Then, having obtained an assemblage of conditions, they pass into the present state. Then, having ceased, they pass into the past state. Cessation is ceasing. The destruction of their nature is called dissolution, impermanence, death. Whatever is the birth of consciousness, that itself is the birth of contact and the others. Whatever is the aging of consciousness, the death of consciousness, the object and basis of consciousness, that itself is the object and basis of contact and the others. Thus, in the way stated above, they have one arising, thus they are 'of single arising.' They have one cessation, thus they are 'of single cessation.' They are of single arising and of single cessation, thus 'of single arising and cessation.' In the latter part of the compound, there is elision of 'eka.' The same applies in other cases. They have one object, thus 'of single object.' They have one basis, thus 'of single basis.' They are of single object and of single basis, thus 'of single object and basis.' Herein, the object, even for a single consciousness, can be multiple. However, it should be understood that it is spoken of as 'a single object' by bringing them together under a unity.

[71] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[71] But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Ekato uppādoca nirodhoca yesaṃ, te ekuppādanirodhā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

it is said: 'Those for whom arising and cessation occur together, they are of single arising and cessation.' That is not well-said.

Na hi ekakkhaṇe ekato uppādamattena ekuppādatā idha adhippetā. Athakho vuttanayeneva adhippetā. Vuttañhetaṃ mūlaṭīkāyaṃ –

For 'singleness of arising' is not intended here merely by arising together at a single moment. Rather, it is intended in the way that has been stated. For this has been said in the Mūlaṭīkā:

Ekakalāpapariyāpannānaṃ rūpānaṃsahevauppādādippavattito

Ekassakalāpassauppādādayo ekekāva hontīti.

Since the arising, etc., of the material phenomena included in a single kalāpa proceed together, the arising, etc., of a single kalāpa are indeed singular.

Tatrāyaṃ yojanā. Ekuppādanirodhāca ekālambaṇavatthukā ca hutvā yedhammā cetoyuttā. Te dvipaññāsadhammā cetasikā matāti. Bhāvapadhānaṃpivā ettha yuttaṃ. Visesaneca nissakkavacanaṃ. Ekuppādanirodhabhāvena ekālambaṇa vatthuka bhāvenaca yedhammā cetoyuttā. Te dvipaññāsadhammā cetasikānāma matā ñātāti. Etthaca ye cetoyuttā. Te cetasikāti vutte cittassa sahajātapaccayuppannarūpānipi tadāyattavuttitāya ekantena cittasambandhīni hutvā cetoyuttāni cetasikāni nāma siyuṃ. Tasmā tesaṃ nivattanatthaṃ ekuppādanirodhāca, ekā lambaṇavatthukāti vuttaṃ. Tānihi cittena khaṇato sahuppannānipi bhinnasantānattā yā cittassa jāti, sāeva tesanti imaṃ lakkhaṇaṃpi nānubhonti. Aññaṃhi rūpasantānaṃ. Aññaṃ arūpasantānanti. Phassādīnaṃpana uppādamattameva cittena saha ekaṃ nahoti. Athakho nirodhopi ālambaṇaṃpi vatthupi sabbaṃ ekamevāti ñāpanatthaṃ eka nirodhādiggahaṇaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi evaṃ avutte sakkā tathā jānitunti. Yasmāpana yathā bahujanasantako eko goṇo tissassa goṇo dattassa goṇoti evaṃ visuṃ visuṃpi vattabboyeva hoti. Evamevaṃ uppādo nirodhoca ekasmiṃ rūpārūpakalāpe ekovasamānopi phassassa uppādo vedanāya uppādo pathavidhātuyā uppādo āpodhātuyā uppādoti evamādinā nayena visuṃ visuṃpi vattabboyeva. Tasmā suttantesu –

Herein, this is the construction: Those states which, having a single arising and cessation and a single object and basis, are associated with consciousness—those fifty-two states are considered mental factors. Or, a construction with an abstract noun is also suitable here, and the adjective is an absolute expression. Those states which are associated with consciousness by way of having a single arising and cessation and by way of having a single object and basis—those fifty-two states are known as mental factors. Here, if it were said, 'Whatever is associated with consciousness is a mental factor,' then even the material phenomena that are products of the co-nascence condition with consciousness, being dependent on it for their occurrence and thus entirely connected with consciousness, would be called mental factors. Therefore, to exclude them, it is said, 'of single arising and cessation, and of single object and basis.' For although they arise simultaneously with consciousness for a moment, because their continuities are different, they do not experience this characteristic: 'Whatever is the birth of consciousness, that itself is their birth.' For the continuity of matter is one thing, and the continuity of non-matter is another. However, it is not only the arising of contact and the others that is one with consciousness. Rather, it should be understood that the inclusion of 'single cessation,' etc., is stated to make known that the cessation, the object, and the basis are all one and the same. For if it were not stated thus, it would not be possible to know it so. Furthermore, just as a single ox owned by many people can be referred to individually as 'Tissa's ox' and 'Datta's ox,' so too, although arising and ceasing are single within a material-and-immaterial group, the arising of contact, the arising of feeling, the arising of the earth element, the arising of the water element, and so on, can each be referred to separately. Therefore, in the suttas:

Vedanāya uppādo paññāyati. Vayo paññāyati. Ṭhikāya aññatthaṃ paññāyati. Saññāya. Saṅkhārānaṃ. Viññāṇassa. La. Paññāyatīti vuttaṃ. Tathā yo bhikkhave pathavidhātuyā uppādo [M 0.0089] ṭhitiabhinibbatti pātubhāvo. Dukkhasseso uppādo rogānaṃ ṭhiti jarā maraṇassa pātubhāvo. Yo bhikkhave āpodhātuyā. Yo bhikkhave tejo dhātuyā. Yo bhikkhave vāyodhātuyā. Yo bhikkhave cakkhussa.La. Manassa uppādo.La. Jarāmaraṇassa pātubhāvoti.

'The arising of feeling is discerned, its passing away is discerned, its alteration while it persists is discerned. Of perception... of formations... of consciousness... is discerned,' it is said. Similarly: 'Bhikkhus, whatever is the arising, persistence, production, and manifestation of the earth element, that is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, the manifestation of aging and death. Bhikkhus, of the water element... Bhikkhus, of the fire element... Bhikkhus, of the air element... Bhikkhus, of the eye... of the mind... the manifestation of aging and death.'

Vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Itarathā jīvitindriyādīnapi ekasmiṃ kalāpe bahubhāvo vattabbo siyā. Yo arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ āyu ṭhiti avaṭṭhitīti hi vuttaṃ. Tathā vikārarūpānaṃ. Sabbesaṃpivā cakkhādīnaṃ upādārūpānaṃ. Catunnaṃ cahābhūtānaṃ upādāyarūpantica catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādotica vuttanti. Kāyalahutā cittalahutādayopana atthavisesadīpanatthaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā vuttā. Soca atthavisesoupari āvi bhavissatīti. Ayametthaparamatthadīpanā.

It should be understood that this has been said. Otherwise, a multiplicity would have to be acknowledged for the life faculty and others within a single kalāpa. For it has been said: 'That which is the life-span, duration, and persistence of immaterial states...' Similarly for derivative matter, and for all derived matter such as the eye, etc. And it is said: 'matter derived from the four great elements' and 'sensitivity derived from the four great elements.' But lightness of body, lightness of mind, etc., are stated as divided into two for the purpose of clarifying a specific meaning. And that specific meaning will become clear below. This is the elucidation of the ultimate meaning here.

[72] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[72] But in the Vibhāvanī,

Imamatthaṃ asallakkhetvā yaṃ vuttaṃ “yadi ekuppādamatteneva cetoyuttāti adhippetā. Tadā cittena saha uppajjamānānaṃ rūpadhammānampi cetoyuttatā āpajjeyyāti eka nirodhaggahaṇaṃ. Evampi cittānuparivattino viññattidvayassa pasaṅgo nasakkā nīvāretuṃ. Tathā ekato uppādo vā nirodhovā etesanti ekuppādanirodhāti parikappentassa puretaramuppajjitvā cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe nirujjhamānānampi rūpadhammānanti ekālambaṇaggahaṇaṃ. Ye evaṃ tividhalakkhaṇā. Te niyāmato ekavatthukā yevāti dassanatthaṃ. Ekavatthukaggahaṇanti. Alamatipapañcenā”ti. Sabbaṃ taṃ niratthakameva.

Not having discerned this meaning, what was said—'If “associated with consciousness” is intended to mean merely arising together, then association with consciousness would also apply to material states arising together with consciousness; for this reason, there is the inclusion of “single cessation.” Even so, the contingency of the two intimations that follow upon consciousness cannot be prevented. Similarly, for one who conceives “of single arising and cessation” as “their arising or cessation is together,” the inclusion of “single object” is to exclude even those material states that, having arisen earlier, cease at the moment of consciousness's dissolution. To show that those with these three characteristics are, by necessity, of a single basis, there is the inclusion of “single basis.” Enough of this excessive proliferation!'—all of that is quite meaningless.

69. Kathañca dvipaññāsa hontīti pucchitvā pathamaṃ dvipaññāsa sarūpaṃ tīhi rāsīhi vibhajitvā dassento kathantiādimāha. Tattha phusatīti phasso. Phusanti sampayuttakā dhammā etenāti phasso. Phusanamattamevavā etanti phasso. Phusanañcettha ārammaṇassa iṭṭhāniṭṭharasaṃ āhacca upahacca gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yato tadanubhavanti [M 0.0090] vedanā pātubhavati. Phassapaccayā vedanāti hi vuttaṃ. Svāyaṃ phusanalakkhaṇo. Nanucāyaṃ arūpadhammo. Naca arūpadhammā appaṭighasabhāvā kiñci phusantīti. Saccaṃ, ayaṃpana phusanā kārenaca pavattati. Yañca phusantehi sādhetabbaṃ. Tañca kiccaṃ sādheti. Tasmā ayaṃ phassotica phusanalakkhaṇotica vutto. Kiṃpana sādhetīti. Ārammaṇarasānurūpaṃ cittassa vikārapatti. Vedanāvisesuppattiṃvā. Ayañca attho ambilakhādādike disvā aparassa kheḷuppādādīsu pākaṭoti.

69. Having asked, 'And how are there fifty-two?' he first states the passage beginning 'How?' to show the nature of the fifty-two by dividing them into three groups. Therein, 'it contacts' (phusati), hence 'contact' (phasso). 'Associated states contact by means of it,' hence 'contact.' Or, 'it is mere contacting,' hence 'contact.' And here, contacting should be seen as the grasping of the object's agreeable or disagreeable flavor by striking it. From which feeling, which experiences that, arises. For it is said: 'With contact as condition, feeling arises.' Thus, this has the characteristic of contacting. But is this not an immaterial state? And do immaterial states, being non-resistant by nature, contact anything? True. But this proceeds in the manner of contacting, and it accomplishes the function that is to be accomplished by things that contact. Therefore it is called 'contact' and 'having the characteristic of contacting.' What does it accomplish? The undergoing of a modification by consciousness in conformity with the object's flavor, or the arising of a specific feeling. And this meaning is evident in such cases as the production of saliva in another person upon seeing someone eating a sour fruit.

[73] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[73] But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Kheḷuppādādiviya daṭṭhabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Evañcasati idaṃ upamā mattaṃ siyā. Atipākaṭāyapana phassappavattiyā dassana midanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

it is said: 'It should be seen as like the production of saliva, etc.' This being so, this would be a mere simile. But it should be understood that this is a demonstration of the occurrence of contact which is extremely evident.

70. Vedayatīti vedanā. Ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavati. Aviditaṃvā ārammaṇarasaṃ sampayuttānaṃ taṃsamaṅgipuggalānaṃ vā viditaṃpākaṭaṃ karotīti attho. Vindantiva etāya sattā sātaṃvā asātaṃvā labhantīti vedanā. Vedayitamattamevavā etanti vedanā. Pāḷiyaṃpana –

70. It feels, thus it is feeling. It experiences the taste of the object. Or, it makes the taste of the object, previously unknown, known and manifest to those associated with it or to the individuals endowed with it—this is the meaning. Or, beings obtain through it what is agreeable or disagreeable; thus, it is feeling. Or, it is merely the act of feeling; thus, it is feeling. For in the Pāli it is said:

Vedayati vedayatīti kho bhikkhave tasmā vedanāti vuccati. Kiñca vedayati, sukhaṃpi vedayati. Dukkhaṃpi vedayati. Adukkhamasukhaṃpi vedayatīti vuttaṃ.

‘It feels, it feels,’ thus, bhikkhus, it is called feeling. And what does it feel? It feels pleasure, it feels pain, it feels neither-pain-nor-pleasure—thus it is said.

Nanu sabbepi cittacetasikā dhammā ārammaṇarasānubhavanappa katikāevāti tepi vedanānāma siyunti. Nasiyuṃ. Tehi kiccantarabyāvaṭā honti. Ārammaṇarasaṃ ujuṃ anubhavituṃ nasakkonti. Attano attano kiccaṃ karontāva ekadesamattena anubhavanti. Vedanāyevapana anaññakiccatāya anubhavanakicce ādhipaccayogatāyaca issarabhāvena anubhavatīti sāeva vedanānāma bhavituṃ arahatīti. Evañcakatvā rājaggabhojana rasānubhavane tesaṃ sūdasadisatā vedanāyaevaca rājasadisatā vuttāti.

But are not all consciousness and mental factors by nature those that experience the taste of an object? Should they too be called ‘feeling’? No, they should not. They are engaged in other functions. They cannot directly experience the taste of an object. While performing their own functions, they experience it only partially. But feeling, due to its having no other function, its pre-eminence in the act of experiencing, and its sovereignty, experiences in a dominant manner; thus, it alone deserves to be called ‘feeling.’ Having explained thus, just as cooks are compared to the other mental factors in experiencing the tastes of the royal meal, so feeling itself is compared to the king.

71. Sañjānātīti [M 0.0091] saññā. Puna jānanatthaṃ saññāṇaṃ karotīti attho. Ayañhi pubbe gahitasaññānena sañjānanakālepi puna jānanatthaṃ saññāṇaṃ karotiyevāti. Sāhi evaṃ punappunaṃ saññāṇaṃ katvā uppajjamānā thirasaññābhāvaṃ patvā yāvatāyukaṃpi bhavantaraṃ patvāpi sattānaṃ appamuṭṭhabhāvaṃ sādheti. Micchā bhinivesasaññābhāvaṃ patvāca ime satte sabbaññu buddhehipi bodhetuṃ asakkuṇeyye karotīti. Tathāhi sā puna sañjānanatthaṃ nimittakaraṇe dārutacchakasadisātica. Yathāgahita nimittavasena abhinivesakaraṇe hatthidassaka andhasadisātica. Upaṭṭhitavisayaggahaṇe tiṇapurisakesu migapotakasadisātica vuttāti. Pāḷiyaṃpana –

71. It perceives, thus it is perception (saññā). It means that it makes a sign for the purpose of knowing again. For even at the time of perceiving by means of a previously grasped sign, it indeed makes a sign for the purpose of knowing again. Thus, arising having repeatedly made a sign in this way, and having attained the state of firm perception, it accomplishes for beings the state of not being forgotten, even throughout their lifespan and having reached another existence. And having attained the state of wrong, stubborn perception, it makes these beings incapable of being enlightened even by omniscient Buddhas. Indeed, it is said that in making a sign for the purpose of repeated recognition, it is like a wood-carver; and in forming fixed views based on the grasped sign, it is like the blind men shown an elephant; and in grasping presented objects, it is like a young deer towards scarecrows. For in the Pāli it is said:

Sañjānāti sañjānātītikho bhikkhave tasmā saññāti vuccati. Kiñca sañjānāti. Nīlaṃpi sañjānāti. Pītakaṃpi sañjānātītiādi vuttanti.

‘It perceives, it perceives,’ thus, bhikkhus, it is called perception. And what does it perceive? It perceives blue, it perceives yellow, and so forth—thus it is said.

72. Cetayatīti cetanā. Sampayuttadhamme tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇevā kiccevā abhisandahati punappunaṃ ghaṭeti, tattha pabandhavasena nirantaraṃ pavattamāne karotīti attho. Pakappeti vā te. Saṃvidahati ārammaṇapaṭilābhāyavā kammasiddhiyā abhisaṅkharoti. Āyūhativā te. Ārammaṇe sampiṇḍeti ekato samo sarante karotīti attho. Tathāhi sā āyūhanarasāhica saṃvidhānapaccupaṭṭhānātica vuttā. Tāyahi tasmiṃ nirantaraṃ ussukkana byāpāravasena pavattamānāya taṃ sampayuttāpi attano attano kiccaṃ kurumānā tasmiṃ tatheva pavattantīti. Teneva sā sakicca parakicca sādhaka jeṭṭhasissa mahāvaḍḍhaki ādisadisāti vuttāti.

72. It intends, thus it is volition (cetanā). It repeatedly directs and connects the associated phenomena to each respective object or function, making them act continuously in an unbroken stream there; this is the meaning. Or, it plans them. It arranges or constructs for the sake of obtaining an object or accomplishing an action. Or, it accumulates them. It consolidates them on the object, making them proceed together as one and uniformly; this is the meaning. Indeed, it is said to have the characteristic of accumulation and the manifestation of arrangement. For, when it operates continuously through persistent effort and striving, the associated factors, while performing their respective functions, also operate in the same way therein. Therefore, it is said to be like a chief carpenter or a senior student who accomplishes their own tasks and the tasks of others.

[74] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[74] However, in the Vibhāvanī,

Ceteti saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇe byāpāramāpajjatīti vatvā tadatthasādhanatthaṃ yaṃ vuttaṃ “vibhaṅge suttantabhājaniye saṅkhā rakkhandhaṃ [M 0.0092] vibhajantena saṅkhatamatisaṅkharontīti saṅkhārāti vatvā”ti. Taṃ na yujjati.

Having stated that ‘[volition] intends, it engages in the activity of forming the conditioned,’ and to support that meaning, what was said—‘In the Vibhaṅga, in the Suttanta division, while analyzing the aggregate of formations, it is said that “they construct the conditioned, hence they are called formations (saṅkhārā)”’—that is not appropriate.

Na hi vibhaṅge suttantabhājaniye saṅkhatama bhisaṅkharontīti saṅkhārāti vuttaṃ atthi. Khandhasaṃyuttake panetaṃ vuttanti.

For in the Vibhaṅga’s Suttanta division, it is not stated that ‘they construct the conditioned, therefore they are called formations (saṅkhārā).’ Rather, this is stated in the Khandhasaṃyutta.

73. Ekattārammaṇasaṅkhāto aggo koṭṭhāso koṭi vā etassāti ekaggaṃ. Cittaṃ, tassa bhāvo ekaggatā. Ārammaṇañhi nāma ekaṃpi nānāsabhāvaṃ hoti. Tasmā tassa ekassapi nānāsabhāvesu vikkhepaṃ apatvā ekasmiṃ sabhāve khaṇamattaṃpi pavattassa cittassa yoniccalākāro atthi ayaṃ tasmiṃ ekaggābhidhānassa ekaggabuddhiyāca pavattihetubhāvena gayhatīti. Te neva hi sā nivāte dīpaccīnaṃ ṭhitiviya cetaso ṭhitīti daṭṭhabbāti vuttā.

73. That which has a single object as its peak, part, or culmination is called one-pointedness (ekagga). It is a mental factor. Its state is one-pointedness (ekaggatā). For an object, even a single one, can have diverse aspects. Therefore, when the mind, without being scattered among the diverse aspects of even a single object, arises even for a moment focused on a single aspect, its characteristic of immobility is the reason why it is regarded as one-pointedness and why there is the understanding of one-pointedness. Indeed, for that reason it is said to be the steadiness of the mind, like the stability of a lamp flame in a windless place.

[75] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[75] However, in the Vibhāvanī,

“Ekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ aggaṃ imassāti ekagga”nti vuttaṃ. Tatthapi aggasaddo koṭṭhāsevā koṭiyaṃvā pavattoti yutto. Kecipana ārammaṇe pavattoti vadanti. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It was said, ‘It has a single object as its peak, hence it is one-pointed (ekagga).’ Here too, the word ‘agga’ is appropriately used in the sense of a part or culmination. Some, however, say it refers to the object. That is not sound.

Na hi aggasaddo ārammaṇapariyāyo katthaci diṭṭhoti.

For nowhere is the word ‘agga’ seen to be a synonym for ‘object.’

74. Jīvanti sampayuttādhammā etenāti jīvitaṃ. Indoti issaro. Idha pana issarabhāvo vuccati. Indaṃ issarabhāvaṃ kāretīti indriyaṃ. Jīvitañca taṃ indriyañcāti jīvitindriyaṃ. Tañhi mayā vinā tumhākaṃ jīvitaṃ natthi. Tasmā tumhākaṃ jīvanakicce maṃ issaraṃ karothāti vadantamiva sahajātadhamme abhibhavitvā pavattatīti. Tathā hi taṃ pavattasantatādhipateyyanti ca padumuppa lānupālakamudakaṃ viyātica vuttaṃ. Tattha yāva khandhaparinibbānā anuppabandhavasena pavattamānā cittasantati pavattasantatināma. Adhipatibhāvo ādhipateyyaṃ. Pavattasantatiyaṃ ādhipateyyaṃ assāti samāso. Punappunaṃ niruddhaṃpi hi cittasantānaṃ tassa balena punappunaṃ jīvantaṃ hutvā yāva khandhaparinibbānā punappunaṃ pavattatiyeva.

74. Associated phenomena live by means of it, thus it is life (jīvita). ‘Inda’ means lord. Here, however, it refers to the state of lordship. That which makes one exercise lordship is called faculty (indriya). Both life and that faculty are termed life faculty (jīvitindriya). For it functions as if saying to the co-nascent phenomena, overcoming them: ‘Without me, your life would not exist. Therefore, make me your lord in the task of living.’ Indeed, it is said to be the sovereignty of the continuing stream, and like water that sustains lotuses and water lilies. There, the stream of consciousness that persists until the final passing away of the aggregates without cessation is called the ‘continuing stream.’ The state of being a lord is sovereignty. Sovereignty is in the continuing stream—thus the compound. For even though the stream of consciousness ceases repeatedly, by its power, having become alive again and again, it persists until the final passing away of the aggregates, repeatedly continuing to function.

Na [M 0.0093] hi jīvitarahitesu anindriyabaddhadhammesu tādiso pavattasantati visesonāma atthīti.

For in those devoid of life, in phenomena not bound by faculties, there is no such particular continuity of occurrence.

75. Manasmiṃ ārammaṇaṃ asuññaṃ manaṃvā ārammaṇe niccaninnaṃ karotīti manasikāro. So pana tividho vīthipaṭipādako javanapaṭipādakoārammaṇapaṭipādakoti. Tattha pañcadvārāvajjanaṃ vīthi paṭipādako nāma. Tañhi pañcadvārika cittasantatiṃ ārammaṇe paṭipādeti yojetīti. Manodvārāvajjanaṃ javanapaṭipādako nāma. Taṃpi javana santatiṃ ārammaṇe paṭipādeti yojetīti. Idameva dvayaṃ tattha tattha yoniso manasikārotica ayoniso manasikāro tica vuttaṃ. Tañhi pakatiyā samudāciṇṇaninnaniyāmitādīhi paccaye hi upatthambhitaṃ hutvā cittasantānaṃ yoniso ayonisovā ārammaṇe ninnaṃ karotīti. Paṭisandhicittato pana paṭṭhāya pavattamānā cittasantati ārammaṇaṃ muñcitvā nirujjhitvāpi puna uppajjamānā yassa dhammassa vasena tasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe uppajjati asati kāraṇavisese. So ārammaṇapaṭipādakonāma. Ayamidhā dhippeto. Ayañhi ārammaṇaṃ citte cittaṃvā ārammaṇe paṭipādeti yojetīti. Tathā hi ayaṃ sāraṇa lakkhaṇoti ca sampayuttānaṃ ārammaṇena saṃpayojanarasotica ārammaṇapaṭipādakaṭṭhena sampayuttānaṃ sārathīviya daṭṭhabbotica vutto. Tattha sāraṇalakkhaṇoti sārathīviya assānaṃ sampayuttadhammānaṃ ujuṃ ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ pavattayanalakkhaṇoti attho. Samaṃ dhārentiti sādhāraṇā. Sabbesaṃ cittānaṃ sādhāraṇā sabbacittasādhāraṇā.

75. It makes the mind not empty of the object, or it constantly inclines the mind to the object; thus it is attention (manasikāra). It is threefold: that which leads to the cognitive process, that which leads to the impulsive moments, and that which leads to the object. Among these, five-door adverting is called ‘that which leads to the cognitive process.’ For it directs and connects the stream of five-door consciousness to the object. Mind-door adverting is called ‘that which leads to the impulsive moments.’ It too directs and connects the stream of impulsive consciousness to the object. These two are referred to in various places as wise attention and unwise attention. For when supported by habitual tendencies, predispositions, fixed tendencies, and other conditions, it makes the stream of consciousness incline wisely or unwisely towards an object. However, the stream of consciousness that arises from the rebirth-linking consciousness onwards, even after releasing and ceasing with respect to an object, yet arises again towards the same object in the absence of any special cause, by virtue of a certain phenomenon. That is called ‘that which leads to the object.’ This is what is intended here. For this directs the object towards the mind or connects the mind to the object. Indeed, it is said to have the characteristic of guiding, the function of associating connected states with the object, and should be seen as the charioteer of the connected states in the role of leading to the object. Here, ‘guiding characteristic’ means the characteristic of making associated phenomena proceed straight towards the object, like a charioteer guiding horses. They sustain equally, thus they are common. Common to all minds, they are common to all consciousness.

76. Vitakketīti vitakko. Tathā tathā saṅkappetvā ārammaṇaṃ ārohatīti attho. Tasmiṃ pana taṃ kathā ārohante sampayuttadhammāpi taṃ ārohanti. Tadā soyeva te ārammaṇaṃ abhiniropentonāma hotīti katvā ārammaṇā bhiniropanalakkhaṇo vitakkoti vutto. Rājavallabhaṃ nissāya janapadagāsino rājagehārohanañcettha nidassanaṃ. Avitakkaṃpi hi cittaṃ savitakkadhammasantāne vitakkena saha pavattaparicaya balena ārohanato vitakkena atinirovitamevanāma hotīti. Apica, [M 0.0094] avitakkaṃpi pañcaviññāṇaṃ vatthārammaṇa saṅghaṭṭanavasena ārohati. Dutīyajjhānādīnica upacārabhāvanāvasena ārohanti. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana kiṃvā etāya yuttiyāti vatvā imamatthaṃ dasseti. Cittaṃpi hi ārammaṇaṃ āruhatiyeva. Tassa pana niccaṃ sahāyo manasikāro. Tasmiñhi asati taṃ niyāmakarahi tā nāvāviya yaṃvātaṃvā ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā pavatteyyāti. Iti pañcaviññāṇaṃ manasikārasahāyaṃ hutvā attano ārammaṇavijānanasattivaseneva ārammaṇaṃ ārohati. Akusalaṃ patvā pana cittaṃpi lobhādayopi ārammaṇāruhane thāmavatā eva honti. Pāpasmiṃ ramate manoti hi vuttaṃ. Dutīyajjhāna cittādīnica manasikāra vīriyassatīnaṃpi vasena ārohanti. Vitakko pana tathā tathā saṅkappetvā attasahite dhamme ārammaṇāruhane suṭṭhutaraṃ balavante karoti. Iti tasmiṃ kicce aññesaṃ sābhisayabyāpāratāyaeva ayaṃ vitakkoti vuttoti. Evaṃ pana vattabbaṃ. Nanu aññepi arūpadhammā sārammaṇasabhāvā ārammaṇaṃ ārohanti. Atha ca pana kasmā ayameva vitakkoti vuttoti. Aññesaṃ pana āruhanaṃ kiccantarayogavaseneva siddhaṃ. Imassa pana ito aññaṃ kiccaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmā ayameva tathā vuttoti.

76. “Applied thought” (vitakko) means ‘to apply thought’ (vitakketi). The meaning is that by conceiving in various ways, it ascends to the object. When it thus ascends, the associated states also ascend with it. At that time, it is indeed what fixes the mind on the object; thus, applied thought is said to have the characteristic of fixing the mind on the object. Here, the example is the country folk ascending to the royal palace relying on the king’s favorite. Even thought-free consciousness, due to the strength of familiarity arising together with applied thought in a thought-associated continuum, is indeed as if fixed by applied thought. Moreover, even the five sense-consciousnesses ascend by way of the impingement of the base and object. And the second jhāna, etc., ascend through access development. But in the Majjhima commentary, one might ask, “What is the point of this reasoning?”, and then this meaning is shown: Consciousness too ascends to the object. Its constant companion is attention. Without it, like a boat without a helmsman, it would drift aimlessly, taking any object. Thus, the five sense-consciousnesses, aided by attention, ascend to the object merely by the power of knowing their own object. But when unwholesome consciousness arises, greed, etc., are indeed powerful in ascending to the object. For it is said, “The mind delights in evil.” And the second jhāna consciousness, etc., ascend through attention, energy, and mindfulness. But applied thought, by conceiving in various ways, makes the states associated with itself more powerful in ascending to the object. Thus, in this function, because the activity of others is dependent on it, this is called “applied thought.” But it should be said thus: “Do not other immaterial states, which have the nature of being object-related, ascend to the object? Yet why is only this called ‘applied thought’?” For others, their ascending is accomplished in connection with other functions. But this has no other function besides this. Therefore, it is said thus.

77. Vicaratīti vicāro. Vicāretivā sampayuttakedhamme, te vā dhammā vicaranti etenāti vicāro. Vicaraṇañcettha vitakkā ruḷhe tasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe sabhāvākārapātubhāvatthaṃ punappunaṃ anumajjanavasena pavattanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etthaca vitakko oḷāriko pubbaṅgamo ārammaṇe cittassa pathamābhinipātabhūtoca hotīti ghaṇḍābhighāto viya daṭṭhabbo. Vicāro sukhumo anucaro tasmiṃyeva ārammaṇe cittassa anubandhanabhūto ca hotīti ghaṇḍānuravoviya daṭṭhabboti.

77. “Sustained thought” (vicāro) means ‘to sustain thought’ (vicarati). It is called sustained thought because it makes the associated states ponder, or those states ponder by means of it. Here, sustained thought should be seen as its repeated movement by way of rubbing over, for the manifestation of its own characteristic aspect, on that same object in which applied thought is already established. And here, applied thought is coarse, a forerunner, and is the mind’s initial impingement on the object—like the striking of a bell. Sustained thought is subtle, the follower, and is the mind’s subsequent adherence to that same object—like the reverberation of a bell.

78. Adhimuccanaṃ adhimokkho. Ārammaṇe evaṃ nukho no nukhoti evaṃ pavattaṃ saṃsappanaṃ adhibhavitvā vicchinditvā pakkhako muccanavasena cittassa pavattīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evañca katvā so ārammaṇe [M 0.0095] sanniṭṭhānalakkhaṇoti ca ārammaṇe niccalabhāvena indakhīlasadisotica vutto.

78. Adhimokkha is determination. It is said that the mind’s activity consists in overcoming and cutting off the wavering that occurs regarding the object, thinking, “Is it thus or is it not thus?”, and then proceeding by way of its decisive release. Thus, it is characterized by settling upon the object and is described as being like an Indra’s pillar in its immovability regarding the object.

79. Vīrassa kammasūrassa bhāvo kammavā vīriyaṃ. Taṃsamaṅgī puggalo hi kammasūro hoti. Mahantaṃpi kammaṃ appakato gaṇhāti. Dukkaraṃpi sukarato, bhāriyaṃpi abhāriyato gaṇhāti. Attakilamathaṃ nagaṇeti. Kammasiddhiyā niccaṃ paggahita kāya cittova hoti. Tasmā taṃ tassa puggalassa tathāpavattiyā hetubhāvoceva tathāpavattassa ca tassa puggalassa kāya cittakriyābhūtaṃ hotīti. Vidhināvā nayena upāyena vīriyavato kiṃ nāmakammaṃ na sijjhatītiādikena pubbābhisaṅkhārena īrayitabbaṃ pavattayitabbanti vīriyaṃ. Visesenavā sakaparahitahetu īranti kampanti taṃ samaṅgino etenāti vīriyaṃ. Etthaca vīriyu patthambhitā sampayuttadhammā sadā anikkhittadhurā paggahitasīsāviya hutvā attano attano kiccasampattiyā niccaṃ ussāhajātāva honti, tesuca tathāhontesu taṃsamaṅgino puggalāpi attanovā paresaṃvā hitahetu niccaṃ byāvaṭakāyacittā honti. Tasmā īranti kampantīti vuccantīti. Tathā hi taṃ upatthambhanalakkhaṇanti ca paggahalakkhaṇanti ca ussāhalakkhaṇanti ca gehassa thūṇūpatthambhana sadisanti ca sammā āraddhaṃ sabbasampattīnaṃ mūlanti ca vuttanti.

79. Energy (viriya) is the state of a hero, of one zealous in action. A person endowed with this is indeed zealous in action. Even a great task is undertaken as if small, a difficult task as if easy, and a heavy burden as if light. They do not consider their own fatigue. Their body and mind are always exerted for the success of their work. Therefore, this energy is both the cause of such behavior in that person and the bodily and mental activity of that person when so behaving. Alternatively, energy is that which should be aroused and maintained by prior preparation, as in “What task is not accomplished by one who has energy?” Or, energy is that by which those endowed with it move and shake especially for their own or others’ benefit. Here, the associated states, supported by energy, are always unremitting in their duty, as if with heads held high, constantly generating enthusiasm for the fulfillment of their tasks. And when they are thus, the persons endowed with it are also always active in body and mind for their own or others’ welfare. Therefore, they are said to move and shake. Indeed, it is characterized by support, by exertion, and by enthusiasm, like a pillar supporting a house. It is rightly said to be the root of all success when properly commenced.

80. Vinayati kāyacittaṃ tappeti, tuṭṭhaṃ suhitaṃ janeti, supupphitapadumaṃviyavā vaḍḍhetīti pīti, vinantivā etāya taṃ samaṅgino puṇṇacandoviya virocamāna kāyacittā hontīti pīti. Sā pañcavidhā khuddikā pīti, khaṇikāpīti, okkantikā pīti, ubbegā pīti, pharaṇāpītīti.

80. Joy (pīti) removes weariness from body and mind, satisfies them, produces contentment and comfort, or makes them grow like a fully bloomed lotus; or because those endowed with it shine like a full moon with their body and mind, therefore it is joy. It is fivefold: minor joy, momentary joy, showering joy, transporting joy, and all-pervading joy.

81. Chandanaṃ chando. Icchā patthanā abhisandhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sopana duvidho taṇhāchando, kattukamyatā chandoti. Idha kattukamyatā chando adhippeto. Etthaca kattuṃ kāmeti icchatīti kattukāmo. Chandasamaṅgipuggalo. Tassa bhāvo kattukamyaṃ. Tadeva kattukamyatā, yathā devoyeva devatāti. Etthaca kattusaddo sabbesaṃ dhātusaddānaṃ atthe saṅgahetvā pavatto. [M 0.0096] Tasmā kattukamyatāti etena kathetukamyatā cintetukamyatā daṭṭhukamyatā sotukamyatāti evamādīni sabba kriyāpadāni saṅgahitāni hontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. So pana ārammaṇaṃ icchantopi taṇhā viya assādana rajjana laggana vasena naicchati. Yena yena pana atthiko hoti. Taṃ taṃ atthaṃ ārādhetu kāmatāvaseneva icchati. Yathā rañño issāsā dhanenavā yasenavā atthikā rājaverīnaṃ vijjhanavasena chaḍḍitabbayuttakepi sare bahū icchantiyeva. Evamevaṃ ayaṃpi parassa vissajjitabbayutta kānipi dānavatthūni aladdhānipi laddhuṃ icchati. Laddhānipi rakkhituṃ icchatīti. Ayañca attho vibhāvaniyaṃpi vuttoyeva.

81. The act of wishing is chanda. It is said to be desire, aspiration, or intention. And it is twofold: craving-chanda and desire-to-act-chanda. Here, desire-to-act-chanda is intended. In this context, one who wishes to act, who desires to act, is one who is eager to act (kattukāmo), a person endowed with chanda. His state is eagerness to act (kattukamyaṃ). That very state is kattukamyatā, just as a god (devo) is divinity (devatā). Here, the word 'kattu' (to do) is used to encompass the meaning of all verbal roots. Therefore, it should be understood that by 'eagerness to act,' the eagerness to speak, the eagerness to think, the eagerness to see, the eagerness to hear, and so forth—all verbal actions are included. However, even when desiring an object, this chanda does not desire in the manner of craving—by way of relishing, being dyed, or clinging. Rather, for whatever one has need, one desires it simply by way of the wish to accomplish that purpose. Just as the king’s archers, having need of wealth or glory, desire many arrows, even those fit to be shot and discarded for the purpose of piercing the king’s enemies. Even so, this person desires to obtain items for giving, even those not yet received, which are fit to be given away to others, and desires to protect those already obtained. This meaning is also stated in the Vibhāvanī.

Vuttañhi tattha

For it was said there:

Dānavatthuvissajjanavasena pavattakālepi cesa vissajji tabbena tena atthikoyeva. Khipitabbausūnaṃ gahaṇe atthiko issāsoviyāti.

Even at the time of giving away items for giving, he is indeed desirous of that which is to be given away, like an archer who is desirous of taking up arrows that are to be shot.

Tattha yadaggena dānaṃ dassāmīti dānavatthupariyesanādivasena pavattā pubbabhāgacetanā dānavatthuvissajjana saṅkāte dāne saṅgahitā hoti. Tadaggena tassā pubbabhāgacetanāya pavattikālo idha dānavatthu vissajjanavasena pavatta kāloti veditabbo. Vissajjitabbenāti vissajjitabba yuttakena. Tena atthikoyeva parassa vissajjanatthāyāti adhippāyo. Khipitabbausūnaṃ gahaṇeti tesaṃ akatānaṃ karaṇavasena aladdhānaṃ pariyesanavasena gahaṇe. Ettha pana keci issāso usūnikhipitvāpi labhamāno tehi usūhi atthikoyevāti eva matthaṃ vadanti. So nayujjati. Evañhi sati khipitausūnanti vuttaṃ siyā. Yathā kathitaṃ lapitaṃ tathāgatenāti. Tathā vissajjitabbe nāti etthapīti. Keci issāso usūhi anatthiko khipanto nahoti. Atthikoyeva samāno aññaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ icchanto khipatīti evaṃ atthaṃ vadanti. Sopi nayujjati. Evañhi sati usūhi atthikoyeva tāni khipanto issāsoviyātivuttaṃ siyāti. Atthato [M 0.0097] pana tadubhayaṃpi avahasitabbameva hotīti. Yasmāca chandasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gaṇhantaṃ chandavasena ati icchamānaṃ viya viluppamānaṃ viya gaṇhāti. Tasmā ayaṃ ārammaṇaggahaṇe cetaso hatthappasāraṇaṃviyāti vutto. Etthaca hatthappasāraṇaṃviyāti idaṃ abhūtaparikappavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi cittassa hatthonāma atthi. Atthavisesapākaṭatthaṃ pana abhūtaṃpi bhūtaṃ viya kappetvā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Apica, ayaṃ chandonāma thāmapatto taṇhāya balavataro hoti. Tathā hesa adhipatibhūto iddhipādabhūtoca hotīti. Yadi hi so taṇhāya samānabalo siyā. Ime sattā taṇhāya hatthe ṭhitā taṇhā pariggahitāni dhanabhogarajjasukhānivā dibbabrahmasampattiyovā chaḍḍetvā vaṭṭadukkhato niyyātuṃ nasakkhissanti yevāti.

Therein, the preliminary volition that proceeds by way of searching for an item for giving, with the thought, 'I will give a gift,' is included in the giving known as the relinquishing of the item for giving. On account of that, the time of the proceeding of that preliminary volition should be understood here as the time that proceeds by way of relinquishing the item for giving. 'By that which is to be relinquished' means by that which is suitable to be relinquished. The meaning is that one has need of it for the purpose of relinquishing it to another. 'In the taking of arrows to be shot' means in the taking of them by way of making those not yet made, or by way of searching for those not yet obtained. Here, however, some say this meaning: 'An archer, even having shot arrows, if he obtains them, indeed has need of those arrows.' That is not fitting. For if that were so, it would have been said 'shot arrows,' as in 'spoken, uttered by the Tathāgata.' So too here with 'to be relinquished.' Some say this meaning: 'An archer is not one who shoots without need of the arrows. Being one who has need, he shoots desiring some other benefit.' That too is not fitting. For if that were so, it would have been said: 'like an archer who, having need of the arrows, shoots them.' In meaning, however, both of these should be dismissed. And because a mind associated with chanda, when taking an object, takes it by the power of chanda as if desiring it excessively, as if plundering it. Therefore, this is said to be like the stretching forth of the mind's hand in the grasping of an object. Here, 'like the stretching forth of a hand' should be understood as a statement of unreal imagining. For the mind has no such thing as a hand. But it should be understood that for the sake of making a specific meaning clear, the unreal is spoken of as if it were real. Moreover, this so-called chanda, when it has attained strength, becomes more powerful than craving. For thus it becomes a dominant factor and a basis of psychic power. For if it were of equal strength to craving, these beings, standing in the hand of craving, having been seized by craving, would never be able to escape from the suffering of the round of existence by abandoning wealth, enjoyments, the pleasure of kingship, or divine and Brahmā-like attainments.

82. Sobhaṇā sobhaṇesu cittesu pakirantīti pakiṇṇā. Keeva pakiṇṇakā. Aññehi aññesaṃvā samānā aññasamānā. Yadā sobhaṇacittesu yuttā, tadā tehi asobhaṇato aññehi samānā. Yadā asobhaṇacittesu yuttā, tadā tehi sobhaṇato aññehi samānā sadisāti vuttaṃ hoti.

82. They are called 'miscellaneous' (pakiṇṇā) because they are scattered (pakiranti) in beautiful and unbeautiful minds. In what way are they miscellaneous? They are 'common to others' (aññasamāna). When associated with beautiful minds, they are common with those that are other than the unbeautiful ones. When associated with unbeautiful minds, they are common with those that are other than the beautiful ones. Thus it is said they are alike.

Aññasamānarāsimhi paramatthadīpanā.

The explanation of the ultimate meaning in the section on the miscellaneous mental factors.

83. Idāni akusalarāsiṃ dassento mohotiādimāha. Tattha muyhatīti moho. Muyhanti sattā etenātivā moho. Muyhanamattaṃvā moho, caturaṅgatamassa viya cakkhussa sabbaso kalyāṇapakkhaṃ paṭicchādetvā cittassa andhabhāvakaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāpapakkhaṃ pana patvā so ñāṇagatiko hotīti daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hesa pāḷiyaṃ micchāñāṇanti vutto. Aṭṭhakathāsuca micchāñāṇanti pāpakriyāsu upāyacintāvasenapavatto mohoti vuttaṃ. Avijjāyaca appaṭipatti micchāpaṭipattivasena duvidhabhāvo vutto. [M 0.0098] Etthaca appaṭipattīti kalyāṇapakkhe aññāṇameva vuccati. Micchāpaṭipattīti pāpapakkhe micchāñāṇameva vuccatīti, tathā hi pāpapakkhaṃ patvā pañcadhammā ñāṇagatikā honti moho, lobho, diṭṭhi, vitakko, vicāroti. Cittena pana saddhiṃ chabbidhā honti. Tehi pakatiyā viññujātikesu sutapariyattisampannesuca uppannā pāpakriyāsu taṃ taṃ upāyadassanavasena tesaṃ tattha chekabhāvaṃ paṭibalabhāvañca sādhentīti.

83. Now, showing the group of unwholesome states, he says 'delusion,' and so on. Therein, 'one is deluded' (muyhati), thus it is delusion (moho). Or, beings are deluded by this, thus it is delusion. Or, delusion is the mere state of being deluded; it is said to be the causing of blindness to the mind by completely concealing the wholesome side, like a film over the eye. But having reached the evil side, it should be understood that it becomes knowledge-oriented. Thus, in the Pāli, it is called wrong knowledge. And in the commentaries it is said: 'Wrong knowledge is delusion that proceeds by way of thinking of means in evil actions.' And for ignorance, a twofold nature is stated by way of non-realization and wrong realization. And here, non-realization is called simply ignorance regarding the wholesome side. Wrong realization is called specifically wrong knowledge regarding the evil side. For, having reached the evil side, five states become knowledge-oriented: delusion, greed, wrong view, initial thought, and sustained thought. And together with consciousness, they become sixfold. When these have arisen in those who are naturally intelligent and accomplished in scriptural learning, they accomplish skillfulness and competence in evil actions by showing them this or that means.

84. Nahiriyati kāyaduccaritādīhi nalajjati najigucchatīti ahirī. Hirippaṭipakkhāvā ahirī, sāeva ahirikaṃ. Tañhi pāpa kriyāsu paccupaṭṭhitāsu hiriyā okāsaṃ adatvā tāsu ruciṃ uppādetvā pavattatīti. Tathā hi taṃ kāyaduccaritādīhi ajigucchanalakkhaṇantica alajjālakkhaṇantica vuttaṃ.

84. 'One is not ashamed' (na hiriyati) of bodily misconduct, etc., 'one does not feel shame' (na lajjati), 'one is not disgusted' (na jigucchati)—this is shamelessness (ahirī). Or, shamelessness is the opposite of shame (hiri); that very state is shamelessness (ahirikaṃ). For when evil actions are present, it proceeds without giving an opportunity for shame, having generated delight in them. Thus, it is said to have the characteristic of not being disgusted by bodily misconduct, etc., and the characteristic of not feeling shame.

85. Naottappatīti anottappaṃ. Kāyaduccaritādīhi nabhāyati nautrasatīti attho. Ottappappaṭipakkhaṃvā anottappaṃ. Taṃpi hi tāsu paccupaṭṭhitāsu ottappassa okāsaṃ adatvā cittaṃ tāsu asārajjamānaṃ katvā pavattatīti. Tathā hetaṃ kāyaduccari tādīhi asārajjalakkhaṇanti ca anuttāsalakkhaṇanti ca vuttaṃ. Vuccati ca –

85. 'One does not dread' (na ottappati)—this is lack of moral dread (anottappaṃ). The meaning is: one does not fear or tremble at bodily misconduct, etc. Or, lack of moral dread is the opposite of moral dread (ottappa). For it too, when those evil actions are present, proceeds without giving an opportunity for moral dread, having made the mind unshrinking in regard to them. Thus, it is said to have the characteristic of being unshrinking in regard to bodily misconduct, etc., and the characteristic of not trembling. And it is said:

Ajegucchī ahiriko, pāpāgūthāva sūkaro;

Abhīruca anottappī, salabho viya pāvakāti.

Not disgusted and shameless, like a pig in the excrement of evil; fearless and without moral dread, like a moth in a fire.

86. Uddharatīti uddhaṭaṃ. Pāsāṇapiṭṭhe vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭha geṇḍuko viya nānārammaṇesu vikkhittaṃ cittaṃ, uddhaṭassa pana cittassa uddharaṇākārappavattiyā paccayabhūto dhammo uddhaccaṃ. Taṃ pana vāteritaṃ jalaṃ viya dhajapaṭākā viyaca daṭṭhabbaṃ.

86. 'It is agitated' (uddharati), thus it is the agitated state (uddhaṭaṃ). The mind is scattered among various objects like a ball released after being rolled on a stone surface. However, the mental factor that is the condition for the proceeding in the manner of agitation of an agitated mind is restlessness (uddhaccaṃ). And that should be seen like water stirred by the wind, or like a banner and a flag.

87. Lubbhatīti lobho, lubbhanti sampayuttā dhammā ete nāti lobho, lubbhanamattamevavā etanti lobho. Etthaca lubbhanaṃnāma ārammaṇābhisajjanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sopana ārammaṇe lagga naṭṭhena [M 0.0099] makkaṭālepoviya abhikaṅkhaṭṭhena tattakapāle khittamaṃsa pesi viya aparicāgaṭṭhena telañjana rāgoviya taṇhānadibhāvena vaḍḍhitvā sattānaṃ apāyāvahaṭṭhena sabbāni sukkhakaṭṭha sākhāpalāsa tiṇakasaṭāni mahāsamuddaṃ vahantī sīghatotā nadī viya daṭṭhabbo.

87. Greed is so called because it is greedy; or because associated states are greedy by means of it; or because it is simply the state of being greedy. And here, being greedy should be understood as clinging to an object. It should be regarded as like a monkey stuck with birdlime, due to its attachment; like a piece of meat thrown onto a hot pan, due to its longing; like an oil-and-soot stain, due to its tenacity; and like a swift-flowing river which, having swelled by its nature as a river of craving, carries all dry wood, branches, leaves, and rubbish to the great ocean, due to its bringing beings to the states of loss.

88. Dassanaṃ diṭṭhi. Dhammānaṃ yāthāvasabhāvesu ñāṇadassanaṃ viya tesameva ayāthāvasabhāvesu micchādassananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāhi ekaccānaṃ paṇḍitamānīnaṃ micchāvitakkabahulānaṃ uppannā thāmagatā ayāthāvapakkhe paṭivedhaññāṇagatikā hotīti. Sāpana micchābhinivesalakkhaṇā paramaṃvajjanti daṭṭhabbā.

88. Seeing is view (diṭṭhi). It is said that just as there is knowledge and vision regarding the true nature of things, so too there is wrong vision regarding their untrue nature. For this, born in some self-styled intellectuals abounding in wrong thoughts, becomes strong, having the nature of penetrative knowledge in the untrue aspect. But it should be seen that it is characterized by stubborn adherence to wrong beliefs and is the ultimate fault.

89. Maññatīti māno. Ahaṃ loke eko puggalo asmi. Na kaṭṭhakaliṅgaroviya avamaññanārahoti evaṃ attānaṃ daḷhaṃ paggahetvā samanupassatīti attho. Sopana jāti kuladhana bhoga yasa issariyādīhi ceva sīla suta lābhasakkārā dīhica guṇehi upatthambhito atirekataraṃ vaddhitvā attānaṃ janamajjhe ketuṃviya accuggataṃ maññati. Tasmā so unnatilakkhaṇotica ummādoviyātica vutto.

89. Conceit is so called because it conceives (maññatīti māno). The meaning is: thinking, "I am a unique person in the world, not contemptible like a piece of wood or a scrap," one firmly grasps and regards oneself thus. That conceit, supported by birth, family, wealth, enjoyment, fame, and dominion, as well as by virtues such as morality, learning, gains, and honors, grows exceedingly, making one think of oneself as towering above others like a banner in the midst of people. Therefore, it is said to have the characteristic of haughtiness and to be like madness.

90. Dussatīti doso. Sopana caṇḍikkaṭṭhena pahatā sivisoviya visappanaṭṭhena asanipātoviya attano nissaya dahanaṭṭhena dāvaggiviya dussanaṭṭhena laddhokāso sapattoviya sabbaso ahitarāsi bhāvaṭṭhena visa saṃsaṭṭha pūtimuttaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo.

90. Hatred is so called because it corrupts (dussatīti doso). It should be regarded as like a struck venomous snake, due to its ferocity; like a thunderbolt, due to its pervasiveness; like a forest fire, due to its burning of its own support; like an enemy who has found an opportunity, due to its harmfulness; and like putrid urine mixed with poison, due to its being entirely a mass of what is unbeneficial.

91. Issatīti issā. Parasampattiṃ ussūyatīti attho. Sāhi paresaṃ pakatiyā laddhasampattiṃ disvā vā sutvāvā nasahati. Tassā sampattiyā vipattiṃ icchati ākaṅkhati. Asuko idaṃnāma labhissatīti sutvāpi nasahati. Tassa alābhaṃ icchati ākaṅkhati. Tasmā sā parasampattīnaṃ ussūyanalakkhaṇāti vuttā.

91. Envy is so called because it is envious (issatīti issā). It means being jealous of others' success. When one sees or hears of others' naturally acquired prosperity, one cannot bear it. One wishes and longs for the ruin of their prosperity. Even hearing, "So-and-so will gain such-and-such," one cannot endure it and wishes and longs for their failure to gain it. Therefore, it is said that envy is characterized by jealousy toward others' success.

92. Mama [M 0.0100] eva idaṃ guṇajātaṃvā vatthuvā hotu. Mā aññassāti evaṃ attano sampattihetu avipphārikatāvasena carati pavattatīti maccharaṃ, tathā pavattaṃ cittaṃ. Maccharassa bhāvo macchariyaṃ. Idaṃca issā viya duvidhaṃ attanā laddhasampatti labhitabbasampatti vasena. Tattha pakatiyā laddhasampattiyaṃ tāva taṃ parehi sā dhāraṇaṃvā yena kenacivā kāraṇena attasantakabhāvato muccitvā paresaṃ santakabhāvaṃ gamissamānaṃ disvā vā sutvāvā cintetvā dukkhī dummano hoti, labhitabbasampattiyaṃpi asukasmiṃ dese vākālevā idaṃnāma bhavissatīti sutvāvā cintetvāvā taṃ attanāva laddhuṃ icchati. Aññesaṃ lābhaṃ naicchati. Aññe labhissantīti sutvāvā cintetvāvā dukkhī dummano hotīti. Tathā hetaṃ laddhānaṃvā labhitabbānaṃvā attano sampattīnaṃ nigguhanalakkhaṇanti vuttaṃ. Etthaca labhitabbasampattiyaṃ yassa lābhaṃ naicchati. Solabhatītivā labhissatītivā sutvāvā cintetvāvā cittavighāto issānāma. Yaṃ yaṃ attanā laddhuṃ icchati. Taṃ taṃ attanā alabbhamānakaṃ cintetvā cittavighāto macchariyaṃnāma. Na hi ete dve ekato uppajjantīti.

92. "Let this abundance of virtues or possessions be mine alone, not others'." Thus, one acts and proceeds with a mind that is ungenerous, motivated by personal gain; this is called stinginess (maccharaṃ), and the state of being stingy is avarice (macchariyaṃ). This, like envy (issā), is twofold: regarding possessions one has attained and possessions one hopes to attain. Regarding possessions one has already attained, one becomes sorrowful and distressed when one sees, hears, or reflects that they might slip from one's possession and pass into the possession of others, whether through sharing or any other reason. Regarding possessions one hopes to attain, upon hearing or reflecting that such-and-such will exist in a certain place or time, one desires to obtain it for oneself alone. One does not wish for others to gain it. Upon hearing or reflecting that others might obtain it, one becomes sorrowful and distressed. Thus, it is said that avarice has the characteristic of concealing one's own prosperity, whether attained or to be attained. Here, regarding possessions one hopes to attain, the mental vexation that arises upon hearing or reflecting that another—whose gain one does not wish for—is obtaining or will obtain something, is called envy (issā). The mental vexation that arises upon reflecting that one cannot obtain for oneself what one desires to obtain, is called avarice (macchariyaṃ). These two do not arise simultaneously.

93. Kukkuccanti ettha kiriyā kataṃ. Kucchitaṃ katanti kukataṃ. Kucchitakiriyāti attho. Paṇḍitehi ekantena ninditabbo cittappavattivisesoti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthato pana akataṃ vata me kalyāṇaṃ kataṃ pāpanti evaṃ anusocanavasena pavatto kukkucca sampayuttacittuppādoyeva, so hi tathā pavattamānopi pubbe akataṃvā kalyāṇaṃ puna kataṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Pubbe kataṃ vā pāpaṃ puna akataṃ kātuṃ nasakkoti. Athakho kusaladhammesu cittapariyādānāyaeva saṃvattati. Tasmā kucchitakiriyā mattattā kukatanti vuccatīti. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭha kathāyaṃ katākatassa sāvajjānavajjassa abhimukhagamanaṃ paṭisāronāma. Yasmā paneso kataṃvā pāpaṃ akataṃ nakaroti. Akataṃvā kalyāṇaṃ kataṃ nakaroti. Tasmā virūpo kucchito vā paṭisāroti vippaṭisāroti. Etthaca vippaṭisāroti kukkucca meva. [M 0.0101] Kukkucceca kucchite sati taṃ sampayuttacittuppādopi kucchitoyeva. Yenaca kāraṇena kukkuccaṃ kucchitaṃnāma hoti. Teneva kāraṇena so cittuppādopi kucchitonāma hotīti katvā so cittuppādova kukatapade gahetuṃ yuttoti veditabbo. Sudinnakaṇḍaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ayamattho ujukatova vutto. Yathāha-viññūhi akattabbatāya kucchitakiriyābhāvato kukkuccanti.

93. Herein, 'kukkucca' (remorse) is 'a deed done badly.' 'Kucchitaṃ kataṃ' means 'a badly done deed,' which is to say, 'a reprehensible action.' It is said to be a specific mental state that is entirely condemned by the wise. Essentially, it is the arising of a mental state associated with remorse, proceeding by way of lamenting, "Alas, good was not done by me; evil was done." This mental state, even when arising in that way, cannot make good what was not done before, nor can it undo the evil that was done before. Instead, it only leads to the mind's exhaustion regarding wholesome states. Therefore, because it is merely a reprehensible action, it is called 'kukata' (a bad deed). As stated in the Commentary: "Turning one's attention to what was done and not done, whether blameworthy or blameless, is called regret (paṭisāra)." Since this regret neither undoes past evil nor accomplishes past good, it is a distorted or reprehensible regret, and thus called 'vippaṭisāra' (remorse). Here, 'vippaṭisāra' is 'kukkucca' itself. When reprehensible remorse exists, the associated mental state is also reprehensible. For the same reason that remorse is called reprehensible, that mental state is also termed reprehensible. Therefore, it should be understood that that mental state itself is properly included in the term 'kukata'. In the Commentary to the Sudinnakaṇḍa, however, this meaning is stated straightforwardly: "Because it is something that should not be done by the wise, due to its nature as a reprehensible action, it is called 'kukkucca'."

[76] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[76] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Imamatthaṃ asallakkhetvā yaṃ vuttaṃ “kucchitaṃ katanti kukataṃ. Katākata duccaritasucarita”nti. Taṃ na yujjatiyeva. Etena yañca tattha vuttaṃ “akataṃpi hi kukatanti voharanti. Yaṃ mayā akathaṃ. Taṃ kukatantica. Idha pana katā kataṃ ārabbha uppanno vippaṭisāracittuppādo kukata”ntica. Taṃpi sabbaṃ paṭikkhittameva hotīti.

Not recognizing this meaning, what was said—"'What is done badly' is 'kukataṃ' (a bad deed). Done and not done, bad conduct and good conduct"—is not appropriate at all. By this, what was also said there—"Indeed, even what is not done is called 'kukataṃ'. 'What I did not do, that too is kukataṃ.' Here, however, the arising of a mind of remorse with regard to what was done and not done is 'kukataṃ'"—all that is entirely refuted.

Kukatassa yathāvuttacittuppādassa tathāpavatti hetubhāvo kukkuccaṃ. Apica, dhātupāṭhesu kucasaddaṃ saṅkocana mano vilekhanatthesu paṭhantiyeva. Tasmā kucchitena ākārena kocati saṅkocati na pāpajigucchanākārenāti kukkuco. Kucchitenavā ākārena kocati vilikhati nakilesasallīkhanā kārenāti kukkuco. Tathā pavattadhammasamūho. Sohi kucchitena akataṃ vata me kalyāṇaṃ kataṃ pāpanti evaṃ pavattena anutthunanākārena saṅkocati. Kusaladhammasamādāne cittaṃ namituṃpi nadeti. Manaṃvā vilekhati. Saddhādīnaṃ sāradhammānaṃ tanukaraṇena cittaṃ kusaladhammasamādāne pariyādinnathāmabalaṃ karoti. Tasmā kukkucoti vuccati. Yena pana dhammena yuttattā so tathā pavatto hoti. So kukkuccaṃnāma kukkucassa bhāvoti katvā. Taṃ pana yasmā pubbe akatañca kalyāṇaṃ katañca pāpaṃ ārabbha pacchā anutāpanavasena anusocanavasenaca pavattati. Tasmātaṃ pacchānutāpalakkhaṇaṃ katākatānuyocana rasanti ca vuttaṃ. [M 0.0102] Etthaca pacchānutāpalakkhaṇanti pubbe kalyāṇañca akatvā pāpañca katvā āgatattā pacchime kāle anutāpalakkhaṇanti attho. Tena kukkuccassa ekantena atītārammaṇatā siddhā hoti. Paccuppannānāgatārammaṇatāca paṭisiddhāti. Katākatā nusocanarasanti ettha katañca pāpaṃ akatañca kalyāṇanti yo jetabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ mahāniddese –

Remorse (kukkucca) is the causal state for the occurrence of the aforementioned mental state of 'kukata'. Moreover, in the Dhātupāṭha, the root 'kuc' is indeed read in the meanings of 'contracting' and 'scraping the mind'. Therefore, it is called 'kukkuco' because it contracts in a reprehensible manner, not in the manner of disgust toward evil. Alternatively, it is called 'kukkuco' because it scrapes the mind in a reprehensible way, not in the manner of cleansing defilements. Such is the group of phenomena that occurs.
