For it contracts the mind in a reprehensible manner, proceeding by way of lamenting thus: 'Alas! I have not done good, but have done evil.' It does not allow the mind even to incline toward undertaking wholesome actions. Or it scrapes the mind. By weakening the essential qualities like faith, it renders the mind exhausted of strength and power for undertaking wholesome actions. Therefore, it is called 'kukkuco'. That which occurs in such a way due to its connection with a certain phenomenon is called 'kukkucca', it being the state of 'kukkuco'. Since it arises afterward by way of subsequent regret and lamentation concerning good deeds not done and evil deeds done in the past, it is said to have the characteristic of subsequent regret and the function of reproaching what was done and not done. Here, 'the characteristic of subsequent regret' means that because one has come to a later time having not done good and having done evil in the past, it is the characteristic of regret. This establishes that remorse (kukkucca) exclusively takes the past as its object, while present and future objects are refuted. Here, 'the function of lamenting over what was done and not done' should be understood as 'evil done and good not done'. Indeed, it is stated in the Mahāniddesa:—

Dvīhākārehi kukkuccaṃ uppajjati katattā ca akatattā ca. Kathañca dvīhā.La. Akatattāca. Akataṃ me kāyasu caritaṃ. Kataṃ kāyaduccaritanti uppajjati kukkuccaṃ. Akataṃ me vacīsucaritaṃ.La. Kataṃ manoduccaritanti uppajjati kukkuccaṃ. Akatāme pāṇātipātā veramaṇī. Kato pāṇāti pātoti uppajjati kukkuccaṃ.La. Akatā me sammādiṭṭhi. Katā micchāmiṭṭhīti uppajjati kukkuccanti.

Remorse arises in two ways: from what has been done and from what has not been done. And how is it twofold? 'I have not practiced good bodily conduct; I have practiced bad bodily conduct'—thus remorse arises. 'I have not practiced good verbal conduct... I have practiced bad mental conduct'—thus remorse arises. 'I have not undertaken abstinence from killing living beings; I have killed living beings'—thus remorse arises. 'I have not cultivated right view; I have cultivated wrong view'—thus remorse arises.

Etena pana akatasucaritā rammaṇatāya kataduccaritā rammaṇatāyaca vasena kukkuccassa dvidhābhāvoyeva siddho hoti. Dvīhākārehīti hi vuttaṃ. Soca kho pubbe pāpaṃ katvā pacchā apāyabhayatajjitānañceva apāyesu patitvā pubbe attanā katakammaṃ anussarantānañca hoti. Naaññesaṃ, akataṃ me kāyasucaritaṃ. Kataṃ kāyaduccaritanti hi vuttaṃ. Yathā pana māno duvidho hoti yāthāvamāno ayāthāvamānoti. Tathā kukkuccaṃpi, yāthāvakukkuccaṃ, ayāthāva kukkuccanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha ayāthāva kukkuccaṃpi uppajjamānaṃ dvīhākāreho uppajjati akataṃ vata me kalyāṇaṃ kataṃ pāpanti. Katamaṃ pana tanti. Yañca pubbe kalyāṇakammepi pāpasaññī pāpadiṭṭhi akatvā pāpakammepi kalyāṇasaññī kalyāṇadiṭṭhi katvā pacchā anusocanavasena uppajjati. Yañca pubbe kalyāṇe kalyāṇasaññī katvā pacchā pāpasaññino pāpeca pāsaññī akatvā pacchā kalyāṇasaññino uppajjati. Idaṃ ayāthāvakukkuccaṃnāma. Anavajje sāvajjasaññī, kappiye akappiyasaññī, anāpattiyaṃ āpattisaññītiādināpi [M 0.0103] yojetabbaṃ. Idañca sabbaṃ uppajjamānaṃ dvīhā kāreheva uppajjati. Tasmā dvīsueva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana mahāniddeseyeva hatthakukkuccakaṃpi kukkuccaṃ. Pādakukkuccakaṃpi kukkuccaṃ. Hatthapādakukkuccakaṃpi kukkuccanti niddiṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ asaṃyata kukkuccaṃnāma. Yaṃ pana taṃ bhikkhu kukkuccāyantā napaṭiggaṇhiṃsūti vinaye āgataṃ. Yañca kathaṃ kukkuccappakatatāya āpajjati kappiye akappiyasaññitā akappiye kappiyasaññitāti āgataṃ. Taṃ vinayakukkuccaṃnāma. Taṃpana vinayasaṃsayoeva. Soca kho attano avisaye kappati nukho nonukhoti saṃsappanākārena pavatto kusala kriya cittuppādo. Sopana yesaṃ uppajjati. Tesu ye sikkhākāmā, te taṃkammaṃ nakaronti. Te sandhāya kukkuccāyantā napaṭiggaṇhiṃsūti vuttaṃ. Ye pana karontiyeva. Te kappiyavatthusmiṃpi āpattiṃ āpajjanti. Te sandhāya kukkuccappakatatāya āpattiṃ āpajjatīti vuttaṃ.

By this, the twofold nature of remorse is established: having unperformed good conduct as its object and having performed bad conduct as its object. For it is said to be of two kinds. It occurs to those who, having previously done evil, are later terrified by the fear of the lower realms, and to those who, having fallen into the lower realms, recollect the deeds they themselves have done in the past; it is not for others. For it is said, 'I have not done bodily good conduct; I have done bodily misconduct.' Just as conceit is twofold—proper conceit and improper conceit—so too is remorse twofold: proper remorse and improper remorse. Here, even improper remorse, when it arises, arises in two ways: 'Alas, I have not done good,' and 'I have done evil.' But what is that? It is the remorse that arises by way of subsequent lamentation in one who, having previously regarded wholesome deeds as unwholesome due to wrong perception and wrong view, did not do them, or in one who, having regarded unwholesome deeds as wholesome due to wrong perception and wrong view, did them. And it is that which arises in one who, having done wholesome deeds with wholesome perception in the past, later has unwholesome perception of them, or in one who, having not done unwholesome deeds with unwholesome perception, later has wholesome perception of them. This is called improper remorse. It should also be applied thus: perceiving fault where there is none, perceiving the unallowable where it is allowable, perceiving an offense where there is none, and so on. All this, when it arises, arises in two ways. Therefore, it should be seen as included in these two. But what is described in the Mahāniddesa as 'hand-remorse', 'foot-remorse', and 'hand-and-foot-remorse'—that is called 'unrestrained remorse'. As for what is stated in the Vinaya: 'Those monks, being scrupulous, did not accept it,' and what is stated as 'how one falls into an offense due to being prone to scrupulousness, perceiving the allowable as unallowable or the unallowable as allowable'—this is called Vinaya-remorse. That, however, is simply a Vinaya-doubt. And that is a wholesome functional mental state that proceeds in the manner of hesitation regarding what is not one’s domain: 'Is it allowable or not?' For those in whom this arises, if they are desirous of training, they do not do that action. Concerning them, it is said, 'Being scrupulous, they did not accept it.' But those who do it anyway commit an offense even in an allowable matter. Concerning them, it is said, 'One falls into an offense due to being prone to scrupulousness.'

94. Thiyaticittaṃ mandamandaṃ katvā ajjhottharatīti thinaṃ. Thiyiyanā thiyitattanti hi pāḷiyaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ.

94. It is called 'thina' (sloth) because it makes the mind slow and sluggish and overwhelms it. For in the Pāli it is described as 'thiyiyanā' (sluggishness) and 'thiyitattaṃ' (the state of being sluggish).

95. Medhati cetasike dhamme akammaññabhūte katvā vihiṃ satīti middhaṃ. Tathā hi ārammaṇe vipphāravasena taṃ taṃ iriyā pathaṃ sandhāretvā pavattamānesu sampayuttadhammesu muggarena pothetvā viya te ārammaṇato oliyāpetvā iriyāpathaṃpi sandhāretuṃ asamatthe katvā thinaṃ cittaṃ abhibhavati. Middhaṃ cetasiketi.

95. It is called 'middha' (torpor) because it afflicts and harms mental states by rendering them unworkable. For, when associated states are occurring while maintaining this or that posture, it is as if torpor, spreading over the object, strikes them with a mallet, causing them to withdraw from the object and making them unable even to maintain their posture. Sloth overwhelms the mind; torpor, the mental factors.

96. Vicikicchāti ettha. Cikicchanaṃ cikicchā. Ñāṇappaṭikā roti attho. Tikicchituṃ dukkaratāya vigatā cikicchā etāyāti vicikicchā. Sabhāvaṃ vicinantā kicchanti kilamanti etāyātivā vicikicchā. Vicikicchativā dveḷhakabhāvena pavattatīti vicikicchā. Sā nīvaraṇabhūtā, paṭirūpakāti duvidhā. Tattha buddhādīsu aṭṭhasu vatthūsu vimativasena pavattamānā nīvaraṇabhūtā. Tato aññāpana asabbaññūnaṃ tesu tesu ārammaṇesu kathaṃ nukho evaṃ nukho [M 0.0104] idaṃnukhoti vematikabhāvena pavattā sabbā vicikicchā paṭirūpakānāma. Sā pana kusalāpi hoti, akusalāpi khīṇā savānaṃ uppanna kriyābyākatāpīti. Idha pana ekantākusalabhūtā nīvaraṇavicikicchāva adhippekāti.

96. Regarding 'vicikicchā' (doubt): 'Cikicchā' is healing; the meaning is 'the remedy of knowledge'. It is called 'vicikicchā' because healing is gone from it (vi-gatā cikicchā), it being difficult to cure. Or, it is 'vicikicchā' because those investigating (vicinantā) a nature suffer (kicchanti) and are wearied by it. Or, it is 'vicikicchā' because it proceeds in a state of perplexity. It is twofold: that which is a hindrance and that which is a counterfeit. Of these, that which proceeds as perplexity regarding the eight objects, such as the Buddha, is a hindrance. Other than that, all doubt that proceeds as uncertainty for those who are not omniscient regarding various objects—'How is it? Is it so? What is this?'—is called a counterfeit. This can be wholesome, unwholesome, or, for those whose taints are destroyed, it can arise as functionally indeterminate. Here, however, only the doubt that is exclusively unwholesome, the hindrance of doubt, is intended.

Akusalarāsimhi paramatthadīpanā.

The Exposition of the Ultimate Meaning in the Section on the Unwholesome.

97. Saddahatīti saddhā. Yathā acchaṃ pasannaṃ nisinnaṃ udakaṃ canda sūriyādīni rūpanimittāni suṭṭhu attani dahati. Evaṃ ayaṃ buddhaguṇā dīni suṭṭhu attani dahati dhāreti thapetivāti attho. Saddahantivā etāyāti saddhā. Saddahanamattamevavā etanti saddhā. Sāpi buddhā dīsu saddheyyavatthūsu akālussiyabhāvena pavattamānāeva idha adhippetā. Tato aññāpana titthiyesuvā titthiyadhammesu vā evarūpesu asaddheyyavatthūsu saddahanavasena pavattā okappanā saddhā paṭirūpakānāma hoti. Sā pana atthato micchādhimokkho yevāti. Yathā pana manussā hatthe asati ratanāni disvā pi-gahetuṃ na sakkonti. Vitte asati tesaṃ sabbabhogā na sampajjanti. Bīje asati sassādīni nasampajjanti. Evaṃ saddhāya asati puññakriyāvatthūni nasampajjanti. Tasmā esā hatthavittabīja sadisāti vuttā.

97. Faith (saddhā) is that which believes. Just as clear, serene, and still water perfectly receives the images of the moon, sun, and other forms within itself, so too does this faith perfectly receive, hold, and establish the qualities of the Buddha and so forth within oneself—this is the meaning. Or, it is saddhā because one believes by it; or, it is saddhā because it is merely the act of believing. Here, however, only that faith which arises with clarity regarding proper objects of faith, such as the Buddha and so forth, is intended. On the other hand, the blind faith that arises by way of believing in unsuitable objects of faith—such as in heretical teachers or their doctrines—is called a counterfeit faith. In reality, it is simply wrong conviction. Just as people, without hands, cannot grasp jewels even when seeing them, or without wealth cannot attain all enjoyments, or without seeds cannot obtain crops, so too, without faith, meritorious actions do not succeed. Therefore, it is said that faith is comparable to hands, wealth, and seeds.

98. Saratīti sati. Attanā katāni kattabbāni ca kalyāṇakammāvā buddhaguṇādīnivā appamajjanavasena upagacchatīti attho. Sāpi sammāsati micchāsati duvidhā hoti. Tattha sammāsati idha adhippetā. Itarā pana satiyeva na hoti. Katassa kattabbassaca pāpakammassa appamajjanavasena pavatto satipaṭirūpako akusalacittuppādoyeva. Yasmā panesā cittaṃ sabbehi akusaladhammehica rakkhituṃ kusaladhammehica yojetuṃ sakkoti. Tasmā sā rañño sabbakammika mahāamacco viya daṭṭhabbāti. Satiṃkhvāhaṃ bhikkhave sabbatthikaṃ vadāmīti hi vuttaṃ.

98. Mindfulness (sati) is that which remembers. Its meaning is that it approaches, by way of non-negligence, good deeds done or to be done by oneself, or the qualities of the Buddha and so forth. This mindfulness is of two kinds: right mindfulness (sammāsati) and wrong mindfulness (micchāsati). Here, right mindfulness is intended. The other, however, is not truly mindfulness. For that which proceeds by way of non-negligence regarding evil deeds done or to be done is merely a counterfeit of mindfulness, an unwholesome arising of consciousness. But because this mindfulness can protect the mind from all unwholesome states and connect it with wholesome states, it should be regarded like a king's chief minister, a superintendent in all matters. For it has been said: 'Monks, I declare mindfulness to be useful in all cases.'

99. Hiriyatīti [M 0.0105] hiri. Kāyaduccaritādīhi lajjati jigucchati ukkaṇṭhatīti attho.

99. Moral shame (hiri) is that which is ashamed. Its meaning is to be ashamed of, disgusted with, and repelled by bodily misconduct and the like.

100. Tehiyeva ottappatīti ottappaṃ. Ubbijjatīti attho. Etthapi hiriottappappaṭirūpakānāma atthi, vuttañhi –

100. Moral dread (ottappa) is that by which one dreads those very things. Its meaning is to be alarmed. Here too, there are counterfeits of moral shame and moral dread, as it has been said:

Lajjitabbe nalajjanti, alajjiyesu lajjareti ca;

Bhāyitabbe nabhāyanti, abhaye bhayadassinoti ca.

They are not ashamed of what is shameful, yet are ashamed of what is not. They do not fear what is fearful, yet see fear in what is not fearful.

Yasmā pana sappurisā hiriyā attani ottappenaca paresu ārakkhadevatādīsu gāravaṃ uppādetvā pāpato vajjetvā suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharanti. Tasmā ime dve lokapāladhammāti vuttā.

Since good people, by means of moral shame in themselves and moral dread regarding others, and by generating respect for guardian deities and so on, avoid evil and keep themselves pure, therefore these two are called the guardian principles of the world.

101. Lobhappaṭipakkho alobho. So hi yesu attano hitasaññitesu ārammaṇesu lobho lagganavasena pavattati, tesveva taṃ lobhaṃ vidhamitvā lobhavatthubhūtā bhavabhogasampattiyo gūtharāsiṃviya hīḷetvā jigucchitvā ekānekkhamma dhātunāma hutvā pavattatīti.

101. Non-greed (alobha) is the opposite of greed. For, in those objects perceived as beneficial to oneself, where greed arises by way of clinging, non-greed dispels that very greed. It despises and loathes the attainments of existence and enjoyment, which are the basis of greed, like a heap of excrement. Thus, it proceeds having become what is called the element of renunciation.

102. Dosappaṭipakkho adoso. Sopi hi yesu attano ahitasaññitesu ārammaṇesu doso dussanavasena pavattati. Tesveva taṃdosaṃ vidhamitvā diṭṭhadiṭṭhesu sattesu puṇṇacandasadisaṃ sommahadayaṃ uppādetvā ekā abyāpādadhātu nāma hutvā pavattatīti. Ayamevaca brahmavihāresu mettāti vuttā. Amohopi idha vattabbo. Mohappaṭipakkho amoho. Sopi hi yesu dhammesuvā atthesuvā catūsu ariyasaccesuvā moho andhakāraṃ katvā pavattati. Tesveva taṃ mohaṃ vidhamitvā candasūriyasahassaṃ uṭṭhāpentoviya vijjānāma hutvā pavattatīti.

102. Non-hatred (adosa) is the opposite of hatred. For, in those objects perceived as harmful to oneself, where hatred arises by way of aversion, when that hatred is dispelled with regard to those very objects, a heart as gentle as the full moon arises towards beings seen and unseen, and it proceeds having become what is called the element of non-ill will. This is what is called loving-kindness among the divine abidings. Non-delusion (amoha) should also be mentioned here. Non-delusion is the opposite of delusion. For, in those phenomena, meanings, or the Four Noble Truths where delusion arises creating darkness, when that delusion is dispelled with regard to those very things, it proceeds having become what is called knowledge, as if raising a thousand suns and moons.

103. Tatramajjhattatāti ettha attā vuccati sabhāvo. Līnuddhaccādīnaṃ ubhinnaṃ visamapakkhānaṃ majjhe pavatto attā etassāti majjhattā. Samappavatto sampayuttadhammasamūho. Tassa bhāvo majjhakkatā. [M 0.0106] Tesu tesu sampayuttadhammesu dissamānā majjhattatā tatramajjhattatā tesu tesuvā hitakammesu cittacetasikānaṃ majjhattatā tatramajjhattatā. Tathā hi sā samappavattānaṃ sampayutta dhammānaṃ ajjhupekkhanavasena samappavattānaṃ ājāneyyānaṃ ajjhupekkhanasārathīviya daṭṭhabbāti vuttā. Ayamevaca brahmavihāresu upekkhāti vuttā.

103. Here, in the term 'tatramajjhattatā', 'attā' is said to mean 'sabhāva' (nature). Equanimity (majjhattā) is that whose nature (attā) proceeds in the middle of two dissimilar sides, such as sluggishness (līna) and restlessness (uddhacca). The group of associated mental factors that proceeds evenly is 'samappavatto'. The state of that is 'majjhattatā'. The equanimity visible in those various associated mental factors is specific equanimity (tatramajjhattatā); or, the equanimity of mind and mental factors in those various beneficial actions is specific equanimity. For it is said that it should be seen as a charioteer impartially observing well-trained thoroughbreds that proceed evenly, by way of its impartial observation of the evenly proceeding associated mental factors. And this very thing is called equanimity (upekkhā) among the divine abidings.

104. Kāyappassaddhādīsu kāyoti vedanādikkhandhattaya saṅkhāto cetasikasamūho vuccati. Cittanti sobhaṇacittaṃ. Kāyassa passaddhi kāyappassaddhi. Cittassa passaddhi cittappassaddhītiādinā samāso. Passambhanaṃ passaddhi. Santasītalabhāvoti attho. Yesaṃ idaṃ dvayaṃ dubbalaṃ hoti. Te puññakammesu cittasukhaṃ napindanti. Bahiddhāeva nesaṃ cittaṃ pakkhandati. Santatte pāsāṇapiṭṭhe thapitamacchoviya hoti. Yesaṃ pana balavaṃ hoti. Teyeva tattha taṃ vindanti. Tesaṃ cittaṃ sītale udake pakkhitta maccho viya hoti.

104. In 'tranquility of the body' (kāyappassaddhi) and similar terms, 'kāya' (body) refers to the group of mental factors reckoned as the three aggregates beginning with feeling. 'Citta' (mind) means wholesome consciousness. Tranquility of the body is 'kāyappassaddhi,' and tranquility of the mind is 'cittappassaddhi,' and so on by way of compounding. Passaddhi means calming; its meaning is the state of being peaceful and cool. For those in whom this pair is weak, their minds do not find happiness in meritorious deeds. Their minds incline outward, like a fish placed on a hot stone slab. But for those in whom this pair is strong, they find that happiness there. Their minds are like a fish placed in cool water.

105. Lahubhāvo lahutā. Agarutā adandhatāti attho. Yesaṃ idaṃ dubbalaṃ. Tesaṃ cittaṃ puññakammesu napasāreti saṅkocati. Tattapāsāṇe pakkhittapadumapupphaṃ viya hoti. Yesaṃ pana balavaṃ. Tesaṃ cittaṃ tattha pasāreti. Sītale udake pakkhitta padumapupphaṃ viya hoti.

105. Lightness (lahutā) is the state of being light; its meaning is non-heaviness, non-slowness. For those in whom this is weak, their minds do not extend to meritorious deeds but shrink, like a lotus flower placed on a hot stone. But for those in whom this is strong, their minds extend there, like a lotus flower placed in cool water.

106. Mudubhāvo mudutā. Yesaṃ idaṃ dubbalaṃ. Tesaṃ cittaṃ puññakammesu thaddhaṃ hoti. Verīnaṃ majjhe gatamahāyodhoviya hoti. Yesaṃ pana balavaṃ. Tesaṃ cittaṃ tattha mudu hoti. Viyaññātīnaṃ majjhe gatamahāyodho viya hoti.

106. Pliancy (mudutā) is the state of being soft. For those in whom this is weak, their minds become rigid regarding meritorious deeds, like a great warrior who has gone into the midst of enemies. But for those in whom this is strong, their minds become soft regarding that, like a great warrior who has gone into the midst of relatives.

107. Kammani sādhu kammaññaṃ. Tadeva kammaññatā. Yesaṃ idaṃ dubbalaṃ. Tesaṃ cittaṃ puññakammesu yathicchitaṃ thapetuṃ nalabbhati, vikkirati. Paṭivāte khittathusamuṭṭhiviya hoti. Yesaṃ pana balavaṃ. Tesaṃyeva taṃ tattha yathicchitaṃ thapetuṃ labbhati navikkirati. Paṭivāte khittasuvaṇṇakkhandhoviya hoti.

107. Workableness (kammaññatā) is that which is fit for action; that itself is workableness. For those in whom this is weak, their minds cannot be fixed as desired on meritorious actions; they scatter, like a handful of chaff thrown against the wind. But for those in whom this is strong, their minds can be fixed as desired there without scattering, like a nugget of gold thrown against the wind.

108. Paguṇassa [M 0.0107] bhāvo pāguññaṃ. Tadeva pāguññatā. Yesaṃ idaṃ dubbalaṃ. Tesaṃ cittaṃ puññakammesu vikampati vihaññati. Gambhīre udake khittavānaroviya hoti. Yesaṃ pana balavaṃ, te saṃ taṃ tattha navikampati navihaññati. Gambhīre udake khitta kumbhilo viya hoti.

108. Proficiency (pāguññatā) is the state of being proficient; that itself is proficiency. For those in whom this is weak, their mind wavers and is agitated in meritorious deeds, like a monkey thrown into deep water. But for those in whom it is strong, their mind does not waver or become agitated there, like a crocodile thrown into deep water.

109. Ujueva ujukaṃ, ujukassa bhāvo ujukatā. Yesaṃ idaṃ dubbalaṃ. Tesaṃ cittaṃ puññakammesu visamagahikaṃ hoti. Kadāci līnaṃ. Kadāci uddhaṭaṃ. Kadāci onataṃ. Kadāci unnataṃ. Surāmadamattassa maggagamanaṃ viya hoti. Yesaṃ pana balavaṃ, tesaṃ taṃ vuttavipariya yena veditabbanti.

109. Straightforwardness (ujukatā) is what is straight; the state of being straight is straightforwardness. For those in whom this is weak, their mind in meritorious deeds becomes crooked—sometimes sluggish, sometimes agitated, sometimes depressed, sometimes elated. It is like the walking of a drunkard on a road. But for those in whom it is strong, the opposite of what was said should be understood.

110. Etthaca siddhesupi cittappassaddhādikesu vuttesu visuṃ kāyappassaddhādīnaṃ vacanaṃ tesaṃ vasena rūpakāyassapi passaddhādi dīpanatthanti veditabbaṃ. Tattha taṃ taṃ suttantaṃ sutvā gelaññavuṭṭhā nādīsu rūpakāyassa passaddhabhāvo pākaṭo iddhimantānaṃ iddhiyā ākāsagamanādīsu lahu bhāvo. Kāyaṃ khuddakaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā katvā nimminanesu mudubhāvo. Antopathaviyaṃvā antopabbate suvā asajjamānaṃ katvā gamanādīsu kammaññabhāvo. Nāgavaṇṇaṃvā garuḷavaṇṇaṃvā katvā nimminanādīsu paguṇabhāvo tesveva sabbesu yathānimmitavasena cirappavattibhāvesu ujukabhāvo pākaṭo hotīti veditabbo. Samaṃ dhārentīti sādhāraṇā, sabbehi sobhaṇacittehi, tesaṃvā sādhāraṇā sobhaṇa sādhāraṇā.

110. Here, although mental tranquility and so forth have been mentioned as accomplished, the separate mention of bodily tranquility and so forth is to be understood as for the purpose of indicating that the material body also attains tranquility and so forth by means of them. In this regard, having heard various discourses, the tranquility of the material body becomes evident in cases like recovery from illness. For those possessing psychic powers, their lightness in traversing the sky and so forth by means of psychic power, their softness in creating bodies small or large, their wieldiness in moving unobstructed through the earth or mountains, their proficiency in creating forms like a nāga or a garuḍa—in all these, their straightness in maintaining for a long duration whatever form they have created becomes evident. They are held in common, thus they are 'common' (sādhāraṇā). They are common to all beautiful consciousnesses, or common to them, hence they are 'beautiful-common' (sobhaṇasādhāraṇā).

111. Sammāvācāti ettha tividhā sammāvācā kathā, cetanā, virativasena, tattha atthadhammappaṭisaṃyuttā subhāsitā vācā kathā sammāvācānāma. Taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā kusalakriyacetanā cetanāsammāvācānāma. Yā pana musāvādā veramaṇādīni sikkhāpadāni samādiyantassavā adhiṭṭhahantassavā sampattaṃ vatthuṃ avītikkamantassavā pāpaviramaṇākārena cittassa pavatti. Ayaṃ virati sammāvācānāma. Sā idha adhippetā. Sammā vadanti etā yāti [M 0.0108] sammāvācā. Etāyāti cettha karaṇatthe hetuatthe vā karaṇavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha vācāya sikkhāpadāni samādiyantassa samādānavacanāni sandhāya karaṇattho hetuattho ca yujjati. Tato yathāsamādinnānivā yathādhiṭṭhitānivā sikkhāpadāni suṭṭhurakkhāmāti yāni anavajjānieva vacanāni vadantā vicaranti. Tāni sandhāya karaṇatthānukūlo hetu atthoyeva yujjatīti. Athavā, tathā vadantuvā māvā. Ayaṃpana vadamānesu sati tesaṃ sammā vattuṃeva deti. Namicchā vattunti katvā sammā vācātveva vuccati. Apica, ayaṃ vacīduccaritānaṃ pajahanavasena pavattamānā vacīdvārasuddhiyā eva hotīti sammāvācāti vuccatīti.

111. Here, right speech (sammāvācā) is threefold: by way of speech, volition, and abstinence. Herein, speech that is connected with the meaning and the Dhamma, and is well-spoken, is called right speech by way of speech. The wholesome volition that gives rise to it is called right speech by way of volition. As for the occurrence of the mind in the mode of abstaining from evil for one who undertakes or resolves upon the training rules, such as abstinence from false speech, or for one who does not transgress a situation that has arisen—this abstinence is called right speech by way of abstinence. This is what is intended here. 'They speak rightly by this (etāya),' hence it is right speech (sammāvācā). Here, the instrumental case 'by this' should be understood in the sense of either instrument or cause. In this context, with reference to the words of undertaking for one who undertakes the training rules by speech, both the instrumental and causal senses are applicable. Therefore, with reference to those who live speaking only blameless words, guarding well the training rules as undertaken or resolved upon, the causal sense, which is conducive to the instrumental sense, is applicable. Alternatively, whether they speak thus or not, this abstinence, when they are speaking, enables them to speak rightly and prevents them from speaking wrongly; therefore, it is called right speech. Moreover, since this abstinence occurs by way of abandoning verbal misconduct, it is for the purification of the verbal door, and thus it is called right speech.

112. Sammākammantopi tividho kriyā, cetanā, virati vasena. Tattha yaṃkiñci anavajjaṃ kammaṃ karontassa kāyikakriyā kriyākammantonāma. Taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā cetanākammanto nāma. Yā pana pāṇātipātā veramaṇādīni sikkhāpadāni samādi yantassavā adhiṭṭhahantassavā sampattaṃ vatthuṃ avītikkamantassavā pāpaviramaṇākārena cittassa pavatti. Ayaṃ virati sammākammanto nāma. Sammā karonti etenāti sammākammaṃ, tadeva sammā kammanto suttanto vanantoviya. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

112. Right action (sammākammanta) is also threefold: by way of action, volition, and abstinence. Herein, whatever blameless bodily action is performed by one who acts is called right action by way of action. The volition that gives rise to it is called right action by way of volition. As for the occurrence of the mind in the mode of abstaining from evil for one who undertakes or resolves upon the training rules, such as abstinence from killing, or for one who does not transgress a situation that has arisen—this abstinence is called right action by way of abstinence. 'They act rightly by this (etena),' hence it is right action (sammākammaṃ). That same right action is sammākammanto, the suffix -anta being used as in suttanta (discourse) or vananta (forest). The rest here is to be understood in the same way as previously explained.

113. Sammāājīvopi vīriya, virativasena duvidho. Tattha pakatiyā anavajjāni kasikammādīnivā bhikkhācariyādīnivā katvā jīvitaṃ kappentānaṃ uṭṭhānabalasaṅkhāto vāyāmo vīriyasammāājīvonāma. Yā pana ājīvasuddhiṃ apekkhitvā attano ājīvasīlavipattikāraṇāni kāyavacīduccaritāni pajahantānaṃ pāpaviramaṇākārena cittassa pavatti. Ayaṃ virati ājīvonāma. Ayamidhādhippeto. Sammā ājīvanti jīvitaṃ pavattenti etenāti sammāājīvo. Sesamettha vuttanayamevāti.

113. Right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) is also twofold: by way of effort and by way of abstinence. Herein, the exertion, defined as the strength of initiative, of those who make a living by performing naturally blameless actions such as farming or seeking alms, is called right livelihood by way of effort. But for those who, seeking purity of livelihood, abandon bodily and verbal misconduct that are causes of corruption in their livelihood and morality, the occurrence of the mind in the mode of abstaining from evil—this abstinence is called right livelihood. This is what is intended here. 'They live rightly, they sustain their life by this (etena),' hence it is right livelihood (sammā-ājīva). The rest here is to be understood in the same way as previously explained.

114. Ekekāpi cettha sampatta virati, samādāna virati, samucchedavirativasena tividhā. Tattha yā sikkhāpadāni asamā diyitvāvā [M 0.0109] samādinnānipivā tāni anapekkhitvā kevalaṃ hiri ottappabaleneva sampattaṃ vatthuṃ avītikkamantānaṃ uppannā virati. Ayaṃ sampattaviratināma. Sā paccuppannārammaṇāyeva. Pañcasikkhā padā paccuppannārammaṇāti hi vuttaṃ. Yā pana sikkhāpadāni samādi yantassavā adhiṭṭhahantassavā yathāsamādinnānivā yathādhiṭṭhitāni vā suṭṭhurakkhāmīti sampatta vatthuṃ apītikkamantassavā uppannā. Ayaṃ samādānaviratināma. Sā pana paccuppannārammaṇāvā hoti anāgatārammaṇāvā. Tathā hi pañcasikkhāpadā paccuppannārammaṇāti idaṃ sampattavirativasena vuttanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Maggakkhaṇe pana sabbaduccaritānaṃ paccayasamucchedavasena uppannā samucchedaviratināma. Sā pana nibbānārammaṇāeva. Phalaviratipi ettheva saṅgahitāti. Tattha lokiyaviratiyo jīvitindriyādīni vītikkamitabbavatthūni ārammaṇaṃ katvā pāṇātipātādīni viramitabbavatthūni pajahanti. Lokuttaraviratiyo pana nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā tāniyeva viramitabbavatthūni pajahantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

114. Each of these abstinences is threefold here: as abstinence by encounter, abstinence by undertaking, and abstinence by eradication. Among these, the abstinence that arises in those who, without having undertaken the training rules, or even having undertaken them but without relying on them, refrain from transgressing an encountered situation solely through the power of moral shame and moral dread—this is called abstinence by encounter. It has only a present object, for it is said, 'The five training rules have a present object.' On the other hand, the abstinence that arises in one who undertakes or resolves upon the training rules, thinking, 'I will properly guard what I have undertaken or resolved,' and thus refrains from transgressing an encountered situation—this is called abstinence by undertaking. It may have either a present or a future object. For it is stated in the commentary that the statement, 'The five training rules have a present object,' is said with reference to abstinence by encounter. At the moment of the path, the abstinence that arises through the eradication of the conditions for all misconduct is called abstinence by eradication. This has only Nibbāna as its object. The abstinence of fruition is also included here. In this context, mundane abstinences abandon the things to be refrained from, such as killing living beings, by taking as their object things that are to be transgressed, such as the life faculty. Supramundane abstinences, however, abandon those same things to be refrained from by taking Nibbāna as their object. This should be understood.

115. Paradukkhe sati kāruṇikānaṃ hadayakhedaṃ karotīti karuṇā. Kirativā paradukkhaṃ vikkhipati, kiṇātivā paradukkhaṃ hiṃsatīti karuṇā. Kirīyati dukkhitesu pasārīyatītivā karuṇā. Apica kali uṇāti chedo. Kalīti dukkhaṃ vuccati, yathā-kali sambhave bhaveti. Kalītivā pāpapi parājayopi vuccati. Pāpe kali parājayeti hi vuttaṃ. Sabbañcetaṃ kāruṇikā naṃ kāruññahetubhūtameva hoti. Iti kaliṃ dukkhaṃvā pāpaṃvā sabbasampattito parājayaṃvā sattehi avanti rakkhanti, sattevā tato vidhakalito avanti rakkhanti kāruṇikā janā etāyāti karuṇā.

115. When there is suffering in others, it causes (karoti) distress in the hearts of the compassionate—thus it is compassion (karuṇā). Or it scatters (kirati) the suffering of others; or it destroys (kiṇāti), that is, harms, the suffering of others—thus it is compassion. Or it is spread (kirīyati) or extended (pasārīyati) to those who are afflicted—thus it is compassion. Moreover, 'kali' and 'uṇā' mean 'cutting'. 'Kali' is said to mean suffering, as in 'arising from kali.' Or, 'kali' is also said to mean evil or defeat, for it is said, 'In evil there is kali, defeat.' All this is indeed the cause of compassion for the compassionate. Thus, compassionate people protect beings from 'kali'—whether it be suffering, evil, or defeat from all prosperity; or they protect beings from that destructive 'kali'—by this (etāya) it is compassion.

116. Parasampattiṃ disvā modanti etāyāti muditā. Natthi pamāṇaṃ etesanti appamāṇā, sattā. Appamāṇesu bhavāti appamaññā. Etāhi ettakesuyeva sattesu pavattetabbā. Na ito aññesūti evaṃ paricchedappamāṇassa abhāvā ekasmiṃ satte pavattāpi appamaññāevanāma hontīti.

116. Seeing the prosperity of others, they rejoice by this (etāya)—thus it is sympathetic joy (muditā). There is no measure (pamāṇa) for these beings (sattā), thus they are immeasurable (appamāṇā). That which occurs in relation to the immeasurable is an 'immeasurable' (appamaññā). It is not the case that these should be applied to only so many beings and not to others; thus, because there is no such limiting measure, even when applied to a single being, they are still called 'immeasurables.'

[77] Ṭīkāsu pana

[77] But in the subcommentaries,

Appamāṇasattā [M 0.0110] rammaṇattā appamāṇā. Tāeva appamaññāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

They are 'immeasurable' because they have immeasurable beings as their object. It is said that they themselves are the 'immeasurables'. That is not a sound explanation.

117. Paññindriyanti heṭṭhā vutto amohoeva. So hi pajānanaṭṭhena paññā, adhipatiyaṭṭhena indriyañcāti katvā paññindriyanti vuccatīti.

117. The faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is simply the non-delusion mentioned previously. For it is called the faculty of wisdom because it is wisdom (paññā) in the sense of understanding, and a faculty (indriya) in the sense of exercising dominance.

Sobhaṇarāsimhi paramatthadīpanā.

The Exposition of the Ultimate Meaning in the Section on the Beautiful.

118. Ettāvatātiādi tiṇṇaṃ rāsīnaṃ saṅgaho. Evaṃ dvipaññāsa sarūpaṃ dassetvā idāni cetoyuttappakāraṃ dassento tesantiādimāha. Ito cetasikānaṃ sarūpadassanato paraṃ tesaṃ cittāviyuttānaṃ cittena aviyuttānaṃ cetasikānaṃ cittuppādesu paccekaṃ sampayogo tathāyogaṃ vuccateti yojanā. Cittuppādesūti cittesu icceva attho. Uppajjanti cetasikā etesūti uppādā. Cittānieva uppādā cittuppādāti katvā. Dvipañcaviññāṇānaṃ sabbadubbalattā tesu cha pakiṇṇakā nuppajjanti. Bhāvanābalena pahīnattā vitakko dutīyajjhānikādīsu, vicāro tatīyajjhānikādīsu, pīti catutthajjhānikādīsu nuppajjati. Sanniṭṭhānasabhāvattā adhimokkho asanniṭṭhānasabhāve vicikicchā citte nuppajjati. Vīriyaṃ balanāyakattā dubbalesu pañcadvārāvajjanā dīsu soḷasacittesu nuppajjati. Pīti sampiyāyanasabhāvattā domanassupekkhā sahagatesu nuppajjati. Chando icchāsabhāvattā icchārahitesu ahetukesu momūhacittesuca nuppajjatīti āha pakiṇṇakesupana vitakko.La. Momūhavajjitacittesūti. Te pana cittuppādā pakiṇṇakavivajjitā sapakiṇṇakāti sambandho.

118. The phrase 'up to this point' and so forth is a summary of the three groups. Having thus shown the nature of the fifty-two mental factors, now, explaining the manner of their connection with consciousness, he says 'of these' and so forth. From here, after showing the nature of the mental factors, the individual association of those mental factors, which are inseparable from consciousness, with the consciousness-arisings (cittuppāda) is called 'such association'—this is the connection. 'In the consciousness-arisings' means simply 'in the consciousnesses.' Mental factors arise in these, thus they are 'arisings.' Because consciousnesses themselves are arisings, they are called 'consciousness-arisings.' Due to the extreme weakness of the two sets of fivefold consciousnesses, the six occasional mental factors do not arise in them. Because they are abandoned through the power of meditation, initial application (vitakka) does not arise in the second jhāna and beyond, sustained application (vicāra) in the third jhāna and beyond, and joy (pīti) in the fourth jhāna and beyond. Because decision (adhimokkha) has the nature of resolution, it does not arise in consciousness that lacks resolution, such as in doubt-accompanied consciousness. Because energy (vīriya) has the nature of being the leader of strength, it does not arise in the sixteen weak consciousnesses, such as the five-door adverting consciousnesses. Because joy (pīti) has the nature of delight, it does not arise in consciousness accompanied by displeasure or equanimity. Because desire (chando) has the nature of longing, it does not arise in rootless consciousnesses that are devoid of desire, nor in deluded consciousnesses. Thus he says, 'But among the occasional factors, initial application... except in deluded consciousnesses.' The connection is that those consciousness-arisings are either devoid of the occasional factors or accompanied by them.

119. Akusalesūti akusalacetasikesu. Sabbākusala sādhāraṇānāma. Tasmā sabbesupi dvādasākusalacittesu labbhantīti yojanā.

119. 'In unwholesome states' means in unwholesome mental factors. They are called 'common to all unwholesome' factors. Therefore, the connection is that they are found in all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.

[78] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[78] But in the Vibhāvanī,

Pacchimaṃ [M 0.0111] purimassa samatthanavacananti adhippetaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

The latter is intended as a statement supporting the former. That is not sound.

Idañhi ṭhānaṃ cittesu labbhamānatādassanapadhānanti. Yasmā pana sabbāni akusalacittāni imehi catūhi vinā nuppajjanti. Na hi tāni pāpesu ādīnavaṃ passitvā ṭhitānaṃ uppajjanti. Naca tehi lajjāyavā bhayenavā ukkaṇṭhitānaṃ. Nāpi kusalesu dhammesu samāhitānanti. Tasmā te sabbesu tesu labbhantīti. Yasmāca diṭṭhimānā khandhesu assādaṃ amuñcitvāva tesu tathā tathā āmasitvā pavattanti. Tasmā te lobhamūlacittesveva uppajjanti. Tattha uppajjantesu pana tesu diṭṭhi khandhesu attaggāhaṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā taṃ attaṃ niccatādīhi micchāsabhāvehieva parāmasantī pavattati. Māno pana khandhe ahanti daḷhaṃ gahetvā taṃ gahitākāraṃ seyya tādīhieva āmasanto pavattati. Tasmā te āmasanākārato asadisavuttinoeva hontīti āha. Diṭṭhicatūsu.La. Vippayuttesūti. Ye pana diṭṭhigatikā diṭṭhiyā yathāgahitaṃ attānameva ahanti gaṇhanti. Tesaṃpi diṭṭhimānā āmasanākāraṃ patvā asadisavuttikāeva honti. Na hi mānassa viya diṭṭhiyā atta saṃpaggahaṇe byāpāro atthi. Na ca diṭṭhiyā viya mānassa dhammānaṃ ayāthāvapakkhaparikappaneti. Teneva hi ahaṃgāho māno anāgāmīnaṃpi pavattati. Attaggāhabhūtā pana diṭṭhi puthujjanāna mevāti.

This is indeed a section primarily concerned with showing what is found in consciousnesses. For all unwholesome states of mind do not arise without these four mental factors. Indeed, they do not arise in those who, seeing the danger in evil, remain steadfast; nor in those who are ashamed of, afraid of, or disheartened by them; nor in those who are composed in wholesome states. Therefore, they are found in all of them. And because wrong view and conceit, without letting go of the savoring of the aggregates, engage with them in various ways, they arise only in consciousnesses rooted in greed. When they arise there, wrong view, having firmly grasped the aggregates as self, persists in misapprehending that self with false characteristics such as permanence. Conceit, however, having firmly grasped the aggregates as 'I am,' persists in engaging with them by way of such notions as 'I am better.' Therefore, they are dissimilar in their mode of engagement—thus it is said: '[They are found] in the four [consciousness-types] dissociated from wrong view.' But even for those who hold to wrong view and grasp 'I am' as the very self grasped by that view, for them too, wrong view and conceit become dissimilar in their mode of engagement. For conceit does not have the function of grasping a self in the same way as wrong view; nor does wrong view have the distorted conceptualization of phenomena in the same way as conceit. For this very reason, the 'I am' conceit persists even in non-returners, whereas wrong view in the form of grasping a self is only for ordinary people.

[79] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[79] But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Mānopi ahaṃmānavasena pavattanato diṭṭhisadisova pavattatīti diṭṭhiyā saha ekacittuppāde napavattatī”ti vatvā kesara sīho pamāya taṃ atthaṃ sādheti. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

Having said, 'Because conceit, operating by way of the 'I am' conceit, operates similarly to wrong view, it does not operate in the same consciousness-arising together with wrong view,' Kesarasīha establishes that meaning through reasoning. That is not sound.

Sadisappavatti hi nāma sahapavattiyā eva kāraṇanti. Macchariyaṃ pana attasampattīsu lagganalobhasamuṭṭhitaṃpi tāsaṃ parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ [M 0.0112] asahanākārena pavattattā ekantena paṭighasampa yuttameva hotīti vuttaṃ doso.La. Cittesūti. Akammañña lakkhaṇaṃ thinamiddhaṃ kammaññasabhāvesu asaṅkhārikesu nasambhavatīti vuttaṃ thinamiddhaṃ pañcasu sasaṅkhārika cittesūti. Cattāro sabbā kusalasādhāraṇā. Tayo lobha diṭṭhimānā. Cattāro dosādayo. Dvayaṃ thinamiddhaṃ. Vicikicchā cittecāti casaddo avadhāraṇe. Vicikicchācitteevāti attho. Catuddasa akusala cetasikā.

For similar occurrence is indeed the cause of co-occurrence. Miserliness, however, though arising from clinging and greed regarding one's own attainments, is entirely associated with aversion because it manifests as an inability to tolerate sharing those attainments with others—thus it is said: '[It is found] in consciousnesses rooted in aversion, etc.' Sloth and torpor have the characteristic of unworkability. It is said that sloth and torpor do not arise in unprompted consciousnesses which have the nature of being workable; hence, sloth and torpor occur in the five types of prompted consciousness. Four mental factors are common to all unwholesome consciousness-types. Three are greed, wrong view, and conceit. Four are aversion and so on. Two are sloth and torpor. In the phrase 'in the doubt-consciousness and' (vicikicchācitte ca), the word 'and' (ca) is used for emphasis, meaning 'only in the doubt-consciousness.' These are the fourteen unwholesome mental factors.

120. Sobhaṇesūti sobhaṇacetasikesu. Lokuttare aṭṭhaṅgikamagge tīsu khandhesu paññākkhandhe sammāsaṅkappo nāma sammādiṭṭhipacchimakova hoti. Tasmā pādakajjhānādivasena tasmiṃ asatipi paññākkhandho naparihāyati. Sīlasamādhikkhandhadhammesu pana eko ekassa kiccaṃ nasādheti. Tasmā lokuttara maggo sattaṅgikato heṭṭhā napavattatīti āha viratiyo pana tissopi.La. Labbhantīti. Niyatāva ekatova sabbathāpi labbhantīti yojanā. Tattha niyatāvāti na lokiyesuviya kadācieva labbhanti. Athakho sabbadāpi niyatā hutvāva labbhanti. Kasmā, lokuttaradhammānaṃ niccaṃ sīlesu paripūrakāritāvasena pavattattā. Na hi te lokiyā viya kadāci dānavasena kadāci sutapariyattivasena kadāci kasiṇabhāvanādivasena pavattantīti. Ekato vāti nalokiyesu viya visuṃ visuṃ labbhanti. Athakho tissopi ekato hutvāva labbhanti. Kasmā, abhinnārammaṇattā. Na hi te lokiyā viya vītikkamitabbavatthusaṅkhātāni jīvitindriyādīni nānārammaṇāni ārabbha pavattanti. Ekaṃpana nibbānameva ārabbhapavattantīti. Sabbathāpīti na lokiyesu viya ekade sappahānavasena labbhanti. Athakho tissopi anavasesa duccarita durājīvappahānākārena labbhanti. Lokiyesuhi sakiṃ uppannā sammāvācā catubbidhāni vacīduccaritāni sabbāni ekato pajahituṃ nasakkoti. Musāvādavirati musāvādameva pajahituṃ sakkoti. Na itarāni. Musāvādaṃpi samūlaṃ sānusayaṃ pajahituṃ nasakkoti. [M 0.0113] Tathā pisuṇavācā virati pisuṇavācameva pajahituṃ sakkoti. Na itarāni. Pisuṇavācaṃpi samūlaṃ sānusayaṃ pajahituṃ na sakkoti. Sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Lokuttaresu pana sakiṃ uppannā sammāvācā sabbāni vacīduccaritāni samūlāni sānusayāni pajahati. Sakiṃ uppanno sammākammanto sabbāni kāyaduccaritāni samūlāni sānusayāni pajahati. Sakiṃ uppanno sammāājīvo sabbāni ājīvahetukāni kāyavacīduccaritāni samūlāni sānusayāni pajahati. Iti tisso lokuttaresueva sabbathāpi labbhantīti. Visaddo avayavasampiṇḍanattho. Sakiṃ uppannā ekā sammāvācā musāvādappahānavasenāpi labbhati. Nakevalañca tappahānavaseneva. Athakho pisuṇavācāpahānavasenapi labbhatīti sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Etthaca duccaritāni samūlāni sānusayānīti ettha kāyavacīcopana bhāgiyāni kāmarāgānusayādīni uparimaggavajjhāni kilesajātāni arūpasekkhānaṃpi santiyeva. Kāmarūpasekkhānaṃ pana vattabbameva natthi. Tasmā tesaṃ pajahanavasena uparimagga phalaviratīnaṃ duccaritappahānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāmāvacarakusalesveva, napana kāmāvacaravipākakriyacittesu, nāpimahaggatacittesūti adhippāyo. Kāmāvacarakusalesupi kāmabhūmiyaṃ uppannesueva, narūpārūpabhūmiyaṃ uppannesu. Na hi brahmānaṃ viramitabbavatthu saṅkhātāni kāyavacīduccaritānināma atthi. Naca lokiyaviratiyo viramitabba vatthurahitesu puggalesu pavattantīti. Upari chakāmāvacaradeve supi napavattantīti vadanti. Taṃ kathāvatthumhi vicāritameva. Yadi evaṃ manussalokepi tīsu heṭṭhimaphalaṭṭhesu tāsaṃ appavatti āpajjati. Na hi tesaṃpi pāṇātipātādīni viramitabbavatthūnināma atthīti. Saccaṃ, idha pana sattavidhaāpattikkhandhāpi viramitabbavatthuṭṭhāne ṭhitā. Tathā tividhakuhanavatthūnica. Tānica kānici tesaṃ phalaṭṭhānaṃpi sādhāraṇānieva. Manussānañca yāni kānici tassa tassa samādinnassa sikkhāpadassa vatthūnipi viramitabbavatthūnieva. Yānipi kāmasekkhānaṃ kāyavācā vipphandanakarāni kilesajātāni samucchedaviratīnaṃ vatthubhūtāni santi. Tāni tesaṃ tadaṅga viratīnaṃpi [M 0.0114] vatthūnievāti. Kadāci sandissantīti samādānasampattaviratīnaṃ aññataravasena pavattakāleeva sandissanti. Evaṃ sandissa mānāpi bhinnārammaṇattā naekato hutvā sandissantīti vuttaṃ visuṃ visunti. Visuṃvisuṃ sandissamānāpi ekekaduccaritappahānavaseneva sandissanti. Na lokuttaresu viya sabbathāpīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

120. “In the beautiful” means in the beautiful mental factors. In the supramundane Noble Eightfold Path, within the three aggregates, in the wisdom aggregate, right intention is indeed subsequent to right view. Therefore, even if it is absent by way of the foundational jhānas and so forth, the wisdom aggregate is not diminished. However, among the factors of the virtue and concentration aggregates, one does not accomplish the function of another. Therefore, the supramundane path does not proceed with fewer than seven factors; thus it is said: “The three abstinences, however, are obtained.” The explanation is that they are obtained invariably, together, and in every way. Herein, “invariably” means they are not obtained only occasionally, as in the mundane sphere; rather, they are always obtained, having become fixed. Why? Because supramundane phenomena always proceed by way of completely fulfilling virtue. Indeed, they do not proceed like mundane virtues, sometimes by way of giving, sometimes by way of studying the scriptures, sometimes by way of kasiṇa meditation, and so forth. “Together” means they are not obtained separately, as in the mundane sphere; rather, all three are obtained as one. Why? Because of having an identical object. Indeed, they do not proceed like mundane abstinences, taking as objects various things to be transgressed, such as the life faculty and so forth. Rather, they proceed taking only Nibbāna as their object. “In every way” means they are not obtained by way of partial abandonment, as in the mundane sphere; rather, all three are obtained in the manner of abandoning misconduct and wrong livelihood without remainder. In the mundane sphere, right speech, having arisen once, is not able to abandon all four kinds of verbal misconduct at once. Abstinence from false speech is able to abandon only false speech, not the others. It is not able to abandon even false speech with its root and latent tendency. Similarly, abstinence from divisive speech is able to abandon only divisive speech, not the others. Nor is it able to abandon even divisive speech with its root and latent tendency. All this should be elaborated in full. In the supramundane sphere, however, right speech, having arisen once, abandons all verbal misconduct with their roots and latent tendencies. Right action, having arisen once, abandons all bodily misconduct with their roots and latent tendencies. Right livelihood, having arisen once, abandons all bodily and verbal misconduct due to livelihood with their roots and latent tendencies. Thus, the three are obtained in every way only in the supramundane sphere. The word ‘vi’ has the meaning of combining the parts. A single right speech, having arisen once, is obtained by way of abandoning false speech. And not only by way of abandoning that, but it is also obtained by way of abandoning divisive speech, and so on—all this should be stated. And here, regarding “misconduct with roots and latent tendencies,” the kinds of defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths, such as the latent tendency of sensual desire and so forth, which are connected with bodily and verbal actions, exist even for trainees in the formless realm. For trainees in the sense-sphere and form realms, however, there is nothing more to be said. Therefore, the abandonment of misconduct by the abstinences of the higher paths and fruitions should be seen by way of abandoning them. The intention is: only in wholesome sense-sphere states, not in sense-sphere resultant or functional consciousness, nor in sublime consciousness. Even among wholesome sense-sphere states, only in those arisen in the sense-sphere plane, not in those arisen in the form or formless planes. For Brahmās, there are indeed no things to be abstained from, designated as bodily and verbal misconduct. And mundane abstinences do not proceed in individuals who are without things to be abstained from. They say they do not proceed even in the six sense-sphere heavens above; that is indeed discussed in the Kathāvatthu. If so, in the human world too, for those established in the three lower fruitions, their non-occurrence would follow. For them too, there are indeed no things to be abstained from, such as killing living beings and so forth. True, but here the sevenfold classes of offenses also stand in the place of things to be abstained from, as do the three grounds of deceit. And some of those are common even to those established in the fruitions. For humans, whatever are the objects of this or that training rule undertaken by them are also things to be abstained from. Also, whatever kinds of defilements that cause bodily and verbal agitation for trainees in the sense-sphere exist, which have become the basis for the abstinences by eradication, those are also the basis for their abstinences by substitution of opposites. “They appear sometimes” means they appear only at the time of proceeding by way of either abstinence by undertaking or abstinence by attainment. Even when appearing thus, because of having different objects, they do not appear as one; thus it is said, “separately.” Even when appearing separately, they appear only by way of abandoning each single misconduct, not in every way as in the supramundane sphere—this should be understood.

121. Appanāpattānaṃ appamaññānaṃ somanassasahagatabhāvova vibhaṅge vuttoti vuttaṃ pañcamajjhānavajjitamahaggatacittesūti. Etāhi parasattānaṃ hetu adhimattabyāpārā honti, tasmā atisantāya nibyāpārāya pañcamajjhānupekkhāya saha napavattantīti. Appanāpubbabhāgabhūtānaṃ pana tāsaṃ upekkhāvedanāyapi sampayogo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ anuññātoyevāti vuttaṃ kāmāvacara.La. Cittesucāti. Kadācīti kāruññappakatikassa anissukinoca paresaṃ vipattisampattidassanakāle. Nānāhutvā jāyantīti tesaṃ vipattidassanakāle anukampanavasena karuṇā eva jāyati, namuditā. Sampattidassanakāle pana modanavasena muditāva jāyati, nakaruṇāti evaṃ visuṃ visuṃ hutvā jāyantīti attho. Yasmā panetā dosasamuṭṭhitānaṃ vihiṃsā aratīnaṃ nissaraṇabhūtāti suttantesu vuttā. Domanassapaṭipakkhañcaso manassameva hoti. Tasmā tāsaṃ appanāpubbabhāgabhūtānaṃpi niccaṃ somanassayogameva keci icchantīti vuttaṃ upekkhāsahagatesu.La. Keci vadantīti. So pana tesaṃ vādo aṭṭhakathāyapi saha viruddho. Tasmā taṃ bahū viññuno na sampaṭicchantīti katvā sovādo therena kecivādonāma kato. Yasmāca sabbesaṃpi lokiya lokuttarajjhānānaṃ pubbabhāga bhāvanā nāma appanāsannakāleeva somanassajjhānānaṃ pubbabhāgā somanassasahagatā honti. Upekkhājhānānaṃ pubbabhāgā upekkhāsahagatā honti. Anāsannakāle pana sabbesaṃpi tesaṃ pubbabhāgā kadāci somanassasahagatā, kadāci upekkhāsahagatāhonti. Tasmā so vādo kecivādova kātuṃ yuttoti. Etthaca sabbānipi samathavipassanābhāvanācittānināma ādimhi yebhuyyena upekkhāsahagatānieva [M 0.0115] bhaveyyuṃ, yadiyi tāni āditoyeva paṭṭhāya somanassasahajātāni siyuṃ. Tadā ime sattā so manassajātesu kammesu anabhiratānāma natthīti aññaṃ kammaṃ chaḍḍetvā bhāvanākammameva anuyuñjeyyunti. Pacchā pana attano bhāvanāya pubbāpariyavisesadassanakāleeva somanassa sahajātāni bhavanti. Paṭikūlā rammaṇesu pana asubhabhāvanācittesu dukkhitasattārammaṇesuca karuṇābhāvanācittesu vattabbameva natthi. Apica imā karuṇāmuditānāma pakatikālepi uppajjantiyeva. Tāsu pana muditā tāva iṭṭhasampattivisayāti sāyebhuyyena somanassa sahajātāti yuttametaṃ. Karuṇā pana aniṭṭhavipattivisayāti sā yebhuyyena upekkhāsahajātā eva siyā. Naca etā parasattahetu adhimatta byāpārāti katvā upekkhāvedanāya saha viruddhāevāti sakkā vattuṃ. Sā hi appanaṃ apattā vedanupekkhānāma ārammaṇarasānubhavaneeva nibyāpārāhoti. Na aññakiccesu. Tathā hi sattā upekkhāsahagata cittehi adinnaṃpi ādiyanti, dānaṃpi denti, aññānipi mahantāni puññāpuññakammāni karontiyevāti. Tasmā appanā pattānaññeva tāsaṃ vedanupekkhāya saha viruddhabhāvo vattuṃ yuttoti.

121. In the Vibhaṅga, it is stated that for the immeasurables that have attained absorption, the state is accompanied by joy. This is said regarding the exalted minds, excluding the fifth jhāna. These immeasurables have excessive engagement on account of other beings, and therefore, they do not occur together with the extremely tranquil and disengaged equanimity of the fifth jhāna. However, for those immeasurables in the preliminary stages leading to absorption, their association with equanimous feeling is permitted in the commentaries. This is stated regarding the sense-sphere minds. Sometimes, for one naturally compassionate and not envious, when seeing the misfortunes or successes of others, they arise separately: when seeing their misfortune, compassion alone arises by way of sympathy, not appreciative joy; but when seeing their success, appreciative joy alone arises by way of rejoicing, not compassion. This is the meaning of their arising distinctly. Moreover, since these immeasurables are stated in the suttas to be the escape from violence and aversion born of ill will, and since joy is the opposite of sorrow, some desire that even for those immeasurables in the preliminary stages leading to absorption, they are always associated with joy. This is stated in relation to those accompanied by equanimity: 'Some say...' But their view conflicts even with the commentaries. Therefore, because many wise ones do not accept it, that view is called 'the view of some' by the Elder. And since, for the preliminary cultivation of all mundane and supramundane jhānas, when near absorption, the preliminary stages of joy-jhānas are accompanied by joy, and the preliminary stages of equanimity-jhānas are accompanied by equanimity; but when not near absorption, their preliminary stages may sometimes be accompanied by joy and sometimes by equanimity. Therefore, that view is rightly considered 'the view of some'. And here, all serenity and insight meditation minds would mostly be accompanied by equanimity at the beginning. If they were accompanied by joy from the very start, then there would be no beings who do not delight in actions born of joy, and they would abandon all other deeds to engage solely in meditation. Later, however, joy arises only when one sees the specific progress of one's own meditation. However, in the case of meditation minds on foulness with repulsive objects, and meditation minds on compassion with suffering beings as objects, there is nothing to be said about joy. Furthermore, this compassion and appreciative joy arise even at ordinary times. Among them, appreciative joy, being concerned with desirable success, is mostly accompanied by joy, which is fitting. But compassion, being concerned with undesirable misfortune, would mostly be accompanied by equanimity. Nor can it be said that these immeasurables are in conflict with equanimous feeling merely because they have excessive engagement on account of other beings. For equanimous feeling, when it has not attained absorption, is disengaged only in experiencing the flavor of the object, not in other activities. Indeed, beings with minds accompanied by equanimity may still take what is not given, give gifts, and perform other great wholesome and unwholesome deeds. Therefore, it is proper to say that their conflict with equanimous feeling exists only for those that have attained absorption.

[80] Ettāvatā yaṃ vuttaṃ vibhāvaniyaṃ

[80] Thus far, what was stated that needed clarification is:

“Karuṇāmuditā bhāvanākāle appanāvīthito pubbe paricayavasena upekkhāsahagatacittehipi parikammaṃ hoti. Yathātaṃ paguṇaganthaṃ sajjhāyantassa kadāci aññavihi tassāpi sajjhāyanaṃ, yathāca paguṇavipassanāya saṅkhāre sammasantassakadāci paricayabalena ñāṇavippayuttacittehipi sammasananti upekkhā sahagatakāmāvacaresu karuṇā muditānaṃ asambhavavādo kecivādo kato”ti. Taṃ paṭikkhittaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

"At the time of developing compassion and appreciative joy, even before the absorption path-process, preliminary work occurs with minds accompanied by equanimity due to familiarity. Just as one reciting a familiar text occasionally recites another text, or as one contemplating formations with practiced insight occasionally contemplates with minds dissociated from knowledge due to the power of familiarity—thus, the view of some has been put forth that compassion and appreciative joy are impossible in the sense-sphere accompanied by equanimity." This should be seen as refuted.

Kiñcāpi kasiṇanimittādīni ārammaṇāni agambhīrānieva honti. Tathāpi yogakammabalena cittasamādhānabalena kilesa dūrībhāvenaca [M 0.0116] tadārammaṇesu jhānacittesu ñāṇaṃ ekantena pavatta tiyevāti āha sabbesupi pañca.La. Cittesucāti.

Although kasiṇa signs and other objects are indeed not profound, yet through the power of meditative work, the strength of mental concentration, and the distancing of defilements, knowledge certainly arises in the jhāna minds focused on those objects. Thus, it is said that it arises in all five kinds of minds.

122. Tayo viratidhammā. Dvayaṃ appamaññāyugaḷaṃ. Evaṃ so bhaṇacetasikā sobhaṇesveva cittesu catudhā catūhi pakārehi sampayuttāti yojanā. Idāni sabbesaṃpi ceto yuttānaṃ niyatā niyatayogivibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ issātiādimāha. Karuṇā ādi yassāti karuṇādi. Appamaññā dvayaṃ. Issāmaccherakukkuccānica viratiyoca karuṇādica issāmacche rakukkuccaviratikaruṇādayo. Te nānāca jāyanti, kadācica jāyanti. Mānoca kadācieva jāyati. Thinamiddhañca tathā kadāci eva jāyati. Jāyamānaṃ pana aññamaññaṃ saheva jāyati. Nanānāti yojanā. Etthaca appamaññāviratīnaṃ nānā kadāci yogo heṭṭhāca vutto. Uparica vakkhati. Issādīnaṃca upari vakkhati. Mānathinamiddhānaṃ pana idha vattabboti. Tattha māno catūsu diṭṭhivippayuttesu labbhamānopi kadāci tesaṃ seyyo hamasmītiādinā pavattakāleeva labbhati, naaññadā. Thinamiddhaṃ pañcasu sasaṅkhārikesu labbhamānaṃpi kadāci tesaṃ niddātibhūtavasena akammaññatāya pavattikāleeva labbhati. Na aññadā. Tadā labbhamānaṃpana dvayaṃ saheva labbhati. Na nānāti.

122. There are three abstinences. The two immeasurables. Thus, the connection is: those beautiful mental factors are associated in four ways, by four modes, only with the beautiful minds. Now, to show the division of all associated mental factors into fixed and unfixed associations, he begins by saying 'envy,' etc. That which has compassion as its beginning is 'compassion, etc.' The two immeasurables. Envy, stinginess, worry, and the abstinences, and compassion, etc.—these are envy, stinginess, worry, the abstinences, compassion, and so on. They arise separately and sometimes they arise. Conceit also arises only sometimes. Sloth and torpor likewise arise only sometimes. But when they arise, they arise together, not separately. This is the connection. Here, the separate and occasional association of the immeasurables and abstinences has been stated below and will be stated above. Regarding envy, etc., it will be stated above. But conceit, sloth, and torpor should be stated here. There, conceit, though obtainable in four types dissociated from wrong view, is obtained only at the time of its manifestation as 'I am better,' etc., not at other times. Sloth and torpor, though obtainable in five types with prompting, are obtained only at the time of their manifestation due to excessive sleepiness and unwieldiness, not at other times. When they are obtained then, both are obtained together, not separately.

[81] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[81] However, what needs to be clarified is:

“Thinamiddhaṃ kadāci issāmaccherakukkuccehiceva mānenaca saha jāyati. Kadāci tehi tenaca nānā jāyatī”ti yojanā vuttā. Sā sārato na paccetabbā.

"Sloth and torpor sometimes arise together with envy, stinginess, worry, and conceit. Sometimes they arise separately from them." This is the stated connection. It should not be accepted as essentially correct.

Na hi tehi tenaca tassa sahabhāvo nānābhāvoca kiccārammaṇavirodhāvirodhabhāvena siddhoti.

For their co-existence or separateness is not established by the opposition or non-opposition of function and object.

Yāca ṭīkāyaṃ

And in the subcommentary:

Mānoca thinamiddhañca kadāci nānā jāyati. Kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Yojanā vuttā. Sāpi na sundarā. Kadāci sahajāyatīti.

"Conceit, and sloth and torpor, occasionally arise separately. The reason has been stated. The connection has been stated. That too is not sound. It should be: 'Sometimes they arise together.'"

Yathāvuttānusārenāti sattasabbatthayujjantītiādinā vuttappakāraṃ anusārena sesāti ekādasahi aniyata yogīhi avasesā ekacattālīsadhammā. Te yathāvuttānusārena attanā labbhamāna cittuppādesu aniyatayogino veditabbāti yojanā.

The phrase 'Following what has been said' refers to the method explained beginning with 'the seven are associated everywhere,' etc. Accordingly, the remaining forty-one phenomena, apart from the eleven indeterminate factors, are to be understood as having unfixed associations in the mind-moments where they are obtained. This is the connection.

123. Evaṃ cetasikānaṃ yogaṭṭhānaparicchindanavasena sampayoganayaṃ dassetvā idāni yuttadhammarāsiparicchindanavasena saṅgaha nayaṃ dassento saṅgahañcātiādimāha. Idāni tesaṃ saṅgahañca yathārahaṃ pavakkhāmīti yojanā. Chattiṃsātiādi saṅgahanayassa uddesagāthā. Sattapaññattārammaṇā appamaññā nibbānā rammaṇesu nalabbhantiti vuttaṃ appamaññāvajjitāti tathā aṭṭhasu dutīyajjhānikacittesu vitakkavajjā aññasamānā dvādasaceta sikā appamaññāvajjitā tevīsati sobhaṇacetasikāceti pañcattiṃsa dhammā saṅgahaṃ gacchantītiādinayaṃ tathāsaddena niddisati. Teevāti vitakka vicāra pītisukhavajjā upekkhāsahagatā te eva tettiṃsadhammā. Aṭṭhasūti ettha aṭṭhaca aṭṭhaca aṭṭhāti ekasesaniddeso, vicchālopaniddesovā daṭṭhabbo. Pañcakajjhāna vasenāti pāḷiyaṃ pañcakanayena vuttassa jhānabhedassa vasena, catukkanayena vuttassa jhānabhedassa vasena pana catudhāva saṅgaho hotīti adhippāyo. Dvīsu rūpapathamajjhānalābhīsu dutīyajjhānaṃ uppādentesu mando vitakkamo atikkamituṃ sakkoti. Tassa caturaṅgikaṃ dutīyajjhānaṃ uppajjati. Tikkhapañño pana vitakka vicāre ekato atikkamituṃ sakkoti. Tassa tiyaṅgikaṃ dutīyajjhānaṃ uppajjatīti ayaṃ tesaṃ nayānaṃ viseso.

123. Having thus shown the method of association by defining the places of association of mental factors, now, to explain the method of classification by defining the groups of associated phenomena, he begins with 'and the classification,' etc. The connection is: 'Now, I will explain their classification appropriately.' 'Thirty-six,' etc., is the summary verse for the method of classification. It is stated that the immeasurables, which have the concept of beings as their object, are not found in states having Nibbāna as their object—hence, 'excluding the immeasurables.' Similarly, in the eight second-jhāna minds, the twelve other-equal mental factors excluding initial thought, and the twenty-three beautiful mental factors excluding the immeasurables—these thirty-five phenomena are included. This is indicated by the word 'such' (tathā). 'Those very' refers to those very thirty-three phenomena, excluding initial thought, sustained thought, joy, and happiness, and accompanied by equanimity. Here, 'in the eight' (aṭṭhasu) should be understood as a specification by the ekaśeṣa method (eight and eight and eight), or as a specification by alternation. 'According to the fivefold jhāna method' means according to the division of jhāna stated in the Pāli canon by the fivefold method; however, according to the division of jhāna stated by the fourfold method, the classification is fourfold—this is the intention. Among those who have attained the first jhāna in the form realm and are developing the second jhāna, one of dull faculties can overcome initial thought. For such a one, the second jhāna with four factors arises. But one of sharp wisdom can overcome initial thought and sustained thought together. For such a one, the second jhāna with three factors arises—this is the distinction between their methods.

124. Kiccārammaṇaviruddhattā viratiyo mahaggatesu nuppajjantīti āha viratittayavajjitāti. Viratiyo hi kāyavacī visodhanakiccā honti. Mahaggatajjhānāni pana suvisuddhakāyavacī payogasseva cittavisodhanakiccāni. Viratiyoca vītikkamitabba vatthuṃvā nibbānaṃvā ārabbha pavattanti. Mahaggatajjhānāni pana paññatti yovā mahaggatadhammevāti.

124. Because they are incompatible in function and object, the abstinences do not arise in the sublime states—thus it is said, ‘excluding the three abstinences.’ For the abstinences have the function of purifying bodily and verbal action. The sublime jhānas, however, have the function of purifying the mind for one whose bodily and verbal conduct is already very pure. The abstinences, moreover, arise having as their object either a basis for transgression or Nibbāna. The sublime jhānas, however, have as their object either concepts or the sublime phenomena themselves.

125. Kiccārammaṇavi [M 0.0118] ruddhattāyeva viratiappamaññāyo ekasmiṃ citte dve nalabbhantīti vuttaṃ. Appamaññā viratiyo panettha.La. Yojetabbāti. Viratiyo ekantena dussilyappahāna kiccattā tappahāna kiccarahitesu lokiyābyākatesu nalabbhantīti vuttaṃ virativajjitāti. Pañcasikkhāpadā kusalāyevāti hi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Idañca lokiyasikkhāpadāni sandhāya vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Appamaññānaṃ sattapaññattārammaṇattā mahāvipākānañca ekanta parittārammaṇattā tāsaṃ tesu sambhavo natthīti vuttaṃ appamaññā virativajjitāti. Nanu kāmakusalaṃ sattapaññattādi ārammaṇaṃpi hotīti tabbipākenapi tena sadisā rammaṇena bhavitabbanti. Na. Vikapparahitattā. Paññattiyo hi avijjamānattā mahaggatānuttaradhammāca saṇhasukhumadhammattā tathā tathā vikappetvāvā paṭivijjhitvāvā gaṇhantānaṃ kusalādīnaṃ eva ārammaṇabhūtā honti. Kāmavipākāni pana sayaṃ atidubbalatāya ārammaṇaṃ vikappetvā vigahetuṃ nasakkonti, kuto paṭivijjhitvā gahetuṃ. Tasmā tāni paññattiyovā mahaggatānuttaradhammevā ālambituṃ na sakkontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahaggatavipākāni pana vikapparahitānipi appanāpattakammavise sanibbattattā bhāvanābalanimmitāni paññattivisesāni ālambituṃ sakkontīti.

125. It is said that the two—the abstinences and the immeasurables—are not found in a single consciousness precisely because their functions and objects are contradictory. Here, the immeasurables and the abstinences... should be connected. The abstinences are said not to be found in worldly indeterminate states because their function is solely the abandonment of immoral conduct, and those states lack the function of that abandonment—thus it is said, ‘excluding the abstinences.’ For it is stated in the Pāli canon that the five precepts are exclusively wholesome. This should be understood as referring to worldly precepts. The immeasurables are said not to arise in those states because their objects are the concepts of beings, whereas the great resultants have exclusively sense-sphere objects. Therefore, their occurrence in those states is not possible—thus it is said, ‘excluding the immeasurables and abstinences.’ But does not sense-sphere wholesome consciousness also have the concept of beings, etc., as its object? Should not its resultant consciousness also have a similar object? No, because it lacks conceptual activity. For concepts, being non-existent, and the sublime and supramundane states, being subtle and refined phenomena, become objects only for wholesome states, etc., which apprehend them by variously conceptualizing or penetrating them. Sense-sphere resultants, however, being themselves extremely weak, cannot conceptualize and grasp an object, let alone penetrate and grasp it. Therefore, it should be understood that they cannot take concepts or sublime and supramundane states as objects. Sublime resultants, however, though lacking conceptual activity, can take special concepts created by the power of meditation as objects because they are produced by the special quality of kamma that has attained absorption.

[82] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[82] However, in the Vibhāvanī:

Kāmataṇhādhinakammajanitattā kāmavipākāni kāmataṇhāya ārammaṇabhūte kāmadhammeeva ālambituṃ labhantīti adhippāyena “kāmataṇhādhinassa phalabhūtattā”ti vatvā dāsiputtopamāya tadatthaṃ vibhāveti. Taṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

With the intention that sense-sphere resultants, being produced by kamma under the sway of craving for sense pleasures, can only take as their object sense-sphere phenomena, which are the objects of craving for sense pleasures, he clarifies that meaning by stating, ‘because they are the fruit of what is under the sway of craving for sense pleasures,’ and by means of the simile of the slave woman’s son. This should be investigated.

Evañhi sati mahaggatavipākānipi rūpārūpataṇhādhina kammajanitāni eva hontīti tānipi rūpārūpataṇhānaṃ ārammaṇabhūte mahaggata dhammeeva ālambeyyunti. Apica, kāmataṇhāpi kāmadhammeeva ārammaṇaṃ karoti. Na paññattidhammeti natthi. Naca itthipurisādi hattha pādādi paññattīsu assādavasena pavattā taṇhā kāmataṇhā nāma [M 0.0119] nahotīti atthi. Subheti kusale. Maneti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Subhe kriye pāketi niddhāraṇīyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sahetu. La. Mane dvādasadhāva saṅgahotivā yojetabbaṃ. Navijjantetthāti vajjitānaṃ saṅgaho. Etthāti sobhaṇacittesu. Dvayanti viratiappamaññādukaṃ. Anuttareti visesakānaṃ saṅgaho. Jhāna dhammāti vitakkādayo. Majjhime mahaggate appamaññāca jhānadhammā ca. Parittesu kāmasobhaṇesu appamaññāca virati ñāṇapīti yoca visesakā, saṅgahanaya bhedakārakāti attho.

For if this were so, then the sublime resultants, being produced by kamma under the sway of craving for form and formlessness, would also take as their object only the sublime phenomena that are the objects of craving for form and formlessness. Moreover, craving for sense pleasures also takes sense-sphere phenomena as its object. It is not the case that it does not take conceptual phenomena as its object. And it is the case that craving which arises through enjoyment in concepts such as 'man,' 'woman,' 'hand,' 'foot,' etc., is indeed called craving for sense pleasures. 'In the beautiful' refers to the wholesome. 'In the mind' is the locative of determination. 'In the beautiful, functional, and resultant' should be understood as the determinable. 'With roots... in the mind' should be connected as 'the classification is of twelve kinds.' 'Are not found here' means the inclusion of what is excluded. 'Here' refers to the beautiful consciousnesses. 'The two' refers to the pair of abstinences and immeasurables. 'In the supramundane' means the inclusion of the distinguishing factors. 'Jhāna factors' refers to initial thought and so on. In the intermediate sublime states, there are the immeasurables and the jhāna factors. In the limited sense-sphere beautiful states, the immeasurables, abstinences, wisdom, and joy are the distinguishing factors, meaning they are the factors that differentiate the method of classification.

126. Sattarasadhammā lobhadiṭṭhīhi saddhiṃ ekūnavīsati hutvā saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti yojanā. Pītivajjitā aññasamānā dvādasa cetasikā akusalasādhāraṇā cattārocāti soḷasadhammā lobhadiṭṭhīhi saha aṭṭhārasa hutvā saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti yojanā. Issāmacchariya kukkuccāni kiccato ārammaṇato ca bhinnāni hontīti vuttaṃ issā.La. Yojetabbānīti. Sabbesupi akusalacittuppādesu sampayuttadhammā dhammato asadisāeva honti. Gaṇanato pana ekacce ekaccehi sadisā eva hontīti vuttaṃ dvādasa.La. Saṅgahitābhavantīti. Etthaca pañcasu asaṅkhārikesu pathamadutīyesu ekūnavīsati. Tatīyacatutthesu aṭṭhārasa. Pañcame vīsati. Pañcasu sasaṅkhārikesu pathamadutīyesu ekavīsati. Tatīyacatutthesu vīsati. Pañcame dvāvīsati. Momūhadvaye pannarasāti evaṃ akusalesu satta saṅgahā bhavanti. Tenāha ekūnavīsātiādiṃ. Sādhāraṇāti sabbā kusalasādhāraṇā. Samānāti aññasamānā. Apareti chandapītiadhimokkhe thapetvā ekacce.

126. The connection is: the seventeen factors, together with greed and wrong view, become nineteen and are classified together. The connection is: the sixteen factors—namely, the twelve other-equal mental factors excluding joy, and the four unwholesome universals—together with greed and wrong view, become eighteen and are classified together. It is said that envy, stinginess, and remorse are distinct in function and object—thus, ‘envy... should be connected.’ Although all factors associated with unwholesome consciousnesses are dissimilar in nature, some are similar in enumeration—thus it is said, ‘the twelve... are classified together.’ Here, among the five unprompted types, the first and second have nineteen factors; the third and fourth have eighteen; the fifth has twenty. Among the five prompted types, the first and second have twenty-one; the third and fourth have twenty; the fifth has twenty-two. In the two types rooted in delusion, there are fifteen. Thus, there are seven classifications among the unwholesome states. Therefore, he says, ‘nineteen,’ etc. ‘Universals’ refers to all unwholesome universals. ‘Equal’ refers to the other-equals. ‘Others’ refers to some, excluding intention, joy, and decision.

127. Hasanacitteti hasituppādacitte. Voṭṭhabbaneti manodvārāvajjane. Sukhasantīraṇeti somanassa santīraṇe. Mano dhātuttikā hetuka paṭisandhi yugaḷeti pañcadvārāvajjana sampaṭicchanadvayasaṅkhāte manodhātuttikeceva upekkhā santīraṇa dvayasaṅkhāte ahetuka paṭisandhiyugaḷeca. Sabbattha sabbesu ahetukesu [M 0.0120] satta, tato sesā pakiṇṇakā pana yathārahaṃ yujjanti, iti tettiṃsa vidhasaṅgaho mayā vuttoti yojanā.

127. ‘In the smile-producing consciousness’ refers to the consciousness that produces smiling. ‘In the determining consciousness’ refers to the mind-door adverting consciousness. ‘In the joyful investigating consciousness’ refers to the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy. ‘The mind-element triad and the rootless rebirth-linking pair’ refers to the mind-element triad itself, which consists of the five-door adverting consciousness and the two receiving consciousnesses, and to the rootless rebirth-linking pair, which consists of the two investigating consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity. In all rootless consciousnesses, the seven universal mental factors are found; thereafter, the remaining particular mental factors are combined as appropriate. The connection is: 'Thus, the thirty-threefold classification has been explained by me.'

128. Idāni ayaṃ cetasikaniddesoti katvā cittassa viya ekassapi cetasikassa bhūmijāti sampayogādi bhedena vibhāgo kathetabboti taṃ dassetuṃ antimagāthamāha. Itthaṃ iminā yathāvuttappakārena cittāviyuttānaṃ cetasikānaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ sampayogañca tettiṃsavidhaṃ saṅgahañca ñatvā tesaṃ yathā yogaṃ cittena samaṃ bhedaṃ uddiseti yojanā. Phasso tāva ekūnanavutiyā ekavīsasatesuvā cittesu yuttattā ekūnanavuti ekavīsasatavidhevāti evaṃ dvipaññāsacetasike visuṃ visuṃ uddharitvā yathāyogaṃ bhūmijātisampayogādibhedehi tesaṃ vibhāgaṃ katheyyāti attho.

128. Now, considering this to be an exposition of mental factors, and that even a single mental factor, like consciousness, should be classified by way of distinctions such as plane, class, association, and so forth, he speaks the final verse to show this. The construction is that, having thus understood the sixteen kinds of association and thirty-three kinds of inclusion of mental factors inseparable from consciousness in the manner described, one should set forth their distinctions together with consciousness as is appropriate. For instance, contact, being connected with eighty-nine or one hundred and twenty-one types of consciousness, is thus eighty-ninefold or one hundred and twenty-onefold. In this way, taking up each of the fifty-two mental factors separately, one should explain their classification according to distinctions such as plane, class, association, and so forth, as is appropriate—this is the meaning.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus, of the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, in the commentary named ‘Paramatthadīpanī’,

Catutthavaṇṇanāya cetasika saṅgahassa

of the fourth exposition, the Compendium of Mental Factors,

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

the Paramatthadīpanī is completed.

Pakiṇṇaka saṅgaha paramatthadīpanī

The Compendium of Miscellanea: An Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning

129. Evaṃ [M 0.0121] visuṃ visuṃ cittacetasikānaṃ niddesaṃ dassetvā idāni puna ubhinnaṃ niddesaṃ dassento sampayuttāyathāyogantiādimāha. Yathāyogaṃ sampayuttā sabhāvato tepaññāsa cittacetasikā ye dhammā mayā visuṃ visuṃ niddiṭṭhā. Idāni yathā rahaṃ tesaṃ ubhinnaṃ saṅgahonāma niyyateti yojanā. Tattha attano attano bhāvo sabhāvo. Dhammānaṃ āvenikalakkhaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Cittaṃ tāva bhūmijātisampayogādibhedena ekūna navutividhaṃpi attano ārammaṇa vijānanasaṅkhātena āvenikalakkhaṇena ekameva hoti. Phassopi bhūmijātisampayo gādibhedena ekūnanavutividhopi phusanalakkhaṇena ekova hoti tathā vedanāsaññādayoti evaṃ sabhāvato tepaññāsa eva hontīti. Vedanāhetuto kiccadvārālambaṇavatthuto pavatto saṅgahoti sambandho. Tattha vedanāhetutoti vedanābheda hetubhedato. Evaṃ kiccadvārālambaṇa vatthutoti etthapi. Cittuppādavasenevāti cittavaseneva niyyateti sambandho. Evasaddena cetasike nivatteti. Ettāvatā channaṃ pakiṇṇakasaṅgahānaṃ vacanattho idheva tāva therena dassito hoti vedanābhedena cittacetasikānaṃ saṅgaho vedanāsaṅgaho, hetubhedena cittacetasikānaṃ saṅgaho hetusaṅgahotiādinā.

129. Having thus shown the separate exposition of consciousness and mental factors, he now proceeds to show their combined exposition, beginning with the words, 'Associated according to suitability...'. The construction is as follows: The fifty-three phenomena—consciousness and mental factors—which I have separately expounded, are associated according to suitability by their intrinsic nature. Now, the grouping of these two is set forth as is appropriate. Therein, one’s own nature is its intrinsic characteristic. It is said to be the unique characteristic of phenomena. For instance, consciousness, though of eighty-nine kinds based on the division of plane, class, association, and so forth, is one by its unique characteristic of cognizing an object. Similarly, contact, though of eighty-nine kinds based on the division of plane, class, association, and so forth, is one by its characteristic of touching. The same applies to feeling, perception, and so on. Thus, by their intrinsic nature, there are only fifty-three. The connection is that the grouping proceeds by way of feeling, root, function, door, object, and base. Herein, 'by way of feeling and root' means by way of the division of feelings and the division of roots. Similarly, this applies to 'by way of function, door, object, and base.' The connection is that it is set forth only by way of the arising of consciousness, that is, by way of consciousness itself. By the word 'eva' (only), he excludes the mental factors.
