Thus far, the meaning of the words of the six miscellaneous groupings has been shown here by the Elder: the grouping of consciousness and mental factors by way of the division of feelings is the feeling-grouping; the grouping of consciousness and mental factors by way of the division of roots is the root-grouping, and so on.

[83] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[83] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Cittuppādasaddena cetasikadhammepi gahetvā aññaṃ nivatte tabbaṃ apassanto “na katthaci taṃvirahenā”ti vadati. Taṃ nayujjatiyeva.

By the term ‘cittuppāda’ (arising of consciousness), having also included mental factors, and not seeing anything else to exclude, he says, “It is nowhere without that.” That is indeed not suitable.

Na hi idha ettakā cetasikā sukhasahagatā, ettakā dukkha sahagatātiādinā ekopi saṅgaho cetasikehi nīto nāma [M 0.0122] atthi. Sukhasahagataṃ kusalavipākaṃ kāyaviññāṇamekamevātiādinā pana cittenaeva nīhoti. Citte pana siddhe ceta sikāpi siddhāevāti katvā cittuppādavasenevāti idaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For here, there is no single grouping that is led by mental factors, such as ‘so many mental factors are associated with pleasure,’ ‘so many are associated with pain,’ and so on. But it is led by consciousness itself, as in ‘the wholesome-resultant body-consciousness associated with pleasure is just one,’ and so on. But since when consciousness is established, mental factors are also established, it should be understood that this is said 'by way of the arising of consciousness'.

130. Tatthāti tesu chasu saṅgahesu. Vedanābhedena taṃsampayuttānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ saṅgaho vedanāsaṅgaho.

130. ‘Therein’ means in those six groupings. The grouping of consciousness and mental factors associated with them by way of the division of feelings is the feeling-grouping.

[84] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[84] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Sukhādivedanānaṃ taṃsahagatacittuppādānañca vibhāgavasena saṅgaho vedanāsaṅgaho”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha casaddena vedanāsaṅgahoca vedanāsahagata cittuppāda saṅgahocāti imasmiṃ atthe vedanāsaṅgahoti ekasesaniddeso hotīti dasseti. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: “The grouping of pleasant and other feelings and the arisings of consciousness associated with them, by way of division, is the feeling-grouping.” Therein, he shows that by the word ‘ca,’ in the sense of 'both the grouping of feelings and the grouping of arisings of consciousness associated with feelings,' ‘feeling-grouping’ is an elliptical exposition. That is not elegant.

Idha hi vedanābhedo imassa saṅgahassa nissayadhammapariggahatthaṃeva vutto. Na vedanānaṃca visuṃ saṅgahadassanatthanti. Tatthatividhā vedanāti kasmā vuttaṃ. Nanu saṃyuttake dvepi tissopi pañcapi chapi aṭṭhārasapi chattiṃsapi aṭṭhasataṃpi vedanā vuttāti. Saccaṃ. Anubhavanalakkhaṇena pana vedanā tividhāeva hoti. Ye hi keci yaṃkiñci ārammaṇaṃ anubhavanti. Te taṃ sātatovā anubhavanti asātatovā majjhattatovā. Tato añño pakāro natthīti. Aññe pana pabhedā tena tena pariyāyena vuttā. Tattha hi dve kāyikacetasikavasena vuttā. Yathāha-katamāca bhikkhave dve vedanā kāyikāca cetasikācāti. Sukhadukkha vasenavā upekkhaṃ sukhe saṅgahetvā. Yathāha-dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā sukhāvedanā dukkhāvedanā. Yāyaṃ bhante adukkha masukhā vedanā. Santasmiṃ esāpaṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatāti.

For here, the division of feelings is stated solely for the purpose of encompassing the supporting phenomena of this grouping, not for the purpose of showing a separate grouping of feelings. Why then is it said, “Feelings are threefold”? Are not feelings spoken of in the Saṃyutta Nikāya as twofold, threefold, fivefold, sixfold, eighteenfold, thirty-sixfold, and even one hundred and eightfold? That is true. However, by the characteristic of experiencing, feelings are only threefold. For whatever object beings experience, they experience it either agreeably, disagreeably, or neutrally. There is no other way. But other classifications are stated in various ways. There, they are spoken of as twofold—bodily and mental—as it is said: “And what, monks, are the two feelings? Bodily and mental.” Or, by way of pleasure and pain, by including equanimity under pleasure, as it is said: “Two feelings were spoken of by the Blessed One—pleasant feeling and painful feeling. And this, venerable sir, this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, was it spoken of by the Blessed One as included in that which is peaceful and sublime pleasure?”

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī:

Anavajjapakkhikaṃ upekkhaṃ sukhe sāvajjapakkhikañca dukkhe saṅgahetvā dve vuttāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pāḷiyaṃ anāgataṃpi yujjatiyeva.

It is said that by including equanimity on the blameless side in pleasure and that on the blameworthy side in suffering, two are spoken of. That is suitable even if not found in the Pāli Canon.

Indriyabhedavasena [M 0.0123] pañca. Phassabhedavasena cha. Upavicārabheda vasena aṭṭhārasa. Cha gehassitāni cha nekkhammassitānīti evaṃ paccekaṃ dvādasannaṃ somanassa domanassaupekkhānaṃ vasena chattiṃsa. Tāyeva kālattayavasena aṭṭhasataṃ vedanā vuttāti. Yañca katthaci sutte yaṃkiñci vedayitaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhasminti vuttaṃ. Taṃ saṅkhāradukkhatāvasena vuttanti. Heṭṭhā pana cittaniddese cittāni indriyabhedavasena niddiṭṭhānīti katvā idhapi indriyabhedavaseneva cittāni saṅgahetuṃ puna sukhaṃ.La. Pañcadhā hotīti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca yesu dhammesu ādhi paccavasena sukhadukkhāni indriyāni nāma honti. Tesaṃ kāyika mānasikavasena duvidhattā tānipi sukhindriyaṃ somanassindriyaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ domanassindriyanti dvidhā vuttāni. Upekkhāya pana ādhipaccaṭṭhānabhūtā dhammā mānasikāeva hontītisā upekkhindriyanti ekadhāva vuttāti. Apica, tepi pariyāyena duvidhā honti. Cakkhādipasādakāya nissitānaṃpi sabbhāvato. Vedanāpana ekarasattā ekadhāva vuttāti.

By way of the division of faculties, there are five. By way of the division of contact, there are six. By way of the division of investigation, there are eighteen. Six are connected to household life, and six are connected to renunciation—thus, with twelve each of joy, displeasure, and equanimity, there are thirty-six. The same, when divided by way of the three periods of time, makes one hundred and eight feelings spoken of. And that it is said in a certain Sutta, 'Whatever is felt, all that is within suffering'—that is spoken of by way of the suffering inherent in formations. But below, in the exposition of consciousness, since consciousnesses are explained by way of the division of faculties, here too, in order to group consciousnesses by way of the division of faculties, it is again said: 'Pleasure, etc., is fivefold.' And here, those phenomena wherein pleasure and pain are predominant are called faculties. Since these are twofold, being bodily and mental, they too are spoken of as twofold: the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of joy, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of displeasure. But the phenomena that are the basis of predominance for equanimity are purely mental, and thus it is spoken of as one: the faculty of equanimity. Moreover, even these are in a certain sense twofold, due to their existence being dependent on the sensitive matter of the eye and so forth. Feeling, however, is spoken of as one due to its single essence.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Kāyika mānasika sātabhedato sukhadukkhāni dvidhā vuttānī”ti vuttaṃ.

It is said: “Pleasure and pain are spoken of as twofold by way of the division into bodily and mental agreeableness.”

Tattha sabhāvato iṭṭhāniṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbā nubhavanalakkhaṇāni sukha dukkhāni. Sabhāvatovā parikappanatovā iṭṭhāniṭṭhamajjhattānubhavana lakkhaṇāni itarānīti. Sesānīti yathāvutta sukhadukkhato manassa domanassayuttehi sesāni bāttiṃsa kāmāvacaracittāni tevīsati pañcamajjhānikacittānicāti sabbāni pañcapaññāsacittāni. Ekatthāti ekasmiṃ citte. Itarā hi upekkhāvedanā.

Therein, pleasure and pain are by nature characterized by the experience of desirable and undesirable tangibles. The others are characterized by the experience of desirable, undesirable, or neutral objects, either by nature or by conceptualization. ‘The rest’ means the remaining thirty-two sense-sphere consciousnesses and the twenty-three fifth-jhāna consciousnesses, apart from those associated with the aforementioned pleasure, pain, and displeasure—thus all fifty-five consciousnesses. ‘In one’ means in one consciousness. For the other is the feeling of equanimity.

131. Hetūnaṃ bhedena taṃsampayuttānaṃ cittacetasikāna saṅgaho hetusaṅgaho.

131. The grouping of consciousness and mental factors associated with them by way of the division of roots is the root-grouping.

[85] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[85] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Lobhādihetūnaṃ vibhāgavasena taṃsampayuttadhammavasenaca saṅgaho hetusaṅgaho”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: “The compendium by way of the division of roots beginning with greed and by way of the phenomena associated therewith is the Compendium of Roots.” That is not well-stated.

Kāraṇaṃ [M 0.0124] vuttameva. Hetūnāma chabbidhā bhavantīti sambandho. Tattha hetukiccaṃnāma ārammaṇe sampayuttadhammānaṃ suppatiṭṭhitabhāva sādhanaṃ. Yathā hi rukkhassa mūlāni sayaṃ anto pathaviyaṃ vaddhitvā pathaviraseca āporaseca gahetvā rukkhaṃ yāva aggā abhiharanti. Vātevā mahoghevā āgate rukkhaṃ suṭṭhu ākaḍḍhitvā tiṭṭhanti, evaṃ rukkho vuddho viruḷho vipulo ciraṭṭhitikoca hoti. Evamevaṃ imepi dhammā sayaṃ ārammaṇesu thirapattā hutvā sampayuttadhamme tattha vuddhe viruḷhe vipule ciraṭṭhitikeca sādhentīti. Ahetukacittānipana jalatale amūlakasevā lāni viya ārammaṇe suṭṭhu patiṭṭhitāni na hontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Apare pana dhammānaṃ kusalādibhāvasādhanaṃ hetukiccanti vadanti. Evaṃsante yesaṃ sahajātahetu natthi. Tesaṃ akusalabhāvo abyākatabhāvoca nasampajjeyya. Yānica laddhahetupaccayāni rūpāni. Tesañca kusalādibhāvo āpajjeyyāti vatvā taṃvādaṃ paṭipakkhipanti. Yathā pana loke andhakāronāma kenaci paccaya visesena sādhetabbo na hoti. Yattha āloko natthi. Tattha so attano dhammatāya siddho hoti. Evamevaṃ dhammesu muyhanakriyābhūto mohandhakāropi attano dhammatāya eva akusalo bhavituṃ arahati. Tathā hi icchānāma atthi. Sāmuyhanakriyāya yuttā lagganabhāvaṃ patvā lobho akusalo nāma hoti. Saddhāya yuttā pana dhammacchandabhāvaṃ patvā kusalacchandonāma hoti. Tathā akkhantināma atthi. Sāpi muyhana kriyāya yuttā paṭighabhāvaṃ patvā doso akusalonāma hoti. Saddhāya yuttā pana uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetītiādinā nayena pāpadhamma pāpārammaṇa virodhabhāvaṃ patvā alobho kusalonāma hoti. Muyhanakriyā pana asukena yuttā akusalonāma. Asukena yuttā kusalonāmāti natthi. Ambilatthāya aññena saṃyogakiccarahito jātiambilaraso viya ekantaakusalajātikāeva hotīti. Yoca dhammo kusalo akusaloca na hoti. So abyākatoti ettakameva [M 0.0125] dhammānaṃ abyākatabhāvasiddhiyā kāraṇaṃ. Tasmā ahetukacittānaṃ rūpanibbānānañca abyākatabhāvopi attano dhamma tāyaeva siddho. Tattha moho sesamūlānaṃpi mūlaṃ hoti. Rajjanadussanānipi hi muyhananisandānieva honti. Alobhādīnañca kusalabhāvo avijjānusayena saheva siddhoti. Tāni pana lobhādīni lobhasahagatādīnaṃ visesamūlāni honti. Rajjanādi nisandāni hi diṭṭhimānādīni. Arajjanādinisandāni ca saddhādīnīti. Yasmā pana hetuyonāma sampayuttesu padhānadhammā honti. Tasmā sahetukavipākakriyānaṃ abyākatabhāvo pana hetu mukhenapi vattuṃ yutto.

The reason has been stated. The connection is that roots are of six kinds. Herein, the function of a root is to establish the firm-footing of associated phenomena in their object. For just as the roots of a tree, growing deep into the earth and drawing up the essences of earth and water, sustain the tree up to its very top, and when strong winds or great floods come, they hold the tree fast and stand firm, thus the tree grows, flourishes, becomes great, and is long-lasting; even so, these phenomena, having become firmly established in their objects, bring about the growth, flourishing, greatness, and long-lastingness of the associated phenomena therein. It should be understood that rootless consciousnesses, like rootless water-plants on the surface of the water, are not well-established in their objects. Others, however, say that the function of roots is to establish the wholesome, etc., nature of phenomena. If that were so, then for those phenomena that have no conascent root, their unwholesome or indeterminate nature would not come to be. And for those material phenomena that have obtained root-condition, a wholesome, etc., nature would result. Having said this, they refute that view. Just as in the world, darkness does not need to be brought about by any special condition—wherever there is no light, there it is established by its own nature—even so, the darkness of delusion, which is the activity of bewilderment regarding phenomena, is fit to be unwholesome by its very own nature. For instance, there is desire. When conjoined with the activity of bewilderment, having reached a state of clinging, it is called unwholesome greed. But when conjoined with faith, having reached a state of wholesome desire for the Dhamma, it is called wholesome desire. Likewise, there is intolerance. When conjoined with the activity of bewilderment, having reached a state of aversion, it is called unwholesome hatred. But when conjoined with faith, by the method of 'one does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual pleasure,' etc., having reached a state of opposition to evil phenomena and evil objects, it is called wholesome non-greed. The activity of bewilderment, however, is not such that it is called unwholesome when conjoined with one thing and wholesome when conjoined with another; just as the natural taste of sourness is devoid of the need for combination with another to be sour, so too is it exclusively of an unwholesome nature. And whatever phenomenon is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, that is indeterminate. This much alone is the reason for the establishment of the indeterminate nature of phenomena. Therefore, the indeterminate nature of rootless consciousnesses, of material form, and of Nibbāna is also established by their very own nature. Therein, delusion is the root of the other roots as well. For attraction and repulsion are indeed consequences of bewilderment. And the wholesome nature of non-greed and so on is established together with the latent tendency of ignorance. Those, however, greed and so on, are the specific roots for states accompanied by greed, etc. For the consequences of attraction and so on are wrong view, conceit, and so on; and the consequences of non-attraction and so on are faith and so on. And since roots are the principal phenomena among associated states, it is therefore proper to speak of the indeterminate nature of resultant and functional consciousnesses with roots also by way of the roots.

[86] Ettāvatā yaṃ vuttaṃ vibhāvaniyaṃ

What has been said thus far is to be elucidated.

“Apare pana kusalādīnaṃ kusalādibhāvasādhanaṃ hetu bhāvo”ti vadanti. Evaṃ sati hetūnaṃ attano kusalā dibhāvasādhano añño hetu maggitabbo siyā. Atha sesasampayuttahetupaṭibaddho tesaṃ kusalādibhāvo, evampi momūha cittasampayuttassa hetuno akusala bhāvo appaṭibaddho siyā. Atha tassa sabhāvato akusalabhāvopi siyā. Evaṃsati sesahetūnampi sabhāvato kusalādibhāvoti tesaṃ viya sampayutta dhammānampi so hetupaṭibaddho nasiyā, yadica hetupaṭibaddho kusalādibhāvo. Tadā ahetukānaṃ abyākatabhāvo nasiyāti alamatinippīḷanenāti taṃ paṭikkhittaṃ hoti.

“Others, however, say that the nature of a root is to establish the wholesome, etc., state of wholesome, etc., phenomena.” If this is so, then for the roots to establish their own wholesome, etc., state, another root would have to be sought. Or, the wholesome, etc., state of those phenomena would be dependent on the remaining associated roots. Even so, the unwholesome state of a root associated with a very deluded mind might not be dependent on anything. Or perhaps its unwholesome nature would exist by its own nature. If this were so, then the remaining roots too would have their wholesome, etc., nature by their own nature; and like them, for the associated phenomena too, that nature would not be dependent on the root. And if the wholesome, etc., nature is dependent on the root, then the indeterminate state of rootless phenomena would not be established. Enough of this excessive straining; thus that view is rejected.

Yathāca laddhajjhānapaccayesu rūpārūpadhammesu jhānaṅgāni arūpadhammesueva upanijjhānaṭṭhaṃ pharanti, na rūpadhammesu. Te pana jhānadhamma samuṭṭhi tattāeva jhānapaccayuppannesu vuttā. Evameva hetuyopi arūpa dhammesueva kusalādibhāvaṃ pharanti. Na rūpadhammesu. Te pana hetu samuṭṭhitattāeva hetupaccayuppannesu vuttāti na tesaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ kusalādibhāvāpatti codetabbāti.

And just as, among material and immaterial phenomena that have obtained jhāna-condition, the jhāna factors pervade only the immaterial phenomena for the purpose of contemplation, not the material phenomena—yet they are said to be arisen from jhāna-condition because they are originated by jhāna-phenomena—even so, the roots too pervade only the immaterial phenomena with their wholesome, etc., nature, not the material phenomena—yet they are said to be arisen from root-condition because they are originated by roots. Therefore, the objection that those material phenomena would acquire a wholesome, etc., nature should not be raised.

[87] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

And what is to be elucidated.

“Kusalādibhāvo pana kusalākusalānaṃ yoniso ayoniso manasikārapaṭibaddho”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi vicāre tabbaṃ.

It is said: “The wholesome, etc., nature of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, however, is dependent on wise and unwise attention.” That too should be examined.

Tathā hi sūriyāloke āgate divā balānaṃ haṃsādīnaṃ okāso hoti. Rattandhakāle āgate rattibalānaṃ ulūkādīnaṃ okāso hoti. Naca te ālokandhakārā tesaṃ vaṇṇādivisesaṃ sāmenti. Taṃ pana tesaṃ yoniyoeva sādhenti. Tattha āloko viya yonisomanasikāro daṭṭhabbo. Andhakāro viya itaro. Te sattā viya kusalākusalā. Vaṇṇādiviseso viya kusalādibhāvo. Yoniyo viya hetuyo daṭṭhabbāti. Abyākatānaṃ panāti sabbaṃ yo dhammo kusalo akusaloca na hoti. So abyākatoti vuttapakkhe patatiyevāti. Tatthāti hetusaṅgahe. Sahetukānaṃ pariggahasukhatthaṃ idha vajjetabbānipi ahetukāni pathamaṃ uddhaṭāni. Tenāha sesāni pana. La. Sahetukā nevāti. Tesaṃvā ahetukanāmaṃpi hetūnaṃ vaseneva visuṃ siddhanti tesaṃpi idha saṅgahaṇaṃ aviruddhaṃ hoti. Tenāha ahetu kāṭṭhārasekātiādi. Sabhāva bhedena chabbidhāpi hetuyo kusalā kusalā byākatajātibhedena navadhā hontīti vuttaṃ lobho dosocātiādi.

For when sunlight arrives, it is the occasion for those strong by day, such as swans and the like. When the darkness of night arrives, it is the occasion for those strong by night, such as owls and the like. Yet, that light and darkness do not establish their distinctions of color and so forth. Rather, it is their own natures that establish it. Here, wise attention should be seen as the light, and the other as the darkness. The wholesome and unwholesome states are like the beings. The state of being wholesome and so on is like the distinctions of color and so forth. The roots should be seen as the natures. But as for the indeterminate, all this falls into the stated category that 'whatever phenomenon is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, that is indeterminate.' Therein, that is, in the Compendium of Roots, for the sake of easily grasping those with roots, the rootless phenomena, which should have been excluded, were set forth first. Therefore, it is said: “The rest, however... are with roots.” Or, since their name 'rootless' is also established separately by the power of the roots, their inclusion here is not contradictory. Hence, it is said: “The rootless are eighteen,” and so on. It is said that the roots, though sixfold by distinction of nature, become ninefold by the distinction of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate classes, thus: “Greed and hatred,” and so on.

132. Cuddasannaṃ kiccānaṃ bhedena taṃkiccavantānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ saṅgaho kiccasaṅgaho.

132. The Compendium of Functions is the grouping of consciousness and mental factors that possess those functions, by way of the division into fourteen functions.

[88] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

Furthermore, what is to be elucidated:

“Paṭisandhādīnaṃ kiccānaṃ vibhāgavasena taṃkiccavantānañca paricchedavasena saṅgaho kiccasaṅgaho”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: “The grouping is a functional grouping by way of dividing the functions such as rebirth-linking, etc., and by way of delimiting those possessing those functions.” That is not well-stated.

Yena ekakammena eko upapattibhavonibbattati. Tasmiṃ sarasenavā laddhavibādhanenavā parikkhīṇe so bhavo nirujjhati. Ekassa [M 0.0127] kammassa okāso hoti. Tasmā tato nibbatta bhavato cutassa antarā khaṇamattaṃpi aṭṭhatvā laddhokāsena ekena kammena puna bhavantarādi paṭisandhāna vasena abhinibbatti paṭisandhikiccaṃ. Tathā nibbattassa upapattibhavasantānassa yāva taṃ kammaṃ nakhiyyati. Tāva aviccheda pavattipaccayaṅgabhāvena pavatti bhavaṅgakiccaṃ. Tassa hi tathā pavattiyā sati āyupabandhāca usmā pabandhāca pavattantiyevāti ete tayo dhammā imaṃ kāyaṃ abhijjamānaṃ rakkhantīti. Yathāha –

By one kamma, one rebirth-existence is produced. When that existence is exhausted, either by its own nature or by an afflicting factor, that existence ceases. An opportunity arises for one kamma. Therefore, for one who has passed away from that produced existence, without remaining even for a moment in between, a new existence is produced again by one kamma that has found its opportunity, by way of rebirth-linking; this is the function of rebirth-linking. Similarly, for the continuum of the existence thus produced, as long as that kamma is not exhausted, the uninterrupted occurrence as a condition for continuity is the function of the life-continuum. For when such an occurrence exists, the bond of life and the bond of heat continue, and these three things protect this body from breaking apart. As it is said:

Āyu usmāca viññāṇaṃ, yadā kāyaṃ jahanti maṃ;

Apaviddho tadā seti, niratthaṃva kaliṅgaranti.

“When life, heat, and consciousness leave this body, then it lies discarded, like a useless log.”

Āvajjanaṃ cittasantānassa āvaṭṭanaṃ, taṃvā āvajjeti āvaṭṭeti, āvaṭṭativā taṃ ettha etenātivā āvajjanaṃ. Bhavaṅga vīthito okkamitvā ārammaṇantarābhimukhaṃ pavattatīti attho. Āvajjetivā ārammaṇantare ābhogaṃ karotīti āvajjanaṃ. Dassanādīni pākaṭāni. Voṭṭhabbananti visuṃ avacchinditvā thapanaṃ idaṃ nīlantivā pītakantivā subhantivāasubhantivā asaṅkaratothapanaṃ niyamananti vuttaṃ hoti. Javanantivā javotivā vegotivā atthato ekaṃ. Asaninipāto viya vegasahitassa ekekassa pittassa pavatti javanakiccaṃ.

Adverting is the turning of the continuum of consciousness; or it adverts, or it turns, or it turns to this by means of this—thus, adverting. It means, having departed from the life-continuum, it proceeds towards another object. Or, because it directs attention to another object, it is adverting. Seeing and so forth are evident. Determining is the act of establishing by separately defining, such as ‘this is blue,’ or ‘this is yellow,’ or ‘this is beautiful,’ or ‘this is ugly,’ establishing without confusion; this is what is meant by defining. Impulsion, or quickness, or speed, are the same in meaning. The occurrence of each single consciousness with speed, like the fall of a thunderbolt, is the function of impulsion.

[89] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[89] Now, what is to be elucidated:

“Ārammaṇe taṃtaṃkiccasādhanavasena anekakkhattuṃ ekakkhattuṃvā javamānassa viya pavatti javanakicca”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

“Impulsion is the function of the occurrence as if running, repeatedly or once, to accomplish its respective function in the object,” it is said. That is not well-stated.

Na hi javamānassa cittassa ekavāramattena nivattināma atthi. Maggātiññājavanānipi hi ekāvajjanaparikammacittato paṭṭhāya ekavegena pavattajavamānacittasantānapatitāni eva honti. Na pana tāni visuṃ siddhena javena javantīti.

For there is no such thing as a turning back of the impelling consciousness with just a single occurrence. For even the impulsions of path and higher knowledge, starting from the single adverting and preparatory consciousness, fall into a continuum of impelling consciousnesses proceeding with a single impetus. But they do not impel with a distinct, independently established impulsion.

[90] Tattha ca

[90] And in that regard:

Javamānassa [M 0.0128] viya pavattīti etena visuṃ visuṃ uppajjitvā niruddhā naṃ khaṇikadhammānaṃ sīghagamanasaṅkhāto javonāma visuṃ natthi. Bahukkhattuṃ pavattivasena pana sīghagacchantapurisa sadisattā eva javananti vuccatīti dassitaṃ hoti. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

By the phrase 'occurrence as if running,' it is shown that for momentary phenomena that arise and cease individually, there is no separate thing called 'speed' characterized by rapid movement. However, it is also shown that it is called 'impulsion' (javana) only because of its similarity to a swiftly moving man, due to its repeated occurrence. This too is not well-stated.

Asaninipāto viya vegasahitassa ekekassa cittassa pavattijavanakiccanti hi heṭṭhā vuttaṃ. Bhavaṅgacittañhi dīghaṃ addhānaṃ pūretvā pavattaṃpi nadisote vuyhamānaṃ sukkhapaṇṇaṃ viya vegarahitaṃ hoti. Javanacittaṃ pana ekamekaṃpi samānaṃ indena vissaṭṭha vajiraṃ viya vegasahitameva pavattatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃ ārammaṇaṃ etassāti tadārammaṇaṃ. Yaṃ javanena gahitaṃ, tadevassa ārammaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Yaṃ javanena gahitārammaṇaṃ, tasseva gahitattā tadārammaṇaṃ nāmāti hi vuttaṃ. Tassavā javanassa ārammaṇaṃ assa ārammaṇanti tadārammaṇaṃ. Idha pana tadārammaṇabhāvo adhippeto. Nibbattamānabhavato vacanaṃ muccanaṃ parigaḷanaṃ cuti. Idāni tāni kiccāni aniyamato na pavattanti. Ṭhānaniyameneva pavattantīti dassetuṃ ṭhānabhedo vutto. Tiṭṭhati pavattati taṃtaṃ kiccavantaṃ cittaṃ etthāti ṭhānaṃ. Okāso. Taṃtaṃ antarākāloti vuttaṃ hoti. Kālopi hi kālavantānaṃ pavattivisayattā ṭhānanti vuccati. Paṭisandhiyā ṭhānaṃ paṭisandhiṭṭhānaṃ. Paṭisandhakālo paṭisandhikkhaṇoti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ sesesupi.

For it was stated previously: “Like the fall of a thunderbolt, the occurrence of each single consciousness with speed is the function of impulsion.” The life-continuum consciousness, even when it occurs filling a long duration, is devoid of speed, like a dry leaf carried along by a river current. But each single impulsion consciousness, even when occurring individually, proceeds with speed, like a thunderbolt hurled by Indra—this should be understood. Its object belongs to it—thus it is called 'tadārammaṇa' (that which has that object). What is grasped by the impulsion, that indeed is its object—this is what is meant. Because what was grasped by the impulsion is taken as its object, it is called 'tadārammaṇa.' Or, the object of that impulsion is its object, thus 'tadārammaṇa'. Here, however, the state of being tadārammaṇa is intended. The term 'cuti' (death) means the ceasing, the release, the falling away from the present existence. Now, these functions do not occur without a fixed order; they occur only according to a definite sequence—to show this, the differentiation by position is stated. 'Position' (ṭhāna) is that wherein a particular consciousness, endowed with its function, stands and occurs. It is an opportunity, an interval—this is what is meant. Time, too, is called 'position' because it is the sphere of occurrence for things that exist in time. The position of rebirth-linking is the rebirth-linking position. The time of rebirth-linking is the moment of rebirth-linking—this is what is meant. The same applies to the rest.

[91] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[91] Now, what is to be elucidated:

“Paṭisandhiyā ṭhānaṃ paṭisandhiṭṭhānanti vatvā kāmaṃ paṭisandhivini muttaṃ ṭhānaṃnāma natthi. Sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ pana silā puttakassa sarīrantiādīsu viya abhedepi bhedaparikappanāti daṭṭhabba”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

Having stated, 'The position of rebirth-linking is the rebirth-linking position,' [it is said:] 'Indeed, there is no such thing as a position separate from rebirth-linking. However, for the sake of easy comprehension, it should be understood that a division is conceived even where there is no division, as in cases like 'the body of a stone doll'.' This should not be accepted.

Kālo hi nāma sabhāvato avijjamānopi cittassa visuṃ ārammaṇabhūto eko paññattidhammo. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ mahāvipākacittānaṃ vipaccanaṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Etāni hi catūsu [M 0.0129] ṭhānesu vipaccanti. Paṭisandhiyaṃ bhavaṅge cutiyaṃ tadārammaṇeti vatvā taṃ vitthārentena paṭisandhiggahaṇakāle paṭisandhihutvā vipaccanti. Asaṅkhyeyyaṃpi āyu kālaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā maraṇa kāle cuti hutvāti kālova vuttoti. Itarathā kiccāni viya ṭhānānipi cuddasavidhānieva vattabbāni siyunti. Ṭhānānaṃ vitthārabhedo pana upari dvīsu pavattisaṅgahesu cittapavattividhānānusārena veditabboti. Yasmā omakaṃ dvihetukakusalaṃ sayaṃ so manassayuttaṃpi samānaṃ atidubbalattā somanassa paṭisandhiṃ dātuṃ nasakkoti. Tasmā somanassasantīraṇaṃ paṭisandhiṭṭhānaṃ nagacchatīti vuttaṃ dveupekkhāsahagatasantīraṇānicevāti. Tathā hi paṭṭhāne pītisahagatattike paṭiccavāre hetupaccanike taṃ paṭi sandhiṭṭhānena uddhaṭanti. Manodvārāvajjanaṃ parittārammaṇevā avibhūtā rammaṇevā dvattikkhattuṃ pavattamānaṃpi vipāka santānato laddhapaccayabhāvena dubbalattā javanavegarahitameva hotīti vuttaṃ āvajjana dvaya vajjitānīti.

For time, though non-existent by its own nature, is a single concept that serves as a separate object for consciousness. Indeed, in the commentary, it is said that the ripening-place of these eight great resultant consciousnesses should be understood. They ripen in four places: at rebirth-linking, in the life-continuum, at death, and as registering consciousness. Expanding on this, it is said that at the time of grasping rebirth-linking, they ripen by becoming rebirth-linking; for an incalculable lifespan, they ripen by becoming the life-continuum; and at the time of death, by becoming the death consciousness—thus, time itself is spoken of. Otherwise, like the functions, the positions too would have to be stated as fourteenfold. The detailed distinctions of these positions, however, should be understood from the two subsequent summaries of process, according to the method of the occurrence of consciousness. Because an inferior two-rooted wholesome consciousness, even when associated with joy, is too feeble to produce a rebirth-linking with joy, it is said that the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy does not reach the rebirth-linking position; hence, only the two investigating consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity are mentioned. Indeed, in the Paṭṭhāna, in the triad associated with joy, in the dependent section, in the negative section of the root condition, it is excluded by the rebirth-linking position. It is said that mind-door adverting, even when occurring two or three times with a limited or indistinct object, is indeed devoid of the speed of impulsion due to its weakness, having obtained its condition from the resultant continuity; hence, the two adverting consciousnesses are excluded.

[92] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[92] Now, what is to be elucidated:

“Ārammaṇarasānubhavanā bhāvato”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ a kāraṇaṃ.

The reason is stated as: 'due to the absence of experiencing the flavour of the object.' That is not the reason.

Na hi ārammaṇa rasānubhavanaṃ javanakicca siddhiyā javananāma lābhassaca kāraṇaṃ hoti. Taṃ pana javanakiccasiddhiyā phalame vahotīti. Yasmā pana phalacittaṃ āsevanabhāvarahitaṃpi magga cetanāya mahānubhāvattā parikammabhāvanābalena ca pavattattā ārammaṇe vegasahitameva patatīti tassajavanesu gahaṇaṃkataṃ.

For experiencing the flavour of the object is not the cause for the accomplishment of the impulsion-function or for obtaining the name 'impulsion'. Rather, it is the result of the accomplishment of the impulsion-function. However, because fruition-consciousness, though devoid of the nature of repetition, falls upon the object with speed due to the great power of the path-volition and because of its arising through the strength of the development of preparation, its inclusion among the impulsions is made.

[93] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[93] Now, what is to be elucidated:

Maggābhiññājavanānaṃ ekavārameva pavattattā javanakiccaṃ na sampajjatīti adhippāyena “ekacittakkhaṇikaṃpi lokuttara maggāditaṃ taṃsabhāvavantatāya javanakiccaṃ nāmā”ti vatvā sabbaññutaññāṇopamāya tamatthaṃ vibhāveti. Taṃ na yujjatiyeva.

With the intention that the impulsion-function is not accomplished because the path and higher knowledge impulsions occur only once, he says, 'Even the supramundane path, etc., which is of a single mind-moment, is called the impulsion-function because of its possessing that nature.' He elucidates that meaning by the analogy of the knowledge of omniscience. That is indeed not correct.

Idāni [M 0.0130] samānakiccagaṇanāni cittāni saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ tesu panātiādimāha. Paṭisandhādayo nāma cittuppādāti sambandho.

Now, to present the consciousnesses by grouping them according to the count of their similar functions, he says, beginning with 'tesu pana...' The connection is: 'Rebirth-linking and so on are called arisings of consciousness'.

[94] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[94] Now, what is to be elucidated:

Nāmakiccabhedenātipi yojeti. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

He also connects it by way of the distinction of function in name. That is not well-stated.

Nāmabhedassa visuṃ vattabbābhāvatoti. Ekakiccaṭṭhāna dvikiccaṭṭhāna tikiccaṭṭhāna catukiccaṭṭhāna pañcakiccaṭṭhānāni cittāni yathākkamaṃ aṭṭhasaṭṭhica tathā dveca navaca aṭṭhaca dveca niddiseti yojanā.

Because there is no need to state the distinctions of names separately. The states of consciousness with one function, two functions, three functions, four functions, and five functions are enumerated in order as sixty-eight, two, nine, eight, and two, respectively. This is the connection.

133. Cakkhādīnaṃ dvārānaṃ bhedena cittacetasikānaṃ saṅgaho dvārasaṅgaho.

133. The collection of consciousness and mental factors through the distinctions of the doors beginning with the eye is the door-collection.

[95] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[95] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

“Dvārānañca dvārapavattacittānañca paricchedavasena saṅgaho dvārasaṅgaho”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

"The grouping by way of delimiting doors and consciousness occurring at the doors is called the door-grouping." This is not well-stated.

Dve janā aranti gacchanti etenāti dvāraṃ. Nagarassa anto janā bahijanāca yena chiddamaggena nikkhamanti pavisantica, tassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Dve janā aranti gacchanti etthāti dvārantipī vadanti. Apica, duvidhaṃ dvāraṃ ākāsadvāraṃ maṇḍadvāranti. Tattha ākāsadvāraṃnāma yathāvutto chiddamaggo. Maṇḍadvāraṃnāma ādāsa paṭṭamayo ālokamaggo. Taṃ pana puññavantānaṃ gehesu yojīyati. Yathā ca tesu, tathā sattānaṃ sarīresupi dveeva honti. Navadvāro mahāvaṇoti hi chiddadvāraṃ vuttaṃ. Navanavutilomakūpasahassā nipi chiddadvārānieva. Idha pana ādāsapaṭṭasadisaṃ maṇḍadvāraṃ adhippetaṃ. Taṃpi hi ārammaṇikadhammānaṃ ārammaṇadhammānañca niggamana pavisana mukhapathabhāvato dvārasadisattā dvāranti vuccatīti. Taṃ pana rūpamaṇḍa dvāraṃ arūpamaṇḍadvāranti duvidhaṃ. Rūpamaṇḍadvāraṃpi kammavisesamahābhūta visesasiddhena maṇḍabhāvavisesena pañcavidhanti dassetuṃ cakkhudvārantiādimāha. Tattha cakkhumevacakkhudvāranti yasmiṃ cakkhumhi canda maṇḍalādīni rūpa nimittāni paññāyanti. Āvajjanādīnica yamhi paññātāni tāni nimittāni gaṇhanti. Tasmā tadeva cakkhu tesaṃ dvinnaṃ visayavisa yibhāvupagamanassa [M 0.0131] mukhapathabhūtattā cakkhudvāraṃnāmāti attho. Athavā, yena cakkhumaṇḍena bahiddhā candamaṇḍalādīni rūpāni anto āvajjanādīnaṃ visayabhāvaṃ upagacchanti. Yenaca anto āvajjanādīni bahiddhā tesaṃ rūpānaṃ visayibhāvaṃ upagacchanti. Tameva yathāvutta kāraṇena cakkhudvāraṃ nāmāti attho. Evaṃ sesesupi.

Two people go and come by this, hence it is called a door. Inside the city, people and outsiders exit and enter through whichever passageway, hence it is named so. Two people go and come here, hence it is also called a door—so they say. Furthermore, there are two kinds of doors: the space-door and the aperture-door. Among them, the space-door refers to the passageway as previously mentioned. The aperture-door refers to a path of light made of mirror-plates. This is employed in the houses of the meritorious. Just as in those cases, so too in the bodies of beings, there are two kinds. The nine-doored great wound refers to the hole-door. Even the ninety-nine thousand hair-pores are just hole-doors. Here, however, the aperture-door, similar to a mirror-plate, is intended. That too, because it serves as the entrance and exit for subjective and objective phenomena, it is called a door due to its resemblance to a doorway. Moreover, the aperture-door is of two kinds: the form-aperture door and the formless-aperture door. To show that the form-aperture door is fivefold by means of the specific nature of the aperture, accomplished by specific kamma and specific great elements, he says, beginning with 'eye-door'. Herein, 'the eye itself is the eye-door' means that in the eye, forms such as the moon-disk appear as signs; and adverting, etc., grasp those manifested signs in that eye. Therefore, that very eye is called the eye-door because it serves as the entrance-path for the coming together of these two—the object and the subject. Alternatively, by means of the eye-aperture, external forms like the moon-disk enter internally as objects of adverting, etc., and by means of it, internal adverting, etc., go out to those forms as subjects. For this reason, it is called the eye-door. The same applies to the rest.

[96] Ṭīkāsu pana

[96] In the sub-commentaries, however,

“Āvajjanādīnaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ pavattimukhabhāvato dvārasadisattā dvārānī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

"Because non-material phenomena such as adverting, etc., have the characteristic of being an opening for their occurrence, like a door, they are called 'doors'." This is not well-stated.

Rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇānaṃpi pavattimukhabhūtattā. Vakkhati hi chabbidhā visayapavattiyoti. Etthaca visayānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ dvāresu āpātā gamana saṅkhātā pavattiyo visayapavattiyoti vuccantīti. Tattha cakkhumeva cakkhudvāranti etena cakkhussa dvāraṃ cakkhudvāranti atthaṃ nivatteti. Tathā sotādayo sota dvārādīnīti etena sota meva sotadvāraṃ.La. Manoeva manodvāraṃ. Na manānaṃ dvāraṃ manodvāranti imamatthaṃ atidissati. Tassa pana manassa bahuvidhattā idha adhippetaṃ manaṃ dassento manodvāraṃ pana bhavaṅganti pavuccatīti vuttaṃ.

Because it is also an opening for the occurrence of objects such as forms. For it will be said: "There are six kinds of object processes." Here, the processes of objects—forms and so on—are called object processes because they involve the falling upon and going of objects to the doors of perception. In this context, "the eye itself is the eye-door" — with this, he refutes the meaning that the door belonging to the eye is the eye-door. Similarly, the ear and so on are the ear-door and so forth; with this, he indicates that the ear itself is the ear-door... so too, the mind itself is the mind-door, not that the door of minds is the mind-door. He points out this meaning. However, due to the multifaceted nature of the mind, here, indicating the mind intended, it is said that the mind-door is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

[97] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[97] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

“Āvajjanādīnaṃ manānaṃ dvāranti manodvāra”ntipi vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is also said, "The mind-door is the door of minds such as adverting." But that is not satisfactory.

Kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Tattha sabbaṃ ekūnanavutividhaṃpi cittaṃ manodvāra mevanāma hoti. Idha pana upapattidvārameva adhippetanti katvā bhavaṅganti pavuccatīti vuttaṃ. Paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya yāvatāyukaṃ nadisotamiva pavattamānaṃ ekūnavīsatividhaṃ bhavaṅgacittameva idha manodvāranti vuccati, kathīyatīti attho.

The reason has already been stated. There, all eighty-nine types of consciousness are indeed called the mind-door. Here, however, it is said that the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is so called because only the door of rebirth (upapattidvāra) is intended. From rebirth-linking onwards, throughout life, flowing like a river's stream, the nineteen types of life-continuum consciousness alone are here called the mind-door; this is the meaning.

[98] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[98] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

Yathā gāmassa dvāraṃnāma gāmānantarameva hoti. Evaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ manānaṃ pavattimukhaṭṭhena dvāraṃnāma āvajjanānantaraṃ bhavaṅgameva siyā. Na tato purimāni bhavaṅgānīti adhippāyena yaṃ vuttaṃ “bhavaṅganti āvajjānānantaraṃ bhavaṅga”nti. Taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

Just as the door of a village is indeed right at the boundary of the village, so too, the door for mental processes such as adverting, in the sense of being the beginning of the process, would indeed be the life-continuum immediately following adverting. What was said with the intention that the preceding life-continuum states are not meant, namely, ‘the life-continuum is the life-continuum immediately following adverting,’ should not be accepted.

Evañhi [M 0.0132] sati yesu cakkhupasādādīsu rūpādīni āpātaṃ nāgacchanti. Tānipi āvajjanādīnaṃ vīthicittānaṃ pavattimukhāni eva na hontīti katvā dvārānināma nasiyuṃ. Na ca tathā sakkā vattuṃ. Pāḷiyameva tesaṃ dvārarūpabhāvassa vuttattā. Idhaca vakkhati pasādaviññattisaṅkhātaṃ sattavidhaṃpi dvārarūpaṃnāmāti.

For if this were so, then in cases where forms and so forth do not impinge on the eye-sensitivity and other sense bases, those too would not indeed be the starting points for the occurrence of adverting and other process-minds, and thus would not be called doors. But this cannot be said, because the Pāḷi itself states their being the nature of doors. And here it will be stated that the sevenfold door-materiality, known as sensitivity and intimation, is called a door.

[99] Yañca tattha

[99] And as for what is said there:

Sāvajjanaṃ bhavaṅgantu, manodvāranti vuccatīti –

Sādhakavacanaṃ āhaṭaṃ; Taṃpi idha nayujjatiyeva.

‘The life-continuum together with adverting is called the mind-door’—this is a statement cited by proponents; but it does not apply here.

Tañhi āvajjanaṃpi manodvārapakkhikaṃ katvā dīpetīti. Yattha pana cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpeca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Sotañca. La. Manañca paṭicca dhammeca uppajjati manoviññāṇanti vuttaṃ. Tattheva taṃ yuttaṃ. Tattha hi cakkhuviññāṇuppattiyā catūsu paccayesu cakkhurūpāni eva sarūpato vuttānīti itare āvajjanañca sampayuttakkhandhā cāti dve paccayā casaddena gahitā, evaṃ sotaviññāṇādīsupi. Manoviññāṇe pana manañcāti ettha bhavaṅgacittena saha āvajjanaṃ gahetvā casaddena sampayuttakkhandhā gahitā. Evañhi sati cattā ropaccayā hontīti. Vuttañhetaṃ dhātuvibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭiccāti nāma āgataṭṭhāne āvajjanaṃ visuṃ nakātabbaṃ. Bhavaṅganissitakameva kātabbanti. Tasmā idha manoti sahāvajjanakaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ. Mano viññāṇanti javanamanoviññāṇanti. Etthaca paṭiccātināma āgataṭṭhāneti etena aññattha pana āvajjanaṃ dvārapakkhikaṃ nakātabbanti siddhaṃ hoti. Paṭiccāti āgatattāyevaca bhavaṅgaṃpi āvajjanā nantaraṃ bhavaṅgadvayameva imissaṃ pāḷiyaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Sannihitapaccayānaṃ eva tattha adhippetattāti. Idha pana dvārabhāvā rahassa sabbassa upapattidhammassa pariggahitattā sabbaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ adhippetaṃ. Na hi kiñci bhavaṅgaṃ nāma atthi. Yaṃ manodvārabhāvārahaṃ na siyāti niṭṭhamettha gantabbanti. Tatthāti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ, tesu chasu dvāresu cakkhu dvāreti sambandho. Yathārahanti ārammaṇabhūmipuggalamanasikārā dīnaṃ anurūpavasena. Sabbathāpīti visuṃ visuṃ chacattālīsa bhedasaṅkhātena [M 0.0133] sabbapakārenapi agahita gahaṇa vasena, catupaññā sāti sambandho. Sabbathāpītivā āvajjanādi tadārammaṇa pariyo sānavasena anekakiccabhedayuttena sabbapakārenapi, kāmāvacarānevāti sambandho. Yāni āvajjanādīni kiccāni dvāravikāraṃ paṭicca pavattanti, taṃ kiccavantānieva dvāre niyuttānīti atthena dvārikānināma honti. Paṭisandhi bhavaṅga cuti kiccānipana dvāravikārena vinā kevalaṃ kammavaseneva sijjhanti. Tasmā taṃkiccavantāni dvārikānināma nahontīti vuttaṃ ekūna.La. Dvāravimuttānīti ettha ca dvāravikāronāma attani ārammaṇānaṃ āpātāgamanavasena bhavaṅgassa calanaṃ, cakkhādīnañca attani viññāṇuppādana sattivisesa yogo daṭṭhabbo.

For it explains that by treating adverting as also belonging to the mind-door side. Where, however, it is said: ‘Eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and forms; ear-consciousness... mind-consciousness arises dependent on the mind and mental objects,’ there alone is that appropriate. For there, in the arising of eye-consciousness, among the four conditions, the eye and forms are stated by their own nature; the other two conditions—adverting and the associated aggregates—are included by the word ‘and.’ Similarly for ear-consciousness and so forth. But in the case of mind-consciousness, in the phrase ‘dependent on the mind,’ here, adverting is taken along with the life-continuum consciousness, and by the word ‘and,’ the associated aggregates are taken. Thus, when this is the case, there are four conditions. This is stated in the Commentary on the Analysis of Elements: ‘In the place where the term “dependent” (paṭicca) occurs, adverting should not be treated separately; it should be treated as based on the life-continuum.’ Therefore, here ‘mind’ refers to the life-continuum together with adverting. ‘Mind-consciousness’ refers to javana mind-consciousness. And by this statement, 'in the place where the term "dependent" occurs,' it is established that elsewhere adverting is not to be treated as belonging to the door-side. And because the term ‘dependent’ occurs, in this Pāḷi passage, only the two moments of life-continuum immediately after adverting should be taken, because only the proximate conditions are intended there. Here, however, since every phenomenon subject to arising is included as being fit to be a door, the entire life-continuum is intended. For there is no life-continuum whatsoever that is not fit to be a mind-door; this conclusion should be reached here. ‘Therein’ is a locative of determination; the connection is with ‘eye-door’ among those six doors. ‘As appropriate’ means in a manner suitable to the object, plane, person, attention, and so forth. ‘In every way’ means in every possible manner, by way of grasping the forty-six kinds separately without omission; the connection is with ‘fifty-four.’ Or ‘in every way’ means in every possible manner, possessing a variety of functions from adverting up to registering; the connection is with ‘only sense-sphere.’ Those functions such as adverting, which occur dependent on the modification of a door, are called ‘door-related’ (dvārika) in the sense that they are employed at the door by way of their function. The functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, however, are accomplished solely by the power of kamma, without any modification of a door. Therefore, it is said that those with such functions are not called ‘door-related.’ Here, in the phrase ‘freed from doors’ (dvāravimutta), the ‘modification of a door’ should be understood as the vibration of the life-continuum due to the impingement of objects upon it, and the connection of the eye and so forth with the specific power to produce consciousness in themselves.

[100] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[100] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

“Cakkhādidvāresu apavattanato manodvārasaṅkhāta bhavaṅgato ārammaṇantaragahaṇavasena apavattitoca dvāravimuttānī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyapi saha nasameti.

it is said, ‘Because they do not occur at the eye-door and so forth, and because they do not occur by way of grasping a different object from the life-continuum known as the mind-door, they are “freed from doors” (dvāravimutta).’ This does not align with the commentary.

Paṭisandhi bhavaṅga cuti vasenāti hi vuttaṃ. Etena hi kiccasīseneva cittānaṃ dvārika dvāravimuttabhāgo therena dassito. Teneva hi heṭṭhāpi pañcadvārāvajjana.La. Tadārammaṇavasenātiādinā kiccasīseneva cittānaṃ cakkhudvārikādibhāvo vuttoti. Nanu cakkhādidvāresu apavattanatoti iminā etadatthova vuttoti ce. Na. Adhippetatthavirahassa apasaṅga nivattakassaca saṃvaṇṇanā vākyassa payojanābhāvatoti. Chadvārikāniceva santīraṇa tadārammaṇakiccānaṃ vasena dvāravimuttānica paṭisandhādikiccānaṃ vasenāti adhippāyo. Pañcadvārikānica chadvārikānica pañcachadvārikāni. Kadāci chadvārikāniceva tāni kadāci dvāravimuttānicāti chadvārikavimuttāni. Dvārasaddo cetthaadhikāravasena yojīyati.

For it is said, ‘by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death.’ By this, indeed, the Elder has shown the division of consciousness into door-related and door-freed by way of the heading of function. For this reason, even below, the nature of consciousness as eye-door-related and so forth has been stated by way of the heading of function, in the passage beginning ‘by way of the five-door adverting... up to registering.’ If it is said, ‘But is not this very meaning stated by the phrase “because it does not occur at the eye-door and so forth”?’, it is replied, ‘No.’ Because the intended meaning is absent, and because a descriptive statement that averts an absurd conclusion serves no purpose here. The intended meaning is that by way of the investigating (santīraṇa) and registering (tadārammaṇa) functions, certain consciousnesses are six-door-related, and by way of the functions of rebirth-linking and so forth, others are door-freed. Consciousnesses that are both five-door-related and six-door-related are called five-and-six-door-related. Consciousnesses that are sometimes six-door-related and sometimes door-freed are called six-door-related-and-freed. And here the word ‘door’ is to be applied in the sense of predominance.

[101] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[101] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

“Chadvārikānica chadvārikavimuttānicā”tipi vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

it is also said, ‘six-door-related and six-door-related-and-freed.’ That is not well said.

Heṭṭhā cuṇṇiyavākye tathā asutattāti. Ekadvārikacittāni. La. Sabbathā dvāravimuttānica yathākkamaṃ chattiṃsati.La. Navadhā ceti pañcadhā paridīpayeti yojanā.

Because it is not found thus in the prose passage below. The application is to be explained thus: ‘The single-door consciousnesses... and those entirely freed from doors, are respectively thirty-six... and ninefold and fivefold.’

134. Rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇānaṃ bhedena cittacetasikānaṃ saṅgaho ārammaṇasaṅgaho.

134. The compilation of consciousness and mental factors according to the distinction of objects such as forms is the Compilation of Objects.

[102] Ṭīkāsu pana

[102] In the subcommentaries, however,

“Ārammaṇānaṃ sarūpato vibhāgato taṃvisayacittato ca saṅgaho ārammaṇasaṅgaho”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

it is said, ‘The Compilation of Objects is the compilation by way of the objects' own nature, their distinction, and the consciousness that takes them as object.’ That is not well said.

Ayañhi cittacetasikānaṃ eva saṅgaho. Na ārammaṇānanti. Rūpādīnaṃ vacanattho upari āgamissati. Dubbalapurisena daṇḍādiviya cittacetasikehi ālambīyati amuñcamānehi gaṇhīyatīti ālambaṇaṃ. Ārammaṇasadde pana sati cittacetasikāni āgantvā ettha ramantīti ārammaṇaṃ.

For this is indeed a compilation of consciousness and mental factors, not of objects. The meaning of the words ‘forms and so forth’ will come later. Just as a stick and so forth is depended upon by a weak man, so too it is depended upon by consciousness and mental factors; it is grasped by them without their letting go, therefore it is called a support (ālambana). But when the word ‘object’ (ārammaṇa) is present, consciousness and mental factors come and delight in it; thus it is called an object (ārammaṇa).

[103] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[103] As for what is in the Vibhāvanī, however,

“Dubbalapurisena daṇḍādiviya cittacetasikehi ālambīyati. Tānivā āgantvā ettha ramantīti ālambaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

it is said, ‘Just as a stick and so forth is depended upon by a weak man, so too it is depended upon by consciousness and mental factors; or they come and delight in it; therefore it is called a support (ālambana).’ That is not well said.

Visuṃ siddhāni hi etāni padānīti. Rūpamevāti vaṇṇāyatanameva. Pañcārammaṇavimuttaṃ yaṃkiñci dhammajātaṃ vijjamānaṃpiavijjamānaṃpi bhūtaṃpi abhūtaṃpi dhammārammaṇameva. Taṃ pana sabhāga koṭṭhāsato saṅgayhamānaṃ chabbidhaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ pana.La. Chadhā saṅgayhatīti. Tatthāti tesu rūpādīsu chasu. Cakkhudvāre ghaṭṭayamāna rūpānusāreneva uppannāni cakkhudvārikacittāni aññāni ārammaṇāni ālambituṃ nalabhanti. Rūpānipi ghaṭṭanarahitāni atītānāgatāni ālambituṃ nalabhantīti vuttaṃ cakkhudvārikacittānaṃ sabbesaṃpi rūpameva ārammaṇaṃ. Tañha paccuppannanti. Sotadvārikā dīsupi esevanayo. Tattha taṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ paccuppannaṃ. Vattamānanti attho. Chabbidhaṃpīti rūpādivasena chabbidhaṃpi. Atikkantabhāvaṃ itaṃ gataṃ [M 0.0135] pavattanti atītaṃ. Āgacchati āgacchitthāti āgataṃ. Paccuppannaṃ, atītañca. Na āgatanti anāgataṃ. Uppādajātikā saṅkhatadhammāeva tīsu kālesu anupatanti. Tasmā uppādarahitā asaṅkhatabhūtā nibbānapaññattiyo kālavimuttaṃnāmāti veditabbā.

For these words are indeed distinct. ‘Form only’ means the visible-form base alone. Whatever phenomenon, freed from the five sense objects—whether existing or non-existing, real or unreal—is merely a mental object (dhammārammaṇa). But that mental object, when compiled into its homogeneous divisions, is said to be sixfold; thus it is said, ‘The mental object, however... is compiled in six ways.’ ‘Therein’ refers to those six, namely forms and so forth. Eye-door-related consciousnesses, having arisen solely in accordance with a form impinging on the eye-door, cannot take other objects as their support. It is said that they cannot take as objects even forms lacking impingement—past or future. Thus, for all eye-door-related consciousnesses, form alone is the object, and that too must be present. The same principle applies to ear-door-related consciousnesses and so forth. There, what has arisen dependent on this or that cause is ‘present’ (paccuppanna). The meaning is ‘currently occurring’ (vattamāna). ‘Also sixfold’ means sixfold by way of forms and so forth. That which has gone beyond, departed, passed, is the past (atīta). That which comes or will come is ‘come’ (āgata). The present and the past. That which has not come is the future (anāgata). Only conditioned phenomena, which have the nature of arising, fall within the three times. Therefore, the unconditioned realities—Nibbāna and concepts—which are devoid of arising, should be known as ‘freed from time’ (kālavimutta).

[104] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[104] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

“Vināsābhāvato atītādikālavasena navattabbattā nibbānaṃ paññattica kālavimuttaṃnāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

it is said, ‘Because of the absence of destruction, and because they cannot be expressed in terms of past time and so forth, Nibbāna and concepts are called “freed from time” (kālavimutta).’ That should be examined.

Sabbepi hi saṅkhatadhammā anāgatabhāva pubbakāeva honti. Tasmā te yadā paccayasāmaggiṃ labhitvā uppajjissantīti vattabbapakkhe tiṭṭhanti, tadā anāgatānāma. Yadā paccayasāmaggiṃ labhitvā uppannā, yadā paccuppannānāma. Yadā niruddhā, tadā atītānāma. Evaṃ uppādajātikānaññeva uppādamūlikā tekālikatā siddhā. Uppādarahitānaṃ pana anāgatāvatthāpi natthi. Kuto paccuppannātītā vatthāti. Tasmā nibbānapaññattīnaṃ kālattaya vimuttatā hotīti. Vināsābhāvatoti idaṃ pana atītakālavimuttiyāeva kāraṇanti na tena tāsaṃ itarakālavimuttiṃ sādhetīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathārahavibhāgo pana idheva tesūtiādinā pacchā āgamissati. Dvāravimuttānañca chabbidhaṃpi ārammaṇaṃ hotīti sambandho. Yathā pana āvajjanādīnaṃ chadvārikacittānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ bhavantarepi imasmiṃ bhavepi purimabhāge kenaci dvārena gahitaṃpi agahitaṃpi hoti. Na tathā imesanti dassetuṃ bhavantare chadvāragahitanti vuttaṃ. Bhavavisesañhi patthetvā kammaṃ katvā tattha nibbattānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ bhavantarepi kenaci dvārena gahitaṃpi hoti yevāti.

All conditioned phenomena are indeed preceded by their future state. Therefore, when they stand on the verge of arising, having obtained the concordance of conditions, they are then called 'future.' When they have arisen, having obtained the concordance of conditions, they are then called 'present.' When they have ceased, they are then called 'past.' Thus, for things whose nature is to arise, their being subject to the three times, which is rooted in arising, is established. But for those devoid of arising, there is no future state. How much less a present or past state? Therefore, Nibbāna and concepts are free from the three times. That there is no destruction, however, is a reason only for their freedom from past time; it should be understood that this does not thereby establish their freedom from the other times. The appropriate classification, however, will come later, beginning with 'in these very things,' etc. And for the door-free (consciousnesses), the object is also of six kinds; this is the connection. Just as the object of the six-door consciousnesses, such as adverting, may be apprehended or not apprehended by some door in another existence or in an earlier part of this existence, it is not so for these. To show this, it is said, 'apprehended by the six doors in another existence.' For those who, aspiring to a particular existence, perform kamma and are reborn there, their object is indeed apprehended by some door in another existence.

[105] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[105] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Taṃ pana nesaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na āvajjanassa viya kenaci agahitameva gocarabhāvaṃ gacchatīti dassetuṃ chadvāra gahitanti vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

It is said: 'However, to show that their object does not become an object while still unapprehended by anything, as in the case of adverting, it is said to be “apprehended by the six doors.”' That is not correct.

Pañcadvārā vajjanassapi hi ārammaṇaṃ pubbe kenaci dvārantarena gahitaṃpi agahitaṃpi hotiyeva. Tathā hi idaṃ nāma labhissāmi [M 0.0136] bhuñjissāmi passissāmīti pubbe gahitaṃ pacchā āvajjanassa ārammaṇaṃ na na hotīti. Naca ekāvajjanavīthiyaṃ pubbe kenaci cittena agahitabhāvo idha pamāṇanti. Yathā ca pañcadvārikacittānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ekantapaccuppannameva hoti. Yathā ca manodvārikacittānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ tekālikaṃvā kālavimuttasā maññaṃvā hoti. Na tathā imesanti dassetuṃ paccuppannamatītaṃ paññattibhūtaṃvāti vuttaṃ. Yathā ca chadvārikacittānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ āgamasiddhavohārayuttaṃpi tabbohāravinimuttaṃpi hoti. Na tathā imesanti dassetuṃ kamma kamma nimitta gatinimitta sammatanti vuttaṃ.

For the object of five-door adverting may indeed have been previously grasped by some other door, or not grasped. For example, an object previously grasped with the thought, 'I will obtain this, I will enjoy this, I will see this,' does not fail to become an object for a subsequent adverting. Nor is the fact that an object was not previously grasped by any consciousness in a single adverting process a valid criterion here. And, to show it is not so for these, it is said 'present, past, or conceptual,' unlike the object of the five-door consciousnesses, which is exclusively present, and unlike the object of mind-door consciousnesses, which may be of the three times or considered time-free. And, to show it is not so for these, it is said 'designated as kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign,' unlike the object of six-door consciousnesses, which may be connected with conventional usage established by tradition or be free from such usage.

[106] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[106] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Nāpi nesaṃ ārammaṇaṃ maraṇāsannato purimabhāgajavanānaṃ viya kammakammanimittādivasena āgamasiddhavohāravinimuttanti dassetuṃ kamma.La. Sammatanti āhā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

It is said: 'He said “designated as kamma, etc.” to show that their object is not, like that of the javanas in the period prior to the time near death, free from conventional usage established by tradition by way of kamma, kamma-sign, and so on.' But that too is not well-stated.

Maraṇā sannato purimabhāgepi hi sattā attanā katakammaṃvā cetiyādīni kamma, pakaraṇānivā ārammaṇaṃ karontiyeva. Tadāpi hi kammaṃ kammameva, kammupakaraṇānica kammanimittāniyeva. Kamma siddhiyānimittaṃ kāraṇaṃ kammanimittanti katvā. Kammassa nimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ kammanimittantipi vadanti. Ajātasatturājā viyaca supinadassanādivasena gatinimittānipi ārammaṇaṃ karontiyeva. Rājā hi dvīsu bhavesu pitaraṃ māreti. Māritakālatoca paṭṭhāya tassa niddāyantassa gatinimittāni upaṭṭhahantīti. Tattha yathāsambhavanti taṃ taṃ paṭisandhādīnaṃ chadvāragahitādivasena sambhavantassa ārammaṇassa anurūpato. Yathāsambhavavibhāgo pana upari maraṇuppattiyaṃ āgamissati. Yebhuyyenāti bāhullena. Bhavantareti atītānantarabhave tatthaca maraṇāsannakāle. Chadvāra gahitanti chahi dvārehi maraṇāsannajavanehi gahitaṃ. Ettha ca yebhuyyenāti etena bhavantare chadvāragahitanti imassa vidhānassa anekaṃsabhāvaṃ viseseti. Kasmā. Agahitassapi sambhavato. Yañhi asaññibhavato cutānaṃ kamma kammanimitta gatinimitta sammataṃ [M 0.0137] arūpabhavato cutānañca gatinimittasammataṃ kāmapaṭisandhi bhavaṅgacutīnaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Taṃ bhavantare kenaci dvārena agahita meva hotīti. Etthaca yasmā paṭṭhāne arūpabhave duvidhopi purejātapaccayo paṭisiddho. Aṭṭhakathāsuca tato cutānaṃ kāmapaṭisandhiyā paccuppannagatinimittārammaṇatāpi vuttā. Gatinimittañca nāma rūpārammaṇameva dīpenti. Tasmā tesaṃ kāmapaṭisandhiyāpi gatinimittasammataṃ bhavantare kenaci dvārena agahitameva hotīti veditabbaṃ. Apica, maraṇāsannakāle kammabalena kammādīnaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃnāma yebhuyyena saṃmuḷhamaraṇena marantānameva hoti. Itaresaṃ pana paresaṃ payogabalenapi attanā pakatiyā suṭṭhu āsevitānaṃ anussaraṇabalenapi dhammikaupāsakādīnaṃ viya devalokato āgantvā gaṇhantānaṃ devānaṃ ānubhāvenapi hotiyeva. Nirayapālāpi nirayato āgantvā gaṇhantiyeva. Revativimānañcettha vattabbaṃ. Tañhi dve nirayapālā gahetvā pathamaṃ tāvatiṃsābhavanaṃ netvā pacchā nirayaṃ nayiṃsu. Te hi yakkha jātikattā vessavaṇaparisāviya tāvatiṃsā bhavanaṃpi gantuṃ sakkontiyeva. Yamassa dūtā dve yakkhāti hi pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Vessavaṇadūtā idha yamassa dūtāti vuttātipi vadanti. Tasmā ye kasiṇāsubhādīni samathanimittāni suṭṭhu āsevitvā upacārajjhāne ṭhatvā tāneva nimittāni gahetvā maranti. Tesaṃpi kāmapaṭisandhiyā ārammaṇaṃ bhavantare kenaci dvārena agahitameva siyā. Upacārajjhānabaleneva brahmalokato idhauppajjantānaṃpi esevanayoti.

For even in the period prior to the time near death, beings make their own deeds, or shrines and so on which are accessories to deeds, their object. Even then, a deed is just a deed, and the accessories to a deed are just kamma-signs, because the cause which is the sign for the accomplishment of kamma is the kamma-sign. They also say that the object which is the sign of kamma is the kamma-sign. And like King Ajātasattu, they make destiny-signs their object by way of dreams, visions, and so on. For the king killed his father in two existences, and from the time he killed him, destiny-signs appeared to him while he was sleeping. Therein, this is in accordance with the object that occurs, according to possibility, by way of being grasped by the six doors, etc., for this or that rebirth-linking and so on. The classification according to possibility, however, will come later in the section on death and rebirth. 'For the most part' means 'generally.' 'In another existence' refers to the immediately preceding existence, and there, at the time near death. 'Grasped through the six doors' means grasped by the death-proximate javanas through the six doors. Here, by the words 'for the most part,' he qualifies the non-absolute nature of the statement, 'apprehended by the six doors in another existence.' Why? Because of the possibility of it being unapprehended. For the object designated as kamma, kamma-sign, or destiny-sign for those fallen from the non-percipient existence, and the object designated as the destiny-sign for those fallen from the formless existence—which becomes the object for rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death in the sense-sphere—is indeed unapprehended by any door in another existence. And here, since in the Paṭṭhāna the twofold pre-nascence condition is denied in the formless existence, and since in the commentaries it is said that for those fallen from there, the sense-sphere rebirth-linking has a present destiny-sign as its object, and since they explain that a destiny-sign is only a form-object, it should therefore be understood that for them, the object designated as the destiny-sign for sense-sphere rebirth-linking is indeed unapprehended by any door in another existence. Furthermore, the presentation of kamma and so on at the time near death by the power of kamma occurs, for the most part, only for those who are dying a deluded death. For others, it can also occur by the power of another's effort, or by the power of recollection for those who have thoroughly practiced, like devout lay followers, or by the power of devas who come from a deva world to take them. The guardians of hell also come from hell to take them. The story of Revatī's mansion should be mentioned here. Two guardians of hell took her first to the Tāvatiṃsa celestial realm and afterwards led her to hell. Being of yakkha birth, they were able to go to the Tāvatiṃsa realm like Vessavaṇa's retinue. For it is said in the Pāli, 'Yama's two messengers are yakkhas.' Some also say that Vessavaṇa's messengers are here called Yama's messengers. Therefore, for those who, having thoroughly practiced serenity signs such as kasiṇas and the unattractive meditations, die while in access concentration, taking those very signs as their object, the object for their sense-sphere rebirth-linking could indeed be unapprehended by any door in another existence. This is the same method for those who are reborn here from a Brahmā world by the power of access concentration.

Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

But as for what is said in the Vibhāvanī:

“Kevalaṃ kammabaleneva tesaṃ asaññibhavato cutānaṃ paṭisandhiyā kammanimittādikaṃ ārammaṇaṃ upaṭṭhātī”ti vuttaṃ.

It was said: 'Solely by the power of kamma, for those who have passed away from the non-percipient existence, the object of rebirth-linking, such as the kamma-sign, etc., presents itself.'

Tattha kammanimittādikanti ettha ādisaddena kammaṃpi gahetabba meva. Na hi tassa agahaṇe kāraṇaṃ atthīti. Tāni pana sabbānipi kevalaṃ paṭisandhijanakassa kammassa ānubhāveneva paṭisandhiyaṃ upaṭṭhahantīti [M 0.0138] veditabbaṃ. Anāgataṃ pana nimittaṃ upaṭṭhahamānaṃ gatinimittameva siyā. Naca tassa visuṃ upaṭṭhātabbakiccaṃ atthi. Paccuppanna gatinimitte siddhe siddhameva hotīti vuttaṃ paccuppannamatītaṃ paññatti bhūtaṃvāti.

Therein, in the phrase 'kamma-sign, etc.,' kamma itself should certainly be included by the word 'etc.' For there is no reason for not including it. It should be understood that all these appear at rebirth-linking solely through the power of the kamma that generates that rebirth. However, a future sign that appears would only be a destiny-sign, and there is no separate function for it to appear. When the present destiny-sign is established, it is established indeed; thus it was said, 'present, past, or become a concept.'

[107] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[107] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Anāgataṃnāma atītaṃ viya anubhūtañca na hoti. Naca paccuppannagatinimittaṃ viya āpātamāgata”nti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ.

The reason is stated: 'The future, unlike the past, has not been experienced, nor has it come into view like a present sign of destiny.' That is no reason.

Pasaṅgassa anivattitattā. Gatinimittañhi nāma paccuppannaṃpi anubhūtaṃ na hoti. Taṃpi kammabaleneva āpātamāgataṃ. Evaṃsante anāgataṃpi kammabalena āpātamāgatameva siyāti ayaṃ pasaṅgo pākatikoeva hotīti. Tesūti yathāvuttesu ārammaṇikacittesu. Rūpādīsu pañcasu ekekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ etesanti samāso. Rūpādīni pañca ārammaṇāni etassāti viggaho. Sesānīti pañcaviññāṇasampaṭicchana dvayato sesāni santīraṇa mahāvipākāni. Sabbathāpi kāmāvacarā lambaṇānevāti paṭisandhādīhi nānākiccehi rūpādīsu nānārammaṇesu pavattena sabba pakārenapi kāmāvacarālambaṇikāniyeva. Tāni hi sabbaññubuddhānaṃ uppannānipi vikappasattirahitattā avijjamāne paññattidhammeca sukhume mahaggatadhammeca gambhīre lokuttaradhammeca ālambituṃ na sakkontīti. Tattha santīraṇattayaṃ tāva santīraṇakiccavasena rūpādipañcālambaṇe pavattati. Tadārammaṇādivasena pana sabbānipi ekādasavipākāni chasu parittārammaṇesu pavattantīti.

Because the implication is not averted. For a sign of destiny, though present, is not experienced. That too comes into range only through the power of kamma. This being so, that the future too might come into range through the power of kamma—this implication is merely natural. Among these—that is, among the aforesaid object-taking consciousnesses. The compound is: 'Each of the five, such as form, is an object for these (consciousnesses).' The analysis is: 'The five, such as form, are objects for this (consciousness).' The rest—that is, the investigating and great resultant consciousnesses remaining from the five sense-consciousnesses and the pair of receiving consciousnesses—in every way have only sense-sphere objects. This is because, operating with various objects such as form through various functions like rebirth-linking, they in every way have only sense-sphere objects. Indeed, even when they arise for Omniscient Buddhas, being devoid of the power of conceptualization, they are unable to take as object non-existent conceptual phenomena, subtle sublime phenomena, or profound supramundane phenomena. Therein, the triad of investigating consciousnesses, for its part, operates with the five objects, such as form, by way of the investigating function. However, by way of the registration function and so on, all eleven resultant consciousnesses operate in relation to the six limited objects.

[108] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[108] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Vipākāni tāva santīraṇādivasena rūpādipañcālambaṇe”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha santīraṇādivasenāti navattabbaṃ. Santīraṇavasena icceva vattabbanti.

It is said: 'Resultant consciousnesses, for their part, operate with the five objects such as form by way of investigation, etc.' Therein, 'by way of investigation, etc.' should not be said. It should be said only 'by way of investigation.'

Yo panettha cittānaṃ ārammaṇesu pavattivibhāgo vattabbo. So aṭṭhakathākaṇḍe gahetabbo. Lokuttaradhammā atigambhīrattā [M 0.0139] ñāṇasseva visayabhūtāti vuttaṃ. Akusala.La. Lokuttara vajjita sabbā rammaṇānīti. Tattha tāni laddhasamāpattīnaṃ uppannakāleeva mahaggatārammaṇāni. Tesuca dve dosamūlacittāni parihīnajjhānāni ārabbha uppannakāleti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ñāṇaṃpi anadhigatāni lokuttarāni ālambituṃ na sakkotīti vuttaṃ ñāṇasampayutta.La. Vajjitasabbā rammaṇānīti. Tattha ñāṇasampayuttakāmakusalāni puthujjanānaṃ ajjhānalābhīnaṃ uppannakāle paññattiyā saha kāmāvacarārammaṇāni. Tāneva sotāpattimaggato pure gotrabhukkhaṇe puthujjanānaṃ nibbānārammaṇāni. Jhānalābhīnaṃ tāneva abhiññākusalañca mahaggatārammaṇānipi. Heṭṭhimaphalaṭṭhānaṃ attanā adhigata maggaphalanibbānā rammaṇānipīti veditabbāni. Yathā cettha ariyā attanā adhigata maggaphalāniyeva ālambituṃ sakkonti. Tathā jhānalābhinopi attanā adhigatajjhānānieva ālambituṃ sakkontīti veditabbaṃ. Ettha siyā-ye ca jhānāni patthenti. Jhānaparikammaṃpi karonti. Yeca jhānasuttāni saṃvaṇṇenti. Te alābhino mahaggatajjhānāni ālambituṃ sakkonti, nasakkontīti. Na sakkonti. Te hi jhānānināma evaṃ mahānubhāvāni evaṃ mahānisaṃsānīti sutvāvā sutapariyattibalena siddhe ākāra sallakkhaṇaññāṇe ṭhatvā vā anumānavaseneva tāni patthenti. Parikammaṃpi karonti. Suttānipi saṃvaṇṇentīti. Itarathā puthujjanāpi lokuttaradhamme patthenti, maggaparikammaṃpi karonti. Maggaphala nibbānavacanānivikathenti saṃvaṇṇentīti tesaṃpi te ārammaṇabhūtā eva siyunti. Tesaṃ pana cittāni jhānādīnaṃ paññattiguṇe eva anubhontīti veditabbāni. Paṇītadhammānañhi paññattiyopi paṇitarūpāeva hontīti. Mahiddhiko hi paracittavidū. Māro deva puttopi rūpajjhānacittaṃ vaṭṭanissitameva passati. Vivaṭṭanissitaṃ na passati. Arūpajjhānacittaṃ pana vaṭṭanissitaṃpi napassatīti aṅguttare navanipāte aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ye pana aggamaggaphalāni paṭivijjhanti. Tesaṃ uppannāniññaṇasampayuttakāmakriyajavanāni kriyābhiññājavanañca puggalānurūpaṃ paññattiyā saha catubbhūmakadhammesu kiñci ārammaṇaṃ [M 0.0140] kātuṃ nasakkontīti natthi. Tathā tesaṃ purecāri kamanodvārāvajjanañcāti vuttaṃ ṭhāṇasampayutta.La. Sabbathāpisabbā rammaṇānīti. Tattha sabbathāpīti sabbakāmāvacara sabbamahaggata sabbalokuttara sabbapaññatti sabbapaccuppannādi pakārenapītiattho. Idañca sabbaññubuddhānaṃ uppannāni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Itarāni pana pacceka buddhānaṃ uppannānipi padesasabbārammaṇānieva honti. Tāni hi ekaṃ pathavidhātuṃpi sabbehi anavasesapakārehi jānituṃ nasakkontīti. Āruppesu dutīyacatutthāni pathamatatīyāruppa viññāṇā rammaṇattā mahaggatā rammaṇāni. Sesānīti abhiññā dvaya dutīyacatutthāruppehi avasesāni sabbānipi ekavīsatividhāni mahaggatacittāni kasiṇādi paññattārammaṇānīti attho. Pañcavīsāti pañcadvārāvajjana tevīsati kāmavipāka hasanacittāni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Parittamhīti kāmāvacarā lambaṇe evāti attho. Tañhi appānubhāvato paṭibandhakadhammehi parisamantato dīyati avakhaṇḍīyati nittejabhāvaṃ pāpīyatīti parittanti vuccati.

The analysis of the functioning of consciousnesses in relation to their objects, which is the question here, is to be understood from the commentary section. The supramundane phenomena, due to their extreme profundity, are said to be the domain of knowledge alone. Unwholesome consciousnesses are all-object-taking, excluding the supramundane. Therein, they take sublime objects only at the time of arising for one who has attained absorption. And among these, it should be understood that the two consciousnesses rooted in aversion arise taking as object the lost absorptions. It is said that even knowledge is unable to take as object supramundane states that have not been realized; knowledge-associated consciousnesses are all-object-taking, excluding the supramundane. Therein, for ordinary people who have not attained jhāna, knowledge-associated wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses, at the time of arising, have sense-sphere objects along with concepts. Those same consciousnesses, for ordinary people at the moment of change-of-lineage before the stream-entry path, have Nibbāna as their object. For those who have attained jhāna, those same consciousnesses and the wholesome supernormal knowledge consciousness also have sublime objects. It should be understood that for those established in the lower fruitions, they also have as object the path, fruition, and Nibbāna realized by themselves. Just as noble ones can take as their object only the path and fruition they have realized, so too should it be understood that those who have attained absorption can take as their object only the absorptions they have attained. Here it might be asked: those who aspire for jhānas, engage in preliminary work for jhāna, and praise the discourses on jhāna, but have not attained them—can they take sublime jhānas as object, or not? They cannot. For they, having heard that 'jhānas are of such great power and benefit,' or by standing in the knowledge of discerning characteristics established by the power of scriptural learning, aspire to them only by way of inference; they also engage in preliminary work and praise the discourses. Otherwise, ordinary people also aspire to supramundane phenomena, engage in preliminary work for the path, and explain and praise the words on path, fruition, and Nibbāna, and so these would become objects for them too. But it should be understood that their minds experience only the conceptual quality of the jhānas and so on. For the concepts of sublime phenomena are themselves of a sublime nature. For a mind-reader of great psychic power, such as the devaputta Māra, sees form-jhāna consciousness only when it is dependent on the round; he does not see it when it is independent of the round. But he does not see formless-jhāna consciousness even when it is dependent on the round; so it is said in the commentary to the Ninth Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. But as for those who penetrate the highest paths and fruitions, it is not that their arisen knowledge-associated sense-sphere functional javanas and functional supernormal knowledge javana are unable to take as object, according to the individual, any of the phenomena of the four planes along with concepts. Similarly, it is said that their preceding mind-door-adverting consciousness is in every way all-object-taking. Therein, 'in every way' means in all modes: all sense-sphere, all sublime, all supramundane, all conceptual, all present, etc. And this is said with reference to what has arisen for Omniscient Buddhas. But for others, even what has arisen for Paccekabuddhas are only partially all-object-taking. For they are unable to know even one earth element in all its modes without remainder. Among the formless attainments, the second and fourth have sublime objects because they have the first and third formless consciousnesses as their object. The rest—that is, all the twenty-one types of sublime consciousnesses remaining apart from the two supernormal knowledges and the second and fourth formless attainments—have concepts such as kasiṇas as their object. 'Twenty-five' is said with reference to the five-door-adverting consciousness, the twenty-three sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, and the smile-producing consciousness. 'In the limited' means 'having only sense-sphere objects.' For that, due to its weak power, is torn apart, fragmented, and brought to a state of powerlessness by surrounding obstructive phenomena; therefore it is called 'limited.'

135. Cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ bhedena tabbatthukānaṃ cittacetasi kānaṃ saṅgaho vatthusaṅgaho.

135. The Compendium of Bases is the grouping of consciousness and mental factors dependent on those bases, according to the classification of the bases such as the eye and so on.

[109] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[109] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Vatthuvibhāgato tabbatthukacittaparicchedavasenaca saṅgaho vatthusaṅgaho”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: 'The Compendium of Bases is the grouping determined by the classification of the bases and by the delimitation of the consciousnesses dependent on those bases.' That is not well-stated.

Vasantipatiṭṭhahanti cittacetasikāetesūtivatthūni, cakkhuvatthuca. La. Kāyavatthucahadayavatthucātiyojanā. Cakkhumeva cakkhuvatthu tathā sotādīniyeva sotavatthādīni. Vākyasaṅkhepo hesa pāṭho. Peyyālanayotipi antadīpakanayotipi vattuṃ yujjati. Keci pana dvandasamāsaṃ maññanti. Tesaṃ casaddo nayujjati. Parato vatthusaddo casaddoca pubbapadesu ānetabbotipi vadanti. Tesaṃ hadayavatthūti samāsapadaṃ nayujjati. Avibhattikaniddesotipi apare. Tāni kāmaloke sabbānipi labbhantīti kāmataṇhā dhina kammanibbattānaṃ attabhāvānaṃeva paripuṇṇindriyatā sambhavato sabbānipi [M 0.0141] tāni cha vatthūni kāmalokeeva labbhanti. Tathā hi cakkhādīsu vatthūsu santesu evarūpādīnaṃ paribhogo sampajjati. Tasmā rūpādīsu kāmavatthūsu abhiratā kāmataṇhā sadā cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ vatthūnaṃpi sampattiṃ patthetiyeva. Yathāca sabbakammiko amacco sadā rañño icchameva pūrayamāno sabbāni rājakammāni sampādeti. Evameva kāmāvacarakammaṃpi sadā kāmataṇhāya icchameva pūrayamānaṃ paripuṇṇindriyaṃ attabhāvaṃ nibbatteti. Tasmā kāmataṇhādhinakammanibbattā kāmasattāeva paripuṇṇindriyā hontīti. Yathā ca dassanasavanānuttariya dhammabhūtāni cakkhusotāni buddhadassana dhammassavanā divasena sattānaṃ visuddhiyāpi honti, na tathā ghānādittayaṃ. Taṃ pana kevalaṃ kāmaparibhogatthāyaeva hoti. Tasmā taṃ kāmavirāgabhāvanā kammanibbattesu brahmattabhāvesu naupalabbhatīti vuttaṃ rūpaloke pana ghānādittayaṃ natthīti. Idañca pasādarūpattayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sasambhāraghāna jivhā kāya saṇṭhānānipana suṭṭhuparipuṇṇānieva hontīti. Arūpalokepana sabbānipi nasaṃvijjantīti rūpavirāga bhāvanā kammanibbatte tasmiṃ loke ajjhattabahiddhāsantānesupi sabbena sabbaṃ rūpapavattiyāeva abhāvato. Tattha nibbattā hi sattā suddhe ākāsataleeva cittapabandhamattā hutvā tiṭṭhantīti. Imasmiṃ saṅgahe pana cittāni sattaviññāṇa dhātuvasena gahetuṃ tattha pañcaviññāṇadhātuyotiādi vuttaṃ.
