Tatthāti tesu chasu vatthūsu. Pañcaviññāṇāni eva nisattanijīvaṭṭhena dhātuyoti viggaho. Evaṃ sesesupi. Vijānanakiccābhāvato mananamattā dhātūti manodhātu. Pañcadvāre āvajjanamatta sampaṭicchanamatta kiccāni hi visesajānana kiccāni nahontīti. Pañcaviññāṇāni pana paccakkhato dassanādivasena thokaṃ visesajānanakiccāni honti. Avasesā pana santīraṇādayo ārammaṇasabhāva vicāraṇā divasena atireka visiṭṭhajānanakiccayuttattā na manodhātuyo viya mananamattā honti. Nāpi pañcaviññāṇadhātuyoviya vijānana mattā. Athakho mananaṭṭhena manoca taṃ vijānanaṭṭhena viññāṇañcāti katvā [M 0.0142] manoviññāṇadhātuyonāma. Atisaya visesajānana dhātuyoti attho. Pariyāyapadānañhi visesana samāse atisayattho viññāyati. Yathā padaṭṭhānanti.

Bases (vatthūni) are so called because consciousness and mental factors dwell and are established in them; this is the explanation for the eye-base, etc., the body-base, and the heart-base. The eye itself is the eye-base, so also the ear, etc. are the ear-base, etc. This is a condensed expression. It is suitable to explain it by the peyyāla method or by the antadīpaka method. Some, however, consider it a compound. For them, the word "ca" is not appropriate. Others say that the word "vatthu" and the word "ca" should be brought forward to the previous terms. For them, the compound "hadayavatthu" is not appropriate. Others explain it as an undivided designation. All these are obtainable in the sensual realm. Because beings born of kamma dominated by sensual craving have fully developed sense faculties, all six bases are obtainable only in the sensual realm. For only when these bases—eye, etc.—exist, does the enjoyment of forms, etc. occur. Therefore, sensual craving, delighting in sensual objects, always desires the attainment of the perfection of the five bases—eye, etc. Just as a competent minister, always fulfilling the king’s wishes, accomplishes all royal duties, so too, kamma in the sensual realm, always fulfilling the desires of sensual craving, produces a being with fully developed sense faculties. Therefore, sentient beings born of kamma dominated by sensual craving are indeed endowed with complete sense faculties. Just as the eye and ear, supreme in seeing and hearing, bring about the purification of beings daily through seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dhamma, the remaining three—nose, tongue, and body—do not. These exist solely for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. Therefore, it is said that they are not found in the Brahma realms born from kamma through the cultivation of dispassion for sensual pleasures. In the form realm, the nose and the other two are absent. This refers to the three sensitive pasāda forms. But the nose, tongue, and body, along with their respective support, are indeed fully complete. In the formless realm, none of these exist at all, because in that realm the cultivation of dispassion for form results in beings born of kamma having no form whatsoever, internally or externally, due to the complete absence of the arising of form in all ways. For beings born there dwell purely in the sphere of space, existing only as a stream of consciousness. In this compendium, consciousness is classified into seven elements of consciousness, taking the cittas. There, it is said, "the five elements of consciousness," etc. "There" means in those six bases. The five consciousnesses themselves are "elements" in the sense of being lifeless and without a living entity; this is the explanation. The same applies to the rest. Because they lack the function of knowing distinctly, the mind element is merely reflective. The functions of adverting at the five doors and receiving are not specialized acts of knowing. The five consciousnesses, however, have a slight specialized function of knowing through direct experience like seeing, etc. But the remaining cittas, such as the investigating consciousness (santīraṇa), are not merely reflective like the mind element, nor are they merely discerning like the five consciousness elements, because they possess an exceptionally refined function of knowing through examining the nature of the object, etc. Therefore, what is "mind" in the sense of reflecting and "consciousness" in the sense of discerning is called the "mind-consciousness element." The meaning is: an element of exceedingly specialized knowing. For in a determinative compound of synonymous terms, a sense of excellence is understood, as in the word padaṭṭhāna.

[110] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[110] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Manoyeva viññāṇaṃ manoviññāṇanti vā. Manaso viññāṇaṃ manoviññāṇa”nti vā vuttaṃ. Tattha manoyeva viññāṇanti idaṃ tāva na yujjati.

It is said, "Mind itself is consciousness, hence mind-consciousness," or "Consciousness of mind is mind-consciousness." Here, the statement "mind itself is consciousness" is not appropriate.

Na hi aññamaññaṃ visesetvā abhirekaṭṭhadīpake padaṭṭhānantiādike visesanasamāse avadhāraṇa viggaho katthaci dissati yujjaticāti.

For in determinative compounds that indicate a special meaning by one term qualifying another, such as 'proximate cause' and so on, an emphatic analysis is nowhere seen or justified.

[111] Manaso viññāṇanti idaṃpi nayujjatiyeva.

The analysis 'consciousness of mind'—this too is indeed not justified.

Manasoti hi manodhātuttikasaṅkhātassa manassa. Tattha sampaṭicchanadvayaṃ santīraṇādikassa manoviññāṇapabandhassa paccayabhūtaṃ hoti. Pañcadvārāvajjanaṃ pana parato dvārantare pavattamānaṃ tasseva manoviññāṇapabandhassa paccayuppannabhūtaṃ hotītikatvā ādimhi paccayabhūtassa ceva ante dvārantare paccayuppannabhūtassa ca manassa sambandhiviññāṇanti attho. Athavā, pañcaviññāṇavajjitāni sabbāni viññāṇāni mananakiccattā manonāma. Ārammaṇe pana abhinipāta mattāni pañcaviññāṇāni mananakiccāni nahontīti dassanādīni eva nāma. Pañcadvārāvajjanañca manato jātaṃpi manassa paccayo nahoti. Dassanādīnaṃ eva paccayo. Sampaṭicchanadvayañca manassa paccayo hontaṃpi manato jātaṃ nahoti. Dassanādito eva jātaṃ. Santīraṇādīni pana attano pure pacchāpavattānaṃ dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ manānaṃ eva majjhe jātānīti attano paccaya paccayuppannabhūtassa manassa sambandhiviññāṇanti attho. Evañca sati pañcaviññāṇaṃpi dvinnaṃ manodhātūnaṃ antare pavattattā manaso paccaya paccayuppannabhūtassa sambandhiviññāṇaṃ manoviññāṇanti vattabbameva siyāti.

By 'of mind' (manaso) is meant the mind (manassa) designated as the triad of mind-elements (manodhātuttika). There, the two receiving moments serve as conditions for the series of mind-consciousness beginning with the investigating consciousness. The five-door adverting, occurring subsequently at another door, is a conditionally arisen state for that same series of mind-consciousness. Thus, the meaning is that it is the consciousness related to the mind which is a condition in the beginning and a conditionally arisen state at the end, at another door. Alternatively, all consciousnesses except the five sense consciousnesses are called 'mind' because they perform the function of thinking. However, the five sense consciousnesses, which merely incline towards their objects, do not perform the function of thinking; hence, they are simply called seeing, etc. The five-door adverting, even though it arises from the mind, is not a condition for the mind; it is only a condition for seeing, etc. The two receiving moments, though being conditions for the mind, do not arise from the mind; they arise only from seeing, etc. But the investigating and subsequent moments, arising in the middle of two preceding and two succeeding minds, are the consciousness related to a mind that is both a condition and conditionally arisen. Thus, when this is the case, even the five sense consciousnesses, occurring between the two mind-elements, could rightly be called mind-consciousness, as it is the consciousness related to a mind that is both a condition and conditionally arisen.

[112] Ṭīkāyaṃ pana

[112] In the Ṭīkā, however,

Manato jātaṃ viññāṇantipi vuttaṃ. Taṃpi vuttanayena nayujjatiyeva.

The analysis 'consciousness arisen from mind' is also stated. That too is not justified according to the method mentioned.

Avasesā pana manoviññāṇadhātusaṅkhātāca santīraṇa.La. Pannarasarūpāvacaravasena tiṃsadhammā hadayaṃ nissāyeva pavattantīti yojanā. Casaddo panettha avasesānaṃ chasattati dhammānaṃ manoviññāṇadhātubhāvaṃ sambhāveti.

The remaining thirty states, however, designated as the mind-consciousness element—namely, the investigating consciousnesses, etc., and the fifteen form-sphere consciousnesses—arise dependent solely on the heart-base; this is the explanation. The word 'ca' here suggests that the remaining seventy-six states are states of the mind-consciousness element.

[113] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[113] In the Vibhāvanī, however,

Sampiṇḍanatthaṃ gahetvā “na kevalaṃ manodhātuyevā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

Having taken it for the purpose of condensation, it was said, 'Not only the mind-element.' That is not justified.

Evañhi sati avasesāca manoviññāṇadhātusaṅkhātāti vuttaṃ siyāti.

For if this were so, it would have been stated: 'and the remaining are designated as the mind-consciousness element.'

[114] Yāca ṭīkāsu

[114] And in the sub-commentaries,

Santīraṇa.La. Rūpāvacaravasena pavattā, avasesā manoviññāṇa dhātusaṅkhātāca tiṃsa dhammāti yojanā. Sāpi na sundarā.

The explanation is: 'The investigating consciousnesses, etc., and the form-sphere consciousnesses function, and the remaining thirty states are designated as the mind-consciousness element.' That too is not appropriate.

Atthagatiyā avisadattāti. Tattha kasmā te nissāyeva pavattantīti. Āruppesu anuppajjanato, kasmāca tattha nuppajjantīti vuccate. Santīraṇamahāvipākāni tāva tattha nuppajjanti pañcannaṃ dvārānaṃ attano kiccānañca tattha abhāvato. Paṭighacittadvayaṃpi nuppajjati. Anīvaraṇāvatthassa paṭighassa abhāvato. Ekanta nīvaraṇānañca jhānabhūmīsu asambhavato. Ettha pana yadi anīvaraṇāvattho paṭigho natthi. Pāḷiyaṃ dutīyajjhāneeva domassindriyassa aparisesanirodhavacanaṃ aṭṭhakathāsuca dutīyajjhānūpacāre tassa uppattisambhavavacanaṃ viruddhaṃ siyā. Tasmā attano sahāyapaccaya bhūtassa oḷārikassa kāmarāgassa jhānabhūmīsu abhāvato paṭighacittadvayaṃ tattha nuppajjatīti yuttantipi vadanti. Ṭīkākārāpana dutīyajjhānūpacāre tassa uppattisambhava vacanaṃ parikappavacanamattanti katvā [M 0.0144] purimakāraṇameva icchanti. Yadi panetaṃ parikappavacanamattaṃ siyā pāḷivacanaṃpi parikappavacanamattameva siyā. Tasmā pacchimakā raṇameva yuttarūpanti amhākaṃ khanti. Hasanacittaṃpi nuppajjati arūpīnaṃ hasanakiccassa abhāvato. Kāyābhāvatotipi yujjati. Sotāpattimaggacittaṃpi nuppajjati. Paratoghosābhāvena tatthuppannassa puthujjanassa dhammābhisamayābhāvato buddhapaccekabuddhānañca tattha anuppajjanato. Teneva hi tatthuppanno puthujjano aṭṭhasu akkhaṇayuttesu vuttoti. Rūpāvacaracittānipi tattha nuppajjanti rūpavirāgabhāvanāya rūpanimittārammaṇānaṃ tesaṃ samatikkantattāti.

Because of the unclarity of the meaning. There, why do they arise only dependently? Because they do not arise in the formless realms. And why is it said that they do not arise there? Firstly, the investigating and great resultant consciousnesses do not arise there due to the absence of the five sense doors and their respective functions. The two consciousnesses accompanied by aversion also do not arise, because of the absence of aversion in a state free from hindrances, and because absolute hindrances are impossible in the jhāna planes. Here, however, if there is no aversion in a state free from hindrances, then the statement in the Pāli that in the second jhāna there is the remainderless cessation of the faculty of displeasure, and the statement in the commentaries that its arising is possible in the access concentration of the second jhāna, would be contradictory. Therefore, some say that the two consciousnesses accompanied by aversion do not arise there because coarse sensual desire, which is their supporting condition, is absent in the jhāna planes. The subcommentators, however, considering the statement about its possible arising in the access concentration of the second jhāna as merely a conceptual statement, prefer the former reason. But if this is merely a conceptual statement, then the Pāli statement should also be merely a conceptual statement. Therefore, our preference is that the latter reason is more suitable. The smiling consciousness also does not arise because formless beings lack the function of smiling. This is also fitting due to the absence of a physical body. The path consciousness of stream-entry also does not arise there, because an ordinary person born there lacks the breakthrough to the Dhamma due to the absence of a voice from another, and because Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas do not arise there. For this very reason, an ordinary person born there is said to be included among the eight inopportune moments. The form-sphere consciousnesses also do not arise there because they, which have form-signs as their objects, have been transcended by means of developing dispassion for form.

Avasesā manoviññāṇadhātusaṅkhātā kusalākusalakriyānuttaravasena dve cattālīsadhammā hadayaṃ nissāyavā anissāyavā pavattantīti yojanā. Nissāyavā pañcavokāre anissāyavā catuvokāreti adhippāyo. Kusalānica akusalānica kriyānica anuttarānicāti viggaho. Tattha kusalānīti pañcarūpa kusalato avasesāni dvādasalokiyakusalāni. Akusalānīti paṭighadvayato avasesāni dasaakusalāni. Kriyānīti pañcadvārāvajjana hasana pañcarūpakrito avasesāni terasakriyacittāni. Anuttarānīti pathamamaggato avasesāni sattaanuttaracittāni. Kāme chavatthuṃ nissitā sattadhātuyo matā. Rūpe tivatthuṃ nissitā catubbidhā dhātuyo matā. Āruppe kiñcivatthuṃ anissitā ekā dhātu matāti yojanā. Tecattālīsāti pañcaviññāṇa manodhātuttikehi saddhiṃ santīraṇādike tiṃsadhamme sandhāya vuttanti.

The remaining forty-two states, designated as the mind-consciousness element—classified as wholesome, unwholesome, functional, and supramundane—arise either dependent on the heart-base or not dependent on it; this is the connection. The meaning is that they arise dependently in the five-aggregate realm and not dependently in the four-aggregate realm. The analysis is: 'wholesome, and unwholesome, and functional, and supramundane.' Therein, 'wholesome' refers to the twelve mundane wholesome states remaining after the five form-sphere wholesome states. 'Unwholesome' refers to the ten unwholesome states remaining after the two consciousnesses accompanied by aversion. 'Functional' refers to the thirteen functional consciousnesses remaining after the five-door adverting consciousness, the smiling consciousness, and the five form-sphere functional states. 'Supramundane' refers to the seven supramundane consciousnesses remaining after the first path consciousness. In the sense-sphere realm, seven elements are held to be dependent on six bases. In the form-sphere realm, four kinds of elements are held to be dependent on three bases. In the formless-sphere realm, one element is held to be not dependent on any base; this is the connection. The phrase 'forty-three' is stated with reference to the thirty states beginning with the investigating consciousness, together with the five sense-consciousnesses and the triad of the mind-element.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus, of the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, in the commentary named Paramatthadīpanī,

Catutthavaṇṇanāya pakiṇṇakasaṅgahassa

of the explanation of the fourth chapter, the Compendium of Miscellaneous Items.

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The Paramatthadīpanī is concluded.

Vīthi saṅgaha paramatthadīpanī

The Paramatthadīpanī on the Compendium of Processes

136. Evaṃ [M 0.0145] cittappabheda saṅgaho, cetasikappabheda saṅgaho, ubhayappabheda saṅgahoti cittacetasikānaṃ kayopabheda saṅgahe dassetvā idāni vīthicittappavattisaṅgaho vīthimutta cittappavattisaṅgahoti te saññeva dve pavattisaṅgahe dassetuṃ cittuppādānamiccevantiādimāha. Tattha uppajjantīti uppādā. Tattha uppajjanti. Aññassa asu tattācitte icceva labbhati. Iti cittañca citteuppādācāti cittuppādā. Cittacetasikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tesaṃ cittuppādānaṃ. Iccevantiādito paṭṭhāya vuttappakārena. Saṅgahamuttaranti jātiniddeso yaṃ. Uttare uttame tayo pabhedasaṅgahe katvāti sambandho. Bhūmipuggalabhedenāti sahatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Kāmāvacarādibhūmibhedena duhetukādi puggalabhedena saddhinti attho. Pubbāparaniyāmitanti āvajjanādi cakkhuviññāṇādi pubba cittāparacittānukkamena niyāmitaṃ vavatthitaṃ. Pavattisaṅgahaṃnāmātipi jātiniddesoyeva. Evaṃ nāmake dve pavattisaṅgaheti attho. Paṭisandhipavattiyanti paṭisandhipavattīsu. Vacanavipallāso hesa. Paṭisandhikālepavattikālecāti attho. Paṭisandhikāle pavattisaṅgahañca pavattikāle pavattisaṅgahañcāti dve saṅgahepavatti pavakkhāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañca attho uparisaṅgahe ārabbha gāthāya pākaṭo. Keci pana niddhāraṇe bhummanti vadanti. Evaṃsati upari saṅgaho paṭisandhisaṅgahonāma siyā. Na pavatti saṅgaho nāma. Evañca sati upari vīthimuttasaṅgahe ārabbha gāthāyaṃ sandhiyaṃ pavattisaṅgahonāma idāni vuccatīti iminā na sameti.

136. Thus, having shown the compendium of the classification of consciousness, the compendium of the classification of mental factors, and the compendium of the classification of both—that is, the compendium of the divisions of consciousness and mental factors—now, to explain the two compendia of processes, namely, the compendium of the process of consciousness in a cognitive series and the compendium of the process of consciousness free from a cognitive series, the text begins with 'of the arisings of consciousness,' and so on. Here, 'uppajjanti' means 'they arise.' They arise there. Because another does not exist, the term 'in consciousness' (citte) is thus obtained. Thus, both consciousness and what arises in consciousness are called 'arisings of consciousness.' This is said to mean consciousness and mental factors. 'Of those arisings of consciousness' means in the manner stated starting from 'thus' and so on. 'The further compendium' is a designation of kind. The connection is: 'having made the three classifications in the further, supreme section.' 'By division of planes and individuals' is the instrumental case in the sense of 'together with.' The meaning is: 'together with the division of planes, such as the sense-sphere plane, and the division of individuals, such as the two-rooted individual.' 'Determined by preceding and succeeding' means regulated, established by the sequence of preceding consciousness and succeeding consciousness, such as adverting, eye-consciousness, and so on. 'Called the compendium of processes' is also a designation of kind. The meaning is 'two compendia of processes with this name.' 'In rebirth-linking and in process' means 'in rebirth-linking and in processes.' This is an inversion of grammatical number. The meaning is 'at the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of life.' It is said, 'I will explain two compendia of processes: the compendium of process at the time of rebirth-linking and the compendium of process during the course of life.' And this meaning is evident in the verse that introduces the subsequent compendium. Some, however, say it is the locative case in the sense of specification. If so, the subsequent compendium would be called 'the compendium of rebirth-linking,' not 'the compendium of process.' And if that were so, it would not accord with the statement in the verse introducing the subsequent compendium free from a cognitive series: 'Now the compendium of process with reference to rebirth-linking is spoken of.'

[115] Ṭīkāsu pana

[115] But in the subcommentaries,

“Uttaraṃ vedanāsaṅgahādivibhāgato uttama”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

It is said: '"The further" is supreme because of the classification beginning with the compendium of feelings.' That should be investigated.

Evañhi [M 0.0146] sati pakiṇṇakasaṅgahova idha saṅgahasaddena gahito siyāti. Yasmāpana tiṇṇaṃ dvinnañca pabhedasaṅgahānaṃ majjhe ṭhatvā ayaṃ anusandhigāthā pavattā. Tasmā pubbe tayopi pabhedasaṅgahā idha saṅgahasaddena gahetuṃ yuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Ayaṃ pana pavattisaṅgaho vatthudvārālambaṇehi saddhiṃ yojetvā vutto suvuttoti tāni tīṇi chakkānipi puna idha nikkhittāni.

For if this were so, only the Compendium of Miscellaneous Items would be taken here by the word 'compendium.' But since this connecting verse occurs standing between the three and the two compendia of classifications, it should therefore be understood that it is fitting for all three prior compendia of classifications to be taken here by the word 'compendium.' Moreover, this compendium of processes is said to be well-spoken because it is taught in connection with base, door, and object; thus those three groups of six are set down here again.

[116] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[116] But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Vatthudvārālambaṇa saṅgahā heṭṭhā kathitāpi paripuṇṇaṃ katvā pavattisaṅgahaṃ dassetuṃ puna nikkhittā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: 'Though the compendia of base, door, and object have been discussed before, they are set down again in order to show the compendium of processes in its entirety.' That is not well-stated.

Na hi sakalā vatthudvārālambaṇasaṅgahā idha nikkhittāti. Visayānaṃ dvāresu pavatti visayapavatti. Etthaca pavattīti āpātāgamanameva vuccati. Vakkhati hi ekacittakkhaṇā tītānivātiādiṃ. Sā pana kāci sīghatamā, kāci sīghatarā, sīghā, dandhā, dandhatarā, dandhatamāti chadhā hotīti. Kammādīnaṃ visayānaṃ dvāresu pavatti paccupaṭṭhānaṃ āpātāgamanaṃ visayappavatti. Vakkhati hi kammaṃvā kammanimittaṃvā gatinimittaṃvā kammabalena channaṃ dvārānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ paccupaṭṭhātīti.

For not the entire compendium of base, door, and object is set down here. The process of objects at the doors is 'object-process.' And here, 'process' is simply called 'coming into range.' For it will be said, 'past by one mind-moment,' and so on. And this is sixfold: very fast, faster, fast, slow, slower, and very slow. The process of objects such as kamma at the doors, their presentation, their coming into range, is 'object-process.' For it will be said: 'Through the force of kamma, either kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of destiny presents itself at one of the six doors.'

[117] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[117] But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Visayesuca cittānaṃ pavatti visayappavattī”tipi vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is also said: 'The process of consciousnesses with regard to objects is object-process.' That is not well-stated.

Evañhi sati atiparittārammaṇe visayappavattināma anupapannā āpajjatīti. Tatthāti tesu chakkesu. Dhātubhedaṃ patvādhātunānattaṃ pamāṇanti mananaṃ vijānanato visuṃ katvā manodhātu visuṃ vuttā. Viññāṇabhedaṃ patvā pana yaṃkiñci mananaṃ vijānane anto gadhamevāti vuttaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ.La. Chaviññāṇānīti chavīthiyo pana dvārappavattā cittapavattiyo yojetabbāti sambandho. Cakkhudvāre pavattā vīthi cakkhudvāravīthi. Cakkhudvāravikāraṃ paṭicca pavatto [M 0.0147] cittappabandhoti attho. Evaṃ sesesu. Asādhāraṇena cakkhuviññāṇena upalakkhitā vīthi cakkhuviññāṇavīthi. Suddho pana manoviññāṇapabandho manoviññāṇavīthi.

For if this were so, the designation 'process-occurrence with an extremely small object' would become untenable. Therein, 'in those' means in those sixes. Having arrived at the distinction of elements, with the diversity of elements as the measure, having separated thinking (manana) from knowing (vijānana), the mind-element is stated separately. But having arrived at the distinction of consciousness, whatever thinking there is, is entirely included within knowing; thus it is said 'eye-consciousness,' and so forth. The six consciousnesses, these six cognitive series, however, are cognitive processes occurring at the doors, and they should be connected thus; such is the connection. The cognitive series occurring at the eye-door is the eye-door cognitive series. The meaning is: the stream of consciousness occurring dependent on the modification of the eye-door. Similarly for the rest. The cognitive series characterized by the specific eye-consciousness is the eye-consciousness cognitive series. But the pure stream of mind-consciousness is the mind-consciousness cognitive series.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Cakkhuviññāṇasambandhinī vīthi tena saha ekārammaṇa eka dvārikatāya saha caraṇabhāvato cakkhuviññāṇa vīthī”ti vuttaṃ.

It is said: 'The cognitive series associated with eye-consciousness is the eye-consciousness cognitive series because of its nature of proceeding together with it, having a single object and a single door.'

Dvārappavattāti dvāre uppannā. Taṃ taṃ dvāravikāraṃ paṭicca uppannāti attho. Cittappavattiyoti cittapabandhā. Atimahantanti sāmi atthe paccattavacanaṃ. Atimahantassa pañcālambaṇassa pavatti.La. Atiparittassa pañcālambaṇassa pavatticāti pañcadvāre catudhā. Manodvāre pana vibhūtassa chaḷārammaṇassa pavatti avibhūtassa chaḷārammaṇassa pavatticāti dvidhāti chadhāvisayappavatti veditabbāti yojanā. Atimahantādibhāvo cettha ālokādi paccaya vasenavā vatthu atimahantādivasenavā veditabbo. Tattha saṇhasukhumaṃpi dūraṃpi rūpādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānavatthunāma ālokādi paccaya sampattiyā sati atimahantameva. Tathā hi buddhassa bhagavato pathamāti nīhārakālādīsu loka vivaraṇa pāṭihāriyapavatti kāle avīcinirayepi akaniṭṭhepi paracakkavāḷesupi saṇhasukhumānica dūrānica rūpāni idha ṭhitāva passanti. Tadā hi uḷāro obhāso pāturahosi. Tassa vasena sabbepi pathavisineru cakkavāḷa siluccayādayo jātiphalikakkhandhā viya sampajjanti. Mahanto uḷāro obhāso pāturahosi atikammadevānaṃ devānubhāvanti hi vuttaṃ. Upapattidevabrahmādīnaṃ pana pasādanissayabhūtānaṃ obhāsajātatāyapi pathavipabbatādayo cakkhurūpādīnaṃ antaraṃ kātuṃ nasakkontīti. Tathā dūrepi pabbatādirūpāni vatthu atimahantatāya candasūriya tārakādi rūpāni visaya vatthu mahantatāya obhāsa jātatāya ca ati mahantāni nāma hontīti. Ālokādipaccayānaṃ pana adhiṭṭhānavatthūnañca dubbala dubbalatara [M 0.0148] dubbalatamānukkamena mahantādibhāvo vattabboti. Yāni pana pañcālambaṇāni ekacittakkhaṇaṃ atikkamma āpātaṃ āgacchanti, tāni atimahantārammaṇānināma. Yāni dvatticittakkhaṇāni atikkamma, tāni mahantārammaṇāni. Yāni catu pañca cha satta aṭṭha nava cittakkhaṇāni atikkamma, tāni parittārammaṇāni. Yānipana dasekādasadvādasa terasa cuddasa pannarasa cittakkhaṇāni atikkamma āpātaṃ āgacchanti. Tāni atiparittā rammaṇānīti. Pakkhatica ekacittakkhaṇātītānivātiādi. Vibhūtassāti pākaṭassa, avibhūtassāti apākaṭassa. Evaṃ chachakkāni sarūpato niddisitvā idāni tāni sabbāni ekato yojetvā vīthicittappavattiṃ vitthārento kathanti pucchitvā rūpārūpānaṃ tāva addhānaparicchedaṃ dassetuṃ uppādaṭṭhitītiādi māha. Tattha kathanti kena pakārena vīthicittappavatti hotīti attho.

'Occurring at the door' means arisen at the door. The meaning is: arisen dependent on the modification of that particular door. 'Cognitive processes' means streams of consciousness. 'Extremely large' is a subjective expression in the sense of mastery. The occurrence of the fivefold object that is extremely large... and the occurrence of the fivefold object that is extremely small—thus, in the five doors, it is fourfold. However, in the mind-door, the occurrence of the sixfold object that is clear and the occurrence of the sixfold object that is unclear—thus, it is twofold. Thus, the process-occurrence with an object should be understood as sixfold; this is the connection. Here, the state of being extremely large, etc., should be understood either by way of conditions such as light, or by way of the physical basis being extremely large, etc. In this regard, even a subtle and distant form, etc., which is a support-basis, is indeed extremely large when there is the attainment of conditions such as light. For example, at the time of the Buddha's first aspiration, etc., at the moment of the manifestation of the miracle of opening the world, even in the Avīci hell or the Akaniṭṭha heaven, or in other world-systems, subtle and distant forms are seen as if present here. At that time, a magnificent radiance appeared. Due to that, all the earth, Mount Sineru, the world-spheres, mountain ranges, etc., became like masses of natural crystal. 'A great and magnificent radiance appeared, surpassing the divine majesty of the gods'—so it is said. But for the gods and Brahmās born by rebirth, whose support is the sensitive matter, even with the arising of radiance, the earth, mountains, etc., are not able to create an obstruction for the eye and for forms. Similarly, distant forms such as mountains, due to the great size of their physical basis, and forms such as the moon, sun, and stars, due to the great size of their object-basis and the arising of radiance, are called extremely large. However, the state of being large, etc., should be stated in sequence as weak, weaker, and weakest in accordance with the conditions such as light and the support-bases. Those fivefold objects that arrive at the avenue of apprehension after surpassing one mind-moment are called extremely large objects. Those that arrive after surpassing two or three mind-moments are called large objects. Those that arrive after surpassing four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine mind-moments are called small objects. Those that arrive after surpassing ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, or fifteen mind-moments are called extremely small objects. And it is said, 'those that are past one mind-moment,' etc. 'Clear' means manifest; 'unclear' means unmanifest. Having thus pointed out the six sixes according to their nature, now, combining them all together, while explaining the process of consciousness in the cognitive series, having asked 'How?', he then states 'arising, presence,' etc., in order to show the time-limit of form and formless phenomena. Therein, 'how?' means: In what way does the process of consciousness in the cognitive series occur? This is the meaning.

[118] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Kathanti kena pakārena atimahantādivasena visaya vavatthānaṃ hotīti pucchitvā cittakkhaṇavasena taṃ pakāsetuṃ uppādaṭṭhitītiādi āraddha”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ yuttaṃ viya na dissati.

It is said: 'Having asked, "How, in what way, does the establishment of the object occur by way of being extremely large, etc.?", the passage beginning "arising, presence," etc., was undertaken in order to explain that by way of the mind-moment.' That does not seem quite appropriate.

Evañhi satiādito pañcannaṃ chakkānaṃ okāsonāma nasiyā. Naca uppādaṭṭhiti.La. Rūpadhammānamāyūti idaṃ visaya vavatthānatthameva vuttanti sakkā viññātunti. Uppajjanaṃ uppādo. Sabhāva paṭilābhoti attho. Ṭhānaṃ ṭhiti. Yathāladdhasabhāvassa anivattīti attho. Bhañjanaṃ bhaṅgo. Tassa parihāyitvā antaradhānanti attho. Ekacittakkhaṇaṃnāmāti ekassa cittassa khaṇonāma. So pana khaṇo accharāsaṅghāṭakkhaṇassa akkhinimmilanakkhaṇassaca anekakoṭi satasahassabhāgo daṭṭhabbo. Accharāsaṅghāṭakkhaṇe anekakoṭisatasahassasaṅkhā vedanā uppajjantīti hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ācariyānandattheramatena panettha uppādabhaṅga vasenakhaṇadvayaṃ ekacittakkhaṇaṃnāmāti vattabbaṃ. Yathā hi loke [M 0.0149] vijjunāma vaddhanānantarameva bhijjati. Na panassā vaddhanassa bhijjanassaca antarā ṭhitināma visuṃ paññāyati. Yathā ca uddhaṃ ujuṃ khittaṃ leḍḍu uppatitvā patati. Na pana uppatanassa patanassa ca antarā ṭhitināma visuṃ dissati. Tathā cittaṃpi. Taṃpi hi udaya bhāgānantarameva vayabhāge patati. Na panassa rūpadhammānaṃ viya tesaṃ dvinnaṃ bhāgānaṃ majjhe visuṃ eko gaṇanūpago ṭhitibhāgonāma upalabbhati. Evañca katvā yamakesu cittassa uppādabhaṅgāva tattha tattha vuttā. Visesato pana cittayamake uppannaṃ uppajjamānanti. Bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ. No ca uppajjamānaṃ. Uppādakkhaṇe uppannañceva uppajjamānañcātiādinā bhaṅguppādāva cittassa vuttā. Kathāvatthumhica ekaṃ cittaṃ divasaṃ tiṭṭhatīti āmantā. Upaddhadivaso uppādakkhaṇo. Upaddhadivaso vayakkhaṇoti. Na hevaṃ vattabbe. Ekaṃ cittaṃ dve divase tiṭṭhatīti āmantā. Eko divaso uppādakkhaṇo. Eko divaso vayakkhaṇoti nahevaṃ vattabbe. Ekaṃ cittaṃ cattāro divase tiṭṭhatīti āmantā. Dve divasā uppādakkhaṇo. Dve divasā vayakkhaṇoti na hevaṃ vattabbe.La. Māsaṃ. Dve māse. Cattāromāse.La. Saṃvaccharaṃ, dve saṃvaccharāni. Cattāri saṃvaccharāni.La. Kappaṃ. Dve kappe. Cattāro kappetiādinā dve uppādavayabhāgāva cittassa vuttā. Na ṭhitibhāgo. Yadi so visuṃ upalabbheyya. Ekaṃ cittaṃ divasaṃ tiṭṭhatīti āmantā. Divasassa pathamo bhāgo uppādakkhaṇo. Dutīyo ṭhitikkhaṇo. Tatīyo vayakkhaṇoti evaṃ mahātherena vicārito siyā. Tayo divase tayo māse tīṇi saṃvaccharāni tayo kappeti imānipi avajje tabbānieva siyunti. Ettha siyā, nanu suttantesu tīṇi māni bhikkhave saṅkhatassa saṅkhata lakkhaṇāni. Katamānitīṇi, uppādo paññāyati. Vayo paññāyati. Ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyatīti vuttaṃ. Tathā vedanāya uppādo paññāyati. Vayo paññāyati. Ṭhitāya aññathattaṃ paññāyati. Saññāya. Saṅkhārānaṃ. Viññāṇassa uppādo.La. Paññāyatīti vuttaṃ. Tasmā cittassa tatīyo ṭhitibhāgo visuṃ upalabbhati yevāti.Na. Pabandhaṭhitiyā eva tattha [M 0.0150] vuttattāti. Kathaṃ viññāyatīti ce, uppādavaye pathamaṃ vatvā pacchā puna visuṃ ṭhitassa aññathatthaṃ paññāyatīti imassa vuttattāti. Itarathā uppādo paññāyati. Ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyati. Vayo paññāyatīti vuttaṃ siyāti. Nanu pabandhaṭhiti nāma paññatti hoti. Sāca asaṅkhatā, suttantānica saṅkhata lakkhaṇa visayāni. Tasmā sā pabandhaṭṭhiti tattha vuttāti nasakkā viññātunti ce. Na na sakkā. Abhidhammepi saṅkhatadhammaniddesesu samūha saṇṭhāna santati paññattīhipi niddesassa diṭṭhattā. Tathā hi rūpāyatananiddesādīsu dīghaṃ rassaṃ saṇhaṃ thulaṃ vaṭṭaṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ caturassaṃ chaḷaṃsaṃ aṭṭhaṃsaṃ soḷasaṃsaṃ ninnaṃ thalantiādinā, vibhaṅge ca kesā lomā nakhā dantātiādinā paññattisisena saṅkhatadhammā niddiṭṭhāti. Suttantesu vattabbameva natthi. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu paññattivasena pavattāpi desanā saṅkhatadhammameva āhacca tiṭṭhati. Tasmā yathā uppādabhaṅgānaṃ paccekaṃ ekeko khaṇo cittassa labbhati. Na tathā ṭhitiyāti. Ayaṃ ācariyānandatthe rassa adhippāyo. Ayañca vādo saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ eva āgato. Soca saṅgahakārena paṭikkhitto. Vuttañhi tattha, apare pana vadanti. Arūpadhammānaṃ jarākhaṇonāma nasakkā paññapetuṃ. Sammā sambuddhoca vedanāya uppādo paññāyati. Vayo paññāyati. Ṭhitāya aññathatthaṃ paññāyatīti vadanto arūpadhammānaṃpi tīṇi lakkhaṇāni paññapeti. Bhāniatthikkhaṇaṃ upādāya labbhantīti vatvā –

For if this were so, there would be no opportunity from the outset for the five sixes. Nor for arising and duration. The phrase 'the life-span of material phenomena' (rūpadhammānamāyu) is stated merely for the purpose of defining the scope; it can be understood thus. Arising (uppāda) is the coming into being; its meaning is the acquisition of its own nature. Duration (ṭhiti) is abiding; its meaning is the non-reversal of its obtained nature. Dissolution (bhaṅga) is breaking up; its meaning is its decay and disappearance. A single mind-moment (ekacittakkhaṇa) is the moment of a single mind. That moment, however, should be regarded as one of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of parts of the moment of a snap of the fingers or a blink of the eye. For it is said in the commentary that hundreds of thousands of koṭis of feelings arise in the moment of a snap of the fingers. In the opinion of the Elder Ācariya Ānanda, here, it should be said that a single mind-moment consists of two moments, namely, arising and dissolution. Just as in the world, a lightning flash breaks up immediately after its appearing, and no separate duration is discerned between its appearing and breaking up; and just as a clod of earth thrown straight upward rises and falls, and no separate duration is seen between its rising and falling; so too is the mind. For it too, immediately after the phase of arising, falls into the phase of dissolution. And, unlike material phenomena, no distinct phase of duration that can be reckoned is found between these two phases. Thus, in the Yamakas, only the arising and dissolution of the mind are mentioned in various places. Specifically, in the Cittayamaka, concerning 'what has arisen' and 'what is arising,' it is said that at the moment of dissolution, it 'has arisen' but is not 'arising,' and at the moment of arising, it both 'has arisen' and 'is arising'; in this way, only the dissolution and arising of the mind are mentioned. And in the Kathāvatthu: 'Does a single mind last for a day?' 'Yes.' 'Is half a day the moment of arising and half a day the moment of dissolution?' 'This should not be said.' 'Does a single mind last for two days?' 'Yes.' 'Is one day the moment of arising and one day the moment of dissolution?' 'This should not be said.' 'Does a single mind last for four days?' 'Yes.' 'Are two days the moment of arising and two days the moment of dissolution?' 'This should not be said.' Similarly, 'a month, two months, four months,' 'a year, two years, four years,' 'an eon, two eons, four eons,' etc.; in this way, only the two phases of arising and dissolution are mentioned for the mind. There is no phase of duration. If it were separately discernible, one could say: 'Does a single mind last for a day?' 'Yes.' 'The first part of the day is the moment of arising, the second is the moment of duration, and the third is the moment of dissolution.' The great elder might have reasoned thus. Similarly, for three days, three months, three years, three eons, etc., these too would be liable to the same objection. Here, one might object: 'But in the suttas, it is said: "Monks, there are these three characteristics of the conditioned. What three? Arising is discerned, dissolution is discerned, and the alteration of what endures is discerned." Likewise, for feeling, arising is discerned, dissolution is discerned, and the alteration of what endures is discerned. And so for perception, formations, and consciousness, arising is discerned.' Thus it is said. 'Therefore, the third phase, duration, is indeed separately discernible for the mind.' No, because what is spoken of there is merely continuity of duration. If it is asked, 'How is this known?', it is because, having first spoken of arising and dissolution, then afterwards the alteration of what endures is spoken of separately. Otherwise, it would have been said: 'Arising is discerned, the alteration of what endures is discerned, dissolution is discerned.' But is not 'continuity of duration' a concept? And that is unconditioned, while the suttas have as their subject the characteristics of the conditioned. Therefore, it cannot be understood that this 'continuity of duration' is what is spoken of there. No, it can be understood. For even in the Abhidhamma, in descriptions of conditioned phenomena, we see descriptions by way of aggregates, configurations, continuity, and concepts. For instance, in the descriptions of the sense-spheres and so on, through terms such as long, short, smooth, coarse, round, circular, square, hexagonal, octagonal, sixteen-sided, low-lying, and high-lying; and in the Vibhaṅga, through terms such as hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, and teeth, conditioned phenomena are described by way of concepts. There is no need to say anything about the suttas. For even teachings that proceed in terms of concepts in such instances still pertain to conditioned phenomena. Therefore, while individual moments of arising and dissolution can be obtained for the mind, it is not so with duration. This is the opinion of the Elder Ācariya Ānanda. And this view has come down only in the Saṃyuttaṭṭhakathā, and it is rejected by the compiler. For it is said there, 'But others say: "A moment of aging cannot be designated for immaterial phenomena. Yet the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha, in saying, 'Arising is discerned in feeling, dissolution is discerned, and the alteration of what endures is discerned,' designates three characteristics even for immaterial phenomena." They say that these can be obtained by taking the moment of change.'

Atthitā sabbadhammānaṃ, ṭhitināma pavuccati;

Tasseva bhedo maraṇaṃ; Sabbadā sabbapāṇinanti.

The existence of all phenomena is called duration; their breaking up is death; for all beings, always.

Imāya ācariyagāthāya tamatthaṃ sādhenti. Athavā, santativasena ṭhānaṃ veditabbantica vadanti. Imasmiṃ pana sutte ayaṃ viseso natthi. Tasmā ācariyagāthāya suttaṃ appaṭibāhetvā suttameva pamāṇaṃ kātabbanti. Tattha jarākhaṇonāma uppādakkhaṇabhaṅgakkhaṇānaṃ majjhe visuṃ jarāya khettabhūto ṭhītikkhaṇo vuccati. Aññathattanti jarāeva. Atthikkhaṇanti khaṇadvayameva. Paṭikkhittopi pana ayaṃ vādo kathāvatthu pāḷiyā saddhiṃ suṭṭhu sametiyeva. [M 0.0151] Apica, uddhaṃ uppatitassa leṭṭussa uppatananivatti viya yā cittassa udayasaṅkhātassa vaḍḍhanassa nivattināma atthi. Na hi udaye anivattante vayonāma sambhavatitī. Sā eva udaya pariyantamattabhūtā idha ṭhitipariyāyoti sakkā vattuṃ. So pana visuṃ gaṇanūpago eko khaṇonāma nahotīti katvā abhidhamme dveeva khaṇā cittassa vuttā. Udayabhāgassa pana ādi koṭiṃ vayabhāgassaantakoṭiñca thapetvā majjhebhāgadvayanissitā paripaccana lakkhaṇā jarānāma arūpadhammānaṃpi labbhatiyeva. Taṃ sandhāya dhātukathāyaṃ jarādvīhikhandhehisaṅgahitātivuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

They establish that meaning by means of this teacher’s verse. Alternatively, they say that duration should be understood in terms of continuity. However, in this Sutta, there is no such distinction. Therefore, without setting aside the teacher’s verse, the Sutta itself should be taken as the authority. Here, the moment of aging (jarākhaṇa) is called the moment of duration (ṭhitikkhaṇa), which is a separate field for aging in the middle of the moment of arising and the moment of dissolution. Alteration (aññathatta) is aging itself. The moment of existence (atthikkhaṇa) refers to just two moments. Yet, even this rejected view aligns well with the Kathāvatthu Pāḷi. Furthermore, just as there is a cessation of the upward motion of a clod thrown straight up, so too there is a cessation of the mind's growth, which is reckoned as arising. For dissolution cannot occur if arising does not cease. That very cessation, being merely the limit of arising, can here be called a synonym for duration. But since that is not a single moment that can be separately reckoned, only two moments of the mind are mentioned in the Abhidhamma. However, setting aside the initial point of the arising phase and the final point of the dissolution phase, aging—characterized by maturing and dependent on the two middle portions—is indeed found even for immaterial phenomena. With reference to this, it should be understood that in the Dhātukathā it is said that aging is included in two aggregates.

[119] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[119] But whatever is to be clarified,

“Uppādabhaṅgāvatthāhi bhinnā bhaṅgābhimukhāvatthāpi icchitabbā. Sā ṭhitināmā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ kathāvatthupāḷiyā saha na sameti.

It was said: 'A state distinct from the states of arising and dissolution, a state facing towards dissolution, should also be accepted. That is called duration.' This does not agree with the Kathāvatthu Pāḷi.

Upaddhadivaso uppādakkhaṇo. Upaddhadivaso vayakkhaṇo. Pathamo divaso uppādakkhaṇo. Dutīyo vayakkhaṇoti hi vicārentena uppādabhaṅgāvatthā hi bhinnā tatīyā avatthā tassaṃ pāḷiyaṃ paṭikkhittāyeva hotīti.

For one who considers thus: 'Half a day is the moment of arising, half a day is the moment of dissolution; the first day is the moment of arising, the second day is the moment of dissolution,' a third state distinct from the states of arising and dissolution is indeed rejected in that Pāḷi text.

[120] Etena yañca tattha

[120] By this, whatever was said there,

“Pāḷiyaṃ pana veneyyajjhāsayā nuromato nayadassanavasena sā na vuttā. Atidhammadesanāpi hi kadāci veneyyajjhāsayānurodhena pavattati. Yathā, rūpassa uppādo upacayo santatīti dvidhā bhinditvā desito”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi paṭikkhittaṃ hoti. Vibhāgārahassa hi dhammassa vibhāgakaraṇaṃnāma veneyyavasenātipi dhammavasenātipi yujjati. Vijjamāne sati visuṃ katvā vattabbassa abhidhamme avacanaṃ pana veneyyavasenāti na yuttametanti.

It was said: 'In the Pāḷi, however, it was not stated in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained, or by way of showing the method. For even the Abhidhamma teaching sometimes proceeds in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained. For example, the arising of form, its accumulation, and continuity are taught by dividing it into two.' That too is refuted. For making a division of a phenomenon that merits division is justifiable both on account of those to be trained and on account of the Dhamma itself. But the failure to speak in the Abhidhamma of what exists and should be stated separately, on account of those to be trained, is not appropriate.

[121] Yampi tattha

[121] And whatever was said there,

“Sutteca tīṇi māni bhikkhave saṅkhatassa saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni. Katamāni tīṇi. Uppādo paññāyati. Vayo paññā yati. [M 0.0152] Ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyatīti evaṃ saṅkhatadhammasseva lakkhaṇadassanatthaṃ uppādādīnaṃ vuttattā nasakkā pabandhassa paññattisabhāvassa asaṅkhatassa ṭhiti tattha vuttāti viññātu”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na gahetabbaṃ.

It was said: 'In the Sutta: "Monks, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. What three? Arising is apparent, passing away is apparent, and alteration of what is established is apparent." Thus, because arising and so on are stated for the purpose of showing the characteristics of conditioned phenomena themselves, it cannot be understood that the duration spoken of there is the duration of a continuum, which has the nature of a designation and is unconditioned.' That too is not to be accepted.

Abhidhammepi heṭṭhā vuttanayena paññattisīsena saṅkhatadhammānaṃ niddesassa diṭṭhattāti.

In the Abhidhamma too, the exposition of conditioned phenomena is seen under the heading of designation, according to the method stated earlier.

[122] Yampi tattha

[122] And whatever there,

“Upasaggassaca dhātvattheyeva pavattanato paññāyatīti etassa viññāyatīti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yuttaṃ.

And it was said: 'Because a prefix functions only in the meaning of the root, the meaning of "paññāyati" is "viññāyati".' That too is not appropriate.

Yathānulomasāsanañhi suttaṃ. Tasmā tattha vineyyānaṃ suṭṭhu paññāyanameva adhippetanti. Arūpaṃ arūpisabhāvattā lahupariṇāmaṃ. Rūpaṃ pana rūpidhammattāyeva dandhapariṇāmanti vuttaṃ tānipana.La. Rūpadhammāna māyūti.

For the Sutta is indeed in accordance with proper instruction. Therefore, there, the intention is simply that the trainees understand clearly. The immaterial, due to its immaterial nature, changes swiftly. But form, because it is of the nature of form, changes slowly—so it is said. These, however, are the life of material phenomena.

[123] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[123] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Gāhakagahetabba bhāvassa taṃtaṃ khaṇavasena nippajjanato”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ.

It is said: 'The reason is that the nature of the grasper and the grasped arises due to individual moments.' But that is no reason.

Na hi gāhakaṃ arūpaṃ gahetabbañca rūpaṃ gahaṇasampajjanatthaṃ lahuṃ pariṇamati garuṃ pariṇapatīti sakkā vattunti. Tāni tādisāni sattarasannaṃ cittānaṃ khaṇāni sattarasavā tāni cittakkhaṇāni rūpa dhammānamāyūti yojanā. Sattarasa cittakkhaṇasamapamāṇāni khaṇāni viññatti rūpalakkhaṇa rūpavajjānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ āyunāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Khaṇamattato pana aṭṭhakathānayena ekapaññāsakhaṇāni honti, mūlaṭīkānayena dvattiṃsakhaṇāni. Tatthaca ādimhi dve khaṇāni rūpadhammānaṃ ekaṃ uppādakkhaṇameva. Ante dve ekaṃ bhaṅgakkhaṇameva. Majjhe aṭṭhavīsa khaṇāni tesaṃ ekaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi dandhapariṇatānaṃ rūpānaṃ uppādabhaṅgāpi cittassa viya lahukā bhavituṃ arahantīti. Tattha viññattidvayaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ. Upacayasantatiyo uppādamattā aniccatā bhaṅgamattā. Jaratā rūpa dhammānaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇamattāti daṭṭhabbā. Mūlaṭīkānayena panettha tāni pana [M 0.0153] soḷasacittakkhaṇāni rūpadhammānamāyūti vattabbaṃ. Ṭīkācariyo hi paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅge āgataṃ mahāṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ patiṭṭhapento soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukabhāvaṃ sambhāveti, evaṃ santepi khandha vibhaṅgeyeva tāva rūpānaṃ uppādanirodhavidhānassa mahāaṭṭhakathā vādassa yamakapāḷivirodhaṃ dassetvā saṅgahakārena paṭisiddhattā na sakkā taṃ patiṭṭhapetunti. Tasmiṃ vāde hi paṭisiddhe tattha āgatā soḷasāyukatāvā atirekasoḷasāyukatāvā paṭisiddhāyeva hotīti.

For it cannot be said that the formless, being the grasper, and form, being the grasped, transform swiftly or slowly for the sake of accomplishing the grasp. The connection is that those moments, being seventeen moments of consciousness, are the life-span of material phenomena. It is said that seventeen moments, equal in measure to moments of consciousness, are the life-span of material phenomena, excluding communicative form and the characteristics of form. However, from the perspective of moments, according to the commentary method, there are fifty-one moments; according to the root subcommentary method, there are thirty-two moments. And there, at the beginning, two moments are just one arising moment for material phenomena. At the end, two moments are just one dissolution moment. In the middle, twenty-eight moments are to be seen as their one duration moment. Indeed, the arising and dissolution of material phenomena, which transform slowly, cannot be as swift as those of consciousness. Here, the two types of communicative form are of one mind-moment's duration. Accumulation and continuity are merely arising; impermanence is merely dissolution. Aging should be seen as merely the duration moment of material phenomena. According to the root subcommentary method here, however, it should be stated that those sixteen moments of consciousness are the life-span of material phenomena. For the subcommentary teacher, while establishing the statement from the great commentary found in the Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga, considers it probable that material phenomena have a lifespan of sixteen moments of consciousness. Even so, in the Khandhavibhaṅga itself, because the great commentary’s explanation of the arising and cessation of material phenomena contradicts the Yamaka Pāḷi, and because it was rejected by the author of the Saṅgaha, it is not possible to establish that view. For when that view is rejected, the sixteen-moment lifespan or the more-than-sixteen-moment lifespan mentioned there is also rejected.

[124] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[124] But what is in the Vibhāvanī:

Taṃ ṭīkānayaṃ tayidamasāranti paṭikkhipitvā tadatthaṃ sā dhentena “paṭisandhicittena sahuppannaṃ rūpaṃ tato paṭṭhāya sattarasamena saddhiṃ nirujjhati. Paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannaṃ rūpaṃ aṭṭhārasamassa uppādakkhaṇe nirujjhatītiādinā aṭṭhakathāyameva sattarasacittakkhaṇassa āgatattā”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

Rejecting that subcommentary method as 'this is unsubstantial,' and establishing its meaning, the reason is stated: 'The material form that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases from that point onwards together with the seventeenth [moment]. The material form that arises at the duration moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases at the arising moment of the eighteenth [moment],' and so on, because the seventeen moments of consciousness are mentioned in the commentary itself. That is not good.

Yañhi saṅgahakārassa sattarasāyukavacanaṃ ṭīkākārena vicāritaṃ. Tadeva dassetvā ṭīkānayo paṭikkhittoti na yuttame tanti. Ekacittassa khaṇaṃ viya khaṇaṃ ekacittakkhaṇaṃ. Atthato abhinnaṃpi hi khaṇaṃ idaṃ cittassa idaṃ rūpānanti kappanāvasena bhinnaṃ viya katvā upacarīyatīti. Ekacittakkhaṇaṃ atītaṃ etesanti ekacittakkhaṇātītāni. Atimahantabhūtāni pañcārammaṇāni.

For the statement of the author of the Saṅgaha about the seventeen-moment lifespan has been examined by the subcommentary writer. To say that the subcommentary method is rejected after having shown that very thing is not fitting. A moment of a single mind, like a moment, is a single mind-moment. Indeed, though a moment is non-different in meaning, it is treated figuratively as if it were different by way of conceptualization, saying 'this belongs to mind, this belongs to form.' Those for whom a single mind-moment has passed are 'passed beyond a single mind-moment.' These are the exceedingly great five objects.

[125] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[125] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Etānivā taṃ atītānīti ekacittakkhaṇātī kānī”tipi vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is also said: 'Or, "these have passed it," thus they are "passed-beyond-a-single-mind-moment".' That is not good.

Na hi niruddhadhammavisayo atītasaddo kiñci atikkamitvā uddhaṃ āgatāni paccuppannarūpāni dīpetīti sakkā vattunti. Bahūni cittakkhaṇāni atītāni etesanti bahucittakkhaṇātītāni. Mahantādi bhūtāni pañcārammaṇāni. Rūpadhammānaṃ pana rūpadhammesveva āpātāgamane thokaṃ balavantatā icchitabbā. Teca ṭhitikkhaṇeyeva paripuṇṇapaccayupaladdhā [M 0.0154] hutvā balavantā hontīti vuttaṃ ṭhitipattānevāti. Evasaddena ṭīkākārassa vādaṃ nīvāreti. So hi uppajjamānameva rūpaṃ pasāde ghaṭṭetīti icchatīti. Pañcālambaṇāni pañcadvāre āpātamāgacchantīti ettha rūpasaddārammaṇāni asampatta vasena itarānica sampattavasena gocarabhāvaṃ upagacchanti. Ayañca visesoghaṭṭanavisesena veditabbo. Purimānihi dve nimittavaseneva ghaṭṭenti. Na vatthuvasena. Pacchimāni pana tīṇivatthuvasena ghaṭṭenti. Na nimittamattavasena nimittaghaṭṭanañcanāma asampattānaññeva na sampattānaṃ. Vatthughaṭṭanaṃ pana sampattānaññeva. No asampattā hoti. Nanti. Yathā hi tīre gacchantānaṃsarīranimittāni pokkharaṇi yāudake dissanti. Tasmiṃ udake orohantānaṃ pana tāni tattha na dissanti. Evameva sampattāni rūpasaddārammaṇāni naghaṭṭenti. Kasmā, visayavisayīnaṃ majjhe ālokassa ākāsassaca abhāvena nimittokāsassa abhāvato. Asampattāniyeva pana attano nimittupaṭṭhāpanavasena ghaṭṭenti. Kasmā, nimittokāsassa laddhattā. Itarāni pana tīṇi yathājātavatthuvaseneva ghaṭṭenti. Tasmā tāni sampattāniyeva ghaṭṭenti. No asampattānīti. Tattha yāni asampattāniyeva hutvā ghaṭṭenti. Tāni sayaṃ dūre ṭhatvā nimitta appanāvasena ghaṭṭitattā ekekasmiṃ pasāde candamaṇḍala sūriya maṇḍalādivasena asanisaddamaṇḍala meṇḍasaddamaṇḍalādivasena ca mahantānipi bahūnipi āpātamāgacchantiyeva. Itarāni pana tīṇi sampattāniyeva ghaṭṭentīti ekekasmiṃ pasāde ekekameva āpātamāgacchantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idañca pañcadvāravasena vuttaṃ. Mano dvāre pana sabbānipi ārammaṇāni asampattāniyeva āpātamāgacchantīti. Etthaca pañcadvāreti idaṃ asādhāraṇa dvāradassanavasena vuttaṃ. Tāni pana pañcālambaṇāni yadāsakasakadvāre ghaṭṭenti. Tadā manodvārepi apāta māgacchantiyeva. Ekekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ dvīsu dvīsu dvāresu apāta māgacchatīti hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā yadā candaṃvā sūriyaṃvā pabbataṃvā rukkhaṃvā yaṃkiñcivā passanti. Tadā ekekasmiṃ cakkhupasāde ekekāni manodvāre ekanti anekāni [M 0.0155] candamaṇḍalādīni ekakkhaṇe upaṭṭhahanti, evaṃ sesārammaṇe sūti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Apātāgamanañcettha lañchakānaṃ tālapaṇṇe lañchanakhandhaṃ thapetvā muggarena paharaṇakāle lañchanakhandhassa tālapaṇṇe āpātetvā akkharupaṭṭhāpanaṃ viya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yato dvārānaṃ vikārappatti hotīti.

Indeed, it cannot be said that the word 'past,' whose domain is ceased phenomena, illuminates present forms that have come up after passing beyond anything. Those for whom many mind-moments have passed are 'passed beyond many mind-moments.' The five objects are large, etc., and are existent. However, regarding material phenomena, a slight strength should be desired in their approach to other material phenomena. And it is said that they become strong only when they have attained stability, having obtained full conditions at the moment of stability. By this word, the subcommentary writer refutes the view of the commentary writer. For he holds that material form strikes the sense sensitivities only at the moment of its arising. Here, when the five objects approach the five sense doors, visual and auditory objects enter the range of cognition by way of not having arrived, and the others by way of having arrived. And this distinction should be understood by the difference in striking. For the former two strike only by way of their signs, not by way of the physical base. The latter three, however, strike by way of the physical base, not merely by their signs. Striking by signs applies only to those not yet arrived, not to those that have arrived. Striking by the physical base, however, applies only to those that have arrived, not to those not yet arrived. Just as, indeed, the reflections of bodies of those walking on the bank are seen in the water of a pond, but when they descend into that water, those reflections are not seen there—even so, visual and auditory objects that have arrived do not strike. Why? Because there is no light and no space between the object and the subject, and thus no opportunity for a sign. But those not yet arrived strike by projecting their own signs. Why? Because the opportunity for the sign is obtained. The other three, however, strike according to their inherent physical bases. Therefore, they strike only when arrived, not when not arrived. Among these, those that strike without having arrived, because they strike by projecting signs while remaining at a distance, large and numerous objects such as the disk of the moon, the disk of the sun, the disk of thunder-sound, and the disk of a ram's sound, approach each sense sensitivity. The other three, however, strike only when arrived; thus, it should be understood that only one object approaches each sense sensitivity at a time. And this is said with reference to the five sense doors. In the mind door, however, all objects approach without having arrived. And here, 'five sense doors' is said to show the uncommon doors. But when these five objects strike their respective sense doors, they also approach the mind door. For it is said in the commentary that each object approaches two doors. Therefore, when one sees the moon, or the sun, or a mountain, or a tree, or anything else, then in each eye-sensitivity there is one, and in the mind door there are one or many disks—such as the moon's disk—that appear simultaneously. The same should be understood for the remaining objects. And here, this approach should be understood to be like the imprinting of letters when a stamper, having placed a stamp-block on a palm leaf, strikes it with a mallet, causing the stamp-block to fall upon the palm leaf. Because an alteration of the doors occurs.

[126] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[126] But as to the clarification:

“Ābhogānurūpaṃ anekakalāpagatāni āpātaṃ āgacchantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha ābhogānurūpanti idaṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

It is said: 'In accordance with the attention, they approach, having gone into many groups.' Here, 'in accordance with the attention'—this should be examined.

Yattakāni hi pañcālambaṇāni cakkhādipathe ālokādi sahitāni hutvā ṭhitāni honti. Tattakāni sabbāni niddāyantassapi visaññi bhūtassapi aññavihitassapi yaṃkiñci jhānaṃvā phalaṃvā nirodhaṃvā samāpajjantassapi ābhogena vinā attano dvāresu āpātamāgacchantiyeva. Nakevalaṃ attanodvāresu eva. Athakho manodvārepi. Nakevalaṃ bhavaṅgamanodvāreeva. Āvajjanādīsu pana catubbhūmaka vīthicittesupi āpātaṃ āgacchantiyeva. Ayaṃnāma mano manodvāraṃ nahotīti navattabboti hi dvārakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayañca attho pathamajjhānassa saddo kaṇṭakoti iminā pāṭhena dīpetabbo. Pathamajjhānaṃ samāpannassa hi saddo sotamhi ghaṭṭetvā jhānacittasaṅkhāte manodvāre āpātamāgacchati. Tadā jhānacitta santati calitvā vocchijjati. Jhānā vuṭṭhāti. Bhavaṅgapāto hoti. Taṃ saddārammaṇaṃ vīthicittaṃ pavattatīti. Dutīyajjhānādīni samāpajjanto pana appakena saddena navuṭṭhāti. Adhimattasaddena pana vuṭṭhātiyeva. Na hi tāni āneñjapattānināma honti. Arūpajjhānānieva pana āneñjapattānināma honti. Tasmā tāni samāpajjanto adhimattasaddenapi navuṭṭhātiyevāti. Tesu pana tathā āpātamāgatesu tadārammaṇāni vīthicittāni pavattantiyevāti navattabbaṃ. Bhavaṅga santatiyāvā javanasantatiyāvā vocchinnāya pavattanti. Avocchinnāya napavattanti. Pavattamānānipi ārammaṇā dhimattādivasena laddhapaccayavisese ekekasmiṃ ārammaṇeeva pavattanti. [M 0.0156] Na ekakkhaṇe pañcasūti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etthaca atthavasā vibhatti pariṇāmoti katvā ekacittakkhaṇātītāni ṭhitipattāneva pañcā lambaṇāni ekacittakkhaṇātīte ṭhitippatte eva pañcadvāre bahu cittakkhaṇātītāni bahucittakkhaṇātīteti yojetabbaṃ.

For as many as the five sense objects—visible forms, sounds, etc.—that are present along with light, etc., in the eye-door and other sense pathways, all of them come into range at their respective doors without any attention, even for one who is asleep, unconscious, or distracted, or for one who has entered any jhāna, fruition, or cessation attainment. Not only at their own doors but also at the mind-door. Not only at the life-continuum mind-door but also in the four-plane cognitive processes beginning with adverting. For in the Discourse on Doors it is said: 'This mind is indeed the mind-door; it should not be said that it is not.' This meaning should be illustrated by the passage: 'For the first jhāna, sound is a thorn.' For when one has attained the first jhāna, a sound striking the ear comes into range at the mind-door, which is considered the jhāna-consciousness. Then the continuity of jhāna-consciousness is disturbed and interrupted. One emerges from the jhāna. There is a descent into the life-continuum. Then a cognitive process with that sound as its object occurs. But one who attains the second jhāna or higher does not emerge due to a slight sound. However, one does emerge due to a loud sound, for those attainments are not called 'imperturbable.' Only the formless attainments are called 'imperturbable.' Therefore, one who attains them does not emerge even due to a loud sound. However, when they have thus come into range, it should not be said that cognitive processes with those objects as their object necessarily arise. They occur when the continuity of the life-continuum or the impulsion is interrupted; they do not occur when it is uninterrupted. Even when they occur, due to differences in conditions such as the intensity of the object, they arise only for one object at a time, not for five objects in a single moment. Here, it should be understood that the grammatical case is altered according to the meaning; thus one should connect the description 'having passed one mind-moment and reached the static phase' to both the five objects and the five doors, and likewise the description 'having passed many mind-moments.'

[127] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[127] But as to the clarification:

“Te pana pasādā bhavaṅgacalanassa anantarapaccayabhūtena bhavaṅgena saddhiṃ uppannā”ti vuttaṃ.

'But those sensitivities arise together with the life-continuum that is the proximate condition for the vibration of the life-continuum,' it was said.

Evaṃ pana sati bahucittakkhaṇātītānipi pañcālambaṇāni ekacittakkhaṇātīteeva pañcadvāre āpātamāgacchantīti āpajjati. Eta rahi pana ekakkhaṇe sahuppannānaññeva vatthārammaṇānaṃ ghaṭṭanaṃ icchanti. Sahuppannānivā pana hontu nānuppannānivā, balavabhāvoyeva pamaṇanti amhākaṃ khanti. Sabbaṃ vicāretvā gahetabbaṃ.

However, if that is the case, it follows that even the five objects that have passed through many mind-moments would arrive at the five sense-doors that have passed through only one mind-moment. But here, some desire the impingement of only co-arisen bases and objects in a single moment. However, whether they arise simultaneously or not, our view is that strength is the measure. All this should be carefully investigated and understood.

[128] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[128] But as to the clarification:

“Āvajjanena saddhiṃ uppannāti apare”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

'Others say it arises together with adverting.' That is not tenable.

Evañhi sati aññadeva pañcārammaṇānaṃ āpātāgamanavatthu. Aññadeva pañcaviññāṇānaṃ nissayavatthūti evaṃ viruddhassa atthassa āpajjanatoti. Evaṃ pañcadvāre visayapavattiyā ādilakkhaṇaṃ dassetvā idāni sabbapāripūraṃ visayapavattivibhāgaṃ vīthicittapavattiñca dassento tasmātiādimāha. Tatoti tasmā cakkhussa āpātāgamanapaccayā. Cakkhussa āpātāgamanena saheva bhavaṅgassapi āpātaṃ āgacchatiyevāti vuttaṃ dvikkhattuṃbhavaṅgecaliteti. Calanañcettha yathā gahitaṃ kammādi ārammaṇaṃ muñcitvā idāni attani āpātaṃ āgacchantaṃ abhinavārammaṇaṃ gahetuṃ ussāhajātassa viya bhavaṅgasantānassa vikārappatti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etthaca cakkhussa āpātāgamanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇuppattiyā eva kāraṇaṃ. Na āvajjanuppattiyā. Bhavaṅgassa āpātāgamanameva pana āvajjanuppattiyāpi kāraṇaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For if this were so, it would follow that the basis for the arrival of the five objects is one thing, and the support-basis for the five consciousnesses is another, which leads to a contradiction. Having thus shown the initial characteristic of the object process at the five doors, now, to show the complete analysis of the object process and the cognitive process, he says 'Therefore,' etc. Here, 'tato' means 'from the condition of the arrival at the eye.' It is said 'the life-continuum vibrates twice' because with the arrival at the eye, it arrives at the life-continuum as well. And here, the vibration should be seen as the alteration of the life-continuum stream, like one in whom effort has arisen to release a previously grasped object, such as a kamma-object, and to grasp a new object now arriving. And here, the arrival at the eye is the cause only for the arising of eye-consciousness, not for the arising of adverting. But it should be understood that the arrival at the life-continuum is also the cause for the arising of adverting.

[129] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[129] But as to the clarification:

Manodvārepi [M 0.0157] āpātāgamanaṃ visuṃ apatvā rūpādīnaṃ cakkhādisu ghaṭṭanaṃnāma yogyadesāvaṭṭhānaṃ eva. Tamevaca bhavaṅgu pacchedassapi kāraṇaṃ hotīti katvā “pañcasu hi pasādesu yogyadesāvaṭṭhāna vasena ārammaṇe ghaṭṭite pasādaghaṭṭanānubhāvena bhavaṅgasantati vocchijjamānātiādi” vuttaṃ. Taṃ tathā na daṭṭhabbaṃ.

That the arrival at the mind-door does not occur separately, but that the impingement of form, etc., on the eye, etc., is merely their presence in a suitable location, and that this itself is the cause for the interruption of the life-continuum—because of which it was said, 'For when an object has impinged on the five sensitivities by way of being present in a suitable location, the life-continuum stream is interrupted by the power of the impingement on the sensitivity, etc.'—this should not be understood in that way.

Na hi yogyadesāvaṭṭhānameva ghaṭṭananti sakkā vattuṃ. Yogyadesepana ṭhatvā nimittaghaṭṭanavasena vatthughaṭṭanavasenaca asani nipātoviya pasādesu yujjhanaṃ manthanaṃ khobhakaraṇaṃ ghaṭṭananti ca āpātāgamananti ca vuccatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayañca attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva. Etthaca ayaṃpi eko dhammaniyāmoyevāti katvā nānā ṭhāniyesu dvīsu dvīsu dvāresu saheva āpātāgamanaṃ paccetabbaṃ. Rūpādinā pasāde ghaṭṭite taṃ nissitasseva pañcaviññāṇassa calanaṃ siyā. Kathaṃ pana hadayavatthunissitassa bhavaṅgassāti na codetabbanti.

For it cannot be said that impingement is merely presence in a suitable location. Rather, it should be understood that while it is present in a suitable location, the clashing, churning, and agitating at the sensitivities—like the falling of a thunderbolt—by way of impingement on the sign and impingement on the physical base, is called 'impingement' and 'arrival.' This meaning has already been stated previously. And here, accepting this as just a fixed order of phenomena, the simultaneous arrival at two doors at a time in various locations should be acknowledged. When a sensitivity is struck by a form, etc., there might be a vibration of the fivefold consciousness dependent on it. Therefore, one should not object, 'But how is the life-continuum, which is dependent on the heart-base, affected?'

[130] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[130] But as to the clarification:

Tameva codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā taṃ pariharanto “santati vasena ekābaddhattā”tiādimāha. Tattha santativasenāti navattabbaṃ. Saṇṭhānavasenāti pana vattabbaṃ. Sabbañcetaṃ sārato na paccetabbaṃ.

Having raised that very objection and refuting it, he says, 'Because of being bound as one by way of continuity,' and so on. Here, 'by way of continuity' should not be said. Rather, 'by way of configuration' should be said. And all this should not be accepted in its essence.

Kasmā, tādisassa anukkamacalanassa aṭṭhakathāyameva daḷhaṃ paṭikkhittattā. Vuttañhi tattha ekekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ dvīsu dvīsu dvāresu āpātamāgacchatīti. Rūpārammaṇañhi cakkhupasādaṃ ghaṭṭetvā taṅkhaṇeyeva manodvāre āpātaṃ āgacchati. Bhavaṅgacalanassa paccayo hotīti attho. Sadda gandha rasa phoṭṭhabbesupi eseva nayo. Yathā hi sakuṇo ākāsenāgantvā rukkhagge nilīyamānova rukkhasākhañca ghaṭṭeti. Chāyācassa pathaviyaṃ paṭihaññati. Sākhāghaṭṭana chāyāpharaṇāni apubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva bhavanti. [M 0.0158] Evaṃ paccuppannarūpādīnaṃ cakkhupasādādighaṭṭanañca bhavaṅgacālana samatthatāyamanodvāreāpātāgamanañcaapubbaṃ acarimaṃ ekakkhaṇeyeva hotīti. Evaṃ sakuṇopamāya sahataṅkhaṇeyevāti ca apubbaṃacarimaṃ ekakkhaṇe yevātica vatvā daḷhaṃ paṭibhiddhattā taṃ anukkamacalanaṃ acintetvā dhammaniyāmavasena ekappahāracalanameva paccetabbanti. Bhavaṅgasotaṃvocchinditvāti bhavaṅgapavāhaṃ sabbaso avacchinnaṃ katvā. Āvajjantanti adisvāva kiṃnāmetanti āvajja mānaṃ. Passantanti atta paccakkhaṃ kurumānaṃ. Sampaṭicchantanti muñcituṃ adatvā yathādiṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ paṭi gaṇhantaṃ. Santīrayamānanti suṭṭhu tīrentaṃvicārentaṃ. Vavatthapentanti suṭṭhu asaṅkarato thapentaṃ sallakkhentanti attho. Yonisomanasikārādivasena laddhopaccayo yenāti laddhapaccayaṃ. Yaṃkiñci javanaṃ javatīti sambandho. Taṃ pana javanaṃ ārammaṇassa dubbalakālevā mucchā maraṇāsannakālesuvā chakkhattuṃ vā pañcakkhattumevavā javatīti vuttaṃ yebhuyyenāti. Javatīti asaninipātasadisena javena pavattati. Tattha pathamajavanaṃ aladdhā sevanattā sabbadubbalaṃ hoti. Tato dutīyaṃ balavaṃ. Tato tatīyaṃ. Tato catutthaṃ. Idaṃ pana sabbabalavaṃ muddhapattaṃ hoti. Ito paṭṭhāya anukkamena parihāyamānaṃ pavattati. Sattamavāre gate parikkhīṇajavaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Javanā nubandhāniti yathā paṭisotaṃ gacchantiṃ nāvaṃ udakaṃ thokaṃ anubandhati anugacchati. Evaṃ javanaṃ anubandhāni. Dve tadārammaṇapākānīti dvikkhattuṃ tadārammaṇakiccāni vipākacittāni pavattanti. Yathārahanti ārammaṇajavana sattānurūpaṃ. Bhavaṅgapātoti imasmiṃ atihantārammaṇe āvajjanato pathamabhavaṅgacalanatoyevavā paṭṭhāya uṭṭhitaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ cittasantānaṃ yāvacatutthajavanā samuṭṭhahitvā pañcamajavanato paṭṭhāya patitameva hoti. Evaṃ santepi samuṭṭhitavegassa sabbaso aparikkhīṇatāya patitanti navuccati. Dutīyatadārammaṇato paraṃ pana samuṭṭhitavegassa sabbaso parikkhīṇattā tadā eva taṃcittasantānaṃ patitaṃnāma hoti. Tasmā patanaṃ pāto. Bhavaṅgabhāvenacittasantānassa pāto bhavaṅgapāto, bhavaṅgaṃ hutvā pātoti [M 0.0159] attho daṭṭhabbo. Bhavaṅgakicce bhavaṅgaṭṭhāne bhavaṅgārammaṇeca pāto bhavaṅgapātotivā. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne dovārikopamā, gāmillopamā, ambopamāca vattabbā. Tāsabbāpi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ gahetabbā. Ettāvatā sattarassa cittakkhaṇāni paripūrepāti sambandho. Etthaca chachakkayojanā vattabbā. Yattha hi rūntī rammaṇaṃ ghaṭṭeti. Taṃ cakkhuvatthuṃ nissāya tattha ghaṭṭitaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ ārabbha cakkhuviññāṇaṃ uppajjati. Itarāni pana āvajjanādīni mano viññāṇāni attano attano atītānantaracittena sahuppannaṃ hadayavatthuṃ nissāya tamevārammaṇaṃ ārabbha uppajjanti. Cakkhudvāra manodvārāni sabbesaṃpi vīthicittānaṃ dvārakiccaṃ sādhenti. Ayañca vīthi cakkhudvāre uppannattā cakkhudvāravīthīti. Cakkhuviññāṇena upalakkhitattā cakkhuviññāṇavīthītica vuccati. Ekacittakkhaṇaṃ atikkamma ghaṭṭanasamatthe atibalavā rammaṇe uppannattā atimahantārammaṇa vīthītica vuccatīti. Etthaca yattakāni rūpārammaṇāni cakkhupathe uppajjitvā ṭhitippattāni honti. Tāni tattakāni ṭhitippattesu pubbāparabhūtesu ekūna paññāsaparimāṇesu cakkhupasādesu kismiṃci naghaṭṭentīti navattabbāni. Tesu pana yadeva ekaṃ cakkhu imissā vīthiyā yathārahaṃ vatthubhāvaṃ dvārabhāvañca sādheti. Yatthaca ghaṭṭitaṃ rūpaṃ ārabbha ayaṃ vīthi pavattati. Etadeva kicca sādhanaṃ nāma hoti. Yaṃ majjhimāyukanti vadanti, itarāni pana mogha vatthūnināma honti, yānimandāyukānītiamandāyukānītica vadanti. Tānipana yathāvutta kicca sādhanato purimāni pacchimānīti duvidhāni honti, tadubhayānipi cakkhuviññāṇassa uppādakkhaṇe ṭhitibhāvena labbhamānāni aṭṭhacattālīsamattāni veditabbānīti. Avasesāni pana tato purimatarāni pacchimakarānica laddhaghaṭṭanānipi vatthudvārakiccasiddhibhāve anāsaṅkitabbattā idha nagahitānīti. Ettha siyā imāya vīthiyā uppattisamaye so puggalo ahaṃ idaṃ nāma passāmīti jānāti, na jānātīti. Najānāti. Kadā pana jānātīti. Sallakkhaṇavīthiyā pavattamānāya. Tathā hi [M 0.0160] sabbapathamaṃ cakkhudvāravīthi pavattati. Tato tadanuvattikā manodvāravīthi. Tato samudāyagāhikā. Tato vaṇṇasallakkhaṇā. Tato vatthugāhitā. Tato vatthusallakkhaṇā tato nāmagāhikā. Tato nāmasallakkhaṇāti. Tattha vaṇṇasallakkhaṇāya pavattamānāya ahaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ passāmītiādinā vaṇṇaṃ sallakkheti. Vatthusallakkhaṇāya saṇṭhānaṃ sallakkheti. Nāma sallakkhaṇāya nāmaṃ sallakkhetīti. Iti taṃtaṃ sallakkhaṇavīthi yā pavattamānāyaeva taṃtaṃpassāmīti jānātīti. Etthaca alātacakkassa gāhikāviya purimāhi dvīhi vīthīhi punappunaṃ gahitānaṃ rūpānaṃ samudāyato gāhikā tatīyā manodvāravīthi samudāya gāhikānāma, na hi samudāyagahaṇena vinā paribyattavaṇṇagahaṇaṃ sambhavatīti. Yāva tadārammaṇuppādā pana appahontātītakanti dvikkhattuṃ yāva tadārammaṇuppādā pavattituṃ appahontaṃ hutvā atītadvatticittakkhaṇikaṃ. Yassa hi dvevā tīṇivā cittakkhaṇāni atītāni honti. Taṃ yāva tadārammaṇuppādā pavattituṃ nappahoti na sakkoti. Evaṃ appahontaṃ hutvā atītakanti attho. Apātamāgatanti cakkhudvāre manodvāreca āpātaṃ āgataṃ. Natthi tadārammaṇuppādoti ettha yassa tīṇi cittakkhaṇāni atītāni honti. Tassa cuddasa cittakkhaṇāyukāvase sassa ārammaṇassa sattamajavanena saheva niruddhattā tasmiṃ natthi tadārammaṇuppādoti yuttametaṃ. Na hi ekāvajjanavīthiyaṃ cittāni dhammavasena viya kālavasenāpi nānārammaṇāni icchanti aṭṭhakathācariyāti. Yassa pana dve cittakkhaṇāni atītāni. Tasmiṃ sattamajavanato paraṃ ekacittakkhaṇāyukāvasese ārammaṇe ekena tadārammaṇena uppajjitabbanti ce.Na. Na hi tādisaṃ nirodhā sannaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ekavāraṃpi tadārammaṇuppattiyā paccayo bhavituṃ sakkotīti. Tathā hi mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vipākuddhāre cittappavattigaṇanāyaṃ tadārammaṇāni dveti dveeva tadārammaṇa vārā āgatāti.

Why is such a sequential movement firmly rejected in the commentary itself? For it is stated there that each object comes into range at two doors, in pairs. For a visual object, having struck the eye-sensitivity, comes into range at the mind-door in that very moment. This means it becomes a condition for the stirring of the life-continuum. The same method applies to sound, smell, taste, and touch. Just as a bird, having come through the air and alighting on a treetop, strikes a tree branch, and its shadow is cast on the ground—the striking of the branch and the spreading of the shadow occur simultaneously, without prior or subsequent occurrence—so too, the striking of present visual objects, etc., on the eye-sensitivity, etc., and their coming into range at the mind-door with the capability of stirring the life-continuum, occur simultaneously, without prior or subsequent occurrence. Thus, by the simile of the bird and by saying “in that very moment” and “simultaneously, without prior or subsequent occurrence,” it is firmly refuted that one should consider such sequential movement, but rather one should accept only a single-impact movement in accordance with the natural law of phenomena. “Having cut off the stream of the life-continuum” means having completely interrupted the flow of the life-continuum. “Adverting” means adverting, thinking, “What is this?” without having seen it. “Seeing” means making it directly perceptible to oneself. “Receiving” means receiving the seen form without letting it go. “Investigating” means thoroughly investigating and examining. “Determining” means clearly establishing without confusion, discerning—this is the meaning. “Having obtained a condition through wise attention, etc.” means that condition which has been obtained, with which whatever impulsion arises is connected. That impulsion, however, when the object is weak, or in cases of fainting or near death, arises six times or only five times—this is generally said. “It impels” means it proceeds with the speed of a lightning strike. Here, the first impulsion is weakest because it has not yet gained strength through repetition. Then the second is stronger. Then the third. Then the fourth. This, however, is the strongest, reaching its peak. From then on, it proceeds, gradually declining. It should be understood that by the seventh occurrence, the impulsion is exhausted. “Followed by impulsions” means that, just as water slightly follows a boat moving upstream, so too they follow the impulsions. “Two resultant registering consciousnesses” means that resultant consciousnesses performing the function of registering occur twice. “As is appropriate” means in accordance with the object, the impulsion, and the being. “The falling into the life-continuum” means that, in the case of this very intense object, the stream of consciousness that has arisen and emerged, starting from the adverting or from the first stirring of the life-continuum, having emerged up to the fourth impulsion, is indeed fallen from the fifth impulsion onwards. Even though this is so, because the force of the arisen stream is not entirely exhausted, it is not called “fallen.” Only after the second registering consciousness, however, because the force of the arisen stream is entirely exhausted, is that stream of consciousness truly called “fallen.” Therefore, “falling” is the fall. The fall of the stream of consciousness into the state of the life-continuum is the “falling into the life-continuum”; the meaning should be understood as “having become the life-continuum, it falls.” Alternatively, the falling into the life-continuum is so called because it is a fall in the function of the life-continuum, in the place of the life-continuum, and in the object of the life-continuum. In this context, the simile of the gatekeeper, the simile of the villager, and the simile of the mango should be stated. All of them are to be taken from the commentary. Up to this point, the seventeen moments of consciousness are completed—this is the connection. And here, the sixfold application should be stated. Wherever a visual object strikes, depending on that eye-base, eye-consciousness arises with that visual object, which has struck there, as its object. The other processes, however, such as adverting, are mind-consciousnesses, each arising depending on the heart-base that has co-arisen with its own immediately preceding consciousness, and taking that very same object. The eye-door and the mind-door perform the door-function for all process-consciousnesses. And this process, because it has arisen at the eye-door, is called the “eye-door process.” Because it is characterized by eye-consciousness, it is also called the “eye-consciousness process.” And because it has arisen with an extremely strong object capable of striking beyond a single moment of consciousness, it is called the “process of a very intense object.” And here, however many visual objects arise and attain persistence in the eye-path, it should not be said that they do not strike any of the forty-nine eye-sensitivities that have attained persistence and are prior or posterior. Among them, however, only that one eye which appropriately fulfills the roles of base and door for this process, and where the struck visual object gives rise to this process, is called the one that accomplishes the function. Those that are called “of middling lifespan” are the ones that accomplish the function, while the others are called “useless bases”—those that are called “of short lifespan” and “of long lifespan.” These, however, are of two kinds: prior and posterior to the accomplishment of the function as stated. Both of these, amounting to forty-eight, are to be understood as being obtained in a state of persistence at the moment of the arising of eye-consciousness. The remaining ones, however, those that are even earlier or even later, even if they have been struck, are not taken here because they are not relevant to the accomplishment of the base and door functions.
