Here, it might be asked whether, at the time of the arising of this process, that person knows, “I am seeing such-and-such,” or not. He does not know. When, then, does he know? When the discerning process is occurring. For thus, first of all, the eye-door process occurs. Then, the mind-door process that follows it. Then, the one that apprehends the aggregate. Then, the one that discerns color. Then, the one that grasps the substance. Then, the one that discerns the substance. Then, the one that grasps the name. Then, the one that discerns the name. There, when the color-discerning process is occurring, he discerns the color, thinking, “I see a blue color,” etc. When the substance-discerning process is occurring, he discerns the shape. When the name-discerning process is occurring, he discerns the name. Thus, it is only when the respective discerning processes are occurring that he knows, “I see this or that.” And here, the third mind-door process, which apprehends the aggregate, is called the “apprehender of the aggregate,” like the apprehension of a firebrand circle, because it apprehends the visual forms repeatedly grasped by the first two processes collectively. For without the apprehension of the aggregate, distinct color apprehension is not possible. “Past, being unable to reach the arising of registering” means having been unable to proceed up to the arising of registering, being of two or three past moments of consciousness. For whatever has two or three past moments of consciousness, that cannot proceed up to the arising of registering, it is not capable. Thus, having been unable, it is “past”—this is the meaning. “Having come into range” means having come into range at the eye-door and the mind-door. “There is no arising of registering”—here, for one whose three moments of consciousness have passed, it is fitting to say that there is no arising of registering in that case, because the object, which has a remaining lifespan of fourteen moments of consciousness, has ceased together with the seventh impulsion. For the commentary teachers do not wish that, in a single adverting process, the consciousnesses should have different objects even due to time, as in the case of phenomena. But for one whose two moments of consciousness have passed, if it were to be said that a single registering consciousness should arise in that case, in the object with a remaining lifespan of one moment of consciousness after the seventh impulsion—No. For such an object, being near cessation, cannot be a condition for even a single arising of registering. Thus, in the Great Commentary, in the enumeration of consciousness processes in the section on results, only two instances of registering consciousness are mentioned.

Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

That, however, which is to be explained:

“Dvikkhattumeva [M 0.0161] hi tadārammaṇuppatti pāḷiyaṃ niyamitā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha pāḷiyanti aṭṭhakathātantiṃ sandhāya vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Na hi sā nāma pāḷi atthi, yattha dvikkhattuṃ tadā rammaṇuppatti niyamitāti.

It is said, “The arising of tadārammaṇa is limited to only twice, as determined in the Pāḷi.” Here, “Pāḷi” should be understood as referring to the commentary tradition. For there is no such Pāḷi text where the arising of tadārammaṇa is determined to be only twice.

Majjhimabhāṇakāpana tadārammaṇaṃ ekaṃpi icchanti. Saṅgahakārena pana taṃ paṭisiddhanti idhapi taṃ therena paṭikkhittanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā paramatthavinicchaye sakiṃdvevā tadālambanti therena vuttanti. Majjhimabhāṇakānaṃ matena vuttanti daṭṭhabbanti. Ācariyānandatthero pana ekaṃpi icchatiyeva. Yathā hi āgantukabhavaṅgaṃ ekaṃ pavattati. Tathā tadārammaṇaṃpi ekaṃ napavattatīti nasakkā vattuṃ. Yañca cittappavattigaṇanāyaṃ tadārammaṇāni dveti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena vuttanti, na nasakkā vattunti. Yāva javanuppādāpi pavattituṃ appahontātītakanti sambandho. Yassa hi ārammaṇassa cattāri pañca cha satta aṭṭhanava vā cittakkhaṇāni atītāni honti. Taṃ yāva javanuppādā pavattituṃ nappahoti. Evaṃ appahontaṃ hutvā atītakanti attho. Javanaṃpi anuppajjitvāti javanassapi anuppajjanato. Ayañhi tvāpaccayo bhāvattheeva daṭṭhabbo. Na kattuatthe. Kasmā. Attano padhānakriyāya samānakattukatāya abhāvatoti.

The Majjhima reciters, however, accept even one tadārammaṇa. But the compiler has rejected this, and here too it should be seen that the Elder has refuted it. If so, why is it said by the Elder in the Paramatthavinicchaya that tadālambana occurs once or twice? It should be understood that this was said according to the opinion of the Majjhima reciters. The teacher, the Elder Ānanda, however, accepts even one. For just as the guest life-continuum arises once, so too it cannot be said that tadārammaṇa does not arise once. And as for what is said in the enumeration of the processes of consciousness that tadārammaṇa occurs twice—that too is said with reference to the maximum limit; it is not impossible to say so. The connection is this: that which is unable to persist up to the arising of javana is past. For an object of which four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine mind-moments have elapsed cannot persist up to the arising of javana. Thus, the meaning is that being unable to persist, it is past. 'Javanaṃpi anuppajjitvā' means 'because javana also has not arisen.' This 'tvā' suffix should be seen here only in the sense of an abstract state, not in the sense of an agent. Why? Because there is no common agent with the principal action.

[131] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

In the Vibhāvanī, however:

“Hetumhicāyaṃ tvāpaccayo”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said, “This ‘tvā’ suffix is in the sense of cause.” That is not well-put.

Na hi bāhiratthabhūto hetuattho kitakapaccayānaṃ visayo hotīti. Tasmā idha bhāvattheeva tvāpaccayo. Tatoca hetuatthe paccattavacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etena yā lakkhaṇe hetumhicamānantapaccayānaṃpi pavatti katthaci vuttā. Sāpipaṭikkhittā hoti. Nahi bāhiratthabhūtā lakkhaṇahetuyo tesaṃ visayā hontīti. Etthaca yassa ārammaṇassa navacittakkhaṇāni atītāni honti. Tassa avasesa aṭṭhacittakkhaṇā yukassa dutīya voṭṭhabbanena saheva [M 0.0162] niruddhattā tasmiṃ javanaṃpi anuppajjitvāti yuttametaṃ. Kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Yassa pana cattāri.La. Aṭṭhavā cittakkhaṇāni atītāni. Tasmiṃ javanena uppannena bhavitabbanti ce.Na. Avasesachacittakkhaṇāyukaṃpi hi ārammaṇaṃ javanuppattiyā paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti. Javanañhi uppajjamānaṃ sattakkhattuṃ pavattituṃ pahonake ārammaṇe eva uppajjati. Pakatiniyāmena javanassa sattakkhattu paramatāya sambhavatoti. Ettha pana yathā visaññikāla mucchākāla maraṇakālesu vatthussa avisadatāya dubbalatā yaca javanaṃ chapañcavārepi pavattati. Tathā pakatikālepi ārammaṇassa dubbalabhāve sati chapañcavārepi pavattatiyevāti. Dvattikkhattunti dvikkhattuṃvā tikkhattuṃvā. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ voṭṭhabbane ṭhatvā ekaṃvā dvevā cittāni pavattanti. Tato āsevanaṃ labhitvā javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā puna bhavaṅgaṃ otaratīti vuttaṃ. Ettha hi tato āsevanaṃ labhitvā javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvāti etena tatīyassa voṭṭhabbanassa pavattiṃ dasseti. Itarathā ekaṃvā dvevā cittāni pavattanti. Tato bhavaṅgaṃ otaratīti vuttaṃ siyāti. Ekaṃvāti pana vācā siliṭṭhamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā diratta tirattaṃti. Athavā, tatoti ekacittatovā dvicittatovāti attho. Tattha pathamena dvikkhattuṃ dutīyena tikkhattuṃ voṭṭhabbanassa uppatti vuttā hotīti. Āsevanaṃ labhitvāti idaṃ pana upacāravacanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi voṭṭhabbanassa āsevanatā paṭṭhāne vuttāti. Ācariyānandattherena panettha voṭṭhabbanato paraṃ catupañca cittakkhaṇāvasese ārammaṇe catupañcajavanuppattiyā eva parittārammaṇavāro icchito. Na voṭṭhabbana pariyosānavasena. Paṭṭhānehi bhavaṅgaṃ āvajjanāya anantarapaccayena paccayo tvevavutto. Na pana vutto āvajjanā bhavaṅgassa anantarapaccayena paccayoti. Yathā ca mucchāmaraṇakālesu vatthudubbalatāya cha pañcajavanavārā icchitabbā. Tathā idhapi ārammaṇadubbalatāyāti na na sakkā vattunti. Ettha ca santīraṇato paraṃ ekacittakkhaṇā vasese ārammaṇe ekaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ dvicittakkhaṇāvasese dve taduttari [M 0.0163] tīṇīti yuttaṃ siyā. Etarahi pana dvivoṭṭhabbanikā chaparittārammaṇavīthiyoti voṭṭhabbanikā pañcāti yojesuṃ. Evaṃ sante kīdise parittārammaṇe dvivoṭṭhabbanikā, kīdise tivoṭṭhabbanikāti vicāretabbā siyunti. Yaṃ pana ārammaṇaṃ dvattikkhattuṃvoṭṭhabbanuppattiyā appahonakaṃ hoti. Taṃ āvajjanappattiyāpi paccayo na hotīti vuttaṃ tattha bhavaṅgacalanameva hoti. Natthi vīthicittuppādoti. Tattha bhavaṅgacalanamevāti dvikkhattuṃ bhavaṅgassa calanamattameva hoti. Iccevaṃ cakkhudvāreti iti evaṃ yadi ekacittakkhaṇātītakaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ cakkhussa apātamāgacchatītiādinā vuttanayena cakkhudvāre catunnaṃ vārānaṃ vasena catudhā visayappavatti veditabbā, tathā sotadvārādīsu cātiyojanā. Sabbathāpi catudhā veditabbāti sambandho. Atiparittārammaṇaṃpi āpātāgatamattena moghavārassa ārammaṇaṃnāma hoti. Na ārammaṇakaraṇavasena. Itarāni pana ubhayathāpi itaresaṃ vārānaṃ ārammaṇānināma hontīti vuttaṃ catunnaṃ vārānaṃ yathākkamaṃ ārammaṇabhūtāti.

For an external meaning of 'cause' is not the domain of primary derivative suffixes. Therefore, here the 'tvā' suffix is only in the sense of an abstract state, and from that, it should be understood as a specific term used in the sense of cause. By this, any occurrence of the present participle suffixes (like '-māna' and '-anta') in the sense of 'characteristic' and 'cause' that is mentioned anywhere is also rejected. For characteristics and causes that are external things are not their domain. And here, regarding an object of which nine mind-moments have passed, it is fitting that javana also does not arise in it, because that which has a remaining lifespan of eight mind-moments has ceased together with the second determining consciousness. The reason has already been stated. But if it is said that in an object of which four... or eight mind-moments have passed, javana must have arisen, this is not so. For even an object with a remaining lifespan of six mind-moments cannot be a condition for the arising of javana. For javana, when arising, arises only in an object capable of lasting for seven moments, since by natural rule, the maximum occurrence for javana is seven times. Here, however, just as at the time of unconsciousness, fainting, or death, javana occurs only five or six times due to the indistinctness and weakness of the physical base, so too in normal circumstances, if the object is weak, it occurs only five or six times. 'Dvattikkhattuṃ' means 'twice or thrice.' For in the commentary it is said: “Having stood in the determining moment, one or two consciousnesses arise. Then, having obtained repetition, having stood in the place of javana, it again descends into the life-continuum.” Here, by the phrase 'having obtained repetition, having stood in the place of javana,' the occurrence of a third determining moment is shown. Otherwise, it would have been said: “one or two consciousnesses arise, then it descends into the life-continuum.” The phrase 'ekaṃ vā' should be seen as merely for euphonic effect, as in 'diratta-tirattaṃ' (two or three nights). Alternatively, 'tato' means 'from that one consciousness or from those two consciousnesses.' In that case, by the first the arising of determining twice is stated, and by the second, thrice. 'Having obtained repetition' should be seen as merely a figurative expression, for the repetition of determining is not mentioned in the Paṭṭhāna. Here, the teacher, the Elder Ānanda, has accepted the limited-object process only through the arising of four or five javanas in an object with four or five mind-moments remaining after the determining moment, not by way of the process ending with the determining moment. For in the Paṭṭhāna it is indeed said that the life-continuum is a condition for adverting by way of the proximity condition, but it is not said that adverting is a condition for the life-continuum by way of the proximity condition. And just as at the times of fainting and death, six or five javana processes are to be accepted due to the weakness of the physical base, so too here, due to the weakness of the object, it cannot be said that this is not possible. And here, it would be fitting that after the investigating consciousness, in an object with one mind-moment remaining, one determining moment arises; with two mind-moments remaining, two; and with more than that, three. But now, some have construed it thus: “The six limited-object processes are those with two determining moments,” and “The five are those with determining moments.” If so, it should be investigated in what kind of limited object there are two determining moments, and in what kind there are three. It is said that an object which is insufficient for the arising of determining twice or thrice is not a condition even for the attainment of adverting. In that case, there is only a vibration of the life-continuum; there is no arising of process-consciousness. There, 'bhavaṅgacalanameva' means there is merely a vibration of the life-continuum twice. Thus, in the eye-door, in accordance with the method stated in the passage beginning, “If a visual object of which one mind-moment has passed comes into the range of the eye...,” the occurrence of the object should be understood as fourfold, by way of the four processes; and the application is similar in the ear-door and so on. The connection is that it should be understood as fourfold in all cases. An extremely limited object, merely by having come into range, is called the object of the frustrative process, not by way of functioning as an object. The others, however, are objects of the other processes in both ways. It is said that they are the objects of the four processes in sequence.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

In the Vibhāvanī, however:

Ārammaṇabhūtāti imassa atiparittārammaṇaṃ sandhāya paccayabhūtāti attho vutto. Tañhi moghavāra paññā panāya paccayo hotīti.

It is said that the meaning of 'ārammaṇabhūtā' is 'being a condition' with reference to an extremely limited object. For that object is indeed a condition for the manifestation of the frustrative process.

Pañcadvārevīthicittāni yathārahaṃ kiccavasena satteva. Cittuppādā cittānaṃ uppattikhaṇavasena catuddasa. Vitthārā cittasarūpavitthārato catupaññāsāti yojanā. Etthāti parittajavanavāre.

In the five sense-doors, the process-consciousnesses, according to their respective functions, are only seven. The arisings of consciousness, in terms of the arising-moment of consciousnesses, are fourteen. In detail, according to the expansion of the nature of consciousness, they are fifty-four—this is the application. Here, this refers to the limited javana process.

137. Manodvāre pana ārammaṇadhammā parittakhaṇāpi atītānāgatāpi kālavimuttāpi āpātaṃ āgacchantiyeva. Tasmā tattha ekacittakkhaṇātītānivā bahucittakkhaṇātītānivā ṭhitippattāneva āpātamāgacchantīti idaṃ vidhānaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ manodvārepana yadivibhūtamālambaṇaṃ āpātamāgacchatīti. Tattha manodvāreti suddhamanodvāre. Cakkhādīsu hi ghaṭṭanena saheva yattha apātamāgacchati. [M 0.0164] Taṃ missakadvāranti vuccati. Idha pana suddhamevā dhippetanti. Taṃpi pañcadvārānubandhakaṃ visuṃ siddhanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha yathā ghaṇḍe daṇḍakena ekavāraṃ pahaṭe ghaṇḍasarīrabhūtā rūpa kalāpā ciraṃpi kālaṃ aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭetvā anuravasaddasantānaṃ pavattenti. Tathā pañcadvāre ārammaṇena ekavāraṃ ghaṭṭite pañca dvārikavīthiyā niruddhāyapi atītaṃ pañcālambaṇaṃ manodvāre yathā pātāgatameva hutvā anekasahassānipi manodvārikavīthicitta santānāni pavattetiyeva. Tesaṃ pana dvārabhūtaṃ bhavaṅgasantānaṃ anubandhakaṃnāma hoti. Tānica cittāni anubandhakavīthicittānināma honti. Yattha pana pañcadvāraghaṭṭanā nubandhabhāvena vinā kevalaṃ tathā tathā chaḷārammaṇadhammā āpātaṃ āgacchanti. Taṃ visuṃ siddhaṃ nāma hoti. Kathaṃ pana tasmiṃ visuṃ siddhe manodvāre ārammaṇa dhammā āpātaṃ āgacchantīti. Vuccate. Diṭṭhato diṭṭhasambandhato sutato sutasambandhato saddhāya ruciyā ākāraparivitakkena diṭṭhinijjhānakhantiyā nānākammabalena nānāiddhibalena dhātukkhota vasena devatopasaṃhāravasena anubodhavasena paṭivedhavasenāti evamādīhi kāraṇehi āpātaṃ āgacchantīti. Tattha diṭṭhaṃnāma pubbe pañcahidvārehi gahitaṃ pañcālambaṇaṃ. Taṃpi kālantare kāraṇalābhe sati suddhe manodvāre āpātaṃ āgacchatiyeva. Diṭṭhasambandhaṃnāma diṭṭhasadisaṃ vuccati. Pubbe hi kiñci disvā aññaṃ yaṃkiñci anumānentassa adiṭṭhaṃpi taṃsadisaṃ atītaṃpi anāgataṃpi paccuppannaṃpi bahuāpātaṃ āgacchatiyeva. Sutaṃnāma parato sutvā gahitaṃ chaḷārammaṇaṃ. Taṃ pana mahāvisayaṃ hoti. Sabbaññudesanaṃ sutvā gahitaṃ na kiñci anārammaṇaṃnāma atthīti. Sutasambandhaṃnāma sutasadisaṃ. Saddhānāma parassa saddahanā. Rucināma attano mati. Ākāra parivitakko nāma atthacchāyaṃ byañjanacchāyaṃ kāraṇacchāyañca nissāya tathā tathā parivitakkanaṃ. Diṭṭhinijjānakhantināma paññāyavā attano laddhiyāvā punappunaṃ upaparikkhitvā evamevāti sanniṭṭhānaṃ pāpetvā gahaṇaṃ. Sesaṃ pākaṭameva. Etthaca anantarūpanissaya paccayabhāvonāma cittasantānassa mahāvipphāro hoti. Sakiṃpi ārammaṇaṃ [M 0.0165] suṭṭhu āsevitvā niruddhakālato paṭṭhāya vassasatepi vassasahassepi bhavantarepi taṃārammaṇaṃ paṭicca bhavaṅga calanassa paccayo hoti. Cittañcanāma diṭṭhādīhi yathāvuttakāraṇehi saṃvaddhitaṃ mahāvipphāraṃ hoti. Kiñci nimittaṃ labhitvā ekasmiṃ khaṇe anekasahassesupi diṭṭhādīsu ārammaṇesu pharamānaṃ pavattati. Tehica kāraṇehi niccaṃ codīyamānaṃ cittasantānaṃ kāyagelaññādike cittadubbalapaccaye asati niccakālaṃpi bhavaṅgato vuṭṭhātuṃ ajjhāsayayuttaṃ hoti. Na hi cittaṃnāma avibhūte ārammaṇe ramati. Vibhūteeva ramati. Tasmā bhavaṅgasampayutto manasikāro punappunaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ cāletvā laddhapaccayesu ārammaṇesu punappunaṃ āvajjanaṃ niyojetiyeva. Tadā tāni ārammaṇāni tadabhininnākāra pavattamanasikāra sampayuttassa bhavaṅga cittassa āpātaṃ āgacchanti. Na hi aññaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā pavattamānassa cittassa ārammaṇantare abhininnākāronāma natthīti sakkā vattunti. Tadārammaṇapākāni pavattantīti idaṃ kāmasattavasena vuttaṃ. Rūpārūpasattānaṃ pana vibhūtārammaṇepi tadārammaṇuppādo natthiyeva. Yathā cettha. Evaṃ pañcadvārepi rūpasattānaṃ atimahantārammaṇesu tadārammaṇuppādo natthīti. Avibhūte panā lambaṇe javanāvasāne bhavaṅgapātova hotīti idañca ukkaṭṭha paricchedavasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ñāṇavibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana dvattikkhattuṃ voṭṭhabbanappavattivasena avibhute ālambaṇe voṭṭhabbanavāropi āgato. Yoca pañcadvārebhavaṅgacalanamattavasena moghavāro nāma catuttho vāro vutto. Sopi idha laddhuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Suddhamanodvārepi hi ārammaṇe āpātamāgate vīthicittaṃ anuppajjitvā dvikkhattuṃ bhavaṅge calite nivattanakavārānaṃ pamāṇaṃ nabhavissatiyeva, visayeca āpātāgate bhavaṅgeca calite sati visayappavattināma na na hotīti. Iti imasmiṃ manodvārepi tadārammaṇa javana voṭṭhabbana moghavāra saṅkhātānaṃ catunnaṃ vārānaṃ yathākkamaṃ āraṇabhūtā visayappavatti catudhā veditabbāti. Tattha tadārammaṇavārassa ārammaṇabhūtā abhivibhūtānāma javana vārassa [M 0.0166] vibhūtānāma. Voṭṭhabbanavārassa avibhūtānāma. Moghavārassa ārammaṇabhūtā atiavibhūtānāmāti yojetabbā.

137. At the mind door, however, even momentary objects, whether past, future, or timeless, come into range. Therefore, it is said that there is no such rule that only objects that have passed one or many mind-moments, or have reached the static phase, come into range there; rather, at the mind door, if the object is clear, it comes into range. Here, 'mind door' refers to the pure mind door. For in the case of the eye and other sense doors, where objects come into range only with contact, that is called a mixed door. But here, only the pure mind door is intended. That too is of two kinds: that connected to the five doors, and that independently arisen. For example, when a gong is struck once by a stick, the material aggregates constituting the gong, by repeatedly striking one another for a long time, produce a continuous stream of reverberating sound. Similarly, when an object strikes the five sense doors once, even after the five-door cognitive process has ceased, the past fivefold object can still appear as if in range at the mind door, giving rise to thousands of mind-door cognitive processes. The life-continuum that serves as the door for these is called 'connected'. And those thoughts are called 'connected cognitive process thoughts'. But when the six types of objects appear at the mind door merely without being connected to a five-door impact, that is called 'independently arisen'. How, then, do objects come into range at this independently arisen mind door? It is explained thus: Through what has been seen, through association with what has been seen, through what has been heard, through association with what has been heard, through faith, through preference, through reflection on aspects, through patient acceptance of views after scrutiny, through the power of various kamma, through various psychic powers, through elemental disturbance, through divine presentation, through subsequent understanding, or through penetration—by such causes, objects come into range. Here, 'what has been seen' refers to the fivefold object previously grasped by the five sense doors. Even after a long time, when a cause is obtained, it can reappear at the pure mind door. 'Association with what has been seen' is said to be something similar to what was seen. For instance, after seeing something previously, when one infers something else, even if unseen, but similar to that, whether past, future, or present, it can come into range abundantly. 'What has been heard' refers to the sixfold object received from others. This, however, has a vast range. For having heard and grasped the teaching of the Omniscient One, there is nothing that is not an object. 'Association with what has been heard' is something similar to what was heard. 'Faith' is trusting another. 'Preference' is one's own inclination. 'Reflection on aspects' is reflecting in various ways based on the hint of meaning, the hint of expression, and the hint of cause. 'Patient acceptance of views after scrutiny' is grasping (a view) after repeatedly examining it with wisdom or one's own doctrine and bringing it to the conclusion 'it is indeed so'. The rest are self-evident. Here, the nature of the immediate proximate condition is of great expansion for the mental continuum. Even if an object is well attended to just once, from the time it ceases, it can be a condition for the stirring of the life-continuum hundreds or thousands of years later, or even in another existence. The mind, when strengthened by the aforementioned causes, becomes highly expansive. Seizing upon a single sign, it spreads and occurs among thousands of objects, such as those seen, in a single moment. Constantly stimulated by these causes, the mental continuum, when there is no condition for mental weakness such as bodily illness, is always disposed to emerge from the life-continuum. For the mind does not delight in unclear objects; it delights only in clear ones. Therefore, the attention associated with the life-continuum repeatedly stirs the life-continuum and directs repeated attention toward objects for which conditions have been obtained. Then, those objects come into range of the life-continuum consciousness associated with attention that is inclined towards them. For it cannot be said that there is no inclination towards another object for a mind that is occurring having taken another object. The occurrence of resultant registering consciousnesses is stated here with reference to sense-sphere beings. For form and formless realm beings, however, even with a clear object, the arising of registering consciousness does not occur. Just as here, so too at the five doors, for form realm beings, the arising of registering consciousness does not occur with extremely vast objects. But when the object is unclear, after the impulsion phase, there is only a falling into the life-continuum. This should be understood as stated by way of the highest classification. In the Ñāṇavibhaṅgaṭṭhakathā, however, the phase of determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana-vāra) is also mentioned as occurring two or three times even with unclear objects. And the fourth phase, called 'futile phase' (mogha-vāra), which is stated as merely the stirring of the life-continuum at the five doors, is also suitable to be taken here. For even at the pure mind door, if an object comes into range but no cognitive process arises, and the life-continuum is stirred twice, there will be no measure for the phases of turning back. And when an object has come into range and the life-continuum has been stirred, the occurrence of the object is certainly not absent. Thus, in this mind door as well, the occurrence of objects, which are the basis for the four phases, namely, registering, impulsion, determining, and futile, should be understood as fourfold respectively. Here, the objects that are the basis for the registering phase are called 'very clear'; for the impulsion phase, 'clear'; for the determining phase, 'unclear'; and for the futile phase, 'extremely unclear'—thus should it be connected.

Etthaca ārammaṇassavā cittassavā atibalavatāya abhivibhūtatā veditabbā. Dubbalepi hi citte pathavipabbatādivasena atibalavantaṃ ārammaṇaṃ ativibhūtaṃnāma hoti. Atibalavante ca citte atisukhumaṃpi nibbānaṃ ativibhūtaṃnāma hotīti. Evaṃ sesesupīti. Vārabhedo panettha anubandhako, visuṃ siddhoti duvidho. Tattha anubandhako cakkhudvārānubandhakādivasena pañcavidho. Ekekasmiñcettha atītagahaṇaṃ, samudāya gahaṇaṃ, vatthugahaṇaṃ, nāmagahaṇanti cattāro cattāro vārā. Tesuca tadārammaṇavārādayo yathārahaṃ yojetabbā. Visuṃ siddho pana diṭṭha vāro, diṭṭhasambandhavāro, sutavāro, sutasambandhavāro, viññātavāro, viññātasambandhavāroti chabbidho hoti. Etthaca saddhā ruci ākāra parivitakkādi vasena pavattavārā viññātavāro, viññāta sambandhavāroti vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ pana saddhāruciyādiva senagahitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ tathāpi hoti. Aññathāpi hoti. Tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na gahitanti vuttaṃ. Tathāvā hotu aññathāvā. Vīthicittapavattiyā sati gahetabbameva. Tattha ekekasmiṃvāre tadārammaṇavārādivasena cattāro cattāro vārā. Tesuca kāma mahaggatā nuttara paññatti vasena paccuppannātītānāgatakāla vimuttavasenaca ārammaṇadhammā yathārahaṃ yojetabbāti. Etarahi pana atītabhavaṅgavasena tadārammaṇavasena ca vārabhedaṃ kappenti. Tattha atītabhavaṅgavasena vārabhedakappanaṃ niratthakaṃ. Na hi manodvāre pañcadvāre viya ārammaṇānaṃ khaṇavasena balava dubbalatā sambhavo atthi. Tadā avijjamānānaṃpi atītānāgatānaṃ kālavimuttānañca tattha āpātāgamanatoti. Ettha siyā, ekāvajjanavīthiyā ārammaṇaṃnāma dhammatoca kālatoca abhinna meva icchanti aṭṭhakathācariyā. Imeca sattā taṃ taṃ ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā aññamaññassa cittaṃ jānantiyeva. Paracittaviduniyo pana devatā ākārasallakkhaṇena vināpi jānanti. Tattha paccuppannaṃ parassa [M 0.0167] cittaṃ jānanakāle āvajjanaṃ bhāvayaṃ parassa cittaṃ attanā sahuppannaṃ. Taṃ vā āvajjati. Udāhu parato taṃ taṃ javanena sahuppannaṃvā. Javanānica yaṃ āvajjanena sahuppannaṃ taṃ vā jānanti, paccekaṃ attanā sahuppannaṃvāti. Kiñcettha, yadi tāva āvajjanena sahuppannaṃ āvajjati jānantica. Evaṃ sati dhammato abhinnaṃ hoti. Kālato bhinnaṃ. Tañhi cittaṃ āvajjanassa paccuppannaṃ hoti. Javanānaṃ pana atītanti. Atha paccekaṃ attanā sahuppannaṃ āvajjati jānantica. Evañca sati kālato abhinnaṃ hoti. Dhammato bhinnameva. Athapi yaṃ paccekaṃ sahuppannaṃ jānanti. Tadeva āvajjati. Evaṃpi bhinnameva hotīti. Ettha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tāva yaṃ āvajjanena sahuppannaṃ. Tadeva āvajjati jānanticāti dhammato abhinnaṃ vatvā taṃ cittaṃ niruddhaṃpi addhāvasena santativasenaca gahitaṃ javanānaṃpi paccuppannameva hotīti vinicchitaṃ. Ācariyānandamatena pana parassa taṃ taṃ ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā taṃ taṃ adhippāyajānanakāle āvajjanajavanāni paccekaṃ attanā sahuppannaṃ cittaṃ āvajjati jānanti ca. Na cettha dhammato kālatoca bhinnaṃnāma hoti. Sabbesaṃpi hi ārammaṇaṃ cittameva hoti paccuppannañcāti. Naca javanāni nirāvajjanānināma honti. Āvajjanenapi hi cittanteva āvajjitaṃ hoti. Javanānica cittanteva jānantīti. Yadi pana āvajjane na cittanti āvajjite javanāni rūpanti jānanti. Rūpantivā āvajjite cittanti jānanti, nīlantivā āvajjite pītanti jānanti. Evaṃ sati javanāni dhammato nirāvajjanāni nāma honti. Tathā atītanti āvajjite paccuppannanti. Evañca sati tāni kālato nirāvajjanānināma hontīti. Yasmā ca atīto dhammo paccuppannassa dhammassa anantarapaccayena paccayoti paṭṭhāne vutto. Tasmā idha khaṇavaseneva paccuppannaṃ vattuṃ yuttaṃ. Na addhāsantati vasenāti. Itarathā sabba vīthicittavāresupi ārammaṇānaṃ atītādibhāvo addhāsantativaseneva vattabbo siyāti. Gāthāyaṃ tīṇevāti kiccavasena tīṇi eva. Cittuppādā daseritāti cittuppattikkhaṇavasena dasa īritāni kathitāni. Vitthā renāti [M 0.0168] cittasarūpavitthārena. Etthāti manodvāre. Ekacattālīsāti pañcaviññāṇamanodhātūhi vajjitānaṃ kāmāvacaracittānaṃ vasena ekacattālīsaṃ. Etthāti parittajavanavāre. [Parittavāro]

Herein, the overwhelmingness of the object or of the mind due to its extreme strength should be understood. For even when the mind is weak, an extremely strong object, such as the earth or a mountain, is indeed called very overwhelming. And when the mind is very strong, even the subtlest Nibbāna is indeed called very overwhelming. Thus also in the rest. Herein, the division of turns is twofold: connected and separately established. Among these, the connected is fivefold, in the manner of being connected to the eye-door, and so forth. And in each of these, there are four turns each: grasping the past, grasping the aggregate, grasping the base, and grasping the name. And among these, the tadārammaṇa turn and so forth should be applied appropriately. The separately established, however, is sixfold: the seen turn, the seen-related turn, the heard turn, the heard-related turn, the cognized turn, and the cognized-related turn. And here, it should be understood that the cognized turn and the cognized-related turn are said to occur in the manner of faith, liking, mode of thinking, and so forth. In the Aṭṭhasālinī, however, an object grasped in the manner of faith, liking, and so forth, may be so or may be otherwise. Therefore, it is said that it is not taken up in the commentary. Whether it is so or otherwise, when there is the occurrence of a thought-process, it must indeed be grasped. Herein, in each turn, there are four turns each, in the manner of the tadārammaṇa turn and so forth. And among these, the object-dhammas should be applied appropriately in the manner of sensual, sublime, supramundane, and concept, and in the manner of being free from present, past, and future time. Nowadays, however, they make a distinction of turns in the manner of past life-continuum and tadārammaṇa. Among these, the making of a distinction of turns in the manner of past life-continuum is meaningless. For in the mind-door, unlike in the five-doors, there is no possibility of strength or weakness of objects in terms of moments, because at that time, there is an apparent occurrence there even of non-existent objects, namely, past, future, and timeless ones. Here it may be said: The commentary teachers desire that in a single adverting thought-process, the object is indeed non-different both in nature and in time. And these beings, having discerned those various aspects, indeed know each other’s minds. But deities skilled in knowing others’ minds know even without discerning aspects. Herein, at the time of knowing another's present mind, does one advert to another's mind that has arisen simultaneously with one's own? Or to that which has arisen simultaneously with the other's various javanas? And do the javanas know that which has arisen simultaneously with the adverting, or do they know that which has arisen simultaneously with themselves individually? Moreover, here, if indeed one adverts to and knows what arises simultaneously with the adverting, then in that case it is non-different in nature but different in time. For that mind is present for the adverting, but past for the javanas. Or if one adverts to and knows what arises simultaneously with oneself individually, then in that case it is non-different in time, but indeed different in nature. Or again, if they know what arises simultaneously with themselves individually, and advert to that very thing, even so, it is indeed different. Here, in the commentary, first, having said that what arises simultaneously with the adverting is that very thing which is adverted to and known, being non-different in nature, it is concluded that even though that mind has ceased, it is taken in terms of duration and continuity, and it is indeed present even for the javanas. According to the view of Ācariya Ānanda, however, when discerning another’s various aspects and knowing their various intentions, the adverting and javanas advert to and know the mind arising simultaneously with themselves individually. And here, there is indeed no difference both in nature and in time. For of all of them, the object is indeed mind and is present. Nor indeed are the javanas without an adverted object. For by the adverting too, only mind is adverted to. And the javanas too know only mind. But if, when 'not mind' is adverted to, the javanas know it as 'form'; or when 'form' is adverted to, they know it as 'mind'; or when 'blue' is adverted to, they know it as 'yellow'; then in that case, the javanas are indeed without an adverted object in nature. Similarly, when 'past' is adverted to, they know it as 'present'. And in that case, they are indeed without an adverted object in time. And since a past dhamma is a condition for a present dhamma by way of proximity condition, as stated in the Paṭṭhāna, therefore, here it is proper to speak of the present only in terms of moments, not in terms of duration and continuity. Otherwise, even in all thought-process turns, the pastness, etc., of objects would have to be spoken of only in terms of duration and continuity. In the verse, 'three indeed' (tīṇeva) means there are indeed three by way of function. 'Ten mind-arisings are declared' (cittuppādā daseritā) means ten are declared by way of the moment of mind's arising. 'In detail' (vitthārena) means by the detailed nature of the mind. 'Here' (ettha) means in the mind-door. 'Forty-one' (ekacattālīsa) means forty-one by way of the sensual-sphere minds, excluding the five sense-consciousnesses and the mind-element. 'Here' (ettha) means in the weak javana turn. [The Weak Turn]

138. Vibhūtāvibhūtabhedo natthi ekaṃ vibhūtameva labbhatīti adhippāyo. Na hi avibhūte ārammaṇe appanānāma sambhavatīti. Tathā tadārammaṇuppādoca natthi. Na hi atisantataraṃ appanājavanaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ anubandhatīti. Tattha hi chabbīsati mahaggata lokuttara javanesu yaṃkiñci javanaṃ appanāvīthimotaratīti sambandho. Ñāṇarahitaṃ dvihetukajavanaṃ athirasabhāvattā appanāya anantarūpanissayo nahotīti vuttaṃ ñāṇasampayutta kāmāvacarajavanānamaṭṭhannanti. Parikammopacārānulomagotratunāmenāti ettha indriyasamatādīhi paritobhāgehi appanā karīyati sajjīyati etenāti parikammaṃ. Appanaṃ upecca caratīti upacāro. Samīpacāroti attho. Samīpacaraṇañcettha āsannekāle appanāvahasamatthabhāvena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yassa pavattiyā aciraṃ kālaṃ appanā sambhavo hotīti. Anulomanti appanāpavattiyā paccanīkadhammavidhamanena appanāya anukūlaṃ appanāhitaṃ appanā vahanticceva attho, yassa pavattiyā appanā vibandhako paccanī konāma natthīti. Gamīyati bujjhīyati attho etenātivo. Abhidhānaṃ buddhica. Taṃ duvidhaṃpi gavaṃ tāyati rakkhatīti gottaṃ. Paritta jātisaṅkhāto anvayo. Gottaṃ abhibhuyyati chijjati etthāti gotrabhu. Ettha ca cattāripi javanāni parikammajavanānīti vā upacārajavanānitivā anulomajavanānītivā vuccantiyeva. Gotrabhūti pana pacchimasseva nāmaṃ. Idha pana catunnaṃpi nāmānaṃ saṅgahaṇatthaṃ parikammo pacārānuloma gotrabhunāmenāti evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañca katvā kasmā pathamameva parikammaṃnāma. Nanu itarānipi appanaṃ parisaṅkharontiyevāti evamādikā codanā anokāsā hotīti. Catukkhattuṃ tikkhattumevavāti catukkhattumevavā tikkhattumevavā. Tattha pathamena eva saddena pañcamaṃ gotrabhusambhavo paṭikkhitto hoti. Tadā hi javanaṃ patitaṃnāma hoti. Pavedhati [M 0.0169] kampati. Kāmagottaṃ abhikkamitvā uparibhūmantarappattiyā paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkotīti. Dutīyena dutīyaṃ gotrabhu sambhavo paṭikkhitto hoti. Tadā hi aladdhāsevanaṃ anulomaṃ attano anantare cittaṃ gotrabhubhāvaṃ pāpetuṃ na sakkotīti. Eteneva pañcamato paraṃ catutthatoca oraṃ appanāya asambhavo sādhito hotīti. Vāsaddena pana mandapaññassa catukkhattumeva. Na tikkhattuṃ. Tikkhapaññassa tikkhattumeva. Na catukkhattunti dassitaṃ hoti. Aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ pana mandamajjhima mahāpaññavasena tidhā bhinditvā pañcakkhattuṃpi parikammajavanānaṃ uppatti anuññātā viya dissati. Itaraṭṭhakathāsu pana suṭṭhu vicāretvā paṭisiddhattā sā na gahetabbāvāti.

138. There is no distinction between a manifest and an unmanifest object; the intention is that only a manifest object is obtained. For absorption cannot arise with an unmanifest object. Likewise, the arising of retention consciousness (tadārammaṇa) does not occur. Indeed, the absorption javana, being exceedingly tranquil, is not followed by retention consciousness. Here, the connection is that any one of the twenty-six sublime and supramundane javanas descends into the absorption process. It is said that a two-rooted javana devoid of wisdom, due to its unstable nature, does not serve as an immediately proximate support for absorption; this concerns the eight sense-sphere javanas associated with wisdom. Here, by the terms 'preparation' (parikamma), 'access' (upacāra), 'adaptation' (anuloma), and 'change-of-lineage' (gotrabhū): that by which absorption is performed and prepared through contributory factors such as the balancing of faculties, is 'preparation.' It approaches and moves near absorption, thus it is 'access,' meaning 'proximate movement.' Proximate movement here should be understood as the capacity to bring about absorption in a short time, that is, its occurrence makes the arising of absorption possible without delay. 'Adaptation' (anuloma) is that which is favorable to the occurrence of absorption by dispelling opposing states; it is conducive to absorption, carrying it forth. That is to say, when it occurs, there is no opposing factor that obstructs absorption. By this, the meaning is understood or cognized. This is twofold: designation and wisdom. That which protects (tāyati) the lineage (gavaṃ) is 'lineage' (gotta). The lineage is the succession designated as the limited state of existence. That by which the lineage is overcome or cut off is 'change-of-lineage' (gotrabhu). Here, all four javanas are also called 'preparation javanas,' 'access javanas,' or 'adaptation javanas.' However, 'change-of-lineage' is the name of the last one only. But here, to include the names of all four, it is stated as 'by the name of preparation, access, adaptation, and change-of-lineage.' This being so, the objection, 'Why is only the first named preparation? Do not the others also prepare for absorption?' is rendered baseless. 'Four times or only three times' means four times or three times. Here, by the first word 'eva' (only), the possibility of a fifth [preliminary] javana is rejected. For then the javana is said to have fallen; it trembles and wavers. Having transcended the sense-sphere lineage, it cannot become a condition for reaching a higher plane. By the second 'eva', the possibility of a second [preliminary] javana is rejected. For then, adaptation, not having gained repeated practice, cannot cause the consciousness immediately following it to attain the state of change-of-lineage. By this, it is established that absorption cannot occur after the fifth javana or before the fourth javana of the process. By the word 'vā' (or), it is shown that for one of dull wisdom, it is four times only, not three; for one of sharp wisdom, it is three times only, not four. In the Aṭṭhasālinī, however, by dividing into three—dull, middling, and sharp wisdom—the arising of preparation javanas even five times seems to be permitted. But since this is thoroughly examined and rejected in other commentaries, it should not be accepted.

Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

That, however, which is to be explained.

“Chaṭṭhaṃ sattamaṃ bhavaṅgassa āsannabhāvena papātāsannapuriso viya appanāvasena patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkotī”ti vuttaṃ.

It is said: 'Just as a man near a precipice cannot stand firm, so too the sixth and seventh [javanas], due to their nearness to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), are unable to be established by way of absorption (appanā).'

Tattha bhavaṅgassa āsannabhāvenāti bhavaṅgabhāvassa āsanna bhāvenāti attho. Pañcamajavanato hi paṭṭhāya javanasantānaṃ anupubbena parikkhīṇajavaṃ hoti. Bhavaṅgabhāvatthāya pariṇamatīti. Evañca katvā papātāsannapurisopamāpi upapannā hotīti. Niruddhānantaramevāti niruddhe anantaramevāti padacchedo. Kassa anantaranti, aññassa asutattā niruddhassāti atthato laddhamevāti. Yasmā pana appanānāma uppajjamānā catutthatovā pañcamatovā paṭṭhāya uppajjati. Na chaṭṭhatovā sattamatovā. Sāhi vasībhūtāpi catuttha pañcamesu uppattiṃ alabhamānā sabbaso nuppajjatiyeva. Labhamānā pana divasaṃpi nirantaraṃ pavattatiyeva. Tasmā catutthaṃvā pañcamaṃvāti idaṃ ādimattaniyamanatthaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva hi appanāvīthimotaratīti ca tatoparaṃ appanāvasāne bhavaṅgapātova hotīti ca vakkhatīti. Yadi pana pañcamato paṭṭhāya javanaṃ patitaṃ nāma hoti. Evaṃ sati kasmā tato paṭṭhāya patanakhette appanājavanaṃ pavattatīti. Vuccate, hatthe [M 0.0170] thapitaleḍḍussa patanakhettaṃnāma hatthato muttamatte hoti. Evaṃ santepi hatthabalena khipitaṃ leḍḍu dūraṃpi gacchatiyeva. Ettha ca leḍḍussa javonāma hatthajavamūlako hoti. Hatthajavoca sarīrabalamūlako. Tattha leḍḍu viya appanājavanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Leḍḍussa patanakhettaṃ viya catutthato pacchākālo. Hatthajavoviya gotrabhujavo. Sarīrabalaṃ viya purimānaṃ parikammajavanānaṃ balaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uttānaseyyassa bāladārakassa balaṃ viya ādikammikavīthiyaṃ kāmajavanānaṃ balaṃ. Vuddhipattassa purisassabalaṃ viya samāpattivīthiyaṃ kāmajavanānaṃ balaṃ. Yathā ca bāladārakena khittaṃ leḍḍu hatthato muttamattepi patati. Evaṃ ādikammikavīthiyaṃ appanājavanaṃ ekavāraṃ javitvā patati. Yathāvuddhipattena khittaṃ leḍḍu patanakhettepi apatitvā dūraṃpi dūrataraṃpi gacchati. Tathā samāpattivīthiyaṃ appanājavanaṃ ciraṃpi cirataraṃpi pavattatīti. Mūlaṭīkāyaṃ pana appanājavanaṃ patanakhette pavattaṃpi bhūmantarapattiyāvā ārammaṇantaraladdhiyāvā patitaṃnāma nahotīti vuttaṃ. Ettha siyā, kasmā pañcamato paṭṭhāya javanaṃ patitanti vuttaṃ. Nanu apati tattā eva suṭṭhu balavabhāvato sattamajavanacetanā sīghaṃ anantare bhave vipākadāyinīca ānantariyakammañca hoti. Majjhe pañcacetanā tathā balavabhāvābhāvato cirena tatīyabhavādīsu vipākadāyinīca honti, anantariyabhāvañca na gacchantīti. Nakho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yadi hi sīghaṃ vipākadānatāya balavatīnāma siyā. Evaṃsati paṭhamacetanā sabbabalavatīnāma siyā. Sā hi imasmiṃyeva bhave vipākaṃ detīti. Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Eka vassajīvīnaṃ tiṇarukkhānaṃ pariṇāmoviya pathamacetanāya pariṇāmo daṭṭhabbo. Dvivassajīvīnaṃ viya sattamacetanāya. Mahāsālānaṃ viya majjhimacetanānanti. Tattha ekavassajīvino tiṇarukkhānāma asārā honti. Asārattāca dubbalā anaddhaniyā aciraṭṭhikā. Tasmā tesaṃ sīghatarapariṇāmo hoti. Te hi sīghataraṃ ruhanti. Vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ āpajjanti. Sīghataraṃ pupphanti phalanti patanti antaradhāyanti. Ekaṃ nidāghasamayaṃ atikkamituṃ nasakkonti. Dutīyaṃ [M 0.0171] vassaṃ na pāpuṇanti. Etthaca nidāghasamayo viya maraṇakālo veditabbo. Dvivassajīvino pana thokaṃ sārabhūtā honti. Sārabhūtattāca thokaṃ balavantā addhaniyā. Tato yevacatesaṃ cirapariṇāmo hoti. Te hi pathamaṃ vassaṃ ruhanti vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ āpajjanti. Pupphituṃvā phalituṃvā nasakkonti. Dutīyavasseeva pupphanti phalanti patanti antaradhāyanti. Dutīyaṃ pana nidāgha samayaṃ atikkamituṃ na sakkonti. Tatīyaṃ vassaṃ na pāpuṇanti. Mahāsālā pana sabbasārabhūtā honti. Balavantā cirataraṭṭhāyino. Tasmā te saṇikameva pariṇāmaṃ gacchanti. Te hi eka dve vassāni vidatthiratanamattāva honti. Vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ nāpajjanti. Pupphituṃvā phalituṃvā na sakkonti. Aticiraṭṭhāyino pana honti. Cha pañca vassasatāni ṭhatvāva patanti. Evameva pathamajavanacetanā sabbaso aladdhāsevanatāya asārā abalā hoti. Visuṃ ekaṃ bhavaṃ nibbattetuṃ ekañca maraṇakālaṃ atikkamituṃ na sakkoti. Imasmiṃ bhaveeva vipaccitvāvā avipaccitvāvā khiyyati. Sattama javanacetanā pana laddhāsevanatāya thokaṃ sārabhūtā hoti. Visuṃ ekaṃ bhavaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkoti. Sārabhūtattā yevaca saṇikameva pariṇāmaṃ gacchati. Imasmiṃ bhave vipaccituṃ na sakkoti. Bhavantaraṃ patvāva vipaccati. Patitajavanesu pana antima javanatāya dubbalattā dutīyaṃ maraṇakālaṃ atikkamituṃ na sakkoti. Dutīyabhaveeva vipaccitvāvā avipaccitvāvā khiyyati. Avasesānaṃ pana pañcannaṃ majjhimacetanānaṃ suṭṭhu laddhāsevanānaṃ saṇika tara pariṇatabhāvo vuttanayānusārena veditabboti. Naṃ kevalañcettha tiṇa rukkho pamāya pāṇopamāyāpi ayamattho dīpetabbo. Yehikeci gabbhaseyyakā pāṇā appāyukajātikā honti. Te sīghataraṃ gabbhavāsaṃ vasanti, sīghataraṃ vijāyanti. Aṅgamaṅgānica nesaṃ sīghataraṃ thāmagatāni honti. Indriyānica sīghataraṃ paripākagatāni honti. Tadaheva uṭṭhahitvā gacchanti. Gocaraṃ gaṇhanti. Attano attano visaye sīghataraṃ viññuttaṃ āpajjanti. Sīghataraṃ jiṇṇā honti maranti. [M 0.0172] Dīghāyukajātikānaṃ pana gabbhavāsādīni sabbāni saṇika meva sijjhantīti. Etthaca mahaggata kusalāni sattama javanaṭṭhāne ṭhitānīti veditabbāni. Parikammajavanāni hi ciraṭṭhitikaṭṭhena supakka sālidhaññasadisāni. Appanājavanāni aciraṭṭhitikaṭṭhena supakka sālibhattasadisānīti tānipi acirataraṭṭhitikānieva honti. Dutīye bhave vipaccitvāvā avipaccitvāvā khiyyanti. Imasmiṃ bhavepi appakena kāmacchandādinā paccanīkadhammena paṭibāhitāni sabbaso avipākabhāvaṃ āpajjanti. Tasmātāni tena pariyāyena dubbalāni nāma hontīti.

Here, the phrase "due to the proximity of the life-continuum" means "due to the nearness of the state of the life-continuum." For indeed, from the fifth impulsion onward, the stream of impulsions gradually becomes exhausted of its impetus and matures for the sake of the life-continuum state. And having done so, the simile of a man near a precipice also becomes applicable. The phrase "immediately after cessation" (niruddhānantarameva) is to be parsed as "immediately upon cessation" (niruddhe anantarameva). Immediately after what? Since nothing else is mentioned, it is understood by implication to be "after the cessation (of the preceding moment)." However, since absorption, when it arises, arises from the fourth or fifth (impulsion) onwards, not from the sixth or seventh. For indeed, even if it is well-mastered, if it does not obtain arising in the fourth or fifth (moment), it does not arise at all. But if it does obtain (arising), it continues uninterruptedly even for a whole day. Therefore, this "either the fourth or the fifth" should be understood as stated for the purpose of indicating the initial limitation. For that very reason, indeed, it will be said that it descends into the absorption cognitive process, and that thereafter, at the cessation of absorption, there is only the falling into the life-continuum. But if, however, impulsion is said to "fall" from the fifth onward, if that is the case, why does absorption impulsion occur in the "falling" sphere from then on? It is said: The "falling sphere" of a clod placed in the hand is indeed the moment it is released from the hand. Even so, a clod thrown by the force of the hand travels far indeed. And here, the impetus of the clod is indeed rooted in the impetus of the hand. And the impetus of the hand is rooted in bodily strength. In this regard, absorption impulsion should be seen as like the clod. The time after the fourth (moment) is like the falling sphere of the clod. The change-of-lineage impulsion is like the impetus of the hand. The strength of the preceding preparatory impulsions should be seen as like bodily strength. Like the strength of a child lying on its back is the strength of the sense-sphere impulsions in the initial cognitive process. Like the strength of a grown man is the strength of the sense-sphere impulsions in the absorption cognitive process. And just as a clod thrown by a child falls even the moment it is released from the hand, so too, in the initial cognitive process, absorption impulsion, having impelled once, falls. Just as a clod thrown by a grown man, without falling even in the falling sphere, travels far or even farther, so too, in the absorption cognitive process, absorption impulsion continues for a long or even longer time. However, in the Mūlaṭīkā, it is said that even if absorption impulsion occurs in the falling sphere, it is not called "fallen" until it has reached another plane or obtained another object. Here, one might ask: Why is it said that impulsion "falls" from the fifth onward? Is it not because the seventh impulsion volition, being very strong due to its non-falling nature, quickly gives results in the immediately succeeding existence and becomes immediate kamma, while the middle five volitions, due to not having such strength, give results slowly in the third existence and so forth, and do not attain the state of immediate (kamma)? Indeed, this should not be seen thus. For if (a volition) were indeed strong by reason of giving results quickly, then the first volition would indeed be the strongest. For it gives results in this very existence. Here, the conclusion is this: The maturation of the first volition should be seen as like the maturation of one-year-living grasses and trees. That of the seventh volition is like two-year-living (plants). And that of the middle volitions is like great sāla trees. In this regard, one-year-living grasses and trees are indeed insubstantial. And because they are insubstantial, they are weak, not long-lasting, and short-lived. Therefore, their maturation is very quick. For they grow very quickly, attain growth and development, flower, fruit, fall, and disappear very quickly. They cannot pass one dry season and do not reach a second year. And here, the dry season should be understood as the time of death. Two-year-living (plants), however, are somewhat substantial. And because they are somewhat substantial, they are somewhat strong and long-lasting. And for that very reason, their maturation is slow. For they grow and attain growth and development in the first year, but cannot flower or fruit. Only in the second year do they flower, fruit, fall, and disappear. But they cannot pass a second dry season and do not reach a third year. Great sāla trees, however, are fully substantial. They are strong and very long-lasting. Therefore, they mature very slowly. For they are only about a span or a cubit for one or two years. They do not attain growth or development, cannot flower or fruit, but they are very long-lasting. They stand for five or six hundred years before falling. Just so, the first impulsion volition, due to having absolutely no opportunity for development, is insubstantial and weak. It cannot produce a separate existence or pass one death-moment. It ripens in this very existence or perishes without ripening. The seventh impulsion volition, however, due to having obtained some opportunity for development, is somewhat substantial. It can produce a separate existence. And because it is substantial, it matures slowly. It cannot ripen in this existence but ripens only upon reaching another existence. But among the 'fallen' impulsions, due to its weakness as the last impulsion, it cannot pass a second death-moment. It ripens in the second existence or perishes without ripening. But the remaining five middle volitions, having very well obtained development, their state of ripening more slowly should be understood according to the method explained. And here, this meaning should be illustrated not only by the simile of grasses and trees, but also by the simile of living beings. For indeed, whatever beings are born in the womb and are short-lived: They dwell in the womb very quickly, are born very quickly. And their limbs quickly become strong. And their faculties quickly reach maturity. They rise and walk immediately. They take food. They quickly attain skill in their respective spheres. They quickly become old and die. But for long-lived beings, all stages, beginning with dwelling in the womb, are accomplished slowly. And here, the exalted wholesome states should be understood as standing in the position of the seventh impulsion. For the preparatory impulsions, by reason of being long-lasting, are like well-ripened sāli grains. The absorption impulsions, by reason of being short-lasting, are like well-cooked sāli rice, and thus they are indeed even shorter-lasting. They ripen in the second existence or perish without ripening. Even in this existence, being obstructed by a small opposing state like sensual desire, they entirely attain the state of non-ripening. Therefore, in that sense, they are indeed weak.

Yasmā ca ānantariyakammānaṃ phaladānaniyatatānāma kālaniyamena vinā na sambhavati. Kālaniyamocanāma ekantena sattamajavanasseva hoti. Na majjhimajavanānaṃ. Tesañhi asukasmiṃ bhaveeva vipaccantīti evaṃ niyamo natthīti. Tasmā duvidhassa niyamassa siddhattā eva sattamajavanacetanāya anantariyakammatā siddhā hoti. Na balavataratāyāti niṭṭhametthagantabbanti. Mūlaṭīkāyaṃ pana nanuca sattamajavanacetanāya balavatāya upapajjavedanīyabhāvo hoti ānantariyatāpīti codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā tatthāyaṃ adhippāyo siyā. Paṭisandhiyā anantarapaccayabhāvino vipākasantānassa anantarapaccayabhāvena antimajavanacetanāya susaṅkhatattāsā sattamajaganacetanā upapajjavedanīyā ānantariyakāca hoti. Na apatitajavanacetanā viya balavatāyāti uttaraṃ vadati. Taṃ yuttaṃ viya na dissati. Evañhi sati pathamajavanacetanā kassa anantarapaccayabhāvena susaṅkhatattā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyānāma jātāti vattabbā hotīti. Mahāṭīkāyaṃ pana dubbalāpi antimajavana cetanā sanniṭṭhānakiccavisesayuttatāya phalavipaccane sattivise sayuttā hotīti upapajjavedanīyā ānantariyakāca sā hotīti vuttaṃ. Yathārahanti taṃ taṃ puggalānurūpaṃ. Yathābhinīhāra vasenāti tassa tassa parikammabhāvanā cittassa kasiṇanimittā dīsuvā aniccalakkhaṇādīsuvā abhinīharaṇānurūpaṃ. Appanāvīthinti appanāpabandhaṃ. Idañca anekavāre pavattānaṃ appanājavanānaṃ saṅgahaṇatthaṃ [M 0.0173] vuttaṃ. Tenevāha tatoparaṃ appanāvasāne bhavaṅgapātova hotīti. Tattha tatoti catutthatovā pañcamato vā. Imasmiṃ atthe sati pañcamevā chaṭṭhevā ekantena bhavaṅgapāto hotīti āpajjati. Tasmā puna appanāvasāneti vuttaṃ. Bhavaṅgapātovahoti. Natthi tadārammaṇuppādoti adhippāyo.

Because the fixedness of giving results for kamma of immediate effect is not possible without a fixed time for its fruition. A fixed time for its fruition occurs exclusively with the seventh javana, not with the intermediate javanas. For with them there is no such fixed rule as, 'they will ripen in such-and-such an existence.' Therefore, due to the establishment of this twofold fixedness, the characteristic of being kamma of immediate effect is established only for the volition of the seventh javana. It is not due to greater strength—this is the conclusion to be drawn here. However, in the Mūlaṭīkā, the question is raised: 'Is it not because the volition of the seventh javana is strong that it has the nature of producing results in the immediately subsequent existence, and also the nature of kamma of immediate effect?' There, the intended meaning might be this: Because the volition of the final javana is well-prepared by being the immediately preceding condition for the stream of resultant consciousness connected with rebirth-linking, that volition of the seventh javana has the nature of producing results in the immediately subsequent existence and also the nature of kamma of immediate effect. It is not through strength, as is the case with the volition of an untimely javana—this is the answer given. This does not appear fitting. For if this were the case, then the volition of the first javana, being well-prepared by virtue of its immediately preceding condition, should be said to be of the nature of producing results experienced in the present life. But in the Mahāṭīkā, it is said that even a weak volition of the final javana, due to its association with a special decisive function and being endowed with a special power in the ripening of its fruit, has the nature of producing results in the immediately subsequent existence and also the nature of kamma of immediate effect. 'According to what is suitable' means according to what is appropriate to that particular individual. 'According to the mode of directing' means in accordance with the directing of that particular preparatory mind-moment towards the kasiṇa-sign, or impermanence, and so forth. 'The absorption process' refers to the sequence of absorption. This is stated to include the multiple occurrences of absorption javanas. Hence, it is said: 'After that, at the cessation of absorption, there is only the falling into the life-continuum.' Therein, 'that' refers to either the fourth or fifth [javana]. If this were the meaning, it would follow that the falling into the life-continuum occurs exclusively after the fifth or sixth [javana]. Therefore, it is said again: 'At the cessation of absorption, there is only the falling into the life-continuum.' The meaning is that there is no arising of a tadārammaṇa consciousness at that time.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī.

“Katthaci appanāvāre sattajavana paripūraṇatthaṃ appanāvasānepi kāmāvacarajavanappavattiṃ vadantānaṃ nikāyantarikānaṃ vādo idha evasaddena nivattito”ti vuttaṃ.

“The view of other schools, who assert that in certain instances of absorption, in order to complete the seven javanas, sense-sphere javanas occur even after the cessation of absorption, is here refuted by the word ‘eva’.”

Tatthāti tasmiṃ appanājavanavāre. Nirantarapavattānaṃ javanānaṃ bhinnavedanatānāma natthīti vuttaṃ somanassasahagata javanā nantarantiādi.

“There,” that is, in that absorption javana process. It was said that there is no difference in feeling among continuously occurring javanas, with reference to the passage beginning, “after a javana accompanied by joy…”

[132] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[132] But in the Vibhāvanī.

“Bhinnavedanānaṃ aññamaññaṃ āsevanapaccayabhāvassa anuddhaṭattā”tikāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

“Because the condition of mutual repetition among those with different feelings has not been refuted,” this reason was stated. That is not sound.

Na hi idha āsevanapaccayabhāvo pamāṇaṃ. Kasmā, āsevana paccanikānaṃ phalajavanānaṃpi parikammajavanehi aññamaññañca abhinnavedanatāya icchitabbattāti. Pāṭikaṅkhitabbāti avassaṃ icchitabbā.

Indeed, here the repetition condition is not the standard. Why? Because it is required that even the fruition javanas, which are contrary to repetition, have the same feeling as the preparatory javanas and as each other. 'Pāṭikaṅkhitabbā' means 'it must necessarily be desired'.

[133] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[133] But in the Vibhāvanī.

“Pasaṃsitabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

“It should be praised,” was said. That is not sound.

Na hi tādiso saṃvaṇṇanāpadeso dissatīti. Arahatta phale maggavīthiyaṃ maggakusalānantaraṃ pavattamānepi ayaṃ pubbāpara niyamo parikammajavanehi eva saha appanājavanānaṃ hotīti katvā kriyajavanānantaraṃ arahattaphalañcāti vuttaṃ. Sukhapuññamhā paraṃ dvattiṃsa appanājavanāni sambhavanti. Upekkhakā puññamhā paraṃ dvādasa, sukhitakriyato paraṃ aṭṭha. Upekkhakā kriyato paraṃ cha appanājavanāni sambhavantīti yojanā. Tattha dvattiṃsāti arahattaphalasabbapañcamajjhānavajjitānaṃ catunnaṃ rūpakusalānaṃ soḷasannaṃ [M 0.0174] maggakusalānaṃ dvādasannaṃ heṭṭhimaphalānañca vasena dvattiṃsa. Dvādasāti pañcamajjhānikānaṃ rūpārūpamaggakusalānaṃ heṭṭhimaphalānañca vasena dvādasa. Aṭṭhāti pañcamajjhānavajjitānaṃ catunnaṃ rūpakriyānaṃ catunnaṃ arahattaphalānañca vasena aṭṭha. Chāti pañcamajjhānikānaṃ pañcannaṃ rūpārūpakriyānaṃ arahattaphalassaca vasena cha. Puthujjanānaṃ sekkhānañca kāmapuññatihetuto paraṃ catucattālīsa appanā sambhavanti. Vītarāgānaṃ arahantānaṃ tihetukāmakriyato paraṃ cuddasa appanā sambhavantīti yojanā.

Indeed, such a laudatory description is not seen. Because, even when in the path process for the fruit of Arahantship the fruition arises after the wholesome path-consciousness, this rule of sequence before and after applies only to the preparatory javanas together with the absorption javanas, it was therefore said, 'and the fruit of Arahantship after the functional javanas.' After pleasant wholesome javanas, thirty-two absorption javanas are possible. After equanimous wholesome javanas, twelve; after pleasant functional javanas, eight. After equanimous functional javanas, six absorption javanas are possible—this is the interpretation. Therein, 'thirty-two' refers to the four fine-material wholesome javanas excluding the fifth jhāna, the sixteen path-wholesome javanas, and the twelve lower fruition javanas—totaling thirty-two. 'Twelve' refers to the path-wholesome and lower fruition javanas associated with the fifth fine-material jhāna and the immaterial jhānas—totaling twelve. 'Eight' refers to the four fine-material functional javanas excluding the fifth jhāna and the four arahantship-fruition javanas—totaling eight. 'Six' refers to the five functional javanas associated with the fifth fine-material jhāna and the immaterial jhānas, and the arahantship-fruition javana—totaling six. For ordinary persons and trainees, after triple-rooted sense-sphere wholesome javanas, forty-four absorption javanas are possible. For the passionless arahants, after triple-rooted sense-sphere functional javanas, fourteen absorption javanas are possible—this is the interpretation.

139. Sabbathāpīti atimahantādinā sabbapakārenapi. Etthāti etesu yathāvuttesu pañcadvāra manodvāresu. Sabbatthāpi pana aniṭṭhe tivā pāṭho. Teneva ṭīkāsu sabbatthāpīti pañcadvāra manodvārepīti vuttaṃ. Icchitabbanti iṭṭhaṃ. Kena icchitabbanti. Lokiyamahājanena. Tattha ca atiukkaṭṭhe atiduggateca jane agahetvā majjhimakena mahājanena. Evañhi sati iṭṭhāniṭṭhānaṃ suṭṭhuvavatthānaṃ hotīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmiṃ ārammaṇekusala vipākaṃ uppajjati, tadeva iṭṭhaṃnāma. Yasmiṃ pana akusalavipākaṃ uppajjati, tadeva aniṭṭhaṃnāma. Na hi sakkā iṭṭhaṃvā aniṭṭhaṃvā ārammaṇaṃ vipākacittaṃ vañcetuntica. Apica dvāravasenāpi iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā veditabbāti ca vuttaṃ. Tasmā indriyānindriyabaddhasantānagate eke kasmiṃ rūpakalāpe vaṇṇādīsu rūpesu kiñci iṭṭhaṃ hoti. Kiñci aniṭṭhaṃ. Kadāci iṭṭhaṃ hoti. Kadāci aniṭṭhaṃ, tattha kiñci iṭṭhaṃ hoti kiñci aniṭṭhanti yathā kiṃsmiṃci ekasmiṃ pupphe vaṇṇo iṭṭho. Gandho aniṭṭho, raso aniṭṭho, phoṭṭhabbo aniṭṭho, kharasamphasso. Kiṃsmiṃci vaṇṇopi iṭṭho, gandhopi iṭṭho, rasādayo aniṭṭhāyeva. Tathā buddhassa sarīragatepi ekasmiṃ kalāpe vaṇṇo iṭṭho hoti. Gandho aniṭṭho. Matakaṇhasunakhassa uddhumātasarīrepi vaṇṇo iṭṭho hoti. Gandho aniṭṭho. So hi vaṇṇo yadi nivatthapārutassa vatthassa bhaveyya. Taṃ vatthaṃ mahagghaṃ hotīti. Kadāci iṭṭhaṃ kadāci aniṭṭhanti aggināma hemante iṭṭho sukhavipākassa paccayo. Gimhe aniṭṭho dukkhavipākassa paccayo. Sītudakaṃ gimhe [M 0.0175] iṭṭhaṃ. Hemante aniṭṭhaṃ. Tathā sukha samphassaṃ vatthaṃ pakatikāye iṭṭhaṃ hoti. Vaṇaṃ patvā aniṭṭhaṃ. Tenavā saṇikaṃ phusantassa iṭṭhaṃ, gāḷhaṃ phusantassa aniṭṭhanti. Naiṭṭhanti aniṭṭhaṃ. Tasmiṃ aniṭṭhe. Iṭṭheti iṭṭhamajjhatte, kusalavipākāni pañcaviññāṇa sampaṭicchana santīraṇa tadārammaṇānīti sambandho. Santīraṇa tadārammaṇāni cettha upekkhāsahagatānieva veditabbāni. Tenevāha atiiṭṭhepanātiādi. Tattha abhiiṭṭheti suvaṇṇa rajata maṇivaṇṇādike haritālavaṇṇādike koseyya vatthavaṇṇādi ke devaccharāvaṇṇādikeca ativiya lokiyamahājanena icchitabbe chaḷārammaṇe. Yasmā cettha aniṭṭhārammaṇa samāyogo akusalakammasseva vipaccanokāso hoti. Iṭṭhārammaṇasamāyogoca kusalakammasseva, tasmā aniṭṭhe akusalavipākāneva. Iṭṭhe kusalavipākānevāti ayaṃ niyamo siddho. Vedanāniyamo pana ādāse mukhanimittassa viya attano ussāha balena vinā kevalaṃ kammabalena nibbattānaṃ vipākānaṃ paridubbalattā tathā tathā kappetvā pakappetvā gahaṇā bhāvato yathārammaṇameva siddho hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na kevalañca vipākānaṃ eva. Athakho vipallāsarahite khiṇāsavasantāne pavattānaṃ kāmakriyajavanānaṃ viyathārammaṇameva vedanāyogo hotīti adhippāyena vuttaṃ tatthāpi somanassasahagata kriyajavanāvasāne tiādi. Tatthāpīti tesu vipākesupi. Somanassasahagata kriya javanā vasāneti buddhavaṇṇādike atiiṭṭhārammaṇe pavattānaṃ somanassa sahagata kriyajavanānaṃ avasāne. Upekkhāsahagata kriya javanā vasāneti aniṭṭhe iṭṭhamajjhatteca pavattānaṃ upekkhāsahagatakriyajavanānaṃ avasāne. Ayañca kriyajavanāvasāne tadārammaṇaniyamo aṭṭhakathāyaṃpi vuttoyeva. Vuttañhi tattha kāmāvacara tihetuka somanassa sahagatakriyadvayaṃ tadārammaṇavasena pañcannaṃ somanassasahagata vipākānaṃ anantarapaccayotiādi. Idañca pakatinīhārena pavattānaṃ kriyajavanānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Tathā rūpena pana cittātisaṅkhārena pavattānaṃ [M 0.0176] kriyajavanānaṃ iṭṭhepi upekkhāvedanāyogo aniṭṭhepi somanassa vedanāyogo hotiyeva. Yathāha –

139. “Sabbathāpi” means “in every way,” such as with the extremely great. “Ettha” means “here,” in these five sense-doors and mind-door as mentioned. However, the reading “tivā” for “aniṭṭhe” (undesirable) is found everywhere. Therefore, in the sub-commentaries, it is said that “sabbatthāpi” (in all cases) refers to the five sense-doors and mind-door. “Icchitaṃ” means “desirable.” “By whom is it desired?” By worldly people. And in that, excluding extremely exalted and extremely lowly persons, it is desired by the average majority. For thus, the distinction between the desirable and the undesirable is well established, as stated in the commentary. That object in which a wholesome resultant arises is called desirable. That object in which an unwholesome resultant arises is called undesirable. For it is not possible to deceive the resultant consciousness concerning a desirable or undesirable object. Moreover, it is also said that desirability and undesirability should be understood based on the sense-doors. Therefore, in a certain form-aggregate belonging to a continuum bound by faculties and non-faculties, among the forms such as colors, some are desirable, some are undesirable. Sometimes it is desirable, sometimes it is undesirable. There, something is desirable, something is undesirable, for example, in a certain flower, the color is desirable, the smell is undesirable, the taste is undesirable, the tangible is undesirable (a rough contact). In some, the color is desirable, the smell is also desirable, but the taste and so forth are undesirable. Similarly, even in the Buddha’s body, in one aggregate, the color is desirable, but the smell is undesirable. Even in the bloated corpse of a black dog, the color is desirable, but the smell is undesirable. For if that color were on a cloth that is worn or wrapped, that cloth would be very valuable. “Sometimes desirable, sometimes undesirable”—for example, fire in winter is desirable, being a condition for a pleasant resultant, but in summer, it is undesirable, being a condition for a painful resultant. Cold water in summer is desirable, but in winter, it is undesirable. Similarly, a cloth with a pleasant touch is desirable for a healthy body, but undesirable when touching a wound. Therefore, for one touching gently, it is desirable; for one touching roughly, it is undesirable. “Naiṭṭhaṃ” means undesirable. In that undesirable [object]. “Iṭṭha” refers to the desirable and the neutral. The connection is with the five sense-consciousnesses, receiving consciousness, investigating consciousness, and registering consciousnesses, which are wholesome resultants. Here, the investigating and registering consciousnesses should be understood as accompanied by equanimity. Therefore, it is said, “even in the extremely desirable,” etc. There, “extremely desirable” refers to the six objects exceedingly desired by worldly people, such as the colors of gold, silver, and gems; orpiment colors; silk cloth colors; and the colors of celestial nymphs. Because here, contact with an undesirable object provides an opportunity for the ripening of only unwholesome kamma, and contact with a desirable object provides an opportunity for the ripening of only wholesome kamma, therefore, this rule is established: in the undesirable, only unwholesome resultants arise; in the desirable, only wholesome resultants arise. The rule of feeling, however, should be understood to be established according to the object itself, like the reflection of a face in a mirror, because the resultants—which arise solely by the power of kamma without one's own effort—are extremely weak, and thus there is an absence of grasping them by arranging and conceiving them in various ways. And not only for resultants. Rather, for the functional impetuses occurring in the continuum of an Arahant, who is free from perversions, the association with feeling is according to the object. This is the intention of what is said: “Also at the end of the functional impetuses accompanied by joy,” etc. “Tatthāpi” means “in those resultants also.” “The end of functional impetuses accompanied by joy” refers to the conclusion of functional impetuses accompanied by joy that arise in extremely desirable objects like the Buddha’s complexion, etc. “The end of functional impetuses accompanied by equanimity” refers to the conclusion of functional impetuses accompanied by equanimity that arise in undesirable or desirable-neutral objects. This rule regarding the registering consciousness at the end of functional impetuses is also stated in the commentary. For it is said there: “The two types of triple-rooted, joy-accompanied functional consciousnesses of the sense-sphere are, by way of registering, the immediate condition for the five types of joy-accompanied resultant consciousnesses,” etc. This is said with reference to functional impetuses occurring naturally. However, when functional impetuses occur due to such excessive mental exertion, even in desirable objects, the association with feeling is equanimity, and even in undesirable objects, the association with feeling is joy. As it is said—

Kathañcānanda ariyo hoti bhāvitindriyo. Idhānanda bhikkhuno cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjati manāpaṃ uppajjati amanāpaṃ. Uppajjati manāpāmanāpaṃ. So sace ākaṅkhati paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyyanti. Appaṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati. Sace ākaṅkhati appaṭikūle paṭikūla saññī vihareyyanti. Paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharatīti.

And how, Ānanda, is a noble one one with developed faculties? Here, Ānanda, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, there arises what is agreeable, there arises what is disagreeable, there arises what is both agreeable and disagreeable. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive.

Sabbaṃ uparipaṇṇāsake indriyabhāvanāsuttaṃ āharitabbaṃ. Tattha uppajjati manāpaṃ uppajjati amanāpaṃ. Uppajjati manāpāmanāpanti etena khīṇāsavānaṃ kāmakriyajavanānaṃ pakatinīhārena iṭṭhe so manassayogo aniṭṭhe upekkhā yogo dassito hoti. Sosace ākaṅkhati paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyyanti. Appaṭikūlasaññī tattha viharatītiādinā pana tesaṃ tathārūpe cittābhisaṅkhāre sati iṭṭhepi upekkhāyogo aniṭṭhepisomanassa yogo vutto hotīti. Yaṃ pana khīṇāsavānaṃ satatavihārasutte idha bhikkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti. Na dummano. Upekkhako viharati sato sampajānotiādinā chasudvāresu somanassa paṭikkhipanaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃpi tesaṃ tathā rūpacittābhisaṅkhārabāhullavasena vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Yasmā vā khīṇālavāpi buddharūpadassanādīsu padhānasāruppaṭṭhānadassanādīsu ca somanassitā hontiyeva. Tasmā kevalaṃ rāgādivatthu bhūtāni rūpārammaṇādīni iṭṭhāniṭṭhāni sandhāya idaṃ vuttantipi yuttaṃ. Ettha ca. Kathaṃ paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī viharati. Aniṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ mettāyavā pharati. Dhātutovā upasaṃharati. Evaṃ paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī viharati. Kathaṃ appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī viharati iṭṭhasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ asubhāyavā pharati. Aniccato vā upasaṃharati. Evaṃ appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī viharatītiādinā paṭisambhidāmagganayena idha tathārūpo cittābhisaṅkhāro nāma [M 0.0177] veditabbo. Apare pana vadanti-khīṇāsavā yadā devaccharā vaṇṇādikaṃ atiiṭṭhārammaṇaṃ āpātamā gacchati. Tadā tattha asubhāyavāpharanti. Aniccatovā upasaṃharanti tattha aniṭṭhabhūtaṃ asubha lakkhaṇaṃvā aniccalakkhaṇaṃvā upekkhā kriya javanānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Na atiiṭṭhārammaṇabhūtaṃ devaccharāvaṇṇādikaṃ.

The entire Indriyabhāvanā Sutta from the Uparipaṇṇāsaka should be cited. Therein, 'the agreeable arises, the disagreeable arises, the agreeable and disagreeable arise'—by this, it is shown that for the Arahants, the functional javanas in the sense-sphere, when occurring naturally, have association with joy in the desirable and association with equanimity in the undesirable. But by 'If he wishes, "May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive," he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive there,' etc., it is stated that when such mental formations are present in them, there is association with equanimity even in the desirable, and association with joy even in the undesirable. Moreover, in the Satatavihāra Sutta concerning the constant abiding of Arahants, the rejection of joy at the six sense-doors is stated by 'Here, a bhikkhu, having seen a form, is neither elated nor dejected, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and fully aware,' etc. That too should be understood as spoken with reference to them due to the predominance of such mental formations. Or, because even Arahants experience joy upon seeing the Buddha’s form, etc., and upon seeing objects conducive to diligence, etc., therefore it is fitting to say that this teaching is spoken solely with reference to desirable and undesirable objects such as forms that are truly grounds for lust, etc. And here: How does one dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive? One pervades the disagreeable object with loving-kindness, or reflects on it as elements. Thus, one dwells perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive. How does one dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive? One pervades the agreeable object with the perception of foulness, or reflects on it as impermanent. Thus, one dwells perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive—and so on. Herein, such mental formations should be understood according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Others, however, say: When Arahants encounter an exceedingly desirable object, such as the beauty of celestial nymphs, they then pervade it with the perception of foulness or reflect on it as impermanent. There, an undesirable phenomenon—the characteristic of foulness or the characteristic of impermanence—becomes the object for the equanimous functional javanas, not the exceedingly desirable object like the beauty of celestial nymphs.

Tathā yadā kudhibhakuṭṭhasarīrādikaṃ atianiṭṭhārammaṇaṃ āpātamāgacchati. Tadā tattha mettāyavā pharanti. Dhātutovā upasaṃharanti. Tattha iṭṭhabhūtaṃ averatāvādilakkhaṇameva somanassakriyajavanānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti. Na atianiṭṭhabhūtaṃ kudhita kuṭṭhasarīrādikaṃ. Tasmā tāni javanāni kāmavipākāniviya sabbadāpi ārammaṇānurūpameva vedanāyuttāni hontīti. Taṃ nayujjati. Na hi tāni lakkhaṇāni devaccharāvaṇṇādīhi vinā visuṃ labbhanti. Tehi pana saheva labbhanti. Tasmā yathā ānisaṃsadassanena bhāvanāya pubbāpariyavisesadassanenaca uddhumātakādīsu ati aniṭṭhesupi somanassuppatti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttā. Yathāca mahā moggalānattherassa buddhasubuddhatādassanena attasampattidassanenaca aniṭṭhabhūtepi aṭṭhikaṅkalikapetarūpe somanassuppatti pāḷiyaṃ vuttā. Yathā ca mahākassapattherassa tathārūpena cittābhi saṅkhārena kuṭṭhino hatthato laddhe aniṭṭhabhūte pūtikummāsepi somanassuppatti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttā. Evamevaṃ idhapi asubhapharaṇādiko cittābhisaṅkhāro atiiṭṭhe upekkhājavanānaṃ atianiṭṭheca somanassajavanānaṃ uppattiyā paccayo hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayañhi ārammaṇānaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāvonāma lokiyamahājanānaṃ icchāvasena siddho hoti agambhīro vipallāsadhammānaṃ kilesānañca vatthubhūto. Yathāha-tattha katamaṃ rūpaṃ hīnaṃ. Yaṃ rūpaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ uññātaṃ avaññātantiādi. Ettha hi tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānanti etena ārammaṇadhammānaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāvo nāma lokiyamahājana sammutiyā siddhoti dasseti. Tasmā yañca appahīnavipallāsānaṃ lokiyamahājanānaṃ devaccharāvaṇṇā dīsu ati iṭṭhesu atiiṭṭhākārato gahaṇaṃ. Yañca buddhavaṇṇā dīsu [M 0.0178] atiiṭṭhesu aniṭṭhākārato gahaṇaṃ. Tadubhayaṃpi tesaṃ vipallāsavaseneva hoti. Yaṃpana paññavantānaṃ buddhasāvakānaṃ devaccharāvaṇṇādīsu aniṭṭhākārato gahaṇaṃ. Yañca buddhavaṇṇādīsu atiiṭṭhākārato gahaṇaṃ. Tadubhayaṃpi paññābaleneva hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Likewise, when an extremely disagreeable object such as the body of an angry leper and so forth comes into view, they then radiate it with loving-kindness or reflect on it as elements. There, only the agreeable characteristic of non-ill-will and so forth becomes the object of the joy-accompanied functional javanas, not the extremely disagreeable body of an angry leper and so forth. Therefore, those javanas, like sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, always arise with a feeling appropriate to their object. This is not fitting. For those characteristics cannot be found separately from the appearance of celestial nymphs and so on—they are found only together with them. Thus, just as the arising of joy in the extremely disagreeable, such as bloated corpses, is mentioned in the commentaries through seeing the benefits of meditation and through seeing distinctions before and after; and just as the arising of joy in the extremely disagreeable, such as skeletons and ghostly forms, is mentioned in the Pāli canon regarding the great Elder Mahāmoggallāna through seeing the Buddha's perfect enlightenment and his own accomplishments; and just as the arising of joy in the extremely disagreeable, such as the putrid gruel received from a leper’s hand, is mentioned in the commentaries regarding the great Elder Mahākassapa through such mental formations—in the same way, here too, the mental formation of pervading with foulness and so on becomes a condition for the arising of equanimity-accompanied javanas in the extremely agreeable and joy-accompanied javanas in the extremely disagreeable. This should be seen. For this agreeable or disagreeable nature of objects is established according to the desires of worldly people—it is shallow, subject to distortion, and a basis for defilements. As it is said: 'Here, what is inferior form? That form which is disdained and scorned by various beings,' and so on. Here, 'by various beings' indicates that the agreeable or disagreeable nature of objects is established by the convention of worldly people. Therefore, the perception of the extremely agreeable aspect in celestial nymphs and so on by worldly people who have not abandoned distortions, and the perception of the disagreeable aspect in the Buddha’s appearance and so on—both are due to their distortions. On the other hand, the perception of the disagreeable aspect in celestial nymphs and so on by the wise disciples of the Buddha, and the perception of the extremely agreeable aspect in the Buddha’s appearance and so on—both are due to the power of wisdom. This should be understood.

[134] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[134] Now, concerning the Vibhāvaniya,

“Kusalākusalānaṃ pana appahīnavipallāsesu santānesu pavattiyā atiiṭṭhepi iṭṭhamajjhattaaniṭṭhākārato aniṭṭhepi iṭṭhaiṭṭhamajjhattākārato gahaṇaṃ hotīti” vuttaṃ.

"Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome, in the continuities of those with unabandoned distortions, even in what is extremely agreeable, there is perception of it as agreeable, neutral, or disagreeable; and even in what is disagreeable, there is perception of it as agreeable, extremely agreeable, or neutral." Thus it is said.

Yañca tattha

And what is said there:

“Khīṇāsavānaṃ cittavipallāsābhāvena kriyajavanānipi yathārammaṇameva pavattantī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ vicāretabbameva.

"It is said that for those whose taints are destroyed, due to the absence of mental distortion, even functional javanas occur in accordance with the object." This should be examined.
