Ye hi te dhamma cakkhurahitā honti. Teyeva vipallāsa vasena cittavasānugā ārammaṇavasānugāca hontīti kusalā kusalāniyeva yebhuyyena yathārammaṇaṃ pavattanti. Na pana kriya javanāni. Na hi khīṇāsavā lokiyamahājanasammatesu iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu cittavasānugā ārammaṇavasānugāca hontīti. Yathāha –

For those states that are devoid of the eye of Dhamma, they are indeed subject to distortion, to the mind's control, and to the object's control. Thus, wholesome and unwholesome states mostly proceed according to the object, but not functional javanas. For those whose taints are destroyed are not subject to the mind's control or the object's control in worldly matters deemed agreeable or disagreeable by the multitude. As it is said:

Rūpā saddā gandhā rasā, phoṭṭhabbāca manoramā;

Iṭṭhadhammā aniṭṭhāca, na pavedhanti paṇḍitāti.

Forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and delightful things—whether agreeable or disagreeable—do not agitate the wise.

Tasmā somanassa kriya javanānantaraṃpi tadārammaṇāni somanassupekkhā vedanāyuttāni eva siyuṃ. Tathā upekkhākriyajavanānantaraṃpīti. Mūlaṭīkāyaṃ panettha paṭṭhāne-kusalākusale niruddhe vipāko tadārammaṇatāuppajjatīti kusalakusalānantaraṃ eva tadārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Na abyākatānantaraṃ naca katthaci kriyānantaraṃ tadārammaṇassa vuttaṭṭhānaṃ dissati. Vijjamāneca tasmiṃ avacane kāraṇaṃnatthi. Bhavaṅgañcanāmetaṃ nadisotoviya paṭisotagāmināvaṃ savipphārikaṃ evajavanaṃ anubandhatīti yuttaṃ. Na pana chaḷaṅgupekkhāvato khīṇāsavassa santavuttikriyajavanaṃ. Tasmā kriyajavanānantaraṃ tadārammaṇavidhānaṃ [M 0.0179] upaparikkhitabbanti vuttaṃ. Paṭṭhāne pana kusalattike pañhā vāre ārammaṇapaccayavibhaṅge tīsu abyākatapadāvasānavāresu sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ tadārammaṇameva padhānaṃ hoti. Na kusalā kusalajavanaṃ. Tasmā dvīsupi vāresu sekkhāvā puthujjanāvā kusalaṃ aniccato vipassanti kusalaṃ assādentītiādikaṃ vatvā punaca kusale niruddhe akusale niruddhe vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjatīti vuttaṃ. Arahato pana javanaṃpi tadārammaṇaṃpi padhāna meva hoti. Tasmā arahā kusalaṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassati icceva vuttaṃ. Napana vuttaṃ kriyābyākate niruddhe vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjatīti. Yadi cetaṃ vucceyya tadārammaṇameva padhānaṃ kataṃnāma siyā. Avuttepica tasmiṃ vipassatīti iminā tadārammaṇaṃpi gahitameva hotīti. Tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ paṭṭhāne kusalā.La. Uppajjatīti kusalākusalānantarameva tadārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Na abyākatānantarantica. Vijjamāneca tasmiṃ avacane kāraṇaṃ natthīti ca vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjatiyeva. Anantarapaccayavibhaṅgesu pana kusalaṃ vuṭṭhānassa akusalaṃ vuṭṭhānassa kriyaṃ vuṭṭhānassātica vipākadhammadhammā khandhā vuṭṭhānassa nevavipāka nāvipākadhammadhammā khandhā vuṭṭhānassātica evamādinā kriyajavanānantaraṃ bhavaṅgena saha tadārammaṇassapi vuṭṭhānanāmena vuttaṭṭhānaṃ dissatiyeva. Tasmā yañca vuttaṃ na katthaci kriyānantaraṃ tadārammaṇassa vuttaṭṭhānaṃ dissatīti. Taṃpi na yujjatiyeva. Naca chaḷaṅgupekkhāva to khīṇāsavassa santavuttipi kriyajavanaṃ savipphārikaṃ na hoti. Kusalajavanassa viya tassapi oḷārikakāyavacī payogasamuṭṭhā panatoti.

Therefore, after joyful functional impulsions, the registering consciousnesses may be associated with either joy or equanimity. Similarly, after equanimous functional impulsions. In the Mūlaṭīkā, it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna that when wholesome and unwholesome states cease, resultant registering consciousness arises. Thus, registering consciousness is mentioned only after wholesome and unwholesome states, not after indeterminate states, nor is any place seen where it is mentioned after functional states. And if it were present, there would be no reason for not mentioning it. It is appropriate that a forceful impulsion follows the life-continuum, like a boat going against the river's current; but not so the functional impulsion of an arahant with six-limbed equanimity and a tranquil disposition. Therefore, it is said that the arrangement of registering consciousness after functional impulsions should be examined. In the Paṭṭhāna, however, in the wholesome triad, in the question section, in the analysis of the object condition, in the three sections concluding with indeterminate terms, the registering consciousness of trainees and ordinary persons is the primary focus, not wholesome or unwholesome impulsion. Thus, in both sections, whether for trainees or ordinary persons, having said that they contemplate the wholesome as impermanent, delight in the wholesome, and so on, it is further stated that when the wholesome ceases, when the unwholesome ceases, resultant registering consciousness arises. For an arahant, however, both impulsion and registering consciousness are primary. Thus, it is only said that an arahant contemplates the wholesome as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. But it is not stated that after functional-indeterminate states cease, resultant registering consciousness arises. If this were said, then registering consciousness alone would be made primary. And even without this being stated, by the words 'he contemplates,' registering consciousness is also included. Therefore, what was stated—that in the Paṭṭhāna, 'when wholesome... arise,' registering consciousness is mentioned only after wholesome and unwholesome states, and not after indeterminate states, and that if it were present, there would be no reason for not mentioning it—that is not justified. In the analyses of the immediate condition, however, a place is indeed seen where registering consciousness, along with the life-continuum, is mentioned by the name 'emergence' after functional impulsion, in such phrases as 'wholesome for emergence,' 'unwholesome for emergence,' 'functional for emergence,' 'aggregates of resultant phenomena for emergence,' and 'aggregates of neither-resultant-nor-non-resultant phenomena for emergence.' Therefore, what was said—that no place is seen where registering consciousness is mentioned after functional impulsion—that also is not justified. Furthermore, it is not the case that the functional impulsion of an arahant with six-limbed equanimity and a tranquil disposition is not forceful, for, like wholesome impulsion, it also arises from gross bodily and verbal preparatory efforts.

[135] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

Now, in the Vibhāvaniya:

Ṭīkāvādassa uttaraṃ vadantena yaṃ vuttaṃ “yadi abyākatā nantaraṃpi tadārammaṇaṃ vucceyya. Parittārammaṇe voṭṭhabbanā nantaraṃpi tassa pavattiṃ maññeyyunti kriyajavanānantaraṃ tadā rammaṇaṃ na vutta”nti. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

What was said in answering the Ṭīkāvāda—'If registering consciousness were to be mentioned even after indeterminate states, one might think it could occur even after the determining consciousness in the case of a limited object; for this reason, registering consciousness is not mentioned after functional impulsions'—that is not sound.

Na [M 0.0180] hi paṭṭhāne imasmiṃ vutte idaṃnāma maññeyyunti avuttaṃnāma atthi. Na ca arahā kusalaṃ aniccato dukkhato anattato vipassatītiādinā vipassanācāravasena vuttaṭṭhāne pañcadvārika parittārammaṇa vārapasaṅgo atthīti. Domanassa.La. Upekkhā sahagatāneva bhavanti. Na somanassasahagatāni. Kasmā, somanassa domanassānaṃ aññamaññaviruddhattā. Teneva hi paṭṭhāne tesaṃ itarītarānantarapaccayatā navuttāti. Etthaca kriyajavana domanassajavanāna meva anantaraṃ tadārammaṇa niyamaṃ dassentena therena itaresaṃ kusalākusalajavanānaṃ anantaraṃ pana tādiso niyamo natthīti dassito hoti. Tasmā aṭṭhannaṃ kāmakusalānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ lobhamūlānaṃ dvinnaṃ mohamūlānanti aṭṭhārasannaṃ javanānaṃ anantaraṃ ārammaṇānurūpaṃ sabbāni tadārammaṇāni bhavaṅgāni ca pavattanti. Yebhuyyena pana akusalajavanānantaraṃ tadārammaṇaṃ ahetukameva. Dvihetukajavanānantaraṃ dvihetukameva. Tihetukajavanānantaraṃ tihetukamevāti ayaṃ yebhuyyaniyamo. Yassa pana dvihetukānivā tihetukānivā kusalajavanāni bahulaṃ samudācaranti. Tassa kadāci akusalajavanesu javitesu akusalānantaraṃpi dvihetukānivā tihetukānivātadārammaṇāni pavattanti. Yassa akusalajavanāni bahulaṃ samudācaranti. Tassa kadāci dvihetukesuvā tihetukesuvā kusalajavanesu javitesu kusalānantaraṃpi ahetukatadārammaṇāni pavattanti. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭṭhāne-ahetuke khandhe aniccato.La. Domanassaṃ uppajjati. Kusalākusale niruddhe sahetuko vipāko tadā rammaṇatā uppajjati. Ahetuko vipāko tadārammaṇatā uppajjatīti. Ekānihi tadārammaṇānināma paṭisandhijanakena ekena kammena nibbattānipi nānāvīthīsu nānāppakārāni honti. Pavatti vipākajanakehi pana nānākammehi nibbatthesu vattabbameva natthīti. Tasmāti yasmā domanassānantaraṃ somanassuppatti nāma natthi, tasmā. Somanassapaṭisandhikassāti catūsu somanassamahā vipākesu ekamekena gahita paṭisandhikassa sattassa. Tadā rammaṇasambhavoti [M 0.0181] tadārammaṇuppatti kāraṇaṃ. Tadārammaṇuppatti yevavā. Yaṃkiñcīti iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhūtesu rūpārammaṇādīsu yaṃkiñci. Paricitapubbanti imasmiṃ bhaveyeva taṅkhaṇato purimakhaṇesu gahaṇa bahulatā vasena paricitaṃ. Abhiṇhasevitanti attho. Parittārammaṇanti parittadhammabhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ. Ārabbhāti ālambitvā. Upekkhāsahagata santīraṇanti dvīsu upekkhāsahagatasantī raṇesu iṭṭhe kusalavipākaṃ aniṭṭhe akusalavipākaṃ upekkhā sahagata santīraṇaṃ. Yesaṃ pana pakatiyā itarāni cattāri upekkhāsahagata vipākāni bahulaṃ pavattanti. Tesaṃ tānipi āgantukabhavaṅgaṃ nahontīti na vattabbāni. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana mahādhammarakkhitattheravāde yebhuyyaniyamasote patitattā akusalajavanānurūpaṃ ahetukaṃ upekkhā santīraṇa dvaya meva vuttaṃ. Teneva hi parato theravādānaṃ vicāritaṭṭhāne akusalajavanānantaraṃ ahetuka tadārammaṇa meva dīpentassa tassa theravādassa aparipuṇṇavādabhāvaṃ dassetvā yadā kusalajavanānaṃ antarantarā akusalaṃ javati, tadā kusalāvasāne āciṇṇa sadisameva akusalāvasāne sahetukaṃ tadārammaṇaṃ yuttanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tadārammaṇecayutte etaṃpi yujjatiyeva. Tasmā chapi upekkhāsahagatavipākāni āgantukabhavaṅgaṃ hontiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etthaca upekkhāpaṭisandhikassa tāva atimahantāti vibhūtesupi buddhavaṇṇādīsu abhiiṭṭhārammaṇesu domanassaṃ uppādentassa tadārammaṇasambhavo natthīti domanassa javanānantaraṃ bhavaṅgapātova hoti. Somanassapaṭisandhikassa pana sabbesupi iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhūtesu mahantesu avibhūtesuca chaḷārammaṇesu domanassa uppādentassa neva tadārammaṇasambhavo atthi. Nacamūlabhavaṅga sambhavoti katvā domanassānantaraṃ chasu upekkhāsahagatavipākesu yathārahaṃ ekaṃ āgantuka bhavaṅgabhāvena pavattati. Tathā tasseva buddhavaṇṇādīsu atiiṭṭhabhūtesu atimahantesu ativibhūtesuca chaḷārammaṇesuvā mahaggatapaññattīsuvā domanassaṃ uppādentassāti. Ettha ca yasmā abhidhamme dhātuvibhaṅge sabbadhammesuvā pana [M 0.0182] pathama samannāhāroti vuttaṃ. Mahāhatthipadopama sutteca ajjhatti kañceva āvuso cakkhu aparibhinnaṃ hoti. Bāhirāca rūpāāpātaṃ āgacchanti. Noca tajjo samannāhāro hoti. Neva tāva tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Yatoca kho āvuso ajjhattikañceva cakkhu aparibhinnaṃ hoti. Bāhirāca rūpā āpāta māgacchanti. Tajjoca samannāhāro hoti. Evaṃ tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Ajjhattikañceva āvuso sotaṃ.La. Ghānaṃ.La. Jivhā.La. Kāyo.La. Mano aparibhinno hoti. Bāhirāca dhammā āpātaṃ āgacchanti. Noca tajjo samannāhāro hoti. Neva tāva tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hoti. Yatoca kho āvuso ajjhattikoceva mano aparibhinno hoti. Bāhirāca dhammā āpātaṃ āgacchanti. Tajjoca samannāhāro hoti. Evaṃ tajjassa viññāṇabhāgassa pātubhāvo hotīti vuttaṃ. Tasmā vīthicittānināma āvajjanenavinānauppajjanti. Sace āvajjanena dhammatovā kālabhovā yaṃyaṃ niyametvā āvajjitaṃ hoti. Taṃ tadeva tānipi gaṇhanti. Yadi aniyametvā yaṃkiñci āvajjitaṃ hoti. Tānipi āvajji tappakārameva gaṇhanti. Na pana ekāvajjana vīthiyaṃ sabbāni vīthicittāni āvajjanenavā aññamaññaṃvā dhammatovā kālatovā bhinnā lambaṇāni hontīti veditabbanti.

For indeed, in the Paṭṭhāna, when this is stated, there is nothing left unsaid such that one should think, 'this is what is meant.' Nor, in places where insight practice is described, such as “an Arahant contemplates the wholesome as impermanent, suffering, and non-self,” does the problem of a five-door process with a limited object arise. Consciousnesses accompanied by mental pain are followed only by those accompanied by equanimity; they are not followed by those accompanied by joy. Why? Because joy and mental pain are mutually opposed. Hence, in the Paṭṭhāna, their reciprocal immediate conditionality is not stated. Here, by showing the rule that registration consciousness follows immediately only after functional impulsions and impulsions accompanied by mental pain, the Elder indicates that for other wholesome and unwholesome impulsions, no such fixed rule exists. Therefore, after the eighteen types of impulsions—eight sense-sphere wholesome, eight rooted in greed, and two rooted in delusion—all registration consciousnesses and life-continuum consciousnesses arise according to the object. Generally, after unwholesome impulsions, the registration consciousness is rootless (ahetuka). After two-rooted (dvihetuka) impulsions, it is two-rooted; after three-rooted (tihetuka) impulsions, it is three-rooted. This is the general rule. For one in whom two-rooted or three-rooted wholesome impulsions frequently arise, even after unwholesome impulsions, the registration consciousness may be two-rooted or three-rooted. Conversely, for one in whom unwholesome impulsions frequently arise, even after wholesome impulsions, the registration consciousness may be rootless. As stated in the Paṭṭhāna: “Regarding rootless aggregates as impermanent… mental pain arises. When a wholesome or unwholesome state has ceased, a rooted resultant arises as registration consciousness, or a rootless resultant arises as registration consciousness.” These registration consciousnesses (tadārammaṇa), though produced by a single kamma that generates rebirth, are diverse in different processes. It is needless to speak of those produced by different kammas that generate resultant consciousness in the active life period. `Tasmā` (Therefore) means: since there is no such thing as the arising of joy immediately after mental pain, therefore... `Somanassapaṭisandhikassa` (For one with a rebirth-linking accompanied by joy) means: for a being who has taken rebirth-linking with one of the four great resultants accompanied by joy. `Tadārammaṇasambhava` (The possibility of registration consciousness) means: the cause for the arising of registration consciousness, or the arising of registration consciousness itself. “Whatever” means any object—pleasant or unpleasant, such as a visual form. “Previously familiar” (paricitapubba) means familiar in this very existence due to frequent engagement in the moments before the present. The meaning is “repeatedly frequented.” “Limited object” (parittārammaṇa) refers to an object consisting of limited phenomena. `Ārabbha` means having taken as an object. The equanimity-accompanied investigating consciousness (upekkhāsahagata santīraṇa), among the two types, is the wholesome resultant for pleasant objects and the unwholesome resultant for unpleasant objects. For those in whom the other four equanimity-accompanied resultants frequently arise by nature, it should not be said that these too cannot be an adventitious life-continuum (āgantukabhavaṅga). In the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), in the view of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, because it falls into the stream of the general rule, it is said that corresponding to unwholesome impulsions, only the two types of rootless equanimity-accompanied investigating consciousness arise. Therefore, later, in the section discussing the views of the Elders, after showing that the Elder’s view—which indicates only rootless registration consciousness after unwholesome impulsions—is an incomplete view, it is stated in the commentary that when unwholesome impulsions occur occasionally between wholesome impulsions, then at the end of the unwholesome, a rooted registration consciousness is fitting, similar to what is habitual at the end of the wholesome. And when registration consciousness is fitting, this too is fitting. Therefore, it should be understood that all six equanimity-accompanied resultants can indeed serve as adventitious life-continuum. Here, for one with a rebirth-linking of equanimity, when generating mental pain even towards supremely desirable objects like the Buddha’s complexion, which are very great and distinct, there is no possibility of registration consciousness; thus, after the impulsion with mental pain, only a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅgapāta) occurs. For one with a joy-linking rebirth, however, when generating mental pain towards any of the six sense-objects—whether desirable or undesirable, great or indistinct—there is neither the possibility of registration consciousness nor the possibility of the root life-continuum. Therefore, after the mental pain, one of the six equanimity-accompanied resultants arises as an adventitious life-continuum, according to suitability. Likewise for that very person when generating mental pain in relation to the Buddha’s complexion, etc.—which are supremely desirable, supremely great, and supremely distinct among the six sense-objects—or in relation to sublime or conceptual objects. Here, because in the Abhidhamma, in the Dhātuvibhaṅga, it is said “or however, for all phenomena, the initial bringing-together,” and in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta: “When, friends, the internal eye is intact, and external forms come into range, but there is no appropriate gathering, then the corresponding part of consciousness does not manifest. But when the internal eye is intact, external forms come into range, and there is appropriate gathering, then the corresponding part of consciousness does manifest.” The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Therefore, process consciousnesses (vīthicitta) do not arise without adverting (āvajjana). If, by nature or time, adverting is directed according to some rule, then those consciousnesses take up exactly that object. If adverting is undirected, they too grasp it in the very manner it was adverted to. However, it should be understood that in a single-adverting process, it is not the case that all process consciousnesses have different objects due to adverting, mutual influence, nature, or time.

Ettha siyā. Yadi ce taṃ āgantukabhavaṅgaṃ ekavīthiyaṃ ādimhi āvajjanena āvajjitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ agahetvā aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci paricitapubbaṃ parittārammaṇaṃ ārabbha uppajjati. Evaṃ sati nirāvajjanaṃnāma etaṃ siyā. Āvajjanādīhica saddhiṃ dhammato kālato ca bhinnārammaṇaṃnāma siyāti. Saccaṃ, yathā pana maggavīthiyaṃ gotrabhuvodānāni phalasamāpattivīthiyaṃ phalāni nirodhato vuṭṭhahantassaca phalacittaṃ nirāvajjanameva honti bhinnārammaṇañca. Evametassapi natthi nirāvajjanatāya bhinnārammaṇatāyaca dosoti. Yañca ekasmiṃbhave bhavaṅgassa paṭisandhiyā saha dhammatoca ārammaṇa toca abhinnattaṃ tattha tattha vuttaṃ. Taṃpi mūlabhavaṅgaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. [M 0.0183] Idañca āgantukabhavaṅganti natthi dosoti. Tamanantaritvāti taṃ āgantukabhavaṅgaṃ attano anantarapaccayaṃ katvā. Vadanti ācariyā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃca etaṃ vidhānaṃ natthīti adhippāyo. Kāmāvacarajavanāvasāneyeva tadārammaṇaṃ icchanti. Na mahaggatānuttarajavanāvasāne. Kasmā iti ce. Kāmāvacara javanānaṃ eva savipphandanattā. Itaresañca avipphandanattā.

Here it might be said: If that adventitious life-continuum, at the beginning of a single cognitive process, arises based on some previously familiar, limited object, without grasping the object adverted to by adverting—in such a case, this would be called 'without adverting.' Moreover, it would have a different object from adverting and so on, due to nature and time. True, just as in the path process, the change-of-lineage and the purification, and in the fruition attainment process, the fruition minds that emerge from cessation, are indeed without adverting and also have a different object. Similarly, in this case too, there is no fault in its being without adverting or having a different object. And what has been said elsewhere about the life-continuum in a single existence, and its non-difference in nature and object with rebirth-linking—that refers to the root life-continuum. This, however, is the adventitious life-continuum, so there is no fault. The teachers say that the phrase 'having made it immediately subsequent' refers to making that adventitious life-continuum its own immediate condition. But in the Pāḷi and the Great Commentary, this arrangement is not found; this is the intention. They desire that registering consciousness occurs only at the end of sense-sphere impulsions, not at the end of sublime or supramundane impulsions. Why? Because sense-sphere impulsions alone are characterized by agitation, whereas the others are not characterized by agitation.

[136] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[136] But in the Vibhāvaniya,

“Kāmataṇhā nidāna kammanibbattattā”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ.

The reason is stated: ‘Because it is produced by kamma having sensual craving as its cause.’ That is not a valid reason.

Apica abhiññāvajjitāni mahaggatānuttarajavanāni aparittārammaṇāni honti. Tadārammaṇāni pana parittārammaṇānevāti natesaṃ avasāne tadārammaṇuppatti pasaṅgo atthi. Abhiññājavanānica kānici parittārammaṇānipi santatarāni hontīti tesaṃpi avasāne taduppatti natthiyevāti.

Moreover, the sublime and supramundane impulsions that are devoid of direct knowledges have unlimited objects. But registering consciousnesses have only limited objects, so there is no occasion for the arising of registering consciousness at their end. And although some impulsions of direct knowledge have limited objects, they are very serene; therefore, at their end too, there is no such arising.

[137] Etena

[137] By this,

Ajanakattā janaka samānattābhāvatotiādipi paṭikkhittaṃ hoti.

By this, the argument, 'because it is not a producer and because there is an absence of similarity to a producer,' and so on, is also refuted.

Kāmāvacarasattānaṃeva tadārammaṇaṃ icchanti. Na rūpārūpasattānaṃ. Na hi tesu uppannānaṃ parittārammaṇānaṃpi kāmāvacarajavanānaṃ avasāne tadārammaṇuppatti atthi. Tadārammaṇūpa nissayassa kāma bhavaṅgassa abhāvato mahaggata bhavaṅgassa ca santa tarassa tadārammaṇa kiccā bhāvatoti. Cakkhuviññāṇa sota viññāṇāni pana rūpasattānaṃ cakkhusotaindriya pavattiānubhāvato sampaṭicchanasantīraṇānica dvāravīthibhede cittaniyamasiddhito rūpasattesu pavattanti yevāti. Kāmāvacaradhammesveva ārammaṇabhūtesu tadārammaṇaṃ icchanti, na mahaggatānuttarapaññattidhammesu. Ekantaparittārammaṇattā tadārammaṇānaṃ. Tesaṃ pana ekantaparittā rammaṇabhāve kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttamevāti.

They desire registering consciousness only for beings of the sense-sphere, not for beings of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. For even when sense-sphere impulsions with limited objects arise in them, there is no occurrence of registering consciousness at their end, because of the absence of a sense-sphere life-continuum as a support for registering consciousness, and because the sublime life-continuum, being very serene, does not perform the function of registering consciousness. However, eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness do occur in beings of the fine-material sphere by the power of the functioning of the eye and ear faculties; and receiving and investigating consciousnesses also occur in them, this being established by the fixed order of mind in the classification of door processes. They desire registering consciousness only when sense-sphere phenomena serve as objects, not in relation to sublime, supramundane, or concept phenomena, because registering consciousnesses have exclusively limited objects. The reason for their having exclusively limited objects has indeed been stated below.

[138] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[138] But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Aparicitattā”ti [M 0.0184] kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ.

“Because of unfamiliarity” is stated as the reason. That is not the reason.

Cittañhi nāma vikappabalevā appanāpattabhāvanākammavisese vā sati nibbāne viya aparicitepi ārammaṇe pavattatiyevāti.

For the mind, by the power of conception, or when there is a special meditative practice that has reached absorption, does indeed operate even on an unfamiliar object, such as Nibbāna.

[139] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

[139] And what in the Vibhāvanī,

“Kāmataṇhāyattakammajanitattāpī”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃpi heṭṭhā paṭikkhittameva. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ kiṃvā etāya yutticintāyāti vatvā sabbāni vibhāvaniyaṃ vutta kāraṇāni paṭikkhittānīti.

“Because it is produced by kamma dependent on craving for sensual pleasures,” the reason has been stated. That too has indeed been refuted below. For that very reason, in the commentary, after saying, “Or what is the use of this line of reasoning?” all the reasons stated in the Vibhāvanī have been refuted.

Kāme javana sattālambaṇānaṃ niyamesatīti kāmabhūmipariyāpannānaṃ javanānaṃ sattānaṃ ārammaṇānañca vasena tividhe niyame sati. Vibhūte timahanteca tadārammaṇamīritanti etena tadārammaṇaṃnāma pavattamānaṃ vibhūtārammaṇevā atimahantārammaṇe vā pavattatīti ayameva niyamo dassito. Na pana yattha tadā rammaṇaṃ pavattati. Etadeva vibhūtañca atimahantañca nāmāti niyamo. Tasmā uḷārakammanibbattānaṃ suvisadavatthukānaṃ rūpabrahmānaṃ uppannāvīthiyo yebhuyyena vibhūtārammaṇāeva atimahantā rammaṇāevaca hontīti veditabbā. Keci pana imamatthaṃ asallakkhetvā rūpārūpabhūmīsu vibhūtārammaṇavīthiyo atimahantārammaṇavīthiyoca nalabbhantīti vadanti. [Tadārammaṇaniyamo].

Regarding the rule for impulsions, beings, and objects in the sense-sphere: this means when there is a threefold rule concerning impulsions included in the sense-sphere, beings, and objects. By the statement, 'When the object is clear and very great, tadārammaṇa is said to occur,' this very rule is shown: that registering consciousness, when it occurs, does so only with a clear object or a very great object. It is not, however, that registering consciousness occurs just anywhere; the rule is that its object must be precisely this: clear and very great. Therefore, it should be understood that the cognitive processes arising in the fine-material Brahmās, who are born of sublime kamma and have very clear physical bases, for the most part have clear objects and very great objects. But some, not understanding this point, say that cognitive processes with clear objects and cognitive processes with very great objects are not found in the fine-material and immaterial planes. [The Rule of Registering Consciousness].

140. Javanesucāti casaddo pana saddattho. Chakkhattu mevavā javanti. Pakatikālepi ārammaṇassa dubbalabhāve satīti adhippāyo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpi hi pakatikāle ārammaṇadubba laṭṭhāneeva kāmāvacarajavanānaṃ chakkhattuṃ pavatti vuttāti. Keci pana chakkhattunti idaṃ mucchākālavasena vuttanti maññanti. Mandavattiyanti maraṇāsannakāle bahucittakkhaṇātītakassa vatthussa dubbalattā itarakālesuca mudutarabhāvena kenaci upadduta bhāvena ajjhotthaṭabhāvenaca vatthussa dubbalattā tannissitānaṃ javanānaṃ [M 0.0185] mandībhūtavegatā vasena pavattikāle. Maraṇakālādīsūti maraṇāsannakāle mucchākāle visaññibhūta kāle atitaruṇakāleca, tattha mucchākālonāma asayha rūpehi dukkhadhammehi atibhūtānaṃ adhimattato karajakāyassa vihaññappattikālo. Visaññi bhūtakālonāma pītivegenavā niddābhibhūtatāyavā yakkhagahaṇenavā surāmadādi vasenavā pakatisaññāya vigatakālo. Atitaruṇakālonāma gabbhagatassavā sampatijātassavā dārakassa ajjhatta vatthūnaṃ atimudukālo. Tādisesu hi kālesu antarantarā chadvārikavīthiyo pavattamānāpi yebhuyyena paripuṇṇajavanavārā na pavattanti. Dvattivoṭṭhabbanikāvā catupañcajavanikāevavā pavattantīti. Etthaca dvattivoṭṭhabbanikavārā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttā. Catupañca javanikavārā mūlaṭīkāyaṃ vuttā. Pañcavāramevāti idaṃ pana maraṇā sannakālavasena vuttaṃ. Namucchākālādivasena. Tañca khopākatikasattānaṃ vaseneva. Ye pana jhānasamanantaraṃvā paccavekkhaṇa samanantaraṃvā abhiññāsamanantaraṃvā cavantivā parinibbāyantivā. Tesaṃ jhānādīniyeva pañcavārato adhikānivā ūnānivā maraṇā sannajavanānināma hontīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayañca attho upari maraṇuppattiyaṃ āvibhavissatīti. Bhagavato pana yamakapāṭihāriya kālādīsūti ettha aññesaṃpi mahāmoggalānattherādīnaṃ evarūpo lahuppavattikālo ādisaddena saṅgahitoti daṭṭhabbo. Vuttañhi visuddhimagge ayaṃ pana matthakapattā vasī bhagavato yamakapāṭihāriye labbhati. Aññesaṃvā evarūpe kāleti. Sakalena pana vākyena thapetvā yamakapāṭihāriyasadisaṃ lahuka pavattikālaṃ aññasmiṃ kāle bhagavatopi chavā sattavā paccavekkhaṇacittāni pavattanti. Aññesaṃ pana vattabbameva natthīti dasseti. Cattāri pañcavā paccavekkhaṇacittāni bhavantīti etthapi bhagavatopi lahukappavattiyaṃ pañca paccavekkhaṇacittāni bhavanti. Lahukatarapavattiyaṃ cattārīti atthopi yujjatiyeva.

140. The particle 'ca' in 'javanesucāti', however, has the meaning of 'pana'. They impel six times. The meaning is that even in ordinary times, when the object is weak, they impel six times. Indeed, in the commentary too, it is stated that the sense-sphere javanas occur six times precisely when the object is weak in ordinary times. Some, however, think that this statement of 'six times' is said with reference to the time of fainting. By 'slow functioning' is meant the time of occurrence when the javanas dependent on that base function with diminished speed, due to the weakness of the physical base at the time near death (because the object is one for which many mind-moments have passed), and at other times due to the weakness of the physical base on account of its being more tender, afflicted by some condition, or overwhelmed. By 'at the time of death, etc.' is meant the time near death, the time of fainting, the time of being unconscious, and the time of extreme youth. Here, the time of fainting is when the physical body reaches a state of distress due to being excessively overwhelmed by unbearable painful states. The time of being unconscious is when normal perception is lost due to the force of joy, being overpowered by sleep, possession by a yakkha, or due to intoxication from liquor, etc. The time of extreme youth is when the internal bases of a child in the womb or just born are extremely tender. Indeed, during such times, even if six-door cognitive processes occur intermittently, they usually do not run as full javana courses. Instead, they occur as courses with two or three determining moments or with four or five javana moments. Here, the course with two or three determining moments is mentioned in the commentary, and the course with four or five javana moments is mentioned in the Mūlaṭīkā. 'Five times only'—this, however, is said with reference to the time near death, not with reference to the time of fainting, etc. And this, indeed, applies only to ordinary beings. However, for those who pass away or attain final Nibbāna immediately after jhāna, reviewing, or supernormal knowledge, it should be understood that their death-proximate javanas—which are precisely those jhānas, etc.—may be more or less than five. And this meaning will become clear later in the section on death and rebirth. 'At the time of the Blessed One’s Twin Miracle, etc.'—here, it should be understood that the term 'etc.' includes such a time of rapid occurrence for others as well, such as for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and others. As it is said in the Visuddhimagga: 'This mastery, having reached its peak, is obtained by the Blessed One at the Twin Miracle, or by others at such a time.' However, the entire statement shows that, except for a time of rapid occurrence similar to the Twin Miracle, at other times even for the Blessed One, reviewing cognitions occur six or seven times. For others, there is nothing to be said. 'Four or five reviewing cognitions occur'—here too, even for the Blessed One, five reviewing cognitions occur during rapid functioning, and during more rapid functioning, four occur—this meaning is also appropriate.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī,

Bhagavato [M 0.0186] cattāri aññesaṃ pañcapīti yuttaṃ viya dissatīti vuttaṃ.

it is said that it appears fitting that for the Blessed One there are four, and for others, five.

Tattha yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karonto bhagavā aggikkhandhaudaka dhārādīnaṃ dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ pāṭihāriyānaṃ pavattanatthaṃ pathamaṃ tejokasiṇe pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajji. Tato dve jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhi. Tato uparimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattatūti adhiṭṭhāsi. Tato tasmiṃyeva kasiṇe abhiññaṃ samāpajji. Abhiññāvasena uparimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattati. Tato āpokasiṇe pādakajjhānaṃ samāpajji. Tato dve jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhi. Tato heṭṭhimakāyato udakadhārā pavattantūti adhiṭṭhāsi. Tato tasmiṃyeva kasiṇe abhiññaṃ samāpajji. Abhiññāvasena heṭṭhima kāyato udakadhārā pavattanti. Sesayamakesupi eseva nayo. Etthaca lahukappavattiyā icchitattā dve dve paccavekkhaṇavārā catupañcajavanikāeva bhavanti. Dvinnañca javanavārānaṃ antarā dve eva bhavaṅgāni bhavanti. Tānica dve pāṭihāriyāni passantānaṃ ekappahāreneva pavattāni viya paññāyantīti. Etarahi pana keci ādikammikajjhānapaccavekkhaṇesupi cattāri pañcavājavanāni vadanti. Ādikammikassāti yogakammasiddhiyā ādimhi niyuttassa. Pathamaṃ uppannā appanā pathamakappanā. Tassaṃ pathamakappanāyaṃ. Ādikammikaappanāvīthiyanti attho. Tadā hi sabbānipi mahaggatajavanāni puna āsevanābhāvato paridubbalāni hontīti ekavārameva javantīti. Abhiññājavanāni pana iddhivikubbanādi. Kiccasiddhiyāeva payuttānīti kiccasiddhito paraṃ kattabbābhāvato ādikammikakālepi vasībhūtakālepi ekavārameva javantīti vuttaṃ abhiññājavanānica sabbadāpīti. Yathāca abhiññājavanādi evaṃ maggajavanānipi taṃ taṃ kilesappahānakiccasiddhito paraṃ kattabbā bhāvato ekavārameva javantīti vuttaṃ cattāro pana.La. Eka cittakkhaṇikāvāti. Athavā, maggacetanāya anantarikaphalattā sakiṃ [M 0.0187] uppanneyeva magge phalassavāro āvatoti natthi maggacittassa punuppattiyā okāsoti vuttaṃ cattāro pana.La. Ekacittakkhaṇikāvāti. Javanuppattiyā pakatiyā sattakkhuparamattā mandassa pañcamaṃ uppannamaggato paraṃ dve phalacittāni uppajjanti. Tikkhassa catutthaṃ uppannamaggato paraṃ tīṇīti vuttaṃ tato paraṃ.La. Uppajjantīti. Nirodhasamāpattikāle pana pubbabhāgeyeva tādi sassa payogābhisaṅkhārassa katattā dvinnaṃ vārānaṃ upari cittappavatti natthīti vuttaṃ nirodha.La. Javatīti. Etthaca dvikkhattunti idaṃ ukkaṭṭha niddesavasena vuttaṃ. Ekaṃvā dvevā cittavāre atikkamitvā acittako hotīti hi vuttaṃ. Catutthāruppajavananti anāgāmino kusalabhūtaṃ arahato kriyabhūtaṃ nevasaññānāsaññā yatana javanaṃ. Vuṭṭhānakāleca nirodhassa nisandamattattā ekavārameva vajanaṃ pavattatīti vuttaṃ vuṭṭhānakālecātiādi. Tattha anāgāmi phalaṃvā arahattaphalaṃvāti anāgāmiphalevā arahattaphalevā. Bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe hetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Tenāha niruddheti. Sabbatthāpi samāpattivīthiyanti jhānasamāpatti phalasamāpattivasena sakalāyapi samāpattivīthiyaṃ. Bhavaṅgasotoviya vīthiniya mo natthīti idaṃ ciṇṇavasībhūtakālaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Akatā dhikārassa pana jhānasamāpattiyaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya dve tīṇi cattārītiādinā jhānajavanāni anukkamena vaddhamānāni pavattanti. Katā dhikārānaṃ pana mahāpurisajātikānaṃ paṭiladdhakālato paṭṭhāya ciṇṇavasībhāvāneva honti. Tathā phalajavanānica sabbesaṃpi phalaṭṭhānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bahūnipīti pisaddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena ādikammikakālādīsu ekavārādivasenapi avasesānaṃ pavattiṃ sampiṇḍetīti. [Jānaniyamo].

There, while performing the Twin Miracle, the Blessed One first attained the foundational jhāna in the fire kasina in order to manifest the two miracles, namely, masses of fire and streams of water, and so forth. Then he reviewed the two jhāna factors. Then he determined, 'Let a mass of fire arise from the upper part of the body.' Then in that very kasina, he attained the higher knowledge. By means of the higher knowledge, a mass of fire arose from the upper part of the body. Then he attained the foundational jhāna in the water kasina. Then he reviewed the two jhāna factors. Then he determined, 'Let a stream of water flow from the lower part of the body.' Then in that very kasina, he attained the higher knowledge. By means of the higher knowledge, a stream of water flowed from the lower part of the body. The same method applies to the remaining twin miracles. And here, because of the desire for swift performance, the two reviewings occur in just four or five javanas. Between the two javana sequences, there are only two bhavaṅga moments. And these two miracles appear to those who see them as if they occurred simultaneously. But nowadays, some say that even in the initial reviewings of jhāna for a beginner, there are four or five javanas. 'For a beginner' means for one who is newly engaged in the practice for the accomplishment of spiritual development. The first arising of appanā is the first appanā. In that first appanā, the initial appanā process is meant. At that time, indeed, all the sublime javanas are very weak due to the lack of repeated practice, so they occur only once. But the higher knowledge javanas, such as the exercise of psychic power and transformation, are applied solely for the accomplishment of the task. Since there is nothing further to be done after the accomplishment of the task, even in the initial period and also when mastery has been attained, it has been said that they occur only once, and that higher knowledge javanas always do so. Just as the higher knowledge javanas do, so too the path javanas, having accomplished their task of abandoning particular defilements, there being nothing further to do, occur only once. It is said, 'The four (path moments) are of a single moment of consciousness.' Alternatively, because the path consciousness is immediately followed by fruition, there is no opportunity for the path consciousness to arise again, as the turn for fruition has arrived with the single arising of the path. Therefore it is said, 'The four (path moments) are of a single moment of consciousness.' By nature, the arising of javana is limited to a maximum of seven moments. For a person with dull faculties, after the path consciousness has arisen as the fifth javana, two fruition consciousnesses arise. For a person with keen faculties, after the path consciousness has arisen as the fourth javana, three arise. It is said that thereafter they arise. But in the attainment of cessation, since the volitional formation of such an effort has been made in the preceding phase, there is no arising of consciousness beyond two sequences. It is said that in cessation, the mind does not run. And here, 'twice' is said in terms of an extreme designation. For it is said that after one or two cognitive processes have passed, one becomes without consciousness. The fourth arūpa-jhāna javana is the karmically wholesome state for the non-returner and the functional state for the arahant, namely, the javana of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And at the time of emerging from cessation, because it is merely the outflow of cessation, only a single javana occurs. It is said, 'And at the time of emergence, etc.' There, 'whether it is the fruition of the non-returner or the fruition of the arahant' means in the fruition of the non-returner or in the fruition of the arahant. This is a locative statement indicating the characteristic of being. Therefore, he said, 'when ceased'. 'In all cases of the attainment process' means in the entire attainment process, whether jhāna attainment or fruition attainment. There is no fixed sequence like the stream of the life-continuum. This is said with reference to a time when one has become accustomed and mastered. But for one who has not yet gained proficiency, in jhāna attainment, from the very beginning, two, three, four, etc., jhāna javanas arise successively, increasing in number. But for those who have gained proficiency, for those of the nature of great persons, from the time of having attained the ability, they are always in a state of practiced mastery. Similarly, fruition javanas should be understood as occurring for all those who have attained fruition. In 'bahūnipi' (many also), the particle 'pi' has the meaning of inclusion. Thus it includes, by grouping them together, the occurrence of the remaining javanas in the initial period and so on, which may occur only once, and so forth. [Regulation of Knowledge].

141. Evaṃ pubbāparaniyāmavasena vīthicittānaṃ pavattiṃ dassetvā idāni puggalabhedavasena bhūmibhedavasenaca tesaṃ pavattiṃ dassento duhetukānantiādimāha. Paṭisandhiviññāṇasahagatā dve hetuyo etesanti duhetukā. Catūhi ñāṇavippa yuttamahāvipākehi [M 0.0188] gahitapaṭisandhikā. Dvīhi pana ahetuka vipākehi gahita paṭisandhikā ahetukā natthi paṭisandhihetu etesanti katvā. Tesaṃ dvinnaṃpi vipākāvaraṇasabbhāvato mahagga tajjhānānipi tāva nuppajjanti. Kuto lokuttarāni. Kriyajavanāni pana khīṇāsavānameva āvenika bhūtānīti vuttaṃ kriyajavanāni cevaappanājavanānica na labbhantīti. Tattha vipākā varaṇaṃ nāma ahetuka paṭisandhikatā dvihetuka paṭisandhikatāca. Tathā ñāṇasampayuttavipākānica sugatiyanti sugati bhave pariyāpannānaṃ tesaṃ dvinnaṃ tathā ñāṇampayuttamahāvipākānica na labbhantīti attho. Etthaca sugatiyanti etena duggatipariyāpanne ahetuka puggale nivatteti. Na hi tesaṃ imasmiṃ vākye itaresaṃ anuññātāni ñāṇavippayuttavipākānipi labbhantīti. Tenāha duggati yaṃ panātiādi. Tattha duggatiyaṃ pariyāpannānaṃ ahetukānaṃ ñāṇasampayuttavipākānica ñāṇavippayuttāni mahāvipākānica na labbhantīti paripuṇṇa yojanā daṭṭhabbā. Ettha siyā. Kasmā panettha sugatipariyāpannānaṃ ahetukānaṃ cattāri ñāṇasampayuttavipākāni duggatipariyāpannānañca aṭṭhapi sahetuka mahāvipākāni na labbhantīti vuttaṃ. Nanu paṭṭhāne sahetukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ ahetukassa bhavaṅgassa anantarapaccayena paccayoti vuttaṃ. Ettha hi ekasmiṃ bhave ekassa sattassa kadāci sahetukaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ kadāci ahetukaṃ bhavaṅganti evaṃ mūlabhavaṅge pavattibhedo natthīti katvā sahetukaṃ bhavaṅganti idaṃ tadārammaṇasaṅkhātaṃ āgantukabhavaṅgaṃ sandhāya vuttanti viññāyati. Sahetukantica sāmaññavacanattā dvihetukaṃ tihetukañca tadārammaṇaṃ viññātabbaṃ hoti. Ahetukassa bhavaṅgassāti idha pana tassa tadārammaṇassa anantaraṃ uppannaṃ mūlabhavaṅgameva adhippetaṃ. Idhapi sāmaññavacanattā dvīsu a- ahetukabhavaṅgesu yaṃkiñci gahetabbamevāti. Tasmā dvinnaṃ ahetukānaṃpi aṭṭhasahetuka tadārammaṇānipi labbhamānānieva siyuṃ. Duhetukānaṃ pana vattabbameva natthīti. Vuccate, ahetu kesu [M 0.0189] tāva duggatipariyāpannānaṃ sahetukatadārammaṇasambhavo sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhitto. Tasmā ahetukassa bhavaṅgassāti idaṃ kusalavipākabhūtaṃ ahetukabhavaṅgaṃ sandhāya vuttanti yuttaṃ. Ayañhi paṭṭhāne dhammatā. Yadidaṃ yathālābhagahaṇanti. Itarathā sabbaaṭṭhakathāvirodho siyāti. Yathāca kusalānaṃ yogasādhanīyattā pavattiyaṃpi yogakammavasena ñāṇayogo hoti. Na tathā vipākānaṃ. Tesaṃ pana ayogasādhanī yattā pavattiyaṃ bhavaṅgañāṇasaṅkhātena upanissayaññāṇena vinā ñāṇayogo na sambhavati. Tasmā sahetukaṃ bhavaṅganti idhapi ñāṇavippayuttabhūtaṃ sahetukatadārammaṇameva gahetuṃ yuttanti katvā dvihetukānaṃ ahetukānañca ñāṇasampayuttatadārammaṇa paṭikkhepo therena katoti. Ācariyabuddhadattattherena pana yena vipākacittena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti. Tena sadisaṃ vā tato hīnaṃ vā tadārammaṇaṃ tesaṃ sambhavati. Na paṇītanti katvā dvinnaṃpi ahetukānaṃ aṭṭhamahāvipākāni paṭikkhipitvā sattatiṃsacittapaṭi lābho vutto. So pana yathā vuttapaṭṭhānapāḷiyā virujjhati. Apare pana yathā ahetukānaṃ sugatipariyāpannānaṃ dvihetuka tadārammaṇaṃ hoti. Evaṃ dvihetukānaṃpi tihetukatadārammaṇaṃ sambhavatīti vadanti. Taṃ yuttaṃviya dissati. Aṭṭhakathāyañhi katthaci tesaṃ dvinnaṃpi avisesena aṭṭhamahāvipākapavatti vuttāti. Paṭisandhiviññāṇa sahagatā tayo hetū etesanti tihetukā. Te pana kāmarūpārūpavasena tividhā honti. Puthujjano aṭṭhaariyācāti navavidhā. Tesu khīṇāsavānaṃ kusalākusala javanānica nalabbhanti. Sabbaso anusayapahānena sabbesaṃ kusalākusalānaṃ saha niruddhattā anusaya paṭibaddho hi tesaṃ tabbhāvoti. Tathāsaddo pakkhantarattho. Apariniṭṭhitasikkhākiccatāya sikkhanasīlayuttā sattaariyā sekkhānāma. Idha pana tayo heṭṭhimaphalaṭṭhā adhippetā. Tesañhi ādito sotāpattimaggeneva diṭṭhivicikicchānaṃ pahīnattā taṃ sahagatāni [M 0.0190] pañcajavanāni nalabbhantīti. Anāgāmipuggalānaṃ pana paṭighajavanānica na labbhanti. Anāgāmimaggena pahīnattā. Maggassa pana ekacittakkhaṇikattā. Catunnaṃ maggaṭṭhānaṃ paccekaṃ yathāsakaṃ maggajavanānieva labbhanti. Uparimānañca phalānaṃ heṭṭhimehi puggalehi anamigatattā heṭṭhimānañca uparimesu puggalantaresu anuppajjanato catunnaṃ phalaṭṭhānaṃpi paccekaṃ yathāsakaṃ phalajavanānieva labbhantīti vuttaṃ lokuttara.La. Samuppajjantīti. Etthaca uparimagge āgate heṭṭhimamaggānubhāvassa sabbaso paṭipassaddhivasena uparimānaṃ puggalantaratāsiddhi veditabbāti. Idāni tesaṃ tesaṃ puggalānaṃ pārisesato labbhamānavīthicittāni dassetuṃ gāthamāha. Pariniṭṭhi tasikkhākiccattā natthi sikkhitabbakiccaṃ etesanti asekkhā. Khīṇāsavā. Tesaṃ tevīsatikāmavipāka vīsatikriya arahattaphala vasena catucattālīsa vīthicittāni sambhavā yathāsambhavaṃ uddise. Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ diṭṭhivicikicchājavanavajjitānaṃ sattannaṃ akusalānaṃ ekavīsatiyā kusalānaṃ tevīsatiyā kāmavipākānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ heṭṭhimaphalānaṃ āvajjanadvayassaca vasena chapaññāsa vīthicittāni sambhavā uddise. Avasesānaṃ catunnaṃ puthujjanānaṃ kāmavipāka lokiyakusalākulāvajjana dvayavasena catupaññāsa vīthicittāni sambhavā uddiseti yojanā. Puggala bhedena vīthicittānaṃ bhedo puggalabhedo.

141. Having thus shown the occurrence of thought-processes according to the sequence of prior and subsequent moments, he now states their occurrence based on the distinctions of individuals and planes, beginning with 'those with two roots.' Those whose rebirth-consciousness is accompanied by two roots are called 'duhetuka' (two-rooted). They have taken rebirth with the four great resultant consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge. However, those who have taken rebirth with the two rootless resultant consciousnesses are called 'ahetuka' (rootless), because there are no roots for their rebirth. For these two, even the sublime jhānas do not arise due to the presence of resultant obstruction. How much less the supramundane states! But functional impulsions are exclusively for the arahants; thus it is said that functional impulsions and absorption impulsions are not obtained. Here, 'resultant obstruction' refers to rootless rebirth and two-rooted rebirth. Similarly, it is meant that for those two types of individuals (ahetuka and duhetuka) who are included in happy destinies, resultant consciousnesses associated with knowledge, including the great resultant consciousnesses associated with knowledge, are not obtained. Here, by 'in happy destinies,' he excludes rootless individuals included in unhappy destinies. For indeed, in this statement, even resultant consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge, which are permitted for others, are not obtained by them. Therefore, he says, 'But in the unhappy destinies,' etc. There, the complete explanation should be understood as: for the rootless beings included in the unhappy destinies, neither resultant consciousnesses associated with knowledge nor great resultant consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge are obtained. Here, one might ask: Why is it said here that for the rootless beings included in happy destinies, the four resultant consciousnesses associated with knowledge are not obtained, and for those included in unhappy destinies, the eight great resultant consciousnesses with roots are not obtained? Surely, in the Paṭṭhāna, it is said that a rooted bhavaṅga is a condition for a rootless bhavaṅga by way of the immediately contiguous condition. For in this case, it is understood that in one existence, for one being, there is no difference in the occurrence of the fundamental bhavaṅga, such that sometimes it is rooted and sometimes rootless. Therefore, 'rooted bhavaṅga' is said here with reference to the adventitious bhavaṅga known as tadārammaṇa. And since 'rooted' is a general term, both two-rooted and three-rooted tadārammaṇa should be understood. But here, by 'rootless bhavaṅga,' only the fundamental bhavaṅga that arises immediately after that tadārammaṇa is intended. Here too, due to its generality, any of the two rootless bhavaṅgas must be taken. Therefore, even for the two types of rootless beings, the eight rooted tadārammaṇas could be obtained. For the two-rooted, it goes without saying. It is said that in all the commentaries, the possibility of rooted tadārammaṇa for rootless beings included in unhappy destinies is rejected. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that 'rootless bhavaṅga' here refers to the rootless bhavaṅga that is a wholesome resultant. For this is the natural principle in the Paṭṭhāna, namely, 'taking what is available.' Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with all the commentaries. And just as in the occurrence of wholesome states, there is an association with knowledge due to their being attainable by effort and by way of the action of effort, it is not so with resultant states. But since their occurrence is not attainable by effort, an association with knowledge is not possible without the supporting knowledge, which is called bhavaṅga-knowledge. Therefore, considering that here too 'rooted bhavaṅga' should be taken only as the rooted tadārammaṇa dissociated from knowledge, the Elder made the rejection of tadārammaṇa associated with knowledge for both the two-rooted and the rootless. But Ācariya Buddhadatta Thera, having stated that the tadārammaṇa for those beings is possible if it is similar to or inferior to the resultant consciousness by which they take rebirth, but not superior, and having rejected the eight great resultant consciousnesses for both rootless types, mentioned the attainment of thirty-seven consciousnesses. However, that contradicts the aforementioned Paṭṭhāna text. Others, however, say that just as two-rooted tadārammaṇa occurs for rootless beings included in happy destinies, similarly, three-rooted tadārammaṇa is possible for two-rooted beings. That appears reasonable. For in the commentaries, the occurrence of the eight great resultant consciousnesses for both types is sometimes mentioned without distinction. Those whose rebirth-consciousness is accompanied by three roots are called 'tihetuka' (three-rooted). They are threefold according to the sense-sphere, form sphere, and formless sphere. They are ninefold: ordinary persons and the eight noble ones. Of these, neither wholesome nor unwholesome impulsions are obtained by arahants, because all wholesome and unwholesome states have entirely ceased with the abandonment of latent tendencies, for their existence is bound to those tendencies. The word 'tathā' (similarly) has the meaning of another aspect. Because their task of training is not yet completed, the seven noble ones endowed with the practice of training are called 'sekkhā' (trainees). But here, the three lower fruition-attainers are intended. For them, from the very beginning, with the path of stream-entry, the five impulsions accompanied by wrong view and doubt are not obtained, because those have been abandoned. But for non-returners, impulsions connected with aversion are also not obtained, because they have been abandoned by the path of non-returning. But since the path is momentary (of one citta-moment), for the four path-attainers, only their respective path impulsions are obtained. And since the higher fruitions are not attained by the lower individuals, and since the lower fruitions do not arise in the higher individuals as intermediate states, it is said that for the four fruition-attainers, only their respective fruition impulsions arise as supramundane states. Here, it should be understood that when a higher path has arisen, the distinct attainment of higher individuals is due to the complete subsidence of the influence of the lower path. Now, to show the thought-process consciousnesses obtainable by each of those individuals by way of remainder, he speaks a verse: Because their task of training is completed, and there is no task to be trained for by them, they are called 'asekhā' (non-trainees). They are the arahants. For them, you should point out the forty-four thought-process consciousnesses that are possible, namely, twenty-three sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, twenty functional consciousnesses, and the fruition of arahantship. For the seven trainees, you should point out the fifty-six thought-process consciousnesses that are possible, namely, the seven unwholesome impulsions excluding those associated with wrong view and doubt, twenty-one wholesome impulsions, twenty-three sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, the three lower fruitions, and the two adverting moments. For the remaining four ordinary persons, you should point out the fifty-four thought-process consciousnesses that are possible, namely, the sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses, mundane wholesome and unwholesome impulsions, and the two adverting moments. This is the explanation. The distinction of thought-process consciousnesses by way of individual distinction is individual distinction.

142. Sabbānipi vīthicittāni upalabbhanti puggalānaṃ dvārānañca ettheva paripuṇṇasambhavato. Yathārahanti taṃ taṃ bhūmipuggalānaṃ uppattiarahānurūpaṃ. Rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ vajjitabbesu soḷasavīthi cittesu channaṃ cittānaṃ uparivākye vuccamānattā paṭighajavana tadārammaṇa vajjitānīti vuttaṃ. Arūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ pathamamagga rūpāvacarahasana heṭṭhimāruppavajjitāni paṭighajavana tadārammaṇavajjitānica vīthi cittāni labbhantīti yojanā. Etthāpi vajjitabbesu aṭṭhatiṃsa vīthicittesu soḷasannaṃ cittānaṃ uparivuccamānatā daṭṭhabbā. Sabbatthāpīti sabbāsupi rūpārūpabhūmīsu. Taṃtaṃ pasādarahitānaṃ taṃtaṃdvārika vīthicittāni [M 0.0191] na labbhantevāti rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ tāva ghānādittayaṃ natthīti ghānajivhākāyapasāda rahitānaṃ rūpībrahmānaṃ ghāna jivhākāyadvārikāni cha vīthicittāni nalabbhanteva. Yāni sandhāya channaṃ cittānaṃ uparivākye vuccamānattāti heṭṭhā vuttaṃ. Arūpabhūmiyaṃ pana pañcapi pasādā natthīti pañcadvārikāni dvipañcaviññāṇa manodhā tuttika santīraṇattayavasena soḷasavīthicittāni nalabbhanteva. Yāni sandhāya soḷasannaṃ cittānaṃ upari vuccamānatāti vuttaṃ. Kāmabhūmiyaṃ pana taṃtaṃ pasādarahitatā jaccandhādīnaṃ vasena yo jetabbā. Kāme asīti vīthicittāni yathārahaṃ labbhare labbhanti. Rūpe catusaṭṭhi tathā yathārahaṃ labbhare. Arūpe dve cattālīsa yathārahaṃ labbhareti yojanā. Etthaca brahmalokevā upari chakāmāvacara devalokesuvā aniṭṭhārammaṇāni nāma natthi. Tasmā rūpāvacarabhūmiyaṃ catunnaṃ akusalavipākānaṃ labbhamānatāvacanaṃ tattha ṭhatvāvā idha āgantvāvā idha anaṭṭhehi rūpasaddehi samāgacchantānaṃ vasena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Keci pana idha āgatānaṃyeva brahmānaṃ aniṭṭhārammaṇasamāyogo hotīti thāni cattāri rūpabhūmiyaṃ laddhānināma na honti. Tasmā tattha saṭṭhiyeva vīthicittānīti vadanti. Taṃ na yujjati. Idha āgatānaṃyeva uppannānipi brahmattabhāve uppannattā brahmaloke uppannāni icceva vattabbattā. Naca tattha ṭhitāpi idha aniṭṭhāni nagaṇhanti. Dūrepi ārammaṇaṃ gahetuṃ samatthattā brahmānanti.

142. All process-consciousnesses are found in individuals and their doors, as their complete arising is possible in this very place. They are appropriate according to the suitability of arising for those individuals in their respective planes. In the fine-material plane, among the sixteen process-consciousnesses to be excluded, it is said that six consciousnesses are excluded—as mentioned in the preceding passage—because aversion javanas and tadārammaṇa are excluded. In the immaterial plane, process-consciousnesses are found, excluding those of the first path, the fine-material smile, and the lower immaterial states, and also excluding aversion javanas and tadārammaṇa; such is the connection. Here too, among the thirty-eight process-consciousnesses to be excluded, the sixteen consciousnesses mentioned above should be understood. 'In all places' means in all fine-material and immaterial planes. For those lacking the respective sense faculties, the respective door-process-consciousnesses are not found. For instance, in the fine-material plane, the three faculties—nose, tongue, and body—are absent. Thus, for the Rūpa Brahmās who lack the nose, tongue, and body sense faculties, the six process-consciousnesses of the nose-, tongue-, and body-doors are not found. This is what was stated below, referring to the six consciousnesses mentioned in the preceding passage. In the immaterial plane, however, the five sense faculties are absent. Therefore, the sixteen process-consciousnesses—namely, the ten sense-consciousnesses, the mind-element triad, and the three investigating consciousnesses—do not arise. This is what was meant by the statement above regarding the sixteen consciousnesses. In the sense-sphere plane, however, the lack of respective sense faculties should be connected with cases such as those of the congenitally blind. In the sense-sphere, eighty process-consciousnesses are found as appropriate. In the fine-material sphere, sixty-four are found accordingly. In the immaterial sphere, forty-two are found as suitable; such is the connection. And here, in the Brahmā worlds or in the six higher sense-sphere divine realms, there are no disagreeable objects. Therefore, the statement that the four unwholesome resultant consciousnesses are found in the fine-material plane should be understood with reference to those who, while abiding there or having come here, encounter disagreeable forms and sounds here. Some, however, say that only Brahmās who have come here experience disagreeable objects, and therefore these four types are not considered to be found in the fine-material plane. Thus, they say only sixty process-consciousnesses are found there. This is not correct. For even those consciousnesses that arise for those who have come here are said to arise in the Brahmā world because they arise within the Brahmā existence. And it is not that those who abide there do not grasp disagreeable objects here, for Brahmās are capable of grasping an object even from afar.

[140] Yañca vibhāvaniyaṃ

That which is to be explained.

Tassa vādassa paṭikkhipanatthaṃ vuttaṃ “idha pana tattha ṭhatvāpi imaṃ lokaṃ passantānaṃ aniṭṭhārammaṇassa asambhavo na sakkā vattu”nti. Tena tattha ṭhatvā imaṃ lokaṃ passantānaṃ uppannāni tāni cattāri cittāni tattha laddhānināma honti. Idha āgatānaṃ uppannāni idha laddhānināma hontīti anuññātaṃ hoti. Tañca na yuttaṃ.

To refute that view, it is said: 'Here, however, it is not possible to state the non-occurrence of a disagreeable object for those who, while abiding there, see this world.' By this, those four consciousnesses that arise for those who, abiding there, see this world, are said to be obtained there. And it is acknowledged that those that arise for those who have come here are said to be obtained here. But that is not correct.

Taṃ taṃ bhūmipariyāpanne sattasantāne uppannānieva taṃtaṃbhūmiyaṃ uppannānīti siddhattā. Iccevantiādi mahānigamanaṃ. Yathāsambhavanti taṃ taṃ bhūmipuggaladvārārammaṇesu sambhavānurūpaṃ. Bhavaṅgena antaritā bhavaṅgantaritā. Yāvatāyukanti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave bhavanikanti vīthito paṭṭhāya yattakaṃ kālaṃ jīvitasantānaṃ pavattati. Tattakaṃ kālanti attho. Abbhocchinnā pavattati asati nirodha samāpattiyanti adhippāyo.

Because it is established that whatever arises in the mental continuum of a being included in a particular plane is indeed what arises in that particular plane. 'Thus, and so forth' is the great conclusion. 'According to possibility' means according to the suitability of arising in the respective planes, individuals, doors, and objects. 'Interrupted by the life-continuum' means separated by the life-continuum. 'For as long as life lasts' means for as long as the life-continuum persists in that particular existence, from the cognitive process onwards; 'for that length of time' is the meaning. 'It flows unbroken'—the intention is that it persists without interruption, in the absence of the attainment of cessation.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus, of the commentary on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, named the Paramatthadīpanī,

Catutthavaṇṇanāya vīthi saṅgahassa

of the fourth exposition on the Compendium of Cognitive Processes,

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The Paramatthadīpanī is concluded.

Vīthimutta saṅgaha paramatthadīpanī

The Paramatthadīpanī on the Compendium of the Process-Freed.

143. Evaṃ [M 0.0193] pavattikāle pavattisaṅgahaṃ dassetvā idāni paṭisandhiyaṃ pavattisaṅgahaṃ dassetuṃ ādigātha māha. Evaṃ vuttanayena pavattiyaṃ pavattisaṅgahonāma vīthicittavasena udīritokathito. Idāni sandhiyaṃ pavattisaṅgaho nāma vīthimutta cittānaṃ vasena vuccatīti yojanā. Etthaca paṭisandhiyaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ pavattiyā kathitāya tato paraṃ bhavaṅgakāleca cutikāleca tesaṃ pavatti kathitāyeva hotīti katvā sandhiyamicceva vuttaṃ.

143. Having thus shown the Compendium of Occurrence during the course of life, now, to show the Compendium of Occurrence at rebirth-linking, he states the initial verse. In this way, the Compendium of Occurrence during the course of life has been declared and explained in terms of process-consciousnesses. Now, the Compendium of Occurrence at rebirth-linking is stated in terms of process-freed consciousnesses; such is the connection. And here, since by explaining the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors at rebirth-linking, their occurrence during the life-continuum and at death is also thereby explained, only 'at rebirth-linking' is stated.

[141] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[141] Now, the explanation:

Parato maraṇuppattiyaṃ pathamaṃ cutiṃ dassetvā pacchā anantare paṭisandhiyā vakkhamānattā idha sandhiggahaṇena atītā nantara cutipi gahetabbāti adhippāyena yaṃ vuttaṃ “tadāsannatāya taṃgahaṇeneva gahitacutikālecā”ti. Taṃ na yujjatiyeva.

Because decease is first shown in the subsequent section on the process of dying, and rebirth-linking is to be spoken of immediately after, the intention here is that by the term 'rebirth-linking', the immediately preceding decease should also be included. Thus, what was said—'and the moment of decease is included by that very term due to its proximity'—is not correct at all.

Vīthimuttānañhi visayappavattināma atītānantarabhave maraṇuppattiyaṃeva siddhāti ekasmiṃ bhave visayappapattiyā saha tesaṃ paṭisandhipamukhānaṃ vīthimuttacittānaṃ pavattidassanatthaṃeva tāya atītānantaracutiyā saddhiṃ maraṇuppattividhānaṃ therena dassitanti. Bhavanti sattā saṅkhārāca etāsūti bhūmiyo. Ayoti vaḍḍhi. Atthato pana sukhaṃca sukhahetu sukhapaccayāca veditabbā. Yebhuyyena tato ayato apagatā ettha nibbattā sattāti apāyo. Soeva bhūmīti apāyabhūmi. Oḷārikena kāmarāgena kāmīyatīti kāmo. Gantabbā upagantabbāti gati. Gacchanti sattā etthātivā gati. Anekavidhasampattīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānatāya sobhaṇāgati sugati. Kāmoca so sugaticāti samāso. Natthi yathāvutto ayo etthāti nirayo. Niccaṃ vā rayanti kampanti phandanti [M 0.0194] sattā dukkhappattā etthāti nirayo. Manussā viya uddhaṃ uccā ahutvā tiro añcitā āyatāti tiracchānā. Yuvanti nānā vaṇṇasaṇṭhānāpi sattā samānajātitāya ekībhūtāviya honti etāyāti yoni. Jāti.

Indeed, the occurrence of an object for the process-freed consciousnesses is established only at the process of dying in the immediately preceding existence. It is precisely to show the occurrence of those process-freed consciousnesses—headed by rebirth-linking—together with the presentation of an object in a single existence, that the Elder has shown the procedure of the process of dying along with that immediately preceding decease. 'Beings and formations exist in these'; therefore, they are planes (bhūmi). 'Ayo' means prosperity. By meaning, however, happiness, the cause of happiness, and the conditions for happiness should be understood. Because beings born here are for the most part devoid of that prosperity, it is a state of loss (apāya). That very plane is the plane of loss (apāyabhūmi). It is desired through gross sensual passion; therefore, it is sensuality (kāma). 'It is to be gone to, to be approached'; therefore, it is a destination (gati). Or, 'beings go here'; therefore, it is a destination. Because it is the basis for many kinds of success, a good destination is a happy state (sugati). 'Kāma' and 'sugati' form a compound. 'There is no aforementioned prosperity in it'; therefore, it is hell (niraya). Or, 'beings who have met with suffering constantly cry out, tremble, and throb in it'; therefore, it is niraya. 'Not being upright and tall like humans, they move horizontally'; therefore, they are animals (tiracchāna). 'Beings of various colors and forms become as if mixed and unified by it through common birth'; therefore, it is an origin (yoni). It also means birth (jāti).

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

Now, the explanation:

Khandhānaṃ pavattivisesoti vuttaṃ.

It is said to be the distinctive occurrence of the aggregates.

Tiracchānānaṃ yoni tiracchānayoni. Pecca itā gatāti petā. Ito apakkamma cavitvā bhavantare gatāti attho. Yekeci kālaṅkatā. Divaṅgatāpi hi loke kālaṅkatā petāti vuccanti. Idha pana sukhasamussayato pecca pakaṭṭhaṃ pavāsaṃ dūraṃ gatāti atthena yāva tato na muccanti. Tāva niccaṃ dukkhappattā lakkhaṇasaṃyuttādīsu āgatā tatīyā apāyikasattā adhippetā. Petānaṃ samūho petti. Pettiyā visayoti petti visayo. Visayotica pavattideso vuccati. Asurakāyoti ettha surā vuccanti upari devā suranti iddhivisesehi dibbanti, suṭṭhuvā ramanti kāmasukharatiṃ paccanubhavantīti katvā. Na surāti asurā. Vepacitti pahārādādayo sandhāya surapaṭipakkhā sura sadisāvāti attho. Viyaṅkaramātā uttaramātādayo vini pātike sandhāya khuddakasurā cūḷakasurāti attho. Yamarājā dayo vemānikapete sandhāya ekadesena surasadisāti attho. Vemānikapetāpi hi katthaci asurakāyāti āgatā. Lokantarika nerayike sandhāya sabbaso suraguṇa rahitāti attho. Tepi hi buddhavaṃsanidānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ jātidukkha niddesesuca asurakāyāti vuttā. Tathā kālakañcikapete sandhāya sabbaso surabhāvarahitāti attho. Iti pañcannaṃ asurānaṃ vasena atthavibhāgo veditabbo. Dibbā vata bhokāyā parihāyissanti, paripūrissanti asurakāyāti imasmiṃ suttapade cattāropi apāyā asurakāyāti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vaṇṇitā.

The origin of animals is the animal origin. Having passed away from here, they are gone; thus they are petas. The meaning is: having departed from here, passed away, and gone to another existence. Whoever has died. Indeed, even those who have gone to heaven are, in the world, called 'the departed' or 'the gone' (petas). Here, however, it is intended to mean the third class of beings of the woeful states, mentioned in the Lakkhaṇasaṃyutta and so forth, who, having passed away from an accumulation of happiness, have gone far away to a wretched state, and for as long as they are not freed from that, they are constantly afflicted by suffering. The collection of petas is petti. The domain of petti is the petti domain. And visaya is called the place of occurrence. As for the asura-host: herein, the gods above are called suras because they shine with special powers and revel, greatly delighting in and experiencing sensual joys. Not suras are asuras. With reference to Vepacitti, Pahārāda, and others, the meaning is that they are opponents of the suras or resemble the suras. With reference to Viyaṅkaramātā, Uttaramātā, and others among the fallen ones, the meaning is that they are minor asuras or lesser asuras. With reference to Yamarāja and others among the vemānika-petas, the meaning is that they are in some respects like the suras. Indeed, vemānika-petas are also sometimes referred to as the asura-host. With reference to the lokantarika hell-beings, the meaning is that they are entirely devoid of the qualities of the suras. Indeed, they too are called the asura-host in the commentary on the introduction to the Buddhavaṃsa and in the expositions on the suffering of birth. Similarly, with reference to the kālakañcika-petas, the meaning is that they are entirely lacking in the state of suras. Thus, the division of meaning should be understood according to these five kinds of asuras. In this Sutta passage, 'Alas, the divine hosts of enjoyers will decline, the asura hosts will flourish,' all four woeful states are described in the commentary as the asura-host.

Tattha [M 0.0195] vepacitti pahārādādayo asurā tāva tiṃsesu devesu saṅgahitā. Vinipātikāsurā cātumahārājikadevesu. Tathā vemānikapetāsurā. Tepi hi vinipātikāsurā viya tihetukāpi duhetukāpi ahetukāpi hontīti aṭṭhakathāsu vuttā. Yamarājāno pana vessabhū nottica petti rājā somo yamo vessavaṇoca rājāti evaṃ kathā vatthupāḷiyaṃ āgatā vessabhūādayo sayaṃ mahiddhikā mahānubhāvā vemānikapetarājāno hutvāpi nerayikesu sattesu kāruññataṃ paṭicca heṭṭhā nirayalokesupi rajjaṃ kārentiyeva. Teneva hi sabbe petalokāpi nirayalokāpi yamalo kātica yamavisayātica vuccantīti. Yeca cātumahārājikapari yāpannā pāpajjhāsayā kururakammakārino revativimāne yakkhāti āgatā saṃkiccajātake rakkhasāti āgatā yakkharakkhasānāma ito gantvā ussadanirayesu nerayikānaṃ nānākamma kāraṇāyo karonto vicaranti. Tesaṃpi kālo upakāloti evamādīhi nāmehi nāradajātake āgatānaṃ niraya pālānaṃ upariyamarājānaṃ āṇāpavattatiyevāti. Lokantarikā surā niraye saṅgahitā. Idha pana kālakañcikādayo petāsurāva adhippetā. Tesaṃ asurānaṃ kāyo samūhoti asurakāyo. Etthaca nirayabhūmināma paccekaṃ soḷasussadapari vārānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ mahānirayānaṃ vasena anto pathaviyaṃ ṭhitāti veditabbā. Arañña pabbata samudda dīpakādīsupi nānāniraya bhūmiyo hontiyeva. Tasmā tādisassa visuṃ vavatthitassa okāsassa atthitāya nirayotveva vuttā. Sesānaṃ pana tissannaṃ apāyabhummīnaṃ tādisassa okāsassa natthitāya yoni visaya kāya saddehi yojetvā khandhāvā khandhappavattipadesāvā gahitāti. [Apāyabhūmi]

Therein, the asuras such as Vepacitti and Pahārāda are included among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. The Vinipātika Asuras are among the Cātumahārājika devas. Likewise, the Vemānikapeta Asuras. For they too, like the Vinipātika Asuras, can be with three roots, with two roots, or without roots, as is stated in the commentaries. However, the Yama kings—Vessabhū, Nottica, the Petti king, Soma, Yama, and King Vessavaṇa—are mentioned thus in the Kathāvatthupāḷi. Though they themselves are mighty and powerful vemānikapeta kings, out of compassion for beings in the hells, they also govern the lower hell realms. Therefore, all the peta worlds and hell worlds are called Yama's world and Yama's domain. And those included in the Cātumahārājika realm, of evil disposition and performers of cruel deeds, who are mentioned as yakkhas in the Revativimāna and as rakkhasas in the Saṅkiccajātaka—these yakkhas and rakkhasas, having gone from here, wander about in the Ussada hells, inflicting various torments on the hell-beings. The command of the superior Yama kings prevails even over the hell-guardians mentioned in the Nāradajātake with names such as Kāla and Upakāla. The Lokantarika Asuras are included in hell. Here, however, the Kālakañcika and other peta-asuras are intended. The body (kāyo), meaning the collection, of these asuras is the asura-host. And here, the hell-plane should be understood as being situated within the earth, consisting of the eight great hells, each surrounded by sixteen Ussada hells. Indeed, various hell-planes also exist in forests, mountains, oceans, islands, and so forth. Therefore, because such a distinct, established location exists, they are simply called 'hells.' But for the remaining three woeful planes, because there is no such location, they are understood as aggregates or as the place where aggregates arise, being designated by the terms 'womb,' 'domain,' and 'host.' [Apāyabhūmi]

Ussito uggato ussannovā mano etesanti manussā. Tehi anantesu cakkavāḷesupi itarabhūmikānaṃ sattānaṃ tikkhatarasūra vicitracittā honti. Paripuṇṇānaṃ kusalākusalakamma pathānaṃ [M 0.0196] ānantariyakammānañca ettheva sambhavatoti. Tesupi pana jambudīpavāsinoeva atisayena ussitamanā honti. Itare pana tehi samānavaṇṇāditāya manussā icceva vuccanti. Imasmiṃ cakkavāḷe pana vattabbameva natthi, yathāha-tīhi bhikkhave ṭhāne hi jambudīpakā manussā uttarakuruke manusse adhiggaṇhanti. Deveca tāvatiṃse. Katamehi tīhi ṭhānehi. Sūrāca sati mantoca idha brahmacariyavāsocāti. Akkharacintakā pana vadanti manūti mahāsammatarājā vuccati. Imeca janā tena thapitesu mariyādadhammesu ṭhitā tassa puttaṭṭhāniyā honti. Tasmā manuno apaccā puttāti manussāti. Idha pana bhūmipariyāyoti katvā manussāti itthiliṅgaṃ ekavacanañca katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ sese supi. Yesu pana cattāro mahārājāno rajjaṃ kārenti. Te devā cātumahārājikā. Tattha dhataraṭṭho gandhappānaṃ rājā hoti. Viruḷhako kumbhaṇḍānaṃ. Virūpakkho nāgānaṃ. Kuvero yakkhānaṃ. Tattha paṭisandhivasena gandharukkhesu appenti upagacchantīti gandhappā. Gandharukkhādhivatthā devā. Te mūlagandhādivasena dasadhā pāḷiyaṃ āgatā. Kumbhaṇḍāti dānavarakkhasā. Nāgā yakkhāca pākaṭā. Sabbe te yebhuyyena pāpajjhāsayā kururakammakārino ca honti. Tasmā cattāro mahārājāno aññamaññaṃvā manussānaṃ vā aviheṭhanatthāya tesu nānārājānaṃvā nānāsenāpatiṃvā thapesuṃ.

Their mind is lofty, exalted, or abundant; therefore they are humans (manussā). Therefore, even in endless world-systems, they are sharper, more courageous, and more diverse in mind than beings of other planes. Because it is only here that the complete paths of wholesome and unwholesome kamma and the deeds with immediate result are possible. Yet, among them, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa are especially exalted in mind. The others, however, are called 'humans' simply because of their similar appearance and so forth. In this world-system, however, there is nothing more to be said of their superiority, as it is stated: 'Monks, in three respects the humans of Jambudīpa excel the humans of Uttarakuru and the Tāvatiṃsa devas. What are the three? They are courageous, they are mindful, and here the holy life is lived.' Etymologists, however, say that 'Manu' refers to the great king Mahāsammata. And these people, established in the moral boundaries laid down by him, are in the position of his sons. Therefore, they are called 'humans' (manussā), meaning 'offspring of Manu.' Here, however, because it is a term for the plane of existence, it should be understood that the word manussā is treated as feminine and singular. The same applies to the rest. Those devas over whom the Four Great Kings rule are the Cātumahārājika devas. Therein, Dhataraṭṭha is the king of the Gandhabbas, Virūḷhaka of the Kumbhaṇḍas, Virūpakkha of the Nāgas, and Kuvera of the Yakkhas. Therein, because through rebirth they are attached to or go to fragrant trees, they are gandhabbas; they are devas who dwell in fragrant trees. They are mentioned in the Pāli in ten varieties, based on root-fragrance and so forth. Kumbhaṇḍas are dānavas and rakkhasas. Nāgas and yakkhas are well-known. All of them are for the most part of evil disposition and performers of cruel deeds. Therefore, the Four Great Kings appointed various kings and generals among them to prevent them from harming one another or from harming humans.

Āṭānāṭiyasuttaṃcetthavattabbaṃ. Tattha hi yakkhoyakkhinīgandhappo gandhappī kumbhaṇḍo kumbhaṇḍī nāgo nāgīticatasso avaruddhakajātiyo āgatā. Tattha sarīrobhāsasirisampattiyutto amanusso yakkhotica devotica devatātica vuccati. Sarīro bhāsa sirisampattirahito vigaccharūpo amanusso yakkhotveva vuccati. Rukkhaṭṭhakavimāne jāto rukkhadevatānāma. Rukkhassa abbhantare jāto gandhapponāma. Yo loke kaṭṭhayakkhoti vuccati. Pubbe nihīnakammakatā kāci gandhappiyo manussitthīnaṃ sarīrabbhantaresupi jāyanti. Yā vedaganthesu yoginītica loke [M 0.0197] joginītica vuccanti. Abhilakkhitarattīsu gocarapasuta kāle jutiatthena juṇhātica vuccanti, kubbhaṇḍānāma mahodarā visālakkhā rakkhasāeva. Ye loke dhana rakkhakāti vuccanti. Te hi vepullapabbate maṇiratanaṃ rakkhanti. Anto himavante abbhantara ambarukkhe rakkhanti. Evaṃ ratanaṭṭhānānivā vanappati rukkhevā dibbosadharukkhevā dibbagandharukkhevā udakasarevā rakkhitvā asanti bhakkhanti. Tasmā rakkhasāti vuccanti. Nāgo nāgīti ettha anto pabbatevā anto pathaviyaṃvā nibbattā vasundharadevayakkhajātiyopi idha nāgātveva vuccanti. Yā mahāparinibbāna sutte bhūmicālasuttapade pathavī devatāti vuttā. Yāsaṃ kīḷāpasuta vasena kadāci bhūmicālo hoti. Yāsañca mantapadāni vatthu vijjātica bhūmivijjātica brahmajālasutte vuttāni. Tesuca nānā iddhimantā avaruddhakā pāpātiratā kibbisakammakārino kīḷā soṇḍavasenavā ghāsasoṇḍavasenavā petesucanirayesuca pakati vaṇṇenavā soṇagijjhakākādivaṇṇenavā satte viheṭhayantā vicaranti. Sabbañce taṃ suttantesuvā jātakesuvā vedaganthesuvā kusalehi veditabbanti.

The Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should be mentioned here. In it, four kinds of beings—yakkhas and yakkhinīs, gandhabbas and gandhabbīs, kumbhaṇḍas and kumbhaṇḍīs, nāgas and nāgīs—are mentioned as those who are bound by their birth. Among them, a non-human being endowed with radiant bodily beauty and splendor is called a yakkha, a deva, or a devatā. A non-human being lacking radiant bodily beauty and splendor, appearing in a disgusting form, is simply called a yakkha. Those born in tree-dwelling celestial mansions are called tree devas. Those born inside trees are called gandhabbas—the ones referred to in the world as tree-yakkhas. Some gandhabbīs, having performed inferior deeds in the past, are born even inside the bodies of human women. Those called yoginīs in the Vedic texts and joginīs in the world are known to wander during marked nights, drawn by their search for food—hence called 'juṇhā' due to their radiance. The kumbhaṇḍas are large-bellied, wide-eyed rakkhasas. Those called wealth-protectors in the world guard jewels on Vepulla Mountain. Inside the Himalayas, they protect amba trees. Thus, they guard jewel-places, forest trees, divine medicinal trees, divine fragrant trees, or lakes, eating and consuming. Therefore, they are called rakkhasas. As for nāgas and nāgīs—whether born inside mountains or within the earth—the Vasundhara deva-yakkha beings are also called nāgas here. Those referred to in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, in the Bhūmicāla Sutta passage, as earth devas are the ones whose playful movements sometimes cause earthquakes. Their mantra-verses, object-lore, and earth-lore are mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta. These beings, possessing various psychic powers, are bound, addicted to evil, doers of evil kamma. They roam about harming beings—whether through playful and mischievous conduct, hunger-driven conduct, or in their natural forms like dogs, vultures, or crows, in the peta or niraya realms. All this should be understood by the wise through the suttas, jātakas, and Vedic texts.

Saha puññakārino tettiṃsa janā māghenanāma jeṭṭhapurisena saha ettha nibbattāti tettiṃsā. Sāeva tāvatiṃsā nirutti nayena. Kāmañcettha sabbacakkavāḷesupi ayaṃ dutīyadeva loko janavasatasutte āgata nayena sakkaṭṭhāniyānaṃ pajāpati varuṇa īsānādīnaṃ tettiṃsa devarājūnaṃ nibandhano kāso hoti. Sahassaṃ cātumahārājikānaṃ. Sahassaṃ tāvatiṃsānanti hi aṅguttare vuttaṃ. Māghapurisā pana tesu samudāgatesu devarājaṭṭhānesu paccājātā honti. Etarahi dharamānāca tasmā tesaṃ vasena ayaṃ vacanattho katoti veditabbo. Apare pana yathā indagopakavaṇṇābhā. Tāva dissanti tiṃsatīti imasmiṃ vidhurajātake tāva saddo tiṃsasaddaparivāramatto hoti. Tathā idhāpīti katvā tiṃsamattānaṃ sakkaṭṭhāniyānaṃ devarājakulānaṃ nivāsaṭṭhā nattā [M 0.0198] tāvatiṃsānāmāti yuttaṃ siyā. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana yathāvuttaṃ niruttinayaṃ kappetvā māghavatthūsuca tesu tesuca ṭhānesu sakkānaṃ tettiṃsa saṅkhāeva vuttātipi vadanti. Taṃ na yujjati. Pāḷiyaṃeva brahmāsanaṅkumāro tettiṃse attabhāve abhinimminitvā devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ pallaṅkesu nisīditvāti vuttattā. Yāmoti tasmiṃ devaloke issaradevakulassa nāmaṃ. Tathā suyāmotica. Taṃ sahacaritattā pana so deva lokopi tattha nibbattadevāpi yāmātveva vuccanti. Vipulāya sirisampattiyā samannāgatattā niccaṃ tusanti ativiya haṭṭhatuṭṭhamukhā honti etthāti tusitā. Yathārucite bhoge sayameva nimminitvā nimminitvā ramanti etthāti nimmānaratī. Attano ruciṃ ñatvā parehi nimmitesu bhogesu vasaṃ vattenti etthāti paranimmitavasavattī. Brūhanti vaḍḍhanti atipaṇītehi jhānādi guṇehi vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjantīti brahmāno. Mahantā brahmāno mahābrahmānoti vattabbe mahāsaddassa lopo.

Thirty-three people, doers of merit, together with the chief man named Māgha, were born here—hence, they are called the Thirty-three (Tettiṃsā). This itself becomes Tāvatiṃsa by way of etymological derivation.
