If the going for refuge is broken by committing an act that destroys the characteristic mark of a disciple, the entire undertaking is broken. In the other cases, it should be understood that the restraint is broken only in that specific case of transgression.

Gahaṭṭhasīle pana pakati gahaṭṭhānaṃ gahaṇavaseneva samādānaṃ siddhaṃ hoti. Tasmā ekatogaṇhante sabbāni samādinnāni honti. Ekasmiṃca bhinne sabbāni bhinnāni honti. Sabbāni puna samādātabbāni. Visuṃ visuṃ gaṇhante pana yaṃ vītikkamati, etadevabhijjati. Tadeva puna samādātabbaṃ hotīti. Paricchinnakālā tikkamane pana sabbaṃ samādānaṃ vūpasammatiyeva. Dussīlabhāvo panettha pañcannaṃ niccasīlānaṃ bhedena veditabbo. Niccāniccesu pana yaṃ niccameva vaṭṭati. Aniccaṃ navaṭṭati sāvajjaṃ hoti. Taṃ niccasīlaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana niccaṃpi vaṭṭati. Mahantaṃ puññābhisandaṃ hoti. Aniccaṃpi vaṭṭati sāvajjaṃ na hoti. Taṃ aniccasīlaṃnāma. Tattha bhikkhu bhāve ṭhitassa bhikkhusīlaṃ sāmaṇerabhāve ṭhitassa sāmaṇerasīlaṃ pakatigahaṭṭhānaṃpañcasīlaṃ pabbajitasaṅkhepagatānaṃ upāsakānaṃ tāpasaparibbājakānañca dasasīlaṃ niccasīlaṃnāma. Tesañhi taṃ taṃ yathāsakaṃ sīlaṃ niccaṃ suddhaṃ katvā rakkhitumeva vaṭṭati. Arakkhantānaṃ bhikkhubhāvādiko sāvajjo hoti asuddho. Kasmā, attano anurūpassa ācārassa vipattito. Pakatigahaṭṭhānaṃ pana aṭṭhaṅguposathasīlaṃ aniccasīlaṃnāma. Tañhi tesaṃ vuttanayena niccaṃpi vaṭṭati. Aniccaṃpi vaṭṭati. Tathā dasasīlañca. Tañhi pakati gahaṭṭhānaṃ aniccasīlameva hoti. Gihinivatthaṃ pahāya kāsāyavatthadhāraṇena pabbajitasaṅkhepagatānaṃ eva niccasīlaṃ. Yathā hi pakatimanussānaṃ pañcasīlaṃ samādinnaṃpi asamādinnaṃpi niccaṃ rakkhitumeva vaṭṭati. Vītikkamituṃ navaṭṭati. Tathā pabbajitavesadhārīnaṃ dasasīlaṃ samādinnaṃpi asamādinnaṃpi niccaṃ rakkhitumeva vaṭṭati. Vītikkamituṃ navaṭṭati. Vesadhāraṇena saha siddhattāti.

Regarding householder precepts, the undertaking for ordinary householders is accomplished simply by the act of taking them. Therefore, when one undertakes them all together, all are undertaken. And if one is broken, all are broken. All must then be undertaken again. However, when they are taken separately, only the one that is transgressed is broken. That one alone must be undertaken again. But if the specified time is transgressed, the entire undertaking simply ceases. Here, the state of being unvirtuous is to be understood through the breaking of the five constant precepts. Among constant and non-constant precepts: that which it is always proper to observe, and which it is not proper and is blameworthy to observe non-constantly, is called a constant precept. That which it is proper to observe always, bringing a great flow of merit, and which it is also proper to observe non-constantly without being blameworthy, is called a non-constant precept. Herein: for one established in the state of a monk, the monastic precepts; for one established in the state of a novice, the novice precepts; for ordinary householders, the five precepts; and for lay followers who are reckoned as renunciants, such as ascetics and wanderers, the ten precepts are called constant precepts. For them, it is proper only to keep their respective precepts always pure. For those who do not keep them, their status as a monk or otherwise becomes blameworthy and impure. Why? Because of the failure of conduct appropriate to their state. For ordinary householders, however, the eight Uposatha precepts are called non-constant precepts. For them, as has been said, it is proper to observe them both constantly and non-constantly. Likewise, the ten precepts; for ordinary householders, they are indeed non-constant precepts. Only for those reckoned as renunciants by having abandoned the householder's garments and taken up the ochre robe do the ten precepts become constant. For just as it is always proper for ordinary people to keep the five precepts—whether formally undertaken or not—and not proper to transgress them, so too is it always proper for those who wear the robes of a renunciant to keep the ten precepts—whether formally undertaken or not—and not proper to transgress them. This is because their observance is established together with the wearing of the robes.

Upari [M 0.0236] vuccamānā samathavipassanāvasena duvidhā bhāvanā bhāvanānāma. Sā idha appanaṃ apattāva adhippetā. Dhammavinayapari yattiyā saha anavajjakammasippavijjāṭhānesu paricayakaraṇa cetanāpi ettheva saṅgayhati. Ratanattaye pana mātāpitūsu kulejeṭṭhesu ācariyesu dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇesu aññesuca guṇavayavuddhesu yathārahaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ vandanaṃ añjalikaraṇaṃ sāmicikaraṇaṃ vattapaṭivattakaraṇanti evamādisabbaṃ apacāyanaṃnāma. Tesaññeva aññesañca āgantukagamikaaddhikānaṃ gilānānaṃ jiṇṇānaṃ kicca karaṇīyesu sabrahmacārīnaṃ cīvarakammādīsu paresaṃ taṃtaṃpuñña kammesuca parisuddhena hitapharaṇacittena attanokiccesu viya kāyavācāhi vāyāmakaraṇaṃ veyyāvaccaṃnāma. Attanā katassa yassakassaci puññassa parehi sādhāraṇakaraṇaṃ pattidānaṃnāma. Parehi dinnāya pattiyā anumodanaṃ attamanatāpavedanaṃ pattā numodanaṃnāma. Adinnassa puññassa anumodanaṃ pana anumodanameva hoti. Na pattānumodanaṃ. Pattiyāeva abhāvato. Pattica duvidhā uddisikā anuddisikāti. Tattha attānaṃ uddisikaṃ anumodantasseva diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ jātanti veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ pana dvayaṃ dānapuññesueva visesato pākaṭaṃ. Tañhi uddisakaṃ katvā devatānaṃvā paradattupajīvipetānaṃvā vemānikapetānaṃvā vinipātikāsurānaṃvā dinnaṃ anumoditañca tesaṃ taṅkhaṇeeva diṭṭhadhamma vedanīyaṃ jātanti. Atthahita paṭisaṃyuttāya dhammakathāya yoniso manasikāre ṭhatvā savanañca kathanañca dhammasavanaṃ dhamma desanācanāma. Niravajjakammasippavijjāṭhānānaṃ savanakathanacetanāca etthevasaṅgayhanti.

The development (bhāvanā) mentioned above, twofold by way of serenity and insight, is called development. Here, it is intended as that which has not yet attained absorption. The volition to cultivate the study of the Dhamma and Vinaya, along with blameless actions, crafts, and sciences, is also included here. Reverence (apacāyana) is all such conduct as rising, paying homage, making the añjali salutation, showing respect, and performing duties and counter-duties as is proper towards the Triple Gem, parents, elders in the family, teachers, righteous ascetics and brahmins, and others senior in virtue and age. Service (veyyāvacca) is making an effort with body and speech, with a pure mind suffused with welfare, as if in one's own affairs, in the duties and needs of newcomers, departing ones, and travelers, of the sick and the aged, in the robe-making and other tasks of one's fellows in the holy life, and in the various meritorious deeds of others. The giving of transference of merit (pattidāna) is the sharing with others of any merit one has made. Rejoicing in transferred merit (pattānumodana) is rejoicing in merit given by others and expressing gladness of mind. However, rejoicing in merit that has not been transferred is simply rejoicing, not rejoicing in transferred merit, due to the absence of a transference. Transference of merit is of two kinds: specified and unspecified. Herein, it should be understood that that which is to be experienced in this very life arises only for one who rejoices in merit specified for oneself. These two are especially evident in the meritorious acts of giving. For when a gift, having been specified, is given to deities, or to petas who live on what is given by others, or to celestial petas, or to asuras in a state of downfall, and they rejoice in it, the result arises for them at that very moment, to be experienced in this very life. Listening to the Dhamma (dhammasavana) and teaching the Dhamma (dhammadesanā) are, respectively, listening to and teaching a discourse on the Dhamma connected with what is good and beneficial, having established wise attention. The volition to listen to and teach about blameless actions, crafts, and sciences is also included here.

Natthi dinnaṃ natthiyiṭṭhantiādinayapavattāya dasavatthukāya micchā diṭṭhiyāvā issaranimmānādidiṭṭhiyāvā diṭṭhamaṅgalādidiṭṭhiyāvā visuddhaṃ katvā tehi tehi vatthūhivā yuttīhivā kāraṇehivā kammasakatā ñāṇasaṅkhātāya sammādiṭṭhiyā vodānakaraṇaṃ diṭṭhujukammaṃnāmāti. Yattha pana tividhameva puññakriyavatthu āgataṃ. Tattha pattidānānumodanāni dāne saṅgayhanti. Issāmaccherānaṃ [M 0.0237] paṭipakkhabhāvena taṃ sabhāvattā. Apacāyanaveyyāvaccāni sīle saṅgayhanti. Tesaṃ cāritta sīlattā. Sesāni tīṇi bhāvanāmaye saṅgayhanti. Taṃ sabhāvattā. Kammaṭṭhānavinimutto dhammonāma natthīti hi vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhujukammañca ñāṇa vaḍḍhanamevāti. Tīsvevavā etaṃ saṅgayhati. Diṭṭhujukammaṃ sabbesaṃ niyama lakkhaṇantiti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Satiyeva hi kammasakatāñāṇe dānādīni tīṇi sampajjantīti. Manokammamevāti manasmiṃeva kammapatha kiccasiddhito manokammaṃeva.

The straightening of one’s view is the purification of right view—which is known as the knowledge of ownership of kamma—by means of various grounds, arguments, and reasons, after having purified oneself from the tenfold wrong view that proceeds from the nihilistic tenet, ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered…,’ or from the wrong view of a creator god, or from the wrong view of auspicious signs, and so on. However, where only the threefold basis of meritorious action is presented, there the giving of transference of merit and rejoicing in transferred merit are included in giving, because by their nature they are the counterpart to envy and avarice. Reverence and service are included in virtue, because they are virtue as conduct. The remaining three are included in the category of mental development, because that is their nature. For it is said: ‘There is no Dhamma apart from a meditation subject.’ And the straightening of one’s view is simply the development of knowledge. Thus, this is included in just the three. In the commentary it is said: ‘The straightening of one’s view is the regulating characteristic of all.’ For it is only when there is knowledge of the ownership of kamma that the three—giving and so on—are accomplished. It is mental action because the function of the path of action is accomplished in the mind alone; thus, it is mental action.

[158] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[158] Now, for clarification:

“Viññattisamuṭṭhāpakattā bhāvena kāya dvārādīsu appavattanatoti” vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: ‘Because it is by nature the originator of intimation, and because it does not occur at the body door, etc.’ That is not well-stated.

Na hi viññattisamuṭṭhāpakaṃ abhiññākusalaṃ kāyadvārādīsu pavattamānaṃpi kāyavacīkammasaṅkhyaṃ gacchati, kāyavācānaṃ kammapatha aṅgabhāvāsambhavatoti. Tañca bhāvanāmayanti dānasīlavasena appavattanato. Kevalaṃ bhāvanākammavisesattā tañca mahaggata kusalaṃ bhāvanākamma meva hoti. Yaṃ pana paṭisambhidā magge pathamajjhānena nīvaraṇānaṃ. Dutīyena vitakkavicārānaṃ. Tatīyena pītiyā. Catutthena sukhadukkhānaṃ pahānaṃ sīlaṃ. Veramaṇi sīlaṃ. Cetanā sīlaṃ. Saṃvaro sīlaṃ. Avītikkamo sīlanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pariyāyena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Appanāpattanti bhāvanā balena ārammaṇe anupavisitvā acalaṭṭhitibhāvena pavattanato appanāpattaṃ kammaṃ hoti.

For even when occurring at the body door, etc., the wholesome consciousness of direct knowledge that originates intimation is not reckoned as bodily or verbal kamma, because it is impossible for it to be a factor of the path of action of body and speech. And that is of the developmental type because it does not occur by way of giving and virtue. Simply because it is a special kamma of development, that exalted wholesome kamma is solely a kamma of development. As to what is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga—that by the first jhāna there is the abandonment of the hindrances, by the second the abandonment of applied and sustained thought, by the third the abandonment of joy, and by the fourth the abandonment of pleasure and pain—this abandonment is virtue. It is said: ‘Abstinence is virtue, volition is virtue, restraint is virtue, non-transgression is virtue.’ This should be understood as spoken figuratively. It becomes kamma that attains absorption because it occurs by the power of development, having entered into the object with a state of unshaken stability.

[159] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[159] Now, for clarification:

“Pubbabhāgapavattānaṃ kāmāvacarabhāvatoti” kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

The reason given is: ‘Because of the sense-sphere nature of what occurs in the preliminary phase.’ That is not well-stated.

Na hi tesaṃ kāmāvacaratāmattaṃ appanāpattiyā kāraṇaṃ hotīti. Jhānaṅgabhedenāti vuttaṃ. Jhānabhedenāti pana vattabbaṃ. Jhānaṅgabhedenātivā jhānaṅgasamudāyabhedenāti attho, jhānabhedena icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Kusalakammaṃ

For their mere sense-sphere nature is not the reason for attaining absorption. It was said, ‘by the distinction of jhāna factors,’ but it should be said, ‘by the distinction of jhāna.’ ‘By the distinction of jhāna factors’ means ‘by the distinction of the collection of jhāna factors,’ which is just to say, ‘by the distinction of jhāna.’ Wholesome kamma.

153. Etthāti [M 0.0238] etasmiṃ pākaṭṭhānacatukke. Uddhaccarahitanti uddhaccasahagatacetanāvajjitaṃ. Kasmā pana uddhaccacetanā idha pajjitāti. Paṭisandhianākaḍḍhanato. Kathaṃ viññāyatīti ce. Dhammasaṅgahe dassanena pahātabbesu taṃ avatvā bhāvanāya pahātabbesu eva vuttattā. Yathāha-cattāro diṭṭhigatasampayuttacittuppādā vicikicchāsahagato cittuppādo, ime dhammā dassanena pahātabbātica, uddhaccasahagato cittuppādo, imedhammā bhāvanāyapahā tabbātica, sesā pana cattāro diṭṭhigatavippayuttacittuppādā dve paṭighasampayuttacittuppādāca siyā dassanenapahātabbā siyā bhāvanāya pahātabbāti tattha vuttā. Kathañca viññāyati. Yo dassanenapahātabbesu na vutto, so akusaladhammo paṭisandhiṃ nākaḍḍhatīti. Paṭṭhāne dassanenapahātabbadhammesueva nānākkhaṇika kammapaccayassa uddhaṭattā itarattha tassa anuddhaṭattāti. Yathāha-sahajātā dassanenapahātabbā cetanā sampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ kammapaccayenapaccayo. Nānākkhaṇikā dassanena pahātabbā cetanā vipākānaṃ khandhānaṃ kaṭattāca rūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayotica sahajātā bhāvanāya pahātabbā cetanāsampayuttakānaṃdhammānaṃ cittāsamuṭṭhānānañcarūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayotica. Naca nānākkhaṇika kammapaccayasattiyā vinā vipākuppādanaṃnāma atthīti. Yadievaṃ sā pavattivipākaṃpi najanetīti sakkā vattuntice.Na. Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅge tassā vipākassa uddhaṭattā. Yathāha-katame dhammā akusalā. Yasmiṃ samaye akusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti upekkhāsahagataṃ uddhaccasampayuttaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃvā.La. Ime dhammā akusalā. Imesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidāti. Tenāha pavattiyaṃ pana sabbaṃpi dvādasavidhantiādi.

153. Here means in this fourfold manifest ground. ‘Devoid of restlessness’ means excluding the volition accompanied by restlessness. But why is the volition associated with restlessness excluded here? Because it does not draw forth rebirth-linking. How is this known? Because in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, it is not stated among those things to be abandoned by seeing, but is stated only among those to be abandoned by development. As it is said: ‘The four types of consciousness that arise associated with wrong view, and the type of consciousness accompanied by doubt—these states are to be abandoned by seeing.’ And: ‘The type of consciousness accompanied by restlessness—this state is to be abandoned by development.’ But it is also stated there: ‘The remaining four types of consciousness that arise dissociated from wrong view and the two types of consciousness that arise associated with aversion may be abandoned either by seeing or by development.’ And how is it known that an unwholesome state not mentioned among those to be abandoned by seeing does not draw forth rebirth-linking? Because in the Paṭṭhāna, the different-moment kamma-condition is specified only for states to be abandoned by seeing, and not for the others. As it is said: ‘Co-nascent volition to be abandoned by seeing is a condition for its associated mental states and for mind-originated matter by way of kamma condition. Different-moment volition to be abandoned by seeing is a condition for the resultant aggregates and for kamma-produced matter by way of kamma condition.’ And: ‘Co-nascent volition to be abandoned by development is a condition for its associated mental states and for mind-originated matter by way of kamma condition.’ And there is no such thing as the production of a resultant without the power of the different-moment kamma-condition. If so, could it be said that it does not generate even a resultant in the course of existence? No, because its resultant is specified in the Analysis of Discrimination. As it is said: ‘What are unwholesome states? The time when an unwholesome consciousness has arisen, accompanied by neutral feeling and associated with restlessness, having a form as its object… these are unwholesome states. Knowledge of these states is the discrimination of the Dhamma. Knowledge of their resultant is the discrimination of the meaning.’ Therefore it was said: ‘But in the course of existence, all twelve kinds…,’ etc.

[160] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[160] Furthermore, for clarification:

“Adhimokkhavirahena sabbadubbalaṃpi vicikicchāsahagataṃ paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhati. Adhimokkhasampayogena tato balavantaṃpi uddhaccasahagataṃ nākaḍḍhatīti” vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: ‘Due to the absence of resolution, the state accompanied by doubt, though the weakest of all, draws forth rebirth-linking; but due to its association with resolution, the state accompanied by restlessness, though stronger than that, does not draw it forth.’ This is not well-stated.

Na hi [M 0.0239] adhimokkhavirahamattena vicikicchāsahagataṃ sabbadubbalantica adhimokkhasampayogamattena uddhaccasahagataṃ tato balavantantica sakkā vattuṃ. Satthari kaṅkhati dhamme kaṅkhatīti evamādinā nayena vuttāya vicikicchāya attano visaye mahāhatthināgassa viya balavatarattā ativiya kāḷakadhammattācāti. Tathā hisā ekantena dassanenapahātabbesu padhānabhāvena vuttā. Tatoyevaca paṭisandhiākaḍḍhanaṃpi tassā viññātabbaṃ hotīti. Sabhāvaviruddhattāyeva pana vicikicchāsahagataṃ adhimokkharahitaṃ hotīti yuttaṃ. Tasmā uddhaccasahagatameva sabbadubbalanti veditabbaṃ. Sabbatthāpīti sugatiduggativasena sabbasmiṃpi. Yathārahanti tesu lokesu laddhavatthudvārānurūpaṃ. Vipaccatīti vipāceti vipakkabhāvaṃ āpādeti. Sabbaṃpivādvādasavidhaṃ akusalakammaṃ sattā kusalapākāni hutvā vipaccati, vipakkabhāvaṃ gacchatīti attho.

For it cannot be said that merely due to the absence of resolution, the state associated with doubt is the weakest of all, or that merely due to its association with resolution, the state associated with restlessness is stronger than it. For doubt—spoken of in such terms as, ‘He doubts the Teacher, he doubts the Dhamma’—is extremely powerful in its own domain, like a great elephant, and is of an extremely dark nature. Thus it is spoken of as primary among those things to be abandoned exclusively by seeing. And for that very reason it should be understood that it also draws forth rebirth-linking. Moreover, it is proper that the state accompanied by doubt is devoid of resolution precisely because of its contradictory nature. Therefore, it should be understood that it is the state accompanied by restlessness that is the weakest of all. ‘In all cases’ means in all, by way of good and bad destinations. ‘As is fit’ means in accordance with the object and door obtained in those worlds. ‘It ripens’ means it causes to ripen, it brings to a state of ripeness. The meaning is that all twelve kinds of unwholesome kamma ripen by becoming the seven unwholesome resultants for beings; that is, they reach a state of ripeness.

Yasmā kusalakammāni apāyabhūmiyaṃpi pavattiyaṃ mahāsampattiyo samuṭṭhāpetvā mahiddhikānaṃ nāgasupaṇṇādīnaṃ santāne sayameva attanovipākassa okāsaṃ katvā sukhavipākaṃ janayanti. Aññesaṃpi āpāyikānaṃ tena tena kāraṇena iṭṭhārammaṇa samāyoge sati attano vipākassa okāsaṃ labhitvā sukhavipākaṃ janayanti. Tasmā tathāpavattiyañcātiādi māha. Na hi tāni sukhavipākāni akusakammassa vipākāni bhavituṃ arahanti. Vutteñhetaṃ vibhaṅge aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ kāyaduccaritassa iṭṭho kanto manāpo vipāko nibbatteyyātiādi. Tattha mahāvipākāni sugati kāmaloke ahetukāni aṭṭhapi sabbasmiṃ kāmaloke tesuca pañcacakkhuviññāṇa sotaviññāṇa sampaṭicchana santīraṇa yugaḷāni rūpaloke vipaccatīti vuttaṃ yathārahaṃ vipaccatīti. Rūpāvacara kusalañhi kammasamuṭṭhānarūpāni janayantaṃpi sayaṃ vipaccamānaṃ ārammaṇantare aññabhūmika vipākabhāvena navipaccati. Kāmavirāgabhāvanābhāvena pana appanāpatta kamma visesattā kāmataṇhāya avisayabhūte nimittā rammaṇe attanā sabbaso sadisena mahaggatabhāvapattena rūpa vipākabhāveneva [M 0.0240] vipaccati. Tasmā rūpalokepi tāni pañcavipākāni kāmāvacarakusalassevāti veditabbānīti. Dvīsu kammassa vipaccanaṭṭhānesu paṭisandhināma mahantaṃṭhānaṃ hoti. Tasmā tadā vipaccantaṃ kammaṃ attano sāmatthiyānurūpaṃ nātihīnaṃ vipākaṃ janetuṃ sakkoti. Pavattiyaṃ pana nānāṭhānesu nānākiccehi vipaccati. Tasmā tadā vipaccantaṃ kammaṃ attano sāmatthiyānurūpaṃ vipaccetuṃ nasakkoti. Pañcaviññāṇaṭṭhānādīsu parittakesu vipaccamānaṃ ṭhānā nurūpaṃ vipaccati. Tadārammaṇaṭṭhāne vipaccamānaṃ yebhuyyena javanā nurūpaṃ vipaccati. Tasmā soḷasakamaggo dvādasakamaggo ahetu kaṭṭhakanti evaṃekekassa kammassa vipākappabhedo pavattotitaṃ pabhedaṃdassetuṃ tatthāpītiādimāha.

For wholesome kamma, even in a plane of misery, can, during the course of life, produce great prosperity by giving rise to mighty nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so on, in their continuity, thus creating an opportunity for its own result and generating a pleasant result. For other beings in the woeful states, too, when for some reason or other they encounter an agreeable object, wholesome kamma may find an opportunity for its own result and generate a pleasant result. Therefore, it is said, 'and in such a course of existence,' etc. For these pleasant results cannot be the results of unwholesome kamma. This is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'It is impossible, it cannot be, that bodily misconduct could produce a desirable, lovely, and agreeable result,' and so on. Therein, the great-resultants ripen in the good-destination sensual sphere, and the eight rootless resultants ripen in the entire sensual sphere; and among them, it is said that the five sense-consciousnesses, the pair of receiving consciousnesses, and the pair of investigating consciousnesses ripen in the form sphere as is appropriate. For although wholesome form-sphere kamma generates kamma-born matter, when it ripens itself it does not ripen as a result in another sphere with a different object. But because it is a special kind of kamma that has reached absorption through the development of dispassion for sensual pleasures, it ripens only with a form-sphere result that has attained an exalted state completely similar to itself, with a sign as its object, which is beyond the range of sensual craving. Therefore, it should be understood that even in the form sphere those five results belong only to wholesome sensual-sphere kamma. Between the two occasions for the ripening of kamma, rebirth-linking is the great occasion. Therefore, kamma ripening at that time can generate a result that is not too inferior, in accordance with its own capacity. But during the course of life, it ripens in various places with various functions. Therefore, kamma ripening at that time cannot ripen in full accordance with its own capacity. When ripening in the limited places of the five sense-consciousnesses, etc., it ripens in accordance with the place. When ripening in the place of the registering consciousness, it ripens for the most part in accordance with the impulsion. Therefore, to show this distinction in the proliferation of results for each kamma during the course of life—such as the sixteenfold set, the twelvefold set, and the rootless portion—it is said, 'Even there,' etc.

Kusalaṃ duvidhaṃ sampajānakataṃ asampajānakatanti. Tattha kammā yūhanakāle antamaso heṭṭhā vuttaṃ diṭṭhujukammañāṇaṃpi suṭṭhu yojetvā kataṃ sampajānakataṃnāma. Yathāha-kammañca kammaphalañca saddahitvā kataṃ sampajānakataṃ nāmāti. Diṭṭhujukammañāṇa mattaṃpi ayojetvā taṃ asampajānakataṃ nāma. Yathāha-kammaṃpi kammaphalampi ajānitvā kataṃ asampajānakataṃ nāmāti. Tattha sampajānakataṃ tihetukaṃ hoti. Asampajānakataṃ duhetukaṃ. Yathāha-sampajānakaraṇaṃ pana catuñāṇasampayuttehi hoti. Asampajāna karaṇaṃ catūhi ñāṇavippayuttehīti. Tattha ekamekaṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ omakanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha kusalasamaye pariyuṭṭhite nīvaraṇadhammevā attukkaṃsana paravambhanādike pāpadhammevā suṭṭhu sodhetvā kataṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ nāma. Asodhetvā kataṃ tehivokiṇṇaṃ omakaṃnāma. Apica, yaṃ katvā pacchā lābhā vata me. Naca vata me alābhā. Suladdhaṃ vata me. Naca vata me dulladdhaṃ. Yassa me īdisaṃ puññaṃ pasutanti evaṃ punappunaṃ anumoditaṃ. Taṃ ukkaṭṭhaṃ. Yaṃ katvā pacchā yenakenaci kāraṇena duṭṭhukataṃ mayāti vippaṭisāro uppajjati. Taṃomakaṃ. Evaṃ catubbidhassa kammassa vasena catubbidhaṃ vipāka koṭṭhāsaṃ vibhajitvā dassetuṃ tathāpītiādi māha. Tatthāpīti [M 0.0241] tasmiṃ kāmāvacarakusalepi. Tihetukamukkaṭṭhanti ukkaṭṭhabhūtaṃ paṇītabhūtaṃ catubbidhaṃ tihetukaṃ. Tihetukapaṭisandhinti catubbidhaṃ tihetuka paṭisandhivipākaṃ. Etthaca ekacetanā ekameva paṭisandhiṃ deti. Pavattivipākaṃ pana asaṅkhyeyyesupi bhavesu detiyeva. Ettha siyā –

Wholesome kamma is twofold: that done with comprehension and that done without comprehension. Therein, kamma done at the time of its accumulation by properly applying at least the aforementioned knowledge that consists in straightening one's view is called 'done with comprehension.' As it is said: 'Kamma done with faith in kamma and its fruit is called "done with comprehension."' Kamma done without applying even a modicum of the knowledge that consists in straightening one's view is called 'done without comprehension.' As it is said: 'Kamma done without knowing kamma and its fruit is called "done without comprehension."' Therein, that done with comprehension is three-rooted; that done without comprehension is two-rooted. As it is said: 'Doing with comprehension is done by the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge. Doing without comprehension is done by the four dissociated from knowledge.' Therein, each is twofold: superior and inferior. Therein, kamma done at a wholesome time after having thoroughly purified the arisen hindrances and evil states such as self-exaltation and contempt for others is called 'superior.' Kamma done without such purification, being mixed with those states, is called 'inferior.' Moreover, that kamma is 'superior' which, after being done, is repeatedly rejoiced over thus: 'A gain, indeed, for me, not a loss! Well-gained, indeed, by me, not ill-gained! It is I who have produced such merit!' That kamma is 'inferior' which, after being done, gives rise to regret for some reason or other: 'I have done wrong!' Thus, to show the fourfold division of the portions of resultants on the basis of the fourfold kamma, the text says, 'Even there,' etc. Therein, 'even there' means 'even in that wholesome sensual-sphere kamma.' 'The three-rooted superior' means the fourfold three-rooted kamma that is superior and excellent. 'The three-rooted rebirth-linking' means the fourfold three-rooted rebirth-linking resultant. And here, a single volition gives only one rebirth-linking. But during the course of life, it gives a result even in countless existences. Here, it might be said:

Ekapupphaṃ yajitvāna, sahassakappakoṭiyo;

Devesuca manussesu, sesena parinibbutoti hi vuttaṃ.

Having offered a single flower,

For a thousand crores of eons,

[One reaps the fruit] among gods and humans;

With the remainder one attains final Nibbāna—so it is said.

Tasmā ekā cetanā ekameva paṭisandhiṃ detīti idaṃ na yujjatīti. Na na yujjati. Pubbāparacetanāhi saddhiṃ sahassakappa koṭi parimāṇassa vattabbattā. Cittañhināma ekaccharakkhaṇepi anekasata sahassa koṭisaṅkhaṃ uppajjati. Tatociratarekālevattabbameva natthīti. Sahassa kappakoṭiyoti ca sahassaāyukappakoṭiyo sahassa attabhāvakoṭiyoti nettiaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Pubbāparacetanānañca paṭisandhidānabhāvo kosalasaṃyuttakena dīpetabbo. Ekapiṇḍapātadānasmiṃhi ekācetanādve paṭisandhiyo na deti. Pubbapacchimacetanāvasena sattakkhattuṃ sagge sattakkhattuṃ seṭṭhikule nibbattoti hi saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tihetu kaṃpi kammaṃ paṭipakkhehi abhibhuyyamānaṃ vihatasāmatthiyaṃ hutvā tihetukavipākaṃ janetuṃ na sakkoti. Naca taṃ atidubbalaṃpi samānaṃ kosallasaṅkhātena ñāṇena yuttattā atibyāmuḷhapaccaya bhūhaṃ jaccandhādivipattisahitaṃ ahetukavipākaṃ janetīti vuttaṃ tihetukamomakantiādi. Dvādasavipākānivipaccati. Ayaṃ dvāda sakamaggonāma ahetukavipākāneva vipaccati. Idaṃ ahetu kaṭṭhakaṃnāma. Evaṃ tipiṭakacūḷanāgattheravādavasena vipākappavattiṃ dassetvā idāni moravāpivāsi mahādattattheravādaṃ dassetuṃ gāthamāha. So hi therovipākānaṃ asaṅkhārikatā sasaṅkhārikatāca kammavaseneva siddhāpi katvā asaṅkhāraṃ kammaṃ sasaṅkhāravipākāni na paccati. Sasaṅkhāraṃkammaṃ asaṅkhāravipākāni navaccatīti vadati.

Therefore, [one might object that] the statement, 'a single volition gives only one rebirth-linking,' is not correct. It is not that it is not correct. For this is said with reference to the preceding and subsequent volitions that have a duration of a thousand crores of eons. For consciousness arises many hundreds of thousands of crores of times even in a single finger-snap; what then needs to be said of a much longer time? And in the commentary to the Netti, 'a thousand crores of eons' is explained as 'a thousand crores of life-span eons' and 'a thousand crores of eons of individual existences.' The fact that preceding and subsequent volitions give rebirth-linking should be illustrated by the Kosala Saṃyutta. In the giving of a single alms meal, a single volition does not give two rebirth-linkings. But it is said in the Saṃyutta Commentary that on account of the preliminary and subsequent volitions one is reborn seven times in heaven and seven times in a treasurer's family. Even a three-rooted kamma, when it is overpowered by opposing factors and its capacity is thwarted, cannot generate a three-rooted resultant. Nor, though it is associated with the knowledge called skillfulness, can it, being extremely weak, generate a rootless resultant accompanied by such misfortunes as congenital blindness, which is a condition for extreme bewilderment. This is what is meant by 'the inferior three-rooted kamma,' etc. The twelve resultants ripen. This is called the 'twelvefold set.' It ripens only as rootless resultants. This is called the 'rootless portion of eight.' Having thus explained the occurrence of resultants according to the school of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, he now states a verse to present the school of the Elder Mahādatta, a resident of Moravāpi. For that elder says that although the distinction between unprompted and prompted resultants is established by way of kamma, unprompted kamma does not ripen into prompted resultants, and prompted kamma does not ripen into unprompted resultants.

Yathā [M 0.0242] mukhanimittaṃ nāma mukhe sannisinne sannisīdati. Calante calati. Evaṃ payogena asādhanīyānaṃ vipākānaṃ tikkhamandatā visesabhūto saṅkhārabhedo kammavaseneva vattabbo. Na payogavasena. Itarathā kammavisesena tikkhamandajātānaṃ tesaṃ sannihitapaccayamattena mandatikkhatāpattināma siyāti. Ahetu kavipākānaṃ pana paridubbalattā aparibyattova tikkhamandatā visesoti ubhayakammanibbattanti adhippāyo. Yasmā pana tesaṃ sasaṅkhārāsaṅkhārabhāvo paṭisandhivasenavā tadārammaṇavasenavā uppattikāle pubbapayogasaṅkhātassa paccayavisesassa bhāvābhāvena vattuṃ yutto. Na kammāgamanavasena, na hi kammabhave saṅkhāro bhavantare vipākāni visesetuṃ yutto. Tasmā imaṃ vādaṃ kecivādaṃnāma karonto kecanāti āha.

Just as the reflection of the face is still when the face is still and moves when it moves, so the distinction of formation, which is the specific quality of sharpness or dullness of resultants that are not accomplishable by effort, should be spoken of as due to the power of kamma, not to the power of effort. Otherwise, for those resultants that are by nature sharp or dull due to the specific nature of the kamma, their becoming dull or sharp would be due to a mere proximate condition. But in the case of rootless resultants, because of their extreme weakness, the distinction of sharpness or dullness is not manifest; the meaning is that they are produced by both kinds of kamma. However, since their prompted or unprompted nature is properly spoken of according to the presence or absence, at the time of their arising, of the specific condition called 'prior effort'—either by way of rebirth-linking or by way of the registering consciousness, not by way of the kamma's coming—for a formation in the kamma-process existence is not fit to determine the specific nature of resultants in a future existence. Therefore, treating this as a 'some-say' doctrine, he said 'some...'

Imasmiṃ kecivāde asaṅkhārikakamme sasaṅkhārika vipākāni sasaṅkhārikakammeca asaṅkhārikavipākāni vajjetvā catūsu tihe tukukkaṭṭhesu kammesu asaṅkhārikadvaye vipākāni paṭisandhiyaṃ dve, pavattiyaṃ dvādasa. Sasaṅkhārikadvaye paṭisandhiyaṃ dve, pavattiyaṃ dvādasa. Catūsu dvihetukomakakammesu asaṅkhārikadvaye paṭisandhiyaṃ dve, pavattiyaṃ dasa. Sasaṅkhārikadvaye paṭisandhiyaṃ dve, pavattiyaṃ dasa. Tathā catūsu dvihetukukkaṭṭhesu. Catūsu dvihetukomakesu pana paṭisandhiyaṃ ekaṃ ahetukaṃ pavattiyaṃ aṭṭhaahetukānīti evaṃ vipākānaṃ dve dvādasakamaggā cattāro dasakamaggā ekaṃ ahetukaṭṭhakañca honti, taṃsabbaṃ saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ tesanti gāthamāha.

In this 'some-say' doctrine, excluding prompted resultants from unprompted kamma and unprompted resultants from prompted kamma: among the four superior three-rooted kammas, for the two unprompted ones, the resultants are two at rebirth-linking and twelve during the course of life; for the two prompted ones, two at rebirth-linking and twelve during the course of life. Among the four inferior two-rooted kammas, for the two unprompted ones, two at rebirth-linking and ten during the course of life; for the two prompted ones, two at rebirth-linking and ten during the course of life. Similarly for the four superior two-rooted kammas. But for the four inferior two-rooted kammas, at rebirth-linking there is one rootless resultant, and during the course of life there are eight rootless resultants. Thus, among the resultants, there are two twelvefold sets, four tenfold sets, and one rootless portion of eight. To collect and show all this, he stated the verse beginning 'tesaṃ'.

Tesanti tesaṃ kesañci therānaṃ vāde. Aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ pana tihetukena kammena paṭisandhitihetukāva hoti. Na duhetukā nacaahetukā. Duhetukena kammena paṭisandhi duhetukāpi hoti ahetukāpi. Tihetukā pana nahotīti evaṃ pavatto mahādhammarakkhitattheravādopi āgato. Tattha yathā duhetukena hīnena kammena ahetukā paṭisandhi avassaṃ icchitabbā hoti. Tathā tihetukenapi hīnena kammena duhetukāpi [M 0.0243] paṭisandhi avassaṃ icchitabbāyevāti katvā idha ayaṃvādo therena na gahitoti veditabbo. Paṭisambhidāmagge pana-gatisampattiyā ñāṇasampayutte aṭṭhannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hoti. Kusalassa kammassa javanakkhaṇe tayo hetū kusalā. Nikantikkhaṇe dve hetū kusalā. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe tayo hetū abyākatātica gati sampattiyā ñāṇa vippayutte channaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayā upapatti hohi. Kusalassa kammassa javanakkhaṇe dve hetū kusalā. Nikantikkhaṇe dve hetū akusalā. Paṭisandhikkhaṇe dve hetū abyākatātica evaṃ tihetukena kammena paṭisandhi tihetukāva vuttā. Dvihetukena kammena dvihetukāva. Na pana gatisampattiyā ñāṇavippayutte sattannaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayātiādinā tihetukena kammena dvihetukā paṭisandhi vuttā. Naca catunnaṃ hetūnaṃ paccayātiādinā dvihetukena kammena ahetukā paṭisandhīti.

This is in the doctrine of some of those elders. In the Aṭṭhasālinī, however, rebirth-linking by a three-rooted kamma is only three-rooted. It is not two-rooted nor rootless. Rebirth-linking by a two-rooted kamma can be either two-rooted or rootless, but it is never three-rooted. Thus, the established doctrine of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita has also come down. Therein, just as a rootless rebirth-linking must necessarily be accepted from an inferior two-rooted kamma, so too a two-rooted rebirth-linking must necessarily be accepted from an inferior three-rooted kamma. Therefore, it should be understood that this doctrine was not accepted by the Elder here. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, for one with attainment of a good destination and associated with knowledge, arising occurs through the condition of eight roots. At the moment of impulsion of wholesome kamma, three roots are wholesome. At the moment of desire, two roots are wholesome. At the moment of rebirth-linking, three roots are indeterminate. For one with attainment of a good destination but dissociated from knowledge, arising occurs through the condition of six roots. At the moment of impulsion of wholesome kamma, two roots are wholesome. At the moment of desire, two roots are unwholesome. At the moment of rebirth-linking, two roots are indeterminate. Thus, rebirth-linking by a three-rooted kamma is said to be only three-rooted. By a two-rooted kamma, it is only two-rooted. But it is not said in the passage beginning 'by the condition of seven roots for one with attainment of a good destination but dissociated from knowledge,' etc., that a two-rooted rebirth-linking arises from a three-rooted kamma, nor in the passage beginning 'by the condition of four roots,' etc., that a rootless rebirth-linking arises from a two-rooted kamma.

Tattha pana tīsu khaṇesu sahajāta hetūnaṃ vasena hetu mūlakova ayaṃ desanāvāroti katvā anokāsatāya ahetukapaṭisandhi tattha navuttā. Na pana alabbhamānatāya. Dvihetuka paṭisandhi pana anokāsāyeva nahoti. Alabbha mānattāyeva sā navuttāti sakkā viññātuṃ. Tasmā yuttito pāḷiyeva balavatarāti katvā mahādhammarakkhitattheravādova pāḷiyā sametīti paṭisambhidāmaggaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto. Ṭīkākārā pana kammasarikkhaka vipākadassanatthaṃ sāvasesa pāṭhova mahātherena vuttoti icchanti. Evañca katvā aṭṭhasāliniyaṃpi tipiṭakacūḷanāgattheravādova pamāṇaṃ katvā vuttoti.

Therein, however, because this section of the teaching is founded on roots—by way of co-nascent roots in the three moments—rootless rebirth-linking is not mentioned there due to there being no opportunity, not due to its being unobtainable. But two-rooted rebirth-linking is not unmentioned due to there being no opportunity; it can be understood that it is not mentioned precisely because it is unobtainable. Therefore, because from a logical standpoint the Pāli itself is stronger, it is said in the commentary to the Paṭisambhidāmagga that the doctrine of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita agrees with the Pāli. The sub-commentators, however, hold that the Great Elder taught only a partial text in order to show the correspondence between kamma and its result. And thus, in the Aṭṭhasālinī as well, it is stated by taking the doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga as the authority.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ idāni ekāya cetanāya dvādasavipākāni ettheva dasakamaggopi ahetukaṭṭhakampiti āgatassa moravāpivāsi mahādhammarakkhitattherassāti pāṭho.

Now, in the Vibhāvanī, the reading that has come down from the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, resident of Moravāpi, is as follows: 'By a single volition, twelve results arise. Herein, also the tenfold path and the rootless octad.'

Moravāpivāsimahādattattherassāti pana vattabbo. Mahādhamma rakkhitattheravādopi pana ettha ekadesena saṅgahitoyeva. Tasmiṃpi hi asaṅkhārikaṃ kammaṃ asaṅkhārikavipākameva deti. No sasaṅkhārikaṃ[M 0.0244]. Sasaṅkhārikaṃ kammaṃ sasaṅkhārikavipākameva deti. No asaṅkhārikanti āgatamevāti. [Kāmāvacarakammaṃ]

But the reading should be stated as that of the Elder Mahādatta, resident of Moravāpi. The doctrine of the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita is also included here in part. For in that doctrine, an unprompted kamma gives only an unprompted result, not a prompted one. A prompted kamma gives only a prompted result, not an unprompted one; thus it has come down. [Kāmāvacara Kamma]

154. Rūpāvacarakamme parittanti duvidhaṃ parittaṃ apaguṇatā yavā hīnatāyavā. Tattha yaṃ paṇītehi chandādīhi yuttaṃpi abhāvitaṃ hoti paṭiladdhamattaṃ, taṃ apaguṇatāya parittaṃnāma. Yaṃ sandhāya yaṃ apaguṇaṃ hoti, upari jhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, idaṃ parittaṃnāmāti aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana subhāvitaṃpi samānaṃ hīnehi chandādīhi yuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ hīnatāya parittaṃnāma. Yaṃ sandhāya yassa āyūhanakkhaṇe chandovā hīno hoti. Vīriyaṃvā, cittaṃvā, vīmaṃsāvā, taṃ hīnaṃnāmāti tattheva vuttaṃ. Majjhimaṃpi duvidhaṃ. Tattha nātipaguṇa tāya majjhimaṃ sandhāya nātisubhāvito majjhimoti visuddhimagge vuttaṃ. Majjhimehi chandādīhi yuttatāya majjhimaṃ sandhāya yassa āyūhanakkhaṇe te dhammā majjhimā honti. Taṃ majjhimanti aṭṭha sāliniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Paṇītaṃpi duvidhaṃ. Tattha atipaguṇatāya paṇītaṃ sandhāya subhāvito vasippatto paṇītoti visuddhimagge vuttaṃ. Paṇītehi pana chandādīhi yuttatāya paṇītaṃ sandhāya yassa āyūhanakkhaṇe te dhammā paṇītā honti. Taṃ paṇītanti aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha yāni apaguṇatādi vasena parittādīni vuttāni, tāni idha nādhippetāni. Yāni pana hīnādīhi chandādīhi yuttatāya parittādīni vuttāni, tāneva idhādhippetāni. Imāneva hi tividhāsu bhūmīsu tividhaṃ brahmupapattibhedaṃ sādhentīti. Itthīnaṃ jhānesu vasīpattānaṃpi chandādīnaṃ apaṇītatāya mahābrahmesu anuppajjanañcettha sādhakaṃ. Tenevaca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ chandādivasena siddhāni hīna majjhima paṇītāni aṭṭhārasapabhedena vibhajitvā imāni aṭṭhārasa kammadvārāni nāma imehi pabhāvitattā imesaṃ vasena aṭṭhārasakhattiyā aṭṭhārasa brāhmaṇā aṭṭhārasa vessā aṭṭhārasa suddā aṭṭhacattā līsa gotta caraṇāni veditabbānīti vuttaṃ. Etena hi devānaṃpi brahmūnaṃpi labbhamānaṃ upapattibhedaṃ upalakkhetīti.

154. In fine-material sphere kamma, 'limited' (paritta) is of two kinds: either by lack of proficiency or by inferiority. Herein, that which, though associated with superior factors like zeal, is undeveloped and merely attained, is called 'limited' due to lack of proficiency. With reference to this, it is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī: 'That which is unproficient cannot become a condition for a higher jhāna; this is called 'limited'.' But that which, though well-developed, is associated with inferior factors like zeal, is called 'limited' due to inferiority. With reference to this, it is said in the same text: 'That for which, at the moment of accumulation, zeal, or energy, or consciousness, or investigation is inferior, is called 'inferior'.' The middling is also of two kinds. Herein, with reference to that which is middling due to not being very proficient, it is said in the Visuddhimagga: 'not very well-developed is middling.' With reference to that which is middling due to being associated with middling factors like zeal, it is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī: 'That for which, at the moment of accumulation, those factors are middling, is called 'middling'.' The superior is also of two kinds. Herein, with reference to that which is superior due to being exceedingly proficient, it is said in the Visuddhimagga: 'well-developed and having attained mastery is superior.' But with reference to that which is superior due to being associated with superior factors like zeal, it is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī: 'That for which, at the moment of accumulation, those factors are superior, is called 'superior'.' Here, the terms 'limited' and so on, defined by lack of proficiency, etc., are not intended. Rather, those defined by association with inferior, middling, or superior factors like zeal are intended here. For these alone accomplish the threefold distinction of Brahmā-rebirth in the three planes. And the non-arising among the Great Brahmās for women who have attained mastery in the jhānas, due to the non-superiority of their zeal, etc., is a proof in this matter. Therefore, in the commentary, having divided the inferior, middling, and superior—established by way of zeal, etc.—into eighteen kinds, it is said: 'These are called the eighteen doors of kamma. Because of being influenced by these, by way of them, eighteen kinds of khattiyas, eighteen kinds of brāhmaṇas, eighteen kinds of vessas, eighteen kinds of suddas, and forty-eight clans and conducts are to be understood.' By this, the obtainable distinction of rebirth among both devas and Brahmās is indicated.

[161] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[161] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Paṭiladdhamattaṃ [M 0.0245] anāsevitaṃ parittanti avisesatova aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā nāti subhāvitaṃ amaripuṇṇavasībhāvaṃ majjhimaṃ. Ativiyasubhāvitaṃ pana sabbaso paripuṇṇa vasībhāvaṃ paṇīta”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ idha nayujjatiyeva.

‘“Merely attained, unpracticed, is limited”—this is stated without distinction in the commentary. Similarly, “the middling is not very well-developed, not having attained full mastery.” “But that which is exceedingly well-developed, having in every way attained full mastery, is superior”’—it is said. All of that is not at all applicable here.

Tañhi upari jhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ samatthāsamatthaṃvā hāna bhāgiyatādi visesaṃ vā sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na pana upapatti bhedajanaka visesanti.

For that is said with reference to whether it is capable or incapable of being a condition for a higher jhāna, or with reference to a distinction such as being conducive to decline. But it is not a distinction that generates a difference in rebirth.

[162] Yañca tattha

[162] And what is there stated:

“Ācariyena panettha parittaṃpi īsakaṃ laddhāsevanameva adhippetanti dissati. Tathā hānena nāmarūpaparicchede-

“It is seen that the teacher here intends ‘limited’ to mean even a slight attainment through practice. Thus, by him, in the ‘Analysis of Name-and-Form’:

Samānāsevane laddhe, vijjamāne mahabbale;

Aladdhā tādisaṃ hetu, mabhiññā na vipaccatīti.

‘When similar practice has been gained, and great power is present; not having gained such a cause, higher knowledge does not ripen.’

Samānabhūmikatova āsevana lābhena balava bhāvato mahaggatadhammānaṃ vipākadānaṃ vatvā tadabhāvato abhiññāya avipaccanaṃ vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi vicāretabbameva.

It is said: ‘Having stated the yielding of fruit of the sublime states due to the gaining of practice on the same plane and due to the state of being powerful, the non-ripening of higher knowledge is said to be due to the absence of that.’ That too should indeed be investigated.

Yathā hi ariyamaggacetanā attanā samānabhūmakajavanato aladdhāsevanāpi samānā vipākaṃ na detīti natthi. Tathā ādi kammikavīthiyaṃ ekavāramattabhūtā sabbasamāpatti vīthīsuca sabbapatha mabhūtā mahaggatacetanāpi samānabhūmakadhammato aladdhāsevana tāya dubbalattā vipākaṃ nadetīti natthīti na na sakkā viññātunti. Ettha siyā- tasseva rūpāvacarassa kusalassa kammassa katattā upacitattā vipākaṃ.La. Pathamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatīti vuttaṃ. Na ca sā cetanā upacitānāma hoti. Samānabhūmaka dhammato aladdhāsevanattāti.Na. Maggacetanāyapi avipākatāpattito. Sāpihi tasseva lokuttarassa kusalassa jhānassa katattā bhāvitattā vipākaṃ. La. Pathamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatīti vuttā. Naca sāpi samānabhūmakadhammato laddhāsevanā hotīti. Ubhayattha [M 0.0246] pana pathamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya upacinitvā bhāvetvā āgatattā asamānabhūmika javanehipi laddhāsevana bhāvaṃ paṭicca upacitatā bhāvitatāca vuttāti sakkā vattunti. Tasmā ādi kammikabhūtāpi mahaggatacetanā maraṇā sanne laddhā abbhuṇhā āsannakammabhūtā vipākaṃ nadetīti na vattabbā. Abhiññācetanā ca samānabhūmakehipi nānāvajjanavīthijavanehi suṭṭhutaraṃ laddhāsevanattā tikkhatarabhūtā kathaṃ dubbalānāma siyā. Teneva ayaṃ vādo anuṭīkāyaṃ paṭikkhitto. Vuttañhi tattha keci pana samāna bhūmakato āsevanalābhena balavantāni jhānānīti tāni vipākaṃ denti. Abhiññā pana satipi jhānabhāve tadabhāvato tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe āgantukattāvā dubbalā. Tasmā vipākaṃ na dentīti vadanti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Punappunaṃ parikammavasena abhiññā yapi vasībhāvasambhavatoti. Catutthajjhānasamādhissa pana ānisaṃsabhūtā abhiññācetanā tassa phalasadisā phalaṭṭhāne ṭhitā, tasmā sā vipākaṃ nadetīti icchanti ṭīkākārā. Tassa pana iddhi vikubbanādikiccaṃ vipaccanakiccatopi mahantataraṃ hoti. Sabbathā menaca vikubbanādikiccaṃ sādhentiyā vipaccanathāmepi tena thāmena saha parikkhayaṃ gacchati. Tasmā sā puna vipākaṃ nadetītipi yujjatiyeva. Pañcamajjhānanti abhiññābhāvaṃ apattaṃ parittādibhedena tividhaṃ pañcamajjhānaṃ. Tadevāti pañcamajhānameva. Saññāvirāgaṃ bhāvetvāti citte sati rajjana dussana muyhanāni honti. Tasmiṃ asati diṭṭhadhammanibbānappattonāma hotīti evaṃ citte eva ādīnavaṃ disvā acittakabhavapatthanā sahitaṃ vāyokasiṇevā kesañci matena paricchinnākāsa kasiṇevā saññāvirāgaṃ bhāvetvā. Asaññasattesu uppajjantīti yena yena iriyāpathena idha maranti, teneva tattha uppajjanti. Kammakiriyavādititthiyā evāti adhippāyo. Na hi akammakiriyavādīnaṃ jhānabhāvanā nāma atthīti. Anāgāmino pana suddhāvāsesu uppajjantīti suddhāvāsesu pana anāgāmino eva uppajjanti. Na aññe sakadāgāmiādayoti attho. Etena anāgāmīnaṃ aññasmiṃpi brahmaloke uppatti appaṭisiddhā [M 0.0247] hoti. Anāgāmīsuca saddhādhiko avihesu uppajjati, vīriyādhiko atappesu. Satādhiko sudassesu. Samādhādhiko sudassīsu. Paññādhiko akaniṭṭhesūti. Yathākkamaṃ bhāvetvā yathākkamaṃ arūpesu uppajjantīti yojanā. Etthaca pathamajjhānaṃ parittaṃ bhāvetvātiādi sabbaṃ pathamajjhānādīnaṃ yathā sakaṃ vipaccanabhūmi vavatthānavasena vuttaṃ. Samāpattilābhino pana puthujjana sotāpanna sakadāgāmino attanā laddhasamāpattīnaṃ vipaccanabhūmīsu icchitabhūmiyaṃ nibbattanti. Tesu puthujjano nikantiyā sati kāmalokepi nibbattatiyeva. Itare pana jhāne apari hīne sati kāmalokepi nibbattatiyeva. Itare pana jhāne aparihīne sati kāmabhave nikantināma tesaṃ na sambhavatīti parihīnajjhānāeva tattha nibbattanti.

Just as it is not the case that the volition associated with the noble path gives no result even if it has not gained repeated cultivation from javanas on the same plane, so too, it cannot be understood that a sublime volition—which has occurred only once in an initial practitioner's process and is the very first in all attainment processes—gives no result because it is weak due to not gaining repeated cultivation from states on the same plane. Here, it might be argued: the result arises from the wholesome kamma of the form realm because of its being done and accumulated. It is said that “having attained the first jhāna, he dwells therein.” But that volition is not considered to be accumulated, because it has not gained repeated cultivation from states on the same plane. No, for then the path-volition would also become resultless. For it is said that “having attained the first jhāna, he dwells therein” because that very supramundane wholesome jhāna has been done and developed. But it too has not gained repeated cultivation from states on the same plane. However, in both cases, it can be said that because it has come about through accumulation and development from the initial application onwards, it has gained repeated cultivation even from javanas on different planes, and thus accumulation and development are spoken of. Therefore, it cannot be said that even an initial sublime volition of a practitioner does not give a result if, near death, it has become a fresh, proximate kamma. Furthermore, the volition connected with direct knowledge, having gained repeated cultivation more thoroughly through javanas of various adverting processes on the same plane, is very sharp; how could it be called weak? Therefore, this view has been refuted in the sub-sub-commentary. For it is said there: “Some, however, say that because the jhānas are strong from gaining the benefit of repeated cultivation from states on the same plane, they give rise to a result. But direct knowledge, although there is the jhāna-state, is weak because of the absence of that repetition, being adventitious to this and that object. Therefore, they say, it does not give rise to a result.” That is unreasonable, for the attainment of mastery is possible even for direct knowledge through repeated preliminary practice. The authors of the sub-commentary, however, hold that the volition connected with direct knowledge, which is a benefit of the fourth jhāna concentration and stands in the place of the result, does not give rise to a result. However, its function of magical transformation and so on is greater than its ripening function. In every way, while accomplishing the function of magical transformation and so on, its power of ripening is exhausted along with that power. Therefore, it is indeed reasonable that it does not give rise to a result again. “Fifth jhāna” means the fifth jhāna, which has not attained the state of direct knowledge, and is threefold, distinguished as limited and so on. “That same” means the fifth jhāna itself. “Having developed dispassion for perception” means: when there is mind, there are lust, aversion, and delusion. When it is not there, one is said to have attained Nibbāna in this very life. Thus, seeing the danger in the mind itself, some develop dispassion for perception, together with the aspiration for a mindless existence, through the air kasiṇa or, according to some, the limited-space kasiṇa. “They are reborn among non-percipient beings” means: in whatever posture they die here, they arise there in that same posture. This is the view of the sectarians who are proponents of kamma and action. For there is no such thing as jhāna-development for those who are proponents of non-action. “Non-returners, however, are reborn in the Pure Abodes” means that only non-returners arise in the Pure Abodes. The meaning is that others, such as once-returners, do not. By this, the arising of non-returners in other Brahma-worlds is not prohibited. Among non-returners, one with a predominance of faith arises in Aviha; one with a predominance of energy in Atappa; one with a predominance of mindfulness in Sudassa; one with a predominance of concentration in Sudassī; and one with a predominance of wisdom in Akaniṭṭha. The connection is: having developed them in order, they are reborn in the formless realms in order. Here, all the statements such as “having developed the first jhāna as limited,” and so on, are stated by way of establishing their respective ripening realms for each of the first jhāna and so on. Those who have attained attainments—ordinary persons, stream-enterers, and once-returners—are reborn in a desired realm among the ripening realms of the attainments they have reached. Among them, an ordinary person, if there is craving, is certainly reborn in the sense-sphere world. As for the others, if their jhāna is not lost, craving for sense-sphere existence is not possible for them. Thus, only those whose jhāna has been lost are reborn there.

[163] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[163] But in the Vibhāvanī,

Tesaṃpi sotāpannasakadāgāmīnaṃ nikantivasena kāmabhavenibbattiṃ icchantena “tathā kāmabhavepi kāmāvacara kammabalena. Ijjhati bhikkhave sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattāti hi vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

It is said by one who desires rebirth in the sense-sphere for those stream-enterers and once-returners through craving, 'Thus, in the sense-sphere too, by the power of sense-sphere kamma. For it has been said: “Monks, the heart’s resolve of a virtuous person succeeds because of its purity.”' That is not reasonable.

Tehi jhāne aparihīne ekantena brahmalokagāminoeva honti. Yato te jhānaanāgāminonāmāti vuccanti. Jhānapari hānica tesaṃ taṃtaṃ palibodha vaseneva hoti. Na pana kāma rāgādivasena. Kasmā, maggasahāyena jhānena suṭṭhu vikkhambhitattā. Vuttañhetaṃ aṅguttare-sahadassanuppādā bhikkhave ariyasāvakassa tīṇi saṃyojanāni mahīyanti.La. So vivicceva.La. Pathamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Tasmiṃ ce samaye bhikkhave ariyasāvako kālaṅkareyya. Natthi tassa saṃyojanaṃ. Yena saṃyojanena saṃyutto ariyasāvako puna yimaṃ lokaṃ āgaccheyyāti. Etthaca tasmiṃ ce samayetiādinā so laddhajjhānaṃ aparihāpetvā ce kālaṅkaroti. Ekantena brahmalokameva gamissati. Parihāpentassa pana taṃ saṃyojanaṃ pākatimevāti dasseti. [M 0.0248] Paṭisambhidāmaggaṭṭhakathāyañca jhānalābhīnaṃ pana anāgāmissaca brahmalokeyeva paṭisandhidānato paccayo nahotīti vuttaṃ. Tattha jhānalābhīnanti mahaggatajjhānalābhīnaṃ sotāpanna sakadāgāmīnaṃ. Paccayo nahotīti tesaṃ vipassanānikanti taṇhā kāmasugatipaṭisandhiyā na hotīti attho.

For when their jhāna is not lost, they are certainly bound for the Brahma-world. Therefore, they are called jhāna-non-returners. The loss of jhāna for them occurs only due to certain obstacles, not because of sensual desire or other defilements. Why? Because the jhāna, aided by the path, thoroughly suppresses them. As it is said in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: “Monks, with the arising of vision, three fetters are abandoned by the noble disciple… Quite secluded… Having attained the first jhāna, he dwells therein. If, monks, the noble disciple were to pass away at that time, there is no fetter by which, being fettered, the noble disciple would return to this world.” Here, by the phrase “if at that time,” it shows that if one dies without having lost the attained jhāna, one will certainly go to the Brahma-world. But for one who loses it, that fetter becomes manifest. In the commentary to the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is also stated that for those who attain jhāna, and for non-returners, because they give rebirth only in the Brahma-world, there is no condition for rebirth in the sense-sphere. Here, “those who attain jhāna” refers to stream-enterers and once-returners who attain sublime jhānas. “Not a condition” means that for them, longing for insight is not a condition for rebirth in a happy sense-sphere destination. That is the meaning.

Tasmā tesaṃ dvinnaṃ sekhānaṃ kuppadhammānaṃpi sataṃ jhāne vijjamāne kāmabhave nikanti nāma natthīti veditabbaṃ. Anāgāmissa pana niddāyantasseva satthena gīvaṃ chinditvā mārīyamānassapi jhānaṃ alabhitvā cavanaṃnāma natthi. So hi samādhismiṃ paripūrakārīti vutto. Itthiyo pana aṭṭhasamāpattiyo labhitvā anantare bhave akaniṭṭhe nibbattamānāpi adhipatibhūtesu mahābrahmesu na nibbattanti. Hīnajjhāsayattā purohita pārisajjesueva nibbattanti. Tathāhi aṭṭhakathāsu yaṃ itthī brahmattaṃ kareyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti suttapadassa atthavacane brahmattanti mahābrahmattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Itthī ca idha jhānaṃ bhāvetvā kālaṃ katvā brahmapārisajjānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjati, na mahābrahmānanti vuttaṃ. Brahmapārisajjānanti cettha brahmapurohitānaṃpi saṅgahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Te hi brahmānaṃ parisabhūtā hontīti. Vuttañhetaṃ saṃyuttake –

Therefore, it should be understood that even for those two trainees who are subject to lapse, though they possess jhāna, there is no craving for the realm of sensual desire. As for the non-returner, even if his throat is cut by a sword while he is asleep and he is being killed, there is no passing away without having attained jhāna, for he is said to be one who has fully perfected concentration. However, women, even if they attain the eight meditative attainments and are reborn immediately afterward in the Akaniṭṭha realm, are not reborn among the great Brahmās who are sovereign. Due to their inferior disposition, they are reborn only as Brahmā’s ministers and attendants. Thus, in the commentaries, in the explanation of the statement: “It is not possible for a woman to attain Brahmāhood,” the term “Brahmāhood” refers to the state of a great Brahmā. And here, a woman who develops jhāna and dies is reborn in the company of Brahmā’s attendants, not as a great Brahmā. In this context, “Brahmā’s attendants” should also be understood to include Brahmā’s ministers, for they are part of Brahmā’s assembly. As it is said in the Saṃyutta:

Athakho bhikkhave sikhībhagavā abhituṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi. Paṭibhātu taṃ brāhmaṇa brahmunoca brahmaparisāyaca brahmapārisajjānañca dhammikathāti.

Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī addressed the monk Abhibhū: “May a Dhamma talk occur to you, brahmin, for Brahmā, for the assembly of Brahmā, and for the attendants of Brahmā.”

Parisabhāveca sati parisāsu jātāpināma hontīti. Tattha brahmunoti mahābrahmuno. Brahmaparisāyāti brahmapurohita gaṇassāti attho. Nanu brahmapārisajjānanti vuttattā na mahābrahmānanti ettheva tesaṃ saṅgahaṇaṃ yuttanti ce. Na. Yaṃ itthī sakkattaṃ kareyya, mārattaṃ kareyya, brahmattaṃ kareyya, netaṃṭhānaṃ vijjatīti evaṃ adhipati bhūtehi sakkādīhi saha vuttattā idha adhipatipaṭikkhipanasseva sambhavato. Teneva hi nettiyaṃ-itthī mahābrahmā siyāti, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti vuttaṃ. Ettāvatā vehapphalādīsu [M 0.0249] uparibrahmalokesupi purohitapārisajjabrahmānaṃ atthitā siddhā hoti. Teneva saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ therānañhi bhaṇḍagāhakadaharā viya brahmānaṃpi pārisajjabrahmāno nāma hontīti vuttaṃ.

And when there is an assembly, they are called 'born in assemblies'. Here, 'of Brahmā' means of the Great Brahmā. 'Brahmā's assembly' means the group of Brahmā's ministers—this is the meaning. If it is objected: 'Since it is said "Brahmā's attendants" and "not as a great Brahmā," is it not fitting that their (the ministers') inclusion is right there with the attendants?' No. Because it is said that 'a woman cannot assume the role of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā—such a thing is impossible,' and since this is stated in relation to sovereign beings like Sakka and others, the rejection of sovereignty is what is relevant here. For this very reason, in the Netti, it is said: 'It is impossible that a woman could be a Great Brahmā—such a thing does not exist.' By this much, the existence of minister and attendant Brahmās in the higher Brahmā worlds, such as Vehapphala and others, is established. Therefore, in the Saṃyutta commentary, it is said: 'Just as young novices are like those who handle the requisites for the elders, so too among the Brahmās there are attendant Brahmās.'

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Itthiyopi pana ariyāvā anariyāvā aṭṭhasamāpattilā bhiniyo brahmapārisajjesuyeva nibbattantīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutta”nti vuttaṃ.

It is said: “Moreover, it is stated in the commentary that 'women, whether noble or ignoble, who have gained the eight attainments are reborn only among the retinue of Brahmā.'”

Tattha brahmapārisajjesuyevāti akaniṭṭhe nibbattamānāpi brahmānaṃ paricārika brahmesueva nibbattanti. Na mahābrahmesūti attho daṭṭhabbo.

Here, 'only among the retinue of Brahmā' means that even those reborn in Akaniṭṭha are reborn only as Brahmās who are attendants of Brahmā. The meaning should be understood as 'not as Great Brahmās'.

Maṇimañjūsāyaṃ pana

But in the Maṇimañjūsā,

Brahmapārisajjesuyeva nibbattanti, na brahmapurohitādīsūti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

It is said that 'they are reborn only in the retinue of Brahmā, not among Brahmā's ministers and so forth'. That should not be accepted.

Yañca tattha

And whatever is stated there,

Sāmāvatiyādīnaṃ pathamaṃ brahmapārisajjesu nibbattanaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃpi aṭṭhakathāya na sameti.

The statement about Sāmāvatī and others being reborn first in the Brahmā's retinue—that too does not agree with the commentary.

Yasmā pana tā imasmiṃ attabhāve ariyaphalāni sacchākaṃsu. Tasmā tattha anāgāminiyo suddhāvāsesu uppannā. Itarā kāci tāvatiṃsesu kāci paranimmitavasavattīsu uppannā icceva udānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanti. Apicettha vehapphale akaniṭṭhe catutthāruppeti tīsu bhavaggesu nibbattā ariyā aññattha nuppajjanti. Sesabrahmalokesu nibbattā heṭṭhābhūmīsu nuppajjantīti. [Kammacatukkaṃ].

But since they realized the noble fruits in this very existence, therefore those who were non-returners were reborn in the Pure Abodes, while some others were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa or Paranimmitavasavattī realms, as stated in the Udāna commentary. Moreover, here, noble ones reborn in the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and the fourth formless attainment—these three highest states of existence—are not reborn elsewhere; and those reborn in the remaining Brahmā realms are not reborn in lower realms. [The Tetrad of Kamma].

155. Āyukkhayena maraṇaṃ kammakkhayena maraṇantiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Tattha aparikkhīṇeyeva kammānubhāve tasmiṃ tasmiṃ [M 0.0250] sattanikāye yathāniyamitassa āyuparimāṇassa parikkhayena paripuṇṇena maraṇaṃ āyukkhaya maraṇaṃnāma. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave dubbalena kammena nibbattassa sattassa aparikkhīṇeyeva āyuparimāṇe kevalaṃ kammasattiparikkhayena antarāva maraṇaṃ kammakkhaya maraṇaṃnāma. Tadubhayassa samaṃ parikkhayena maraṇaṃ ubhayakkhaya maraṇaṃnāma. Dharamānepi tadubhaye purimabhavesuvā imasmiṃvābhave katena upaghātakakammena ajjhattabahiddhābhūte nānārogābādha pathavīpavesa asanipātādike jīvitantarāye samuṭṭhāpetvā dussimārakalāburājādīnaṃviya antarāva uparodhita khandhasantānassa sattassa maraṇaṃ upacchedaka maraṇaṃnāma. Nanu cettha marantānaṃ nāma sabbesaṃpi taṃtaṃbhavaṃ janentaṃ kammaṃ khiyyatiyeva. Athakasmā itarepi vuttāti. Vuccate, sarasavaseneva hi kammasāmatthiyassa khayo idha kammakkhayoti adhippeto. Ye pana dasavassa vīsativassa yāva asaṅkhyeyya vassādi vasena nānāāyukappavidhāyakā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sattanikāye sabbajana sādhāraṇā sattānaṃ ajjhattabahiddhasambhūtā utuāhārānāma honti. Te tassa tassa āyukappassa ṭhitikarā vuddhikarā hānikarācāti tividhā honti. Tattha akusalamūlesu vaḍḍhamānesu hānikarā vaḍḍhanti. Kusalamūlesu vaḍḍhamānesu buddhikarā vaḍḍhanti. Ubhayamūlesu samaṃ ṭhitesu ṭhitikarā samaṃ pavattanti. Tesaṃ vasena sattānaṃ āyukappo katthaci sadā ṭhitibhāgo hoti. Katthaci kadāci hānibhāgo kadāci vuddhibhāgo hoti. Tayopi cete ṭhitikarādayo taṃtaṃsattanikāyaṃ ajjhottharamānā āyuṃ paricchindantā pavattantīti asaṅkhyeyyāyuka saṃvattanikaṃ cakkavattisampatti saṃvattanikañca kammaṃ dasavassike kāle vipaccamānaṃ tadanurūpaṃeva bhogañca issariyañca datvā dasavasena khiyyati. Taṃ taṃ sattanikāya pariyāpannā sattā santānabhūtā rūpadhammā sabbaññu buddhānaṃ khandhasantāna bhūtāpi taggatikā tadanūvattikā eva hutvā pariṇamanti aññatra iddhimaya vijjāmaya rasāyanavidhi jīvita saṅkhāra vidūhīti. Vuttañhetaṃ mahāpadānasuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

155. This should be connected with 'death due to the exhaustion of lifespan, death due to the exhaustion of kamma,' and so on. Herein, when the power of kamma is not yet exhausted, death that occurs due to the complete exhaustion of the predetermined lifespan in each class of beings is called 'death due to the exhaustion of lifespan.' In each existence, for a being born with weak kamma, death that occurs in the interim due to the mere exhaustion of the kammic force, even though the lifespan is not exhausted, is called 'death due to the exhaustion of kamma.' Death due to the equal exhaustion of both is called 'death due to the exhaustion of both.' Even while both lifespan and kamma are still present, when destructive kamma performed in previous existences or in this very existence gives rise to life-threatening dangers—such as various internal or external diseases, sinking into the earth, or being struck by lightning—the death of a being whose continuum of aggregates is interrupted, like that of Dussimāra or King Kalābu, is called 'death due to interruption.' Now, if it is asked: 'For all who die, is not the kamma that produced their existence exhausted? Why then are the other types mentioned?' It is answered: Here, 'exhaustion of kamma' is intended to mean the exhaustion of kamma's potential by its own nature. Furthermore, there are conditions common to all people in each class of beings that determine various lifespans, from ten years, twenty years, up to an incalculable age; these are called climate and food, which originate internally and externally. They are of three kinds: those that maintain, increase, and decrease the lifespan of a given age. Therein, when unwholesome roots increase, the decreasing factors increase. When wholesome roots increase, the increasing factors increase. When both roots are balanced, the maintaining factors operate evenly. Due to these, the lifespan of beings is sometimes stable, sometimes decreasing, and sometimes increasing. These three—the maintaining, increasing, and decreasing factors—pervade each class of beings, determining their lifespan. Thus, kamma that leads to an incalculable lifespan or to the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch, when it ripens at a time when the lifespan is ten years, provides corresponding wealth and power and is exhausted in those ten years. The beings comprised within each class, the material phenomena that constitute their continuity, and even the continuum of aggregates of the Omniscient Buddhas, transform according to their particular destiny and conditions, except for those skilled in psychic power, knowledge, elixirs, or the method of prolonging life-formations. This has been stated in the commentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta:

Sabbepi [M 0.0251] sabbaññubuddhā asaṅkhyeyyāyukā. Kasmā te asaṅkhyeyyaṃ na aṭṭhaṃsūti. Utubhojanavipattiyā. Utubhojanavasena hi āyu hāyatipi vaḍḍhatipīti.

All Omniscient Buddhas have incalculable lifespans. Why did they not remain for an incalculable time? Because of the failure of climate and food. For it is due to climate and food that lifespan decreases or increases.

Tasmā padhānanissayabhūtesu dvisamuṭṭhānika rūpadhammesu taṃ taṃ āyukappavasena pariṇamantesu jiyyamānesu yāvamahantaṃpi kammaṃ attano vipākādhiṭṭhānassa abhāvā khiyyatiyeva. Socassa khayo na sarasena hoti. Athakho āyusaṅkhāravipattiyā eva hotīti idha āyukkhayo visuṃ gahitoti. Esanayo upacchedakamaraṇepi netabbo. Tattha upacchedakamaraṇanti akālamaraṇaṃ vuccati. Tañhipavattamānaṃ upacchedakakammunāvā pavattati. Aññehivā aneka sahassehi kāraṇehi. Tāni pana pāḷiyaṃ mūlabhedato saṃkhipitvā aṭṭhadhā vuttāni. Katamāni pana tānīti. Atthi vātasamuṭṭhānā ābādhā. Atthi vittasamuṭṭhānā. Atthi semha samuṭṭhānā. Atthi sannipātikā. Atthi utusamuṭṭhānā. Atthi visamaparihārajā. Atthi opakkamikā. Atthi kammavipākajā ābādhāti. Tattha kammavipākajā keci upapīḷakakammajākeci upacchedakakammajā. Yasmā pana vāto kuppamāno sītuṇhādīhi dasahi kāraṇehi kuppati. Tesuca ekameva kamma vipākajaṃ hoti. Sesāni pana akammavipākajānīti milinda pañhe vuttaṃ. Yasmāca kammavipākajāpi ābādhā uppajjamānā vāta kuppanādīhi vinā na uppajjanti. Tasmā keci vātasamuṭṭhānādayopi kammavipākajā hontiyevāti daṭṭhabbā.

Therefore, when the material phenomena arising from two origins, which serve as the primary support, undergo transformation according to their respective lifespan limits and deteriorate, even the greatest kamma is exhausted due to the absence of a basis for its fruition. The exhaustion thereof does not occur by its own nature. Rather, it occurs precisely due to the failure of the life-sustaining formations. Therefore, here, the exhaustion of lifespan is taken separately. This principle should also be applied to death by interruption. Here, death by interruption is called untimely death. It occurs either due to an interrupting kamma or due to countless other causes. These causes, summarized in the Pāli Canon from their fundamental divisions, are stated as eightfold. What are they? There are illnesses arising from wind, from bile, from phlegm, from their combination, from seasonal changes, from improper care, from external assault, and from the result of kamma. Among these, some illnesses that are the result of kamma arise from oppressive kamma, while others arise from interrupting kamma. Since wind, when agitated, is agitated by ten causes such as cold and heat, and among these, only one is the result of kamma—the rest are not the result of kamma, as stated in the Milinda Pañha. And since even illnesses that are the result of kamma do not arise without the agitation of wind and so on, it should be understood that some illnesses arising from wind and so on are indeed the result of kamma.

Tattha sannipātikāti vātādīnaṃ dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃvā sannipatitānaṃ vasena pavattā. Ye pana loke sattānaṃ payogamuttā sayaṃ jātā nānābhayupaddavā. Te utusamuṭṭhānesu saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Visamaparihārajāti anisammakārīnaṃ anekavidhe visame vipattimukhe attānaṃ payojantānaṃ tato tatovā tattha tattha vā patana pakkhalanādivasena pavattā. Opakkamikāti attanāvā parehi rājacoraverīhivā amanussavāḷayakkhadevatāhivā vāḷamigādīhivā katānaṃ payogānaṃ vasena pavattā. Kuppitā hi devatā [M 0.0252] sakalaṃ rajjaṃvā raṭṭhaṃvā dīpakaṃvā ekappahārena asesaṃ katvā vināsenti daṇḍakaraṭṭha majjharaṭṭha kaliṅgaraṭṭha mātaṅgaraṭṭhesu viya. Anekasahassevā vāḷayakkhe vissajjanti vesāliyaṃ viya. Rakkhasevā vissajjanti suvaṇṇabhūmiyaṃviya. Vuttañhetaṃ aṅguttare yakkhā vāḷe amanusse ossajjanti. Tena bahumanussā kālaṃ karontīti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpi yakkhāti yakkhādhipatino. Vāḷe amanusse ossajjantīti caṇḍe yakkhe manussapathe vissajjanti. Te laddhokāsā mahājanaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpentīti vuttaṃ. Tattha vissajjantīti visamācāra bahule manusse disvā bhinnasaddhā yakkhasenāpatino manussānaṃ atthāya pubbeviya ārakkhaṃna gaṇhantīti attho. Janapadanagaranigamagāmesuceva tasmiṃ tasmiṃ puggaleca vattabbameva natthi. Aṅguttare vuttā satthadubbhikkharoga kappāpi idha vattabbāti. Kammavipākajāti upapīḷakopaghātakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipaccanavasena pavattā ābādhāti attho. Evaṃ akālamaraṇaṃ upacchedakammunāvā aññehivā anekasahassehi kāraṇehi hotīti. Yehi keci loke dissanti. Pāṇaharā jīvitavināsakā nānārogāvā nānābādhāvā nānābhayā nivā nānā daṇḍāvā nānā upaddavu pasaggāvā. Sabbe te sakakamma samuṭṭhitāeva attano sādhāraṇāti natthi. Parakammasamuṭṭhitāpi attano sādhāraṇāeva. Sakakammasamuṭṭhitāpi paresaṃ sādhāraṇāeva. Kammena vinā yato kutoci samuṭṭhitāpi attano vā paresaṃvā sādhāraṇāeva. Sabbasādhāraṇakammasamuṭṭhitesu vattabbameva natthi. Yathāha-visuddhimagge.

Here, 'arising from a combination' refers to those that arise due to the combination of two or three of the humors—wind, and so on. Those various dangers and calamities that arise spontaneously in the world for beings, without human contrivance, should be understood as included under 'arising from the seasons'. 'Arising from improper care' refers to those that arise for those who act without due consideration, exposing themselves to various kinds of dangerous and ruinous situations, leading to falls, slips, and the like. 'Arising from an external assault' refers to those that arise due to actions done by oneself or by others—such as kings, thieves, enemies, non-human beings, fierce yakkhas, deities, or predatory animals. For when angered, deities can utterly destroy an entire kingdom, country, or island in a single strike—as in the Daṇḍaka, Majjha, Kaliṅga, and Mātaṅga countries. Or they may release thousands of fierce yakkhas, as in Vesālī. Or they may unleash ogres, as in Suvaṇṇabhūmi. As it is stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: 'Yakkhas release fierce non-human beings, whereby many people die.' In the commentary, it is explained that 'yakkhas' refers to the yakkha chieftains, and 'they release fierce non-human beings' means they send fierce yakkhas onto human paths. These, having found an opportunity, bring about the destruction of the lives of the great populace. Here, 'they release' means that the yakkha generals, seeing many people engaged in wrong conduct and having lost faith, no longer provide protection for the welfare of humans as they did before. Needless to say, this applies to countries, cities, market towns, and villages, as well as to each and every individual. The weapon-period, famine-period, and disease-period mentioned in the Aṅguttara Nikāya should also be mentioned here. 'Born of kamma-result' means afflictions that arise through the ripening of oppressive and destructive kammas. Thus, untimely death occurs due to a destructive kamma or by countless other causes. Whatever life-taking, life-destroying things are seen in the world—various diseases, various ailments, various fears, various punishments, various calamities and misfortunes—it is not the case that all of them arise from one's own kamma and are exclusive to oneself. Those arising from the kamma of others are also common to oneself. Those arising from one's own kamma are also common to others. Those arising from any source apart from kamma are also common to oneself or to others. Regarding those arising from kamma common to all, there is nothing more to be said. As it is said in the Visuddhimagga.

Yathā catumahāpathe thapite lakkhamhi sabbadisāhi āgatā sarasattitomarapāsāṇādayo nipatanti. Evaṃ kāyepi sabbupaddavā nipatantīti.

Just as arrows, spears, javelins, stones, and so on, coming from all directions, fall upon a target set up at a great crossroads, so too do all calamities fall upon this body.

Yesuca rajjaraṭṭhādīsu te uppajjanti. Tattha yejanā upāya kusalāvā na honti. Naca paṭikārakusalā. Nāpi parihāra kusalā. Kammañca yesaṃ dubbalaṃ hoti. Uppanno anattho bala vā. Tejanā [M 0.0253] vināpi upacchedakakammunā tato na muccanti. Maraṇaṃ vā maraṇamattaṃvā dukkhaṃ pāpuṇantiyeva. Kalyāṇabhūtaṃpi hi kammaṃ attano balavataraṃ yatokutoci samuṭṭhitaṃ rogaṃvā ābādhaṃ vā bhayaṃvā daṇḍaṃvā upaddavupasaggaṃvā paṭibāhituṃ nasakkoti. Rogādayoeva taṃkhepentā pavattanti. Yathā hi udakaṃ attano balavataraṃ aggiṃ paṭibāhituṃ na sakkoti. Aggieva taṃ khepento pavattatīti evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imesañca sattānaṃ pakatiyāpi kammassa dubbalabhāvo mahāniddese jarā suttaniddesena visuddhi maggeca maraṇassati niddese āyu dubbalatoti padassa niddese na dīpetabbo. Yathāha –

And in those kingdoms, countries, and so on, where these calamities arise, there are people who are not skilled in means, not skilled in countermeasures, and not skilled in avoidance. Their kamma is weak, and the calamity that has arisen is powerful. Those people, even without an interrupting kamma, are not freed from it. They inevitably meet with death or suffering equivalent to death. For even wholesome kamma cannot ward off a disease, an ailment, a fear, a punishment, or a calamity and misfortune that has arisen from some source and is more powerful than itself. The disease and the like, overwhelming it, proceed. Just as water cannot extinguish a fire that is more powerful than itself—the fire, overwhelming it, burns on—so should this matter be understood. Moreover, the natural weakness of the kamma of these beings need not be expounded upon, for it is shown in the Mahāniddesa's exposition on the Jarā Sutta, in the Visuddhimagga's exposition on mindfulness of death, and in the exposition of the phrase 'life is weak.' As it is said:

Āyunāmetaṃ abalaṃ dubbalaṃ. Tathā hi sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ assāsapassāsupanibandhañceva iriyāpathupanibandhañca sītuṇhu panibandhañca mahābhūtupanibandhañca āhārupanibandhañcātiādi.

This life-faculty is weak and feeble. For the life of beings is dependent on the in-breaths and out-breaths, dependent on the postures, dependent on cold and heat, dependent on the great elements, and dependent on food, and so on.

Tathā kāyabahusādhāraṇato animittatoti imesaṃ padānaṃ niddesenapi pākaṭoyeva. Kammanibbattassa hi āyuno tiṇagge ussāvabindusseva paridubbalabhāve pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathā yañca vutte kammasāpi tatheva paridubbalatā siddhā hotīti. Evañcetaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Itarathā sabbaṃ pubbekatahetudiṭṭhināma siyā. Yathāha –

Similarly, this is also evident from the exposition of these words: 'because the body is common to many dangers and is indeterminate.' For when it is stated in the Pāli Canon and the commentaries that the lifespan produced by kamma is extremely fragile, like a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass, the extreme fragility of the kamma itself is thereby established. And so this should be accepted. Otherwise, this would amount to the wrong view that everything is due to past action. As it is said:

Idhekacco samaṇovā brāhmaṇovā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃ diṭṭhī. Yaṃ kiñcāyaṃpurisapuggalo paṭisaṃvedeti sukhaṃvā dukkhaṃvā adukkhamasukhaṃvā. Sabbaṃ taṃ pubbekatahetūti.

Here, some ascetic or brahmin holds such a doctrine, such a view: 'Whatever this individual person experiences—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—all that is due to what was done in the past.'

Ayañca attho milindapañhe tīsu ṭhānesu vitthārato āgato. Yathāvuttehi pana anekasahassehi kāraṇehi pavattamaraṇaṃpi akālamaraṇatāsāmaññena idha upacchedakamaraṇe saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And this matter is found in detail in three places in the Milindapañha. However, it should be understood that death occurring from the countless causes as mentioned is also included here under 'death by interruption' by virtue of its general nature as untimely death.
