Rūpayatīti rūpaṃ. Vaṇṇavisesaṃ āpajjitvā hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāseti. Pakatiyāpi vā yaṃkiñcidabbaṃ samavisamaṃvā pakāse tīti attho. Sappati sotaviññeyyabhāvaṃ gacchatīti saddo. Saddayatīti saddo. Taṃ taṃ atthaṃvā attano vatthuṃvā ācikkhatīti attho. Sadativā taṃ taṃ disaṃvā desaṃvā khaṇena vissarati vippharatīti saddo. Gandhayatīti gandho. Attano vatthuṃsūcetīti attho. Gacchatīti go. Vāto. Tena dhārīyatīti gandho. Rasīyati assādīyatīti raso. Rasantivā taṃ assādentīti raso. Phusīyatīti phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Phusanañcettha pasādena saha ghaṭṭanaṃ kalāpantarabhūtehi saddhiṃ paṭihananañca veditabbaṃ. Tadubhayaṃpi āpo dhātuyā natthīti vuttaṃ āpodhātuvivajjitanti. Kasmā pana taṃ tassā natthi. Nanu sītatāvā dravatāvā phusitvā gayhatīti. Vuccate, sītatā hi tejoyeva, na āpo. Yadi hi sā āpoyeva siyā. Pakkumite santatte loharasepissa sītatā labbhamānā siyā. So hi raso āpādhiko hotīti. Evaṃ pana nalabbhati. Tasmā sā tejoyeva, na āpoti. [M 0.0275] Apica, sītuṇhānaṃ ekasmiṃ kalāpe saha appavattanato orapārānaṃ viya tesaṃ anavaṭṭhānatoca viññāyati. Na hi sītakalāpe uṇhaṃ, uṇhakalāpevā sītaṃ saha pavattati. Yasmiṃca vatthumhi pubbe sītasaññā saṇṭhāti. Pacchā tato sītatare āgate tasmiṃyeva puna uṇhasaññā saṇṭhāti. Pubbe uṇhasaññāyaṃpi eseva nayo. Tathā uṇhe mande sītasaññā saṇṭhāti. Sīte mande uṇhasaññāti.

It is altered, thus it is material form (rūpa). It displays various colors and assumes a state that affects the heart. Alternatively, it means that whatever object is naturally even or uneven is made manifest. Sound (sadda) is so called because it moves, entering the range of what can be heard. It makes a sound, thus it is sound. It conveys a particular meaning or indicates its own basis. Alternatively, sound quickly spreads and penetrates in all directions or regions. Smell (gandha) is so called because it scents. It signifies its own basis. It goes (gacchati), thus 'go,' that is, wind. Because it is carried by that, it is smell. Taste (rasa) is so called because it is savored. Or they delight in tasting it, thus it is taste. The tangible (phoṭṭhabba) is so called because it is touched. Here, touching should be understood as contact with the sensitivity, and collision with other material groups. Both of these are absent in the water element, hence it is said to be 'devoid of the water element.' But why is it absent in it? Is it not that coldness or fluidity are grasped by touching? It is said that coldness is actually the fire element, not water. If it were water, then coldness would be found even in boiled, heated molten iron—since that liquid is predominant in water. But this is not found. Therefore, coldness is the fire element, not water. Moreover, this is understood from the fact that heat and cold do not co-exist in the same material group and from their instability, like the near and far banks of a river. Heat does not arise in a cold material group, nor does cold arise in a hot material group simultaneously. In an object where a perception of cold was previously established, if a colder sensation later arises, then in that very same object a perception of heat is established. The same principle applies when a perception of heat was previously established. Similarly, when heat is mild, a perception of cold is established, and when cold is mild, a perception of heat is established.

Atha pana dravabhāvabhūto āpo phusitvā gayhati. Ayo piṇḍādīsu ābandhanabhūtopi phusitvāva gayheyya. Evañca sati yathā tesu itarāni tīṇi bhūtāni vinā itarītarena visuṃ visuṃ kāyika sukhadukkhānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtāni honti. Tathā sopi vinā itarehi visuṃ kāyikasukhadukkhānaṃ ārammaṇabhūtoeva siyā. Na pana hoti. Yañhi tāni ayopiṇḍādīni phusantānaṃ kāyikaṃ sukhaṃvā dukkhaṃvā uppajjati, taṃ saṇhathaddhatā vasenavā uppajjati. Sītuṇhatāvasenavā abbhantarathambhanassa mandagāḷhatāvasenavā. No aññathāti. Tasmā purimabhāge tīṇi bhūtāni phusitvāvā vaṇṇaṃ disvāvā pacchā bhāge suddhena mano viññāṇasantānena dīgharassādisaṇṭhānaṃvā rattiyaṃ alātacakkaṃ vā taṃtaṃchiddavivaraṃvā jānantā viya pathamaṃ dravatāsahitāni vilīnāni mudūni tīṇi bhūtāni pathaviṃ eva vā phusitvā pacchā suddhena mano viññāṇasantānena visuṃ dravabhāvaṃ addatintabhāvaṃ jānanti. Evaṃ santepi taṃ phusitvā jānantā icceva maññanti avisesavidunoti. Gunnaṃ abhiṇhaṃ caraṇaṭṭhānaṃ gocaro. Gocarasadisattā idha gocaro. Gotivā idha cakkhādīni indriyāni vuccanti. Tāni viññāṇādhiṭṭhitāni hutvā etesu caranti. Etānivātesu caranti pavattanti ghaṭṭentīti gocarā. Teyeva idha ekattaṃ upanetvā gocararūpanti vuttaṃ. Imānipana pañca yathākkamaṃ cakkhādīsu paṭihanana lakkhaṇāni rūpādīnīti veditabbāni.

But then, the water element, which has the nature of fluidity, is grasped by touching. Even in iron lumps and the like, that which has the nature of cohesion would be grasped only by touching. This being so, just as the other three primary elements, without one another, separately become objects of bodily pleasure and pain, so too this one, without the others, should separately become an object of bodily pleasure and pain. But it does not. For whatever bodily pleasure or pain arises for those touching iron lumps and the like, it arises by way of softness and hardness, or by way of cold and heat, or by way of the mildness or firmness of the internal stiffness; not otherwise. Therefore, just as one might first touch the three primary elements or see their color, and then afterwards, with a pure continuum of mind-consciousness, cognize shapes such as long and short, or a firebrand-circle at night, or various holes and openings; in the same way, one first touches the three primary elements that are fluid, dissolved, and soft—or just the earth element—and afterwards, with a pure continuum of mind-consciousness, separately cognizes the state of fluidity and the state of cohesion. Even so, those who do not know the distinction think that they cognize it by touching. The resort (gocara) is the place where the faculties frequently range. Because of its resemblance to a pasture, it is here called a resort. Or here the faculties such as the eye are called 'go.' Being established in consciousness, they range among these objects. Or these objects range, proceed, and impinge among them, thus they are resorts. These very things, being brought to oneness here, are called 'resort-form.' But these five—material form, etc.—should be understood as having, in order, the characteristic of impinging on the eye, etc.

Itthī vuccati avisadākārasaṇṭhitaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Yassa pana dhammassa ānubhāvena taṃ tathā saṇṭhāti pavattati. So itthi yā [M 0.0276] bhāvoti itthattaṃ. Puriso vuccati visadākārasaṇṭhitaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Tattha itthiliṅga itthinimitta itthi kutta itthākappānaṃ hetubhāva lakkhaṇaṃ itthattaṃ. Purisaliṅga purisanimitta purisakutta purisākappānaṃ hetubhāva lakkhaṇaṃ purisattaṃ. Tattha liṅganti padhānaṅgabhūtaṃ mahāsaṇṭhānaṃ. Nimittanti paccaṅgabhūtaṃ khuddakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Kuttanti kīḷālilādi kriyāviseso. Ākappoti gamanādiko ākāravikāro. Sabbepete khandhapañcakassa pavattivisesāeva. Ye saddasatthesu liṅganti vuccanti. Yesañca vasena ayaṃ itthīeva, na puriso. Ayaṃ purisoeva, na itthīti sañjānanti. Yasmā panettha saṇṭhānādīnaṃ avisadādibhāvoeva atthato itthipurisatā hoti. Tadubhayamuttabhāvoca napuṃsakatā. Soca akkharapada saṅkhātesu vacanesu ca vacanatthesuca yathārahaṃ sandissatiyeva. Tasmā indriyarahitesupi padesuca rukkhādīsu padatthesuca pariyāyena itthipumanapuṃsakatāsiddhi veditabbāti.

A woman is said to be the five aggregates configured with an indistinct appearance. That phenomenon by the power of which it is so configured and proceeds, that is the female state, femininity. A man is said to be the five aggregates configured with a distinct appearance. The rest is as already stated. Therein, femininity is the characteristic of being the cause for the female gender-mark, sign, deportment, and bearing. Masculinity is the characteristic of being the cause for the male gender-mark, sign, deportment, and bearing. Herein, 'gender-mark' is the major configuration, which is the primary feature. 'Sign' is the minor configuration, which is a secondary feature. 'Deportment' is a specific kind of action, such as playfulness and coquetry. 'Bearing' is a modification of manner, such as in walking. All these are just specific modes of occurrence of the five aggregates. In the grammatical treatises they are called 'genders,' and it is on their basis that one recognizes, 'This is a woman, not a man,' or 'This is a man, not a woman.' For herein, femininity and masculinity consist essentially in the indistinctness or distinctness of the configuration and so on. The state of being devoid of both is the neuter state. And this is found, as is fitting, in words designated as syllables and terms, and in the meanings of words. Therefore, the establishment of the feminine, masculine, and neuter should be understood by way of figurative expression even in things devoid of faculties, such as trees, and in the meanings of terms.

[178] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[178] But what is to be explained:

“Itthīnaṃ aṅgajātaṃ itthiliṅga”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It has been said: 'A woman's genital organ is the female gender-mark.' That is not a sound statement.

Na hi katthaci pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāsuca nimittasaddoviya liṅgasaddo aṅgajāte pākaṭo diṭṭhoti.

For nowhere in the Pāli Canon or the commentaries is the word 'liṅga,' like the word 'nimitta,' clearly seen used for the genital organ.

[179] Yañca tattha

[179] And as to what is stated there:

“Itthisaṇṭhānaṃ itthākappo”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

It has been said: 'A woman's configuration is her bearing.' That too is not a sound statement.

Na hi liṅgasaddo viya ākappasaddo saṇṭhāne pākaṭo diṭṭhoti. Sesaṃpana tattha vuttaṃ yaṃkiñci aṭṭhakathāya asamentaṃpi tena pariyāyena yujjatiyeva. Bhavanti pavattanti taṃsahite khandhasantāne esā itthī, eso purisoti evaṃ pavattā sadda buddhiyo etenāti bhāvo bhavantivā pātubhavanti taṃsahite khandhasantāne liṅgādīni etasmiṃ satīti bhāvo. So eva rūpanti bhāvarūpaṃ. Hadanti sattā taṃtaṃatthaṃvā anatthaṃvā pūrenti etenāti hadayaṃ. Hadantivā sattā ito nānāvikakke osajanti [M 0.0277] muñcantīti hadayaṃ. Harantivā pariharanti taṃ sattā jīvitaṃviya dayanti rakkhanticāti hadayaṃ. Vasanti nivasanti cittaceta sikādhammā etthāti vatthu. Hadayañca taṃ vatthucāti hadayavatthu. Dhātudvayanissayalakkhaṇaṃ vatthurūpaṃ. Taṃ pana hadayakosabbhantare aḍḍhapasatamattaṃ lohitaṃ byāpetvā tiṭṭhatīti veditabbaṃ. Dhammasaṅgaṇiyaṃ pana desanābhedarakkhanatthaṃ avatvā paṭṭhāneeva taṃ vuttaṃ. Yathāha-vatthu kusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ nissayapaccayena paccayo. Vatthu akusalānaṃ khandhānaṃ nissayapaccayena paccayotiādi. Etthaca chahi vatthūhi aññaṃ vatthunāma natthi. Tesuca purimāni pañca kusalādīnaṃ nissayāeva na honti. Tasmā tesaṃ nissayabhāvena tattha vuttaṃ vatthunāma visuṃ ekaṃ vatthurūpamevāti siddhanti.

For the word 'bearing' (ākappa) is not clearly seen used for 'configuration' (saṇṭhāna), unlike the word 'gender-mark' (liṅga). But the rest of what is said there, whatever does not agree with the commentary, is still justifiable by this figurative expression. State (bhāva) is so called because by means of it there come to be and proceed in the continuum of aggregates accompanied by it the words and ideas that occur as 'This is a woman,' 'This is a man.' Or state is so called because when it is present, the gender-marks, etc., come to be or appear in the continuum of aggregates accompanied by it. That very thing is a form, thus it is 'state-form' (bhāvarūpa). Heart (hadaya) is so called because by means of it beings fulfill this or that purpose or non-purpose. Or it is so called because from it beings discharge or release various impulses. Or it is so called because beings carry or bear it, and they cherish and protect it like their own life. Basis (vatthu) is so called because mind and mental factors dwell and reside in it. It is the heart and it is the basis, thus it is the 'heart-basis' (hadayavatthu). The material basis has the characteristic of being the support for the two elements. But it should be understood that this stands pervading the blood amounting to about half a handful inside the heart-cavity. However, in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī it is not mentioned, in order to preserve the division of the teaching, but it is mentioned in the Paṭṭhāna. As it is said: 'The basis is a condition for wholesome aggregates by way of support condition. The basis is a condition for unwholesome aggregates by way of support condition,' and so on. And here there is no other basis apart from the six bases. And among them, the first five are not the support for wholesome states, etc. Therefore, it is established that the 'basis' mentioned there as their support is a single, separate material basis.

[180] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[180] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Yaṃ rūpaṃ nissāyāti pāṭhassa uddhaṭattā rūpasāmaññapasaṅgo hotīti taṃ visodhetuṃ yuttināma vuttā. Paṭṭhāne pana bahūsu anaññasādhāraṇesu ṭhānesu vatthunāmena visesetvā vuttattā sopasaṅgo natthiyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Because the reading 'depending on which material form' has been extracted, there would be the implication of material form in general; to clarify this, a reason has been stated. But in the Paṭṭhāna, it should be seen that since it is stated by specifying with the term 'basis' in many places that are not common to anything else, that implication does not exist.

Jīvanti sahajātadhammā yenāti jīvitaṃ. Tesaṃ jīvane ādhipaccayogena tesu indaṃ issaraṃ attānaṃ karotīti indriyaṃ. Jīvitañca taṃ indriyañcāti jīvitindriyaṃ. Sahajātā nupālana lakkhaṇaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ. Yathā hi bījanibbattāni uppalādīni bījevinaṭṭhepi udakānupālitāni ciraṃpi kālaṃ jīvanti. Evamevaṃ niruddha kammanibbattāni kammajarūpāni kamme asantepi jīvitānupālitāni santativasena vassasataṃpi vassasahassaṃpi kappaṃpi soḷasakappasahassānipi jīvantiyeva, tathā hi jīvitarahitāni itararūpāni jīvantānināma nahonti. Tāni hi yena ekena cittenavā utunāvā āhārenavā jāyanti. Tasmiṃ niruddhe nirujjhanti, paraṃ muhuttamattaṃpi santānaṃ ghaṭetuṃ nasakkonti. Tesu hi cittajarūpānaṃ santatipaccuppannaṃ ekavīthi ekajavanavāra ekasamāpattivārena paricchinnaṃ hoti. Utujāhārajānañca sabhāgeka utuāhāra vasena [M 0.0278] paricchinnaṃ hoti. Kammajarūpānaṃ pana visuṃ santatipaccuppannaṃnāma natthi. Tesaṃ ekabhavaparicchinnaṃ addhāpaccuppannameva hotīti. Yadi evaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ kathanti. Tehi jīvitayogena jīvantāeva honti. Evaṃsantepi tesaṃ santatipaccuppannaṃ dissatīti. Vuccate, arūpadhammesu vipākāni tāva kammajarūpasadisāni. Tānipi hi asati vīthicittuppāde yāvajīvaṃpi ekasantativasena pavattissantiyeva. Itarāni pana yassa ārammaṇassa āpātāgatattā uppajjanti. Tasmiṃ niruddhe tadabhāvepi tadārammaṇā bahū cittasantatiyo jīvitassaaddhānapharaṇānubhāvena pavattantiyeva. Apica, yāvakhandhaparinibbānā anantarapaccayupanibandhena abbocchinnaṃ pavattamānāya cittasantatiyāvasenapi ayamattho vattabbo. Teneva hi kilesasīsaṃ avijjā. Pavattasīsaṃ jīvitindriyanti vuttaṃ.

Co-arisen phenomena live by means of this; hence it is life. Because it exercises lordship over them by way of predominance in their life, it is a faculty. Life and that faculty are the life faculty. The life faculty has the characteristic of maintaining co-arisen phenomena. For just as lotuses and other plants born from seeds continue to live for a long time even after the seeds have perished, being sustained by water, so too, material phenomena born of kamma, even when the kamma has ceased, are maintained by the life faculty and continue to live by way of a continuum for a hundred years, a thousand years, an aeon, or even sixteen thousand aeons. Indeed, other material phenomena that are devoid of life are not called 'living.' For these arise from either mind, temperature, or nutriment, and when that cause ceases, they cease; they cannot sustain their continuum even for a moment. Among these, for material phenomena born of mind, their present continuity is limited by a single cognitive process, a single run of impulsion, or a single attainment. And for those born of temperature or nutriment, it is limited by a single instance of homogeneous temperature or nutriment. But for material phenomena born of kamma, there is no separate present continuity; for them, there is only a temporal present limited to a single existence. If so, what of immaterial phenomena? They live only by connection with life. Even so, is their present continuity observed? It is said: among immaterial phenomena, resultants are similar to kamma-born material phenomena. For even when there is no arising of a cognitive-process consciousness, they continue to occur throughout life in a single continuum. But other immaterial phenomena arise because an object has come into range. When that object has ceased, even in its absence, many consciousness-continuums having that as their object continue to occur through the power of the life faculty's temporal pervasion. Moreover, this meaning should be understood also by way of the consciousness-continuum that proceeds uninterruptedly, bound by the contiguity condition, until the final passing away of the aggregates. For that reason it is said: 'Ignorance is the head of the defilements; the life faculty is the head of the round of existence.'

[181] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[181] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Āhārajādīnaṃ āhārādiyeva uppattiyāpi ṭhitiyāpi kāraṇaṃ hoti. Kasmā, taṅkhaṇe dharamānattā. Kamma jānaṃ pana kammaṃ uppattiyāeva kāraṇaṃ, na ṭhitiyā. Kasmā, taṅkhaṇābhāvato. Jīvitena pana anupālitattā eva tesaṃ khaṇaṭṭhiti siddhāti iminā dhippāyena yaṃ vuttaṃ “yathāsakaṃ khaṇamattaṭṭhāyīnaṃpi hi sahajātānaṃ pavattihetubhāvena anupālakaṃ. Na hi tesaṃ kammaṃyeva ṭhitikāraṇaṃ hoti. Āhārajādīnaṃ āhārādi viya kammassa taṅkhaṇābhāva toti”. Taṃ na yuttaṃ.

For things born of nutriment and so on, nutriment and so on is the cause for both their arising and their presence. Why? Because it is present at that moment. But for things born of kamma, kamma is the cause only for their arising, not for their presence. Why? Because of its absence at that moment. Therefore, the statement made with the intention that 'their momentary presence is established only because they are maintained by life'—namely, 'It is a maintainer of its co-nascent states, which last for only their own moment, by being a cause for their occurrence; for kamma alone is not the cause of their presence, as nutriment and so on is for things born of nutriment, because of kamma's absence at that moment'—that is not correct.

Dhammānañhi khaṇaṭṭhitināma ekakalāpagatasahajātapaccayā yattāeva hoti. Na nānākalāpagatajanakapaccayāyattā. Itarathā uppādakkhaṇe labbhamānānaṃ upacayasantatīnaṃ viya ṭhitikkhaṇe labbhamānāya jaratāyapi kutocisamuṭṭhānatā pāḷiyaṃ vuttā siyāti. Apica, khaṇaṭṭhitināma sabhāvasiddhāeva. Na hi uppannā dhammā paccayavekallena attano khaṇesu paripuṇṇaṃ aṭṭhatvā antarāva bhijjantīti atthi. Naca paccayādhimattena atire kataraṃ [M 0.0279] tiṭṭhantīti atthi. Tasmā khaṇaṭṭhitiyaṃ upatthambhayamānāpi āhārādayo anupālayamānañca jīvitaṃ pacchā balavarūpasantati pavattiatthāyaeva upatthambhenti pāletica. Na khaṇaṭṭhitipavattiyāti. Ettāvatā sabbesaṃpi khaṇaṭṭhitināma dharamānajanakāyattā vā jīvitāyattāvā nahotīti siddhaṃ hoti. Yadi pana taṃ santatipavattimeva sandhāya vuttaṃ siyā, evaṃsati yujjeyyāti. Aṭṭha kathāyaṃpi santepica anupālana lakkhaṇādimhi vidhāne atthikkhaṇeyeva taṃ tedhamme pāletītiādivacane yathāsantatiṭṭhiti labbhati. Tathā vicāretvā gahetabbāti. Idaṃ pana pācakagginā saha sakalaṃ upādinnakasarīraṃ byāpetvā tiṭṭhatīti. Kabaḷaṃ karīyatīti kabaḷīkāro. Āharīyati ajjhoharīyatīti āhāro. Kabaḷīkāroca so āhārocāti kabaḷīkārāhāro. Kabaḷīkāro āhārotipi pāṭho. Idañca savatthuka vacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Athavā, kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkhānaṃ sattānaṃ attabhāvaṃ bhuso harati addhānaṃ pavattetīti āhāro. Khajja bhojjādike kabaḷīkāre āhāro tannissitattā tappariyā pannattācāti kabaḷīkārāhāro. Imasmiṃatthe sati nibbattita ojā eva labbhati. Atthato pana aṅgamaṅgānusārino rasassa sārabhūto upatthambhabalakāro bhūtanissito paramasiniddhasi neho idha āhārarūpaṃnāma. Tattha aṅgamaṅgānusārino rasassāti ajjhoharitvā āmāsaye patiṭṭhitāni āhāravatthūni pācakatejena vivecitāni rasādibhāvena pañcadhā vibhāgaṃ gacchanti. Tattha paṇīta siniddha lahuka sineha koṭṭhāso rasonāma. Ye loke rasadhātūti vuccati. So pācaka tejabalena tato uttaritvā rasaharaṇidhamanijālānusārena heṭṭhāca uddhañca sakalasarīre aṅgamaṅgāni anusaranto anupharanto aṅgamaṅgānusārīti vuccati. Tassa sārabhūto upatthambhaṃ balaṃ karotīti upatthambhabalakāro. So hi āmāsaye patiṭṭhita mattova sakalasarīre bhūtesu upatthambhakabalaṃ janetīti.

For the momentary presence of phenomena is dependent only on co-nascent conditions belonging to a single group, not on generative conditions belonging to different groups. Otherwise, just as growth and continuity are obtained at the moment of arising, so the origination of decay, which is obtained at the moment of presence, would have to be spoken of in the Pāḷi as arising from some source. Moreover, momentary presence is established by its own intrinsic nature. For it is not the case that arisen phenomena, due to a deficiency of conditions, do not stand for their full moment and break up midway. Nor is it the case that they stand for an excessive time due to a surplus of conditions. Therefore, although nutriment and so on support momentary presence and the life faculty maintains it, they support and maintain it only for the sake of the occurrence of a subsequent strong material continuum, not for the occurrence of the momentary presence itself. Thus it is established that the momentary presence of all phenomena is not dependent on a presently existing generative cause or on the life faculty. But if that were said with reference to the occurrence of the continuum, then it would be tenable. Even in the Commentary, in the section on the characteristic of maintaining, in statements such as 'it protects those phenomena only at the moment of presence,' it is the stability of the continuum that is obtained. This should be understood after due consideration. This, however, stands pervading the entire appropriated body together with the digestive fire. 'That which is made into a morsel' is kabaḷīkāra. 'That which is brought in and consumed' is āhāra (nutriment). It is a morsel and it is nutriment, thus kabaḷīkārāhāra (morsel-food nutriment). The reading kabaḷīkāro āhāroti ('morsel-food is nutriment') also exists. And this should be seen as a statement with a physical basis. Alternatively, it is 'nutriment' (āhāra) because it carries (harati) the individual existence of beings who consume morsel-food, causing it to proceed for a long time. In the case of morsel-food such as things to be chewed and eaten, it is 'nutriment' because it is dependent on that and included under that; hence kabaḷīkārāhāra. In this sense, it is the nutritive essence that is produced that is obtained. In meaning, however, the material form of nutriment here is the essential part of the nutrient fluid that courses through the major and minor limbs, which creates supporting strength, is dependent on the primary elements, and is the ultimate fine oiliness. Herein, 'of the nutrient fluid that courses through the major and minor limbs' means: the food items, having been consumed and established in the stomach, are analyzed by the digestive heat and undergo a fivefold division into nutrient fluid, etc. Therein, the refined, smooth, light, oily portion is called 'nutrient fluid,' which is called the 'nutrient fluid element' in the world. Propelled by the power of the digestive heat, it rises from there and, following the network of nutrient-fluid-carrying vessels, it courses through and pervades the major and minor limbs throughout the entire body, below and above; thus it is called 'coursing through the major and minor limbs.' Its essential part creates supporting strength, thus it is called 'creator of supporting strength.' For as soon as it is established in the stomach, it generates supporting strength in the primary elements throughout the entire body.

[182] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[182] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Aṅgamaṅgā nasāri rasahara saṅkhātāti” pāṭho. So duppāṭho.

The reading is: 'Aṅgamaṅgānasārirasaharasaṅkhātāti.' That is a corrupt reading.

Taṃ pana sendriyakāyopatthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ āhārarūpaṃ. Ojālakkhaṇaṃ vā. Tattha udayati pasavatīti ojā. Avasaddovā rakkhaṇe. Rakkhaṇañcettha upatthambhanameva. Avati janeticāti ojā. Kiṃ avati. Attano nissayavatthuṃ. Kiṃca janeti. Āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ. Udayānantaraṃ rūpaṃ janetīti ojātipi vadanti. Aññāpadesarahitena kakkhaḷattādinā attano bhāvena siddhaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvarūpaṃ. Uppādādinā aniccatādināca saṅkhahalakkhaṇena sahitaṃ rūpaṃ salakkhaṇarūpaṃ. Ujukatova kammādīhi paccayehi nipphāditaṃ rūpaṃ nipphannarūpaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇasampannaṃ nippariyāyarūpaṃ rūparūpaṃ. Yathā dukkhadukkhaṃ ajjhattaajjhattanti. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇayutta tāya aniccatādikaṃ lakkhaṇattayaṃ āropetvā sammasanārahaṃ rūpaṃ sammasanarūpaṃ. Te te dabbasambhārāvā rūpakalāpāvā visuṃvisuṃ bhuso kāsanti pakāsanti etenāti ākāso. Nisatta nijīvaṭṭhena dhātu. Ākāsasaṅkhātā dhātūti ākāsadhātu. Parito samantato chindati kalāpantarabhūtāni kalāpantara bhūtehi saddhiṃ asaṃmissaṃ ekattaṃ anupagamanaṃ karotīti paricchedo. Tehivā paricchindīyati attanovā paresaṃvā akatvāmajjhe visuṃ thapīyati. Tesaṃvā chiddavivaramattabhūto. Na visuṃ eko uppādasahito sabhāvadhammo. Nāpi kassaci rūpakalāpassa pakkhabhūtoti paricchedo. Vikāralakkhaṇarūpāni hi asabhāvadhammabhūtānipi taṃtaṃ rūpakalāpesu sandissamānatā taṃtaṃrūpakalāpapakkhikānieva honti. Ayaṃ pana tehi rūpa kalāpehi sabbaso vimuttabhāvena bahibhūtattā kassaci rūpa kalāpassa pakkhabhūto na hotīti. Asabhāvadhammattāca pana kenaci rūpena phusana pariyāyopi tassa sabbaso natthīti katvā so asaṃphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehīti pāḷiyaṃ vutto. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana ghanapiṇḍavatthūsu paṭighaphoṭṭhabbasabhāvānaṃ nānā kalāpagatabhūtānaṃ [M 0.0281] aññamaññasaṃphuṭṭhatā atthīti katvā asaṃphuṭṭhaṃ catūhi mahābhūtehīti etehi asaṃphuṭṭhaṃ ajaṭākāsaṃ kaṃthitanti vuttaṃ. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana ayaṃ niddeso ajaṭākāsaniddeso nahoti, paricchedarūpaniddesoyeva. Soca ghanapiṇḍa vatthūsueva veditabbo. Tesuca bhūtānaṃ asaṃphuṭṭhatānāma natthi. Tasmā bhūtānaṃ aññamaññaabyāpitā ekattaṃ anupagatatāeva. Tattha asaṃphuṭṭhatānāma yuttā siyāti adhippāyena abyāpikatā hi asaṃphuṭṭhatāti vuttaṃ. Atthato pana nānākalāpagatānaṃ bhūtānaṃ pariyantatā saṅkhāto antarāḷadhammo. Rūpaparicchedalakkhaṇaṃ paricchedarūpaṃ. Yā pana calamānena kāyaṅgena attānañca attasamaṅgino puggalassa adhippāyañca paccakkhe ṭhite jane viññāpeti pākaṭaṃ katvā dasseti. Sayañca tena kāyaṅgena tehi janehi viññāyati. Sā kāyaviññattināma. Yā uccārīyamānena vācaṅgena saddena attānañca attasamaṅgino puggalassa adhippāyañca sotapathe ṭhite jane viññāpeti. Sayañca tenavācaṅgena tehi janehi viññāyati. Sā vacīviññattināma. Athavā, viññāpenti janā viññāyantivā janehi aññamaññassa cittāni etāyāti viññatti. Sasambhāre aṅgapaccaṅgabhūte kāye pavattā viññatti kāyaviññatti. Copana kāyasaṅkhāto kāyo evavā viññatti kāyaviññatti. Cittajasaddasaṅkhātāya vācāya pavattā viññatti vacīviññatti. Copanavācā saṅkhātā vācā evavā viññatti vacīviññatti. Tattha cittavasena yaṃkiñci kāyaṅgavikāraṃ karontassa taṃtaṃaṅgaṃ santambhantā sandhārentā cālentā aṅgamaṅgānusārisaṅkhātā cittajavātakalāpā taṃtaṃaṅgaṃ pūretvā uppajjanti. Uppajjantāca yathāvā tathāvā anuppajjitvā yassa tehi cittajavātakalāpeti sahajātassa copanakāyassa ānubhāvena sabbe te kalāpā yathādhippetadisābhimukhāeva uppajjanti. Ayaṃ copanakāyasaṅkhāto ākāravikāro kāyaviññatti nāma. Niyāmakasadisī hi ayaṃ kāyaviññatti. Teca nāvāsadi sāti. Yathā hi niyāmako nāvāya mūlabhāge ṭhatvā ekaṃ mahāphiyaṃ [M 0.0282] daḷhaṃ gahetvā nadisote cāretvā sakalaṃ mahānāvaṃ icchitadisābhimukhaṃ niyojeti. Na yaṃvā taṃvā disaṃ gantuṃ deti. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekacittakkhaṇikā hi viññatti tesaṃ mūlabhāgeeva labbhamānā te yathādhippetadisābhimukhe evaṃ katvā niyojetīti sā niyāmakasadisī hotīti. Etthaca yadetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Ekajavanavīthiyaṃ sattasu javanesu pathama javanasamuṭṭhitā vāyodhātu attanā sahajātarūpakāyaṃ saṃthambhetuṃ sandhāretuṃ sakkoti. Aparāparaṃ pana cāletuṃ nasakkoti. Dutīyādīsupi eseva nayo. Sattamacittena pana samuṭṭhitā vāyodhātu heṭṭhā chahicittehi samuṭṭhitaṃ vāyodhātuṃ upatthambhanapaccayaṃ labhitvāattanāsahajātaṃ rūpakāyaṃ saṃthambhetuṃ sandhāretuṃ cāletuṃ abhikkamāpetuṃ sakkotīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ abhikkamāmīti kāyaṃ paggaṇhantānaṃ anekasahassesu javana vāresu pavattamānesu yasmiṃvāre calanasaṅkhātaṃ desantarapāpanaṃ jāyati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na hi katipayajavanavārehi calanaṃ jāyati. Yadi jāyeyya, iddhimantānaṃ iddhiyāgamanaṃ viya sabbesaṃpi sīghataraṃ gamanaṃ paññāyeyya. Kasmā, ekaccharakkhaṇepi anekakoṭisatasahassacikkapavattiyā sambhavato. Ayañca attho upari akkharuppattivicāraṇāyaṃ pākaṭo bhavissatīti. Tasmā tato purimavāresu saṃthambhanasandhāraṇānieva sampajjantīti veditabbaṃ. Yā cettha sattayugasakaṭopamā vuttā, sāpi nānājavanavīthīsu samuṭṭhitānaṃ vāyodhātūnaṃ aparāparaṃ upatthambhaneca yujjatiyeva. Tathā hi calanacittajarūpasantatiyaṃ pavattāni utujarūpasaṅghāṭānipi viññattisahitāni viya tadākāravantāni savegāni savipphārānieva pavattanti. Tasmā pubbāparapavattānaṃ nānā javanavīthīnaṃ antarantarā bhavaṅgasamayesupi abhikkamanādikaṃ calanaṃ sampajjatiyeva. Ekābaddhapavattānica catusamuṭṭhānikarūpānināma ekassa visaye itarāni ekasamuṭṭhānāni viya sabbaso tadanu parivattīni hontīti cittaje calante itarānipi calanti yevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Calanañcettha pacchimapacchimānaṃ rūpakalāpasaṅghāṭānaṃ purima purimānaṃ [M 0.0283] uppannadesato desantare yathāpavattasannivesākārena aparāparaṃ uppajjamānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na hi rūpārūpadhammānaṃ uppanna dese anirujjhitvā kesaggamattaṃpi desantara saṅkamanaṃnāma atthi. Itarathā khaṇikadhammatā abyāpāradhammatā avasavattitāca tesaṃ nasiyāti. Yaṃkiñci vacībhedaṃ karontassa kaṇṭhaṭṭhānādi gataupādinnaka pathavīdhātūsu calamānakaṇṭhapadesādigatacittaja pathavīdhātūnaṃ saṅghaṭṭanasaṅkhātena ṭhānakaraṇasannipātena sahevayo vacīghosasaṅkhāto cittajasaddo jāyati. So yena attanā saha jātena ākāravikārena yathādhippāyaṃ taṃtaṃ vaṇṇavisesattaṃ upagacchati. Yenaca suṇantānaṃ taṃtaṃatthajotako akkharasannipātabhūto padabyañjanaviseso upalabbhati. So copanavācāsaṅkhāto ākāravikāro vacīviññattināma. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tassā pana cittasamuṭṭhānāya pathavīdhātuyā upādinnaghaṭṭanassa paccayabhūto eko ākāravikāro vacī viññattināmāti vuttaṃ. Tattha upādinnaghaṭṭanassa paccayabhūtoti kammajabhūtāya catujabhūtāyaevavā upādinnapathavīdhātuyā sahaghaṭṭanaṃ paṭicca saddavisesapavattiyā paccayabhūtoti attho. Ghaṭṭanassa paccayo pana calamānakaṇṭhapadesādivikārabhūto kāyaṅgavisesoeva siyā. Vikāradvayañca asaṃmissaṃ katvā veditabbanti. Etthaca upādinnakapathavīhi saha ghaṭṭanaṃ cittajapathavīnaṃ kiccaṃ. Yaṃ pana tāsaṃ yathāvā tathāvā aghaṭṭetvā yathā icchitakkharaṃ sampajjati. Tathā ghaṭṭanapakāravidhānaṃ. Idaṃ kāyaviññattiyā kiccaṃ. Ghaṭṭanena saheva uppannasaddānaṃ taṃtaṃvaṇṇatta pattiyā vidahanameva vacīviññattiyā kiccaṃ. Kumbhathunatalaṃ viyaca upādinnakapathavī. Paharaṇahattho viya cittajapathavī. Hatthapari vattana vikāro viya kāyaviññatti. Saddavikāro viya vacīviññatti. Kumbhathunassa nānāsaddapabhedoviya nānāvaṇṇabhedoti. Etthaca yadetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ idaṃ vakkhāmi etaṃ vakkhāmīti uppajjamānaṃ cittaṃ aṭṭharūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti. Tesaṃ abbhantare citta samuṭṭhānā pathavīdhātu upādinnakaṃ ghaṭṭayamānāva uppajjati. Tena dhātughaṭṭanena [M 0.0284] saheva saddo uppajjatītica purimacittasamuṭṭhā nāya upatthambhanakiccaṃpi natthītica vuttaṃ. Taṃpi anekasatesu javanavāresu pavattamānesu yasmiṃvāre paribyattaṃ akkharaṃ pavattati, taṃ sandhāya vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Teneva hi mūla ṭīkāyaṃ upatthambhanakiccaṃ natthi laddhāsevanena citteneva ghaṭṭanassa balavabhāvatoti vuttaṃ. Etthaca laddhāsevanenāti etena pubbabhāge nānājavanavīthīhi laddhāsevanabhāvaṃ dasseti. Pathama javanacittassapi laddhāsevanatāya adhippetattā. Naca ekajavana vāramattena paribyattaṃ ekakkharaṃ sampajjatīti sakkā viññātuṃ. Kasmā, tassa ekadviaccharakkhaṇamattena kālena vattabbattā ekaccharakkhaṇeca anekasatasahassānaṃ javanavīthīnaṃ pavattisambhavato. Vuttañca –

But that nutritive materiality has the characteristic of supporting the body with its faculties. Or it has the characteristic of nutritive essence. Therein, it is ojā (nutritive essence) because it arises and produces. Or, the word ava is in the sense of protecting. And here protection is simply support. It is ojā because it protects and generates. What does it protect? Its own physical basis. And what does it generate? Materiality produced by nutriment. Some also say it is ojā because it generates materiality immediately after its arising. Materiality established by its own nature—by hardness and so on—devoid of other designations, is intrinsic materiality. Materiality that possesses the characteristic of the conditioned, such as arising, etc., and impermanence, etc., is materiality with its characteristics. Materiality produced directly by conditions such as kamma is produced materiality. Materiality endowed with the characteristic of being afflicted is materiality in the primary sense, materiality as such; just as suffering is suffering, and the internal is internal. Materiality that is fit for comprehension by superimposing upon it the three characteristics of impermanence and so on—because it possesses the characteristic of the conditioned—is materiality for comprehension. It is space (ākāsa) because by it those various collections of substances or material groups are clearly manifest separately. It is an element in the sense of being non-sentient and non-living. The element designated as space is the space element. It is delimitation (pariccheda) because it cuts off all around, causing material groups not to merge with other material groups, not to attain a state of oneness. Or, by it they are delimited, being placed separately in the middle without belonging to one side or the other. Or it is merely the gap and opening between them. It is not a separate, real phenomenon endowed with arising, nor is it an adjunct of any material group; thus it is delimitation. For the material phenomena with the characteristic of alteration, although they are not real phenomena in themselves, are seen within the various material groups and are thus adjuncts of those very material groups. But this [delimitation], being external because of its complete separation from those material groups, is not an adjunct of any material group. And because it is not a real phenomenon in itself, there is absolutely no way for it to be touched by any materiality; therefore in the Pāḷi it is called 'untouched by the four great elements.' In the Commentary, however, it is said that in solid objects, there is mutual contact of the elements that belong to different material groups and possess the nature of resistance and the tangible; therefore, 'untouched by the four great elements' is explained as 'the untangled space untouched by these.' But in the Subcommentary it is said that this exposition is not an exposition of untangled space but of delimiting materiality itself. And that should be understood only in regard to solid objects, for in them there is no such thing as non-contact of the elements. Therefore, what is meant is the non-pervasion of each other, the non-attainment of oneness. With the intention that 'there the term "non-contact" might be suitable,' it was said, 'non-pervasion is non-contact.' In meaning, however, it is the intermediate phenomenon called the boundary of elements belonging to different material groups. Delimiting materiality has the characteristic of delimiting materiality. Bodily intimation is that which, by means of a moving bodily part, makes known oneself and the intention of the person endowed with it to people who are visibly present, and by which one is oneself understood by those people through that bodily part. Vocal intimation is that which, by means of a sound from a vocal organ being uttered, makes known oneself and the intention of the person endowed with it to people who are present in the range of hearing, and by which one is oneself understood by those people through that vocal utterance. Alternatively, it is 'intimation' because by it people make known, or are made to understand, each other's minds. Intimation occurring in the body, which is composed of limbs and minor parts, is bodily intimation. Or, the intimation that is the body itself, called the impelling body, is bodily intimation. Intimation occurring in speech, which consists of mind-produced sound, is vocal intimation. Or, the intimation that is speech itself, called impelling speech, is vocal intimation. Here, when one produces any alteration in a bodily part, mind-born wind-element groups, called 'limb-following,' arise filling that limb, restraining, sustaining, and moving it. Arising thus, they do not arise haphazardly but, by the influence of the co-nascent impelling physical force, all those groups arise facing the intended direction. This alteration of form, called the impelling physical force, is what is termed bodily intimation. This bodily intimation is like a helmsman. And those [wind-element groups] are like a boat. For just as a helmsman, standing at the stern of a boat, firmly grasps a large rudder and, steering it in the river's current, directs the entire great boat in the desired direction and does not let it go in any other direction, so should this be understood. For intimation, which is of a single mind-moment's duration and is found at their base, directs them, making them face the intended direction; thus it is like a helmsman. And here, what is said in the Commentary: 'In a single cognitive series of seven impulsions, the wind element arisen with the first impulsion can stiffen and sustain the co-nascent material body, but it cannot move it. The same applies to the second and the following impulsions. But the wind element arisen with the seventh mind-moment, having received the supporting condition from the wind element arisen with the six preceding mind-moments, can stiffen, sustain, move, and propel its co-nascent material body.' This is said with reference to the particular cognitive series in which movement, defined as the attainment of another location, occurs, among the many thousands of impulsion series that are taking place for those who are lifting up the body thinking, 'I will step forward.' For movement does not arise from just a few impulsion series. If it did, everyone's movement would be perceived as extremely swift, like the travel of those with psychic powers, because of the possibility of the occurrence of many hundred thousands of crores of mind-moments even in a single finger-snap. And this point will become clear later in the investigation of the production of letters. Therefore, it should be understood that in the preceding series, only stiffening and sustaining are accomplished. And the simile of the seven-yoked cart mentioned here is also applicable to the successive support given by wind elements arising in different cognitive series. Thus, in a continuity of mind-produced materiality in motion, even the aggregates of temperature-produced materiality appear to have that same form, as if endowed with intimation, and proceed with velocity and pervasion. Therefore, movement such as stepping forward is accomplished even during the life-continuum moments that occur between the preceding and subsequent series of different cognitive processes. And it should be seen that among the material phenomena born of the four origins that proceed in a single stream, they are entirely subservient to the one [mind-born origin], just as the other single-origin phenomena are; thus when the mind-born materiality moves, the others also move. And here, movement should be understood as the successive arising of later aggregates of material groups in a different location from the place of arising of the earlier ones, in an arrangement and form that accords with their progression. For there is no such thing as the transmigration, even to the extent of a hair's tip, of material or immaterial phenomena to another location without their having ceased in the place where they arose. Otherwise, their momentary nature, their nature of non-agency, and their state of being not subject to will would be lost. When one produces any distinction of speech, the mind-produced sound called vocal utterance arises simultaneously with the event called the conjunction of articulation and place of articulation, which is defined as the collision of mind-born earth elements located in the moving throat area, etc., with the appropriated earth elements located in the throat, etc. It is by means of an alteration of form co-nascent with that sound that it takes on the specific character of this or that phoneme according to one's intention. And it is by this that the specific combination of letters forming words and sentences, which illuminates this or that meaning for the listeners, is perceived. That alteration of form, called impelling speech, is what is termed vocal intimation. In the Commentary, however, it is said: 'One alteration of form, which is a condition for the collision of the mind-produced earth element with the appropriated [earth element], is called vocal intimation.' Here, 'a condition for the collision with the appropriated' means: a condition for the occurrence of distinct sounds dependent on the collision with the appropriated earth element, which is kamma-born or indeed born from the four causes. The condition for the collision, however, would be the specific bodily part itself, which is the alteration of the moving throat area, etc. And the two alterations should be understood as unmixed. And here, the collision with the appropriated earth elements is the function of the mind-born earth elements. But the arrangement of the mode of collision so that the desired letters are produced without their colliding in some random way—this is the function of bodily intimation. The fashioning of the sounds that have arisen simultaneously with the collision into the state of this or that phoneme is the function of vocal intimation. The appropriated earth element is like the head of a pot-drum; the mind-born earth element is like the striking hand; the alteration in the turning of the hand is like bodily intimation; the alteration of the sound is like vocal intimation; the various distinctions of sound from the pot-drum's head are like the various distinctions of phonemes. And here, what is said in the Commentary: 'The mind that arises thinking, "I will say this, I will say that," gives rise to eight material phenomena. Among them, the mind-produced earth element arises while striking the appropriated [earth element]. Simultaneously with that collision of elements, sound arises.' And it is also said that there is no supporting function for the materiality arisen from a preceding mind-moment. This, too, should be taken as said with reference to the particular cognitive series in which a distinct letter occurs, among the many hundreds of impulsion series that are taking place. For this very reason, it is said in the Mūlaṭīkā: 'There is no supporting function, because the collision is forceful on account of the mind's acquired practice.' And here, by the words 'by acquired practice,' he shows the state of having acquired practice through numerous cognitive series in the preliminary stage, since it is intended that even the first impulsion-mind has acquired practice. And it cannot be known that a single distinct letter is accomplished by just a single impulsion series. Why? Because it would have to be spoken in the time of one or two finger-snaps, and because of the possibility of the occurrence of many hundred thousands of cognitive series in a single finger-snap. And it was said:

Ekamattā tayo rassā, dvimattā dīghamuccare;

Timatto tu gīto ñeyyo, byañjanā aḍḍhamattikāti.

A short vowel has one mora; a long vowel is said to have two moras. A sung vowel, however, should be known as having three moras, and a consonant has half a mora.

Milindapañheca sādhike vīhivāhasate vīhibījāni ekaccharakkhaṇe uppannassa cittassa kalaṃpi naupenti. Kalabhāgaṃpi naupentīti dīpitaṃ. Ekakkharaṃ uccārentassaca tattakaṃpi kālaṃ uccāraṇacittabyāpāro sandissatiyeva. Naca paramatthato ekameva saddaṃ uccāremītivā suṇomītivā sakkā niyametvā uccāretuṃ sotuñca. Tathā niyamentassapi saddānaṃ pubbāparato anekasatasahassasseva uccāraṇa savana sambhavato. Ekamevāti abhimāno pana samūhaghana santatighanehi paṭicchannattāeva hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sesamettha kāyaviññattiyaṃ vuttana yena yathāsambhavaṃ veditabbanti. Etthaca viññattisaddo kāyena viññāpeti vācāya viññāpetītiādisu bodhanattho. Sudinna kaṇḍe tikkhattuṃ viññāpetītiādīsu pavattanattho. Idha pana duvidhopi yujjati. Evañhi sati paraṃ bodhetukāmatārahi tesu sabbesu kāyaṅgavācaṅgacopanesupi pavattakaviññattiyā labbhamānatā veditabbā hotīti. Mūlaṭīkāyaṃ pana paraṃ bodhetukāmatāya [M 0.0285] vināpi abhikkamanādipavattanena so citta sahabhūvikāro adhippāyaṃ viññāpeti. Sayañca viññāyatīti dvidhāpi viññattiyevāti vuttaṃ, tattha dvīsu bodhanaviññattīsu purimā kāyaviññatti aṅgapaccaṅgassa calamānavaṇṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇavīthiyā calamānaṅgapaccaṅgaṃ kāyaviññāṇavīthiyā gahetvā pacchā suddhena manodvārikajavanenaeva viññāyati pacchimāca vacīviññatti uccāriyamānaṃ saddaṃ sotaviññāṇavīthiyā gahetvā pacchā suddhena manodvārikajavanenaeva viññāyati, na pañcadvārikajavanena. Sā hi attānaṃ jānanteeva parasatte attanā samaṅgino puggalassa cittaṃ viññāpeti, na ajānante. Ñāpaka hetu hi nāma attānaṃ jānanteeva ñāpetabbaṃ ñāpeti, no ajānante. Evañca katvā kāyaṅga copanaṃ disvāvā parāmasitvāvā saddaṃ sutvāvā parassa taṃtaṃadhippāyaṃ jānantānaṃ tiracchāna gatānaṃpi pathadhaṃ viññattijānanaṃ siddhaṃ bhavati. Taṃjānanena vinā adhippāyajānanassa asambhavato. Viññattiṃ jānantānaṃca purimasiddhasaṅketa sambandha jānanena vinā adhippāyajānanaṃ na sambhavatīti majjhe visuṃ pubbasaṅketa sambandhagahanaṃpi icchanti, dvīsu pana pavattakaviññattīsu paraṃ abhikkamantaṃ cakkhuviññāṇavīthiyā disvā abhikkamanaviññattiñca abhikkamanacittañca manoviññāṇavīthiyā jānanti. Esanayo paṭikkamanādīsu. Tathā parassa kathaṃ sotaviññāṇavīthiyā sutvā kathanaviññattiñca kathanacittañca manoviññāṇavīthiyā jānanti. Paraṃ rattacittena kāyaṅgaṃ cālentaṃ disvā calanaviññattiñca rāgacittañca jānanti. Rattassa kathaṃ sutvā kathana viññattiñca rāgacittañca jānanti. Esanayo sabbāsu kāyikavācasikakriyāsūti. Lahuno bhāvo lahutā. Muduno bhāvo mudutā. Kammani sādhu kammaññaṃ. Kammayogyanti attho. Kammaññassa bhāvo kammaññatā.

In the Milindapañha it is also shown that over a hundred cartloads of paddy grains do not amount to a fraction of the duration of a single thought-moment that has arisen in the time of a single finger-snap. It is explained that they do not amount to even a fractional part. And when one utters a single syllable, the activity of the mind of utterance is evident for just that much time. But in an ultimate sense, it is not possible to regulate and then utter or hear, thinking, 'I utter just one sound' or 'I hear just one sound.' This is because for one who regulates thus, the utterance and hearing of many hundreds of thousands of sounds, one after another, is possible. The conviction 'it is just one' should be understood to arise only because it is concealed by the compactness of the group and the compactness of continuity. The rest here should be understood as is possible by the method stated regarding bodily intimation. Here, the term 'intimation' (viññatti) has the meaning of 'making known,' as in 'one intimates by body, one intimates by speech.' In the Sudinna section, it has the meaning of 'instigating,' as in 'he intimates three times.' Here, however, both are applicable. For when there is a desire to make another understand, it should be understood that in all those bodily and verbal movements, the presence of instigating intimation is to be found. In the Mūlaṭīkā, however, it is said that even without the desire to make another understand, by the mere act of moving forward, etc., that modification co-arisen with the mind intimates the intention. And since it is itself made known, it is said that intimation is twofold. Therein, of the two communicative intimations, the first, bodily intimation—the movement of the major and minor limbs—is known by first apprehending the changing appearance with the eye-consciousness process and the moving limbs with the body-consciousness process, and afterwards by pure mind-door impulsion alone. The latter, verbal intimation, is known by first apprehending the uttered sound with the ear-consciousness process and afterwards by pure mind-door impulsion alone, not by five-door impulsion. For it intimates the mind of another being who is endowed with it only by knowing itself, not to one who does not know. For an informing cause makes known what is to be made known only by knowing itself, not by not knowing. And so, for animals too, having seen or touched a bodily movement or having heard a sound, the initial knowing of the intimation is established, for without knowing that, it is impossible to know the intention. And for those who know the intimation, without knowing the connection with a previously established convention, it is not possible to know the intention; thus some hold that a separate grasping of the connection with a prior convention is necessary in between. As to the two instigating intimations: having seen another moving forward with the eye-consciousness process, they know the intimation of moving forward and the mind of moving forward with the mind-consciousness process. This is the method for retreating, etc. Likewise, having heard another's speech with the ear-consciousness process, they know the intimation of speech and the mind of speech with the mind-consciousness process. Having seen another moving their limbs with a mind of lust, they know the intimation of movement and the lustful mind. Having heard the speech of a lustful person, they know the intimation of speech and the lustful mind. This is the method in all bodily and verbal actions. The state of being light is lightness (lahutā). The state of being soft is softness (mudutā). Fit for work is workable (kammaññaṃ); the meaning is 'suitable for work.' The state of being workable is workability (kammaññatā).

Adandhatālakkhaṇā rūpassa lahutā. Athaddhatā lakkhaṇā rūpassa mudutā. Sarīrakriyānukūlakammaññabhāvalakkhaṇā rūpassa kammaññatā. Aññamaññaṃ avijahantiyopi etā viruddhapaccayasappāya paccayānaṃ vasena asaṃmissato veditabbā. Tathā hi attano kāyaviruddhaṃ [M 0.0286] utuṃvā āhāraṃvā cittakriyaṃvā sevantānaṃ sarīragatā dhātuyo kadāci sakalasarīraṃvā sarīrekadesaṃvā khobhetvā visesato pūtimukha sappasaṅkhātaāpo pariyuṭṭhānaṃ katvā kāyaṃ asayhabhāraṃ viya garuṃ bhāriyaṃ karonti. Iriyā pathaparivattane kāyabhāriyanimittaṃ dukkhaṃ uppādenti. Tadārūpassa lahutā napavattati. Puna attano sarīrasappāyaṃ utuṃvā āhāraṃvā cittakiriyaṃvā sevantānaṃ so dhātukkhobho vūpasammati. Kāyo sallahuko hoti. Iriyāpathaparivattane kāya bhāriyanimittaṃ dukkhaṃnāma natthi. Tadā sā pavattati. Esanayo sesāsupi. Visesanato panettha mudubhāyaṃ kaṭṭhamukhasappasaṅkhāta pathavīpariyuṭṭhānaṃ katvā sukkhakaṭṭhaṃviya kāyaṃ thaddhaṃ kakkhaḷaṃkaronti. Iriyāpathaparivattane aṅgamaṅgānaṃchijjanabhijjanākārapattaṃ thaddhaṃ kakkhaḷanimittaṃ dukkhaṃ uppādentīti vattabbaṃ. Kammaññatāyaṃ satthamukhasappasaṅkhāta vāyo pariyuṭṭhānaṃ vāyovisamaṃ katvā dāmarikacorapariyuṭṭhitaṃ paccantaraṭṭhaṃ viya kāyaṃ vivaṭṭamānaṃ karonti, sabbairiyāpathesu sukhaṃnāma natthīti vattabbaṃ. Tejodhātu pana tāsaṃ sabbāsaṃpi mūlabhūtā hotīti veditabbā.

The characteristic of lightness of material form is non-sluggishness. The characteristic of softness of material form is non-rigidity. The characteristic of workability of material form is the state of being workable, conducive to bodily activities. Although these do not abandon one another, they should be understood as unmingled by way of opposing and favorable conditions. For instance, when one indulges in climate, food, or mental activities that are contrary to the body, the bodily elements may occasionally become disturbed—either throughout the entire body or in a part of it. In particular, when the water element, known as the 'putrid-mouthed snake,' arises, it makes the body heavy and burdensome, like an unbearable load. This results in suffering characterized by bodily heaviness when changing postures. At such times, the lightness of material form does not occur. Conversely, when one engages in climate, food, or mental activities beneficial to the body, that disturbance of the elements subsides. The body becomes very light, and no suffering characterized by bodily heaviness arises when changing postures. Then, lightness occurs. The same principle applies to the rest. Specifically, regarding softness, when the earth element, known as the 'wood-mouthed snake,' arises, it makes the body stiff and rough like dry wood. When changing postures, suffering arises characterized by stiffness and roughness, as if the limbs were being cut or broken. Regarding workability, when the air element, known as the 'sword-mouthed snake,' arises unevenly, it makes the body agitated, like a border country beset by bandits. In all postures, there is no comfort. The fire element, however, should be understood as being the root of all of them.

Imā pana arogino kallabhāvoviya suparimadditacammassa mudubhāvoviya sudandhasuvaṇṇassa kammakkhamabhāvoviya rūpakāyassa iriyāpathaparivattane sallahukatādivasena sandissamānā visesākārā hontīti katvā vikārarūpaṃ nāma. Cayanaṃ cayo. Piṇḍavasena abhinibbattīti attho. Ādito uparitoca cayo upacayo. Pathamābhinibbatti uparuparivaḍḍhicāti attho. Ayañhi upasaddo upaññattantiādīsu viya pathamattho upasittantiādīsu viyaca upari atthoti. Vuttañca mūlaṭīkāyaṃ upasaddo pathamattho upariatthoca hotīti. Tenevahi pāḷiyaṃ yo āyatanānaṃ ācayo, so rūpassa upacayo. Yorūpassa upacayo, sā rūpassa santatīti vuttaṃ. Tananaṃ vitthāraṇaṃ tati. Sambandhā tati punappunaṃvā tati santati. Yathā pavattānaṃ āyatanānaṃ addhānapūraṇavasena pavattīti attho. Tattha gabbhaseyyakānaṃ [M 0.0287] sattānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe rūpānaṃ uppādo pathamānibbattiatthena upacayonāma. Tato paraṃ yāva sabbapathamaṃ uppannānaṃ cakkhu sota ghānajivhānaṃ uppādo, etthantare rūpānaṃ uppādo upari vaḍḍhiatthena upacayonāma. Tato paraṃ yāvajīvaṃ catusantatirūpānaṃ uppādo santatināma. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ nadītīre nikhātakūpasmiṃ udakuggamanakāloviya ācayo nibbatti. Paripuṇṇakāloviya upacayo vaḍḍhi. Ajjhottharitvā gamanakālo viya santati pavattīti.

These, however, are special characteristics that appear in the material body—such as its lightness when changing postures, like the soundness of a healthy person, the suppleness of well-tanned leather, or the workability of refined gold—and thus are called 'alteration-form' (vikārarūpa). Accumulating is accumulation (cayo); it means production in the form of a mass. Increase (upacayo) is accumulation from the beginning and upwards; it means initial production and subsequent growth. For here, the prefix 'upa-' denotes the initial meaning, as in upaññatti, and the 'upon' meaning, as in upasitta. And it is said in the Mūlaṭīkā: 'The prefix “upa-” signifies both the initial and the “upon” meaning.' Therefore, in the Pāḷi texts, it is said: 'The accumulation (ācaya) of the sense bases is the increase (upacayo) of material form. What is the increase of material form is the continuity (santati) of material form.' Extension is tati. Connected or repeated extension is continuity (santati). It means the occurrence of the sense bases that have arisen, filling out a stretch of time. Here, for beings in the womb, the arising of material form at the moment of rebirth-linking is called 'increase' (upacaya) in the sense of initial production. Thereafter, until the arising of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue for the very first time, the arising of material form in this interval is called 'increase' (upacaya) in the sense of subsequent growth. After that, for the rest of life, the arising of the fourfold continuity of material form is called 'continuity' (santati). For it is said in the commentary: 'Just as the emergence of water in a well dug on a riverbank is accumulation (ācaya), its production; the time of fullness is increase (upacayo), its growth; and the time of overflowing and flowing is continuity (santati), its occurrence.'

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī:

Paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya yāvacakkhādi dasakānaṃ uppatti. Etthantare rūpuppādo upacayonāma. Tato paraṃ santati nāmāti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi tena pariyāyena yujjatiyeva.

From rebirth-linking up to the arising of the decades beginning with the eye, the arising of material form in this interval is called 'increase.' After that, it is said, it is called 'continuity.' That too is indeed fitting in that way.

Saṃsedajopavātikānaṃ pana paṭisandhikkhaṇe rūpānaṃ uppādo pathamā bhinibbatti atthena paripuṇṇa vaḍḍhi atthenaca upacayo nāma, tato paraṃ rūpānaṃ uppādo santatināma. Apica, tisamuṭṭhānika rūpānaṃpi visuṃ visuṃ santatipaccuppannaṃnāma atthi. Tassaca ekekassa nibbatti vaḍḍhi pavatti vasena tisso tissoavatthā honti. Tattha ekekasantatiyaṃ ādimhi santatisīsarūpānaṃ sabbapathamaṃ uppādo nibbattināma. Tato vaḍḍhanarūpānaṃ uppādo vaḍḍhīnāma. Vaḍḍhane samatte avaḍḍhitvā pabandhaṭṭhitivasena vattanavasenauppādopavattināma. Tattha ca nibbattivaḍḍhiyo upacayonāma. Pavattisantati nāma. Saṅkhepato pana loke sabbāsu indriyānindriyabaddharūpapavattīsu sandissamāne jāyana vaḍḍhana pavattanasaṅkhāte avatthābhede disvā upacayasanta tiyo veditabbā. Tatrāyaṃ nayo-rukkhatiṇādīnivā sākhā pattapupphaphalādīnivā ādimhi jāyanti. Jāyitvā vaḍḍhanti. Vaḍḍhane samatte avaḍḍhitvā pabandhavasena pavattitvā bhijjantīti. Jīraṇaṃ jarā, jīranti jiṇṇabhāvaṃ gacchanti etāyāti jarā. Sāyeva jaratā. Uppādajarābhaṅgehi niccalati nakampatīti nicco asaṅkhata dhammo. Na nicco anicco, saṅkhatadhammo. Aniccassa bhāvo aniccatā, bhaṅgo.

For beings born from moisture and those born spontaneously, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the arising of material phenomena is called 'increase' (upacaya) in the sense of first manifestation and in the sense of full growth. After that, the arising of material phenomena is called 'continuity' (santati). Moreover, for material phenomena produced by the three origins, there is for each a distinct 'present continuity.' For each of these there are three stages: production, growth, and continuation. Herein, in each continuity, the very first arising of the initial material phenomena is called 'production' (nibbatti). Thereafter, the arising of the material phenomena that grow is called 'growth' (vaḍḍhi). When growth is complete, the arising that occurs by way of persistence as an uninterrupted series without further growth is called 'continuation' (pavatti). Herein, production and growth are called 'increase' (upacaya); continuation is called 'continuity' (santati). In brief, since in the world, in all continuities of material phenomena—whether bound up with faculties or not—one sees the distinct stages designated as arising, growing, and continuing, increase and continuity should be understood. Here is the method: just as trees, grass, and so on, or branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so on, first arise, and having arisen, they grow; when growth is complete, having continued for a while as a series without further growth, they break up. Decaying is aging (jarā); 'they age' means they go to a state of being worn out, thus it is called 'aging' (jarā). This itself is decrepitude (jaratā). Because it is unshaken and unperturbed by arising, aging, and dissolution, the unconditioned phenomenon is 'permanent' (nicca). What is not permanent is 'impermanent' (anicca), the conditioned phenomenon. The state of being impermanent is 'impermanence' (aniccatā), which is dissolution (bhaṅga).

[183] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[183] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Niccadhuvabhāvena [M 0.0288] na iccaṃ anugantabbanti anicca”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It has been said: 'It is impermanent (anicca) because it should not be desirably pursued (na iccaṃ anugantabbaṃ) with a permanent and stable nature.' That is not a good explanation.

Niccasaddo hi sāsane lokeca pākaṭo. So eva idha nakārayutto aniccoti vuttoti. Lakkhīyanti sallakkhīyanti vinicchīyanti dhammā ime saṅkhatāti etenāti lakkhaṇaṃ. Saṅkhata bhāvajānananimitanti attho. Yathāha- aṅguttare tīṇi māni bhikkhave saṅkhatassa saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni. Katamāni tīṇi, uppādo paññāyati, vayo paññāyati, ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyatīti. Nanu pāḷiyaṃ jātināma āgatā. Tasmā sāpi idha vattabbāti vuttaṃ jātirūpamevātiādi. Etthāti rūpasamuddese. Jananaṃ pātubhavanaṃ jāti. Jāyantivā etāyāti jāti, upacaya santati nāmenapavuccati tassājātiyātathā avatthābhedayogatoti adhippāyo. Sā hi ādito paṭisandhirūpāni pātubhavantāni karoti. Puna aparipuṇṇānica āyatanāni pūreti. Pūritāni ca dīghaṃpi addhānaṃ abbocchinnaṃ katvā pavatteti pabandhayatīti. Ekā dasavidhaṃpīti mahābhūtādibhāvena ekattaṃ upanayanavasena ekā dasapabhedaṃpi. Kathaṃ sarūpavasena aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ hotīti pucchitvā bhūtappasāda visayātiādinā ekādasavidhasseva sarūpato dassanaṃ antogadhabhedānaṃ pubbe vuttabhāvena supākaṭattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha-aṭṭhārasavidhanti.

For the term 'permanent' (nicca) is well-known in the Teaching and in the world. It is this very word that is used here with the negative particle 'na' and called 'impermanent' (anicca). By this these conditioned phenomena are marked, noted, and determined; therefore it is a 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa). The meaning is: it is a sign for knowing the conditioned nature. As it is said in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: 'Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of the conditioned. What three? Arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and alteration while it persists is discerned.' But has not the term 'birth' (jāti) come up in the Pāḷi? Therefore, since it should be mentioned here, it is said, 'birth is simply material form,' and so on. Here, in the 'Exposition of Material Form,' 'birth' (jāti) is generation, manifestation. Or, 'that by which they are born' is 'birth'; the intention is that it is called by the names 'accumulation' and 'continuity' because of its connection with such different stages. For from the beginning it makes the material phenomena at rebirth-linking manifest. Then it fills up the incomplete sense bases. And having filled them, it makes them continue uninterrupted for a long time, causing them to persist as a series. The phrase 'Though one, it is also tenfold' means that although it is one by way of being brought to unity through its nature as the great elements and so on, it is also of ten kinds. Having asked, 'How does it become twenty-eightfold by way of its own nature?', the text shows only the eleven kinds (such as elements, sensitivities, and objects) by way of their own nature, because their internal distinctions have been stated before and are thus very clear. This should be understood. Therefore it says: 'eighteenfold.'

Cattāri bhūtāni pañcapasādā agahitagahaṇena cattāro visayā gocarā. Duvidho bhāvo. Ekaṃ hadayaṃ. Iti idaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ rūpaṃ jīvitāhārarūpehi saha aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ hoti tathā eko paricchedo. Duvidhā viññatti. Agahitagahaṇena tividho vikāro. Catubbidhaṃ lakkhaṇanti dasa anipphannācāti rūpaṃ sarūpato aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ bhaveti yojanā. Etthaca pacchimāni dasarūpāni sabhāvato anupalabbhamānattā paccayehi nipphāditāni rūpāni na hontīti anipphannāni nāma. Api cettha abhidhamme visuṃ [M 0.0289] uddiṭṭhāni niddiṭṭhānica etāni sabhāvato anupalabbhamānānīti vā paramatthato avijjamānānītivā nasakkā vattuṃ. Vohārasiddha mattabhāvaṃ atikkamma tādisena suddhadhammagatiyā siddhena paramattha lakkhaṇena upaladdhattā. Itarathā nibbattilakkhaṇarahitaṃ asaṅkhata nibbānaṃpi sabhāvato anupalabbhamānaṃ paramatthato avijjamānañca nāma siyāti. Tasmā nibbatti lakkhaṇarahitattāeva etāni anipphannānināma. Na sabhāvato anupalabbhamānattāti yuttaṃ siyāti. [Rūpasamuddeso]

The four great elements, the five sensitivities, the four objective fields (by taking what has not been taken), the two kinds of sex, and the one heart-base. Thus this is sixteenfold material form. Together with the life faculty and nutriment, it becomes eighteenfold. Also, the one space element, the two intimations, the three alterations (by taking what has not been taken), and the four characteristics—these are the ten unproduced phenomena. The construction is: 'Thus material form, by way of its own nature, becomes twenty-eightfold.' Herein, the latter ten material phenomena are called 'unproduced' because, not being discoverable in their own right, they are not material phenomena produced by causes. And yet, although in the Abhidhamma they are enumerated and explained separately, it cannot be said that they are not discoverable in their own right or that they are non-existent in an ultimate sense. For, transcending a state of being merely established by convention, they are apprehended by an ultimate characteristic that is established by the pure way of phenomena. Otherwise, even Nibbāna, which is unconditioned and devoid of the characteristic of production, would have to be called 'not discoverable in its own right' and 'non-existent in an ultimate sense.' Therefore, it is only because they are devoid of the characteristic of production that they are called 'unproduced,' not because they are not discoverable in their own right. This would be the proper view. [The Exposition of Material Form]

157. Rūpavibhāgesabbañca pana etaṃ yathāsamuddiṭṭhaṃ aṭṭhavīsati vidhaṃ rūpaṃ ahetukaṭṭhena ekavidhameva. Na sahetukā hetuka vasena duvidhaṃ. Tathāsappaccayaṭṭhena ekavidhameva. Na sappaccayāpaccaya vasena duvidhanti evaṃ pavattaṃ ekavidhanayaṃ tāva dassetuṃ sabbañcātiādimāraddhaṃ.

157. In the Analysis of Material Form: And all this twenty-eightfold material form, as enumerated, is of one kind in that it is rootless; it is not twofold, as with roots and rootless. Similarly, it is of one kind in that it is conditioned; it is not twofold, as conditioned and unconditioned. In order to show this singlefold method of classification, the passage beginning 'And all this...' was started.

[184] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[184] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Ekavidhanayopi rūpavibhāgoevāti katvā “yathā uddiṭṭha rūpānaṃ ekavidhādinayaṃ dassanatthaṃ sabbañca panetantiādi vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sameti.

It has been said: 'Thinking, "The singlefold method is also the analysis of material form," the passage beginning "And all this..." was stated in order to show the singlefold and other methods for the material phenomena as enumerated.' But this is not correct.

Vakkhati hi –

For it will be said:

Ajjhattikādibhedena, vibhajanti yathārahanti.

They classify according to internal and other distinctions, as is fitting.

Etena ajjhattikādibhedo eva rūpavibhāgonāmāti viññāyati.

By this it is understood that the analysis of material form is precisely the distinction into internal, etc.

Tattha sabbaṃpi rūpaṃ hetusampayogā bhāvato ahetuka meva, na kiñci sahetukaṃ. Kiñci ahetukanti evaṃ vibhāgo atthīti adhippāyo. Sappaccayaṃ sāsavaṃ saṅkhataṃ lokiyanti pāṭho. Sappaccayaṃ saṅkhataṃ lokiyaṃ sāsavanti pana yutto. Pāḷiyaṃpi tathā diṭṭhattā sabhāgayugaḷasambhavatocāti. Itarāni pana pāḷikamena asamentānipi sabhāga yugaḷattā bhāgato yuttānieva. Tattha attano janakena paccayena saheva vattatīti sapaccayaṃ. Paccayehi saṅgamma karīyatīti saṅkhataṃ. Pañcupādā nakkhandhasaṅkhāte [M 0.0290] lokeeva pariyāpannanti lokiyaṃ. Attānaṃ ārabbha pavattehi āsavehi saheva vattatīti sāsavaṃ. Akaniṭṭha brahmasantāna bhūtaṃpi rūpaṃ kāmataṇhā visayabhāvena kāmeeva pariyāpannattā kāmāvacaraṃ. Natthi attanā gahitaṃ kiñci ārammaṇaṃnāma assāti anārammaṇaṃ. Yo dhammo aññena payogena pahīnopi samudayapahāne asati apahīnova hoti. Puna avassaṃ uppajjamānattā. Appahīnopi tasmiṃ sati pahīnova hoti. Puna anuppajjamānattā. Tādiso dhammo pahānavāyāmassa aṭṭhānattā appahātabbonāma. Rūpaṃpi edisameva hotīti vuttaṃ appahātabba mevāti. Aṭṭhānattā pahāna vāyāmaṃ na arahatīti attho. Athavā, vinā samudayapahānena pahātuṃ asakkuṇeyyoti attho. Yadi evaṃ rūpaṃ bhikkhave na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ dīgharattaṃ atthāya hitāya sukhāya bhavissatīti idaṃ kathanti. Taṃpi tabbisayassa rāgassa pahānaṃ sandhāya vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathāha –

Herein, all material form is rootless because it is devoid of association with roots; none is with roots. The meaning is that there is no such division as 'some is with roots, some is rootless.' The reading is: 'dependent on conditions, with taints, conditioned, worldly.' But 'dependent on conditions, conditioned, worldly, with taints' is the more suitable reading, since it is seen thus in the Pāli and because of the occurrence of similar pairs. The other terms, though not agreeing with the order in the Pāli, are still appropriate in part because they are similar pairs. Therein, 'dependent on conditions' (sappaccayaṃ) is that which exists together with its own generative condition. 'Conditioned' (saṅkhataṃ) is that which is made by a combination of conditions. 'Worldly' (lokiyaṃ) is that which is included in the world, defined as the five aggregates subject to clinging. 'With taints' (sāsavaṃ) is that which exists together with the taints that arise in relation to it. Even material form that has come to be in the continuity of an Akaniṭṭha brahma is of the sense sphere because, by being an object for sensual craving, it is included in the sense sphere. It is 'objectless' (anārammaṇaṃ) because there is no object whatsoever grasped by it. A phenomenon that, though abandoned by some means, is not truly abandoned as long as its origin is not abandoned—since it will inevitably arise again—and that, though not abandoned, is truly abandoned when its origin is abandoned—since it will not arise again—such a phenomenon is called 'not to be abandoned' (appahātabba) because it is not a basis for the effort of abandoning. Material form is of just such a kind, thus it is said to be 'not to be abandoned.' The meaning is that it is not a proper object for the effort of abandoning. Or, the meaning is that it cannot be abandoned without abandoning its origin. If so, how is this statement to be understood: 'Bhikkhus, this material form is not yours. Abandon it. Its abandonment will be for your long-term welfare and happiness'? This should be seen as stated with reference to the abandoning of the lust related to it as an object. As it is said:

Rūpe kho rādha yo chando, yo rāgo, yānandī, yā taṇhā, taṃ pajahatha. Evaṃ taṃrūpaṃ pahīnaṃ bhavissati ucchinnamūlaṃ tālāvatthukataṃ anabhāvaṃkataṃ āyatiṃ anuppādadhammanti.

Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for form, abandon it. In this way that form will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, obliterated, and made subject to no future arising.

Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi kusalādīsu appahātabbesu veditabboti. Evasaddo cettha purimapadesupi yojetabbo. Itisaddo ādiattho, pakāratthovā. Tena pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ na hetu hetuvippayuttantiādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa tassa puggalassa attabhāvapariyāpanno dhammasamūho ajjhattaṃnāma. Tasmiṃpica yattha taṇhāya atirekataraṃ daḷhapariggaho hoti. So cakkhādiko cittena saha chabbidho dhammo ajjhattiko nāma. Ajjhatte vidito pākaṭoti katvā. Tathā hi so ajjhattajjhattantipi vutto. Itarāni pana rūpādini phassādīnica tadupādāya taṇhāpariggahassa mandattā bāhirāni nāma. Yathā hi loke maṇivā suvaṇṇaṃvā rajataṃvā bahigehe nidahitvā thapitaṃ hoti. Pacchivā suppaṃvā ghaṭovā sarāvovā anto gehe thapito. Tattha pacchimāni chaḍḍetvāpi purimāni rakkhanti. Tasmā tāneva taṇhāpariggahadaḷhatāya antoparibhogātveva vuccanti. Pacchimāni pana bāhira paribhogātveva. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idhapi hi yadi sakkuṇeyya. Rūpādīni phassādinica sabbāni chaḍḍetvāpi cakkhādikaṃ chabbidhameva avassaṃ rakkhissantīti. Iti taṇhā pariggahassa daḷhamandatā vaseneva tesaṃ dvinnaṃ ajjhattika bāhiratā vuttā. Na pavattidesavasenāti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

This method should be understood as applicable also to other wholesome states, etc., that are not to be abandoned. The word 'eva' here should also be connected with the preceding terms. The word 'iti' has the sense of 'etc.' or 'in this way,' thereby including Pāli passages such as 'not a cause, dissociated from a cause,' etc. The aggregate of phenomena included in an individual's personal existence is called 'internal.' Within that, wherever craving's grasp is especially strong, that sixfold phenomenon—the eye, etc., along with the mind—is called 'personal.' This is because it is clearly known within oneself; indeed, it is even called 'the utterly internal.' Other things, however, such as forms and contacts, are called 'external' because craving's grasp on them is weaker. It is like in the world: jewels, gold, or silver are kept in an outer treasury, while a basket, winnowing fan, pot, or dish is kept in the inner house. People will protect the former even if it means discarding the latter. Therefore, due to the firmness of craving's grasp, the former are said to be for 'internal use' and the latter for 'external use.' This should be understood accordingly. Here too, if one could, one would discard all forms, contacts, and so on, but would surely protect the sixfold phenomena like the eye, etc. Thus, the distinction between 'personal' and 'external' is said to be based on the strength or weakness of craving's grasp, not on the place of occurrence. This is the conclusion.

[185] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

But as to what is to be explained:

“Ajjhattikarūpaṃ atthabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ attānaṃ adhikicca uddissa pavattattā. Kāmaṃ aññepi ajjhattasambhūtā atthi. Ruḷhīvasena pana cakkhādikameva ajjhattikanti” vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

"Personal matter is so called because it occurs with reference to and directed towards the self, which is designated as one's own being. Granted, there are other things that have arisen internally, but by convention, only the eye, etc., is called 'personal'." This statement is not good.

[186] Yañca tattha

And as to what is said there:

“Attasaṅkhātaṃpā cittaṃ adhikicca tassa dvārabhāvena pavattatīthi ajjhattaṃ. Tadeva ajjhattikanti” vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

"Because it occurs with reference to the mind, which is designated as 'self,' in the role of a door for it, it is 'internal' (ajjhattaṃ). That very thing is called 'personal' (ajjhattikaṃ)." This too is not good.

Tasmiṃ atthe hi sati cittassa ajjhattatā na sampajjati. Ajjhattadhamma ajjhattikammonañca aviseso āpajjatīti.

For if that were the meaning, the internality of the mind itself would not be established, and no distinction would result between an internal phenomenon and a personal phenomenon.

Yaṃ pana tattha

But as to what is said there:

Athavā yadi mayaṃ na homa, tvaṃ kaṭṭhakaliṅgarūpamo bhavissatīti vadantā viya attabhāvassa sātisayaṃ upakārakattā cakkhādineva visesato ajjhattikānīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ yuttataraṃ.

Alternatively: 'It is as if they were saying, "If we did not exist, you would become like a mere log of wood."' Because of their exceptional helpfulness to one's own being, the eye and so on are specifically called 'personal.' This is more reasonable.

Tathā upakārātisayattāeva hi tesu sattānaṃ pariggaha daḷhatā hotīti. Sattavidhaṃpi dvārarūpaṃnāma. Yathākkamaṃ vīthi cittānaṃ pāṇātipātādikammānañca pavattimukhattā. Tattha pana pañca vidhaṃ pasādarūpaṃ upapattidvāraṃnāma. Viññattidvayaṃ kammadvāraṃnāmāti oḷārikarūpaṃ pakatiyā thūlasabhāvattā ghaṭṭanasaṅkhātassaca attano kiccassa oḷārikattā. Santikerūpaṃ dūre pavattassapi sīghataraṃ ñāṇena gahaṇayogyattā. Sappaṭigharūpañcāti ettha paṭihananaṃ [M 0.0292] paṭigho. So duvidho visayavisayīnaṃ paṭighaṭṭanaṃ mahā bhūtānaṃ aññamaññapaṭighaṭṭananti. Tattha yena paṭighaṭṭanena pasāda dvārānaṃ bhavaṅgassaca vikārappatti hoti. Idaṃ visayavisayīnaṃ paṭighaṭṭanaṃnāma. Yena ruppanalakkhaṇānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ ruppana kuppana ghaṭṭana pīḷana bhijjanādayo pavattanti. Idaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ aññamaññapaṭighaṭṭanaṃ nāma. Paṭighena saha vattatīti sappaṭighaṃ.

Indeed, it is because of such exceptional helpfulness that beings' grasp on them is firm. The sevenfold door-materiality is so called because it is the entrance for the occurrence, respectively, of cognitive series and of kamma such as the destruction of life. Among these, the five kinds of sensitive materiality are called the 'door of arising,' and the two intimations are called the 'door of kamma.' Gross materiality is so called because its nature is naturally coarse and because its own function, designated as impact, is gross. Proximate materiality is so called because, though occurring at a distance, it is fit to be grasped very quickly by knowledge. And as to resistant materiality: here, striking is resistance (paṭigha). This is twofold: the impact of object and subject, and the mutual impact of the great primary elements. Here, that impact by which an alteration of the sense doors and of the life-continuum occurs is called the impact of object and subject. That by which affliction, agitation, collision, oppression, and breaking occur in material phenomena, which have the characteristic of being afflicted, is called the mutual impact of the great primary elements. It is 'resistant' (sappaṭighaṃ) because it occurs together with resistance.

[187] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But as to the explanation:

“Yo sayaṃ nissayavasenaca sampattānaṃ asampattānañca paṭimukhabhāvo aññamaññapatanaṃ. So paṭigho viyāti paṭigho. Yathāhi paṭighāte sati dubbalassa calanaṃ hoti. Evaṃ aññamaññapaṭimukhabhāve sati arūpasabhāvattā dubbalassa bhavaṅgassa calanaṃ hotīti” evaṃ mahābhūtaghaṭṭanaṃ upamāmattaṃ katvā visayavisayighaṭṭanameva gahitaṃ. Taṃ anupapannaṃ.

"That which, by way of dependence, is a state of confrontation and mutual impingement between what has arrived at the sense door and what has not, is like resistance, thus it is resistance (paṭigha). For just as when there is an impact the weaker one is shaken, so when there is a state of mutual confrontation, the life-continuum, which is weak because of its formless nature, is shaken." In this way, taking the collision of the great primary elements as a mere simile, only the collision of object and subject has been understood as resistance. That is untenable.

Evañhi sati yāni loke ajjhattabahiddhāsantānesu ghaṭṭanāni dissanti. Yesaṃ vasena rūpadhammesu aññamaññaṃ laggana bandhana thambhana dhāraṇa calanādīnivā vaḍḍhana hāyana chedana bhedana vilīna vikiraṇādīnivā pavattanti. Tāni idha asaṅgahitāni siyuṃ. Naca tāni anuggaha upaghāta vasena pavattibhūta sannipāta saṅkhātaṃ ghaṭṭanaṃvinā aññapakārānieva sakkā bhavitunti. Itaraṃ soḷasavidhaṃ vuttapaṭipakkhavasena sukhumarūpaṃ dūrerūpaṃ apaṭigharūpañca. Upādinnarūpaṃ nāma katthaci yaṃkiñci sarīraṭṭhakarūpaṃ vuccati. Katthaci kammasamuṭṭhāna meva tadubhayaṃpi taṇhādiṭṭhīhi tusaṃ ādinnaparāmaṭṭhattā upādinnaṃ nāma nippariyāyato pana kammasamuṭṭhānameva upādinnaṃnāma. Kasmā tasseva sattasantāne niccakālaṃ pavattivasena sātisayaṃ bhusaṃ ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhatāsambhavatoti vuttaṃ kammajaṃupādinnarūpanti. Etaṃ mamātiādinā taṇhādiṭṭhīhi bhusaṃ ādiyatīti upādinnaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana taṇhādiṭṭhīhi upetena kammunā attano phalabhāvena ādinnaṃ gahitanti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Saha nidassanena [M 0.0293] sanidassanaṃ. Nidassananti cakkhuviññāṇena daṭṭhabbabhāvo vuccati. So pana dhammato anaññattepi aññe viya katvā upacarīyati. Evañhi sati atthavisesabodho hotīti. Nidassanantivā cakkhuviññāṇakiccaṃ vuccati. Tena saha vattatīti sanidassanantipi yujjatiyeva. Cakkhādidvayaṃ asampattavasena gocaraggāhikaṃ. Ghānādittayaṃ sampattavasena gocaraggāhikanti pañcavidhaṃpi gocaraggāhikarūpanti yojanā. Tattha pasāde allīyitvā laggitvā uppannaṃ ārammaṇaṃ sampattaṃnāma. Kesaggamattaṃpi muñcitvā uppannaṃ asampattaṃnāma. Kasmā panettha cakkhādidvayaṃ asampattameva gaṇhāti.
