Ghānādittayaṃ sampattamevāti, paccayavisesato. Āloko hi rūpagahaṇe cakkhussa paccayo. Ākāsoca saddagahaṇe sotassāti cakkhurūpesuca aññamaññaṃ laggitvā uppajjamānesu ālokaparivārassa okāso natthi. Tathā sotasaddesuca ākāsaparivārassāti. Vāyuāpapathaviyo pana ghānādittayassa gandhādigahaṇe paccayā honti. Tattha vāyunāma gandhākaḍḍhanako nāsavātoyeva, soca sampattasseva paccayo. Āponāma jivhātemanako āpo, sopi sampattasseva paccayo. Na hi raso sukkhajivhāya pharatīti. Pathavīca ghaṭṭanatthāya paccayo. Na hi dubbalapathavīsannissayo ālokovā rajovākāye patamānopi pasāde ghaṭṭetīti. Iti paccayavisesato tesaṃ sampattāsampattavasena gahaṇa viseso hotīti. Tattha cakkhussa tāva asampattagahaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Tañhi samīpe akkhivaṇṇaṃvā bhamukamūlaṃvā napassati. Dūre pana mahantaṃ candamaṇḍalādikaṃvā phalikāditirohitaṃvā vaṇṇaṃ passati. Disādesavavatthānañcassa paññāyatīti. Sotassa pana kathanti, tattha hi dūre saddo cirena suyyamāno dissati pacchimadisābhāge uppannopi saddo antarā mahante cetiyādike antarite sati dakkhiṇapassatovā suyyati. Uttarapassatovā. Asuyyamānovā hotīti. Vuccate, uppanno saddasaṅghāṭo āsanne ṭhitānaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya yāva avasānā kamena [M 0.0294] pākaṭībhūto hoti. Paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃsoca balavā hoti. Ahaṃ suṇomīti pavattā sallakkhaṇavīthiyo sīghataraṃ nirantaraṃ viya pavattanti. Dūre ṭhitānaṃ pana paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃso mandataro hoti. Ādito apākaṭo. Majjhevā avasānevā piṇḍavasena pākaṭībhūto. Sallakkhaṇavīthiyo cirena parena pavattanti. Tasmā tesaṃ lahuṃ suto. Cirena sutoti atimāno hotīti. Apica, saddonāma nissayadhātuparaṃparāya pavattitvā dūraṃpi desaṃ gacchatiyeva. Evaṃ gacchantoca gatagataṭṭhāneeva ṭhatvā savanūpacāre ṭhitānaṃ sotasahassaṃpi ghaṭṭeti. Mahante pana cetiyādike antarite sati yato ākāso ujuṃ vivaṭo hoti. Tato dakkhiṇapassatovā uttarapassatovā gatagataṭhānatovasotaṃ ghaṭṭeti. Mandataro pana saddoasuyya mānopi hoti. Evaṃ gacchantoca yāva sotapasāde allīyitvā nuppajjati. Tāva asampattoyeva hoti. Yo pana allī yitvā uppajjati. So sampattonāma hoti. Na so suyyatīti. Yadi pana sotaṃ sampattavisayaṃ siyā. Yathā anto kucchigato gandho bahi naghāyiyati. Tathā anto kucchigato saddopi bahi nasuyeyya. Gandhassa viya disādesavavatthānaṃ vissana siyāti.

For if this were so, the impacts that are seen in the world in internal and external continuums would not be included here. By means of these, material phenomena undergo adhering, binding, stiffening, supporting, moving, and so on, or growing, declining, cutting, breaking, dissolving, scattering, and so on. And it is not possible for them to be of any other kind apart from the impact, known as conjunction, that occurs by way of assistance and affliction. The other sixteen kinds—subtle matter, distant matter, and non-resistant matter—are stated by way of opposition. Clung-to matter (upādinnarūpa) is sometimes said to be any matter that serves as a physical basis. Sometimes it is only matter originated by kamma. However, both are called 'clung-to' because they are grasped and clung to by craving and views. But in the strict sense, only matter originated by kamma is called 'clung-to matter.' Why? Because of the greater possibility of its being intensely grasped, seized, and clung to, as it persists continuously in a being’s continuum of existence. Hence it is said: 'Clung-to matter is kamma-born.' It is called 'clung-to' because it is intensely grasped by craving and views with such thoughts as 'this is mine.' The commentary, however, shows this meaning: 'It is grasped by kamma accompanied by craving and views as its own fruit.' 'With the visible' (sanidassana). The visible (nidassana) is said to be the state of being seeable by eye-consciousness. Though in reality not different from the physical phenomenon, it is treated by convention as if it were different. For if this is so, an understanding of the specific meaning arises. Or, the visible (nidassana) is said to be the function of eye-consciousness. Thus, 'with the visible' (sanidassana) is also appropriate. The five kinds of object-grasping matter (gocaraggāhikarūpa) are to be construed thus: the pair of eye and ear are graspers of the object without having reached it (asampattavasena); the triad of nose, tongue, and body are graspers of the object by having reached it (sampattavasena). Here, an object that has arisen by adhering and clinging to the sensitivity is called 'reached' (sampatta). One that has arisen without even touching it by a hair's tip is called 'unreached' (asampatta). Why is it that the pair of eye and ear grasp only what is unreached, while the triad of nose, tongue, and body grasp only what is reached? Because of a difference in conditions. For light is a condition for the eye in grasping a form, and space is a condition for the ear in grasping a sound. When the eye and a form arise in mutual contact, there is no room for the surrounding light. Similarly for the ear and a sound, there is no room for the surrounding space. But the air, water, and earth elements are conditions for the triad of nose, etc., in grasping odor, etc. Here, the air element is the nasal breath that draws in the odor, and it is a condition only for what is reached. The water element is the moisture that wets the tongue, and it too is a condition only for what is reached; for a taste does not pervade a dry tongue. And the earth element is a condition for the purpose of impact; for a weak basis of earth, or light, or dust falling on the body does not impact the sensitivity. Thus, because of the difference in conditions, there is a difference in their grasping by way of 'reached' and 'unreached.' In the case of the eye, its grasping of the unreached is manifest. For it does not see the color of the eyelid or the root of the eyebrow, which are close, but it sees the great disk of the moon, etc., which is far, or a color hidden by a crystal, etc. And its determination of direction and location is discerned. But how is it for the ear? Here, a sound far away is observed to be heard after a delay. A sound that has arisen in the western direction might be heard from the southern or northern side if a great stupa or the like stands in between, or it might not be heard at all. It is said: When a conglomeration of sound has arisen, for those standing near it becomes manifest in sequence from beginning to end. The impact and friction are strong. The cognitive processes of noting, 'I hear,' occur very quickly, as if uninterruptedly. But for those standing far away, the impact and friction are weaker. At first it is not manifest; it becomes manifest as a lump in the middle or at the end. The cognitive processes of noting occur after a delay. Therefore, for them, the estimation arises, 'It was heard quickly,' or 'It was heard after a delay.' Moreover, sound, having arisen in a succession of supporting elements, does indeed travel to a distant place. And as it travels, standing in each place it has gone to, it can strike even a thousand ears of those who stand in the range of hearing. But when a great stupa or the like stands in between, it strikes the ear from the southern or northern side, or from whatever place it has gone to where the space is directly open. A weaker sound might not be heard at all. And as it travels, so long as it has not arisen by adhering to the ear sensitivity, it is 'unreached.' But what arises by adhering is called 'reached.' That is not what is heard. If the ear were to have a 'reached' object, then just as a smell inside the stomach is not smelled outside, so a sound inside the stomach would not be heard outside. And like a smell, there would be no determination of its direction and location.

[188] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[188] But as to the explanation:

“Gantvā visayadesaṃ taṃ, pharitvā gaṇhatīti ce. Adhiṭṭhāna vidhā nepi, tassa so gocaro siyā.” Tipi vicāritaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

“If it goes to the object’s location, pervades it, and then grasps it; even by the method of determination, that would be its domain.” This too has been considered. That is not sound.

Na hi cakkhādidvayassa bahiddhā visayadesagamanasaṅgo atthīti. Gocaraṃ gaṇhātīti gocaraggāhikaṃ. Pasāda maṇḍabhūtattā āpātamāgataṃ ārammaṇanimittaṃ sampaṭicchatīti attho.

For there is no involvement of the pair, the eye and so on, in going outside to the object’s location. It grasps the object-domain, thus it is an 'object-domain-grasper.' The meaning is that because the sensitivity is like a polished surface, it receives the sign of the object that has come into its range.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But as to the explanation:

Viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ hutvā taṃtaṃ gocaragahaṇa sabhāvattāti vuttaṃ.

It is said that this is because, being supported by consciousness, it has the intrinsic nature of grasping its respective object-domain.

Vaṇṇoti [M 0.0295] rūpārammaṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ojāti āhāra rūpa māha. Vinibhujjatīti vinibbhogo. Ṭhānato desato uppattikāraṇato visuṃvisuṃ vavatthapīyatīti attho. Navinibbho goti avinibbhogo. So eva rūpanti avinibbhogarūpaṃ. Ācariyānandattherenapanettha gandharasaojā katthaci vinībhuttā dissantīti pañcavidhameva avinibbhogarūpaṃ icchitaṃ. Taṃ parato āgamissatīti. [Rūpavibhāgo].

'Color' is a name for the form-object. 'Nutritive essence' (ojā) refers to nutriment-matter. 'Divisible' (vinibbhoga) means that which can be divided. The meaning is that it is determined as distinct with respect to its standing place, location, and cause of origin. 'Not divisible' is 'indivisible' (avinibbhoga). That very matter is indivisible matter. Here, however, the Elder Ācariya Ānanda maintained that only the fivefold indivisible matter is intended, because odor, taste, and nutritive essence are sometimes seen as divided. That will be discussed below. [The Division of Matter].

158. Kammanti ekā cetanāeva. Sāyeva hi paṭṭhāne nānākkhaṇika kammapaccayabhāvena vuttā. Yathāha-nānākkhaṇikā kusalākusalā cetanā vipākānaṃ khandhānaṃ kaṭattāca rūpānaṃ kammapaccayena paccayoti. Cittanti pana sasampayuttadhammaṃ adhippetaṃ. Paṭṭhāne cetasikadhammānaṃpi rūpasamuṭṭhāpanabhāvena vuttattā. Yathāha-hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃ samuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetu paccayena paccayotiādi. Utūti tejoyeva. So hi kappasaṇṭhāpanavasena sakalaṃ okāsa lokaṃpi nānāsarīrasaṇṭhāpanavasena saka laṃ rūpamayaṃ kāyaṃ sattalokaṃpi nānārukkhatiṇādīnaṃ abbhapaṭalameghavuṭṭhijalaaggi vātādīnañca saṇṭhāpanavasena sakalaṃ saṅkhāralokaṃpi udayati pasavati janeti vaḍḍheti. Tasmā utūti vuccatīti. Arati gacchati pavattatīti utūtipi vadanti. Āhāroti ojāeva. Rūpavirāgabhāvanābhūtaṃ arūpakusalaṃ kammajarūpaṃ najanetīti vuttaṃ pañcavīsatividhaṃpīti. Atisaṅkhatanti atītakāle yathākā lantare rūpaṃ janeti, tathā visesetvā suṭṭhukataṃ. Ajjhatti kasantāneti vuttaṃ, ajjhattasantāneti pana vattabbaṃ. Ajjhatta meva ajjhattikantivā ikasaddassa attho daṭṭhabbo. Paṭisandhimupādāyāti paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇaṃ upādāya. Khaṇekhaṇeti ekekassa cittassa tīsu tīsu khaṇesu. Ācariyānandatthero pana sabbesaṃpi catusamuṭṭhānikarūpānaṃ ekekassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇeeva uppādaṃ bhaṅgakkhaṇeeva nirodhañca āha. Ahaṃ panassā [M 0.0296] dhippāyo-sabbānipi catusamuṭṭhānikarūpāni cittassa uppādakkhaṇeeva uppajjanti, na bhaṅgakkhaṇe. Yathāha –

158. 'Kamma' is simply volition. For it is this that is spoken of in the Paṭṭhāna as the different-moment kamma-condition, as when it is said: 'Volitions that are wholesome or unwholesome in different moments are a condition by way of kamma-condition for the resultant aggregates and for matter produced by kamma.' But by 'consciousness' (citta), its associated states are also intended, for in the Paṭṭhāna mental factors too are said to be producers of matter, as when it is said: 'Roots are a condition by way of root-condition for the states associated with the roots and for the matter originated by them,' and so on. 'Temperature' (utu) is just the fire element. For it is this that establishes the entire world of space by way of establishing the eon; the entire material body, the world of beings, by way of establishing the various bodily forms; and the entire world of formations by way of establishing the various trees, grasses, cloud-layers, rain, water, fire, wind, etc. It arises, brings forth, generates, and increases. Therefore it is called 'temperature.' Some also say it is called utu because it proceeds (arati), goes (gacchati), and occurs (pavattati). 'Nutriment' is just nutritive essence. It is said that formless-sphere wholesome kamma, which is the development of dispassion towards matter, does not generate any of the twenty-five kinds of kamma-born matter. 'Exceedingly conditioned' (atisaṅkhata) means specially well-made, in the sense that it generates matter at a later time than when it occurred in the past. 'In the internal continuity' is said, but 'in the internal continuum' should be said. Or the meaning of the suffix '-ika' in ajjhattika should be understood as simply 'internal.' 'From rebirth-linking onwards' means from the arising moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness. 'Moment by moment' means in each of the three moments of each single consciousness. The Elder Ācariya Ānanda, however, said that for all matter originated from the four sources, arising occurs only at the arising moment of each consciousness, and cessation only at its dissolution moment. But my own view is this: all matter originated from the four sources arises only at the arising moment of consciousness, not at the dissolution moment. As it is said:

Yassavā pana samudayasaccaṃ nirujjhati, tassa dukkhasaccaṃ uppajjatīti. Noti.

Or for whomever the truth of the origin is ceasing, for them is the truth of suffering arising? No.

Tathā tāni cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇeeva nirujjhanti. Na uppādakkhaṇe. Yathāha –

Thus, they cease only at the dissolution-moment of consciousness, not at the arising-moment. As it is said:

Yassa kusalā dhammā akusalā dhammā uppajjanti, tassa abyākatā dhammā nirujjhantīti. Noti.

“For one for whom wholesome states or unwholesome states arise, do indeterminate states cease for them?” “No.”

Arūpabhavaṃ sandhāya etaṃ yamakadvayaṃ vuttaṃ. Rūpāni pana cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇepi uppajjanti. Uppādakkhaṇepi nirujjhantīti ce. Na. Evañhi sati –

This pair of Yamaka questions was stated with reference to the formless existence. But material phenomena arise even at the dissolution-moment of consciousness. If it is said that they also cease at the arising-moment, this is not so. For if it were so:

Yassavā pana samudayasaccaṃ nirujjhati, tassa dukkhasaccaṃ uppajjatīti. Arūpe taṇhāya bhaṅgakkhaṇe tesaṃ samudayasaccaṃ nirujjhati. Noca tesaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ uppajjati. Pañcavokāre taṇhāya bhaṅgakkhaṇe tesaṃ samudayasaccañca nirujjhati, dukkhasaccañca uppajjatītica.

“Or for one for whom the truth of the origin is ceasing, is the truth of suffering arising for them? In the formless realm, at the dissolution-moment of craving, the truth of the origin is ceasing for them, but the truth of suffering is not arising for them. In the five-constituent existence, at the dissolution-moment of craving, the truth of the origin is ceasing for them and the truth of suffering is also arising.”

Itaratthaca

And in the other case:

Arūpe kusalānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe tesaṃ kusalā dhammā uppajjanti. Noca tesaṃ abyākatā dhammā nirujjhanti. Pañcavokāre kusalānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe tesaṃ kusalā dhammāca uppajjanti. Abyākatā dhammāca nirujjhantītica.

“In the formless realm, at the arising-moment of wholesome states, wholesome states are arising for them, but indeterminate states are not ceasing for them. In the five-constituent existence, at the arising-moment of wholesome states, wholesome states are arising for them and indeterminate states are also ceasing.”

Evaṃ paripuṇṇapañhāeva uddhaṭā siyuṃ. Noti pana paṭisedhova uddhaṭo. Tasmā nayidaṃ arūpabhavaṃ sandhāya vuttanti sakkā vattunti. Cittajarūpaṃ sandhāya vuttanti ce. Tampi na. Kammajarūpassa vigahaṇe virodhassa yamakapāṭhantarassa abhāvato. Anulomassevaca bhāvato. Yathāha –

Thus, only full questions would be raised. But here only the denial ‘No’ is raised. Therefore, it cannot be said that this was stated with reference to the formless existence. If it is said that it was stated with reference to mind-generated matter, that too is not so. This is because there is no contradictory alternative Yamaka reading in the analysis of kamma-generated matter, and because it is in conformity with the forward method. As it is said:

Yassavāpana yattha manindriyaṃ na uppajjati. Tassa tattha jīvitindriyaṃ nauppajjatīti. Asaññasattānaṃ tesaṃ tattha manindriyaṃ na uppajjati. Noca tesaṃ tattha jīvitindriyaṃ na uppajjati.

“Or for whomever, wherever the mind faculty is not arising, for them, there, is the life faculty not arising? For non-percipient beings, the mind faculty is not arising for them there, but it is not the case that the life faculty is not arising for them there.

Sabbesaṃ [M 0.0297] cavantānaṃ pavatte cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe tesaṃ tattha manindriyañca nauppajjati. Jīvitindriyañca nauppajjatīti.

For all who are passing away, at the dissolution-moment of consciousness in the course of existence, for them there the mind faculty is not arising and the life faculty is also not arising.”

Ettha hi asaññasattānanti etena rūpajīvitindriya meva vuttaṃ. Yadica taṃ cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇepi uppajjeyya, purimakoṭṭhāse pavatte cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe asaññasattānaṃ tesaṃ.La. Jīvitindriyaṃ nauppajjatīti vuttaṃ siyā, pacchimakoṭṭhāseca sabbesaṃ cavantānaṃ icceva vuttaṃ siyāti. Pacchimakoṭṭhāse pana arūpa jīvitindriyaṃ sandhāya vuttanti ce. Na. Tathā gahaṇatthaṃ yamaka pāṭhantarābhāvato sabbaññuvisayeca ṭhāne pāḷiyo saṃsanditvā balavatiyā pāḷiyuttiyāeva ṭhātabbatoti. Yasmāca rūpadhammā nāma dandhapavattino honti. Arūpadhammā lahupavattino ṭhitikkhaṇoca tesaṃ visuṃ gaṇanūpago natthi. Tasmā aññoyeva rūpa dhammānaṃ khaṇapabandho. Añño arūpadhammānaṃ. Tattha sabbepi rūpadhammā ekacittakkhaṇaparimāṇena attano uppādakkhaṇena yuttā khaṇe khaṇe nirantarameva uppajjanti. Paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya sahuppannattāca pana dvinnaṃ tesaṃ uppādādivā nirodhantovā yāvajīvaṃpisaheva hotītipi tassa adhippāyoti. Yamaka pāḷiyo pana nānātthā, nānābyañjanā, gambhīroca satthu adhippāyo. Tasmā suṭṭhu vicāretvā sallakkhetabbo. Na pana dhammatā esā yamakassa. Yadidaṃ yathālābhayojanāti katvā attano adhippāye ṭhatvā diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhaṃ yamakapāṭhaṃ yathālābhayo janāyaeva sakkā yojetunti. Rūpavirāgabhāvanāvisesabhūtaṃ arūpakusalaṃ tasmiṃ loke rūpasahitaṃ paṭisandhiṃ najaneti. Suddhaarūpameva janeti. Tasmā rūpasantatisīsassa sabbaso abhāvā tatruppannāni sabbāni chacattālīsacittāni rūpaṃ janetuṃ na na sakkonti. Arūpavipākā pana tattheva niyamuppannāti arūpapākasseva gahaṇaṃ kataṃ, teneva aṭṭhakathāyaṃ, aññānipi bahūni āruppe uppannāni anokāsatthā rūpaṃ nasamuṭṭhāpentīti vuttaṃ tattha anokāsatānāma ādito paṭṭhāya uppannassa rūpasantatisīsassa abhāvo eva daṭṭhabboti.

Here, by ‘non-percipient beings,’ only the material life faculty is meant. And if that were to arise even at the dissolution-moment of consciousness, then in the first part of the answer it would be said, ‘For non-percipient beings… at the dissolution-moment of consciousness in the course of existence… the life faculty is not arising’; and in the latter part, it would be said just, ‘For all who are passing away.’ But if it is said that in the latter part this is stated with reference to the formless life faculty, that is not so. For, since there is no alternative Yamaka reading for understanding it thus, and since in a matter that is the domain of the Omniscient One one must rely on the stronger scriptural reasoning after comparing the Pāḷi texts, this interpretation is untenable. And because material phenomena are slow in their process while immaterial phenomena are swift, and their moment of duration is not subject to separate reckoning, therefore the sequence of moments for material phenomena is one thing, and for immaterial phenomena, another. There, all material phenomena, endowed with their own arising-moment, arise continuously moment by moment for the duration of a single mind-moment. And since they arise together from rebirth-linking onwards, the arising, etc., up to the cessation of both occurs together for as long as life lasts—this too is its intention. The Yamaka passages, however, have various meanings and various expressions, and the Teacher’s intention is profound. Therefore, it should be carefully investigated and discerned. But it is not the nature of the Yamaka that one can connect any Yamaka passage one sees just as one finds it, standing on one's own opinion, having adopted the principle of ‘application as available.’ The formless wholesome consciousness, which is a special cultivation of dispassion towards material form, does not generate a rebirth-linking accompanied by material form in that world; it generates only a pure formless rebirth. Therefore, due to the complete absence of the head of the material continuity, all forty-six types of consciousness that arise there are by no means able to generate material form. But the formless resultant consciousness is invariably generated there, so only the formless resultant is taken. For that reason it is said in the commentary: ‘Many other states that arise in the formless realm do not produce material form because they are without a location (anokāsa).’ There, ‘being without a location’ should be seen as precisely the absence, from the very beginning, of the arisen head of the material continuity.

[189] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[189] But in the Vibhāvinī:

“Rūpavirāgabhāvanānibbattattā [M 0.0298] hetuno tabbidhuratāyā”tipi kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ.

The reason has also been stated as: “Because it is produced by the cultivation of dispassion for form as its cause, it is destitute of that capacity to produce form.” That is not the reason.

Rūpārūpavirāgabhāvanābhūtamagganibbattassa lokuttaravipākassa rūpokāse sati rūpajanakatādassanatoti. Jhānaṅgavirahena aṅgadubbalānipi rūpaṃ na janentīti dvipañcaviññāṇagahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Itarā nipi pana pannarasakāmarūpa paṭisandhicittāni khīṇāsavānaṃ parinibbānacuti cittanti imāni cittāni rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpentiyeva. Evaṃsantepi tāni sabbānipi bhavaṅgakāle akhīṇāsavānañca cutikāle samuṭṭhāpentīti tesaṃ idha agahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Because it is seen that the supramundane resultant—produced by the path, which is the cultivation of dispassion for form and the formless—has the capacity to generate form when a material basis exists. The two sets of fivefold consciousness are included because, being weak in their factors due to the absence of jhāna factors, they do not generate form. Moreover, these other consciousnesses—the fifteen sense-sphere and form-sphere rebirth-linking consciousnesses, and the final passing-away consciousness of the arahants—do not produce form at all. Even so, since all of them produce form during the life-continuum and at the time of death for those who are not arahants, it should be understood why they are not included here.

[190] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[190] But in the Vibhāvinī:

Paṭisandhicittaṃ pana cuticittañca ekūnavīsati bhavaṅgasseva antogadhattā cittantaraṃ na hotīti na tassa vajjanaṃ kata”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha ekūnavīsati bhavaṅgassevāti na vattabbaṃ.

It is said: “But since the rebirth-linking consciousness and the death consciousness are included within the nineteen types of life-continuum consciousness, they are not other consciousnesses, and thus they are not excluded separately.” Therein, the phrase “within the nineteen types of life-continuum” should not be said.

Arūpavipākassa sarūpato vajjitattāti. Kasmā pana yathā vuttāni pannarasa paṭisandhicittāni paṭisandhikkhaṇe rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpentīti, paridubbalattā. Cittañhināma uppādakkhaṇeeva paripuṇṇaṃ paccayaṃ labhitvā balavaṃ hoti. Rūpañca ṭhitikkhaṇeva.

Because the formless resultant is excluded by its very nature. But why do the fifteen aforementioned rebirth-linking consciousnesses not produce form at the moment of rebirth-linking? Because of their extreme weakness. For consciousness becomes strong only at the arising-moment, having obtained its complete conditions, but material form only at the duration-moment.

Tasmā attano balavantakkhaṇe uppajjamānabhāvena dubbalaṃ vatthuṃ nissāya uppannattā sayaṃpi paridubbalaṃ hotīti sabbānipi tāni tadā rūpaṃ nasamuṭṭhā pentīti. Etthaca keci anantarāsevanādipaccayā cittassa uppādakkhaṇeeva pharanti. Rūpassa pana upatthambhakabhūtā utuāhārā pacchājātapaccayadhammāca ṭhitikkhaṇeevapharantīti tesaṃ yathākkamaṃ uppādakkhaṇe ṭhitikkhaṇeca paripuṇṇapaccayalābho veditabbo.

Therefore, because it arises depending on a weak physical basis and does not arise at its own moment of strength, it is itself very weak; thus at that time none of those consciousnesses produce material form. And here, some say that conditions such as contiguity and repetition pervade consciousness only at the arising-moment. But the supporting temperature and nutriment of material form, and the phenomena that are postnascence condition, pervade it only at the duration-moment. Thus, the acquisition of complete conditions for them should be understood to be at the arising-moment and the duration-moment respectively.

[191] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[191] But in the Vibhāvinī:

“Pacchājāta paccayarahitaṃ pana āhārādīhica anupatthaddhaṃ dubbalavatthuṃ nissāya pavattattā attanoca āgantukatāya kammajarūpehica cittasamuṭṭhānarūpānaṃ ṭhānaṃ gahetvā ṭhitattā”ti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha pacchājāta paccaya rahitanti idaṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

The reason has been stated as: “Because it occurs relying on a weak physical basis that is unsupported by nutriment, etc., and devoid of the postnascence condition; because of its own adventitious nature; and because kamma-generated matter has taken the place of mind-generated matter.” Therein, this phrase “devoid of the postnascence condition” should be investigated.

Paṭisandhicittassa [M 0.0299] ṭhitikkhaṇe pacchājāta paccaya rahitassa piutussa rūpajanakabhāvassa vakkhamānattā. Na hi attanā avijjamānaṃ pacchimacittaṃ purimacittakkhaṇe ṭhitassa kassaci rūpassa pacchājāta paccayo hoti. Atthi paccayekadesattā tassa paccayassāti. Khīṇāsavānaṃ cuticittaṃ pana pakatiyāva vūpasantavaṭṭamūle santāne pavattattā santataraṃ hoti. Puna āyusaṅkhārānaṃ parikkhayena dubbalatare pariyantagate ca vatthumhi nissitattā dubbalatarañca hotīti taṃ rūpaṃ nasamuṭṭhāpetīti, ācariyānandatthero pana sabbasattānaṃpi cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ nasamuṭṭhāpetīti icchati. Yathāha-khīṇāsavānaṃ cuticittanti visesetvā vuttaṃ.

Because it will be explained that temperature, though devoid of the postnascence condition, is able to generate matter at the duration-moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness. For a later consciousness, not yet existing, is not a postnascence condition for any material phenomenon existing at the moment of a prior consciousness. The condition exists because it is a part of the conditionality. The death consciousness of the arahants, however, is more tranquil because it occurs in a continuity where the root of the round of existence has been pacified. Further, it is even weaker because the life-formations are exhausted and it depends on a physical basis that has become weaker and is nearing its end; thus it does not produce material form. The Elder Ācariya Ānanda, however, holds that the death consciousness of all beings does not produce material form. As he says: “The phrase ‘the death-consciousness of the arahants’ is stated with a distinction.”

Kāmāvacarānaṃ pacchimacittassa uppādakkhaṇe yassa cittassa anantarā kāmāvacarānaṃ pacchimacittaṃ uppajjissati. Rūpāvacare arūpāvacare pacchimabhavikānaṃ yeca rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ upapajjitvā parinibbāyissanti, tesaṃ, cavantānaṃ tesaṃ vacī saṅkhāro nirujjhissati, noca tesaṃ kāyasaṅkhāro nirujjhatīti –

At the arising-moment of the final consciousness of a sense-sphere being—that is, the consciousness immediately after which the final consciousness of a sense-sphere being will arise. “For those in the form sphere and the formless sphere who are in their last existence, and for those who will attain final Nibbāna after being reborn in the form sphere or the formless sphere—for them, as they are passing away, their verbal formation will cease, but their bodily formation does not cease.”

Pana vacanato aññesaṃpi cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ nasamuṭṭhāpetīti viññāyati. Na hi rūpasamuṭṭhāpaka cittassa gabbhagamanādi vinibaddhābhāve kāyasaṅkhārāsamuṭṭhāpanaṃ atthi, na ca yuttaṃ cutoca cittasamuṭṭhānañcassa pavattatīti. Nāpi cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti pāḷi atthīti.

From this statement, it is understood that the death consciousness of others too does not produce material form. For a consciousness that produces material form does not fail to produce bodily formation when it is not connected with such events as entering a womb. And it is not proper that death and the mind-generated form produced by it should occur together. Nor is there any Pāli text stating that death consciousness produces material form.

Anuṭīkāyaṃ pana

But in the subcommentary:

Tasmiṃ pāṭhe tesaṃ cavantānaṃ noca kāyasaṅkhāro nirujjhatīti vacanaṃ na kevalaṃ cuticittasseva rūpasamuṭṭhāpanābhāvaṃ sādheti, athakho tato purimānaṃ sabbesaṃ maraṇāsanna cittānaṃ rūpasamuṭṭhāpanābhāvaṃpi sādhetiyevāti dīpeti. Cuti cittasmiṃhi kāyasaṅkhārassa nirodhe paṭisiddhe tato pubbe yāva sattarasamacittā etthantare tassa uppādopi paṭisiddhoeva hotīti. Sabbañcetaṃ vicāretabbaṃ.

In that passage, the statement, “for those who are passing away the bodily formation does not cease,” not only establishes the non-production of matter by the death-consciousness itself, but it also demonstrates the non-production of matter by all the consciousnesses close to death that precede it. For when the cessation of the bodily formation at the death-consciousness is denied, its arising is also denied in the preceding interval up to the seventeenth consciousness-moment. All this should be investigated.

Kāyasaṅkhāroti [M 0.0300] hi assāsapassāso vuccati. Soca suṭṭhu oḷāriko rūpadhammoti nacuticitte tannirodhābhāva vacanena itarāni sukhumānipi rūpāni cuticittaṃ najanetīti sakkā vattuṃ.

For 'bodily formation' is said to be the in-and-out-breaths. And since that is a very gross material phenomenon, it is not possible to say, on the basis of the statement that it does not cease at the death-consciousness, that the death-consciousness does not generate other, subtle material phenomena.

[192] Yañca tattha

[192] And as to what was said there:

Na hi rūpasamuṭṭhāpakacittassa gabbhagamanādi vinibaddhābhāve kāyasaṅkhārāsamuṭṭhāpanaṃ atthīti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yujjati.

It was said: 'For a consciousness that produces material form does not fail to produce bodily formation when it is not connected with entering a womb and so on.' That too is not tenable.

Tānieva hi gabbhagamanādīni imassatthassa sādhakāni bhavituṃ arahanti oḷārikassa kāyasaṅkhārassa asamuṭṭhāpakaṃpi cittaṃ itaraṃ sukhumarūpaṃ pana samuṭṭhāpetiyevāti.

For these very things—entering a womb and so on—are fit to prove this point: that even a consciousness that does not produce the gross bodily formation does indeed produce other, subtle matter.

[193] Yaṃpi tattha

[193] And as to what was also said there:

Na ca yuttaṃ cutoca cittasamuṭṭhānañcassa pavattatīti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi akāraṇaṃ.

It was said: 'And it is not right that both passing away and its mind-originated matter occur.' That too is groundless.

Na hi cutito paraṃ katipayakhaṇamattaṃ cittajarūpapavattiyā koci virodho atthīti.

For there is no contradiction in the occurrence of mind-originated matter for just a few moments after passing away.

Yañca tattha

And as to what was said there:

Nāpi cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti pāḷi atthīti vuttaṃ. Tatthapi cuticittaṃ rūpaṃ nasamuṭṭhāpetītipi natthi, aññatra kāyasaṅkhārāti na na sakkā vattunti.

It was said: 'Nor is there a Pāli text that says, “The death-consciousness produces matter.”' Even so, there is also no text that says, 'The death-consciousness does not produce matter,' and it is not impossible to say, 'except for the bodily formation.'

Evaṃ pana yuttaṃ siyā, yathā rūpadhammā ādito paṭisandhikāle ekacittakkhaṇamatte paccayaparittatāyavā attano dandhavutti tāyavā dubbalā honti, tathā pariyosānepi maraṇakāle parikkhīyamānapaccayatāyavā nirodhāsannatāyavā paridubbalāeva hontīti sakkā vattuṃ. Tasmā vatthussa ādiantanissitāni paṭisandhicuticittāni samadubbalānieva hontīti sakkā viññātunti.

However, it would be proper to say this: Just as material phenomena at the beginning, at the time of rebirth-linking, in a single consciousness-moment, are weak either because of the paucity of their conditions or because of their own sluggish nature, so too at the end, at the time of death, they are very weak either because their conditions are being exhausted or because of their proximity to cessation. Therefore, it can be understood that the rebirth-linking and death consciousnesses, which depend on the physical basis at the beginning and at the end, are indeed equally weak.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

In the Vibhāvanī, however:

Abhidhammatthavikāsaniyañca pāḷivirodhaṃ maññamāno kiñcimattampi avicāretvā ṭīkāsu vuttanayameva suṭṭhu vikāsayitvā gatoti.

The author of the Abhidhammatthavikāsinī, thinking there was a contradiction with the Pāli, proceeded without any investigation, having thoroughly elaborated only the method stated in the subcommentaries.

Pathamabhavaṅgamupādāyāti [M 0.0301] pathama bhavaṅgacittassa uppādakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya. Jāyantamevāti uppādakkhaṇe uppādakkhaṇe uppajja mānameva, na tiṭṭhantaṃ. Naca bhijjamānanti attho. Kāraṇaṃ vuttameva. Tatthāti tasmiṃ pañcasattatividhe citte. Appanājavananti abhiññādvayavajjitaṃ chabbīsatividhaṃ appanājavanacittaṃ. Iriyāpathanti gamanavajjitaṃ tividhaṃpi iriyāpathaṃ.

‘Beginning with the first life-continuum’: this means starting from the arising moment of the first life-continuum consciousness. ‘Just as it is arising’: this means arising at each and every arising moment, not while it is static and not while it is ceasing; this is the meaning. The reason has already been stated. ‘Therein’: this refers to that seventy-fivefold consciousness. ‘Absorption javana’: this means the twenty-six kinds of absorption javana consciousness, excluding the two higher knowledges. ‘Posture’: this means the three kinds of posture, excluding walking.

[194] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[194] In the Vibhāvanī, however:

“Gamanādī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

It is said, 'walking, etc.' That is not correct.

Na hi aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ calanaphandanamattaṃpi viññattiyā vinā sijjhati. Kuto gamanaṃ. Naca yathāvuttaṃ appanājavanaṃ viññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpetuṃ sakkotīti. Pi saddena taṃ nakevalaṃ rūpasamuṭṭhāpakamattaṃti dasseti. Sannāmetīti sandhāreti ayamevavā pāṭho siyā, vakkhamānehi cittehi abhisaṅkhataṃ yathāpavattaṃ iriyāpathaṃ apatamānaṃ acalamānaṃ dhāreti upatthambhetīti attho. Upatthambhanañcettha yathāpavattassa iriyāpathassa rakkhanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Naukkhipitvā viya abhinīharaṇaṃ. Itarathā thambhanaviññattiyā pasaṅgo siyāti. Etthaca yathānisinnassavā ṭhitassavā bhavaṅga citte abbokiṇṇe pavattamāne aṅgāni osīdanti patanti. Na tathā imasmiṃ chabbīsatividhe jāgaraṇacitte vakkhamānesucadvattiṃsa vidhesu jāgaraṇacittesupavattamānesu. Tesu pana pavattamānesu aṅgāni upatthaddhāni honti. Na osīdanti na patanti. Pubbe yathā thapitāneva pavattantīti veditabbaṃ.

For not even the mere moving and trembling of the major and minor limbs is accomplished without intimation; how much less so walking. Nor, as was stated, is the absorption javana able to produce intimation. By the word ‘pi’ (also), it shows that this is not merely a producer of matter. ‘Sannāmeti’ means ‘sustains’ (sandhāreti)—or this might be the reading. The meaning is that it holds or supports the existing posture, which was generated by the consciousnesses to be mentioned, so that it does not collapse or waver. And here, ‘supporting’ should be seen as merely the preservation of the existing posture, not as propelling it forward as if lifting it up. Otherwise, there would be the consequence of an intimation of stiffening. And here, when the life-continuum consciousness occurs uninterruptedly for one who is sitting or standing, the limbs sink and collapse. It is not so when these twenty-six kinds of waking consciousness, or the thirty-two kinds of waking consciousness to be mentioned, are occurring. But when these are occurring, the limbs are supported; they do not sink, they do not collapse. It should be understood that they continue just as they were previously established.

[195] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[195] In the Vibhāvanī, however:

“Na eva metesu dvattiṃsavidhesu vakkhamānesu ca chabbīsati yā jāgaraṇacittesu pavattamānesū”ti pāṭho.

The reading is: 'Not so when these thirty-two kinds to be mentioned and the twenty-six kinds of waking consciousness are occurring.'

Na evametesu chabbīsatiyā jāgaraṇacittesu vakkhamāne suca dvattiṃsa vidhesu pavattamānesūti pana pāṭho yutto. Voṭṭhabbananti manodvāre āvajjanamāha. Na hi pañcadvārikāni javana cittānipi [M 0.0302] viññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpenti. Iriyāpathupatthambhana mattaṃ vā pisaddena gahithaṃ sandhāya voṭṭhabbanādīni pañcadvārikānipi gahitāniti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etthaca iriyāpathonāma gamanādinā tena tena avatthāvisesena pavattā rūpadhammāeva. Evaṃ santepi kiñcicittaṃ rūpa sāmaññameva janeti na tatoparaṃ. Kiñci aññacittassa vasena yathāpavattaṃ iriyāpathaṃ rakkhituṃeva sakkoti, na appavattaṃ iriyāpathaṃ pavattetuṃ. Kiñci viññattiṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā appavattañca iriyāpathaṃ pavattetuṃ sakkoti. Aññānica kāyika vācasika vikārāni janetuṃ sakkoti. Yānica cittāni uttarakiccaṃ janetuṃ sakkonti. Tāni heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimaṃ kiccaṃ janetuṃ sakkontiyevāti dassanatthaṃ ayaṃ vibhāgo katoti veditabbo.

However, the reading, ‘Not so when these twenty-six kinds of waking consciousness and the thirty-two kinds to be mentioned are occurring,’ is the correct one. ‘Determining’ refers to adverting at the mind-door. For not even the javana consciousnesses of the five doors produce intimation. Or, it should be understood that determining and so on of the five doors are also included with reference to the fact that the mere supporting of posture is included by the word ‘pi.’ And here, ‘posture’ is just the material phenomena that occur through this or that particular state, such as walking. This being so, some consciousness generates only matter in general and nothing further. Some consciousness, by the power of another consciousness, is able only to preserve an existing posture, not to initiate a posture that has not yet occurred. Some consciousness, by producing intimation, is able to initiate a posture that has not yet occurred. And others are able to produce bodily and verbal modifications. It should be understood that this classification has been made to show that those consciousnesses that are able to perform a higher function are indeed able to perform each lower function.

[196] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[196] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Yaṃpana cittaṃ viññattijanakaṃ, taṃ ekaṃsato iriyāpathu patthambhakaṃ. Iriyā pathassa viññattiyā saha avinābhāvato”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

It was said: 'Whatever consciousness produces intimation, that is definitely a supporter of posture, because posture is inseparable from intimation.' That is not correct.

Idha hi iriyāpathupatthambhanaṃnāma viññattirahitamevā dhippetaṃ, na viññattisahitaṃ. Itarathā appanājavanānaṃpi viññattijanakatā āpajjeyyāti. Somanassajavanāni terasāti hasituppādena saddhiṃ lobhamūlato mahā kusalato mahā kriyato ca cattāricattārīti terasa somanassajavanāni. Tesupana kusalā kusalato aṭṭhaputhujjanānaṃ. Diṭṭhivippayuttā kusalakusalato chasekkhānaṃ. Kriyato pañcakhīṇāsavānanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbaṃ kāyavacīmanokammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattanti vacanato vicāraṇakiccarahito hasituppādo sabbaññubuddhānaṃ nasambhavatīti evaṃ pavatto vādo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭikkhittoyeva. Tasmiṃvāde hi sati itaresaṃpi ahetukacittānaṃ ñāṇavippayuttamahā kriyajavanānañca buddhānaṃ asambhavo āpajjati. Tasmā tesaṃ hasituppādacittena pavattassa sitakammassa pubbāparapavattānaṃ ñāṇānaṃ vasena ñāṇapubbaṅgamatā ñāṇānuparivattatā ca veditabbāti. Sītuṇhotu [M 0.0303] samaññātāti idaṃ sītaṃ idaṃ uṇhanti evaṃ sabba lokiyamahājanehi suṭṭhu paricchinditvā ñātā. Ṭhitippattāvāti attano ṭhitibhāvaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇaṃvā pattāeva. Na pana cittamiva jāyanta mattāti attho. Kāraṇaṃ vuttameva.

For here, by ‘supporting of posture’ is meant that which is devoid of intimation, not that which is accompanied by intimation. Otherwise, it would follow that even absorption javanas produce intimation. There are thirteen javanas accompanied by joy: the smile-producing consciousness, along with four rooted in greed, four great wholesome, and four great functional. Among these, it should be understood that eight (wholesome and unwholesome) belong to worldlings; six (the wholesome, and the unwholesome dissociated from wrong view) belong to trainees; and five (functional) belong to arahants. Based on the scriptural passage, ‘All bodily, verbal, and mental action is preceded by knowledge and revolves around knowledge,’ the argument that the smile-producing consciousness, being devoid of the function of examination, does not occur in Omniscient Buddhas, has been refuted in the commentary. For if that argument were accepted, it would follow that other rootless consciousnesses and the great functional javanas dissociated from knowledge would not occur in the Buddhas. Therefore, it should be understood that for them, the smiling action that occurs through their smile-producing consciousness has its precedence by knowledge and its revolving around knowledge by way of the knowledges that precede and follow it. ‘Well-known as cold and hot’: this means known by all worldly people, having been well-distinguished as ‘this is cold, this is hot.’ ‘Having reached the static phase’: this means having reached its own state of stability or its static moment, and not, like consciousness, just as it is arising. This is the meaning. The reason has already been stated.

[197] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[197] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Pacchājātādipaccayupatthambhalābhena ṭhitikkhaṇeeva utuojānaṃ balavabhāvoti vuttaṃ tejodhātu ṭhitippattātiādi”. Tattha pacchājātapaccayavacanaṃ heṭṭhā vicāritameva.

It was said: 'Because of gaining the support of conditions such as postnascence, it is at the static moment itself that temperature and nutriment become strong,' and 'The heat element has reached the static phase,' and so on. Therein, the statement about the postnascence condition has already been discussed above.

Apica, yadi utuno balavabhāvo rūpuppādanañca pacchājātapaccayāyattaṃ siyā. Evaṃ sati so paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeyya, tadā pacchājātapaccayasseva abhāvato. Vakkhatica ṭhitikālamupādāya utusamuṭṭhānāti. Etthaca ṭhitikālanti paṭisandhicittassa ṭhītikālo vuttoti. Tasmā pacchājātapaccayavacanaṃ vicāretvā sampaṭicchitabbanti. Ojāsaṅkhāto āhāroti kammasamuṭṭhānādivasena catubbidho ajjhattasantāna gatoasitapītakhāyitasāyitavasena catubbidho, bahiddhasantā nagatoca ojāsaṅkhāto duvidhāhāro. Tadubhayāpica saṃsagga vasena laddhupatthambhā evarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpentīti vuttaṃ ajjhoharaṇa kāleti. Etthaca bahiddhāsambhūtena utunā saha ajjhatta sambhūtānaṃ catusamuṭṭhānānaṃ utuojānaṃ viya bahiddhāsambhūtāya ojāyapi ajjhattaṃ rūpasamuṭṭhānaṃ sabbaaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, if the strong nature of temperature and the production of material form were dependent on the post-nascence condition, then, in that case, it would not produce material form at the moment of the subsistence of the rebirth-linking consciousness, because the post-nascence condition would be absent then. And it will be said: 'Temperature-originated (material form) arises dependent on the moment of subsistence'. And here, 'moment of subsistence' is said to be the moment of subsistence of the rebirth-linking consciousness. Therefore, the statement about the post-nascence condition should be considered and accepted. Nutriment, called 'ojā', is twofold: that which is internal, existing within one's own continuity and of four kinds by way of its origin (kamma, etc.); and that which is external, of four kinds by way of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. Both of these, through their interaction, having gained support, produce material form in this way—this is said 'at the time of ingestion'. And here, just as external temperature, along with the internal temperature and nutriment arising from the four origins, produces material form, so too is it stated in all commentaries that external nutriment also produces internal material form.

Yathāha-majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ

As it is said in the Majjhima Commentary:

Kabaḷīkārāhāro tāva mukhe thapitamatto eva aṭṭharūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti. Dantavicuṇṇitaṃ pana ajjhoharīyamānaṃ ekekaṃ sitthaṃ aṭṭha aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpetīti.

First, a lump of physical nutriment, merely placed in the mouth, produces eight types of material form. However, as it is ground by the teeth and swallowed, each particle produces eight types of material form.

Ācariyadhammapālattherena pana yadi bahiddhasambhūtā ojā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeyya, evaṃ sati yathā bahiddhasambhūto utu ajjhattañca bahiddhāca rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā sā bahiddhāpi rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeyya. Na pana samuṭṭhāpeti. Tasmā sā ajjhattaṃ patvāpi rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhā petiyeva. [M 0.0304] Ekantena pana ajjhattaojāeva samuṭṭhāpeti. Sā pana tassā upatthambhanapaccayoeva hotīti adhippāyena mukhe thapitamattoeva. Na saṅkhādito. Tattakenapi abbhantarassa paccayo hotiyeva, kenāha aṭṭha aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpetīti majjhimaṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana upādinnakā utu ojānāma suṭṭhu paṇītarūpā honti, tasmā bahiddhā ojāpi ajjhattaṃ patvā tena utunā suṭṭhu sediyamānā tāyaca ojāya suṭṭhu upatthambhīya mānā sarīre medasinehupacayavasena rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetiyevāti yuttaṃ. Ajjhoharaṇakāleti idañca suṭṭhu balavabhāvappatta kālaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Visuddhimagge pana mātarā paribhuttāhāropi dārakassa sararaṃ pharitvā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Sarīre makkhitāhā ropi rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti vuttaṃ. Mukhe thapitamattoeva aṭṭharūpāni samuṭṭhāpetītica pubbe vuttanti. Ṭhāna pattovāti attano ṭhitikkhaṇaṃ pattoeva. Etthaca catūsu samuṭṭhānesu utueva mahanto mahāthāmo mahāvipphāroca hoti. So hi sakalassapi okāsalokassa bahiddhā saṅkhāralokassaca samuṭṭhā pako vināsako ca hoti. Sattalokassaca soeva mahanto ajjhattasambhārabhūto hoti. Itarāni pana tīṇi tassa parivāramattānieva sampajjantīti.

However, by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, it is said: 'If external nutriment were to produce material form, then, just as external temperature produces material form both internally and externally, so too should that external nutriment produce material form externally. But it does not produce it. Therefore, even when it enters internally, it does not produce material form at all. Only internal nutriment produces it without exception. However, that external nutriment serves merely as a supporting condition for it—this is the intention. It is merely placed in the mouth, not yet chewed and swallowed. Even by that much, it becomes a condition for the internal nutriment, for which reason it is said in the Majjhima Sub-commentary that it produces eight material phenomena. However, since appropriated temperature and nutriment are exceedingly refined material forms, it is therefore fitting that even external nutriment, upon entering internally, being thoroughly matured by that temperature and well supported by that internal nutriment, certainly produces material form in the body through the accumulation of fat and bodily fluids. And this phrase 'at the time of ingestion' is said with reference to the time when it has attained a sufficiently strong state. However, in the Visuddhimagga, it is said that food consumed by the mother, having permeated the child’s body, produces material form, and that food smeared on the body also produces material form. And it was stated previously that merely placing it in the mouth produces eight material phenomena. 'Having reached its state' means 'having reached its own moment of subsistence'. And here, among the four origins, temperature alone is the most significant, the most powerful, and the most extensive. For it is the producer and destroyer of the entire world of space externally and also of the world of formations. And for the world of beings, it alone is the great internal constituent. The other three, however, become merely its retinue.

Hadaya indriya rūpāni kammajāneva, na cittajādini. Yadievaṃ vippasannāni kho te āvuso sāriputta indriyāni. Katarena tvaṃ etarahi vihārena viharasīti kasmā vuttanti. Indriyasambhārānaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ samāpatti cittasamuṭṭhitānaṃ visadavippasannatāvasena upacari tattāti. Tathā hi ekābaddhapavattāni catujarūpāni ekasmiṃ vippasanne sabbāni vippasannāneva honti. Milāteca milātānevāti. Utucittāhārā pana tesaṃ navannaṃ upatthambhanapaccayā hontīti veditabbaṃ. Ettha ca uppalapadumāni viya kammajarūpāni daṭṭhabbāni. Tesaṃ bījaṃ viya kammaṃ. Kaddamodakāni viya utuāhārādīni. Viññatti dvayaṃ cittajameva. Tathā hi taṃ cittasahabhū cittānuparivattidhammesu bhagavatā niddiṭṭhanti. Saddocittotujoti kasmā vuttaṃ. Nanunidhikaṇḍasutte [M 0.0305] suvaṇṇatā susaratā susaṇṭhānaṃ surūpatātiādinā tādisena kammavisesena saddasampattināma vuttāti. Saccaṃ, kammavisesena pana yathā suvisado sumadhuro saddo pavattati, tathā ṭhānakaraṇagatānaṃ upādinnakasarīrānaṃ susaṇṭhitatā vāta semhādīhi apalibuddhatāca hoti. Tasmā tammūlikāsaddasampatti kammaphalesu pakkhipitvā susaratāti vuttā. Na ekantena saddassa kammajanitattāti veditabbā.

The heart-base and the material qualities of the faculties are born of kamma alone, not of mind and so on. Why then was it said: 'Indeed, friend Sāriputta, your faculties are very clear. By what dwelling do you now dwell?'? This was stated metaphorically on account of the distinct clarity of the complexion of the constituents of the faculties, which are produced by mind. For when material phenomena born of the four causes proceed bound together as one, if one is clear, all become clear; and when one withers, they all wither. But it should be understood that temperature, mind, and nutriment are supporting conditions for these nine. Here, kamma-born material qualities should be seen like lotuses and water lilies. Their seed is like kamma, while mud and water are like temperature, nutriment, and so on. The two kinds of intimation are born of mind alone, for they are taught by the Blessed One as phenomena that co-arise with and follow the mind. Why was it said, 'Sound is born of mind and temperature'? Is it not said in the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta that excellence of sound—such as a golden voice, melodiousness, good form, and beauty—is due to a special kind of kamma? True, but by a special kind of kamma, a sound arises that is very clear and sweet, and similarly, there is the well-formedness of the appropriated body's vocal organs and their freedom from obstruction by wind, phlegm, and so on. Therefore, the excellence of sound rooted in this is included among the fruits of kamma and called 'melodiousness.' But it should be understood that sound is not exclusively born of kamma.

Lahutādittayaṃ utucittāhārehi sambhotīti kasmā vuttaṃ. Nanu appābādhasaṃvattanikā esā māṇava paṭipadā, yadidaṃ avihiṃsāti vuttaṃ. Appābādha paccayasamuṭṭhitañca etaṃ rūpattayaṃ. Tathā hi dandhattādi kara dhātukkhota paṭipakkhapaccaya samuṭṭhānatā etassa vuttāti. Vuccate, kammajarūpānināma udake pakkhittāni satapākatelāni viya pakatiyāva kammānurūpaṃ lahu mudu kammañña bhūtāni honti. Tasmā tesaṃ visuṃ lahutādi vikāronāma natthi. Yato tesaṃ ekasmiṃbhave ekāaddhā paccuppannatāva labbhatīti. Evañca katvā yamakesupi tesaṃ kālabhedo paṭisandhivutiparicchinnena addhā paccuppanneneva gahitoti. Yasmā pana cittaṃnāma nānānīvaraṇabhedavasenavā sukha dukkha pīti passaddhi saddhā paññādi vasenavā nānā khaṇesu nānā avatthā yuttaṃ hoti. Tathā utuāhārāca sappāyā sappāyabhedavasena. Tasmā tehi tīhi samuṭṭhita rūpānieva nānākhaṇesu garukalahukādi vasena nānāvikārayuttāni honti. Yato tesaṃ santati samaya vasena kālabhedo labbhati. Evañca katvā yamakesupi akammajānaṃ pavattikāle khaṇasantativasenapi kālabhedo gahitoti. Nanu kammavipākajā ābādhāti vuttaṃ. Satica kamma samuṭṭhāne ābādharūpe tatovuṭṭhānabhūto kammajo lahutādi guṇopi visuṃ labbhamāno siyāti. Na. Yesañhi vasena imasmiṃ sarīre kammavipākajānāma ābādhā uppajjanti. Tāni upapīḷakupa ghātakakammānipi gatikālapayoga vipattiyo labhamānāni eva sarīraṭṭhakā pathavādayo vātapittādayoca utusamuṭṭhānā dhātuyo [M 0.0306] khobhetvā nānābādhe uppādenti. Utusamuṭṭhānāsu pana khubbhitāsu itarāni tadanugatikāni eva honti. Teneva hi sītenapi ruppati, uṇhenapi ruppati, jigacchāyapi ruppati, vipāsāyapi ruppatītiādinā utupadhānova rūpadhammānaṃ ruppanapaccayo vuttoti. Tasmā kevalaṃ kammasamuṭṭhāno ābādhonāma natthi. Yato yathāvutto kammajo lahutādiguṇonāma visuṃ labbhamāno siyāti.

Why is it said that the triad of lightness, etc., arises from temperature, mind, and nutriment? Is it not said: 'Young man, this is the practice that leads to freedom from affliction, namely, non-harming'? And this triad of material qualities arises from conditions that bring freedom from affliction. For it is said that its production is by conditions that are the opposite of the disturbance of the elements which causes sluggishness, etc. It is said: Kamma-born material qualities, like oil refined a hundred times thrown into water, are naturally light, soft, and workable in accordance with their kamma. Therefore, for them, there is no separate alteration called lightness, etc., since, in one existence, only one period of presence is obtained for them. Thus, even in the Yamaka, their division of time is understood only by the present period defined by rebirth-linking and occurrence. But because the mind, due to the diversity of hindrances or due to pleasure, pain, joy, tranquility, faith, wisdom, etc., is associated with various states at various moments—and likewise, temperature and nutriment, due to differences in suitability and unsuitability—therefore, the material qualities produced by these three are associated with various alterations such as heaviness and lightness at different moments. This is because for them a division of time is obtained by way of the duration of their continuity. Thus, even in the Yamaka, for non-kamma-born phenomena, the division of time is understood by way of the continuity of moments during their occurrence. But is it not said that afflictions are the result of kamma? And if there are afflictive material qualities originated by kamma, might there not also be a distinctly obtainable kamma-born quality of lightness, etc., that arises from them? No. For it is by those very things that afflictions which are the result of kamma arise in this body. Those oppressive and destructive kammas, upon obtaining misfortunes of destiny, time, and means, disturb the earth element, etc., which reside in the body, and the temperature-originated elements like wind, bile, and phlegm, giving rise to various afflictions. But when the temperature-originated elements are disturbed, the others simply follow them. For this reason it is said: 'One is afflicted by cold, one is afflicted by heat, one is afflicted by hunger, one is afflicted by thirst,' and so on, showing that temperature is the dominant condition for the affliction of material phenomena. Therefore, there is no affliction that is solely kamma-originated, from which it would follow that a distinct kamma-born quality of lightness, etc., as described, could be obtained.

Yasmā pana avihiṃsā kammanibbattā sattā tesaṃ upapīḷakādīnaṃ kammānaṃ suvidūratāyaceva sarīrakoṭṭhāsānaṃ ghanasiniddhasaṇṭhitiyā dukkhobhaniyatāyaca nibbattabhave nirābādhā honti. Tasmā tadatthaṃ sandhāya appābādhasaṃvattanikā esā māṇavapaṭipadā. Yadidaṃ avihiṃsāti vuttaṃ, na pana appābādhanimittassa lahutādittayassa kammasamuṭṭhānatāya. Evañca katvā rūpakaṇḍena kammassakaṭattārūpesu eva etaṃ rūpattayaṃ niddiṭṭhanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rūpakalāpānāma ekasmiṃ paramāṇusmiṃpi bahuvidhā hutvā pavattanti. Tasmā catujarūpa kalāpesu ghanabhāvena pavattamānesu kalāpantarabhūtā ākāsadhātupi dissamānāeva hotīti katvā catujesu tassā gahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Kāmaṃ sabbānipi anipphannarūpāni kenaci paccayena anipphāditāni honti. Tesu pana na tathā lakkhaṇarūpāni. Yathā itarāni cittādi paccaya visesena dissamāna visesāni hontīti vuttaṃ lakkhaṇarūpāni na kutoci jāyantīti. Jāyamānādi rūpānanti jāyamāna jiyyamāna miyyamānānaṃ rūpakalāpānaṃ. Sabhāvattāti jātijarāmaraṇasaṅkhātalakkhaṇasabhāvamattattā. Etthaca rūpakaṇḍe utusamuṭṭhānanti ca āhārasamuṭṭhānanti ca vuttaṃ natthi. Paṭṭhāne eva vuttaṃ.

Because beings produced by the kamma of non-harming are, in their resultant existence, free from affliction—due to their great distance from oppressive kammas, the compact and smooth constitution of their bodily parts, and their endurance of suffering—this path of the young man is, with reference to that, conducive to few afflictions. This is what is called non-harming, but not because the triad of lightness, etc., which are signs of few afflictions, is originated by kamma. And so, it should be understood that in the chapter on form, these three types of form are described as belonging to one’s own kamma. Material clusters occur in many ways even in a single atom. Therefore, when the material clusters born of the four causes occur densely, the space element between the clusters is also visible, and for this reason it is included among those born of the four causes. Granted, all unproduced forms are not produced by any specific cause. Among them, however, the characteristic forms are not like that. Just as other forms have visible distinctions due to specific causes such as mind, it is said that characteristic forms do not arise from any cause. 'Forms that are being born, etc.' refers to the material clusters that are being born, aging, and dying. 'By their own nature' means because they are merely the own-nature of the characteristics designated as birth, aging, and death. Here in the chapter on form, it is not said that they are originated by temperature or by nutriment. It is said only in the Paṭṭhāna.

Ettha siyā, jaratā aniccatā pāḷiyameva na kutoci samuṭṭhānāti vuttā. Tasmā idhapi tāsaṃ nakutoci samuṭṭhānesu gahaṇaṃ yuttaṃ. Upacayasantatiyo pana pāḷiyaṃpi kutoci samuṭṭhānesu vuttā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpi tāhi saddhiṃ visati kammajarūpāni sattarasa cittajarūpāni cuddasa utujarūpāni terasa āhāraja rūpāni [M 0.0307] vuttāni. Tasmā idha tāsaṃ nakutocisamuṭṭhānatā navattabbāti. Vuccate, rūpajanakānaṃ jananabyāpāronāma attanā janitarūpānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe eva pharati. Na-tato paraṃ, tasmā tasmiṃ khaṇe labbhamānā upacayasantatiyoyeva kutoci jātapariyāyaṃ arahanti, na jaratā aniccatāyoti katvā pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathā yaṃca tāsaṃeva kutoci samuṭṭhānesu gahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Apica, pubbe ajātā dhammā paccaye sati jāyanti. Asati na jāyantīti atthi. Jātā pana dhammā paccaye sati jiyyanti, miyyanti. Asati najiyyanti namiyyantīti natthi, tasmā purimānaṃ dvinnaṃ pavatti ekantena paccayāyattā hoti. Pacchimānaṃ dvinnaṃ pavatti pana ekantena paccaya nirapekkhā hotīti iminā pariyāyena tāsaṃ tesu gahaṇaṃ agahaṇañca veditabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana suttapadesu jarāmaraṇaṃ bhikkhave saṅkhataṃ paṭicca samuppannanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ jātiyā satieva tadubhayaṃ paññāyati. Asati na paññāyatīti iminā pariyāyena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Idha pana pubbe vuttanayena itara anipphannarūpāni viya cattāripi etāni cittādipaccayavisesena dissamānavisesāni na hontīti catunnaṃpi na kutoci jātatā vuttā. Evaṃsantepi sārataraṃ pāḷinayaṃ atidhāvanto viya hotīti upacayasanta tīnaṃ kutoci samuṭṭhānesu saṅgahoeva seyyoti. [Rūpasamuṭṭhānanayo]

Here, it might be said, in the Pāḷi itself it is stated that aging and impermanence do not originate from any cause. Therefore, here too their inclusion among things not originated from any cause should be accepted. However, accumulation and continuity are said in the Pāḷi to originate from some cause. In the commentaries, along with these, twenty kamma-originated material phenomena, seventeen mind-originated material phenomena, fourteen temperature-originated material phenomena, and thirteen nutriment-originated material phenomena are mentioned. Therefore, here their non-origination from any cause should not be stated. It is said: The generative activity of the producers of material phenomena extends only to the moment of producing the material phenomena themselves, not beyond. Therefore, at that moment, only the accumulation and continuity obtained are worthy of the term 'arisen from some cause,' but not aging and impermanence. Thus, in the Pāḷi and the commentaries, only their (accumulation and continuity's) inclusion among things originated from some cause is made. Furthermore, previously unarisen phenomena arise when a condition is present; they do not arise when a condition is absent. But for phenomena that have arisen, it is not the case that they fail to decay and die when a condition is absent. Therefore, the occurrence of the former two is entirely dependent on conditions, while the occurrence of the latter two is entirely independent of conditions. In this way, their inclusion and exclusion should be understood. As for the statement in the sutta passages, 'Bhikkhus, aging and death are conditioned and dependently arisen,' it should be understood that this was said in the sense that when birth exists, both are evident; when it does not exist, they are not evident. Here, however, as explained before, just like the other unproduced material phenomena, these four are not seen as distinct due to specific conditions like mind, etc. Thus, for all four, their non-origination from any cause is stated. Even so, since this would be like overstepping the more essential Pāḷi method, it is better just to include accumulation and continuity among things originated from some cause. [The Method of Material Origination]

159. Eko eva jāti saṅkhāto uppādo etesanti ekuppādā. Ekoeva aniccatāsaṅkhāto nirodho etesanti ekanirodhā. Ekasaddo cettha saṅkhāne pavatto. Tasmā tena yāni rūpāni ekāyaeva jātiyā jāyanti. Ekāya eva aniccatāya nirujjhanti. Tesaṃ piṇḍi idha rūpakalāponāmāti dasseti. Ye pana kalāpagata rūpagaṇanāya ekasmiṃ kalāpepi anekāni jātiādīni kappenti, tesaṃ mūlaṭīkāya nasameti. Yuttica natthi. Vuttañhi tattha ekekakalāpa pariyāpannānaṃ rūpānaṃ saheva uppādādipavattito ekekakalāpassa uppādādayo ekekāva hontīti yathā ekekassa kalāpassa jīvitindriyaṃ kalāpā nupālakaṃ [M 0.0308] upādāya rūpanti vuccati. Evaṃ kalāpuppādādi sabhāvā jātiādayo upādāyarūpānicceva vuccanti. Evaṃ vikārapariccheda rūpānica yojetabbānīti. Yadica yo āyatanānaṃ ācayo. So rūpassa upacayotica yo rūpassa upacayo. Sārūpassa santatītica vuttattā tāni jātiādīni lakkhaṇarūpāni visuṃvisuṃ rūpānaṃeva, nakalāpassāti vucceyyuṃ. Catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo rūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ āyūtiādinā vuttattā cakkhādi jīvitādīnipi ekasmiṃ kalāpe anekānieva āpajjeyyuṃ. Tasmā tathā kappanaṃ akatvā ekasmiṃ kalāpe aññāni upādārūpāni viya lakkhaṇarūpānipi ekekānievāti niṭṭhaṃ gantabbanti.

159. 'They have a single arising' designated as birth; hence they are called 'of single arising.' 'They have a single cessation' designated as impermanence; hence they are called 'of single cessation.' Here, the word 'single' is used in the sense of counting. Thus it shows that the collection of those material forms that arise with one and the same birth and cease with one and the same impermanence is here called a 'material cluster.' As for those who, for the purpose of counting the material phenomena contained in a cluster, suppose multiple instances of birth, etc., even within a single cluster—their view does not accord with the Mūlaṭīkā, nor is there any logical basis for it. For it is stated there: 'Since the arising, etc., of the material phenomena included in each single cluster occur simultaneously, the arising, etc., of each single cluster are indeed singular.' Just as the life faculty of a single cluster, being the preserver of the cluster, is called 'derived material,' so too birth, etc., which are the nature of the cluster's arising, etc., are also called 'derived material.' In the same way, the alteration and limiting forms should also be connected. And if it were said that, because it is stated, 'The accumulation of the sense bases is the growth of material form, and the growth of material form is the continuity of material form,' those characteristic forms of birth, etc., pertain to the individual material forms themselves and not to the cluster, then, because it is said, 'Sensitivity dependent on the four great elements is the life of material phenomena,' etc., the eye faculty, life faculty, etc., would also become multiple within a single cluster. Therefore, without making such a supposition, it should be concluded that, just like the other derived material phenomena, the characteristic material phenomena in a single cluster are also singular.

Eko samāno mahābhūtasaṅkhāto nissayo etesanti ekanissayā. Ettha pana samānatthe ekasaddo yutto. Catunnaṃ bhūtānaṃ nissayatāsambhavato. Yānicaekuppādatādīhitīhilakkhaṇehi yuttāni. Tāni ekantena sahavuttīni nāma hontīti vuttaṃ sahavuttinoti. Dasaparimāṇāniassātidasakaṃ. Dasannaṃ samūho vā dasakaṃ. Cakkhunā upalakkhitaṃ dasakanti cakkhudasakaṃ. Cakkhupadhānaṃvā dasakaṃ cakkhudasakaṃ. Esanayo sesesupi. Yasmā pana cittajo saddo viññattivikārena vinā napavattati. Viññattivikāroca tena saddena vinā napavattati. Tasmā cittajaṃ saddanavakaṃvā vacīviññattinavakaṃvā nasambhavatīti adhippāyena vacīviññatti sadde hi ca sahavacīviññatti dasakanti vuttaṃ. Ettha pana viññatti vikāro saddena vinā napavattatīti idaṃ tāva yujjati. Yā tāya vācāya viññatti viññāpanā viññāpitattaṃ. Idaṃ taṃrūpaṃ vacīviññattīti hi vuttaṃ. Viññattivikārarahitaṃ pana cittajaṃ saddanavakaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsu āgatameva. Yathāha-paṭiccasamuppāda niddesesu paṭisandhikkhaṇato uddhaṃ pavattaututoceva cittatoca saddanavakanti.

'They have a single, common support designated as the great elements'; hence they are 'of single support.' Here, however, the word 'eka' is appropriate in the sense of 'common,' because it is possible for the four elements to serve as a support. And those things that possess the three characteristics of single arising, etc., are definitely co-existent; thus it is said 'co-existent.' A group of ten is a decad. Or a collection of ten is a decad. The decad marked by the eye is the eye-decad. Or the decad with the eye as principal is the eye-decad. This is the method for the rest as well. Because mind-originated sound does not occur without the alteration of intimation, and the alteration of intimation does not occur without that sound, therefore, with the intention that neither the mind-originated sound-nonad nor the vocal-intimation-nonad can exist, it is said 'the vocal-intimation-decad together with sound.' Here, firstly, the statement that the alteration of intimation does not occur without sound is tenable. For it is said: 'That which is the intimation, the communicating, the state of having been made known by that speech—this is that form called vocal intimation.' But the mind-originated sound-nonad, devoid of the alteration of intimation, is indeed found in the commentaries. As it is said in the expositions of dependent origination: 'From the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, the sound-nonad arises from temperature and from mind.'

Mahāaṭṭhakathā nayena viññatti rahito vitakka vipphāra saddonāma asota viññeyyo cittajo saddo labbhati. So pana saṅgahakārena paṭisiddho. Yathāha-paṭṭhānepi cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ saddāyatanaṃ sotaviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayena paccayoti āvataṃ. [M 0.0309] Tasmā vinā viññattighaṭṭanāya uppajjamāno asota viññeyyo vitakkavipphārasaddonāma natthīti. Visuddhimagge assāsa passāse cittajaṃ saddanavakaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathāha-cittaje assāsa passāsa koṭṭhāsepi ojaṭṭhamakañceva saddocāti navāti, saddanavakeca āgate saddalahutādi dvādasakaṃpi āgatameva hoti. Tasmā suddhaṭṭhakaṃ, saddanavakaṃ, kāyaviññatti nākaṃ, vacīviññatti dasakaṃ, lahutādekā dasakaṃ, saddalahutādidvādasakaṃ, kāyaviññatti lahutādi dvādasakaṃ, vacīviññattisaddalahutādi te rasakanti aṭṭhacittajakalāpā paccetabbāti. Saccasaṅkhepe pana sadda lahutādi dvādasakaṃ visuṃ agahetvā cittaja kalāpā satteva vuttā.

According to the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, a mind-originated sound called 'thought-diffusion sound,' which is devoid of intimation and not cognizable by the ear, is found. But this is rejected by the author of the Compendium. As he says: 'In the Paṭṭhāna too, it is cited that the sound base originated by mind is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of object-condition.' Therefore, there is no such thing as a 'thought-diffusion sound' arising without the impact of intimation that is not cognizable by the ear. In the Visuddhimagga, a mind-originated sound-nonad is mentioned in relation to the in-and-out-breaths. As it is said: 'Even in the section on mind-originated in-and-out-breaths, there are nine: the octad with nutriment as eighth, and sound.' And when the sound-nonad has been included, the sound-lightness-etc.-dodecad is also included. Therefore, the eight mind-originated clusters should be understood as: the pure octad, the sound-nonad, the body-intimation-nonad, the vocal-intimation-decad, the lightness-etc.-hendecad, the sound-lightness-etc.-dodecad, the body-intimation-lightness-etc.-dodecad, and the vocal-intimation-sound-lightness-etc.-tridecad. In the Saccasaṅkhepa, however, without taking the sound-lightness-etc.-dodecad separately, only seven mind-originated clusters are mentioned.

Ṭīkāsu panassa porāṇaṭīkāyaṃ

But in the subcommentaries, in the ancient subcommentary to this,

Mahāṭṭhakathānayena viññattirahite asota viññeyye vitakka vipphārasadde saddanavakaṃ dassetvā puna vādantaraṃ dassentena. Apica, mahājanasannipātassa dūrato apaññāyamānakkharapadabyañjanattho cittasamuṭṭhānanighosasaddo aviññattiko evāti vadanti. Tathā migapakkhīnaṃca aññamaññaṃ bhāsaṃ ajānantānaṃ andhadamiḷādinaṃ aviññattiko cittasamuṭṭhānasaddo atthīti vuttaṃ.

another point of view is presented after showing the sound-nonad in the thought-diffusion sound, which is devoid of intimation and not cognizable by the ear, according to the method of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. It states: 'Moreover, they say that the loud mind-originated sound of a large gathering, whose meaning, syllables, words, and phrases are not discerned from a distance, is indeed a sound without intimation. Similarly, it is said that for beasts and birds who do not know each other's language, and for the blind, Tamils, etc., there exists a mind-originated sound without intimation.'

Tattha viññattirahito asotaviññeyyo vitakkavipphāra saddo aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ paṭikkhitto. Mahājanasannipātassa citta samuṭṭhāna nighosasaddopi āsanne ṭhitānaṃ paññāyamānakkharapada byañjanattho saviññattikoeva hoti. Itarathā sabbepi citta jasaddā dūratare ṭhitānaṃ apaññāyamāna padabyañjanāeva hontīti sabbepi viññattirahitā siyunti. Naca migapakkhiādīnaṃ cittajo saddo viññattirahito hoti. Samānajātiyānaṃ paresaṃ adhippāyattha viññāpanatoti.

Herein, the thought-diffusion sound, which is without intimation and not cognizable by the ear, is rejected in the Aṭṭhasālinī. Even the loud mind-originated sound of a large gathering, for those standing nearby, has discernible syllables, words, and meaning, and is indeed with intimation. Otherwise, all mind-originated sounds, for those standing further away, would have indiscernible words and phrases, and thus all would be without intimation. Nor is the mind-originated sound of beasts, birds, and so on without intimation, because it communicates the intended meaning to others of the same species.

Pacchima ṭīkāyaṃ panassa

But in its later subcommentary,

Saddanavakaṃ panettha accharā saṅghāta pāṇippahārādi sadda sahitaṃ aṭṭhakamevāti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yuttaṃ.

Herein, it is said that the sound-nonad, together with sounds such as the snapping of fingers, the clapping of hands, and so on, is only an octad. That too is not proper.

Tādiso hi saddo cittapaccayo utusamuṭṭhānoeva. Tasmā visuddhimagge vuttanayena assāsapassāsevā avacīghosesu kadāci cittasahitesu ukkāsita khipita vamita chaḍḍitasaddādīsu pivā etaṃ saddanavakaṃ veditabbanti. Utujakalāpesu pacchimā dvepi kasmā bahiddhā nalabbhanti. Nanu bahiddhāpi rūpānaṃ lahu garu mudu thaddha kammaññatā dissantīti. Saccaṃ, tā pana bhūtānaṃ omattādhimatta vasena honti, na pana lahutādittayavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kasmā pana ākāsadhātuca lakkhaṇarūpānica rūpakalāpesu nagahitānīti vuttaṃ kalāpānantiādi. Ākāsadhātukalāpānaṃ pariccheda mattattā kassaci rūpakalāpassa aṅgabhūtā avayavabhūtā na hoti, lakkhaṇarūpānica sabbesaṃpi kalāpānaṃ uppādādi lakkhaṇa mattattā vikārarūpāni viya kalāpānaṃ bhedakarāni aṅgabhūtāni kalāpavisesapaññāpanassa kāraṇabhūtāni na honti. Tasmā tāni tesu nagahitānīti dasseti. Etena ekuppādātiādinā pubbe vuttaniyamo nipphannarūpānaññeva, na anipphannarūpānaṃ. Tesaṃ pana kalāpa bheda karaṇa meva kalāpaṅganti ca dīpeti. Evañca katvā ekanirodhaṅgarahitassapi viññattidvayassa kalāpabheda karattāeva tesu gahaṇaṃ suṭṭhu upapannaṃ hotīti veditabbanti. [Kalāpayojanā]

For such a sound is indeed conditioned by mind and arises from temperature. Therefore, in the manner explained in the Visuddhimagga, this sound-nonad should be understood in relation to in-breaths and out-breaths, in non-vocal sounds, and sometimes in sounds accompanied by mind, such as coughing, sneezing, vomiting, belching, and so on. Why are the last two qualities not found externally among temperature-originated kalāpas? Is it not so that lightness, heaviness, softness, rigidity, and adaptability of material qualities are also seen externally? True, but they arise due to the lesser or greater degree of the primary elements, not due to the triad of lightness, etc.; thus it should be understood. Why is it said that the space element and characteristic material qualities are not included in the material kalāpas? Because the space element, being merely a boundary for kalāpas, is not an integral part or component of any material kalāpa. Similarly, the characteristic material qualities—arising, etc.—being merely the features of all kalāpas, like the transformative material qualities, do not differentiate the kalāpas, are not integral parts, and are not the cause for defining specific kalāpas. Therefore, it is shown that they are not included in them. By this, it is shown that the previously stated rule—'arising together,' etc.—applies only to produced material qualities, not to unproduced ones. Moreover, it clarifies that for them, the very thing that causes the differentiation of kalāpas is a component of the kalāpa. And thus, it should be understood that the inclusion of the two kinds of intimation, even though they lack the component of ceasing together, is well justified precisely because they cause the differentiation of kalāpas. [Kalāpayojanā]

160. Yathārahanti sabhāvakā bhāvakānaṃ paripuṇṇāpari puṇṇindriyānañca arahānurūpato. Anūnānīti paripuṇṇāni. Nañhi idaṃ nāmarūpaṃ kāmaloke pavattiyaṃ na labbhatīti atthīti.

160. 'As is fitting' means: according to what is suitable for those with and without a sexual characteristic, and for those with complete and incomplete faculties. 'Not deficient' means 'complete'. For indeed, it is not the case that this name-and-form is unobtainable in the course of existence in the sense-sphere realm.

[198] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī,

“Yathārahanti sabhāvakaparipuṇṇāyatanānaṃ anurūpato”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ na sundaraṃ.

It is said: ''As is fitting' means according to what is suitable for those with a sexual characteristic and complete sense bases.' That is not well-stated.

Na hi anūnānīti idaṃ puggalavasena visesanaṃ hotīti. Saṃsedajānañcevaopapātikānañcāti ettha mahāsīhanādasutte-

For 'not deficient' is not a qualification referring to individuals. Regarding 'both the moisture-born and the spontaneously born,' in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, it is said:

Catasso kho imā sāriputta yoniyo. Katamā catasso, aṇḍajā yoni jalābujā yoni saṃsedajāyoni [M 0.0311] opapātikā yonīti. Ye kho te sāriputta sattā aṇḍakosaṃ abhinibbhijja abhinibbhijja jāyanti, ayaṃ vuccati sāriputta aṇḍajā yoni. Ye kho te sāriputta sattā vatthikosaṃ abhinibbhijja abhinibbhijja jāyanti. Ayaṃ vuccati sāriputta jalābujā yoni. Ye kho tesāri puttasattāpūtimacchevā jāyanti. Pūtikuṇapevā pūtikummāsevā candanikāyavā oḷigallevā jāyanti, ayaṃ vuccati sāriputta saṃsedajā yoni. Devā nerakā ekacce ca manussā ekacceca vinipātikā ayaṃ vuccati sāriputta opapātikā yonīti vuttaṃ.

"Sāriputta, there are these four modes of generation. Which four? Egg-born generation, womb-born generation, moisture-born generation, and spontaneous generation. Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born by breaking out of an eggshell—this is called egg-born generation. Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born by breaking out of a membrane—this is called womb-born generation. Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born in a rotting fish, in a putrid corpse, in rotten dough, in a cesspool, or in a dirty puddle—this is called moisture-born generation. Gods, hell-beings, some humans, and some of those in states of deprivation—this is called spontaneous generation."

Aṭṭhakathāyañca aṇḍe jātā aṇḍajā. Jalābumhi jātā jalābujā. Saṃsede jātā saṃsedajā. Vinā etehi kāraṇehi uppattitvā viya nibbattā abhinibbattāti opapātikā. Abhinibbhijja jāyantīti bhinditvā nikkhamanavasena jāyanti. Pūti kuṇapetiādīhi aniṭṭhaṭṭhānāneva dassitāni. Iṭṭhesu sappi telamadhuphāṇitādīsu sattā jāyantievāti vuttaṃ. Etthaca purimesu dvīsu pāḷinayena aṇḍaṃ vuccati aṇḍakoso. Jalābuvuccati vatthikoso, tato jātā vijātā nikkhantāti aṇḍajā jalābujātica vuccantīti veditabbā. Tattha jaraṃ jīraṇaṃ bhedaṃ yāti upetīti jalābūti saddanītiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Jalaṃ vuccati kalalaṃ. Taṃ āvunāti paṭicchādeti avativā rakkhatīti jalābu, gabbhapaliveṭhanāsayo. Saṃsīdanti etthāti saṃsedo. Pūtimacchā diko sappitelādiko padumagabbhaveḷugabbharukkhasusirapupphaphalādi koca allakilinnapadeso. Upapattikkhaṇeeva paripuṇṇaaṅgapaccaṅgattā tato tato uppatitvā viya jāyantīti opapātikā.

In the commentary, those born from an egg are called egg-born. Those born from a womb are called womb-born. Those born from moisture are called moisture-born. Those who arise without these causes, as if arisen and manifested, are called spontaneously arisen. 'They are born by breaking out' means they are born by way of breaking and emerging. By 'putrid corpse,' etc., only undesirable places are shown. It is stated that beings are indeed born in desirable places like ghee, oil, honey, and molasses. And here, in the first two cases, according to the Pāli text, 'aṇḍa' is called 'aṇḍakosa' (eggshell). 'Jalābu' is called 'vatthikosa' (membrane-sheath). It should be understood that because they are born, delivered, and have emerged from that, they are called 'egg-born' and 'womb-born'. Therein, it is said in the Saddanīti that 'jalābu' is so called because it undergoes decay, wearing out, and breaking up. 'Jala' is called 'kalala' (the early embryo). 'Jalābu' is so called because it weaves around, covers, or protects it; it is the receptacle that envelops the fetus. 'Saṃsedo' is so called because beings sink down therein. It is any damp and moist place, such as a rotting fish, etc., ghee, oil, etc., the inside of a lotus, the inside of bamboo, a tree hollow, a flower, fruit, etc. 'Opapātikā' are so called because, being complete in their major and minor limbs at the very moment of arising, they are born as if springing up from here and there.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī,

Aṇḍajādayopi aṇḍakosādimhi okkamantā uppatantā eva nāma hontīti tesaṃpi opapātikattapasaṅgaṃ maññamāno upapāto nesaṃ atthīti opapātikāti vatvā ukkaṃsagati [M 0.0312] paricchedavasena cettha visiṭṭhaopapāto gahito. Yathā abhirūpassa kaññā dātabbāti vadati.

The egg-born and others, in descending into an eggshell and so on, are indeed said to be 'arising.'
