Thinking that the designation 'spontaneously arisen' would thus also apply to them, and having stated, 'they are spontaneously arisen because they have an arising,' here a specific type of arising is taken by way of defining a superior destination. It is like one says, 'A maiden should be given to a handsome man.'

Ukkaṭṭhavasenāti paripuṇṇāyatanabhāvasaṅkhātena ukkaṃsatāvena, tattha opapātikā aṅgapaccaṅgehi saha sabbaso paripuṇṇena attabhāvena jāyanti. Puna tesaṃ vaḍḍhanakiccaṃ natthi. Saṃsedajānaṃ pana āyatanāni eva paripuṇṇāni honti. Aṅgapaccaṅgāni pana puna vaḍḍhitvāeva paripuṇṇāni jātānīti veditabbaṃ. Omakavasenāti avakaṃsavasena. Cakkhusotaghānabhāvasekānikadācipi na labbhanti jātibadhira jaccaghānakānaṃ abhāvakānañca sambhavatoti appoyo. Tattha tāni sabbānipi sugati duggati jātiyānaṃ ahetukasaṃsedajānaṃ kadāci nalabbhanti. Sugatiyaṃ pana opapātikabhāvonāma seṭṭho attabhāva paṭilābhoti nayena kenaci omakena kammena labbhati. Tasmā sugatijāti yānaṃ opapātikānaṃ aparipuṇṇindriyatānāma natthi aññatra abhāvakehi ādikappikehiti. Duggatijātiyānaṃpi pana tesaṃ kadāci cakkhu sota bhāva vekallatāeva vattabbā. Na ghānavekallatā. Kāmadhātuyaṃ pana aghānako opapātiko natthīti hi aṭṭha kathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Jivhāvekallatānāma sabbesaṃpi natthi yevāti veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi dhammahadayavibhaṅge –

'By way of excellence' means by way of excellence, designated as the state of complete sense bases. There, apparitional beings arise with all limbs and parts complete, possessing a fully formed body. Moreover, there is no need for further growth for them. However, for moisture-born beings, only the sense bases are fully developed. The limbs and parts, however, must grow further to reach full development—this should be understood. 'By way of inferiority' refers to a state of deficiency. The faculties of the eye, ear, or nose may sometimes not be obtained, due to the possibility of those born deaf, born without a nose, and those lacking faculties; thus, it is not universally applicable. In this regard, all those faculties may sometimes not be obtained for rootless moisture-born beings in happy or unhappy destinations. However, in happy realms, the state of being apparitional, which is indeed the attainment of the best form of existence, is obtained through some inferior kamma. Therefore, among apparitional beings born in happy realms, incomplete faculties do not occur, except for those lacking the sex faculty and those at the beginning of the aeon. For those born in unhappy realms, a deficiency of the eye or ear faculty must sometimes be acknowledged, but never a deficiency of the nose. Indeed, it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā that in the sense-sphere realm, there is no apparitional being without a nose. It should be understood that a deficiency of the tongue never occurs in any being. As stated in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga—

Kāmadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe kassaci ekādasā yatanāni pātubhavanti. Kassaci dasa. Kassaciaparāni dasa. Kassaci nava. Kassaci sattāyatanāni pātubhavantīti vuttaṃ.

At the moment of arising in the sense-sphere realm, for some, eleven bases appear. For some, ten. For some others, ten. For some, nine. For some, seven bases appear—so it is said.

Tattha kāmadhātuyanti kāmaloke. Upapattikkhaṇeti paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇe. Kassaci ekādasā yatanānītiādisu catūsu vākyesu saṃsedajopapātikā vuttā. Kassaci sattāyatanānīti ettha pana gabbhaseyyakova vutto. Tattha yasmā sattāyatanaṃ nāma paṭisandhikkhaṇe na labbhati. Pavatti kāleyeva labbhati. Tasmā ekādasayatanānīti vuttaṃ. Kassaci dasāti cakkhuvekallavasena. Kassaci aparāni dasāti sota vekallavasena. [M 0.0313] Kassaci navāti cakkhusota dvaya vekalla vasena vuttaṃ. Yadica aghānako opapātikonāma siyā. Tadā suddhajaccaghānakena saddhiṃ tayo dasakavārā vuttā siyuṃ. Tathā jaccandhaghānaka jaccabadhiraghānakehi saddhiṃ tayo navakavārā ekoca aṭṭhakavāro vutto siyā tiṇṇaṃ vipannānaṃ vasena. Tathā avuttattā pana natthi aghānako opapāti koti viññāyatīti. Tasmiṃ pana vibhaṅge indriyavāre napuṃsakānaṃ opapātikānanti avuttattā thapetvā ādikappike abhāvakopi opapātiko natthiyevāti. Pāḷiyaṃ avuttaṃpi pana saṃsedajānaṃ vuttapakāraṃ cakkhādivekallaṃ aṭṭhakathāvasena veditabbaṃ. Yathāha-sattati ukkaṃsatova rūpāni saṃsedajopapāta yonīsu. Athavā, avakaṃsato tiṃsāti. Tattha tiṃsāti jivhākāya vatthu dasakānaṃ vasena tiṃsarūpānīti ca vuttaṃ. Idañhi vacanaṃ saṃsedajānaṃ vasena vuttanti mahāṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Ācariyā nandattherena pana yamake ghānajivhānaṃ aññamaññaṃ avinābhāva vuttitā vuttāti jivhā vekallatā viya ghānavekallatāpi natthīti icchitaṃ. Indriya yamake pana –

Here, 'in the sense-sphere realm' means in the sense-sphere world. 'At the moment of arising' means at the moment of the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness. In the four phrases such as 'for some, eleven bases,' moisture-born and apparitional beings are mentioned. In 'for some, seven bases,' however, only womb-born beings are referred to. Herein, because the seven bases are not obtained at the moment of rebirth-linking but only during the course of existence, the phrase 'eleven bases' is said. For some, it is ten—due to a deficiency of the eye. For others, it is ten—due to a deficiency of the ear. For some, it is nine—due to a deficiency of both eye and ear. If a noseless apparitional being existed, then there would be three cases of ten mentioned, along with the one who is merely congenitally noseless. Similarly, with those born blind and without a nose and those born deaf and without a nose, there would be three cases of nine and one of eight, due to the three deficiencies. However, because it is not so stated, it is understood that there is no noseless apparitional being. In that Vibhaṅga, in the section on the faculties, since apparitional neuters are not mentioned, it is understood that apart from those at the beginning of the aeon, there are no apparitional beings without the sex faculty. Though not stated in the Pāḷi, the deficiency of the eye and other faculties in moisture-born beings should be understood according to the commentary, in the manner described. As it is said: 'Seventy at the maximum, concerning forms, in the moisture-born and apparitional modes of birth.' Or, 'At the minimum, thirty.' Here, 'thirty' refers to the thirty forms on account of the decads of tongue, body, and heart-basis. This statement is made concerning moisture-born beings, as stated in the Great Subcommentary. The teacher, the Elder Nanda, however, stated in the Yamaka that the nose and tongue are mutually inseparable; thus, he holds that just as there is no deficiency of the tongue, there is also no deficiency of the nose. But in the Indriya Yamaka—

Yassavā pana itthindriyaṃ uppajjati, tassa ghānindriyaṃ uppajjatīti. Aghānakānaṃ itthīnaṃ upapajjantīnaṃ tāsaṃ itthindriyaṃ uppajjati, noca tāsaṅghānindriyaṃ uppajjatītica. Yassavā pana purisindriyaṃ uppajjati, tassa ghānindriyaṃ uppajjatīti. Aghānakānaṃ purisānaṃ upapajjantānaṃ tesaṃ purisindriyaṃ uppajjati, noca tesaṃ ghānindriyaṃ uppajjatītica vuttaṃ.

Or for whomever the female faculty is arising, for them is the nose faculty arising? For those females without a nose who are being reborn, for them the female faculty is arising, but the nose faculty is not arising for them. Or for whomever the male faculty is arising, for them is the nose faculty arising? For those males without a nose who are being reborn, for them the male faculty is arising, but the nose faculty is not arising for them—so it is said.

Tasmā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayena ghānavekallatāpi atthīti yuttaṃ.

Therefore, it is proper that there is also a deficiency of the nose, in accordance with the method stated in the commentary.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī:

Apare pana yamake ghānajivhānaṃ sahacāritā vuttāti ajivhassa asambhavato aghānakassapi abhāvameva vaṇṇenti. Tatthāpi yathā cakkhusotāni rūpabhave ghāna jivhāhi vinā pavattanti. Na evaṃ ghānajivhā aññamaññaṃ vinā pavattanti. [M 0.0314] Dvinnaṃpi rūpabhave anuppajjanatoti evaṃ visuṃ visuṃ kāmabhave apavatti vasena tesaṃ sahacāritā vuttāti na na sakkā vattunti vuttaṃ. Taṃ yuttaṃ.

Others, however, explain that since the concomitance of the nose and tongue is stated in the Yamaka, they describe the non-existence of one without a nose because of the impossibility of one without a tongue. Therein, just as the eye and ear exist in the form realm without the nose and tongue, so the nose and tongue do not exist without each other. It is said that because both do not arise in the form realm, it is not impossible to say that their concomitance is stated on the basis of their not occurring separately in the sense-sphere realm. That is proper.

Okāsavāre hi ekantasahacāritā vuttamattena puggalesu ekantasahacāritā na sakkā vattunti. Gabbhe mātukucchimhi sentīti gabbhaseyyakā. Rūpādīsu khandhesu sañjanti laggantīti sattā. Yathāha-rūpe kho rādha yo chando, yo rāgo, yā nandi, yā taṇhā, tatra satto, tatra visatto, tena sattoti vuccatītiādi. Gabbhaseyyāca te sattācāti samāso. Aṇḍajāceva jalābujāca. Tīṇidasakāni pātu bhavanti. Yāni kalalanti vuccanti. Bhāvadasakaṃ kadāci nalabbhati napuṃsakassāti adhippāyo. Evañcakatvā dhammahadayavibhaṅge gabbhaseyyakānaṃ sattānaṃ ahetukānaṃ napuṃsakānaṃ upapattikkhaṇe cattārindriyāni pātubhavanti kāyindriyaṃ manindriyaṃ jīvitindriyaṃ upekkhindriyanti vuttaṃ. Tatoparanti gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇato paraṃ. Pavattikāleti ekadasame sattāhe. Tathā hi kathāvatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ sesāni cattāri sattasattati rattimhi jāyantīti vuttaṃ. Tattha sesānīti kāyāyatana manāyatanato avasesāni cattāri cakkhusotaghānajivhā yatanāni. Sattasattatirattimhīti ekādasamasattāhassa pariyosānarattimhi. Ayañca attho yamakaṭīkāya dīpetabbo. Vuttañhi tattha –

'Womb-born' are those who lie in a womb, in a mother's belly. 'Beings' are so called because they are attached to, they cling to, the aggregates such as form. As it is said: 'Rādha, whatever desire, passion, delight, or craving one has for form, there one is attached, there one is bound; therefore one is called a being,' and so on. The compound is: 'they are womb-born and they are beings.' They are both egg-born and viviparous. Three decads appear, which are called the 'kalala.' The meaning is that the sex decad is sometimes not obtained by a neuter. And so, in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga it is said that at the moment of rebirth-linking for rootless, neuter, womb-born beings, four faculties appear: the body faculty, the mind faculty, the life faculty, and the equanimity faculty. 'Thereafter' means after the rebirth-linking moment for womb-born beings. 'During the course of existence' means in the eleventh week. For in the Commentary to the Kathāvatthu it is said: 'The remaining four arise on the seventy-seventh night.' Here, 'the remaining' refers to the four sense bases—eye, ear, nose, and tongue—that remain after the body base and mind base. 'On the seventy-seventh night' means on the final night of the eleventh week. And this meaning should be clarified by the Subcommentary to the Yamaka. For it is said there—

Gabbhaseyyakassa pacchimabhavikassa upapajjantassa ekadasa masattāhā orato ṭhitassa rūpāyatanaṃ nuppajjissati, noca cakkhāyatanaṃ nuppajjissatīti.

For a womb-born being in their final existence who is being reborn and who will exist for less than eleven weeks, the form base will not arise, but it is not the case that the eye base will not arise.

Yaṃ pana yassavā pana yattha rūpāyatanaṃ uppajjittha, tassa tattha ghānāyatanaṃ uppajjatīti. Kāmāvacarā cavantānaṃ aghānakānaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ upapajjantānaṃ rūpāvacarānaṃ tesaṃ tattha rūpāyatanaṃ uppajjittha. Noca tesaṃ tattha ghānāyatanaṃ uppajjatīti ettha aghānakānaṃ kāmāvacaraṃ upapajjantānanti vuttaṃ.

But as to the passage: 'Or for whomever, wherever the form base arose, for them, there, is the nose base arising?' For those passing away from the sense-sphere realm, for those without a nose who are being reborn into the sense-sphere realm, and for those in the form-sphere realm—for them, there, the form base arose. But for them, there, the nose base is not arising. Herein, the phrase 'for those without a nose who are being reborn into the sense-sphere realm' is stated.

Taṃ [M 0.0315] ye ekādasamasattāhā orato kālaṅkarissanti. Tesaṃ ghānāyatanānibbattakakammena gahitapaṭisandhikānaṃ vasena vuttantica vuttaṃ. Etthaca cakkhughānesu vuttesu sotajivhā avuttāpi atthato siddhāeva hontīti.

That is said with reference to those who will pass away before the eleventh week and whose rebirth-linking has been grasped by kamma that does not produce the nose-base. And here, when the eye and nose are mentioned, the ear and tongue, though unmentioned, are indeed established by implication.

[199] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[199] But as to what is in the Vibhāvanī:

“Pavattikāleti sattame sattāheti” vuttaṃ. Taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

It is said: 'During the course of existence means in the seventh week.' That should not be accepted.

Aṭṭhakathā virodhato īdisesu ca ṭhānesu aṭṭhakathā pamāṇatoti.

Because it contradicts the commentary, and in such cases, the commentary is the authority.

[200] Yañca tattha

[200] And as to what is there:

“Ṭīkākāramatena ekādasame sattāhe vāti” vuttaṃ. Tampi na sundaraṃ.

It is said: 'Or in the eleventh week, according to the opinion of the subcommentator.' That too is not good.

Nahi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ niddiṭṭhato vutto vinicchayo ṭīkākāra matonāma sakkā vattunti.

For a decision stated because it is indicated in the commentary cannot be called the subcommentator's own opinion.

[201] Yañca tattha

[201] And as to what is there:

“Kamenāti cakkhudasakapātubhāvato sattāhātikkamena sotadasakaṃ. Tato sattāhātikkamena ghāna dasakaṃ. Tato sattāhā tikkamena jivhādasakanti evaṃ anukkamenāti vuttaṃ”. Taṃpi na daṭṭhabba.

It is said: 'By 'in sequence' is meant: with the passing of a week from the appearance of the eye-decad, the ear-decad; then with the passing of a week, the nose-decad; then with the passing of a week, the tongue-decad—thus in succession.' That too should not be accepted.

Yathāvutta aṭṭhakathāvirodhattā eva.

Precisely because it contradicts the commentary as stated.

[202] Yaṃpi tattha

[202] And as to what is also there:

“Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpi hi ayamattho dassito vā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yuttaṃ.

It is said: 'For has this meaning been shown even in the commentary?' That too is not proper.

Na hi sānāma aṭṭhakathā atthi. Yattha īdiso uppattikkamo dassito siyā. Nanu paṭiccasamuppādaṭṭhakathāsu gabbhaleyyakavasenavā purimaṃbhavacakkaṃ vuttaṃ. Anupubbapavattidīpanatoti vuttanti ce.Na. Tañhi viññāṇādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ aṅgānaṃ paccayapaccayuppannabhāvapavattikkamena pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ pañcapadaṃ sandhāya vuttanti. Āyatananiddesaṭṭhakathāsu [M 0.0316] pana so paṭikkhittoyeva. Naca aṭṭhakathāsu paṭikkhitto uppattikkamo therena idha kamenāti iminā pāṭhena dassitoti sakkā vattunti. Tasmā kamenāti idhapi desanakkamenāti attho. Desitānīti sambandhoca veditabbo.

For there is no such commentary where such a sequence of arising could be shown. (Query:) Is it not said in the commentaries on dependent origination that the previous life-cycle is described on the basis of the womb-born in order to clarify the successive process? (Reply:) No. For that is said in reference to the five-factored causation that comes in the Pāli, with the sequence of the process of the condition-and-conditioned state of the five links, consciousness, etc. But in the commentaries on the Exposition of the Bases, that very sequence is rejected. And it cannot be said that the sequence of arising rejected in the commentaries is shown here by the Elder with this text 'in sequence.' Therefore, here too, 'in sequence' means 'in the order of the teaching.' And the connection should be understood with 'have been taught.'

Saccasaṅkhepa ṭīkāyaṃ pana

But in the Subcommentary to the Saccasaṅkhepa:

Sākhāvatthaṃ atikkamma pacchā sattame sattāhe cakkhu sotaghānajivhādasakāca uppajjanti. Ṭīkākāropana ekādasame sattāheti āhāti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi nayujjati yevāti.

It is said: 'Having passed the stage of branches, afterwards, in the seventh week, the decads of eye, ear, nose, and tongue arise. The subcommentator, however, says: "in the eleventh week."' That too is indeed not logical.

Ettha ca kalalādīnaṃ uppattikkamo saṃyuttake vutto. Yathāha –

And here the sequence of the arising of the kalala, etc., is stated in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. As it is said:

Pathamaṃ kalalaṃ hoti, kalalā hoti abbudaṃ;

Abbudā jāyate pesi, pesiyā nibbattate ghano;

Ghanā pasākhā jāyanti, kesā lomā nakhāpicāti.

First there is the kalala, from the kalala the abbuda; from the abbuda the pesī is born, from the pesī the ghana develops; from the ghana the limbs are born, the hair, body hair, and also nails.

Aṭṭhakathāyañca vuttaṃ. Tattha pathamanti pathamena paṭisandhiviññāṇena tissoti vā phussotivā nāmaṃ natthi. Athakho tīhi jātiuṇṇaṃsūhi katasuttagge saṇṭhitatelabindupamāṇaṃ kalalaṃ hoti. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

And in the commentary it is said: Therein, by 'first' is meant that with the first rebirth-linking consciousness there is no name such as 'Tissa' or 'Phussa.' But rather, there is the kalala, which is like a drop of oil placed on the tip of a thread made from three strands of fine wool. In reference to this it is said:

Tilatelassa yathā bindu, sappimaṇḍo anāvilo;

Evaṃ vaṇṇapaṭibhāgaṃ, kalalaṃ saṃpavuccatīti.

As is a drop of sesame oil, or the clear surface of ghee, undisturbed, such in color and appearance, the kalala is called.

Kalalā hoti abbudanti tasmā kalalā sattāhaccayena maṃsadhovanaudakavaṇṇaṃ abbudaṃnāma hoti, kalalanti nāmaṃ anta radhāyati. Vuttaṃpi cetaṃ –

From the kalala the abbuda: from that kalala, with the passing of a week, there is what is called the abbuda, the color of water in which flesh has been washed; the name 'kalala' disappears. And this too is said:

Sattāhaṃ kalalaṃ hoti, paripakkasamūhakaṃ;

Vivattamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, abbudaṃnāma jāyatīti.

For a week it is a kalala, a fully ripened mass; transforming from that state, what is called the abbuda is born.

Abbudā jāyate pesīti tasmāpi abbudā sattāhaccayena vilīna tipusadisā pesināma sañjāyati. Sā maricaphāṇitena dīpetabbā. Gāmadārakā hi supakkāni maricāni gahetvā sāṭakantare [M 0.0317] bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā pīḷetvā maṇḍaṃ ādāya kapāle pakkhipitvā ātape thapenti. Taṃ sukkhamānaṃ sukkhamānaṃ sabbabhāgehi muccati. Evarūpā pesi hoti. Abbudanti nāmaṃ antaradhāyati. Vuttaṃpi cetaṃ –

From the abbuda, the pesī is born. Thus, after the passing of a week from that abbuda, what is called a pesī, resembling molten tin, is formed. This should be illustrated with pepper molasses. For village boys take fully ripened peppers, make a bundle of them in their cloaks, squeeze them, take the essence, place it in a bowl, and set it in the sun. As it dries, it detaches from all its parts. Such is the pesī. The name 'abbuda' disappears. And this has been said:

Sattāhaṃ abbudaṃ hoti, paripakkasamūhakaṃ;

Vivattamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, pesināma pajāyatīti.

For seven days it is an abbuda, a matured mass; transforming from that state, it is born with the name pesī.

Pesiyā nibbattate ghanoti tato pesito sattāhacca yena kukkuṭaṇḍasaṇṭhāno ghanonāma maṃsapesi piṇḍo nibbattati. Pesītināmaṃ antaradhāyati. Vuttaṃpi cetaṃ –

From the pesī the ghana is produced. Then, after the passing of seven days from that pesī, a solid lump of flesh called a ghana, having the shape of a chicken's egg, is formed. The name 'pesī' disappears. And this has been said:

Sattāhaṃ pesi bhavati, paripakkaṃ samūhakaṃ;

Vivattamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, ghanotināma jāyatīti;

Yathā kukkuṭiyā aṇḍaṃ, samantaṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ;

Evaṃ ghanassa saṇṭhānaṃ, nibbattaṃ kammapaccayātica.

For seven days it is a pesī, a matured mass; transforming from that state, what is called the ghana is born. Just as a hen’s egg is perfectly round all around, so too is the shape of the ghana, produced from kamma as its cause.

Ghanā pasākhā jāyantīti pañcame sattāhe dvinnaṃ hatthapādānaṃ sīsassaca atthāya pañcapīḷakā jāyanti. Yaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃpañcame kho bhikkhave sattāhe pañcapīḷakā jāyanti. Saṇṭhanti kamma toti. Kesā lomā nakhāpicāti dvācattālīsame sattāhe etāni jāyantīti. Ettha ca chaṭṭhasattāhādayo chasattāhā pasādanissayānaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ anukkamena vaḍḍhitvā pariṇatakālā honti. Cakkhādīni pana ekādasama sattāhassa pariyo sānadivase ekato jāyantīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Yaṃ panettha tilatelassa yathābindūtiādinā kalalassa vaṇṇasaṇṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ thokaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na paṭisandhikkhaṇe pavattamānaṃ. Na hi tadā tādisaṃ pakaticakkhunā diṭṭhaṃ vaṇṇajātaṃvā saṇṭhānaṃvā tassa paññāyeyyāti. Anumānato pana evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ekāya ūkāya sattamo bhāgo likkhānāma. Likkhāya chattiṃsatimo bhāgo rathareṇunāma. Rathareṇussa chattiṃsatimo. Tajjārī nāma. Tajjāriyā chattiṃsatimo aṇunāma. Aṇussa chattiṃsatimo bhāgo paramāṇunāma. So pana ākāsakoṭṭhāsiko [M 0.0318] maṃsacakkhussa āpātaṃ nāgacchati. Dibbacakkhusseva āgacchatīti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ chattiṃsa parimāno aṇu pana titticchidda tālacchiddehi paviṭṭhasūriyarasmīsu vaṭṭivaṭṭi hutvā paribbhamanto paññāyatīti vuttaṃ. Sakalaṃ pana kalāpattayaparimāṇamattabhūtaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe paramāṇutopi parittakameva siyā. So hi santānānubandhavasena pavattattā khaṇe khaṇe upacitarūpakalāpasamūhoeva hotīti heṭṭhima koṭiyā ekūnapaññāsakalāpaparimāṇoeva siyā. Tato parittake sati santāna ghaṭanasseva asambhavatoti. Yaṃ pana mahāṭīkāyaṃ te pana kalāpā paramāṇuparimāṇā hontīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ dhātūnaṃ cuṇṇamanasikārānurūpamattavasena vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Dutīyacittanti pathama bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Ṭhitikālanti paṭisandhi cittassa ṭhitikālaṃ. Ojāpharaṇamupādāyāti gabbhaseyyakānaṃ tāva abbudabhāva pesibhāva ghanabhāvādi pattakāle mātuyā āmāsayagatāya ajjhohaṭāhāra sinehabhūtāya ojāya jalābumūlā nusārena vatthusmiṃ pharaṇakālaṃ upādāya, yathāha –

From the ghana, offshoots are born. In the fifth week, five protuberances arise for the sake of the two hands, two feet, and the head. This is what is meant by the statement: 'In the fifth week, bhikkhus, five protuberances arise. They are established by kamma.' 'Head hair, body hair, and nails' arise in the forty-second week. Here, the six weeks beginning with the sixth are the time for the limbs and members, the supports for the sensitive matter, to grow sequentially and mature. But the eye and other sense faculties arise together on the final day of the eleventh week; this conclusion should be reached here. As for what is said here about the color and shape of the kalala, 'like a drop of sesame oil,' etc., that is said with reference to it being slightly developed, not as it occurs at the moment of rebirth-linking. For at that time such a kind of color or shape would not be discernible to the ordinary eye. But it should be understood thus by inference: One-seventh part of a louse is called a likkhā. One-thirty-sixth part of a likkhā is called a rathareṇu. One-thirty-sixth part of a rathareṇu is called a tajjārī. One-thirty-sixth part of a tajjārī is called an aṇu. One-thirty-sixth part of an aṇu is called a paramāṇu. But this paramāṇu, being a portion of space, does not come into the range of the physical eye; it comes only into the range of the divine eye, so it is said in the commentary. But an aṇu, which has the measure of thirty-six of these, is said to be perceived circling round and round in sunbeams that have entered through a lattice-opening or a keyhole. However, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the entire being, consisting of just the measure of the three groups of matter, might be even smaller than a paramāṇu. For since it proceeds by way of the persistence of the continuum, moment by moment it is just a collection of accumulated material groups; thus at the lower limit, it would be of the measure of forty-nine material groups. If it were smaller than that, the formation of the continuum would be impossible. But as to what is said in the Great Subcommentary, 'Those material groups are of the size of a paramāṇu,' that should be taken as said in the sense of a measure suitable for the mental exercise of pulverizing the elements. 'The second consciousness' means the first life-continuum consciousness. 'Duration' means the duration of the rebirth-linking consciousness. Taking the spreading of nutrition as the starting point: for womb-born beings, when they have reached the stages of abbuda, pesī, ghana, and so on, it is the time of the spreading of nutritive essence into the physical basis. This nutritive essence is derived from the food and drink consumed by the mother which has reached her stomach, and it spreads by way of the channel of the umbilical cord. As it is said:

Yañcassa bhuñjati mātā, annaṃ pānañca bhojanaṃ;

Tena so tattha yāpeti, mātukucchigato tiroti.

Whatever food, drink, and nourishment the mother consumes, by that he is sustained there, concealed in the mother's womb.

Aṭṭhakathāyañca tena so tattha yāpetīti tassa hi nātito uṭṭhito nāḷo mātuudara paṭalena ekābaddho hoti. So uppaladaṇḍako viya chiddo. Tena āhāraraso saṃsaritvā āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ so dasamāse yāpeti. Mātukucchigato tiroti mātuyā tiro kucchigato. Mātukucchiyā abbhantaragatoti atthoti vuttaṃ. Tattha pana nābhināḷassa uṭṭhitakālaṃ sandhāya nātito uṭṭhito nāḷoti vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. Na hi abbudādikāle tassa nātināḷonāma uṭṭhito siyāti. Saṃsedajopapātikānaṃ pana yaṃkiñci laddhaṃvā attano kheḷaṃvā ajjhoharaṇakāle ojāpharaṇaṃ upādāya. Tena vuttaṃ ojāpharaṇamupādāyaāhārasamuṭṭhānāti[M 0.0319]. Cuticittopari sattarasamacittassāti cuticittato upari pubbakāle sattarasamassa bhavaṅgacittassa. Kammajarūpāni na uppajjanti tesaṃ tato paṭṭhāya anuppannattāyeva tato satta rasamaṃ cuticittaṃnāma hoti. No aññathāti. Puretaranti tassa sattarasamassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇaṃeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tatoparanti cuticittato parasmiṃ soḷasacittakkhaṇaparimāṇe khaṇe. Cittajāhārajarūpañcāti cittajarūpasantānaṃ āhāraja rūpasantānañca vocchijjati anupādinnakasantāne tesaṃ uppattiyā asambhavato. Yamettha vattabbaṃ taṃ rūpasamuṭṭhāne vuttameva. Bhāvadasakaṃnāma kāmarāganidānakammasamuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti tabbirāga bhāvanākammanibbatte rūpaloke tassa alābho vutto. Āhārajakalāpānica na labbhanti ajjhohaṭā hārā bhāvato, tatoyevaca sarīragatassa ajjhattāhārassapi rūpasamuṭṭhānā bhāvato. Ācariyānandatthero pana tattha labbhamāna rūpakalāpesupi gandharasānaṃ ojāyaca abhāvaṃ vaṇṇeti. Rūpadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe pañcāyatanāni pātubhavanti cakkhāyatanaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ, sotā yatanaṃ, manā yatanaṃ, dhammāyatananti ca, pañcadhātuyo pātubhavanti cakkhudhātu, rūpadhātu, sotadhātu, manoviññāṇa dhātu, dhammadhātūtica, tayo āhārā pātubhavanti phassāhāro, manosañcetanā hāro, viññāṇā hāroti ca vibhaṅgevuttattā. Etthaca pāḷiyaṃ rūpaloke phoṭṭhabbe paṭikkhittepi kiccantarasabbhāvā mahābhūtānaṃ tattha paṭilābho avārito eva hoti. Gandhādīnaṃ pana kiccantarameva natthi. Yena te dhammamattabhāvepi tiṭṭheyyaṃ tasmā tesaṃ avacanaṃ tattha abhāvameva dīpetīti ācariyassa adhippāyo. Tathā pana bhūtacatukkaṃ tattha atthiyeva, yathāha-asaññasattānaṃ ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭicca tayo mahābhūtātiādi. Phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ pana phoṭṭhabba dhātuca tattha paṭikkhittā. Tasmā sabbesaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ dhammabhāve samānepi yena kiccavisesena gandho raso phoṭṭhabbaṃ kabaḷīkārāhārotica vuccati. Tassa natthitāya tesaṃ tena nāme na tattha [M 0.0320] anupalabbhamānataṃ sandhāya vibhaṅge kathāvatthumhi yamake sūti sabbattha tesaṃ tattha paṭikkhepo. Mahābhūtānaṃ pana nisanda dhammamattabhāvena vijjamānānaṃ tesaṃ dhammāyatanadhammadhātūsu anupavesoti yutto siyāti vadanti. Tīṇidasakāni jīvitanavakañcāti ettha ācariyānanda matiyā cakkhusattakaṃ sotasattakaṃ vatthusattakanti evaṃ tīṇi sattakāni jīvitachakkañcāti vattabbaṃ. Abhiricchatīti alabbhamāne pathamaṃ vajjite tattha labbhamānatāvasena avasissati. Atirekaṃvā hotīti attho. Etthaca rūpaloke viya kāmaloke jīvitanavakaṃ kasmā visuṃ na vuttanti. Rūpaloke pana āhārupatthambhakassa aññassaca sakalasarīrabyāpino anupālaka jīvitassa abhāvā etadeva tadubhayaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā sakalasarīraṃ anupāletīti pākaṭaṃ tattha jīvitanavakanti visuṃ vuttaṃ. Kāmaloke pana aññāni upatthambhakā nupālakāni bahūni pākaṭānica honti. Tasmā jīvitanavakaṃ apākaṭanti katvā visuṃ na vuttaṃ siyā. Kāmalokepi pana etaṃ asitādipācakaggivasena tassevaca udayabhūtassa sakalasarī rānupālakassa usmāsaṅkhātassa kāyaggino vasena pākaṭameva. Yaṃ sandhāya –

And in the commentary it is said: 'He sustains himself there.' For the cord that arises from his navel is connected as one with the lining of the mother's womb. It is hollow like a lotus stalk. Through it, the nutrient essence circulates and gives rise to materiality originated from nutriment. In this way he sustains himself for ten months. 'Concealed in the mother's womb' means concealed within the mother's belly; the meaning is that he has gone inside the mother's womb, it is said. There, however, regarding the time when the umbilical cord arises, it should be understood that 'the cord that arises from the navel' is said. For in the early stages, such as the abbuda stage, there would be no such thing as an umbilical cord arisen from the navel. But for moisture-born and spontaneously arisen beings, it is on account of the diffusion of nutriment at the time of ingesting whatever they get or their own saliva. Hence it is said, 'originated from nutriment on account of the diffusion of nutriment.' 'Of the seventeenth consciousness from the death-consciousness' means of the seventeenth life-continuum consciousness in the period prior to the death-consciousness. Kamma-born materiality does not arise for them because from that point onwards it has not arisen; from that point, the death-consciousness is the seventeenth. It is so called, and not otherwise. 'Earlier' is said referring to the very arising-moment of that seventeenth consciousness. 'Thereafter' means in the period of sixteen mind-moments after the death-consciousness. 'And mind-originated and nutriment-originated materiality' means that the continuity of mind-originated materiality and the continuity of nutriment-originated materiality are cut off, because it is impossible for them to arise in a non-grasped continuity. Whatever should be said here has already been stated in the section on the origins of materiality. The sex-decad is said to be originated by kamma that has sensual lust as its cause; its non-acquisition in the fine-material world, where one is reborn by kamma from developing meditation free from that lust, is stated. And nutriment-originated groups are not obtained because of the absence of ingested nutriment, and because of that very reason, the internal nutriment that has entered the body is also not a cause for the arising of materiality. The Elder Ācariya Ānanda, however, explains the absence of odor, taste, and nutritive essence even in the material groups that are found there. Because it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'At the moment of rebirth in the fine-material world, five sense bases appear: the eye-base, form-base, ear-base, mind-base, and mental-object base. And five elements appear: the eye-element, form-element, ear-element, mind-consciousness-element, and mental-object-element. And three kinds of nutriment appear: the nutriment of contact, the nutriment of mental volition, and the nutriment of consciousness.' And here in the Pāli, although the tangible is rejected in the fine-material world, because of the existence of other functions, the acquisition of the great elements there is not prevented. For odor and so on, however, there is no other function at all by which they might exist even in the state of being mere phenomena. Therefore, their not being mentioned indicates their absence there; this is the teacher's intention. However, the four great elements do exist there, as it is said: 'For non-percipient beings, one great element is a condition for the three other great elements,' and so on. But the tangible-object base and the tangible-object element are rejected there. Therefore, although all real phenomena are the same in being phenomena, it is because of the absence of that specific function by which odor, taste, the tangible, and edible food are so called, that they are not found there by that name. This is why their rejection there is stated everywhere in the Vibhaṅga, Kathāvatthu, and Yamaka. But it is reasonable, they say, that the great elements, existing as a mere outflow of phenomena, are not included in the mental-object base and mental-object element. Here, regarding 'three decads and the life-nonad,' according to the view of Ācariya Ānanda, it should be stated as 'the eye-septad, the ear-septad, and the heart-base-septad—thus three septads—and the life-hexad.' The meaning of 'is in excess' (abhiricchatīti) is that when what is unobtainable is first excluded, what is obtainable there remains; or it means there is an excess. And here, why is the life-nonad not mentioned separately in the sensual world as it is in the fine-material world? In the fine-material world, because of the absence of the support of nutriment and of any other life-faculty that pervades and maintains the entire body, this alone stands in place of both and maintains the entire body; thus the life-nonad is prominent there and is mentioned separately. But in the sensual world, there are many other supporting and maintaining factors that are also prominent. Therefore, the life-nonad, being not prominent, might not have been mentioned separately. However, in the sensual world too, this is prominent as the digestive fire for what is eaten, etc., and as the bodily fire, called heat, which arises from that very thing and maintains the entire body. Regarding this—

Āyu usmāca viññāṇaṃ, yadā kāyaṃ jahantimaṃ;

Apaviddho tadā seti, niratthaṃva kaliṅgaranti vuttaṃ.

‘When life, heat, and consciousness abandon this body, then it lies cast aside, useless like a log of wood,’ it is said.

Tattha āyūti tesu dvīsu aggīsu patiṭṭhitaṃ jīvitameva vuccati. Usmāti te dve aggayo vuccanti. Yesu tikkhamandavasena visama bhūtesu kāye nānābādhā uppajjanti. Yathāha-bahvābādho hoti bahvātaṅko. Visamavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannā gato hoti atiuṇhāyaatisītalāyāti. Samabhūtesu pana sattā nirābādhā honti. Yathāha-appābādho hoti. Appātaṅko. Samavepākiniyāgahaṇiyā samannāgatohoti. Nātisītāya naccuṇhāya majjhimāya padhānakkhamāyāti. Keci pana asitādipācakaggismiṃ eva etaṃmaññanti. Therenacanāmarūpaparicchedejīvitanavakaṃ nāma, rūpaloke visuṃ siyāti vuttaṃ.

Therein, 'life' refers to the life faculty itself established in those two fires. 'Heat' refers to those two fires. When these are imbalanced in the body, being too sharp or too dull, various afflictions arise. As it is said: 'He is very sickly, very ailing, endowed with an imbalanced digestive faculty that is too hot or too cold.' But when they are balanced, beings are free from affliction. As it is said: 'He is not very sickly, not very ailing, endowed with a balanced digestive faculty that is not too cold and not too hot, but is moderate and fit for striving.' Some, however, think this pertains only to the digestive fire for what has been eaten, etc. And by the Elder, in the Nāmarūpapariccheda, it has been said: 'The life-nonad would exist separately in the fine-material world.'

Visuddhimagge [M 0.0321] pana sesesu catusamuṭṭhānesu aṭṭhasu jīvitanava kañceva tīṇi ojaṭṭhamakāni cāti tettiṃsa tettiṃsa rūpāni pākaṭāni hontīti vuttaṃ. Tattha aṭṭhasūti pācakaggiassāsa passāsavajjitesu tīsu tejokoṭṭhāsesu pañcasu vāyo koṭṭhāsesūti aṭṭhasu. Iti kāmalokepi sakalasarīrabyāpīsu tejovāyo koṭṭhāsesu labbhamānattā etaṃ sakala sarīreeva daṭṭhabbanti. Ettha siyā, kasmā panettha kāmaloke viya rūpaloke rūpakalāpānaṃ nirodhakkamo na vuttoti. Visesābhāvato, rūpalokepi hi maraṇakāle pana cuticitto pari sattarasamacittassa ṭhitikāla mupādāya kammajarūpāni nuppajjantītiādiko nirodhakkamo kāmalokasadisoyeva. Kevalaṃ panettha āhārajarūpa nirodhonāma natthi, tathā kaḷevara nikkhepoca. Tasmā tatthapi cuticittato paraṃ soḷasacittakkhaṇa parimāṇe ekasmiṃ khaṇe cittajarūpasantānaṃ vocchijjati. Tato paraṃ utusamuṭṭhānarūpaparaṃparā ekadviti accharākālamattaṃpi pavattitvā vocchijjatīti yuttaṃ. Naca ettakamattena kālena pavattamānāyapi rūpasantatiyā matakaḷevaraṃnāma sakkā laddhuṃ. Passantānaṃ ekakkhaṇena viya sarīrassa antaradhānassa paññāyanatoti. Yathāca rūpaloke, tathā kāmalokepi upapattidevānaṃ aññesañca opapātikānanti. Tesañhi sarīrāni paṭisandhikkhaṇeyeva sabbaso paripuṇṇena kammajakāyena nibbattattā kammajarūpehi ghanapūritāni sallahukabharāni ca honti. Itararūpāni kammajarūpesu patiṭṭhāya pavattanti. Tasmā tesaṃ cutikāle kammajarūpesu niruddhesu tāni tinna patiṭṭhāni hutvā ciraṃ santānaṃ ghaṭṭetuṃ nasakkonti. Thokaṃ pavattitvā sabbaso nirujjhanti. Sarīranikkheponāma tesaṃ natthīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

But in the Visuddhimagga it is said that in the remaining cases concerning the four origins, in eight locations, the life-nonad and the three octads with nutritive essence as the eighth—thus thirty-three material phenomena each—are prominent. There, 'in eight' means in the three sections of the heat element (excluding the digestive fire and in-and-out breathing) and in the five sections of the wind element. Thus, since this is found in the sections of the heat and wind elements that pervade the entire body even in the sensual world, it should be seen in the entire body. Here it might be asked: why is the order of cessation of material groups not stated here for the fine-material world as it is for the sensual world? Because there is no difference. For in the fine-material world too, at the time of death, from the static moment of the seventeenth mind-moment prior to the death-consciousness, kamma-born materiality does not arise, and so on; the order of cessation is just the same as in the sensual world. The only difference here is that there is no cessation of nutriment-originated materiality, nor is there the laying aside of a corpse. Therefore, there too, after the death-consciousness, in a period of sixteen mind-moments, the continuity of mind-originated materiality is cut off. Thereafter, the series of temperature-originated materiality, having continued for just the time of one or two finger-snaps, is also cut off. And a continuity of materiality that proceeds for such a short time cannot be called a corpse, because its disappearance is perceived by onlookers as if in a single moment. And as in the fine-material world, so too in the sensual world for deities born by spontaneous generation and for other spontaneously arisen beings. For their bodies, having been produced at the moment of rebirth-linking with a kamma-born body that is complete in every way, are densely filled with kamma-born materiality and are light. The other kinds of materiality arise depending on the kamma-born materiality. Therefore, at the time of their death, when the kamma-born materiality has ceased, those other kinds, being without a support, are unable to maintain their continuity for long. Having proceeded for a short while, they cease completely. It should be understood that for them there is no laying aside of a body.

[203] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

But as for what is said in the Vibhāvinī:

“Maraṇakāle pana brahmānaṃ sarīranikkhepābhāvato sabbesaṃpi tisamuṭṭhānāni dvisamuṭṭhānānica saheva nirujjhantī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

“But at the time of death, because Brahmās do not have the laying aside of a body, for all of them the material phenomena with three origins and with two origins cease together.” This statement is not sound.

Evañhi [M 0.0322] sati sabbesaṃ rūpabrahmānaṃ maraṇāsannacittāni rūpaṃ nasamuṭṭhāpentīti āpajjati. Na hi maraṇāsanna citta samuṭṭhitāni rūpāni kammajarūpehi saheva nirujjhantīti sakkā vattunti. Yathācatāni kammajarūpanirodhato thokaṃ pavattitvā nirujjhanti. Tathā utujarūpānipi cittajarūpanirodhato thokaṃ pavattitvā nirujjhantīti na na sakkā viññātuṃ. Naca tāvattakena kālena tesu pavatta mānesupi sarīranikkheponāma sakkā bhavitunti. Brahmānaṃ pana thina middhādīnaṃ nīvaraṇajātiyānaṃ atthitāya tadanurūpaṃ cittajarūpānaṃ tadanugatikānañca utujarūpānaṃ lahukagarukatādivikāro na na sambhavatīti lahutādittayaṃpi gahetvā vuttaṃ tevīsarūpesūti. Ghānādittayabhāvadvayavajjāni tevīsarūpāni honti. Tāniyeva cakkhu sotavatthu viññattidvayavajjāni asaññīnaṃ sattaraseva rūpāni hontīti yojanā. Asaññīnaṃ pana garulahutādipakāro cinte tabbo. Na vā cintetabbo rūpadhammānaṃ ruppanavikārassa bahukāraṇattāti. Upapattiyanti kāmarūpāsaññīnaṃ paṭisandhiyā uppādakkhaṇe. Uppādakkhaṇoeva hi ekantena upapattikhaṇonāma hotīti. Pavattetūti paṭisandhiyā ṭhitikkhaṇato paṭṭhāya sakale pavattikāle pana nakiñcipi nalabbhati. Labbhatiyevāti adhippāyo. Na hi idaṃnāma rūpaṃ pavatte nalabbhati. Paṭisandhiyaṃeva labbhatīti atthīti. [Rūpapavattikkamo]

If this were so, it would follow that the minds near death of all the Brahmās in the form realm do not produce materiality. For it cannot be said that materiality arisen from a mind near death ceases together with kamma-born materiality. And just as that mind-born materiality ceases after persisting for a short while following the cessation of kamma-born materiality, so too it is indeed possible to understand that temperature-born materiality also ceases after persisting for a short while following the cessation of mind-born materiality. And even if that materiality persists for such a short time, there cannot be what is called the laying aside of a body. However, for Brahmās, due to the existence of things of the nature of hindrances such as sloth and torpor, alteration in lightness or heaviness, etc., is indeed possible in the mind-born materiality that corresponds to them and in the temperature-born materiality that follows their course. Therefore, the triad of lightness, etc., is also included when it is said 'in the twenty-three forms.' Excluding the triad of nose, tongue, and body sensitivities, and the two sex faculties, there are twenty-three forms. And these same forms, excluding eye, ear, heart-base, and the two expressions, are only seventeen forms for non-percipient beings—this is the explanation. For non-percipient beings, the alteration of heaviness, etc., should be considered. Or it need not be considered, because the causes for the alteration of material phenomena are numerous. 'Upapattiyaṃ' means at the arising moment of rebirth-linking for beings in the sensual realm, form realm, and non-percipient realm. For the arising moment is indeed exclusively called the rebirth moment. 'Pavatte' means that from the static moment of rebirth-linking onwards, throughout the entire course of existence, it is not that anything is unobtainable; the intention is that it is indeed obtainable. For it is not the case that this or that form is unobtainable during the course of existence and is obtainable only at rebirth-linking—this is the meaning. [The Sequence of the Process of Materiality]

161. Evaṃ cittacetasika rūpasaṅgahaṃ katvā idāni yathā nuppattaṃ nibbānasaṅgahaṃ karonto nibbānaṃpanātiādi māha. Nibbānaṃ pana nibbānanti pavuccatīti sambandho. Lokuttarasaṅkhātanti lokuttaranti bhagavatā kathitaṃ, yathāha-katame dhammā lokuttarā. Cattāroca ariyamaggā cattārica sāmaññaphalāni asaṅkhatāca dhātu, ime dhammā lokuttarāti. Etena nibbānassa paññattimattabhāvaṃ nivatteti. Na hi lokavohārasiddhā paññatti lokuttarānāma sakkā bhavitunti. Catumaggañāṇena sacchikātabbanti cakkhumantena candamaṇḍalaṃviya cakkhunā paṭiladdhamaggañāṇehi ariyajanehi catūhi ariyamaggañāṇehi paccakkhato daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paṭivijjhitabbanti [M 0.0323] attho. Tattha catumaggañāṇenāti etena tādi samhā paṭipattimaggato vimukhānaṃ andhaputhujjanānaṃ jaccandhānaṃ viya canda maṇḍalassa tassa avisayabhāvaṃ dasseti. Na ca jaccandhānaṃ cakkhumhi anupaladdhamattena candamaṇḍalaṃ natthināma hotīti. Sacchikātabbanti etena paramatthato vijjamānabhāvaṃ dasseti. Yañhi kiñci paramatthato vijjamānaṃ nahoti. Taṃ sarūpato kassa paccakkhaṃnāma bhavissatīti. Tadubhayena panassa paññavantānaṃ kalyāṇakaputhujjanānaṃ anumānato siddhataṃ dīpeti, na hi anumānatopi attano buddhiyaṃ asiddhassa apākaṭassa sacchikiriyāya vāyāmopināma atthi. Yena sacchikiriyā siddhiyāti. Evaṃ nibbānassa paramatthato vijjamānataṃ dassetvā idāni kevalaṃ vijjamānamattameva na hoti. Athakho mahātejavantaṃ mahojavantañca taṃ hotīti dassetuṃ maggaphalānamālambaṇabhūtanti vuttaṃ. Etena nibbānena vināmagga phalānaṃ akiccasiddhiṃ dasseti. Tato tassa mahātejavanta taṃ mahojavantatañca dīpeti. Yathā hi mahiddhiko eko rājā hoti. Tassa raṭṭhe ekasmiṃ mahāgāme eko gāmabhojako ekoca corajeṭṭhako mahāparivāro vasati. Teca aññamaññaṃ vadhāya parisakkantā vicaranti. Tattha gāmabhojako nagaraṃ gantvā rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahi. So na cirasseva rājavallabho hoti. Rājato mahatiṃ āṇaṃ labhati. Taṃ sutvā corajeṭṭhako idāni idhavasantassa mamajīvitaṃ natthīti attano parivārena saddhiṃ aṭṭaviṃ paviṭṭho. Gāmabhojakoca taṃaṭṭaviṃ paviṭṭhaṃpi muñcituṃ adatvā gahetvā vadhi. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahiddhikarājā viya hi nibbānaṃ. Gāma bhojako viya ñāṇaṃ. Corajeṭṭhako viya moho. Parivāra corā viya sesakilesā. Pubbe rañño anupaṭṭhā nakāle gāmabhojako viya puthujjanañāṇaṃ. Upaṭṭhānakāle gāma bhojako viya maggañāṇanti. Taṇhā pavattamānā ajjhattabahiddhādi bhedesu khandhādidhammesu vinandhamānāva pavattati. Yathāha –

161. Having thus made the compilation of mind, mental factors, and form, now, in due course, making the compilation of Nibbāna, he said, 'Nibbāna, etc.' The connection is that Nibbāna is called Nibbāna. It is designated as supramundane because the Blessed One has declared it as supramundane, as he said: 'Which phenomena are supramundane? The four noble paths, the four fruitions of recluseship, and the unconditioned element—these phenomena are supramundane.' By this, the mere conceptual nature of Nibbāna is refuted. For a concept established by conventional usage cannot be supramundane. 'It is to be realized by the knowledge of the four paths' means it is to be seen directly by noble individuals who have attained the knowledge of the path through the eye of wisdom, by the four noble path-knowledges, just as the moon's disk is seen by one with eyes. The meaning is 'it is to be penetrated.' Here, by 'by the knowledge of the four paths,' it shows that for ordinary blind persons who are averse to the path of practice, it is beyond their range, just as the moon's disk is for those born blind. And it is not that the moon's disk does not exist merely because it is not perceived by the eyes of those born blind. By 'it is to be realized,' it shows its existence in the ultimate sense. For whatever does not exist in the ultimate sense—how could that be directly evident in its own nature to anyone? By both of these, it shows that for the wise and virtuous ordinary people, it is established by inference. For there is no effort to realize what is obscure and not established in one's own understanding even by inference, by which realization would be achieved. Having thus shown Nibbāna's existence in the ultimate sense, now, it is not merely existent. Rather, it is of great power and swift efficacy—to show this, it is said to be 'the support for the path and fruition.' By this, it shows the non-accomplishment of the purpose of the path and fruition without Nibbāna. Then, it illustrates its great power and swift efficacy. Just as there is a mighty king. In his kingdom, in a certain large village, there lives a village headman and a bandit chief with a large retinue. They constantly strive to kill each other. There, the village headman went to the city and attended upon the king. He soon became a favorite of the king. He received great authority from the king. Hearing that, the bandit chief thought, 'Now my life is not safe if I stay here,' and entered the forest with his retinue. And the village headman, not letting him escape even after he entered the forest, captured and killed him. This simile should be understood thus: Nibbāna is like the mighty king. Knowledge is like the village headman. Delusion is like the bandit chief. The bandit's followers are like the remaining defilements. Before attending the king, the village headman is like the knowledge of an ordinary person. When attending the king, the village headman is like the knowledge of the path. Craving, when active, continues to bind itself to phenomena such as the aggregates, etc., which are divided into internal, external, and so forth. As it is said:

Antojaṭā bahijaṭā, jaṭāya jaṭitā pajāti.

Inner tangle, outer tangle, this generation is entangled by a tangle.

Tasmā [M 0.0324] sā veḷugumbe veḷusākhā viya vinanaṭṭhena saṃsibbanaṭṭhena vānasamaññaṃ labhatīti vuttaṃ vānasaṅkhātāyataṇhāyāti. Nikkhantattāti nissaṭattā. Tassā visayabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitattāti attho. Etena vānato nikkhantanti nibbānanti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Sabhāvatoti santilakkhaṇena. Ajjhattasambhūtānaṃ tividhavaṭṭasantāpānaṃ nibbutiatthena. Tesaṃ sabbaso abhāvaṭṭhenāti attho. Ekavidhaṃpīti yathā cittaṃ sabhāvato ekavidhaṃpi jātidhammattā jātibhūmisampayogādi bhedena kāla disādesapuggalabhedenaca vatthuto bhinnameva hoti. Na tathā idaṃ nibbānaṃ. Idaṃ pana sabhāvatopi vatthutopi abhinnameva hutvā ekavidhaṃ hoti. Idañhi anamatagge saṃsāre atīte etarahi anāgateca parinibbutānaṃ buddhānaṃvā paccekabuddhānaṃvā buddhasāvakānaṃvā sabbesaṃpi ekameva hoti. Kasmā, aniddisitabbadhammattā. Viññāṇaṃ anidassanaṃ anantaṃ sabbatopabhanti hi bhagavatā vuttaṃ. Tattha viññāṇanti saṅkhatadhammānaṃ khayanirodhabhāvena siddhattā etaṃ tabbhāvenaeva suṭṭhu abhibyattaṃ katvā ñātabbaṃ. Anidassananti animittadhammattā bālaputhujjanānaṃ dassanavisayabhūtena kenacinimittena nidassituṃvā kālabhedena disādesapuggalasantāna bhedena hīnapaṇītādibhedena ca bhinnaṃ katvā nidassituṃvā nārahatīti attho. Anantanti pubbantāparantavirahitaṃ. Sabbatopabhanti vaṭṭadukkhapaṭipakkhasiddhehi anantehi guṇobhāsehi sabbato pabhāvantanti attho. Tathā aniddisitabbadhammattāca pana anamatagge saṃsāre sabbāsuca disāsu asukasmiṃ nāma kāle asukāyanāma disāya natthīti navattabbaṃ. Kasmā, ariyamaggaṃ bhāventena yadā kadāci yattha katthaci avassaṃ adhigantabbatāvasena sabbadā sabbattha ca labbhamānattā. Vuttañhetaṃ vinaye, aṅguttare, udāneca –

Therefore, like bamboo branches in a bamboo grove, it receives the designation 'vana' due to its nature of entangling or binding—thus it is said of craving, which is designated as 'vana.' 'Having departed' means having escaped. The meaning is that it stands beyond the sphere of that craving. By this, it is shown that 'departed from the forest (of craving)' means Nibbāna—this is the meaning. 'By its intrinsic nature' means by its characteristic of peace. It is in the sense of the quenching of the threefold torments of the cycle that have arisen internally. The meaning is in the sense of their complete absence. 'Of one kind': just as the mind, though by its intrinsic nature is of one kind, yet due to its nature of being subject to birth, becomes objectively diverse based on distinctions of class, plane, association, etc., and by differences of time, direction, place, and person. But this Nibbāna is not like that. This Nibbāna, however, remains undivided both by intrinsic nature and objectively, being of one kind. For in this beginningless cycle of existence, for all those who have attained final Nibbāna in the past, present, or future—whether they be Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples of the Buddha—it is just one. Why? Because it is a phenomenon that cannot be indicated. For the Blessed One has said: 'Consciousness that is non-manifesting, infinite, radiant all around.' Here, 'consciousness' should be understood as that which is established as the destruction and cessation of conditioned phenomena, having made that very state clearly manifest. 'Non-manifesting' means that because it is a signless phenomenon, it cannot be pointed out by any sign that is an object of perception for childish ordinary people; nor can it be shown as divided by distinctions of time, direction, person, or by distinctions of inferiority, superiority, and so on. 'Infinite' means without a beginning or an end. 'Radiant all around' means shining everywhere with the infinite radiances of its qualities, which are established as the counterpart to the suffering of the cycle. Moreover, because it is a phenomenon that cannot be indicated, in the beginningless cycle of existence, one cannot say that in such-and-such a time or in such-and-such a direction it does not exist. Why? Because it is necessarily attainable always and everywhere by one who develops the Noble Path, whenever and wherever. This has been stated in the Vinaya, the Aṅguttara, and the Udāna:

Seyyathāpi bhikkhave yākāci loke savantiyo mahāsamuddaṃ appenti. Yāca antalikkhā dhārā papatanti. Na tena mahāsamuddassa ūnattaṃvā pūrattaṃvā paññāyati. Eva meva kho [M 0.0325] bhikkhave bahūcepi bhikkhū anupādisesāya nibbāna dhātuyā parinibbāyanti. Na tena nibbānadhātuyā ūnattaṃ vā pūrattaṃvā paññāyatīti.

Just as, monks, whatever rivers in the world flow into the great ocean, and whatever streams of rain fall from the sky, no decrease or increase of the great ocean is perceived thereby. Even so, monks, even though many monks attain final Nibbāna by the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining, no decrease or increase of the Nibbāna-element is perceived thereby.

Aṭṭhakathāsuca na tena nibbānadhātuyā ūnattaṃvā pūrattaṃvā paññāyatīti asaṅkhyeyyepi mahākappe buddhesu anuppajjantesu ekasattopi parinibbātuṃ nasakkoti. Tadāpi tucchā nibbāna dhātūti nasakkā vattuṃ. Buddhakāle pana ekekasmiṃ samāgame asaṅkhyeyyāpi sattā amataṃ ārādhenti. Tadāpi nasakkā vattuṃ pūrā nibbānadhātūti vuttaṃ. Brahmanimantanasutteca viññāṇaṃ anidassanaṃ anantaṃ sabbatopabhanti vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyañca sabbatopabhanti sabbato pabhāsampannaṃ. Nibbānato hi añño koci dhammo pabhassaratarovā jotivantatarovā parisuddhatarovā paṇḍara tarovā natthi. Sabbatovā pabhūtameva hoti. Nakatthaci natthīti sabbatopataṃ. Puratthimadisādīsu hi asukadisāyaṃnāma nibbānaṃ natthīti navattabbanti vuttaṃ.

And in the commentaries, regarding 'no decrease or increase of the Nibbāna-element is perceived thereby,' it is said: Even in incalculable great eons when Buddhas do not arise, not even a single being is able to attain final Nibbāna. Even then, it cannot be said that the Nibbāna-element is empty. But during the time of a Buddha, in a single assembly, incalculable beings attain the Deathless. Even then, it cannot be stated that the Nibbāna-element is full. And in the Brahmanimantana Sutta it is said: 'Consciousness that is non-manifesting, infinite, luminous all around.' In the commentary, 'luminous all around' means endowed with luminosity in every way. For there is no other state more luminous, more radiant, more pure, or more brilliant than Nibbāna. Or, it is abundant in every way; it is all-pervading, which means it is not that it is nowhere. For it is said that one cannot state, 'Nibbāna does not exist in such-and-such a direction,' such as the east and so on.

Evaṃsantepi etaṃ niruddhatekālikadhamma sannissayena viññāya mānattā niruddhadhammabhedena bhinnaṃ katvā upacarituṃ labbhatīti vuttaṃ saupādisesātiādi. Tattha upādīyati taṇhādiṭṭhīhi bhusaṃ gaṇhīyatīti upādi. Upādinnakhandhapañcakaṃ. Soyeva ekadesenavā anavasesenavā pahīnehi kammakilesehi sesoti upādiseso. Saṃvijjati tasmiṃ santāne upādiseso yassā adhigatakāleti saupādisesā. Nibbānadhātūti nibbūtisa bhāvo. Saupādisesāca sā nibbānadhātucāti samāso. Natthi tasmiṃ santāne upādiseso yassā adhigatakāleti anupādisesā, anupādisesāca sā nibbānadhātucāti viggaho. Vuttañhetaṃ iti vuttake-dve mā bhikkhave nibbānadhātuyo. Katamā dve, saupādisesāca nibbānadhātu, anupādisesāca nibbānadhātūtiādi. Tattha purimā kilesanibbānaṃnāma. Pacchimā khandhanibbānaṃnāma. Purimāvā diṭṭhadhammika nibbānaṃnāma. Pacchimā samparāyika nibbānaṃnāma. [M 0.0326] Yathāha-ekā hi dhātu idha diṭṭhadhammikā saupādisesā bhavanetti saṅkhayā. Anupādisesā pana samparāyikāti. Aṅguttare pana sattanipāte ubhatobhāgavimutta paññāpi muttānaṃ dvinnaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ khandhupādisesavasena kāyasakkhidiṭṭhipatta saddhāvimuttadhammānusārīsaṅkhātānaṃ catunnaṃ sekkhānaṃ āraddhavipassa kassaca yogīkalyāṇaputhujjanassa kilesu pādisesavasena saupādisesatā anupādisesatāca vuttā. Tattheva navanipāte antarāparinibbāyī, upahaccaparinibbāyī, asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, uddhaṃ sotaakaniṭṭhagāmīti pañcannaṃ anāgāmīnaṃ sakadāgāmissa tiṇṇaṃ sotāpannānanti navannaṃ sekkhapuggalānaṃ kilesupādisesavasena saupādisesatā vuttā.

Although it is so, since this can be known by relying on the ceased momentary phenomena, it is said that it can be treated as distinct by way of the distinction of ceased phenomena, thus: 'with residue remaining,' etc. Herein, 'that which is clung to' (upādi) is that which is strongly grasped by craving and views; it is the five aggregates subject to clinging. Those very aggregates are the 'residue' (sesa) from the karma and defilements that have been abandoned either in part or without remainder; hence 'clinging-residue' (upādisesa). She for whom a clinging-residue exists in her continuity at the time of attainment is 'one with clinging-residue remaining' (saupādisesā). 'Nibbāna-element' is the state of extinguishment. 'The Nibbāna-element with clinging-residue remaining' is a compound. She for whom no clinging-residue exists in her continuity at the time of attainment is 'one without clinging-residue remaining' (anupādisesā); the analysis is: 'the Nibbāna-element that is without clinging-residue remaining.' This is stated in the Itivuttaka: 'Bhikkhus, there are these two Nibbāna-elements. What two? The Nibbāna-element with clinging-residue remaining and the Nibbāna-element without clinging-residue remaining…' Herein, the former is called the Nibbāna of the defilements; the latter, the Nibbāna of the aggregates. Or the former is called Nibbāna in this very life; the latter, Nibbāna pertaining to the future. As it is said: 'One element here is seen in this life, with residue remaining, for the destruction of the conduit to existence. But the one without residue remaining pertains to the future.' Further, in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, in the Book of the Sevens, for the two kinds of taint-destroyed ones—the one liberated in both ways and the one liberated by wisdom—the state of having a clinging-residue is spoken of in terms of the aggregates as residue. And for the four kinds of trainees—the body-witness, the one attained to view, the one liberated by faith, and the Dhamma-follower—and for the good worldling who is a yogi who has commenced insight, the state of having a clinging-residue and being without a clinging-residue is spoken of in terms of the defilements as residue. Therein, in the Book of the Nines, for nine kinds of trainees—the five kinds of non-returners (the one who attains parinibbāna in the interval, upon landing, without exertion, with exertion, and the one bound upstream for the Akaniṭṭha realm), the once-returner, and the three stream-enterers—the state of having a clinging-residue is spoken of in terms of the defilements as residue.

Nettiyaṃ pana arahattaphalaṃpi saupādisesanibbānanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ idha nādhippetaṃ. Etthaca maggakkhaṇe kilesānaṃ khayo saupādi sesaṃnāma. Cuti anantare khandhānaṃ anuppādo anupādisesaṃnāma. Yasmā pana paṭisandhivandhānāma kilesesu satieva jāyanti. Asati najāyanti, tasmā tepi kilesakkhayena saheva khiyyanti. Yāvacutiyā pavattamānaṃ paccuppannakhandhasantānaṃ pana khīṇāsavassapi purimabhave pavattakammakilesānaṃ phalanisandabhūtaṃ sabbasattānaṃ dhamma tāsiddhaṃ. Tasmā taṃ khīṇesupi kilesesu yāvacutiyā pavatta tiyeva. Cutikkhaṇe tassa nirodhopi dhammatānirodho eva. Yo pana tadanantare punabhavassa anuppādo. So kilesakkhayena saheva siddho. Na kevalaṃ tadanantare puna bhavasseva. Tato paraṃpi anamatagga saṃsāre bhavaparaṃparāya anuppādopi tena saheva siddho. Sabbañcetaṃ ekameva nibbānaṃ. Evaṃsantepi khandhāvasesassa bhāvā bhāvalesaṃ upādāya ayaṃ bhedo vuttoti vuttaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti kāraṇapariyāyenāti duvidha paññāpanassa kāraṇalesenāti attho.

But in the Netti, even the fruit of arahantship is called Nibbāna-with-residue-remaining. That is not intended here. And here, the destruction of the defilements at the moment of the path is called 'with residue remaining.' The non-arising of the aggregates immediately after the death-moment is called 'without residue remaining.' Because the bonds of rebirth-linking arise only when defilements are present, and do not arise when they are absent, they too are destroyed along with the destruction of the defilements. However, the present continuum of aggregates of one who has destroyed the taints, which continues until the death-moment, is the fruit and result of kamma and defilements performed in a previous existence; this is established by natural law for all beings. Therefore, even when the defilements are destroyed, it continues right up to the death-moment. At the death-moment, its cessation is just a cessation by natural law. But the non-arising of a future existence immediately after that is accomplished along with the destruction of the defilements. Not only the non-arising of the next existence, but also the non-arising of the succession of existences thereafter in beginningless saṃsāra is accomplished along with it. All this is just the one Nibbāna. Although this is so, it is said that this distinction is made on account of a trace of existence due to the presence of the remaining aggregates. Thus, when it is said, 'it is twofold by way of reason,' the meaning is that the twofold designation is on account of a trace of a reason.

Yasmā pana saṅkhatadhammānāma sapalibodhadhammattā nānāpalibodhehi niccakālaṃ janaṃ pīḷenti. Santasukhaṃnāma laddhuṃ nadenti. Sanimitta dhammattāca kilesānaṃ jarāmaraṇādīnañca sabbesaṃ anatthānaṃ vatthu bhūtā [M 0.0327] bhūmibhūtā honti. Sapaṇihitadhammattāca sabbadukkhānaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ āsādukkhaṃnāma niccakālaṃpi janenti. Tasmā tappaṭipakkhasiddhena guṇabhedena tividhaṃbhedaṃ dassetuṃ suññatantiādi māha. Tattha sabbapalibodha vivittattā suññataṃ. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā hi sati bālānaṃ yattakā pāpakammapalibodhā apāya dukkhapalibodhāca sandissanti. Paṇḍitānaṃca tato attānaṃ rakkhanatthaṃ yattakā kalyāṇakammapalibodhā sandissanti. Sakkāyadiṭṭhinirodhoyeva sabbe te sakkāyadiṭṭhimūlake palibodhe nirodhetuṃ sakkoti. Na vinā tena añño koci. Tasmā sonirodho tehi palibodhehi vivitto hoti, tathā rāgakkhayoyeva rāgamūlake palibodhe nirodhetuṃ sakkoti. Na vinā tena añño koci. Dosakkhayoyeva dosamūlake. Mohakkhayoyeva mohamūlaketiādi vattabbaṃ. Iti nibbānaṃ sabbapali bodhehi vivittattā suññataṃnāma.

Because conditioned phenomena, having a nature subject to troubles, constantly afflict people with various troubles and do not allow them to obtain the happiness of peace; and because they have the nature of being with a sign, they become the basis and ground for all calamities such as the defilements, aging, and death; and because they have the nature of being yearned for, they constantly generate the suffering of longing, which is the root of all suffering. Therefore, to show the threefold distinction by way of the distinction of qualities established as its opposite, it is said: 'emptiness,' etc. Herein, it is 'emptiness' because of its seclusion from all troubles. For when identity view exists, fools encounter as many troubles from unwholesome kamma and as many troubles from the suffering of the plane of misery as there are. And the wise, in order to protect themselves from that, encounter as many troubles from wholesome kamma as there are. Only the cessation of identity view can bring to cessation all troubles rooted in identity view; nothing else can do so without it. Therefore that cessation is secluded from those troubles. Similarly, only the destruction of lust can bring to cessation troubles rooted in lust; nothing else can do so without it. Only the destruction of hatred can bring to cessation those rooted in hatred. Only the destruction of delusion can bring to cessation those rooted in delusion, and so on. Thus, because Nibbāna is secluded from all troubles, it is called 'emptiness.'

Nimittaṃ vuccati uppādapavattamūlako oḷārikākāro. Yena samannāgatā saṅkhatadhammā sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ jarāmaraṇānañca vatthubhūtā bhūmibhūtā honti. Tathā sabbesaṃ mārānaṃ sabbesaṃ verānaṃ sabbesaṃ rogādi anatthānaṃ vatthubhūtā bhūmibhūtā honti. Yato te māradheyyātipi maccudheyyātipi vuccanti. Kāla disā desa santānādi bhedena hīnapaṇītādi bhedenaca bhedaṃ gacchanti. Nibbānaṃ pana sabbesaṃ nimittadhammānaṃ khayanirodhabhāvena siddhattā natthi. Tasmiṃ nimittanti animittaṃ. Tañhi sabbesaṃ kile sādīnaṃ anatthānaṃ vatthubhūte nimittadhamme viddhaṃsetvā tesaṃ anatthānaṃ abhāvaṃ sādhentaṃ niccaṃ tiṭṭhati. Naca taṃ kālabhedena bhinnaṃ hoti. Idaṃ atīte asukakappe asukabuddhassa nibbānaṃ, idaṃ anāgate, idaṃ etarahīti. Nāpi disābhedena bhinnaṃ. Idaṃ dasasu disāsu asukāyanāma disāya nibbānaṃ, idaṃ asukāya nāmāti. Nacāpi desabhedenavā santānabhedenavā bhinnaṃ. Idaṃ manussaloke idaṃ devaloke idaṃ brahmaloketi vā idaṃ manussānaṃ idaṃ devānaṃ idaṃ brahmānantivāti. Tathā paṇītādi bhedena [M 0.0328] bhinnaṃ na hoti. Idaṃ sabbaññubuddhānaṃ. Idaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ. Idaṃ buddhasāvakānanti.

'Sign' is the name for the gross feature that is the root of arising and occurrence. Endowed with this, conditioned phenomena become the basis and ground for all defilements, aging, and death. Similarly, they become the basis and ground for all Māras, all enmities, and all calamities such as disease. For this reason they are called 'the domain of Māra' and 'the domain of Death.' They undergo differentiation by way of distinctions of time, direction, location, continuity, etc., and by way of distinctions of inferior and superior, etc. But since Nibbāna is established through the destruction and cessation of all phenomena that are signs, there is no sign in it; hence it is 'the signless.' For, having demolished the phenomena that are signs—which are the basis for all calamities such as the defilements—it abides perpetually, having established the absence of those calamities. And it is not differentiated by distinctions of time, as in: 'This was the Nibbāna of such-and-such a Buddha in a past eon; this will be in the future; this is now.' Nor is it differentiated by distinctions of direction, as in: 'This is the Nibbāna in such-and-such a direction among the ten directions; this is in another.' Nor is it differentiated by distinctions of location or continuity, as in: 'This is in the human world, this in the deva world, this in the Brahma world,' or 'This is for humans, this for devas, this for Brahmas.' Similarly, it is not differentiated by distinctions such as superior, as in: 'This is for the Omniscient Buddhas, this for the Paccekabuddhas, this for the disciples of the Buddha.'

Paṇihitaṃ, paṇidhānaṃ, paṇidhi, patthanā, āsā, jīghacchā, pipāsāti atthato ekaṃ. Saṅkhatadhammāca labbhamānāpi bhijjanadhammattā punappunaṃ laddhuṃ āsā dukkhaṃnāma vaḍḍhenti. Āsādukkhassa pariyantonāma natthi. Sabbañca dukkhaṃ āsāmūlakaṃ hoti. Āsāsadisaṃ dukkhanidānaṃnāma natthi, nibbānaṃ pana sayaṃ pipāsavinayadhammattā āsāsaṅkhātaṃ sabbaṃ taṇhāpaṇidhiṃvā chandapaṇidhiṃvā vinentaṃ vidhamentaṃ vattatīti natthi. Tasmiṃ paṇihitanti appaṇīhitaṃ. Etthaca duvidhaṃ sukhaṃ vedayitasukhaṃ santisukhanti. Tattha manussa dibba brahma sampattiyo labhitvā anubhavanavasena pavattaṃ pītisomanassa sukhaṃ vedayitasukhaṃnāma. Taṃ pana khaṇekhaṇe vijjuviya bhijjanadhammaṃ. Sampattiyoca aniccadhammā. Sabbe te apariyantaṃ āsādukkhaṃ bhiyyo vaḍḍhentiyeva. Tasmā sabbaṃ vedayitasukhaṃnāma āsā dukkhajanakattā ekantena dukkhameva hoti. Yathāha-yaṃkiñci vedayitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhasminti. Dhammasenāpatināca katamaṃ taṃ āvuso sāriputta nibbāne sukhaṃ, yadettha vedayitaṃ natthīti puṭṭhena etadevettha āvuso nibbāne sukhaṃ, yadettha vedayitaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ. Santisukhaṃnāma attani uppannānaṃvā uppajjituṃ paccupaṭṭhi tānaṃvā kilesādīnaṃ apāyadukkhādīnañca attano sammāpayogaṃ paṭicca vimuccanasukhaṃ. Etadevettha ekantasukhaṃ acalasukhaṃ. Etasmiñhi asati puthujjanānaṃ manussa dibbabrahmasampattiyo anubhavantānaṃpi avassaṃ pattabbaṭṭhena paccupaṭṭhitāneva honti aviciniraya bhayādīnīti. Tasmā sabbassa vedayitasukhamūlakassa āsādukkhassa santisukhadīpakaṃ idaṃ appaṇihitapadaṃ nibbānassa ekaṃ mahantaṃ guṇapadaṃ hotīti.

Directed, aspiration, resolve, longing, hope, hunger, and thirst—these are one in meaning. Since conditioned phenomena, even when obtained, are by nature subject to perishing, the hope to obtain them again and again increases what is called suffering. There is no end to the suffering of hope. All suffering is rooted in hope. There is no source of suffering like hope. But Nibbāna, being itself the nature of the removal of thirst, proceeds by dispelling and destroying all that is called hope—whether the resolve of craving or the resolve of desire—so there is no such thing in it. That in which there is no directing is the 'undirected' (appaṇihita). Herein, happiness is twofold: the happiness of feeling and the happiness of peace. Therein, the happiness of joy and gladness that occurs by way of experiencing human, divine, and brahma-attainments is called the happiness of feeling. But this is by nature subject to perishing from moment to moment like lightning. And these attainments are impermanent. All of them only increase the endless suffering of hope all the more. Therefore, all that is called the happiness of feeling, because it generates the suffering of hope, is exclusively suffering. As it is said: 'Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering.' And when the General of the Dhamma was asked, 'Friend Sāriputta, what is the happiness in Nibbāna, since there is no feeling in it?' he replied, 'This itself, friend, is the happiness in Nibbāna: that there is no feeling in it.' The happiness of peace is the happiness of liberation that comes about through one's own right application, from the defilements, etc., and the sufferings of the plane of misery, etc., that have arisen in oneself or are present to arise. This itself is the exclusive happiness, the unshakable happiness. For when this is absent, even for worldlings enjoying human, divine, and brahma-attainments, the dangers of the Avīci hell, etc., are present as things that must inevitably be reached. Therefore, this term 'undirected,' which illuminates the happiness of peace for all suffering of hope rooted in the happiness of feeling, is a great quality-term of Nibbāna.

Ākāra bhedenāti tividhassa suññatādikassa guṇakoṭṭhāsassa bhedena. Etthaca yadetaṃ anamatagge saṃsāre ajjhattaṃ anusayitvā āgatānaṃ kilesānaṃ maggakkhaṇe ajjhattameva nirujjhanaṃ khiyyanaṃ. Taṃ khayadhātu nirodhadhātu saṅkhātaṃ ekaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ hoti. [M 0.0329] Ekā dhammadhātu hoti. Eko paramatthadhammo hoti. Khayaṭṭhena nirodhaṭṭhena sabhāvato vijjamānattā, na hi taṃ paññattirūpaṃ hoti. Kāye ñāṇeca sarūpato upaladdhattā, duvidhañhi nibbānassa sacchikaraṇaṃ kāyasacchikaraṇaṃ ñāṇasacchikaraṇañca. Yathāha-chandajāto ussahati. Ussahitvā tuleti. Tulayitvā padahati. Pahitatto samāno kāyenaceva paramatthasaccaṃ sacchikaroti. Paññāyaca taṃ paṭivijjha passatīti. Tattha anamatagge saṃsāre ajjhattaṃ niccaṃ santāpetvā paridayhitvā āgatānaṃ kilesānaṃ maggakkhaṇe ajjhattameva nirujjhanaṃ nibbāyanaṃ kāyasacchikaraṇaṃnāma. Evaṃ kāyena sacchikatvā puna paccavekkhanto ajjhattaṃ taṃ nirujjhanaṃ ñāṇena paccakkhato passati. Niruddhā me kilesāti jānāti, idaṃ ñāṇasacchikaraṇaṃnāma. Tesu kāya sacchikaraṇaṃ anantaṃ aparimāṇaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ khepeti. Ñāṇasacchikaraṇaṃ anappakaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppādeti. Paññattidhammesu eva rūpaṃ sacchikaraṇaṃnāma natthīti. Tassa pana nirujjhanassa suññatadhammattā mandabuddhīnaṃ tasmiṃ tucchasaññā niratthakasaññā saṇṭhāti. Animitta dhammattā tasmiṃ abhāvamattasaññā paramatthato avijjamānasaññā saṇṭhāti. Appaṇihitadhammattā taṇhāvasikā janā tasmiṃ sukhaṃ nāma kiñci natthīti maññanti.

'By the division of aspects' means by the division of the portion of qualities, such as the threefold emptiness, etc. And here, the destruction and wasting away, at the moment of the path, of the defilements that have come along lying dormant internally in beginningless saṃsāra—this internal cessation is called the destruction element and the cessation element; it is one mind-object base, one Dhamma element, one ultimate reality. Because it exists by its own nature with the meaning of destruction and cessation, it is not a mere concept. And because it is apprehended in its own nature by the body and by knowledge, the realization of Nibbāna is twofold: realization by the body and realization by knowledge. As it is said: 'Having generated desire, one strives. Having striven, one weighs. Having weighed, one exerts oneself. Having exerted oneself, one realizes the ultimate truth with the body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom.' Therein, the internal cessation and extinguishing, at the moment of the path, of the defilements that have come along constantly tormenting and scorching one internally in beginningless saṃsāra, is called 'realization by the body.' Having thus realized it with the body, when reviewing it again, one sees that internal cessation directly with knowledge. One knows, 'My defilements have ceased.' This is called 'realization by knowledge.' Of these, realization by the body brings to an end the endless, immeasurable suffering of the round. Realization by knowledge gives rise to no little joy and gladness. In the case of mere concepts, there is no such thing as realization. But because that cessation has the nature of emptiness, for those of dull wisdom the perception of it as void and the perception of it as useless arise. Because it has the nature of signlessness, the perception of it as mere non-existence and the perception of it as ultimately non-existent arise. Because it has the nature of the undirected, people under the sway of craving think, 'There is no happiness whatsoever in it.'

Ye pana yathāvuttaṃ khayanirodhamattaṃ nibbānaṃnāma nahoti. Tañhi abhāvamattaṃ paññattirūpaṃ hoti. Nibbānañcanāma gambhīrādīnaṃ anantaguṇānaṃ vatthu hoti, naca abhāvamattaṃ tesaṃ vatthu bhavituṃ arahati. Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhanti vuttaṃ. Naca abhāvamatte kiñci sukhaṃnāma sakkāladdhuṃ. Tasmā yo tassa khayanirodhassa paccayo atthi. Yassaca ānubhāvena so khayanirodho sijjhati. Eta deva nibbānaṃ nāmāti icchanti. Tesaṃpi vaṭṭadukkha santito atirekapayojanaṃnāma nalabbhati. Nibbānassaca guṇapadāni nāma anantānaṃ vaṭṭadhammānaṃ paṭipakkhavasena sijjhanti, no aññathā. Tasmā yattakāni aguṇapadāni vaṭṭadhammesu labbhanti, tattakāni tesaṃ khaya nirodhe anantāni guṇapadāni hutvā sijjhanti. Yo khayanirodhopi [M 0.0330] tāva visuṃ dhammabhāvenaviññātuṃ dukkarogambhīro hoti. Yato taṃ abhāvamattaṃ paññattirūpaṃ maññanti. Guṇapadānaṃ panassa gambhīrabhāve vattabbamevanatthi. Santisukhañca nāma vaṭṭadukkhānaṃ vūpasantatāeva. Tesaṃ vūpasamo sukhoti hi vuttaṃ. Vūpasantatātica tesaṃ sabbaso khayanirodhoevāti vaṭṭadukkhapariyāpannānaṃ sabba vedayītasukhānaṃ ukkaṃsagatā tassa khayanirodhassa paramasukhatā siddhā hotīti. Tassa pana paramatthato vijjamānabhāve tāva idaṃ suttaṃ.

But some hold that Nibbāna is not mere destruction and cessation as stated. For that, they say, is a mere concept of non-existence. Nibbāna is the ground for infinite qualities such as profundity, etc., and a mere non-existence is not fit to be the ground for them. It is said, 'Nibbāna is the ultimate happiness,' and no happiness whatsoever can be obtained in mere non-existence. Therefore, they maintain that Nibbāna is that which is the condition for this destruction and cessation, by the power of which that destruction and cessation is accomplished. For them, too, no benefit is found beyond the peace from the suffering of the round. And the quality-terms of Nibbāna are established by way of being the opposite of the infinite phenomena of the round, not otherwise. Therefore, however many terms for bad qualities are found in the phenomena of the round, just so many infinite quality-terms are established in their destruction and cessation. This destruction-cessation itself is profound and difficult to cognize as a distinct reality, which is why they consider it a mere concept of non-existence. But as to the profundity of its quality-terms, there is nothing to be said. And the happiness of peace is just the pacification of the sufferings of the round. For it is said, 'Their pacification is happiness.' And since their pacification is their complete destruction and cessation, the ultimate happiness of that destruction-cessation is established as the supreme state over all happiness of feeling included in the suffering of the round. Now, as to its existing in an ultimate sense, there is this sutta:

Atthi bhikkhave ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhataṃ. No ce taṃ bhikkhave abhavissa ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhataṃ, na yimassa jātassa bhūtassa katassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇaṃ paññāyetha. Yasmāca kho bhikkhave atthi ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhataṃ, tasmā jātassa bhūtassa katassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇaṃ paññāyatīti.

Monks, there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned. If, monks, there were not that unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, an escape from what is born, become, made, and conditioned would not be discerned. But because there is, monks, an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, therefore an escape from what is born, become, made, and conditioned is discerned.

Tattha ajānanaṃ ajātaṃ. Jātikkhayoti attho. Abhavanaṃ abhūtaṃ. Abhāvoti attho. Akaraṇaṃ akataṃ. Asaṅkharaṇaṃ asaṅkhataṃ. Uppādetuṃvā pavattetuṃvā saṅkhāradukkhassa abhāvoti attho. Jātikkhayotivā visuṃ ekā dhammadhātu hoti. Tasmā visuṃ dhammabhāvaṃ sandhāya natthi jātaṃ etthāti ajātantīpi yujjatiyeva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, saṅkhatadhammānāma paccaye sati jāyanti. Asati na jāyantīti jātaṃ viya ajātaṃpi tesaṃ atthi. Paramatthato vijjamānaṃ hotīti attho. Yadica ajātaṃnāma natthi, jātameva atthi. Evaṃsati attani kilesānaṃ ajātatthāya sammā paṭipajjantānaṃpi sabbe kilesadhammā jātāyeva siyuṃ. No ajātā. Kasmā, ajātassanāma natthitāyāti. Esanayo sabbesu duccaritadhammesu apāyadukkhavaṭṭadukkhesu, diṭṭhadhammeca sabbesu rogābādhabhayupaddavesu. Evañca sati loke sabbe purisakārā purisathāmā purisaparakkamā niratthakā eva siyunti imamatthaṃ sandhāya no cetaṃ bhikkhave.La. Paññāyethāti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana [M 0.0331] ajātaṃnāma ekantena atthiyeva. Tasmā attani ajātatthāya sammāpaṭipajjantānaṃ te ekantena najāyanti. Evaṃ sati sabbe purisakārā purisathāmā purisaparakkamā satthakā eva hontīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya yasmāca kho bhikkhavetiādi vuttaṃ. Ettāvatā avijjānirodhā saṅkhāra nirodho. Saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho.La. Dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotīti evaṃ vuttassa nirodhassa paramatthato vijjamānabhāvaṃ dasseti. Atthi saddassa vijjamānatthavacanattā. Tattha nirodho duvidho jātanirodho ajātanirodhoti. Tattha uppajjitvā nirodho jātanirodhonāma. Maccūtica maraṇantica etassevanāmaṃ. Ajjhattapariyā pannānaṃ kilesādīnaṃ uppādassapi sabbaso abhāvo ajāta nironāma. Yo sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbupadhinissaggo taṇhakkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbānanti vuccati. Ayamidhādhippeto, ayameva hi sabbapalibodhehi suññattā suññatonāma. Kilesānaṃ jārāmaraṇādīnañca vatthubhūtassa nimittassa abhāvā animittonāma. Sabbadukkhānaṃ nidānabhūtassa āsādukkhassa abhāvā appaṇihitonāma. Tena vuttaṃ suññataṃanimittaṃ appaṇihitañceti tividhaṃ hotīti. Padantiādi nibbānassa vevacanāni. Tañhi visuṃ asaṃmisso kevalo upalabbhamāno eko paramattha dhammoti padaṃ nāma. Koṭṭhāsattho hi padasaddo. Yathā padaso dhammaṃ vāceyyāti. Cavanābhāvena accutaṃ. Pubbantāparante atikkamma pavattattā accantaṃ. Saṅkharaṇakiccarahitattā asaṅkhataṃ. Attano uttaritarassa kassaci dhammassa abhāvato anuttaranti. Vānamuttā taṇhā vimuttā, mahante sīlakkhandhādike dhamme esiṃsu adhigacchiṃsūti mahesayo, buddhā.

Therein, non-arising is the unborn. The meaning is the destruction of birth. Non-becoming is the unbecome; the meaning is non-existence. Non-doing is the undone. Non-forming is the unformed.
