The meaning is the non-existence of the suffering of formations, whether to be produced or to be continued. Alternatively, the destruction of birth is a distinct element of reality. Therefore, with reference to this distinct nature of phenomena, 'there is no birth in this' is also fittingly called 'the unborn.' This is what is said: Conditioned phenomena arise when a condition is present; when it is absent, they do not arise. Thus, for them, there is the unborn as well as the born. The meaning is that it exists in an ultimate sense. If what is called 'the unborn' did not exist, and only the born existed, then even for those practicing rightly for the non-arising of defilements in themselves, all defilements would be born, not unborn. Why? Because of the non-existence of what is called 'the unborn.' This principle applies to all unwholesome phenomena, to the suffering of the planes of misery and the round of existence, and in the present life to all diseases, afflictions, fears, and calamities. And if this were so, all human effort, strength, and exertion in the world would be meaningless. It is with this meaning in mind that it was said: 'This is not so, monks...' But because the unborn certainly does exist, for those practicing rightly for the non-arising of defilements in themselves, those defilements certainly do not arise. In that case, all human effort, strength, and exertion are indeed meaningful. It is with this meaning in mind that it was said: 'And because, monks...' and so on. To this extent, it shows the ultimate existence of the cessation spoken of thus: 'With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases... the cessation of this whole mass of suffering occurs.' This is because the word 'is' (atthi) denotes existence. Therein, cessation is twofold: cessation of the born and cessation of the unborn. Therein, cessation after having arisen is called 'cessation of the born'; this is another name for death and dying. The complete absence of the arising of internal defilements and so on is called 'cessation of the unborn.' This is what is called the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all substrata, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. This is what is intended here. Indeed, this itself, because of its emptiness of all obstacles, is called 'emptiness.' Because of the absence of the sign that is the basis for defilements, aging, death, and so on, it is called 'the signless.' Because of the absence of the suffering of longing, which is the source of all suffering, it is called 'the desireless.' Therefore it is said to be threefold: emptiness, the signless, and the desireless. 'State' (pada) and so on are synonyms for Nibbāna. For it is a single ultimate phenomenon found separately, unmixed, and alone; thus it is called a 'state.' The word pada has the meaning of a part, as in 'one should recite the Dhamma part by part.' Because of the absence of passing away, it is 'the imperishable' (accutaṃ). Because it proceeds by transcending the beginning and the end, it is 'the ultimate' (accantaṃ). Because it is without the function of forming, it is 'the unformed' (asaṅkhataṃ). Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is higher than it, it is 'the unsurpassed' (anuttaraṃ). They are released from vāna, that is, freed from craving. The great seers (mahesayo)—the Buddhas—are so called because they sought (esiṃsu) and attained (adhigacchiṃsu) great qualities (mahante dhamme), such as the aggregate of virtue and so on.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus in the Paramatthadīpanī on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.

Catutthavaṇṇanāya rūpanibbāna saṅgahassa

In the fourth explanation, of the compendium of material form and Nibbāna.

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The Paramatthadīpanī is concluded.

Samuccaya saṅgaha paramatthadīpanī

The Compendium of Collections: An Elucidation of the Ultimate Meaning

162. Evaṃ [M 0.0332] chahi paricchedehi cattāro paramatthe dassetvā idāni tesaṃ taṃtaṃrāsisaṅkhātaṃ samuccayaṃ dassento ādigātha māha. Ye salakkhaṇā dvāsattatividhā vatthudhammā mayā vuttā. Idāni tesaṃ samuccayaṃ yathāyogaṃ pavakkhāmīti yojanā. Tattha salakkhaṇāvatthudhammāti padehi dasavidhāni anipphannarūpāni paṭikkhipati. Na hi tāni attano āvenikabhūtena sabhāva lakkhaṇena aniccatādi sāmaññalakkhaṇenaca salakkhaṇāni honti. Ekantaparamatthatāya abhāvato. Tatoyevaca vatthudhammāca nahonti. Sarūpato anupalabbhamānattā. Dabbavācako hi idha vatthusaddo. Dabbañcanāma idha sarūpato labbhamāno sabhāvo eva. Etena nibbānassapi maggaphala paccavekkhanañāṇesu sarūpato labbhamāna sabhāvatā vuttā hoti. Anipphannarūpānaṃ viya ca vatthudhamma sannissayena dissamānadhammamattabhāvaṃ vā paññattidhammānaṃ viya parikappitākāramattabhāvaṃvā sasavisāṇa kacchapalomādīnaṃ viya sabbaso abhūta parikappita mattabhāvaṃvā nivāretīti veditabbaṃ. Etthaca dvāsattatividhāsalakkhaṇāvatthudhammāti vacane payojanaṃ nadissati. Tesu hi dvāsattatividhesu ekacce eva dhammā purimesu tīsu saṅgahesu āgatā. Pacchimeca sabbasaṅgahe anipphannarūpānipi adhippetānievāti. Etthaca vatthudhammāsalakkhaṇāti padehi anipphannarūpānaṃ salakkhaṇatā paṭikkhipane yaṃ vattabbaṃ. Taṃ rūpasamuddesa dīpaniyaṃ vuttamevāti. Ekantākusalajātiyānaṃ āsava catukkādīnaṃ saṅgaho akusalasaṅgaho, na akusala sampayuttattāyeva akusalabhūtānaṃ cittaphassādīnanti. Kusalā kusalābyākatamissakānaṃ saṅgaho missakasaṅgaho.

162. Having thus shown the four ultimate realities in six chapters, now, to present their respective collections, reckoned as a compendium, he states the opening verse. The connection is as follows: 'The seventy-two kinds of real phenomena with specific characteristics have been stated by me. Now I will explain their collection as is appropriate.' Here, by the terms 'real phenomena with specific characteristics,' the ten types of underived material form are rejected. For they do not possess specific characteristics by way of their own unique intrinsic nature, nor general characteristics such as impermanence, because they are not exclusively ultimate realities. For that very reason, they are not real phenomena, as they cannot be apprehended in their own nature. Indeed, here the word 'vatthu' (phenomenon) is a term for 'dabba' (substance). And 'dabba' here is simply the intrinsic nature that can be apprehended in its own right. By this it is said that Nibbāna, too, has an intrinsic nature that can be apprehended in its own right in the reviewing knowledges of path and fruition. And it should be understood that this rejects the mere state of a phenomenon that appears dependent on a real phenomenon, like underived material forms; or the mere state of a conceptualized form, like concepts; or the mere state of an entirely unreal fabrication, like a hare’s horn or a tortoise’s hair. Here, the purpose of the phrase 'seventy-two kinds of real phenomena with specific characteristics' is not apparent. For among those seventy-two, only some phenomena are included in the first three compendia, while in the final Miscellaneous Compendium, underived material forms are also intended. Here, what should be said regarding the rejection of the possession of specific characteristics by underived material forms by the terms 'real phenomena with specific characteristics' has already been stated in the Elucidation of the Summary of Material Form. The Unwholesome Compendium is the compendium of the tetrad of cankers and so on, which are of an exclusively unwholesome nature; it is not the compendium of things like consciousness and contact, which become unwholesome merely by association with the unwholesome. The compendium of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate things mixed together is the Mixed Compendium.

Bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ, bujjhanti etāyāti katvā. Bodhiyā pakkhā bodhipakkhā. Bodhisambhārāti attho. Bodhi pakkhesu bhavā [M 0.0333] antogadhāti bodhipakkhiyā. Tesaṃ saṅgahoti bodhipakkhiyasaṅgaho. Sabbesaṃ anavasesānaṃ paramatthadhammānaṃ saṅgaho sabbasaṅgaho. Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena madaniyaṭṭhenaca āsava sadisattā āsavā. Yadica tadubhayaṭṭhena āsavānāma siyuṃ. Ime lobhādayo eva āsavānāma siyuṃ. Pupphāsavādayo hi loke cha pañca rattimattaṃ vā sattaṭṭharattimattaṃ vā sayaṃpi kumbhesu parivāsaṃ gaṇhanti. Kumbheca parivāsaṃ gāhāpenti. Ime pana anamatagge saṃsāre sayaṃpi sattasantāne parivāsaṃ gaṇhanti. Sattasantānañca parivāsaṃ gāhāpenti. Sakalaṃ sattasantānaṃ sadā āsavapūritameva hoti. Yathāha-cakkhuṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati. Ettha nivīsamānā nivīsatītiādi. Tattha esā taṇhā pariyuṭṭhānavasena uppajjamānā ettheva uppajjati. Uppajjitvāca puna anusayabhāvena parivāsaṃ katvā nivīsamānā ettheva nivīsatīti attho. Yāvaca ariyamaggadhovanaṃ nalabbhati. Tāva santānaṃ gūthapūritakūpaṃ viya dubbisodhaṃ katvā pavattati. Pupphāsavādayoca madaṃ janentā muhuttameva janenti. Ime pana yāva ariyamaggaṃ nalabhati. Tāva niccamadaṃ janenti. Tasmā ekantena imeyeva cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena madani yaṭṭhenaca āsavānāma bhavituṃ arahantīti.

Bodhi is called knowledge in the four paths, because one awakens by means of it. The wings of enlightenment are the bodhipakkhā. The meaning is 'requisites of enlightenment.' Those included within the wings of enlightenment are the bodhipakkhiyā. Their collection is the bodhipakkhiyasaṅgaho. The collection of all ultimate realities without omission is the sabbasaṅgaho. Due to their long-standing residence and intoxicating nature, they are similar to āsavas (fermented liquors), hence they are called āsavas (cankers). If indeed they are called āsavas by both these meanings, then this very greed and so forth are truly the āsavas. Indeed, in the world, flower-wines and such reside by themselves in jars for only five or six nights, or at most seven or eight nights, and they cause residence in jars. But these, throughout beginningless saṃsāra, reside by themselves in the continuum of beings, and cause the continuum of beings to take up residence. The entire continuum of beings is always filled with āsavas. As it is said: “The eye in the world is a form that is beloved and agreeable; there this craving arises when it arises, and there it settles when it settles,” and so on. There, this craving, arising by way of obsession, arises right there. And having arisen, it then settles right there, having taken up residence again in the form of latent tendencies; this is the meaning. And until the washing by the noble path is attained, the continuum persists, having become difficult to cleanse like a pit filled with filth. And flower-wines and such, producing intoxication, produce it only for a moment. But these, until the noble path is attained, produce constant intoxication. Therefore, it is absolutely fitting that these alone, due to their long-standing residence and intoxicating nature, are called the āsavas.

Visandanaṭṭhenavā āsavasadisattā āsavā, yathā hi kudhita kuṭṭhino mahāvaṇamukhehi yūsasaṅkhāto āsavo visanditvā pilotikakhaṇḍāni dūseti, evaṃ imepi chahidvārehi visanditvā chaḷārammaṇānidūsentīti. Āyataṃvā saṃsāradukkhaṃ savantipasavanti vaḍḍhentīti āsavā. Athavā, bhavato ābhavaggā dhammato āgotratumhā savanti ārammaṇakaraṇavasena pavattantīti āsavā. Āsaddassa avadhiatthajotakattā. Avadhica duvidho mariyādavisayo abhividhivisayocāti tattha yassa sambandhinīkriyā avadhibhūtaṃ attānaṃ bahikatvā pavattati. So mariyādavisayo nāma. Yathā āpātaliputtā devo vuṭṭhoti. Yassa sambandhinīkriyā avadhibhūtaṃ attānaṃ byāpetvā anto katvā pavattati, so [M 0.0334] abhividhivisayonāma. Yathā ābrahmalokā bhagavato kittisaddo abbhuggatoti. Idha pana abhividhivisayo daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā bhavaggañca gotrabhuñca byāpetvā anto katvā savantīti attho veditabbo.

Or, they are called āsavas because of their similarity to a discharge in the sense of flowing out. Just as the pus from an inflamed leper's large open wounds flows out and soils pieces of cloth, so too these flow out through the six sense doors and soil the six sense objects. Alternatively, they are called āsavas because they make the long-drawn-out suffering of saṃsāra flow, produce it, and increase it. Or, they are called āsavas because they flow up to the peak of existence and up to the state of change-of-lineage, proceeding by way of taking them as object. The prefix 'ā' indicates the meaning of a limit. A limit is twofold: the sphere of boundary and the sphere of pervasion. Therein, that whose related action proceeds by excluding the limit itself is called the sphere of boundary. For example, 'It rained from Pāṭaliputta.' That whose related action proceeds by pervading and including the limit itself is called the sphere of pervasion. For example, 'The Blessed One's fame rose up to the Brahma-world.' Here, however, the sphere of pervasion should be understood. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: they flow pervading and including both the peak of existence and change-of-lineage.

[204] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[204] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Avadhica mariyādaabhividhivasena duvidhoti vatvā puna taṃ vibhāvento “tattha āpātaliputtā devo vuṭṭhotiādīsuviya kriyaṃ bahikatvā pavatto mariyādo. Ābhavaggāsaddo abbhuggatotiādīsuviya kriyaṃ byāpetvā pavatto abhividhī”ti vadati. Taṃ na yujjati.

Having said that the limit is twofold by way of boundary and pervasion, again, explaining it, he says: 'Therein, as in such cases as, "It rained from Pāṭaliputta," the boundary proceeds by excluding the action. As in such cases as, "The sound rose up to the peak of existence," pervasion proceeds by pervading the action.' This is not tenable.

Na hi avavidhivisayabhūto bhavaggo lokattayabyāpakaṃ saddassa abbhuggamanakriyaṃ byāpetvā pavattati. Naca avadhibhūto attho kriyaṃ bahivā antovā katvā pavattatīti yutto. Kriyāeva pana taṃ bahivā antovā katvā pavattatīti yutto. Evañca katvā mūlaṭīkāyaṃ-duvidhohi avadhi abhividhivisayo anabhividhivisayoca. Abhividhivisayaṃ kriyābyāpetvā pavattati, ābhavaggā bhagavato yaso gatoti. Itaraṃ bahikatvā, āpātaliputtā vuṭṭho devoti. Kāmeti icchatīti kāmo. Soeva āsavoti kāmāsavo. Kāmīyativā oḷārikena kāmena icchīyatīti kāmo. Pañcakāmaguṇamukhena desito sabbo kāmāvacaradhammo. Idha pana taṃ nāmena tadārammaṇā taṇhāeva adhippetā, kāmoeva āsavoti kāmāsavo. Kāmāvacaradhammesu assādanābhinandana vasena pavatto kāmarāgo. Therena pana ayamatthova icchito. Vakkhati hi kāmabhava nāmena tabbatthukā taṇhā adhippetāti.

For the peak of existence, being the object of the sphere of pervasion, does not proceed by pervading the action of the sound's rising, which pervades the three worlds. And it is not tenable that the limit proceeds by making the action external or internal; rather, it is the action that proceeds by making the limit external or internal. And so, in the Mūlaṭīkā it is said: 'For a limit is twofold: the sphere of pervasion and the sphere of non-pervasion. The action proceeds pervading the sphere of pervasion, as in: "The Blessed One's fame went up to the peak of existence." It proceeds excluding the other, as in: "It rained from Pāṭaliputta."' One desires (kāmeti), that is, one wishes (icchati), thus it is 'sensual pleasure' (kāma). That itself is the canker (āsava), thus 'canker of sensual pleasure' (kāmāsava). Or, it is desired (kāmīyati), that is, it is wished for (icchīyati) with coarse desire, thus it is 'sensual pleasure.' This refers to all phenomena of the sense-sphere, taught by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Here, however, by this name only the craving that has them as its object is intended. Sensual pleasure itself is the canker, thus 'canker of sensual pleasure.' This is sensual lust, which proceeds by way of savoring and delighting in phenomena of the sense-sphere. But this is the very meaning intended by the Elder. For it will be said: 'By the name "sensual existence," craving based on that is intended.'

[205] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[205] But in the Vibhāvanī:

Purimatthova vutto. So anupapanno, theramatānugatassa idhādhippetassa atthassa avuttattā.

The former meaning has been stated. That is untenable, because the meaning intended here, which follows the Elder's view, has not been stated.

Bhavāsavoti [M 0.0335] ettha duvidho bhavo kammabhavo upapattibhavo ca. Tattha mahaggatakusaladhammā kammabhavo. Taṃnibbattā vipāka dhammā upapattibhavo. Idhapi bhavasaddena tadārammaṇā taṇhāeva adhippetā. Bhavoeva āsavoti bhavāsavo. Tasmiṃ duvidhe bhave nikantivasena pavatto rūpārūparāgo.

Regarding the canker of existence, here existence (bhava) is of two kinds: kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. Among these, wholesome states pertaining to the sublime planes are kamma-existence. The resultant states produced by that are rebirth-existence. Here too, by the word 'existence,' craving that takes those as its object is what is meant. Existence itself is the canker, thus the canker of existence. This is the lust for the form and formless realms, which proceeds by way of desire for those two kinds of existence.

[206] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[206] But as to what is in the Vibhāvanī:

“Sassata diṭṭhisahagatoca rāgo ettheva saṅgayhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yuttaṃ.

'Lust accompanied by the view of eternalism is included right here,' it is said. That is not proper.

Bhavāsavo catūsu diṭṭhigata vippayutta lobhasahagatesu cittuppādesu uppajjatīti hi aṭṭhakathākaṇḍe vuttaṃ. Yattha pana kāmataṇhā bhavataṇhā vibhavataṇhāti āgataṃ. Tattheva sassatadiṭṭhi sahagato rāgo yākāci kusalākusala kammabhavanikanti yākāci upapattibhavapatthanā. Sabbā bhavataṇhāyaṃ saṅgahitāti yuttā. Idha pana yathāvuttaṃ bhavāsavaṃ thapetvā sabbo lobho kāmāsave eva saṅgahitoti yuttoti.

For it is said in the commentary section that the canker of existence arises in the four types of consciousness accompanied by greed and dissociated from views. But where it is said, 'craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence,' there it is fitting that lust accompanied by the eternalist view, any desire for wholesome or unwholesome kamma-existence, and any aspiration for rebirth-existence are all included in craving for existence. Here, however, it is fitting that, apart from the canker of existence as described, all greed is included only in the canker of sensual pleasure.

[207] Eteneva yañca tattha vuttaṃ.

[207] And by this very same reasoning, what was said there:

“Tatiyo bhādiṭṭhisahagato”ti. Taṃpi paṭikkhittaṃ hoti.

'The third is accompanied by view.' That too is rejected.

Yākāci diṭṭhi diṭṭhāsavo. Yokoci moho avijjāsavo. Ettha siyā, kasmā ime eva āsavāti vuttā. Nanu aññepi mānādayo cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhādiyuttā eva hontīti. Saccaṃ. Imesu pana kāmāsave parivuṭṭhe sati sabbekāmavisayā mānādayo parivuṭṭhāeva honti. Tasmiṃ vimutte vimuttāeva, tathā bhavāsave parivuṭṭhe sati bhavavisayā. Diṭṭhāsaveca parivuṭṭhe sati diṭṭhivisayāti. Avijjāpana tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃpi mūlabhūtāti. Iti ime eva pārivāsiyaṭṭhādīsu padhānabhūtā honti. Itare pana tadanubandhamattāeva sampajjantīti na te āsavāti visuṃ vattuṃ arahantīti. Attani patitaṃ janaṃ anassāsikaṃ katvā ajjhottha ranto [M 0.0336] hanati māretīti ogho. Pakatimahogho. Tathā avahananaṭṭhena duttaraṭṭhenaca oghasadisāti oghā. Yadica avahaññanaṭṭheca duttaraṭṭhenaca oghānāma siyuntiādiko pasaṅgo mānādīnañca oghabhāva parihāro vutta nayena veditabbo.

Whatever view there is, that is the canker of views. Whatever delusion there is, that is the canker of ignorance. Here one might ask: 'Why are only these called cankers? Are there not others, like conceit and so on, which are also endowed with the quality of being long-resident, etc.?' True. But when the canker of sensual pleasure is present with its retinue, all things related to sensual pleasure, such as conceit and so on, are also present with their retinue. When one is liberated from that, they are also liberated. Similarly, when the canker of existence is present with its retinue, so are things related to existence; and when the canker of views is present with its retinue, so are things related to views. And ignorance is the root of all three. Thus, these are the primary ones among those that are long-resident, etc. The others, however, arise merely as their attendants and thus do not deserve to be called cankers separately. A flood is that which, having made a person who has fallen into it helpless, overwhelms, strikes, and kills them. It is a great flood by nature. Similarly, because they are like a flood in the sense of carrying away and being difficult to cross, they are called floods. As for the objection, 'If they are called floods because of the characteristic of carrying away and being difficult to cross…,' the refutation of pride and the like being floods should be understood in the way stated.

Vaṭṭasmiṃvā bhavayantakevā satte yojentīti yogā. Bhavantaracutiyā saha bhavantarapaṭisandhiṃ gantenti ghaṭentīti ganthā. Abhijjhāti sabbassa rāgassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā rūpārūpa rāgāpi ettha saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Byāpādotipi sabbo doso eva. Idaṃ saccāti nivesoti idameva saccaṃ, moghamaññanti pavatto micchābhiniveso. Vaṭṭadukkhato vimuttiyā amaggabhūtaṃyeva gosīlagovatādikaṃ parato āmasanaṃ tathā tathā kappetvā gahaṇaṃ sīlabbataparāmāso. Etthaca paratoti bhūtasabhāvapaccanikatoti attho. Kāyasaddo pana sabbattha rūpakāye nāmakāyeca pavattoti atitakāyena paccuppanna kāyaṃ paccuppannakāyenaca anāgatakāyaṃ gantheti ghaṭetīti kāyagantho. Athavā, kāye gaṇṭhoti kāyagaṇṭho. Ajjhatta gaṇṭhoti attho. Nigaṇṭhonāṭaputtotiādīsuviya gaṇṭhasaddo gaṇṭhiyaṃ pavatto. Bhusaṃ ādiyanti amuñcanagāhaṃ gaṇhantīti upādānāni. Kilesabhūto kāmoeva upādānaṃ kāmu pādānaṃ. Vatthubhūtaṃvā kāmaṃ upādiyatīti kāmupādānaṃ.

They yoke beings in the round of existence or in the mechanism of existence, hence they are called 'yokes' (yogā). Together with the passing away from one existence, they tie and join the rebirth-linking to another existence, hence they are called 'knots' (ganthā). 'Covetousness' (abhijjhā) is a name for all lust (rāga). Therefore, it should be understood that lust for the form and formless realms is also included here. 'Ill will' (byāpāda) too is simply all hatred (dosa). 'This is the truth'—this is the wrong adherence that proceeds as 'this alone is true, other things are worthless.' The grasping of what is not the path to liberation from the suffering of the round—such as the cow-practice and cow-vow—by regarding it as such and taking it up from another, is 'clinging to rules and observances' (sīlabbataparāmāso). Here, 'from another' (parato) means contrary to true reality. The word 'body' (kāya) applies everywhere to the material body and the mental body. It ties the past body to the present body, and the present body to the future body, thus it is the 'bodily knot' (kāyagantho). Alternatively, it is a knot in the body (kāye gaṇṭho), thus 'bodily knot'; the meaning is an internal knot. As in 'Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta,' the word 'knot' (gantha) is used for a tangle (gaṇṭhiyaṃ). They grasp strongly, taking a grasp that is not released, thus they are 'clingings' (upādānāni). Sensual pleasure that is a defilement is 'clinging to sensual pleasure' (kāmupādānaṃ). Or, one clings to sensual pleasure as an object, thus 'clinging to sensual pleasure'.

Dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo tividha mahādiṭṭhiyo aññāpivā sāsane lokeca sandissamānā viparītagāhabhūtā diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Yathāgahitaṃvā purimadiṭṭhiṃ idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti upādiyatīti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Goṇakukkurādīnaṃ taṃtaṃpakaticārittaṃ sīlaṃ nāma. Tameva suṭṭhuṃ samādinnaṃ vataṃnāma. Tadubhayaṃ saṃsāramuttiyā maggoti daḷhagahaṇaṃ sīlabbatu pādānaṃ nāma. Attavādupādānanti ettha attā vuccati parikappabuddhiyā gahito ekekasmiṃ satta santāne padhānissaro. Yaṃ lokiyamahājanā sattotivā puggalotivā jīvotivā tathāgatotivā lokotivā sañjānanti. Yañca nānātitthiyā issaranimmitaṃvā adhiccasamuppannaṃvā accantasassataṃvā [M 0.0337] ekaccasassataṃvā ucchedaṃvā paññapentīti. Taṃ attānaṃ abhivadanticeva upādiyantica sattā etenāti attavā dupādānaṃ. Vīsatividhā sakkāyadiṭṭhi. Tattha abhivadantīti visiṭṭhaṃ padhānaṃ katvā vadanti. Upādiyantīti daḷhaṃ ādiyanti. Yathāha –

The sixty-two views, the three great views, and other views seen in the Dispensation and in the world, which constitute a wrong grasp, are clinging to views. Or, clinging to a previously grasped view, thinking, 'This alone is true, all else is false,' is clinging to views. The natural conduct of cows, dogs, and so on, is called a 'practice.' That same thing, when well undertaken, is called a 'vow.' The firm grasping that both of these are the path to liberation from saṃsāra is called clinging to rules and observances. Clinging to the doctrine of self: here 'self' refers to a dominant lord in each individual continuity of being, grasped by speculative thought. It is what the worldly majority conceives of as a 'being,' a 'person,' a 'soul,' a 'Tathāgata,' or the 'world.' It is also what various sectarians proclaim as being created by a lord, arisen by chance, entirely eternal, partly eternal, or subject to annihilation. Because beings declare this self and cling to it, it is called 'clinging to the doctrine of self.' This is the twenty-fold identity view. Here, 'declare' means they speak of it as something special and primary. 'Cling' means they grasp it firmly. As it is said:

Tattha katamā sakkāyadiṭṭhi. Idha assutavā puthujjano rūpaṃ attato samanupassati. Rūpavantaṃvā attānaṃ. Attani vā rūpaṃ. Rūpasmiṃvā attānaṃ. Vedanaṃ attato samanupassati. Vedanāvantaṃvā attānaṃ. Attanivā vedanaṃ. Vedanāpavā attānaṃ. Saññaṃ. Saṅkhāre. Viññāṇanti.

Therein, what is identity view? Here, an uninstructed worldling regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. He regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. He regards formations as self, or self as possessing formations, or formations as in self, or self as in formations. He regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.

Tattha rūpaṃ attato samanupassatīti rūpameva attāti gaṇhāti. Rūpavantaṃvā attānanti attā me rūpavāti gaṇhāti. Attani vā rūpanti attānaṃ paṭicca rūpaṃ tiṭṭhatīti gaṇhāti. Rūpasmiṃvā attānanti rūpaṃ paṭicca attā tiṭṭhatīti gaṇhāti. Kathaṃ rūpakāyaṃ uddissa ajja ahaṃ thaddhomhīti vā ajja ahaṃ mudukomhītivā vadanto pathavi saṅkhātaṃ rūpaṃ attato samanupassatināma. Ajja mama kāyo thaddhotivā mudūtivā vadanto sesadhammevā dhammamuttakaṃvā attānaṃ gahetvā taṃ attānaṃ pathavīvantaṃ samanupassatināma. Ajja thaddhabhāvovā mudubhāvovā mayi jātoti vadanto attani pathaviṃsa manupassatināma. Ajjāhaṃ thaddhabhāve ṭhitomhi mudubhāve ṭhito mhīti vadantopathavimhi attānaṃ samanussatināma. Ayaṃ pathavimhi caturāvatthikāya saṃkkāyadiṭṭhiyā pavattākāro. Sesesu sattavīsatirūpesu yathāsambhavaṃ vattabbo. Ahaṃ marāmi marissāmītiādinā hi aniccatāyaṃpi sādiṭṭhi pavattatiyeva. Sesarūpesu vattabbaṃ natthi. Idaṃ nāma ahaṃ pubbe saṃbhuñjiṃ. Ajja saṃbhuñjāmi. Parato saṃbhuñjissāmītivā sukhitomhi dukkhitomhītivā vedanaṃ attato samanupassati. Ajja mama kāyo sukhito dukkhitotivā mamacittaṃ sukhitaṃ dukkhitantivā attānaṃ vedanāvantaṃ samanupassati. Ajjasukhaṃvā dukkhaṃvā mayijātanti attani vedanaṃ samanupassati. Ajjāhaṃ sukhita bhāve ṭhitomhi dukkhitabhāve ṭhitomhīti vedanāya attānaṃ samanupassatīti.

Herein, one regards form as self: one grasps form as self. Or one regards self as possessing form, grasping 'My self has form.' Or one regards form as in the self, grasping 'Form exists in dependence on the self.' Or one regards the self as in form, grasping 'The self exists in dependence on form.' How so? When, referring to the body of form, one says, 'Today I am stiff' or 'Today I am soft,' this is called regarding the earth-element form as self. When one says, 'Today my body is stiff' or 'Today my body is soft,' having taken the self as something apart from other phenomena or as a phenomenon in itself, one then regards that self as possessing the earth element; this is called regarding self as possessing form. When one says, 'Today stiffness or softness has arisen in me,' this is called regarding the earth element as in the self. When one says, 'Today I am in a stiff state' or 'Today I am in a soft state,' this is called regarding the self as in the earth element. This is the mode of operation of identity view concerning the earth element in its four aspects. The same should be stated for the remaining twenty-seven forms as is applicable. This same view arises even with respect to impermanence through thoughts like, 'I am dying' or 'I will die.' There is nothing further to be said about the other forms. 'In the past, I experienced this; today, I am experiencing it; in the future, I will experience it,' or 'I am happy' or 'I am miserable'—in this way one regards feeling as self. When one says, 'Today my body is happy or miserable,' or 'Today my mind is happy or miserable,' one regards the self as possessing feeling. When one says, 'Today happiness or misery has arisen in me,' one regards feeling as in the self. When one says, 'Today I am in a happy state' or 'Today I am in a miserable state,' one regards the self as in feeling.

Saññāya [M 0.0338] sabbesuca paññāsamattesu saṅkhāresu visuṃ visuṃ vitthāretvā vattabbo. Ahaṃ passāmīti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati. Dassanaṃ meti attānaṃ viññāṇavantaṃ samanupassati. Mayidassanaṃnāma atthīti attani viññāṇaṃ samanupassati, ahaṃ dassane samatthomhīti viññāṇasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassati. Ese vanayo sesesu pañcasu viññāṇesūti. Aha masmi ahaṃ eko satto ekopuggalo eko jīvo eko loko eko naro manusso devosakko brahmātivā ahaṃgacchāmi ahaṃ tiṭṭhāmi ahaṃ nisīdāmi ahaṃ nippajjāmi ahaṃ samiñjemi pasāremītiādinā vā khandhapañcakaṃvā ekamekaṃvā khandhaṃ samūhato gahetvā pavattipi vattabbā. Apariññātavatthukānañhi ekamuhutta mattepi yaṃkiñci attanovā parassavā attapaṭisaṃyuttavacanaṃ kathentānaṃ cittaṃvā vacanaṃvā yathāvutte rūpārūpadhamme kadāci attato upādiyitvā pavattati. Kadāci attaparivāra bhāvena. Kadāci attanissitabhāvena. Kadāci attanissayabhāvena. Kadāci ekekadhammavasena. Kadāci samūhadhammavasenāti.

Regarding perception, and all fifty formations, the explanation should be elaborated for each one separately. 'I see'—thus one regards eye-consciousness as self. 'Seeing is mine'—thus one regards the self as possessing consciousness. 'In me there is this thing called seeing'—thus one regards consciousness as in the self. 'I am capable of seeing'—thus one regards the self as in consciousness. This is the method for the remaining five consciousnesses as well. 'I am; I am a single being, a single person, a single soul, a single world, a single man, a human, a deva, Sakka, or Brahmā'; or 'I go, I stand, I sit, I lie down, I bend, I stretch'—in such ways, the process should be explained by grasping the five aggregates either collectively or individually. For those who have not fully understood the basis, even for a single moment, when they utter any speech concerning themselves, others, or connected with the self, their mind or speech operates by sometimes clinging to these material and immaterial phenomena as self; sometimes as the self's possession; sometimes as dependent on the self; sometimes as a support for the self; sometimes by way of single phenomena; and sometimes by way of a group of phenomena.

Yasmā pana attanimittaṃnāma vasavattanākāraṃ paṭicca upaṭṭhāti. Vasavattanā kāroca rūpārūpadhammānaṃ paccayāyatta vuttikattaṃ khaṇi kattañca suṭṭhu passantānaṃ natthi. Tasmā pariññātavattukānaṃ atta paṭisaṃyuttavacanaṃ kathentānaṃpi cittaṃ paduminipatte udakabindu viya tesu dhammesu alaggitvāeva pavattatīti veditabbaṃ. Sattānaṃ cittasantāne kusale dhamme anuppannevā uppādetuṃ uppannevā vā setuṃ adatvā nīvārentīti nīvaraṇāni. Kāmanaṭṭhena kāmo, chandanaṭṭhenachandoti kāmacchando. Balavarāgo. Soevanīvaraṇanti kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ. Paṭṭhāneāruppekāmacchandaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ paṭiccauddhaccanīvaraṇanti vuttattā pana thapetvā rūpārūparāge avaseso sabbolobho kāmacchande asaṅgahitonāma natthi. Jhānapaṭipakkhabhāvopana pañcakāmaguṇikarāgasseva hotīti veditabbo. Byāpajjanaṃ byāpādo. Cittassa pūtibhāvoti attho. Yokocidoso. Kasmā panettha thinamiddha nīvaraṇanti ca uddhacca kukkucca nīvaraṇanti [M 0.0339] ca dve dve dhammā ekaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ katvā vuttāti. Kiccato paccayato paṭipakkhatoca sadisattā. Tathā hi kiccato tāva thinamiddhadvayaṃ cittuppādānaṃ līnabhāvā pādanakiccaṃ. Uddhaccakukkuccadvayaṃ avūpasantabhāvāpādanakiccaṃ. Paccayato purimadvayaṃ tandivijambhi tatāpaccayaṃ. Pacchimadvayaṃ ñātibyasanādivitakkapaccayaṃ. Paṭipakkhato purimadvayaṃ vīriyapaṭipakkhaṃ. Pacchimadvayaṃ samathapaṭipakkhanti.

Since the sign of self arises in dependence on the mode of exercising control, and since for those who see clearly the dependently arisen nature and momentariness of material and immaterial phenomena this mode of exercising control does not exist, it should therefore be understood that even when those who have fully understood the basis speak words connected with the self, their mind proceeds without clinging to those phenomena, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. They are called 'hindrances' because they hinder beings, not allowing them to arouse unarisen wholesome states in their mental continuums or to maintain arisen ones. 'Sensual desire' (kāmacchando) is 'kāma' in the sense of craving and 'chanda' in the sense of desire. It is strong passion. That itself is a hindrance, thus it is called the hindrance of sensual desire. Since it is said in the Paṭṭhāna, 'In dependence on the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of restlessness arises,' therefore, apart from lust for the form and formless realms, there is no remaining greed whatsoever that is not included in sensual desire. It should be understood, however, that only passion for the five cords of sensual pleasure is an opponent to jhāna. 'Ill will' (byāpādo) is corruption; the meaning is a rotten state of mind. It is any kind of aversion. Why are sloth and torpor, and restlessness and remorse, each spoken of as a single hindrance, though they are pairs of phenomena? Because of their similarity in function, condition, and opposition. For in terms of function, the pair of sloth and torpor has the function of producing a sluggish state for arisings of consciousness. The pair of restlessness and remorse has the function of producing a state of non-tranquility. In terms of condition, the first pair is conditioned by lethargy and drowsiness. The latter pair is conditioned by thoughts about such things as the loss of relatives. In terms of opposition, the first pair is the opponent of energy, and the latter pair is the opponent of calm.

Anusentīti anusayā. Anurūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ labhitvā uppajjantīti attho. Anuanu sentītivā anusayā. Yāva maggaṃ napaṭilabhati. Tāva antarā aparikkhiyyamānā hutvā kāraṇalābhe sati punappunaṃ uppajjantīti attho. Uppajjanañcettha appahīnaṭṭhena uppajjanā rahabhāvo veditabbo. Na pana sarūpato uppatti, kathaṃ viññā yatīti ce. Yassa kāmarāgānusayo uppajjati, tasseva paṭighānusayo uppajjatīti vuttattā. Evañca katvā pāḷiyaṃ puthujjanassa sattapi anusayā anusayavāre saha anusentīti uppajjanavāre saha uppajjantīti vuttā. Yathāha puthujjanassa avijjānusayoca anuseti. Kāmarāga. Paṭigha. Māna. Diṭṭhi. Vicikicchā. Bhavarāganusayoca anusetīti. Tathā uppajjanavārepīti.

They are called 'latent tendencies' because they lie latent. The meaning is that they arise upon obtaining a suitable condition. Or, they are 'latent tendencies' because they lie latent again and again. The meaning is that as long as one has not attained the path, they remain uneradicated, and upon obtaining a condition, they arise again and again. Herein, their 'arising' should be understood as a potential to arise, in the sense of their not having been abandoned; it is not an actual arising in their own nature. If it is asked how this is known, it is because it is said: 'For whomever the latent tendency for sensual desire is present, for that same person the latent tendency for aversion is also present.' And so, in the Pāli canon, it is said of an ordinary person that in the section on latent tendencies the seven latent tendencies 'lie latent together,' and in the section on arising they 'arise together.' As it is said: 'In an ordinary person, the latent tendency of ignorance lies latent, as do the latent tendencies of sensual desire, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, and craving for existence.' The same is said in the section on arising.

Apica, sarūpato pariyuṭṭhānaṃ apatvā santāne pavattamānehi kusalākusalā byākatacittuppādehi saha anurūpā aviruddhā hutvā senti. Visuṃ sampayuttadhammabhāvena avuṭṭhitā hutvā sayitā hontīti anusayā. Anu anu sentītivā anusayā. Pakatiyā yathānusayitesueva kāmarāgādīsu punappunaṃ uppajjitvā diguṇa tiguṇādi vasena punappunaṃ senti. Sayanākārena uparupari paliveṭhentīti attho.

Moreover, without having reached the state of manifest defilement, the latent tendencies lie dormant in the mental continuum in harmony and without conflict with the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states of consciousness that are occurring. They are called latent tendencies because they lie dormant, not having arisen as distinct associated mental states. Or, they are latent tendencies because they lie dormant again and again. By nature, they arise repeatedly in relation to sensual desire and so forth, in accordance with one's dispositions, and lie dormant again and again, becoming double or triple in strength. The meaning is that they envelop the mind layer upon layer in the manner of lying down.

Tīsu rāgādīnaṃ avatthāsu pathamāvatthāya ṭhitānaṃ kāmarāgā dīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tisso hi avatthā anusayāvatthā pariyuṭṭhānāvatthā vītikkamāvatthāti. Tattha ye kāmarāgādayo uppajjitvā kāyaṅgavācaṅgaṃ cālenti, tesaṃ tathāpavattā avatthā vītikkamāvatthānāma. Ye manasmiṃ eva javanacittasahajātā hutvā pavattanti, tesaṃ tathāpavattā avatthā pariyuṭṭhānāvatthānāma. Ye [M 0.0340] pana javanasahajātabhāvaṃpi apatvā vāsanādhātuyo viya cikkasantānā nusayitā hutvā pariyuṭṭhānappattiyā bījabhāvena tiṭṭhanti, subhanimittādikeca ārammaṇe āpātamāgate yesaṃ vasena āvajjanaṃ rāgādipātubhāvatthāya ayoniso bhavaṅgaṃ āvaṭṭeti, abhāvitañca cittaṃ yesaṃ vasena damathaṃ naupeti, tesaṃ tathā pavattā avatthā anusayāvatthānāma. Tadavatthikā kāmarāgādayo anusayānāma. Te pana aparamatthabhūtāpi na honti. Ekantaparamatthajātikattā. Naca kusalābyākatabhūtā ekantākusalajātikattā. Nāpi kusalābyākataviruddhā, visuṃ sampayuttadhammabhāvena anupaladdhattā. Nāpi kālattayavinimuttā, tekālikadhammasannissayena pavattanato. Yadā pana te samuṭṭha hitvā pariyuṭṭhānabhāvaṃ gacchanti, tadā visuṃ sampayuttadhamma bhāvañca gacchanti. Sārammaṇādibhāvoca tesaṃ paribyatto hoti. Etadatthaṃ sandhāya kathāvatthumhi tesaṃ sārammaṇadhammabhāvo saṅkhārakkhandhabhāvoca patiṭṭhāpito hotīti.

This is a designation for sensual desire and the like when they are in the first of their three states. For there are three states: the latent state, the manifest state, and the transgression state. Herein, when sensual desire and the like arise and stir the body and speech, that state of their occurrence is called the transgression state. When they arise in the mind itself, co-arisen with impulsion consciousness, that state of their occurrence is called the manifest state. But when, not having even reached the state of being co-arisen with impulsion, they remain latent like habitual tendencies in the mental continuum, lying dormant as seeds for the attainment of the manifest state; and when, upon the appearance of an object such as a beautiful sign, unwise attention turns the life-continuum toward the manifestation of lust and the like on account of them, and the undeveloped mind does not attain restraint on account of them—that state of their occurrence is called the latent state. Sensual desire and the like in that state are called latent tendencies. They are by no means non-ultimate realities, for they are of a nature that is exclusively ultimate. Nor are they wholesome or indeterminate, because they are of a nature that is exclusively unwholesome. Nor are they opposed to the wholesome and indeterminate, since they are not found as distinct associated phenomena. Nor are they free from the three times, because they proceed in dependence on phenomena of the three times. But when they have arisen and reached the state of manifestation, they also become distinct associated phenomena, and their nature as having an object and so on becomes evident. It is with reference to this that in the Kathāvatthu their nature as phenomena with an object and their inclusion in the aggregate of formations are established.

Yathā pana phaladhārimhi rukkhamhi visakaṇṭake dinne rukkhānusayito phaluppattiyā paccayabhūto sineho parikkhayaṃ gacchati. Samaye uppajjissamānāni phalāni nuppajjanti. Evaṃ sānusaye citta santāne yasmiṃ khaṇe maggo pātubhavati, tasmiṃ sahamagguppādā so so anusayo parikkhayaṃ gacchati. Parikkhīṇassa pana puna pariyuṭṭhānaṃnāma natthi, kuto vītikkamoti imamatthaṃ sandhāya maggo anāgatasāmaññaṃ kilesajātaṃ pajahatīti tattha tattha vutto. Tattha anāgatasāmaññanti anāgatasammataṃ, na ekanta anāgataṃ. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ maggo yekilese pajahati, te atītākivā anāgatātivā paccuppannātivā navattabbāti vuttaṃ. Etenaca maggo kilesamukhena yāni kusalākusalakammānica upādinnakakhandhapañcakeca pajahati, te atītātivāanāgatātivā paccuppannātivā navattabbāti dīpeti. Yadi evaṃ maggena pahīnā sabbe tebhūmakadhammā kālavimuttānāma ataṅkhatā nāma apaccayānāma siyunti.Na. Tekālikajātikattā saṅkhata sapaccayajātikattā [M 0.0341] ca. Te hi magge anuppanne ime nāmadhammā uppajjissanti nirujjhissantīti evaṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ āhacca ñāṇena gahitattā lakkhaṇavasena tebhūmakādibhāvaṃ bhajantīti. Evañca katvā visuṃ sampayuttadhammabhāvaṃ apattānaṃ anusayāvatthāya vā vāsanāvatthāyavā kammasamaṅgītāvatthāyavā āsayajjhāsayā dhimutticaritavatthāsuvā ṭhitānaṃ sabhāvānaṃ jātivasena paramattha dhammatā akusalāditāca paccetabbā hotīti.

Just as when poison is applied to a fruit-bearing tree, the sap that is the condition for the production of fruit, being inherent in the tree, is exhausted. In time, the fruits that would have arisen do not arise. So too, in the mind-continuum with its latent tendencies, at the moment the path arises, simultaneously with the arising of the path that very latent tendency is exhausted. For what has been exhausted, there is no further manifestation; whence could there be transgression? It is with reference to this meaning that it is said in various places that the path abandons the mass of defilements in a general future sense. Here, 'future in a general sense' means 'regarded as future,' not exclusively future. For this reason, it is said in the commentary that when the path abandons defilements, they cannot be said to be past, future, or present. By this it is shown that the wholesome and unwholesome kammas and the five aggregates subject to clinging, which the path abandons by way of the defilements, also cannot be said to be past, future, or present. If so, would all phenomena of the three realms abandoned by the path be liberated from time, unconditioned, and uncaused? No. Because they belong to the three times and because they are conditioned and have a causal origin. For, before the path has arisen, it is known that 'these mental phenomena will arise and will cease'; thus, since they are grasped by knowledge through the characteristic of being conditioned, they partake of the nature of the three realms, etc., by way of their characteristics. And so, for things abiding in the state of latent tendencies, or in the state of residual impressions, or in the state of karmic potential, or in the states of inclination, disposition, resolve, and temperament, their intrinsic nature, their status as ultimate realities, and their being unwholesome, etc., must be understood according to their kind.

[208] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[208] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Appahīnā hi kilesā kāraṇalābhe sati uppajjanā rahā santāne anuanusayitā viya hontīti tadavatthā anusayāti vuccanti. Te pana nippariyāyato anāgata kilesā. Atītapaccuppannāpi taṃsabhāvattā tathā vuccantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha anusayānāma santāne kadācipi anuppanna pubbā anāgata kilesā evāti katvā santāne anu anusayitā viya hontīti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

“For, when they are not abandoned, the defilements are capable of arising when they obtain a cause; they are as if lying dormant in the mental continuum, and in that state they are called ‘latent tendencies.’ But strictly speaking, they are future defilements. Even past and present ones are so called because they have that same nature.” So it is said. Therein, the statement that latent tendencies are exclusively future defilements that have never before arisen in the continuum, and that for this reason they are said to be ‘as if lying dormant’ in the continuum—this is not correct.

Na hi te anuanusayitā viya honti. Ekantena anusayitāeva hontīti.

For they are not merely as if lying dormant; they are absolutely lying dormant.

[209] Yañca tattha

[209] And as to what is said there:

“Te pana nippariyāyato anāgatakilesā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yuttaṃ.

The statement, “But strictly speaking, they are future defilements,” that too is not correct.

Na hi maggena appahīnā anusayā anāgatānāma honti. Pahīnāpica nippariyāyato anāgatāti nasakkā vattuṃ. Anāgata sāmaññassa adhippetattāti. Etena atītapaccuppannāpi taṃsabhāvattātathā vuccantīti idaṃvipaṭikkhittaṃ hoti. Apica, uppādaṭṭhitibhaṅga pattānaṃeva ekantena tekālikatā hotīti tadapattānaṃ anusayānaṃ paccuppannatā pariyāyova vattuṃ yutto. Evañca katvā pāḷiyaṃ yassa kāmarāganusayo uppajjati, tassa paṭighānusayo uppajjatītiādinā paccuppannakāliko uppādavāro eva vutto, na nirodhavāro, naca atītānāgata vārāti. Yaṃ pana [M 0.0342] paṭisambhidāmagge hañci paccuppanne kilese pajahati. Tena hi ratto rāgaṃ pajahati, duṭṭho dosaṃ, muḷho mohanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pariyuṭṭhānapattānaṃ ekantapaccuppannakkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ bhutvā vigatuppannaṃ okāsakatuppannaṃ samudācāruppannanti catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ na maggavajjhaṃ. Bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ ārammaṇā dhiggahi tuppannaṃ avikkhambhituppannaṃ asamugghāṭituppannanti catubbidhaṃ maggavajjhanti vuttaṃ. Tattha vattamānuppannaṃ samudā cāruppannanti idaṃ dvayaṃ khaṇapaccuppannameva. Bhutvāvigatuppannaṃ atītameva. Okāsa katuppannaṃ anāgatameva. Tadubhayaṃ pana paccuppannasamīpattā uppannanti vuttaṃ. Samīpapaccuppannanti vuttaṃ hoti.

For latent tendencies not abandoned by the path are not called ‘future.’ And even those that are abandoned cannot be said to be strictly future, because what is intended is ‘future’ in a general sense. By this, the statement that ‘even past and present ones are so called because they have that same nature’ is refuted. Furthermore, since belonging to the three times applies exclusively to things that have reached arising, presence, and dissolution, it is proper to speak of the presentness of latent tendencies that have not reached that state only in a figurative sense. And so, in the Pāli canon, when it is said, “For one in whom the latent tendency of sensual desire arises, the latent tendency of aversion arises,” etc., only the section on arising in the present time is stated, not the section on cessation, nor the sections on the past and future. As for what is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, “If one abandons defilements in the present, then one who is lustful abandons lust, one who is hateful abandons hatred, one who is deluded abandons delusion,” this should be understood as said with reference to the strictly present moment of those defilements that have reached the state of manifestation. For this reason, it is said in the commentary that four kinds of ‘arisen’ are not to be abandoned by the path: presently arisen, arisen-and-passed, arisen-by-opportunity, and arisen-as-transgression. Four kinds are to be abandoned by the path: arisen-by-attaining-a-plane, arisen-by-grasping-an-object, arisen-as-unsuppressed, and arisen-as-uneradicated. Therein, ‘presently arisen’ and ‘arisen-as-transgression’ are strictly in the present moment. ‘Arisen-and-passed’ is past. ‘Arisen-by-opportunity’ is future. But both of the latter are called ‘arisen’ because of their proximity to the present; that is to say, they are ‘proximately present.’

Bhūmiladdhuppannaṃnāma attano khandhesu anusayitānaṃ maggena appahīnānaṃ anusayānaṃeva nāmaṃ. Ārammaṇādhiggahituppannaṃ nāma subhanimittādike ārammaṇe sakiṃ javitvā yāva tammūlako pariyuṭṭhānavego na vūpasammati, tāva adhimattathāmagata bhāvena ṭhitānaṃ tesaññeva nāmaṃ. Anusayā hi nāma anamatagge saṃsāre punappunaṃ pariyuṭṭhānapattānaṃ kilesānaṃ vasena uparupari thira tara daḷhatara pattiyā pakatiyāpi thāmagatāevanāma honti. Na yenavā tenavā vāyāmena pajahituṃ sakkuṇeyyā. Evaṃ santepi yadā yo yo anusayo paccayalābhena pariyuṭṭhāna bahulo hoti, tadā so so visesena adhimattathāma gatabhāvaṃ patvā ṭhito hoti. Yadā yo yo paṭipakkhadhamma samādānena niggahapatto hoti, tadā so so mandathāma gatabhāvaṃ patvā ṭhito hotīti. Avikkhambhituppannaṃnāma samatha vipassanāhi suṭṭhuaniggahitānaṃ tesaññeva nāmaṃ. Asamugghāṭi tuppannaṃnāma maggena appahīnānaṃ bhūmiladdhānaṃ tesaṃeva nāmanti. Yasmā pana lokuttaradhammānāma kilesānaṃ accantapaṭipakkhā hontīti heṭṭhimā maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhā sekkhā attano maggaphalakkhaṇesu upari maggājjhehipi anusayehi sānusayātivā nirānusayātivā thāmavatātivā athāmagatātivā navattabbā. Tasmā anusayānaṃ tādise paccuppanna bhāve satipi hañci paccuppanne kilese pajahati. [M 0.0343] Tenahi thāmagato anusayaṃ pajahatīti vutta doso natthīti veditabboti. Kāmarāgoeva anusayo kāmarāgānusayo.

‘Arisen-by-attaining-a-plane’ is the name for those latent tendencies lying dormant in one’s own aggregates that have not been abandoned by the path. ‘Arisen-by-grasping-an-object’ is the name for those same tendencies which, having arisen once in relation to an object such as a beautiful sign, persist with excessive strength until the impetus of the manifestation rooted in it subsides. Indeed, latent tendencies, through the power of defilements that have repeatedly reached manifestation in beginningless saṃsāra, by nature become progressively firmer and stronger and are thus powerful. They cannot be abandoned by just any casual effort. Even so, when any latent tendency frequently manifests due to obtaining a condition, it then abides having attained a state of excessive strength. When any latent tendency is restrained by undertaking an opposing quality, it then abides having attained a state of weak strength. ‘Arisen-as-unsuppressed’ is the name for those same tendencies that are not well suppressed by serenity and insight. ‘Arisen-as-uneradicated’ is the name for those same plane-attained tendencies that have not been abandoned by the path. Since supramundane states are the ultimate opponents of the defilements, trainees standing in the lower paths and fruits cannot be described, during the moments of their own path and fruition, as being with or without the latent tendencies to be abandoned by the higher paths, nor as having strong or weak tendencies. Therefore, it should be understood that even though latent tendencies have such a present nature, there is no fault in the statement, “If one abandons defilements in the present, then one abandons a strong latent tendency.” Sensual desire itself is a latent tendency; hence, the latent tendency of sensual desire.

Saṃyojenti bandhantīti saṃyojanāni, tāni pana sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāso kāmacchando byāpādoti pañca orambhāgiyāni. Rūparāgo arūparāgo māno uddhaccaṃ avijjāti pañca uddhaṃbhāgiyānīti suttante abhidhammeca dasasaṃyojanāni āgatāni. Itarāni pana abhidhammeeva āgatānīti tato visesakaraṇatthaṃ suttanteti vuttaṃ. Kamo pana dvinnaṃpi pāḷiyā nasameti. Sabhāga dhammasaṅgahavasena pana idha aññathā kamo vutto siyāti. Cittaṃ kilissanti vibādhenti upatāpenticāti kilesā. Kilissantivā malīnabhāvaṃ nihīnabhāvañca gacchanti sattā etehīti kilesā. Kāmabhavanāmenāti vatthukāmadīpakena kāmanāmena rūpārūpabhavadīpakena ca bhavanāmena. Tādisaṃ kāma bhavasaṅkhātaṃ ārammaṇabhūtaṃ vatthu etissāti tabbatthukā. Tathā pavattanti sīlabbatāni parato āmasanākārena idaṃ me saccaṃ moghamaññanti abhinivisanākārena khandhesu attābhinivesākārenaca pavattaṃ. Vatthutoti sabhāvadhammato. Ayaṃ pāpasaṅgaho akusalaṅgaho navadhā vuttoti yojanā. [Akusalasaṅgaho]

They fetter, they bind, thus they are called ‘fetters.’ These are the five lower fetters: identity view, doubt, attachment to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will. And the five higher fetters: lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. Thus, ten fetters are found in the Suttanta and the Abhidhamma. But other classifications are found only in the Abhidhamma; therefore, to distinguish this list, the text specifies ‘in the Suttanta.’ However, the order in the two canons does not match. But here the order might be stated differently for the purpose of grouping similar states. They stain, oppress, and torment the mind, thus they are ‘defilements.’ Or, beings are stained by them and fall into a corrupt and base state, thus they are ‘defilements.’ By the name ‘kāma-bhava’: this means by the name ‘kāma,’ which indicates the objects of sensual pleasure, and by the name ‘bhava,’ which indicates form and formless existence. ‘Based on that’ (tabbatthukā) means that which has for its object such a basis designated as ‘kāma’ and ‘bhava.’ Similarly, ‘grasping’ (parāmāso) proceeds by way of misapprehending externals as rules and observances, by way of adhering to the view ‘This is my truth, anything else is futile,’ and by way of adhering to a self in the aggregates. ‘From the standpoint of the thing itself’ (vatthuto) means from the standpoint of its intrinsic nature. This collection of evil, this collection of the unwholesome, is said to be ninefold—this is the connection. [The Collection of the Unwholesome]

163. Missaka saṅgahe pāṇātipātādīni pāpakammāni karontānaṃpi cittassa ārammaṇe ujukaraṇaṃnāma jhānena vinā na sijjhatīti vuttaṃ sattajhānaṅgānīti. Kalyāṇevā pāpakevā ārammaṇe ujukaṃ cittapaṭipādanasaṅkhātassa upanijjhāyana kiccassa aṅgānīti attho. Tattha domanassaṃ akusalajjhānaṅgaṃ. Sesāni kusalākusalābyākatānīti. Kalyāṇakamma pāpakammasaṅkhātāsu sugati duggati vivaṭṭasaṅkhātāsuca nānādisāsu taṃtaṃdisāti mukhappavattisaṅkhātā cittassa gatināma sammāvā micchāvā pavattehi dassanādīhi eva sijjhatīti vuttaṃ dvādasamaggaṅgānīti. Cittassa ujugatiyāvā vaṅkagatiyāvā gamanassa pathaṅgāni upāyaṅgānīti attho. [M 0.0344] Tattha micchādiṭṭhi micchāsaṅkappa micchāvāyāma micchāsamādhayo pāpakamma duggatibhava saṅkhātāsu ahitadisāsu cittassa vaṅkagatiyā gamanassa upāyaṅgāni, itarāni kalyāṇakamma sugatibhava vivaṭṭadhammasaṅkhātāsu hitadisāsu ujugatiyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha pāṇātipātakamme vitakka vicāra domanassekaggatā saṅkhātaṃ caturaṅgikajjhānaṃ micchāsaṅkappa micchāvāyāma micchāsamādhi saṅkhāto tiyaṅgīkamaggoca veditabbo. Evaṃ sesesu sucaritaduccaritakammesu jhānamaggā uddharitabbā. Vibhaṅge pana suttantesuca micchāvācā micchākammanto micchāājīvo micchāsatīti imepi cattāro āgatā. Ime pana visuṃ cetasikadhammā nahonti. Tathā tathā pavattānaṃ catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ adhivacananti katvā idha nagahitā.

163. In the Miscellaneous Section, it is said that even for those who perform evil actions such as killing living beings, the straightening of the mind upon its object is not accomplished without jhāna; thus, 'the seven jhānic factors' are mentioned. The meaning is that they are factors of the function of close examination, which is characterized as making the mind straight upon a wholesome or unwholesome object. Among these, grief is an unwholesome jhānic factor; the rest can be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. The mind's course, designated as its proceeding forth towards a particular direction, is accomplished by means of right or wrong seeing and so on in various directions—that is, towards wholesome and unwholesome kamma, happy and unhappy destinies, and the state of liberation; thus, 'the twelve path factors' are mentioned. The meaning is that they are the components of the path, the means for the mind's straight or crooked going. Among them, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration are the means for the mind's crooked going in unbeneficial directions, designated as evil kamma and an unhappy destination. The others should be understood as the means for its straight going in beneficial directions, designated as wholesome kamma, a happy destination, and the Dhamma of liberation. Here, in the kamma of killing a living being, the four-factored jhāna—comprising initial application, sustained application, grief, and one-pointedness—and the three-factored path—comprising wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration—should be understood. Similarly, the jhānic and path factors should be extracted in other cases of good and bad conduct. However, in the Vibhaṅga and in the suttas, these four are also found: wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, and wrong mindfulness. But these are not separate mental factors; since they are designations for the four aggregates as they occur in such and such a way, they are not included here.

[210] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[210] But as to what is to be explained:

“Sugati duggatīnaṃ nibbānassa ca abhimukhaṃ pāpanato maggā; Tesaṃ pathabhūtāni aṅgāni maṅgānī”ti vuttaṃ; Taṃ na sundaraṃ;

Na hi aṅgāni maggānaṃ pathabhūtānināma honti; Maggasaddoyeva pathapariyāyo aṭṭhakathāsu vutto na aṅgasaddoti;

The statement: ‘Because they lead one to face happy and unhappy destinies and Nibbāna, they are paths (maggā); their factors (aṅgāni) are the way (pathabhūtāni) to them, thus they are path factors (maggaṅgāni)’—this is not correct. For the factors are not what is called the way of the paths. In the commentaries, only the word 'magga' is stated as a synonym for 'patha,' not the word 'aṅga.'

[211] Yañca tattha

[211] And as to what is stated there:

“Maggassavā aṭṭhaṅgikassa aṅgāni maggaṅgānī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi anupapannaṃ.

The statement, ‘The factors of the eightfold path are called path factors,’ is also unfounded.

Idha hi katthaci citte tiyaṅgiko katthaci caturaṅgikotiādinā nānāmaggova adhippetoti. Ādhipaccaṭṭhena indriyāni. Kiñca ādhipaccaṃ. Attādhīnavuttike dhamme attano gatiyaṃ sabbaso vattetuṃ samatthabhāvo. Iti tesu tesu kiccesu attano ādhipaccasaṅkhātaṃ indaṭṭhaṃ karonti sādhentīti indriyāni. Indaṭṭhaṃ kārentītipi indriyāni. Issarā adhipatinoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha pañcacakkhādīni dassanādikiccesu cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ issarāhonti. Balavadubbalamanda tikkhādīsu attākārānuvattāpanato. Bhāvadvayaṃ itthākārādivasena pavattiyaṃ catusamuṭṭhānika rūpānaṃ sakalakhandhapañcakasseva vā issaro hoti. Aññathā appavattito. [M 0.0345] Tathā hi yasmiṃ santāne paṭisandhiyaṃ itthibhāvo pavattati. Tasmiṃ sabbe kammādipaccayā catusamuṭṭhānarūpasantatiṃ samuṭṭhāpentā itthākārasahitameva samuṭṭhāpenti, no aññathā. Chandacittādhippāyāpi tasmiṃ mandākārasahitāva pavattanti. Tabbiparītena purisasantānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Jīvitadvayaṃ rūpā rūpasantatīnaṃ ratti diva māsa saṃvaccharānukkamena addhānapharaṇe sahajātadhammānaṃ issaro hoti. Tesaṃ tadāyattavutti kattā. Mano vijānanakicce. Vedanāpañcakaṃ tathā tathā ārammaṇarasānubhavane. Saddhā ārammaṇāvīmuccane. Vīriyaṃ kammani alīna vuttibhāve. Sati ārammaṇupaṭṭhāne. Samādhi ārammaṇe niccalaṭṭhi tiyaṃ. Paññā asammohakicce sampayuttadhammānaṃ issaro hoti. Anaññābhibhavanīyabhāvena pavattanato. Yathā hi silāyaṃ pathavī sahajātehi anabhibhavanīyā hoti. Attanāvate abhibhavitvā visuṃ avijjamāneviya katvā pavattati. Yathā ca udake āpo aggimhi tejo vāte vāyo. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For here various paths are intended, such as a three-factored one in a certain state of consciousness, a four-factored one in another, and so on. They are faculties in the sense of sovereignty. And what is sovereignty? It is the ability to make phenomena that are dependent on oneself proceed entirely in one's own way. Thus, because in their respective functions they perform and accomplish their own sovereignty, which is the meaning of 'inda' (lord), they are faculties (indriyāni). Or, because they cause the meaning of 'inda' to be exercised, they are faculties. This means they are said to be lords, masters. Here, the five sense faculties—the eye, etc.—are lords over eye-consciousness and so on in their respective functions of seeing, etc., because they make consciousness conform to their own nature as strong or weak, dull or sharp, etc. The two sex faculties are lord over the material form arisen from the four causes—or even over the entire five aggregates—in respect of their proceeding with female characteristics and so on, for otherwise they would not proceed. For instance, in a continuity where the female sex faculty arises at rebirth-linking, all the conditions such as kamma, in generating the continuity of material form arisen from the four causes, generate it only with female characteristics, not otherwise. Even will, consciousness, and intention proceed in it only with female characteristics. The male continuity should be understood in the opposite way. The two life faculties are lord over their co-arisen phenomena in the spanning of the life-term—in the sequence of night and day, month and year—of the material and immaterial continuities, for they are the agent on which the functioning of those phenomena depends. Mind is lord in the function of cognizing. The five feeling faculties are lord in the experiencing of the taste of the object in such and such a way. Faith is lord in adhering to the object. Energy is lord in the state of unsluggish functioning in an action. Mindfulness is lord in establishing the mind on the object. Concentration is lord in the state of unwavering stability on the object. Wisdom is lord over its associated phenomena in the function of non-delusion, because it proceeds in a way that cannot be overcome by another. For just as the earth element in a stone cannot be overcome by its co-arisen elements but proceeds by having overcome them, making them as if non-existent, and just as the water element does in water, the fire element in fire, and the air element in air, so too should this be understood.

Aññāyittha paṭivijjhitthāti aññātaṃ. Na aññātaṃ anaññātaṃ. Catusaccadhammo. Amataṃvā padaṃ. Anaññātaṃ ñassāmi jānissāmīti anaññātaññassāmi. Ākhyātikaṃpi hi padaṃ saññāsaddabhāve ṭhitaṃ nāmikaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Yathā makkhaligosālo ehipassi koti. Evañhi sati tassa padantarena saha samāsabhāvo navirujjhatīti. Anaññātaññassāmīti evaṃ paṭipannassa indriyaṃ anaññā taññassāmītindriyaṃ. Ādimanasikārato paṭṭhāya tādisena ussāhena saha vipassanaṃ ārabhantassa tasmiṃ ussāhe apaṭipassaddheyeva sotāmattimaggaṃ paṭilabhantassa indriyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ājānātīti aññaṃ. Tameva indriyanti aññindriyaṃ, pathamamaggena anaññātaṃ ñatvāpi kilesappahānakiccassa apariniṭṭhitattā tassa jānanakiccassa vippakatabhāvena yathā diṭṭhe tasmiṃ catusaccadhamme amatapadeeva vā punappunaṃ jānanakicca yuttānaṃ indriyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññātāvindriyanti aññā tāvino [M 0.0346] pariniṭṭhita ājānana kiccassa khīṇāsavassa indriyanti aññātāvindriyaṃ. Tividhaṃ petaṃ tathārūpe jānane sampayutta dhammānaṃ issaro hotīti veditabbaṃ.

'It has been understood, it has been penetrated,' thus it is 'known' (aññātaṃ). What is not known is 'unknown' (anaññātaṃ), that is, the Dhamma of the Four Truths, or the deathless state. 'I will know the unknown' (anaññātaṃ ñassāmi): this is the derivation of 'anaññātaññassāmi'. For even a verbal phrase, when it stands in the sense of a designation, takes the place of a noun, as in the case of Makkhali Gosāla's 'ehipassiko' ('one who says, "Come and see"'). When this is so, its forming a compound with another word is not incongruous. The faculty of one who has entered upon the way thus, 'I will know the unknown,' is the faculty of one who will know the unknown (anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ). This is said to be the faculty of one who, having started insight meditation with such an endeavor from the initial application of mind onwards, attains the path of stream-entry while that endeavor is still unallayed. 'One knows perfectly' (ājānāti), thus 'perfect knowledge' (aññaṃ). That itself as a faculty is the faculty of perfect knowledge (aññindriyaṃ). This is said to be the faculty of those who are engaged in the task of knowing again and again the Four-Truths-Dhamma or the deathless state, which has been seen as it is; for although they have known with the first path what was previously unknown, their task of knowing is still unfinished because the task of abandoning the defilements is not yet completed. The faculty of one who has known perfectly (aññātāvino): this is the faculty of one who has known perfectly (aññātāvindriyaṃ), that is, the faculty of an Arahant whose task of perfect knowing is completed, whose taints are destroyed. This threefold faculty, it should be understood, is lord over the phenomena associated with such knowing.

Tattha imesaṃ sattānaṃ pākaṭe rūpakāye attagāhadaḷhattaṃ tabbimuttica imesaṃ apariññāya pariññāyaca hotīti dīpetuṃ ādito pañca pasādindriyāni vuttāni. Tassa attassa itthipuma tābhedo imesaṃ vasena hoti. Tasmiṃ vā itthipurisa gāho tabbimuttica imesaṃ apariññāya pariññāyaca hotīti dīpetuṃ kadanantaraṃ bhāvindriyadvayaṃ vuttaṃ. Soca attā imassa vasena jīvasaññaṃ labhati. Tasmiṃvā jīvagāho tabbimuttica imassa apariññāya pariññāyaca hotīti dīpetuṃ tadanantaraṃ jīvitindriyaṃ vuttaṃ. Idaṃ pana bhāvindriyato pure vattabbaṃpi rūpārūpa missakattā idha vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nāmakāye attagāhadaḷhattaṃ tabbimuttica imassa apariññāya pariññāyaca hotīti dīpetuṃ nāmindriyesu manindriyaṃ ādito vuttaṃ. Soca arūpī attā imesaṃ vasena saṃkiliṭṭho vipphanditoca hoti. Tasmiṃvā sukhitadukkhitagāho tabbimuttica imesaṃ apariññāya pariññāyaca hotīti dīpetuṃ tadanantaraṃ pedanindriyapañcakaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa saṃkiliṭṭhassa vodānappattiyā taṃtaṃgāhavimuttiyāvā paṭipattidassanatthaṃ tadanantaraṃ saddhādipañcindriyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tāya paṭipattiyā vodānappatti yā ādi majjha pariyosāna dassanatthaṃ ante tīṇi lokuttarindriyāni vuttānīti.

Here, to show that for these beings the grasping at self in the manifest physical body is firm, and that liberation from it occurs through non-comprehension and comprehension of these, the five sensitive faculties are stated first. The distinction of that self into male and female occurs by means of these. To show that grasping at the self as male or female and liberation from it occurs through non-comprehension and comprehension of these, the two sex faculties are stated immediately after. And that self acquires the perception of a living being by means of this faculty. To show that grasping at the self as a living being and liberation from it occurs through non-comprehension and comprehension of this, the life faculty is stated immediately after. It should be understood, however, that although this should have been stated before the sex faculties, it is stated here because it is mixed, pertaining to both the material and the immaterial. To show that in the mental body the grasping at self is firm, and that liberation from it occurs through non-comprehension and comprehension of this, the mind faculty is stated first among the mental faculties. And that formless self becomes defiled and agitated by means of these faculties. To show that grasping at the self as happy or suffering and liberation from it occurs through non-comprehension and comprehension of these, the five feeling faculties are stated immediately after. To show the practice for attaining purification for that defiled self and for liberation from those various kinds of grasping, the five faculties beginning with faith are stated immediately after. To show the beginning, middle, and end of the attainment of purification by that practice, the three supramundane faculties are stated at the end.

[212] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[212] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Ettāvatā adhippetatthasiddhīti aññesaṃ agahaṇanti” vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

The statement: ‘The others are not included because the intended meaning is accomplished with just this much’—that is not logical.

Nahi santesupi aññesu indriyabhāvārahesu dhammesu ettāvatā adhippetatthasiddhiyā tesaṃ aññesaṃ bhagavato therassaca agahaṇanti yuttaṃ vattuṃ. Indriyabhāvārahassa aññassa asambhavato. Yadi hi sambhaveyya, sataṃpi sahassaṃpi gaṇhissatiyevāti. [M 0.0347] Baliyanti uppannuppanne paṭipakkhadhamme sahanti maddantīti balāni. Yathā abalānaṃ baliyanti. Maddantenaṃ parissayāti. Etthaca abalāti dubbalā. Nanti hīnavīriyaṃ janaṃ. Baliyantīti balasā karonti ajjhottharanti. Parissayāti abalā rāgādi parissayāti attho. Apica, paṭipakkhadhammehi akampiyaṭṭhena akkho bhaṇiyaṭṭhena balānināma. Tasmā assaddhiyasaṅkhātena paṭipakkhadhammena kampetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatā saddhābalaṃnāma. Kosajjasaṅkhātena kampetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatā vīriyabalaṃnāma. Muṭṭhasaccena kampetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāsatibalaṃnāma. Uddhaccena kampetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāsamādhibalaṃnāma. Avijjāyakampetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatā paññābalaṃ nāma. Sesadukadvayaṃ pana aññamaññaṃ paṭipakkhenayojetabbaṃ.

For it is not proper to say that the non-inclusion of others by the Blessed One and the Elder is because the intended meaning is accomplished with just this much, even when other states suitable for being faculties exist. This is because another state suitable for being a faculty is impossible. For if it were possible, he would indeed include hundreds or even thousands. They are strong; they endure and crush opposing states as they arise—thus they are called strengths. As it is said: 'They are strong against the weak. Dangers are crushed by them.' Here, 'weak' means feeble. 'Them' means a person of diminished energy. 'They are strong' means they act forcefully, they overwhelm. 'Dangers' means dangers such as lust, etc., for the weak. Moreover, they are called strengths because they are unshakeable by opposing states, and because they are spoken of as an axle. Therefore: The strength of faith is the inability to be shaken by the opposing state called lack of faith. The strength of energy is the inability to be shaken by the opposing state called laziness. The strength of mindfulness is the inability to be shaken by the opposing state called forgetfulness. The strength of concentration is the inability to be shaken by the opposing state called restlessness. The strength of wisdom is the inability to be shaken by the opposing state called ignorance. The remaining two pairs, however, should be connected with each other by their opposites.

[213] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[213] But in the Vibhāvanī

Pāpabaladukaṃ paṭipakkhena yojetuṃ nalabbhatīti katvā “ahirikānottappadvayaṃ pana sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāve nevāti” vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

Because the pair of evil powers cannot be connected with their opposites, it is said, “But the pair of shamelessness and lack of moral dread are never stable in the associated states.” That is not well said.

Sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvotica paṭipakkhehi akampiyatā tica atthato nānattābhāvatoti. Vīriyasamādhibalāni kusalākusalābyākatāni. Ahirikānottappāni akusalabalāni. Sesāni kusalābyākatānīti. Adhipatīti ettha patīti sāmi issaro. So pana padesa issaro sakalissaroti duvidho. Tattha indriyāni paresaṃ visaye sayaṃ paravase vattitvā attano visayeeva parehi attano vase vattāpentīti padesissarā nāma. Pubbāti saṅkhāravasena pubbāgamanavasena vā visesetvā pavattaṃ adhipatiṭṭhānaṃ patvā pana añño dutiyo issaronāma natthi. Tasmā adhiko patīti adhipati. Attā dhīnavuttīnaṃ patīti adhipatītica vadanti.

Because 'stability in associated states' and 'unshakeability by opposing factors' are not different in meaning. Energy-power and concentration-power are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Shamelessness and lack of moral dread are unwholesome powers. The remaining ones are wholesome or indeterminate. Regarding 'adhipati' (dominance), 'pati' here means lord, master, controller. That controller is twofold: a local controller and a universal controller. Therein, the faculties are called local controllers because, while operating in the domain of others under another's control, in their own domain they cause others to act under their own control. And having attained the state of dominance that has arisen, being distinguished by way of volitional formations or by way of prior occurrence, there is no other second controller. Therefore, 'adhipati' means 'supreme controller' (adhiko pati). They also say 'adhipati' is the controller of those whose conduct is dependent on oneself.

Chandoeva adhipatīti chandādhipati. Chandavato kiṃnāma kammaṃ nasijjhatīti evaṃ pubbābhisaṅkhāravasenavā pubbe atītabhavesu suṭṭhu āsevitachandāgamanavasenavā tesu tesu kalyāṇa pāpakammesu sampayuttadhamme mahoghoviya tiṇapaṇṇakasaṭe attaparādhīne [M 0.0348] niccaṃ paggahitadhure katvā pavatto kattukamyatā chando. Esa nayo sesesupi. Nanu cettha pacchimā tayo dhammā adhipatibhāvaṃ gaṇhantā indriyabhāvaṃ avijahitvāva gaṇhantīti adhipatibhūtāva samānā indriyakiccavasena paravasepi vattantīti. Saccaṃ, aññaṃ pana adhipatikiccaṃ, aññaṃ indriyakiccanti natthettha dosoti. Yathā hi rājā cakkavattī ekassa attano purohitassa santike ekaṃ dibbavijjaṃ gaṇhāti. Na ettāvatā rājā cakkavattināma nahoti. Naca vijjāhetu aññassa vasena vattati. Aññañhi cakkavatti rajjakiccaṃ, aññaṃ vijjāgahaṇa kiccanti. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha adhipatikiccaṃnāma taṃtaṃkicca visesaṃ anapekkhitvā atulyabalena abhibhavitvā sahajāta dhamme attano attano kiccesu anivattamāne katvā dhura vāhitā. Indriyakiccaṃ pana vijānanādikiccaṃ ārabbha pavuccatīti.

Desire itself is the dominant factor; thus it is called 'chandādhipati' (dominance of desire). What action, indeed, does not succeed for one who has desire? Thus, desire is the wish to act, which proceeds by constantly bearing the burden, making the associated states in those various wholesome and unwholesome deeds subservient to itself, like a great flood carrying grass and leaves, either by way of previous volitional formations, or by way of the approach of well-cultivated desire in past existences. This method applies to the rest as well. Indeed, do not the latter three states, when taking on the role of dominance, take it on without abandoning their nature as faculties? That is, though they are dominant, do they also function under another’s influence in regard to the function of faculties? True, but the function of a dominant factor is one thing, and the function of a faculty is another—there is no fault here. For example, a wheel-turning king learns a divine science from his own priest. By this alone, the king does not cease to be a wheel-turning monarch, nor does he act under another’s influence because of that knowledge. For the duties of a wheel-turning king are one thing, and the duty of learning a science is another. This example should be understood similarly. Here, the function of a dominant factor is to bear the burden by overpowering co-arisen states with incomparable strength, without regard to specific duties, and making them fulfill their own tasks without turning back. The function of a faculty, however, is spoken of with reference to activities such as cognizing.

Āharanti sahajātādipaccayasāmaññato atirekena asādhāraṇapaccayasattivisesena haranti pavattentīti āhārā. Āharantivā ajjhattasambhūtā te te paccayadhammā paccayuppannadhammāca attānañceva attano attano paccayakiccaṃ paccayuppannakiccañca suṭṭhu haranti vahanti etehīti āhārā. Yathāhasabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikāti. Etthaca sabbe sattāti etena sabbe ajjhattasambhūtā paccayapaccayuppannadhammā vuttā. Āhāraṭṭhitikāti paccayaṭṭhitikā. Yathārahaṃ catuvīsatipaccayehi ṭhitisabhāvāti attho. Nanucettha paccayāhārova vutto. Na āhārapaccayo. Idha pana catubbidho āhārapaccayadhammova vuttoti. Saccaṃ, paccayaṭṭhena pana āhāranāmakānaṃ sabbesaṃ catuvīsatipaccayadhammānaṃ majjhe yedhammā cattāro āhārāti visesetvā vuttā. Te tesaṃ paccayāhārānaṃpi āhārabhūtāti siddhā hontīti. Imasmiṃ atthe catunnaṃ āhārānaṃ mahanta bhāvo pākaṭo hotīti.

They are called nutriments because they bring forth and cause to proceed by a special power of an uncommon condition, in addition to the commonality of co-arisen and other conditions. Or, they are called nutriments because through these, those various internally arisen conditioning phenomena and conditionally arisen phenomena properly bring and carry themselves and their respective functions as conditions and as conditionally arisen. As it is said: 'All beings subsist on nutriment.' Here, by 'all beings,' all internally arisen conditioning and conditionally arisen phenomena are meant. 'Subsisting on nutriment' means subsisting on conditions; the meaning is that their nature of stability is due to the twenty-four conditions, as appropriate. Now, is it not that only nutriment-as-support is mentioned here, and not the nutriment condition? But here, the fourfold phenomenon of the nutriment condition is spoken of. True, but in the sense of being a condition, among all the twenty-four conditioning phenomena, those four phenomena that are specifically called 'nutriments' are distinguished. They are established as being nutriments even for those nutriments-as-support. In this sense, the great importance of the four nutriments becomes evident.

Tattha yathā yavabījānaṃvā sālibījānaṃvā ānubhāvo nāma kaḷiraṅkurānaṃ uppādāna padhānaṃ hoti. Tatoparaṃ pana sassabhāvaṃ [M 0.0349] patvā cha pañca māse vaḍḍhiyāvā ṭhitiyāvā pathavi rasaāporasānaṃ ānubhāvo padhānaṃ hoti. Evamevaṃ kabaḷī kārāhārūpajīvīnaṃ kāmasattānaṃ kammassa ānubhāvonāma paṭisandhirūpuppādane padhānaṃ hoti. Tatoparaṃ pana yāvatāyukaṃ vaḍḍhīyāvāṭhitiyāvā utuāhārānaṃ ānubhāvo padhānaṃ hoti. Kammajarūpāni hi yāva āsannamaraṇā pavattamānānipi utuāhārehi anuggahitānieva pavattanti. Utuca āhāru patthambhitoyeva attano kiccaṃ karoti. Tasmā tesaṃ sattānaṃ catusantatirūpaṃ kabaḷīkārāhārena anupatthambhīyamānaṃ ciraṃ napavattati. Upatthambhīyamānaṃeva yāvatāyukaṃ pavattati. Yathāca sakuṇāvā ḍaṃsamakasā dayovā tuṇḍena āhāraṃ gahetvā attabhāvaṃ posenti. Tuṇḍe asante āhāraṃ alabhantā maranti. Evameva ime sattā phassena ārammaṇesu rasaṃ gahetvā vedanāsaṅkhātaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ sampādetvā taṇhāvepullaṃ patvā tividhaṃ vaṭṭaṃ pūretvā yāvajjatanāpi vaṭṭe anukaṇṭhamānā pavattanti.

Here, just as the influence of barley seeds or rice seeds is the primary cause for the production of sprouts, thereafter, having reached the state of crops, the influence of the nutritive essence of earth and water is the primary cause for their growth and sustenance over five or six months. In the same way, for beings of the sense sphere who subsist on physical nutriment, the influence of kamma is the primary cause for the production of rebirth-linking form. Thereafter, for as long as they live, the influence of climate and nutriment is the primary cause for their growth and sustenance. For kamma-born forms, even while they continue until near death, they continue only when supported by climate and nutriment. Climate and nutriment, only when mutually supporting, perform their function. Therefore, for these beings, the fourfold continuity of material form, if unsupported by physical nutriment, does not long continue. Only when supported does it continue for the full lifespan. Just as birds, mosquitoes, and the like take food with their beaks and nourish their bodies, but without a beak, they cannot obtain food and die—so too, these beings, through contact, take relish in objects, bring about enjoyment and consumption known as feeling, reach the expansion of craving, fulfill the threefold round, and continue suffering in the round even until today.

Yadi hi phassonāma na siyā, ārammaṇarasaṃ alabhitvā vedanā paribhogarahitena taṇhuppattiyā okāso natthīti tividhavaṭṭameva nasiyāti.
