Yathāca te sakuṇādayo pakkhe viyūhitvā antarā apatamānā rukkhato rukkhaṃ vanato vanaṃ vicaritvā attānaṃ yāpenti. Pakkhesu asantesu gamanaṃ asampādentā patitvā maranti. Evamevaṃ ime sattā āyūhanalakkhaṇāya cetanāya cetayitvā kammasamaṅgitaṃ sampādetvā bhavato bhavaṃ vicaritvā yāvajjatanā vaṭṭe saṃsaranti. Yadi hi cetanānāma na siyā, kammavaṭṭassa abhāvo. Tadabhāveca vipākavaṭṭassa abhāvo. Tadabhāveca tadanusayitassa kilesavaṭṭassa abhāvoti vaṭṭaṃnāma na siyāti. Yathāca te sakuṇādayo cakkhunā gocaraṭṭhānaṃvā taṃtaṃdisābhāgaṃvā vibhāvetvā yāvajīvaṃ attānaṃ yāpenti. Cakkhusmiṃ asante kiñcigahetabbavatthuṃvā gantabbaṭṭhānaṃvā alabhitvā tattheva maranti. Evamevaṃ [M 0.0350] sampayuttā dhammā ārammaṇavijānalakkhaṇena viññāṇena taṃtaṃārammaṇaṃ labhitvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ phassādayo uppādetvā tividhaṃ vaṭṭaṃ vaṭṭenti. Yadi hi viññāṇaṃnāma na siyā, phassādīnaṃ ārammaṇalābhoyeva natthīti vaṭṭameva na siyāti. Tenāha cattāro āhārā.La. Viññāṇaṃ catutthanti. Saṃyuttakeca –

If there were no such thing as contact, then without obtaining the relish of the object, feeling would be devoid of enjoyment, and there would be no opportunity for the arising of craving; thus the threefold round itself would not exist. Just as those birds and other creatures, with their wings spread, fly without falling between, from tree to tree and forest to forest, sustaining themselves, but without wings, unable to accomplish movement, they fall and die. In the same way, these beings, having willed with volition characterized by accumulation, and having brought about the accompaniment of kamma, wander from existence to existence, revolving in the round even until today. If there were no such thing as volition, the round of kamma would not exist. Without that, the round of results would not exist. Without that, the round of defilements dependent on it would not exist—thus, the round itself would not exist. Just as those birds and other creatures, having discerned with the eye their feeding grounds or specific directions, sustain themselves for life, but without the eye, unable to grasp any object or find a place to go, they die right there. In the same way, associated phenomena, through consciousness characterized by the cognition of objects, obtain various objects and generate contact and the rest, thus turning the threefold round. If there were no such thing as consciousness, there would be no obtaining of objects for contact and the rest—thus, the round itself would not exist. Therefore, he said: “The four nutriments... consciousness is the fourth.” And in the Saṃyutta:

Cattārome bhikkhave āhārā bhūtānaṃ vā sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā sambhavesīnaṃvā sattānaṃ anuggahāya kabaḷīkāro āhāro oḷārikovā sukhumovā, phasso dutīyo, manosañcetanā tatīyā, viññāṇaṃ catutthanti vuttaṃ.

It has been said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the sustenance of beings that have come to be and for the support of those seeking to come into existence: physical nutriment, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth.”

Tattha bhūtānanti vuddhippattānaṃ. Sambhavesīnanti kalalādi kāle ṭhitānaṃ. Catunnaṃpana āhārānaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭevā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhavevā ṭhitiyāvā anuggahāyavā pavatti ākāro vuttanayena veditabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana kopanettha āhāro. Kiṃ āhāretīti. Kabaḷīkārā hāro ojaṭṭhamakarūpāni āhāreti. Phassāhāro tisso vedanā. Manosañcetanāhāro tayo bhave. Viññāṇā hāro paṭisandhināmarūpanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pākaṭaphalavasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ojaṭṭhamakarūpuppādanaṃ pana kabaḷīkārāhārassa mahantaṃ kiccaṃ nahoti. Catusantatirūpupatthambhanameva mahantaṃ. Teneva hi pāḷiyaṃ ṭhitiyātica anuggahāyātica vuttaṃ.

Herein, ‘of beings’ (bhūtānaṃ) means of those who have reached full growth. ‘Of those seeking to come into existence’ (sambhavesīnaṃ) means of those existing in the stage of the embryo and so on. Further, the mode of operation of the four kinds of nutriment should be understood according to the stated method as being for the maintenance or for the support of beings in this or that state of existence within the beginningless round of rebirths, as is possible. In the commentary, however, it is asked: “What here is nutriment? What does it nourish?” It is said: “Edible food nourishes the material octads with nutritive essence as the eighth. The nutriment of contact nourishes the three feelings. The nutriment of mental volition nourishes the three kinds of existence. The nutriment of consciousness nourishes name-and-form at rebirth-linking.” This should be understood as stated in terms of the manifest result. However, the production of material octads with nutritive essence as the eighth is not the primary function of edible food. Its main function is the sustaining of the four continuities of material phenomena. For this very reason, it is said in the Pāḷi “for maintenance” and “for support.”

Apica yathā upanissayāsevanapaccayā suttanti kapariyāyā abhidhammapariyāyātica duvidhā honti. Tathā āhārapaccayopi duvidho. Tattha yaṃ vuttaṃ manosañcetanāhāro tayobhaveti. Taṃ suttantikapariyāyaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Nahi paṭṭhāne arūpā hārā asahajātānaṃ dhammānaṃ āhāraṭṭhena paccayānāma hontīti. Pañcaviññāṇesu jhānaṅgāni nalabbhanti. Tāni hi dubbalakiccaṭṭhānavatthukattā rūpādīsu abhinipātamattāni hontīti na tesu vijjamānā vedanā ekaggatā jhānakiccaṃ sādhentīti. Vitakkapacchimakaṃ jhānantica [M 0.0351] vuttaṃ. Jhānaṅgānaṃ nāyakabhūtoca vitakko tesu natthīti tattha tāvedanā ekaggatāyo taṃ na sādhentīti. Vīriyupatthambharahitā dhammā sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvappattā nahontīti avīriyesu soḷasāhetukacittesu samādhibalakiccaṃ na sādheti. Vīriyapacchimakaṃ balanti hi vuttanti āha avīriyesu balāni nalabbhantīti. Heturahitā ca dhammā vaṭṭassa vivaṭṭassaca pattiyā pathabhāvaṃ nagacchanti. Hetupacchimako maggoti hi vuttanti āha ahetukesu maggaṅgāni na labbhantīti. Vicikicchāsampayuttecitte ekaggatā adhimokkharahi tattā ekantena saṃsappanasabhāvāya vicikicchāya abhibhūtattā ca maggindriyabalabhāvāya balavatī nahotīti vuttaṃ vicikicchā citte ekaggatā maggindriyabalabhāvaṃ na gacchatīti. Dvihetuka tihetuka javanesvevāti ettha dvihetuka tihetukasaddena momūhadvayahasanajavanāni nivatteti. Javanasaddena tibhūmakāni dvihetukatihetukavipākāni nivatteti.

Moreover, just as the decisive support and repetition conditions are twofold—by way of the Suttanta method and the Abhidhamma method—so too is the nutriment condition. Herein, when it is said, “The nutriment of mental volition nourishes the three kinds of existence,” this was stated with reference to the Suttanta method. For in the Paṭṭhāna, immaterial nutriments are not conditions in the sense of nutriment for non-conascent states. The jhāna factors are not found in the five sense consciousnesses. For since they have a weak function, basis, and object, and merely fall upon objects such as forms, the feeling and one-pointedness present in them do not accomplish the function of jhāna. And it is said: “Jhāna has initial application as its final component.” Since initial application, the leader of the jhāna factors, is absent in them, that feeling and one-pointedness do not accomplish that function. States devoid of the support of energy do not attain firmness among their associated states; thus in the sixteen rootless consciousnesses, concentration does not accomplish the function of a spiritual power. For it is said: “Spiritual power has energy as its final component.” Hence he says that the spiritual powers are not found in states devoid of energy. And states devoid of roots do not become a path for the attainment of either the round of existence or the transcendence of the round. For it is said: “The path has a root as its final component.” Hence he says that the path factors are not found in rootless states. It is said that in a consciousness associated with doubt, one-pointedness—being devoid of determination and being completely overwhelmed by doubt, which has the nature of wavering—does not become strong enough to be a path faculty or a spiritual power. Thus it is said that in a consciousness associated with doubt, one-pointedness does not attain the state of a path faculty or a spiritual power. In the phrase “only in two-rooted and three-rooted impulsions,” by the words “two-rooted” and “three-rooted” he excludes the impulsions of the pair of delusion-rooted consciousnesses and the smiling consciousness. By the word “impulsions,” he excludes the two-rooted and three-rooted resultant consciousnesses of the three planes.

[214] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[214] But in the Vibhāvanī:

“Dvihetukatihetukagahaṇena ekahetukesu adhipatīnaṃ abhāvaṃ dassetī”ti vuttaṃ, javanabhāvasāmaññattā pana hasanacittepi tesaṃ abhāvo dassetabboyeva hotīti.

It is said: “By the inclusion of the two-rooted and three-rooted, he shows the absence of predominance factors in the one-rooted states.” However, since the smiling consciousness shares the general nature of an impulsion, their absence must also be shown in it.

Yathāsambhavanti laddhapubbāti saṅkhārassa laddhapubbāgamassa ca ekekassa adhipatino sambhavānurūpaṃ ekova labbhati. Na dutiyo. Itarathā adhipatieva nasiyāti. Evañca katvā paṭṭhāne yathā indriyapaccayavibhaṅge arūpinoindriyā sampayuttakānaṃdhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ indriyapaccayena paccayoti vuttaṃ. Na tathā adhipatipaccayavibhaṅge. Tattha pana chandādhipati chandasampayuttakānantiādinā ekekādhipati vibhāgavaseneva vuttanti. Evañhi sati adhipati indriyānaṃ viseso pākaṭo hotīti. Naveritāti nava īritā kathitā. Kusalā kusalā byākatehi samākiṇṇo kusalādi samākiṇṇo. [Missakasaṅgaho]

'As is possible' means that in accordance with the possibility of each single predominance factor—of a previously acquired formation and of a previously acquired attainment—only one is obtained, not a second. Otherwise, predominance itself would be destroyed. And so, in the Paṭṭhāna, in the analysis of the faculty condition, it is said: 'The immaterial faculties are a condition by way of faculty condition for their associated states and for the material forms originated by them.' It is not so in the analysis of the predominance condition. There, however, by way of the phrase 'predominance of desire for the states associated with desire,' etc., each predominance is stated only by way of an individual analysis. For only thus does the distinction between predominance and the faculties become manifest. 'Nine are uttered' means nine are spoken, are stated. 'Mixed with wholesome' means mixed with wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states. [The Compendium of the Miscellaneous]

164. Cattāri [M 0.0352] saccāni bujjhatīti bodhi. Bujjhantivā tāni taṃ samaṅgino etāyāti bodhi. Catumaggañāṇaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ mahā niddese bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu-ñāṇanti. Pakkhoti koṭṭhāso sambhāro. Bodhiyā pakkhe bhavāti bodhipakkhiyā. Adhisīlā dhicittā dhipaññā saṅkhātāsu tīsu sikkhāsu pariyāpannānaṃ satthusāsanadhammānaṃ etaṃnāmaṃ. Te pana koṭṭhāsato satta vidhā hontīti āha cattārosatipaṭṭhānātiādi. Sampayutta dhammesu pamukhā padhānā hutvā kāyādīsu ārammaṇesu tiṭṭhanti nānārammaṇesu cittagamanaṃ nivattetvā tesveva kāyādīsu citta nibandhanavasena pavattantīti paṭṭhānāni. Satieva paṭṭhānānīti sati paṭṭhānāni. Cattārisatipaṭṭhānānīti vattabbe dhammabhāvaṃ apekkhitvā cattārosatipaṭṭhānā tivuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāyeanupassanā kāyā nupassanā. Rūpakāye rūpasamūhe assāsapassāsādikassa avayavakāyassa taṃtaṃkāyabhāvenavā aniccādibhāvenavā yāva tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāye sammoho pahiyyati. Tāva punappunaṃ nirantaraṃ samanupassanāti attho. Navappabhedāsu vedanāsu sukhavedanādi kāyaavayavavedanāya taṃtaṃ vedanābhāvena udayabbayavasena ca anupassanā vedanānupassanā. Soḷasa pabhedesu sarāgā dīsu cittesu sarāgādikassa avayavacittassa taṃtaṃ cittabhāvena udayabbayavasenaca anupassanā cittānupassanā. Pañcapabhedesu nīvaraṇādīsu dhammesu kāmacchandādikassa avayavadhammassa taṃ taṃ dhammabhāvena udayabbayavasenaca anupassanā dhammānupassanā.

164. It awakens to the Four Truths, thus it is 'enlightenment' (bodhi). Or, one endowed with it awakens to them by means of it, thus it is 'enlightenment.' It is the knowledge of the four paths. This is stated in the Mahāniddesa: 'Bodhi is the term for the knowledge in the four paths.' 'Side' (pakkha) means portion, requisite. 'Pertaining to enlightenment' (bodhipakkhiya) is so called because it is on the side of enlightenment. This is a name for the teachings of the Master's Dispensation that are included in the three trainings called higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. He says that these, by way of division, are of seven kinds: 'The four establishments of mindfulness,' etc. Being chief and principal among associated states, they are established on objects such as the body; having prevented the mind from going to various objects, they proceed by way of binding the mind to just those things such as the body, thus they are 'establishments' (paṭṭhānāni). Mindfulness itself is the establishments, thus 'establishments of mindfulness' (satipaṭṭhānāni). It should be understood that although it should be said as 'cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni,' with regard to their nature as dhammas, it is said as 'cattāro satipaṭṭhānā.' 'Contemplation of the body' (kāyānupassanā) is contemplation in the body. The meaning is: the repeated, uninterrupted, close contemplation of the material body—the collection of material phenomena—and of the component body of in-and-out breaths, etc., either in terms of its own specific bodily nature or in terms of impermanence, etc., until delusion regarding that particular body is abandoned. 'Contemplation of feelings' is the contemplation of the component feeling within the nine kinds of feelings, such as pleasant feeling, in terms of its own specific nature as feeling and in terms of arising and passing away. 'Contemplation of mind' is the contemplation of the component mind within the sixteen kinds of mind, such as the mind with lust, in terms of its own specific nature as mind and in terms of arising and passing away. 'Contemplation of dhammas' is the contemplation of the component dhamma within the five kinds of dhammas, such as the hindrances, in terms of its own specific nature as a dhamma and in terms of arising and passing away.

[215] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[215] But as to what is to be clarified in the Vibhāvanī:

“Kucchitānaṃ kesādīnaṃ āyoti kāyo. Assāsa passāsānaṃvā samūho kāyo”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na sundara meva.

It is said: "It is a source (āya) of despicable things such as hair, thus it is a body (kāya). Or, the body is the collection of in-breaths and out-breaths." This is not well stated.

[216] Yañca tattha

[216] And what is said there:

“Kāyassa anupassanā kāyānupassanā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ.

It is said: "Contemplation of the body is body-contemplation." This too is not well-stated.

Kāye [M 0.0353] kāyānupassī viharatīti hi vuttaṃ. Etena hi kāye anupassanā kāyānupassanāti ayamatthova padhānato dassitoti.

For it is said: "He dwells contemplating the body in the body." By this, the meaning "contemplation in the body is body-contemplation" is shown as the primary one.

[217] Yañca tattha

[217] And what is said there:

“Vedanānaṃ vasena anupassanā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundaraṃ. Vedanāsu vedanānupassīti hi vuttaṃ. Tathā cittānupassanā padepi.

It is said: "Contemplation by way of feelings." This too is not well-stated. For it is said: "He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings." The same applies to the passage on contemplation of mind.

[218] Yaṃpi tattha

[218] And also what is said there:

“Saññāsaṅkhārānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhinnalakkhaṇānameva anupassanā dhammānupassanā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na sundarameva.

It is said: "Contemplation of dhammas is the contemplation only of those dhammas with distinct characteristics, namely, perception and formations." This too is not well-stated at all.

Na hi katthaci pāḷiyaṃ saññāsaṅkhārāva visesetvā dhammāti vuttā atthīti. Pāḷiyañhi chanīvaraṇā pathamaṃ dhammāti vuttā. Tato pañcupādānakkhandhā. Tato dvādasāyatanāni. Tato sattabojjhaṅgā. Tato cattāri saccānīti. Yadievaṃ ekāya dhammānupassanāya vuttāya itarāpi siddhāti satipaṭṭhānaṃ ekameva vattabbaṃ, na cattāroti.Na. Yo hi dhammānupassanāyaṃ rūpakkhandho vutto. So ruppanalakkhaṇānupassanavasena vutto. Ruppanalakkhaṇañhi nibbattitapara matthadhammo. Soca tathā anupassantassa visesato sukhumassa attavipallāsassa pahānāya hotīti. Kāyoti pana taṃtaṃ samūhabhūtarūpadhammavasena veditabbo. Naruppanalakkhaṇavasena. Naca taṃtaṃ kāyabhāvena gahito taṃtaṃ rūpadhammasamūho nibbattita paramatthadhammonāma hoti. Paññattimissakattā. Soca tathā anupassantassa visesato oḷārikassa subhādi vipallāsassa pahānāya hotīti. Tathā vedanācittesupi oḷārikavipallāso sukhumavipallāsoti dve dve vipallāsā honti. Tattha attupanibandhā niccasukha vipallāsā oḷārikā. Attavipallāso sukhumo. Tattha vedanā cittā nupassanā oḷārikavipallāsānaṃ pahānāya visuṃ vuttā. Dhammesu vedanākkhandhaviññāṇakkhandhā sukhuma vipallāsa pahānāyāti. Tasmā cattārova satipaṭṭhānā vattabbāti. Sammā padahanti etehīti sammappadhānāni. Kāmaṃ tacoca [M 0.0354] nhāruca, aṭṭhica avasissatu. Upassussatu me sarīre maṃsalohitaṃ. Yantaṃ purisathāmena purisaparakkamena pattabbaṃ. Na taṃ apatvā vīriyassa saṇṭhānaṃ bhavissatīti evaṃ anivattanavutti vasena pavattassa sammāvāyāmassa etaṃ nāmaṃ. So pana tathā pavatto ekopi samāno kiccasiddhivasena catudhā hotīti. Vuttaṃ uppannānantiādi.

Nowhere in the Pāli canon is it said that only perceptions and formations are distinguished as "dhammas." For in the Pāli, the six hindrances are first called "dhammas," then the five aggregates subject to clinging, then the twelve sense bases, then the seven factors of enlightenment, then the four truths. Thus, since by stating one kind of contemplation of dhammas the others are also established, only one foundation of mindfulness should be taught, not four. No. For in the contemplation of dhammas, the aggregate of form is mentioned. It is mentioned in terms of observing the characteristic of being afflicted. The characteristic of being afflicted is an ultimate reality that has been produced. And for one who contemplates thus, it is especially for abandoning the subtle distortion of self. But "body" should be understood as a collection of material phenomena, not in terms of the characteristic of being afflicted. Nor is a collection of material phenomena, taken as a body, an ultimate reality that has been produced, because it is mixed with concepts. And for one who contemplates thus, it is especially for abandoning the gross distortions such as beauty. Similarly, in feelings and mind, there are two kinds of distortions: gross and subtle. There, the distortions of permanence and happiness, bound up with self, are gross; the distortion of self is subtle. There, the contemplations of feeling and mind are separately stated for abandoning gross distortions. In the contemplation of dhammas, the aggregates of feeling and consciousness are for abandoning subtle distortions. Therefore, it should be said that there are four foundations of mindfulness. They strive rightly with these, thus they are called right strivings. "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in my body dry up. Whatever can be achieved by human strength, human energy, human striving, I will not stop my effort until I have attained it." This is the name for the right effort that proceeds with unwavering resolve. But though it is one when proceeding thus, it becomes fourfold by the accomplishment of its tasks. As it is said: "Of arisen states..." and so on.

Tattha uppannānaṃpāpakānanti asukasmiṃ kāle dese ṭhāne vā ahaṃ idañcidañca nāma pāpaṃ akāsiṃ, idañcidañcanāma mayhaṃ uppannanti evaṃ attano santāne uppannabhāvena viditānaṃ akusalānaṃ. Pahānāyāti tesaṃ attano santāne ajjatagge yāvaparinibbānāpuna anuppādadhammatāpādanakaraṇatthaṃ. Vāyāmoti sīla pūraṇa samatha vipassanābhāvanākammesu daḷhaṃ vāyāmo. Anuppannānanti attano santāne uppannapubbanti aviditānaṃ parasantānesuvā suttantesuvā disvāvā sutvāvā viditānaṃ. Anuppādāyāti yesaṃ akusala mūlānaṃ atthitāya imesaṃ sattānaṃ īdisāni kilesajātāni vā pāpakammānivā uppajjanti. Tāni mayi vijjantieva. Ahaṃpi tehi kilesehivā kammehivā aparimuttoyeva. Ahaṃpi svevā parasuvevā bhavantaresuvā tāni attano santāne uppādessā miyevāti evaṃ paccavekkhitvā tesaṃ akusalamūlānaṃ attano santāne uppattiyā paccayasamucchindanatthaṃ. Anuppannānaṃkusalānanti catubhūmakesu kusaladhammesu sattavisuddhipabhedesu imenāma visuddhidhammā mayā appattā anadhigatāeva hontīti evaṃ ñatvā samaye anatikkanteeva appattānaṃ anadhigatānaṃ upari visuddhidhammānaṃ adhigamanatthāya.

Here, 'of arisen unwholesome states' means this: having recognized the unwholesome states that have arisen in one's own continuity—'At such a time, in such a place, I committed such and such an evil deed, and such and such has arisen in me.' 'For the sake of their abandoning' means for the purpose of ensuring they do not arise again in one's own continuity from this day until Parinibbāna. 'He makes an effort' means strong exertion in the tasks of fulfilling virtue and developing serenity and insight. 'Of unarisen unwholesome states' means those not known to have previously arisen in one's own continuity, but known by seeing or hearing of them in the continuities of others or in the suttas. 'For their non-arising' means this: one reflects, 'Due to the existence of these unwholesome roots, such kinds of defilements or evil actions arise in these beings. These exist in me too. I too am not free from these defilements or actions. I too may give rise to them in my own continuity tomorrow, the day after, or in future existences.' Having reflected thus, one strives to cut off the conditions for the arising of these unwholesome roots in one's own continuity. 'Of unarisen wholesome states' means this: concerning the wholesome qualities of the four planes and the seven kinds of purification, one knows, 'Such and such qualities of purification have not yet been attained or realized by me.' Without letting the opportunity pass, one strives to attain the higher qualities of purification not yet attained or realized.

Uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ bhiyyo bhāvāyāti yāni sīlādīni kusalāni mayi uppannāni. Tāni yāva niyāmaṃ naokkamanti, tāva mayhaṃ etānīti vattuṃ nārahanti. Svevā parasuvevā bhavantaraṃ patvāvā bhijjissanti yevāti evaṃ paccavekkhitvā attano santāne uppannānaṃ tesaṃ sabbaso akuppadhammatāpādanavasena suṭṭhutaraṃ vaḍḍhanatthāya. Etesu pana catūsu mukhesu yena kenaci ekena mukhena [M 0.0355] uppanno vāyāmo catukiccasādhakoeva hotīti veditabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana maggakkhaṇe eva ekassa tassa catukiccasādhakatā vuttāti.

'For the further development of arisen wholesome states' means this: Whatever wholesome states such as virtue have arisen in me, so long as they have not entered the fixed course of rightness, they are not fit to be called 'mine.' They will surely be destroyed, either tomorrow, the day after, or having reached a future existence. Reflecting thus, one strives for the sake of further developing them by bringing those that have arisen in one's own continuity to a state of complete unshakeability. However, among these four aspects, it should be understood that effort arisen through any one aspect accomplishes the fourfold task. But in the commentary, it is said that it is at the moment of the path that one effort accomplishes the fourfold task.

Ijjhanaṃ iddhi, tassa tassa yogakammassa siddhi samiddhi nibbattīti attho. Sā pana saṅkhepato abhiññeyyānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhiññāsiddhi, pariññeyyānaṃ pariññāsiddhi, pahātabbānaṃ pahānasiddhi, sacchikā tabbānaṃ sacchikaraṇasiddhi, bhāvetabbānaṃ bhāvanāsiddhīti pañcavidhā hoti. Ijjhatītivā iddhi satthusāsane yogakammena ijjhantānaṃ sabbesaṃ mahaggata lokuttaradhammānaṃ nāmaṃ. Pajjati etenāti pādo. Iddhiyā pādoti iddhipādo. Iddhipattiyā balavupāyo padhānakāraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. So pana catunnaṃ adhipatidhammānaṃ vasena catudhā hotīti vuttaṃ cattāro iddhipādātiādi. Adhipatibhūto chandova iddhipādoti chandiddhipādo. Esanayo sesesupīti. Etthaca sabbe mahaggatānuttarabhūtā uttarimanussa dhammānāma napākatikena chandenavā vīriyenavā cittenavā paññāya vā adhigantabbā honti. Yena kenaci palibodhena paṭibāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyena adhipatibhāvapattena chandādināeva adhigantabbā. Tasmā ime cattāro dhammā adhipatibhūtāva idha adhippetāti daṭṭhabbāti.

Succeeding is spiritual power (iddhi); the meaning is the accomplishment, fulfillment, and production of this or that spiritual task. Briefly, it is fivefold: the success of direct knowledge regarding things to be directly known, the success of full understanding regarding things to be fully understood, the success of abandoning regarding things to be abandoned, the success of realization regarding things to be realized, and the success of development regarding things to be developed. Or, because it succeeds, it is called iddhi, which is a name for all exalted and supramundane states that are achieved by striving in the Teacher’s dispensation. 'One goes by this,' thus it is a 'base' (pāda). The base of spiritual power is a 'base for spiritual power' (iddhipāda). This means it is a powerful means and a principal cause for attaining spiritual power. It is said to be fourfold based on the four dominant factors, hence the phrase 'the four bases for spiritual power,' and so on. When desire is the dominant factor, it is the base for spiritual power through desire (chandiddhipāda). The same principle applies to the others. And here, all exalted and supreme states, the qualities beyond the ordinary human, are not to be attained by ordinary desire, energy, mind, or wisdom. They must be attained only by desire, etc., that has reached a state of dominance, which cannot be obstructed by any hindrance. Therefore, it should be understood that these four states are intended here precisely as dominant factors.

[219] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

Now, as to the explanation:

“Ijjhati adhiṭṭhānādikaṃ etāyāti iddhi, iddhividhaññāṇaṃ. Iddhiyā pādo iddhipādo”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ saṃyuttake katamāca bhikkhave iddhi. Idha bhikkhave bhikkhu anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti. Ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti.La. Yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vatteti. Ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhave iddhīti imāya pāḷiyā sameti. Evaṃsantepi idha abhidhammapariyāyova adhippetoti taṃ na yujjatiyeva.

It is said: "One succeeds in such things as determination by means of it, thus it is iddhi (spiritual power); it is the knowledge of the kinds of spiritual power. The basis of spiritual power is the base for spiritual power (iddhipāda)." This accords with the Pāli passage in the Saṃyutta Nikāya: "And what, bhikkhus, is spiritual power? Here, a bhikkhu experiences the various kinds of spiritual power: having been one, he becomes many ... he wields mastery with the body even up to the Brahmā world. This, bhikkhus, is called spiritual power." Even so, it is not fitting to hold that only the Abhidhamma exposition is intended here.

Vibhaṅge pana pathamavāre lokiya lokuttaramissakā citta cetasikarāsīeva iddhipādāti vuttā. Aṭṭhakathāyañca-pathamajjhāna parikammaṃhi [M 0.0356] iddhipādonāma. Pathamajjhānaṃ iddhināma.La. Nevasaññā nāsaññāyatanajjhānaparikammaṃ iddhipādonāma. Nevasaññānāsaññā yatanajjhānaṃ iddhināma. Sotāpattimaggassa vipassanā iddhipādo nāma. Sotāpattimaggo iddhināma.La. Arahattamaggassa vipassanā iddhipādonāma. Arahattamaggo iddhināmātica. Pathamajjhānaṃ iddhipādonāma. Dutiyajjhānaṃ iddhināma. La. Ākiñcaññāyatanajjhānaṃ iddhi pādonāma. Nevasaññā nāsaññā yatanajjhānaṃ iddhināma. Sotā pattimaggo iddhipādonāma. Sakadāgāmimaggo iddhināma.La. Arahattamaggo iddhināmāti ca vuttaṃ. Taṃtaṃ pādakajjhānaṃ iddhipādonāma. Tato tato vuṭṭhahitvā uppāditamaggo iddhināmātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Idha pana uttaracūḷabhājaniye āgatanayena cattāro adhipatidhammāeva iddhipādāti vuttā.

In the Vibhaṅga, however, in the first section, the aggregates of mind and mental factors, mixed as mundane and supramundane, are called the bases for spiritual power. And in the commentary it is said: the preliminary practice for the first jhāna is called a base for spiritual power; the first jhāna is called spiritual power. ... The insight for the path of arahantship is called a base for spiritual power; the path of arahantship is called spiritual power. And also: the first jhāna is called a base for spiritual power; the second jhāna is called spiritual power. ... The jhāna of the base of nothingness is called a base for spiritual power; the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called spiritual power. The path of stream-entry is called a base for spiritual power; the path of the once-returner is called spiritual power. ... The path of arahantship is called spiritual power. It is also possible to say that this or that jhāna serving as a foundation is called a base for spiritual power, and that the path generated after emerging from it is called spiritual power. Here, however, following the method presented in the Uttaracūḷabhājaniya, the four dominant factors alone are called the bases for spiritual power.

Tattha pana lokuttarabhūtāeva adhippetā. Idha lokiya lokuttara missakabhūtāti. Indriyabalāni atthato heṭṭhā vuttāneva. Pākaṭaṭṭhānato pana catūsu sotāpattiyaṅgesu saddhāya thāmo veditabbo. Yathāha-kattha bhikkhave saddhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Catūsu sotāpattiyaṅgesu ettha saddhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbanti. Catūsu sammappadhānesu vīriyassa. Yathāha-kattha bhikkhave vīriyindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Catūsu sammappadhānesu ettha vīriyindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbanti. Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu satiyā. Yathāha-kattha bhikkhavesatindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Catūsu satipaṭṭhānesuettha satindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbanti. Catūsu jhānesu samādhissa. Yathāha-kattha bhikkhave samādhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Catūsu jhānesu ettha samādhindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbanti. Catūsu ariyasaccesu paññāya thāmo veditabbo. Yathāha-kattha bhikkhave paññindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Catūsu ariyasaccesu ettha paññindriyaṃ daṭṭhabbanti. Sambodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ, samantato bujjhati paṭivijjhati bujjhanti vā etāyāti katvā. Sā hi catusaccadhammaṃ bujjhamānā ekakkhaṇe soḷasahi atthehi saddhiṃ samantato bujjhati, na ekadesa toti tassā sambodhiyā samuṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena sambodhiyā aṅgo sahakārībalavapaccayoti sambojjhaṅgo. Satieva sambojjhaṅgo satisambojjhaṅgo. [M 0.0357] Sā hi kāyādīsu catūsu attano gocaresu bhāvanāvasena suṭṭhusaṃvaḍḍhamānā anupubbena sabbapamāda pakkhaṃ vidhametvā sabbaṃ appamādapakkhañca pūretvā catumaggaññāṇa saṅkhātaṃ sambodhiṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti. Vipassanāya bhūmibhūte ajjhatta bahiddhādhamme vicināti kakkhaḷattaphusanādīhi aniccatādīhica vividhā kārehi cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kurumānoviya tesu daṭṭhabbākāraṃ asesaṃ upadhāretīti dhammavicayo. Soeva sambojjhaṅgoti dhammavicaya sambojjhaṅgo. Sopi hi attano gocarabhūtesu tesu dhammesu bhāvanāvasena suṭṭhusaṃvaḍḍhamāno anupubbena sabbaṃsammoha pakkhaṃ vidhametvā sabbaṃ asammohapakkhaṃ pūretvā sayaṃ catumaggañāṇa sambodhi hutvā samuṭṭhahatīti. Sammappadhānavīriyameva sambojjhaṅgoti vīriyasambojjhaṅgo. Tampi hi catubbidhesu attano gocaresu bhāvanāvasena suṭṭhu saṃvaḍḍhamānaṃ anupubbena sabbaṃ kusalesu dhammesu līnasaṅkoca kosajjapakkhaṃ kilesajātaṃ vidhametvā sabbaṃ dhurasaṃpaggahapakkhaṃ pūretvā vuttappakāraṃ sambodhiṃ samuṭṭhā petīti.

Here, however, only the supramundane is intended. In this context, it is a mixture of the mundane and supramundane. The faculties and powers, in terms of their meaning, have already been explained previously. From the perspective of their manifest place, however, the strength of faith should be understood in the four factors of stream-entry. As it is said: "Where, monks, should the faculty of faith be seen? In the four factors of stream-entry—here the faculty of faith should be seen." The strength of energy should be understood in the four right strivings. As it is said: "Where, monks, should the faculty of energy be seen? In the four right strivings—here the faculty of energy should be seen." The strength of mindfulness should be understood in the four establishments of mindfulness. As it is said: "Where, monks, should the faculty of mindfulness be seen? In the four establishments of mindfulness—here the faculty of mindfulness should be seen." The strength of concentration should be understood in the four jhānas. As it is said: "Where, monks, should the faculty of concentration be seen? In the four jhānas—here the faculty of concentration should be seen." The strength of wisdom should be understood in the four noble truths. As it is said: "Where, monks, should the faculty of wisdom be seen? In the four noble truths—here the faculty of wisdom should be seen." Enlightenment (sambodhi) is called the knowledge in the four paths, because one awakens all-round by it, or penetrates by it, or they awaken by it. For when it awakens to the Dhamma of the four truths, it awakens all-round in a single moment, together with sixteen aspects, and not partially. Because of its function of causing enlightenment to arise, it is a factor of enlightenment (sambojjhaṅga), a strong cooperative condition for enlightenment. Mindfulness itself is an enlightenment factor—mindfulness as an enlightenment factor. For when it is well-developed in its four domains—body and so on—through cultivation, it gradually dispels all that pertains to heedlessness and fulfills all that pertains to heedfulness, giving rise to enlightenment, which is the knowledge of the four paths. Investigation of phenomena (dhammavicaya) is to investigate internal and external phenomena, which form the basis for insight. It is as if pulverizing them into fine powder in various ways by means of their characteristics such as hardness, contact, impermanence, etc., thereby fully discerning all aspects to be seen in them. That itself is an enlightenment factor—investigation of phenomena as an enlightenment factor. For when it is well-developed in its domain of those phenomena through cultivation, it gradually dispels all that pertains to delusion and fulfills all that pertains to non-delusion, and arises itself as the enlightenment of the knowledge of the four paths. The right striving of energy itself is an enlightenment factor—energy as an enlightenment factor. For when it is well-developed in its fourfold domain through cultivation, it gradually dispels all that pertains to the defilements of slackness, contraction, and laziness in wholesome states, and fulfills all that pertains to vigorous exertion, giving rise to enlightenment in the manner described.

Pītiyeva sambojjhaṅgo pīti sambojjhaṅgo. Sāpi hi vuttappakāresu gocaresu suṭṭhu saṃvaḍḍhamānā kusalesu dhammesu sabbaṃ cittassa aratiukkaṇṭhapakkhaṃ vidhametvā sabbaṃ dhammarati dhammanandidhammārāma pakkhaṃ pūretvā vuttappakāraṃ sambodhiṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Passaddhieva sambojjhaṅgo passaddhi sambojjhaṅgo. Sāpi hi vuttapakāresu gocaresu bhāvanāvasena suṭṭhu saṃvaḍḍhamānā sabbaṃ cittassa sārambha darathapakkhaṃ vidhametvā sabbaṃ vūpasantasītalapakkhaṃ pūretvā vuttappakāraṃ sambodhiṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Samādhieva sambojjhaṅgoti samādhi sambojjhaṅgo. Tassa sambodhisamuṭṭhāpanatā pākaṭā. Tatramajjhattatā saṅkhātā upekkhāeva sambojjhaṅgoti upekkhā sambojjhaṅgo. Sāpihi vuttappakāresu satiādīnaṃ gocaresu bhāvanāvasena suṭṭhu saṃvaḍḍhamānā sabbaṃ cittassa līnuddhaccapakkhaṃ vidhametvā samavāhitapakkhaṃ pūretvā vuttappakāraṃ sambodhiṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti. Sammā aviparītato dassanaṃ sammādiṭṭhi. Sā pana dukkhe [M 0.0358] ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhaniro dhagāminipaṭipadāya ñāṇanti catubbidhā hoti. Sammā aviparītato saṃkappanaṃ sammāsaṅkappo. Yathā sammādiṭṭhi daṭṭhabbasabhāvesu pharamānā pavattati tathā tassā saṃvidhānanti attho. Teneva hi so paññākkhandhe saṅgahitoti. Yathāha-yācāvuso visākha sammādiṭṭhi, yoca sammāsaṅkappo, ime dhammā paññākkhandhe saṅgahitāti. Sammāvācā dayo pubbe vuttatthāyeva. Sammā vāyamanti ekenāti sammāvāyāmo. Catukiccasādhakaṃ sammappadhāna vīriyaṃ. Passaddhidvayaṃ passaddhisāmaññena ekaṃ katvā cuddasete sabhāvatoti vuttaṃ. Sattadhāti vuttappakārānaṃ satipaṭṭhānacatukka sammappadhānacatukkādīnaṃ vasena sattadhā. Idāni tesaṃ cuddasannaṃ kiccānaṃ ṭhānabhedaṃ dassetuṃ saṅkappapassaddhicātiādimāha.

Joy itself is an enlightenment factor; joy as an enlightenment factor. For when it is well developed in the aforementioned domains, it dispels all discontent and weariness of mind regarding wholesome states, fulfilling the aspect of delight in the Dhamma, joy in the Dhamma, and pleasure in the Dhamma, thereby arousing enlightenment in the manner described. Tranquility itself is an enlightenment factor; tranquility as an enlightenment factor. For when it is well developed through cultivation in the aforementioned domains, it dispels all agitation and distress of mind, fulfilling the aspect of calm and coolness, thereby arousing enlightenment in the manner described. Concentration itself is an enlightenment factor; concentration as an enlightenment factor. Its role in arousing enlightenment is evident. Equanimity, designated as neutrality, is itself an enlightenment factor; equanimity as an enlightenment factor. For when it is well developed through cultivation in the aforementioned domains of mindfulness and so on, it dispels all sluggishness and restlessness of mind, fulfilling the aspect of being well-balanced, thereby arousing enlightenment in the manner described. Right view is seeing correctly, without distortion. It is fourfold: knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Right intention is intending correctly, without distortion. Just as right view operates by pervading the true nature of what is to be seen, so too is its arrangement—this is the meaning. For that reason, it is included in the aggregate of wisdom, as it is said: "Friend Visākha, right view and right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom." Right speech and the others have the same meaning as previously stated. Right effort is 'striving rightly as one'. It is the energy of right striving that accomplishes the four tasks. The two kinds of tranquility are made one through the general term 'tranquility,' thus it is said, 'these fourteen in essence.' 'Sevenfold' refers to the sevenfold division based on the four establishments of mindfulness, the four right strivings, and so on, as described. Now, to show the distinction of function and place among these fourteen, the text begins with 'intention and tranquility, etc.'

[220] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[220] Now, that which is to be explained:

“Sattadhā tattha saṅgahoti vatvā puna taṃ dassetuṃ saṅkappapassaddhicātiādimāhā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

It is said: "Having stated, 'The grouping there is sevenfold,' and then to show it again, it is said, beginning with 'intention and tranquility, etc.'" That is not correct.

Na hi tattha satta sarūpaṃ labbhatīti. Saṅkappo viratittayañca ekaṃ maggaṅgaṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇāti. Passaddhica pītica upekkhāca ekaṃ bojjhaṅgaṭṭhānaṃ. Chandoca cittañca ekaṃ iddhipādaṭṭhānanti evaṃ navadhammā ekaṭṭhānikā honti. Ekaṃ vīriyaṃ catusammappadhāna iddhi pādindriya balabojjhaṅga maggaṅga vasena navaṭṭhānikaṃ. Ekā sati catusatipaṭṭhāna indriya bala bojjhaṅga maggaṅga vasena aṭṭhaṭṭhānikā. Eko samādhi indriya bala bojjhaṅga maggaṅga vasena catuṭṭhāniko. Ekāpaññā iddhipādindriya bala bojjhaṅga maggaṅga vasena pañcaṭṭhānikā. Ekā saddhā indriya bala vasena duṭṭhānikāti. Te pana sattatiṃsa pabhedā dhammā pubbabhāge nānārammaṇā nānākhaṇikāca honti. Maggaphalesu pana navaṭṭhānikaṃ vīriyaṃ ekameva nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃkatvā navasuṭhānesu atta paṭipakkhānaṃ pāpa dhammānaṃ paccaya yamugghātavasena nava kiccāni sādhayamānaṃ ekameva pavattati. Esa nayo aṭṭhaṭṭhānikādīsu. Tasmā te ekakkhaṇe ekacitte sabbe ekato upalabbhantīti [M 0.0359] vuttaṃ sabbe lokuttare hontīti. Navāsaṅkappa pītiyoti ettha vāsaddo kvaci saddattho. Saṅkappo kvaci dutīyajjhānikā dikepītica kvaci catutthajjhānikādike lokuttare nahontīti attho.

For a sevenfold nature is not found there. Intention and the three abstinences attain a single path-factor status. Tranquility, joy, and equanimity attain a single enlightenment-factor status. Desire and mind attain a single base-of-power status. Thus, these nine states have a single status. One factor of energy, by way of the four right strivings, bases of power, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, and path factors, has nine statuses. One factor of mindfulness, by way of the four establishments of mindfulness, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, and path factors, has eight statuses. One factor of concentration, by way of faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, and path factors, has four statuses. One factor of wisdom, by way of bases of power, faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, and path factors, has five statuses. One factor of faith, by way of faculties and powers, has two statuses. These thirty-seven kinds of states, in the preliminary stage, have diverse objects and are of diverse moments. But in the paths and fruits, the energy that has nine statuses, having made only Nibbāna its object, performs nine functions in nine positions—by way of destroying the conditions for opposing unwholesome states—and proceeds as one. This is the principle for the factor with eight statuses, and so on. Therefore, it is said that all of them are found together in a single moment, in a single consciousness, and all are supramundane. Regarding the phrase `Navāsaṅkappa pītiyo` ('Not always intention and joy'), here the word `vā` has the meaning of `kvaci` (sometimes). The meaning is that intention is sometimes not present in the supramundane states of the second jhāna and so on, and joy is sometimes not present in the supramundane states of the fourth jhāna and so on.

Lokiyepīti sīlavisodhanādivasena pavatte kāmā vacarakusalādike lokiyakusala kriyacittuppādepi. Yathā yoganti sīlavisodhanakamma samathakammanāmarūpapariggahādikammesu yujjitabbānaṃ viratittayādīnaṃ anurūpaṃ. Chabbisuddhipavattiyanti sīla visuddhādīnaṃ channaṃ visuddhīnaṃ anukkamena pavattikāle. Etena diṭṭheva dhamme maggaphalapatiṭṭhābhāvatthāya pūrite catupārisuddhi sīlepi saddhāsatiādayo bodhipakkhiyesu saṅgahitā eva honti. Tathā maggapādakatthāya uppāditesu mahaggatajjhānesu mīti dasseti. Tathā hi bojjhaṅgasaṃyuttake –

'Even in the worldly sphere' means also in the arising of mundane wholesome and functional consciousness, such as those of the sense-sphere, occurring by way of the purification of virtue, etc. 'As appropriate' means in accordance with the threefold abstinence, etc., as suitable for the tasks to be undertaken, such as the work of purifying virtue, the work of serenity, and the discernment of mind and matter. 'During the progression of the six purifications' refers to the time of the successive development of the six purifications, beginning with the purification of virtue. By this, it is shown that even in the fourfold purification of virtue, which is fulfilled without aiming for the establishment in the path and fruit in this very life, factors such as faith and mindfulness are included among the requisites of enlightenment. Similarly, it indicates this also occurs in the exalted jhānas that are produced for the purpose of being a basis for the path. For thus it is said in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta—

Evaṃ bhāvito kho kuṇḍaliya indriyasaṃvaro tīṇi sucaritāni paripūreti. Evaṃ bhāvitāni tīṇi sucaritāni cattāro satipaṭṭhāne paripūrenti. Evaṃ bhāvitā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā satta bojjhaṅge paripūrenti. Evaṃ bhāvitā satta bojjhaṅge vijjāvimuttiyo paripūrentīti vuttaṃ.

Thus cultivated, Kuṇḍaliya, sense-restraint fulfills the three kinds of good conduct. Thus cultivated, the three kinds of good conduct fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness. Thus cultivated, the four foundations of mindfulness fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. Thus cultivated, the seven factors of enlightenment fulfill knowledge and liberation—so it was said.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃpi nakevalaṃ balavavipassanā maggaphalesueva bojjhaṅge uddharanti. Vipassanāpādaka kasiṇajjhāna ānāpāṇā suka brahmavihārajjhānesupi uddharantīti vuttaṃ. [Bodhipakkhiyasaṅgaho]

In the commentary also, it is said that the enlightenment factors are brought forth not only by strong insight in the paths and fruits, but also in insight-supporting kasiṇa jhānas, mindfulness of breathing, and the pleasant abidings of brahma-vihāra jhānas. [The Compendium of the Requisites of Enlightenment]

165. Sabbasaṅgahe pañcakkhandhāti pañca rāsayo. Atītādi bheda bhinnānaṃ rūpānaṃ khandho rāsīti rūpakkhandho. Ekasmiṃ ruppana lakkhaṇe rāsiṃ katvā ñāṇena pariggahitā rūpadhammāeva. Tathā ekasmiṃ vedayitalakkhaṇe sañjānana lakkhaṇe rāsiṃ katvā pariggahitā atītādibhedabhinnā vedanāsaññāyo vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho canāma. Saṅkharontīti saṅkhārā. Phassa cetanā dayo. Tehi chasuvā upapattidvāresu tīsuvā kammadvāresu ekato saṅgamma samāgamma phusanacetayitādīhi attano attano [M 0.0360] kiccehi dassanasavanādīni sādhāraṇakiccānivā kāyika vācasikamānasikānivā sayana nisajjaṭṭhāna gamana kathana cintanādīni sabbāni kiccāni karonti vidahantīti. Vuttañhetaṃ saṃyuttake –

165. In the comprehensive grouping, the five aggregates are called the five heaps. The aggregate of form is the heap of forms differentiated by past, etc. Form phenomena are those comprehended by knowledge, having been heaped together in the single characteristic of being afflicted. Similarly, the aggregate of feeling and the aggregate of perception are names for feelings and perceptions differentiated by past, etc., comprehended as heaps in the single characteristics of experiencing and perceiving, respectively. They are called 'formations' because they construct. These include contact, volition, and so on. Having come together and combined in the six doors of becoming or the three doors of action, by means of contacting, willing, and so forth, they perform all functions—their respective functions such as seeing, hearing, etc., or common functions, or bodily, verbal, and mental functions such as lying down, sitting, standing, walking, speaking, and thinking—thus arranging them. And this was said in the Saṃyutta:

Kiñca bhikkhave saṅkhāre vadetha. Saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkharontīti kho bhikkhave tasmā saṅkhārāti vuccanti. Kiñca saṅkhataṃ abhi saṅkharonti, rūpaṃ rūpatthāya saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkharonti. Vedanaṃ vedanatthāya saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkharonti. Saññaṃ saññatthāya saṅkhata abhisaṅkharonti. Saṅkhāre saṅkhāratthāya saṅkhata mabhisaṅkharonti. Viññāṇaṃ viññāṇatthāya saṅkhata mabhi saṅkharontīti. Saṅkhata mabhisaṅkharontīti kho bhikkhave tasmā saṅkhārāti vuccantīti.

And why, monks, do you call them 'formations'? Because they fabricate the fabricated, monks, therefore they are called 'formations.' And what do they fabricate as fabricated? They fabricate form as fabricated for the sake of form. They fabricate feeling as fabricated for the sake of feeling. They fabricate perception as fabricated for the sake of perception. They fabricate formations as fabricated for the sake of formations. They fabricate consciousness as fabricated for the sake of consciousness. Because they fabricate the fabricated, monks, therefore they are called 'formations.'

Tattha rūpaṃ rūpatthāya saṅkhatamabhisaṅkharontīti yasmiṃ yasmiṃ kāle sayana nisajjādivasena pavattā yā yā rūpavikati icchīyati, tasmiṃtasmiṃ kāle tassā tassā rūpavikatiyā jātatthāya iriyāpatha parivattanādi vasena taṃ taṃ rūpavikatiṃ saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkharontīti attho. Khajjabhojjādikaṃ vatthālaṅkārādikaṃ mañca pīṭha geha rathādikaṃ sabbaṃ upabhoga paribhogabhūtaṃ bāhira rūpaṃpi gahetvā yojetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Vedananti diṭṭhadhammikaṃ samparāyikañca sabbaṃpi vedanaṃ. Tattha diṭṭhadhammikaṃ vedanaṃ saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkharontā cittakammanaccagītādīni taṃ taṃ vedanupakaraṇāni sampādana vasena samparāyikañca abhisaṅkharontā mānusakaṃvā dibbaṃvā taṃtaṃ vedanaṃ patthetvā dāna sīlādi sampādana vasena abhisaṅkharonti. Esanayo sesesupi. Saṅkhāresu pana phassaṃ phassatthāya cetanaṃ cetanatthāyātiādinā dānaṃ dānatthāya sīlaṃ sīlatthāya pāṇātipātaṃ pāṇātipātatthāyātiādinā vā sabbaṃ lokapavattiṃ ñatvā vitthāretabbāti. Ettha siyā, kasmā saṅkhāresu pākaṭā cetanādayo vitakkādayo lobhādayo saddhāsatipaññādayoca dhamme visuṃ visuṃ khandhabhāvena avatvā vedanāsaññāva vuttāti. Vuccate.

Therein, 'they fabricate form as fabricated for the sake of form' means that at whatever time one desires any particular form-modification arising through activities like lying down, sitting, etc., at that very time, they fabricate that particular form-modification as fabricated by changing postures and so on for the sake of its arising. Even external forms such as food, drink, clothing, ornaments, beds, chairs, houses, chariots, and all objects of enjoyment and use can be included and applied here. By 'feeling' is meant all feeling, both in this present life and in future lives. Regarding feeling in this present life, one fabricates it by producing the necessary conditions for it, such as artistic works, dancing, singing, etc. Regarding future feeling, one fabricates it by aspiring for human or divine feelings and fulfilling them through generosity, virtue, and so on. The same method applies to the rest. As for formations, one should elaborate in detail, knowing all worldly conventions, that contact is fabricated for the sake of contact, volition for the sake of volition, and so on; or alternatively, generosity for the sake of generosity, virtue for the sake of virtue, killing for the sake of killing, and so forth. Here, one might ask: 'Why, in the case of formations, are obvious mental factors like volition, initial thought, greed, faith, mindfulness, and wisdom not mentioned separately as aggregates, while only feeling and perception are?' The answer is given.

Yathā [M 0.0361] hi cheko mahābhisakko bhesajjamūlāni gahetvā cuṇṇaṃ karonto tesu mūlesu imāni thūlānipi mudūni honti. Imāni khuddakānipi kakkhaḷāni hontīti ñatvā tato pathamataraṃ kakkhaḷāni visuṃ uddharitvā suṭṭhu koṭṭetvā cuṇṇaṃ karoti. Sesāni pana sabbāni mudūni ekato katvā koṭṭetvā cuṇṇaṃ karoti. Tato ubhayāni missetvā silāyaṃ pisetvā bhesajjakamme upaneti. Evaṃ karonto nakilamati. Evamevaṃ bhagavāpi nāmarūpadhammesu tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā niccasukhaatta vipallāsānaṃ pahānatthāya anuyuñjantā devamanussā vibhāge akate tīsu dhammesu kilamissantīti ñatvā nāmadhammesu vedanāsaññācittasaṅkhāte tayo dhamme visuṃ uddharitvā ekamekaṃ khandhaṃ nāma katvā desesi. Tathā hi yathā macchānāma udake sati ukkaṇṭhitā nāma natthi. Asati pana ekantena ukkaṇṭhitāyeva honti. Yathāvā madhukarāvā bhamarāvā yasmiṃ vane puppharasa phalarase labhanti, tattha ukkaṇṭhitānāma natthi. Alabhamānā pana ekantena ukkaṇṭhitāeva honti. Evameva imesaṃ sattānaṃ sukha saññitesu patisaraṇesu vedanāsadisaṃ patisaraṇaṃnāma natthi. Manussadevabrahmasampattiyo assādentāpi sukhavedanatthāyaeva assādenti. Yadica tāhi vinā yathicchitaṃ sukhavedanaṃ labheyyuṃ. Konāma tā sādiyissati. Tathā phassacetanādīhi vitakkavicāravīriyādīhi lobhadosādīhi saddhāsatipaññādīhi ca saṅkhārakkhandhadhammehi diṭṭhadhammikaṃ samparāyikañca yaṃkiñci saṅkhataṃ abhisaṅkharontāpi sukhavedanatthāyaeva abhisaṅkharonti. Yadica tādisena abhisaṅkharaṇena vināpi yathicchitaṃ sukhaṃ labheyyuṃ, tehi dhammehi attho natthīti konāma te dhamme abhisaṅkharissatīti.

Just as a skilled master physician, taking medicinal roots, grinds them into powder. Among these roots, he knows that some are thick and soft, while others are small and hard. Knowing this, he first separately extracts the hard ones, pounds them thoroughly, and grinds them into powder. The remaining soft ones he combines, pounds, and grinds into powder. Then, he mixes both kinds together, grinds them on a stone slab, and uses them in medicine. By doing so, he does not become weary. Similarly, the Blessed One, having applied the three characteristics to the phenomena of name and form for the sake of abandoning the perversions of permanence, happiness, and self, knew that gods and humans, if these three phenomena were not analyzed in division, would grow weary in their pursuit. Therefore, he separately extracted the three phenomena counted as feeling, perception, and mind from the name phenomena, teaching each as an individual aggregate. For example, just as for fish, when there is water, there is no distress, but when there is not, they are utterly distressed; or as bees, when they obtain flower nectar and fruit juices in a forest, there is no distress, but when they do not obtain them, they are utterly distressed—so too, for these beings, among the resorts perceived as happiness, there is no resort comparable to feeling. Even when enjoying human, divine, or Brahmā attainments, they delight only for the sake of pleasant feeling. And if they could obtain desired pleasant feeling without those attainments, who would savor them? Likewise, whether through contact, volition, and so on; through initial and sustained thought, effort, and so on; through greed, hatred, and so on; through faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and so on—whatever conditioned thing they fabricate from the phenomena of the aggregate of formations, pertaining to this present life or future lives, they fabricate only for the sake of pleasant feeling. And if they could obtain desired happiness without such fabrication, seeing no purpose in those phenomena, who would fabricate those phenomena?

Iti sukhasaññitesu dhammesu vedanānāma imesaṃ sattānaṃ paramukkaṃsagataṃ sukhasaññitaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tasmā bhagavā taṃ visuṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ katvā khandhadesanaṃ desetīti. Tathā imesaṃ sattānaṃ attasaññitesu patisaraṇesu saññāsadisaṃ patisaraṇaṃ nāma natthi. Tathā hi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sattanikāye uppannā te te sattā [M 0.0362] attāno attano visayesu sabbaṃ jānitabbaṃ saññāya sañjānitvā viññuttaṃ āpajjanti. Tathā viññuttaṃ āpajjantā yattakaṃ pare jānanti. Tattakaṃ mayaṃpi jānāma. Ko amhākaṃ uttaritaroti evaṃ loke ñāṇasammabhaṃ saññaṃ paramaṃ attānaṃ katvā vicaranti. Iti attasaññitesu dhammesu saññānāma imesaṃ sattānaṃ paramukkaṃ sagataṃ attasaññitaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tasmā bhagavātaṃpi visuṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ katvā khandhadesanaṃ desetīti. Tathā imesaṃ sattānaṃ niccasaññitesu patisaraṇesu cittasadisaṃ patisaṃraṇaṃ nāma natthi. Tathā hi sattā sukhaṃ dukkhaṃnāma aniccaṃ sukhapattānaṃ dukkhaṃ natthi. Dukkha pattānaṃ sukhaṃ natthītivā. Saññānāma aniccā, kadāci pamussati kadāci napamussatītivā. Vīriyaṃnāma aniccaṃ. Kadāci ārabhati, kadāci na ārabhatītivā. Lobhonāma anicco. Kadāci uppajjati, kadāci nauppajjatītivā. Dosonāma anicco. Kadāci uppajjati, kadāci na uppajjatītivā. Saddhānāma aniccā. Kadāci pasannacitto hoti, kadāci appasannacitto hotītivā. Paññānāma aniccā. Jānitabbaṃpi kadāci jānāti, kadāci na jānātītivā evaṃ cetasikadhammānaṃ anicca bhāvonāma kesañci lokiyajanānaṃpi pākaṭo hoti. Na pana cittassa. Na hi sattā cittaṃnāma aniccaṃ. Kadāci uppajjati, kadāci na uppajjatīti gaṇhanti. Taṃ pana sayaṃ niccaṃ pavattamānaṃ hutvā kadāci sukhena yuttaṃ hoti, kadāci dukkhenātiādinā tasmiṃ niccasaññameva uppādentīti. Iti cittaṃnāma niccasaññitesu dhammesu paramukkaṃ sagataṃ niccasaññitaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tasmā bhagavā taṃpi visuṃ ekaṃ khandhaṃ katvā khandhadesanaṃ desetīti.

Thus, among the phenomena perceived as pleasant, feeling is for these beings the supreme state perceived as pleasant. Therefore, the Blessed One, having made it a separate aggregate, expounded the teaching of the aggregates. Likewise, among the resorts perceived as self for these beings, there is no resort comparable to perception. For in whatever group of beings they arise, those beings, having perceived all that is to be known in their respective spheres through perception, attain understanding. Thus, attaining understanding, they think: 'As much as others know, that much we also know. Who is superior to us?' In this way, they wander in the world possessed of the conceit of knowledge, making perception their supreme self. Thus, among the phenomena perceived as self, perception is for these beings the supreme state perceived as self. Therefore, the Blessed One, having made it a separate aggregate, expounded the teaching of the aggregates. Likewise, among the resorts perceived as permanent for these beings, there is no resort comparable to mind. For beings consider: 'Pleasure and pain are impermanent—when one attains pleasure, there is no pain; when one attains pain, there is no pleasure.' Or: 'Perception is impermanent—sometimes it is forgotten, sometimes not.' Or: 'Energy is impermanent—sometimes one exerts it, sometimes not.' Or: 'Greed is impermanent—sometimes it arises, sometimes not.' Or: 'Hatred is impermanent—sometimes it arises, sometimes not.' Or: 'Faith is impermanent—sometimes one has a confident mind, sometimes not.' Or: 'Wisdom is impermanent—sometimes one knows what should be known, sometimes not.' Thus, the impermanent nature of mental factors is apparent even to some worldly people. But not so for the mind. For beings do not grasp that the mind is impermanent—that it sometimes arises and sometimes does not. Rather, considering it to be continuously proceeding, sometimes associated with pleasure, sometimes with pain, and so on, they thus give rise only to the perception of permanence in it. Therefore, among the phenomena perceived as permanent, the mind is for these beings the supreme state perceived as permanent. Thus, the Blessed One, having made it a separate aggregate, expounded the teaching of the aggregates.

[221] Yaṃpana vibhāvaniyaṃ

That which is to be elucidated:

“Bhājana bhojana byañjana bhattakāraka bhuñjaka vikappavasena pañceva vuttā”ti vatvā taṃ vibhāvantena “rūpañhi vedanā nissayattā bhājanaṭṭhāniyaṃ. Vedanā bhuñjitabbattā bhojanaṭṭhāniyā. Saññā vedanassāda lābha hetuttā byañjanaṭṭhāniyā. Saṅkhārā abhisaṅkharaṇato bhattakārakaṭṭhāniyā. Viññāṇaṃ upabhuñjakattā bhuñjakaṭṭhāniyaṃ. Ettāvatāca adhippe tatthasiddhīti pañceva vuttā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ sārato nadaṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Five are spoken of by way of the classification of vessel, food, condiment, cook, and eater.” Having said this, by one who elucidates it, it is stated: “Form is like a vessel because it is the support for feeling. Feeling is like food because it is to be experienced. Perception is like a condiment because it is the cause for gaining the taste of feeling. Formations are like a cook because they fabricate. Consciousness is like an eater because it partakes. And by this much, the intended meaning is achieved; thus, five are spoken of.” This should not be understood as the essential meaning.

Na hi taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ etapparamavinicchaye āgataṃ. Upamādīpaneeva āgataṃ. Na ca bhagavatā bhājanādivikappasiddhimattaṃ uddissa pañceva khandhā vuttāti sakkā vattuṃ. Tathāsiddhassa atthassa payojanābhāvatoti.

For it is not found in the commentary for the ultimate determination of this. It is found only in the context of an illustration. Nor can it be said that the Blessed One spoke of just the five aggregates intending merely to establish the classification of vessels and so on, because there is no purpose in a meaning thus established.

[222] Yañca tattha

And as to what is said there:

“Desanākkamepi idameva kāraṇaṃ. Yattha bhuñjati, yañca bhuñjati, yenaca bhuñjati, yoca bhojako, yoca bhuñjitā. Tesaṃ anukkamena dassetukāmattā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi asāraṃ.

“Even in the sequence of the teaching, this is the reason: ‘Where one eats, what one eats, with what one eats, who the cook is, and who the eater is.’ It is said to be because of a desire to show them in sequence.” That too is without substance.

Catunnaṃ upādānānaṃ visayabhūtā khandhā upādānakkhandhā. Sabba sabhāgadhamma pariyādānavasena sāsavā anāsavāca dhammā pañcakkhandhāti vuttā, vipassanā bhūmipariggahavasena sāsavāeva pañcupādānakkhandhāti vuttā. Āyatanti attano phaluppattiyā bhusaṃ ussahantā viya hontīti āyatanāni. Āyatanasaddo pana chasu ajjhattikesu dvāradhammesu pavattamāno sañjātidesaṭṭhena nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ākaraṭṭhena, chasu bāhiresu ārammaṇadhammesu pavattamāno samosaraṇaṭṭhena, ubhayatthapi kāraṇaṭṭhena pavattati. Tattha citta cetasikā dhammā ekasmiṃvā bhave anamataggevā saṃsāre punappunaṃ saha jāyamānā cakkhādīsu chasu dvārapadesesueva jāyanti, na aññattha. Santānānubandhavasena nivasantāpi tesveva nivasanti, na aññattha. Ākiritvā thapitā viya pavattamānāpi tesveva pavattanti, na aññattha. Tasmā cakkhādīni chasañjātidesaṭṭhena nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ākaraṭṭhenaca āyatanānināma. Devāyatanaṃ viya adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhenātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

The aggregates that have become the domain of the four kinds of clinging are the aggregates subject to clinging. By way of encompassing all homogeneous phenomena, all phenomena, whether with or without taints, are referred to as the five aggregates. However, by way of comprehending the ground for insight, only the tainted phenomena are called the five aggregates subject to clinging. They are called āyatanas because they are as if striving intensely for the arising of their own fruit. The word 'āyatana,' when applied to the six internal bases as door-phenomena, signifies their role as places of origin, abodes, and sources; when applied to the six external bases as object-phenomena, it signifies meeting places. In both cases, it conveys the sense of being a cause. Here, mind and mental states, having co-arisen repeatedly in one existence after another throughout beginningless saṃsāra, arise only at the six sense-doors, such as the eye, and nowhere else. Even when persisting through continuity, they abide only in these, not elsewhere. Though they proceed as if scattered about and deposited, they proceed only in these, not elsewhere. Therefore, the eye and the other five are called 'āyatanas' because they are places of origin, abodes, and sources. It is also fitting to say they are āyatanas in the sense of a foundation, like a divine abode.

Yathāca sampannapupphaphalesu khemesu rukkhesu tato tato pakkhino nilinatthāya āhāratthāyaca niccaṃ samosaranti. Evaṃ rūpādīsu [M 0.0364] chasuṭhānesu tato tato cittacetasikā dhammā ārammaṇakaraṇatthāya niccaṃ samosaranti. Tasmā rūpādīni cha samosaraṇaṭṭhena āyatanānināma. Tadubhayāni pana tesaṃ citta cetasikānaṃ kāraṇaṭṭhena āyatanānināma. Cakkhuca taṃ āyatanañcāti cakkhāyatanaṃ. Evaṃ sesāni. Tattha cakkhusotāni sattānaṃ hitakriyāsu bahupakārattā kāmarūpa byāpitattā ca pākaṭānītiādimhi vuttāni. Tehi āsannattā tadanantaraṃ ghānaṃ. Tato jivhāti imāni cattāri padesāyatanānināma. Tato sakalakāyabyāpako kāyo. Tato tesaṃ sabbesaṃ gocaravisayaggāhakaṃ manoti. Sesāni pana tesaṃ visayattā tadanukkameneva vuttānīti.

Just as birds constantly gather from various directions in safe trees abundant with flowers and fruits, both for shelter and for food, so too, mind and mental states constantly gather from various directions at the six bases—form and so on—for the purpose of taking them as objects. Therefore, form and the other five are called āyatanas (bases) because they are gathering places. Furthermore, both sets of bases are called āyatanas because they serve as the cause for those mind and mental states. The eye and that base are called the eye-base. The same applies to the rest. Among them, the eye and ear are mentioned first because they are prominent, greatly aiding beings in beneficial actions and pervading both the sense-desire and form realms. Due to their proximity to these, the nose follows next; then comes the tongue—these four are called the particular bases. Next is the body, which pervades the entire physical form. After that comes the mind, which grasps the objective fields of all of those. The remaining bases, in turn, are mentioned in that same sequence because they are the objects of the former.

Kassaci pana puggalassavā sattassavā manussassavā devassavā brahmunovā vase avattitvā attanoeva sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhātuyo. Visuṃ visuṃ vavatthitasabhāvattāvā yathāsabhāvaṃ dhārīyanti sallakkhīyanti vavatthapīyantīti dhātuyo. Apica, nissatta nijjīvaṭṭhena dhātuyo. Tattha nissattaṭṭhenāti sattākārā bhāvaṭṭhena sattakiccābhāvaṭṭhena. Ko panettha sattākāro kiṃ sattakiccanti. Jīvayogo sattākāro. Īhāca byāpāro ca sattakiccaṃ. Nijjīvaṭṭhenāti ekasmiṃ bhave yāva namarati. Bhavaparaṃparāyavā yāva saṃsāro na nivattati. Tāva abhijjamāno acchijjamāno ekova vattatīti evaṃ gahitassa jīvassa abhāvaṭṭhena. Cakkhādayoca dhammā sabbaso sattākārarahitā satta kiccarahitāca honti. Naca sayaṃ jīvānāma honti. Nāpi jīvayogāti. Iti nissattaṭṭhena nijjīvaṭṭhenacatedhātuyonāmāti. Tesaṃ pana daṭṭhabbākāro aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto. Yathāha-bheritalaṃ viya cakkhudhātu daṭṭhabbā. Daṇḍo viya rūpadhātu. Saddoviya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Tathā ādāsatalaṃ viya cakkhudhātu. Mukhaṃ viya rūpadhātu. Mukhanimittaṃ viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Athavā, ucchuyanta kilayantaṃ viya cakkhudhātu. Yantacakkayaṭṭhi viya rūpadhātu. Ucchurasa telāni viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Tathā adharāraṇi viya [M 0.0365] cakkhudhātu. Uttarāraṇi viya rūpadhātu. Aggi viya cakkhuviññāṇadhātu. Esanayo sotaviññāṇadhātuādīsu. Manodhātu pana yathāsambhavato cakkhuviññāṇadhātuādīnaṃ purecarānucarā viya daṭṭhabbā.

Not being under the control of any person, being, human, deva, or Brahmā, they bear their own inherent nature—thus, they are called elements. Because they are distinctly established in their own nature, they are borne, discerned, and determined according to their inherent characteristics—thus, they are called elements. Furthermore, they are called elements because they are devoid of entity and devoid of life. Here, 'devoid of entity' means the absence of the form of an entity and the absence of the function of an entity. What, then, is the form of an entity here? What is the function of an entity? Vitality is the form of an entity. Striving and activity are the function of an entity. 'Devoid of life' means the absence of a 'life-principle' conceived of as existing as a single, unbroken, and undivided entity within one existence until death, or throughout the succession of existences as long as the cycle of rebirth does not cease. The eye and other phenomena are entirely devoid of the form of an entity and the function of an entity. They are not themselves called 'life,' nor do they possess vitality. Thus, they are called elements because they are devoid of entity and devoid of life. The manner in which they should be viewed is explained in the commentary as follows: The eye-element should be viewed like the surface of a drum. The form-element, like a drumstick. The eye-consciousness-element, like the sound. Alternatively, the eye-element should be viewed like a mirror's surface. The form-element, like a face. The eye-consciousness-element, like the reflection of the face. Or, the eye-element should be viewed like a sugarcane crushing machine. The form-element, like the wheel-axle of the machine. The eye-consciousness-element, like sugarcane juice and its products. Similarly, the eye-element should be viewed like the lower fire-stick. The form-element, like the upper fire-stick. The eye-consciousness-element, like the fire. This same method applies to the ear-consciousness-element and so forth. The mind-element, however, should be viewed, as is suitable, as a forerunner and follower of the eye-consciousness-element and the others.

Dhammadhātuyā vedanākkhandho sallamiva sūlamivaca daṭṭhabbo. Saññā saṅkhārakkhandhā vedanāsalla sūlayogā āturā viya daṭṭhabbā. Puthujjanānaṃvā saññā āsā dukkhajananato rittamuṭṭhi viya ayathābhuccanimittagāhato vanamigoviya. Saṅkhārā paṭisandhiyaṃ pakkhipanato aṅgārakāsuyaṃ khipanapurisā viya. Jātidukkhānubandhato rājapurisānubandhacoro viya. Sabbānatthāvahassa khandhasantānassa hetuto visarukkhabījāni viya. Rūpaṃ nānāvidhupaddavanimittato khura cakkaṃviya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asaṅkhatāpidhātu amatato santato khemato ca daṭṭhabbā. Kasmā, sabbānatthapaṭipakkhabhūtattā. Manoviññāṇadhātu gahitārammaṇaṃ muñcitvāpi aññaṃ gahetvā pavattanato vanamakkaṭo viya, duddamanato assakhaluṅgo viya, yattha kāmanipātito vehāsaṃ khittadaṇḍo viya, lobhadosādi nānāppakāra kilesayogato raṅganaṭo viya daṭṭhabbāti. Ariyasaccānīti ettha santassa dhammassa bhāvo saccaṃ. Santassāti bhūtassa tathassa aviparītassa. Apica, kenaṭṭhena saccanti. Tathaṭṭhena avitathaṭṭhena anaññathaṭṭhena. Yañhi cakkhussa dukkhattaṃ, taṃ tathaṃ hoti avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ. Dukkhadukkha saṅkhāradukkha vipariṇāmadukkha saṅkhātehi tīhi dukkhehi taṃ samaṅgipuggalassa abhiṇhapīḷanato. Tattha saṅkhāradukkhaṃ nāma kammajānaṃ uppattiyā pageva taṃtaṃkammā bhisaṅkharaṇadukkhaṃ. Tathā utujādīnaṃ uppattiyā pageva taṃtaṃ utucittāhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇadukkhaṃ.

In the element of phenomena, the aggregate of feeling should be seen as a dart and a stake. The aggregates of perception and formations should be seen as afflicted by the dart and stake of feeling, like one who is sick. For worldlings, perception is like an empty fist because it generates suffering through hope, and like a wild deer because it grasps at unreal signs. Formations are like a man who throws others into a pit of embers because they cast one into rebirth. They are like a thief pursued by the king's men because they are followed by the suffering of birth. They are like the seeds of a poison tree because they are the cause of an entirely harmful continuum of aggregates. Form should be seen as a razor-wheel because it is a sign of various dangers. The unconditioned element should be seen as deathless, peaceful, and secure. Why? Because it is the opposite of all harm. The element of mind-consciousness should be seen like a wild monkey because it releases a grasped object and seizes another; like an untamable horse because it is hard to tame; like a stick thrown into the air, which falls wherever desire leads it; like a dancing performer because it is entangled with various kinds of defilements such as greed and hatred. Regarding the Noble Truths—here, truth is the state of a real phenomenon. By 'real' is meant what is existent, true, and not otherwise. Moreover, in what sense is it truth? In the sense of being real, not false, and unchanging. For the suffering of the eye is real, not false, and unchanging, because it constantly afflicts the individual who is endowed with it through the three kinds of suffering: suffering as pain, suffering due to formations, and suffering due to change. Therein, suffering due to formations refers to the suffering of forming those respective kammas even before the arising of kamma-born phenomena. Similarly, it refers to the suffering of forming those respective conditions of climate, mind, and nutriment even before the arising of phenomena born of climate and so forth.

Cakkhu hi nāma rūpibrahmānaṃpi purimabhave jhānabhāvanā saṅkhātaṃ mahantaṃ kammābhisaṅkharaṇa dukkhaṃ anubhavantānaṃyeva uppajjati. No aññathā. Kāmasattānaṃ pana purimabhave kammasaṅkhāradukkhaṃ anubhavitvā uppannaṃpi yāvajīvaṃ pavattiyā āhārādisaṅkhāradukkhañca paṭijaggana dukkhañca [M 0.0366] anubhavantānaññeva pavattati, no aññathā. Pavattamānañca paccayavekallevā jāte antarāyevā āgate yadākadāci bhijjati. Maraṇakālaṃ patvā pana ekantena bhijjatiyeva. Tasmā taṃ assādetvā tadatthāya kammaṃvā āhārādipaccayaṃvā paṭijagganaṃ vā saṅkharontānaṃ anamatagge saṃsāre saṅkhāradukkhassa pariyantonāma natthi. Iti sabbaṃ cakkhu apariyantena saṅkhāradukkhena puggalaṃ abhiṇhaṃ pīḷetiyeva. Idamassa saṅkhāradukkhaṃ. Idaṃ cakkhu nāma paccayavekallevā jāte antarāyevā āgate yadā kadāci bhijjanajātikaṃ. Tasmā tassa bhijjanabhayena pageva paccaya sampādanadukkhaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttisaṃvidhānadukkhaṃ bhijjananimittāni disvā vā bhijjamānevā bhinnevā socanaparidevanādidukkhañca vipariṇāma dukkhaṃnāma. Iti sabbaṃ cakkhu apariyantena vipariṇāmadukkhena puggalaṃ abhiṇhaṃ pīḷetiyeva. Idamassa vipariṇāmadukkhaṃ. Dukkhadukkhaṃ pana tadubhayena dukkhena saheva sijjhati. Evaṃ cakkhu dukkhadukkha saṅkhāra dukkha vipariṇāma dukkhasaṅkhātehi tīhi dukkhehi taṃ samaṅgipuggalaṃ abhiṇhaṃ pīḷetiyeva. Yañca tassa tathāpīḷanaṃ, taṃ tathaṃ hoti, avitathaṃ, anaññathaṃ. Tasmā cakkhu dukkhasaccaṃnāma. Esa nayo sotādīsu tebhūmakadhammesu.

The eye, indeed, arises only for those who in a previous existence underwent the great suffering of volitional formations called jhāna cultivation, even among the form-realm Brahmās; not otherwise. For beings in the sensual realm, however, though the eye arises after enduring the suffering of kamma-formations in a past life, it persists throughout life only for those who continue to experience the suffering of formations related to food and other necessities, as well as the suffering of maintenance; not otherwise. And while it persists, it breaks at any time when there is a lack of conditions or an obstacle arises. At the time of death, however, it definitely breaks. Therefore, for those who delight in it and form actions, provisions, or maintenance for its sake, there is no end to the suffering of formations in the beginningless cycle of existence. Thus, the eye constantly oppresses a person with endless suffering of formations. This is its suffering of formations. This so-called eye is of a nature to break at any time when there is a lack of conditions or an obstacle arises. Therefore, due to the fear of its breaking, there is the suffering of securing conditions beforehand, the suffering of guarding, protecting, and arranging for its safety, and upon seeing signs of its breaking, or when it is breaking or has broken, there arises the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, and the like—this is called the suffering of change. Thus, the eye constantly oppresses a person with endless suffering of change. This is its suffering of change. The suffering of pain, however, is established together with both these sufferings. In this way, the eye constantly oppresses the person endowed with it through the three kinds of suffering: the suffering of pain, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change. And that oppression is real, not false, not otherwise. Therefore, the eye is called the truth of suffering. This principle applies to the ear and other phenomena in the three realms.

Sesasaccesupi yaṃ lobhasseva dukkhasamudayattaṃ. Yaṃ nibbānasseva dukkhanirodhattaṃ. Yaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikamaggasseva dukkhanirodhamaggattaṃ taṃ kathaṃ hotītiādinā vattabbaṃ. Yāvaca lobho na pahiyyati. Tāva cakkhādīni assādetiyeva. Yāvaca tāni assādeti. Tāva tesaṃ pavattiyā kammādīni saṅkharontiyeva. Yāvaca kammādīni saṅkharonti. Tāva cakkhādīni pavattantiyeva. Yāvacatāni pavattanti. Tāva tesaṃ vuttappakārehi saṅkhāra dukkhādīhi namuccatiyeva. Tasmā lobhassa dukkhasamudayattaṃ tathaṃ hoti. Cakkhādīsuca pavattamānesu vuttappakāraṃ sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ āgacchatiyeva. Apavattamānesu nāgacchati. Tasmā tesaṃ pavattinirodhabhūtassa nibbānasseva dukkhanirodhattaṃ tathaṃ hoti. Tathā lobhapahānato añño dukkhamuttimaggonāma natthi. Aṭṭhaṅgikamaggoca uppajja māno [M 0.0367] ekantena taṃ pajahati. Tasmā aṭṭhaṅgikamaggasseva dukkhanirodhamaggattaṃ tathaṃ hoti, avitathaṃ, anaññathanti.

Regarding the other truths, it should be explained how it is that greed alone is the origin of suffering, that Nibbāna alone is the cessation of suffering, and that the Eightfold Path alone is the path to the cessation of suffering. As long as greed is not abandoned, so long do people relish the eye and other sense bases. As long as they relish them, so long do they form kamma and other things for their continuation. As long as they form kamma and other things, so long do the eye and other sense bases continue to arise. As long as they arise, so long is one not freed from the suffering of formations and other sufferings in the manner described. Therefore, that greed is the origin of suffering is true. When the eye and other sense bases are active, all suffering arises in the manner described. When they are not active, it does not arise. Therefore, that Nibbāna, being the cessation of their activity, is the cessation of suffering is true. Furthermore, apart from the abandonment of greed, there is no other path to liberation from suffering. The Eightfold Path, when it arises, definitely abandons it. Therefore, that the Eightfold Path is the path leading to the cessation of suffering is true, not false, and not otherwise.

Evaṃsantepi saccasaddo pariyāya saccesupi vattatīti vuttaṃ cattāriariyasaccānīti. Tattha dukkhasacce tāva sakkāyapariyā pannā ajjhattadhammāeva ariyasaccaṃnāma. Teyeva hi asmimānassa adhiṭṭhānabhūtā hutvā yāvataṃ mānaṃ na samūhanati. Tāva dukkhakiccaṃ karonti. Dukkhapariññācanāma yāvadeva asmimānasamugghātāya hoti. Asmimānoca tesveva ajjhattadhammesu nivisatīti tesu pariññātesu pariññākiccaṃ siddhameva hotīti. Tabbiparī tena pana anindriya baddhadhammā maggaphaladhammāca aṭṭhaṅgikavajjā udayabbaya pīḷanato saṅkhāradukkhavipariṇāmadukkhehica aparimuttattā dukkhasaccaṃ nāma. Samudayasacce eko lobhoyeva ariyasaccaṃnāma. Sohi attasamaṅgino satte attanica ārammaṇadhammesuca assādaṃ janayitvā niccaṃ vaṭṭadukkhato anukkaṇṭhamāne karotīti tesaṃ lobhasadiso añño ñātivā mittovā sahāyovā attāvā attaniyaṃvā natthiviya khāyati. Tasmā taṃsadiso añño koci vaṭṭadukkhasaṃvidhāyakonāma natthi. Tañca pajahituṃ sakkontassa añño dujjahonāma natthi. Avasesāpana sabbepi sāsavā kusalākusaladhammā samudayasaccaṃnāma.

Even so, the word 'truth' is also used for conventional truths; hence it is said, 'the Four Noble Truths.' Among them, in the truth of suffering, firstly, the internal phenomena included within the existing body are what is called the Noble Truth. For these very phenomena, serving as the basis for the conceit 'I am,' perform the function of suffering for as long as this conceit is not uprooted. The full understanding of suffering is solely for the uprooting of this conceit 'I am.' And since this conceit 'I am' is established in these very internal phenomena, when they are fully understood, the task of full understanding is indeed accomplished. In contrast, however, phenomena not bound to the faculties, and the path and fruition states—excluding the eightfold path—are called the truth of suffering because they are not freed from the oppression of arising and passing away, and from the suffering of formations and the suffering of change. In the truth of the origin, craving alone is what is called the Noble Truth. For by generating delight in beings endowed with a self—in themselves and in objective phenomena—it constantly makes them unwearied by the suffering of the cycle of existence. Consequently, to them, no other relative, friend, companion, self, or possession seems comparable to craving. Therefore, there is no other agent that arranges the suffering of the cycle like it. And for one who is able to abandon it, there is nothing else so difficult to abandon. All other tainted wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are called the truth of the origin.

Ettha siyā, nanu avijjāpi sabbassa vaṭṭadukkhassa mūlabhāvena vuttāti sāpi samudaye ariyasacceeva vattabbāti. Vuccate, yathāhi eko cheko uyyānapālo sampattiyuttaṃ bhūmi bhāgaṃ labhitvā attano ñāṇabalena bhūmibhāgañca nānābījānica abhisaṅkharitvā nandanasadisaṃ uyyānaṃ māpesi. Tattha bhūmi uyyāna pālassa bījānaṃ rukkhānañca patiṭṭhānakiccaṃ sādheti. Bījānica aṅkuruppādanakiccaṃ sādhenti, uyyānapāloyeva pana sabbakiccāni sādheti. So hi bhūmiyaṃ bījesu rukkhesuca yaṃyaṃ kattabbaṃ hoti. Taṃ sabbaṃ karoti. Mametanti pariggaṇhāti rakkhati. Tato uppanne bhoge bhuñjati. Tasmā ko idaṃ māpesi, kassedaṃ uyyānanti vutte uyyānapāloyeva māpesi. Tassedaṃ uyyānaṃ icceva vuccati. [M 0.0368] Na bhūmiṃ māpesi. Bījāni māpenti. Tesaṃ idaṃ uyyānanti vuccati. Kā pana uyyānasampattiyā paccayaparaṃparāti vutte pana bhūmieva ādito vattabbā. Na uyyānapālo. Naca bījānīti. Evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Paṭiccasamuppāda nayañhi patvā paccayaparaṃ paravasena dukkha dhammānaṃ pavatti nivattividhāne avijjāeva ādi pabhavapadhānabhūtā hoti, na taṇhā. Saccadesanāyaṃ pana tesaṃ nibbattakadhammavidhāne taṇhāeva sāmijeṭṭhaka padhānabhūtā hoti. Na avijjāti natthi samudayāriyasaccabhāve avijjāya okāsoti daṭṭhabbo. Kilesānaṃ tadaṅganirodhavikkhambhana nirodhā nirodhasaccaṃnāma. Nibbānaṃ nirodhāriyasaccaṃnāma. Chasu lokiyavisuddhīsu maggaṅgāni maggasaccaṃ nāma. Aṭṭhaṅgiko lokuttaramaggoeva maggaariyasaccaṃnāmāti.
