Here it might be said: 'Is it not so that ignorance is declared to be the root of all suffering in the cycle of existence? Therefore, should it not also be spoken of in the Noble Truth of the Origin?' It is said in reply: Just as a skilled gardener, having obtained a fertile plot of land, uses his knowledge and power to prepare the land and various seeds, and creates a garden like Nandana. There, the ground serves the function of a foundation for the gardener, the seeds, and the trees. The seeds serve the function of producing sprouts. But it is the gardener who accomplishes all the tasks. For he does whatever needs to be done for the land, the seeds, and the trees. He takes possession of it as 'mine,' protects it, and enjoys the produce that arises from it. Therefore, when asked, 'Who created this? To whom does this garden belong?' it is said, 'The gardener created it; this garden is his.' It is not said, 'The ground created it,' or 'The seeds created it,' or 'This garden is theirs.' But when asked, 'What is the causal sequence for the garden's success?' the ground must be mentioned first, not the gardener, nor the seeds. This matter should be understood in the same way. For in the method of dependent origination, regarding the process of the arising and cessation of the phenomena of suffering by way of a succession of conditions, ignorance is the primary, originating, and principal factor, not craving. In the teaching of the Truths, however, regarding the process of the phenomena that produce them, craving is the master, the chief, and the principal factor, not ignorance. Thus, it should be understood that ignorance has no place in being the Noble Truth of the Origin. The cessations of defilements—by substitution of opposites and by suppression—are called the truth of cessation. Nibbāna is called the Noble Truth of Cessation. In the six mundane purifications, the path factors are called the truth of the path. The eightfold supramundane path alone is what is called the Noble Truth of the Path.

Ariyasaddo cettha katthaci kadāci kesañci kutoci kathañci avitathabhāvena uttamatthavācakoti. Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayena saccasaddassa attho vibhāvito dukkhaṃariya saccanti ettha pīḷanaṭṭho, saṅkhataṭṭho, santāpaṭṭho, vipariṇāmaṭṭhoti imehi catūhi atthehi cakkhādikassa ekekassa tebhūmakadhammassa dukkhasaccatā veditabbā. Tattha saṅkhataṭṭha vipariṇāmaṭṭhā pubbe saṅkhāra dukkhavipariṇāmadukkhesu vuttanayāeva. Padatthatopana paccayehi saṅkharīyatīti saṅkhato. Pageva kammādipaccayābhisaṅkharaṇadukkhena vinā na uppajjati, napavattatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Virūpo hutvā pariṇāmo vipariṇāmo. Parihāniceva paribhedoca. Pīḷanaṭṭhoti ettha pīḷitabbanti pīḷanaṃ. Pīḷetīti pīḷanaṃ. Pīḷīyate pīḷanaṃ. Atthoti sabhāvo. Pīḷanaṃ attho yassāti viggaho. Tattha yathā ekissā duggatitthiyā kucchimhi putto uppajjati. Soca nānārogehi sayaṃ niccaṃ pīḷito hutvā paṭijagganadukkhehi mātarañca niccaṃ pīḷetiyeva. Yañca tassā kucchimhi tādisassa puttassa uppajjanaṃ, tañca tassā itthiyā pīḷanakiccameva hoti. Evamevaṃ ye cakkhādayo dhammā jarāmaraṇehi niccaṃ pīḷīyanti, te paṭijagganadukkhehi taṃ samaṅgīnaṃ puggalaṃ niccaṃ pīḷentiyeva. Yañca tassa santāne tesaṃ uppajjanaṃ, tañca tassa pīḷanakiccamevāti. Yathāhayo [M 0.0369] bhikkhave cakkhussa uppādo ṭhiti abhinibbatti pātubhāvo. Dukkhasseso uppādo. Rogānaṃ ṭhiti jarāmaraṇassa pātubhāvo. Yo bhikkhave sotassa ghānassa jivhāya kāyassa manassa uppādotiādi.

Here, the word 'Ariya' (Noble), wherever, whenever, for whomever, from whatever source, and in whatever way, is a term for the highest meaning, in the sense of being unfailing. The meaning of the word 'sacca' (truth) should be explained. In the commentary, it has been explained in the way that is stated. In the phrase 'the Noble Truth of Suffering,' the truth of suffering for each and every phenomenon belonging to the three planes, such as the eye, is to be understood through these four aspects: the aspect of oppression, the aspect of being conditioned, the aspect of torment, and the aspect of change. Therein, the aspects of being conditioned and of change are just as was stated previously in the context of the suffering of formations and the suffering of change. From the meaning of the word, 'conditioned' is that which is formed by conditions. It is said that it does not arise or continue without the suffering of being conditioned by kamma and other causes. Change (vipariṇāma) is a transformation into a different state; it is both decline and dissolution. Regarding the aspect of oppression (pīḷanaṭṭha): 'oppression' means that which is oppressed, that which oppresses, and the state of being oppressed. 'Aspect' (attha) means nature. The analysis is: 'that which has the nature of oppression.' For instance, a son is conceived in the womb of a poor woman. He, being constantly oppressed by various diseases, also constantly oppresses his mother with the suffering of having to care for him. And the very conception of such a son in her womb is an oppressive act for that woman. In the same way, those phenomena such as the eye are constantly oppressed by aging and death, and through the suffering of having to care for them, they constantly oppress the person endowed with them. And their arising in that person's continuum is itself an oppressive act. As it is said: 'Monks, the arising, persistence, production, and manifestation of the eye is the arising of suffering, the persistence of diseases, the manifestation of aging and death. Monks, the arising of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, the mind... and so on.'

Santāpaṭṭhoti rāgaggiādīhi ekādasahi aggīhi bhusaṃ paridayhanaṭṭho. Yathāha –

The aspect of torment (santāpaṭṭha) is the meaning of being intensely burned by the eleven fires, beginning with the fire of lust. As it is said:

Cakkhuṃ ādittaṃ. Kena ādittaṃ. Rāgagginā ādittaṃ. Dosagginā. Mohagginā. Jātiyā. Jarāya. Maraṇena. Sokena. Paridevena. Dukkhena. Domanassena. Upāyāsena ādittanti vadāmi. Sotaṃ ādittaṃ. Ghānaṃ ādittaṃ. Jivhā ādittā. Kāyo āditto. Mano ādittoti.

The eye is burning. With what is it burning? It is burning with the fire of lust, with the fire of hatred, with the fire of delusion. It is burning with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, I say. The ear is burning. The nose is burning. The tongue is burning. The body is burning. The mind is burning.

Ādipanaṃ santāpanaṃ paridayhananti idha atthato ekanti. Ettha siyā, ariyamaggopi cirakālaṃ pāramitābhisaṅkharaṇadukkhena antimabhaveca sīlādivisuddhibhāvanābhisaṅkharaṇadukkhena puggalaṃ susaṃ pīḷetiyeva. Tathā vipariṇāmadhammoca. Tasmā sopi piḷanādiatthena dukkhasaccasaṅgaho siyāti.Na. Sabbadukkhasanti vaṃhattā. So hi vuttappakāraṃ abhisaṅkharaṇadukkhaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ anubhūtassa puggalassa sakiṃ uppajjamāno sabbaṃ kilesajātaṃ khepento uppajjati. Nirujjhamānoca sabbaṃ āyatiṃ anamatagge saṃsāre vaṭṭadukkhaṃ vūpasamento nirujjhati. Vūpasantaṃca anāgata dukkhaṃ upādāya vuttappakāraṃ abhisaṅkharaṇadukkhaṃ gaṇanupagaṃ nahoti. Bhijjantoca anuttaraṃ vimuttisukhaṃ datvāva bhijjati. Tasmā tassa vipariṇāmapaccayāpi puggalassa kāci hānināma natthīti na so dukkhasaccasaṅgahoti. Lokiyadhammā pana uppajjamānā pavatta mānāca pubbe vuttapakārehi saṅkhāradukkhehi bhusaṃ pīḷetvā eva uppajjanti pavattantica. Nirujjhamānā mahantaṃ pariḷāhadukkhaṃ janetvā apariyante khuracakkasadise vaṭṭadukkhayante puggalaṃ yojentāva nirujjhanti. Tasmā teeva pīḷanādiatthehi ekantadukkhā hontīti. Etena nibbānassapi sampāpakapaccayābhisaṅkharaṇalesaṃ gahetvā dukkhasaccattapasaṅgo nivattito hotīti.

Burning, scorching, and intense heat here are essentially the same in meaning. In this context, it might be argued that even the noble path severely torments a person for a long time through the suffering of accumulating perfections, and in the final existence, through the suffering of cultivating purity in virtue and so forth. Moreover, it is subject to change. Therefore, it too could be included in the truth of suffering due to its oppressive nature. No. Because it is the cessation of all suffering. For when it arises just once in a person who has fully experienced the aforementioned suffering of accumulation, it utterly destroys all defilements. And when it ceases, it brings an end to all future suffering in the endless cycle of existence by calming it. Since future suffering is calmed, the aforementioned suffering of accumulation is no longer counted. Moreover, when it dissolves, it dissolves only after granting the unsurpassed bliss of liberation. Thus, even due to its impermanent nature, no loss whatsoever occurs for the person—hence, it is not included in the truth of suffering. Worldly phenomena, however, both when arising and persisting, arise and persist only after severely oppressing beings through the aforementioned types of suffering of formations. When ceasing, they generate great distress and yoke beings to the endless cycle of suffering, sharp as a wheel of razors, before they cease. Therefore, they alone are exclusively suffering due to their oppressive nature and so forth. Through this, the implication that Nibbāna itself is the truth of suffering, which might be inferred by considering the merest formation of conditions that bring it about, is refuted.

Dukkhasamudayo [M 0.0370] ariyasaccanti ettha bhavābhavasaṅkhātaṃ dukkhakkhandhaṃ samudeti. Punappunaṃ abbocchinnaṃ katvā udayati uṭṭhāpeti vaḍḍhetivāti dukkhasamudayo, āyūhanaṭṭho, nidānaṭṭho, saṃyogaṭṭho, palibodhaṭṭhoti catūhi atthehi lobhassa dukkhasamudayatā veditabbā. Tattha āyūhanaṭṭhoti bhavābhava saṅkhātassa ekekasmiṃ bhavepi vatthukāmapaṭisaṃyuttassa dukkhakkhandhassa bhiyyo paribyūhanaṭṭho rāsikaraṇaṭṭho nidānaṭṭhoti tadeva nirantaraṃ katvā anuppadānaṭṭho niyyātanaṭṭhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṃyogaṭṭhoti dukkhakkhandhasmiṃeva daḷhaṃ bandhanaṭṭho. Palibodhaṭṭhoti tato tassa tassa muccanupāyassa nīvāraṇa vasena palibundhanaṭṭho uparundhanaṭṭhoti attho. Dukkhanirodho ariyasaccanti ettha vaṭṭadukkhassa nirujjhanaṃ anuppāda dhammatāpatti vasena khiyyānaṃ dukkhanirodho. Dukkhaṃ vā nirujjhati napavattati etasminti dukkhanirodho. Nissaraṇaṭṭho vivekaṭṭho, asaṅkhataṭṭho, amataṭṭhoti catūhi atthehi nibbānassa dukkhanirodhatā veditabbā. Tattha nissaraṇaṭṭhoti nissaraṇa vimuttiyā vimuccanaṭṭho. Vivekaṭṭhoti vaṭṭadukkhapalibodhato viviccanaṭṭho. Asaṅkhataṭṭhoti saṅkhāradukkhassa abhāvaṭṭho. Amataṭṭhoti maraṇadukkhassa abhāvaṭṭhoti.

The Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering: here, it causes the mass of suffering, designated as existence and non-existence, to arise. Again and again, making it uninterrupted, it arises, produces, and increases—thus, the origin of suffering. It should be understood that craving is the origin of suffering through four aspects: as accumulation, as cause, as connection, and as obstruction. Herein, 'as accumulation' means the further gathering and heaping up of the mass of suffering, connected with objects of desire in each existence, designated as existence and non-existence. 'As cause' means continuously causing and producing it, and delivering it, it is said. 'As connection' means the firm binding to the mass of suffering itself. 'As obstruction' means the hindering and blocking, by way of preventing means of escape from it; the meaning is obstructing. The Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering: here, the cessation of suffering is the stopping of the cycle of suffering, its wasting away by way of attaining the nature of non-arising. Or, suffering ceases and does not recur from this—thus, the cessation of suffering. It should be understood that Nibbāna is the cessation of suffering through four aspects: as escape, as seclusion, as unconditioned, and as deathless. Herein, 'as escape' means liberation by way of final escape. 'As seclusion' means separation from the obstruction of the cycle of suffering. 'As unconditioned' means the absence of the suffering of formations. 'As deathless' means the absence of the suffering of death.

Dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadāti ettha dukkhanirodhaṃ gameti sampāpetīti dukkhanirodhagāminī. Attano santāne paṭilābhakaraṇa vasena paṭipajjitabbāti paṭipadā. Dukkhanirodhagāminīca sā paṭipadā cāti viggaho. Niyyānaṭṭho, hetvaṭṭho, dassanaṭṭho, adhipateyyaṭṭhoti catūhi atthehi aṭṭhaṅgikamaggassa dukkhanirodhamaggatā veditabbā. Tattha niyyānaṭṭhoti avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārātiādikaṃ vaṭṭasotaṃ paṭinivattetvā avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodhotiādikaṃ vaṭṭapaṭisotaṃ abhimukhaṃ niggamanaṭṭho. Hetvaṭṭhoti sabbesaṃ ariyaguṇānaṃ suppatiṭṭhitabhāva sādhanaṭṭho. Dassanaṭṭhoti aññāṇaadassanasaṅkhātassa sammohassa pahāna vasena catusaccadhammassa paṭivijjhanaṭṭho. Adhipateyyaṭṭhoti taṇhā dāsabyavimuttiyā [M 0.0371] bhūjissabhāvapattivasena sayameva attano adhipati hutvā virocanaṭṭho. Lokiyamaggā hi taṇhāya ārammaṇabhāve ṭhitā taṇhādāsabyaṃ nātivattantīti. Etthaca ime sattānāma ekantena dukkhapaṭikūlā honti dukkhabhīrukā. Yeca attani dukkhaṃ janenti. Tesu verisaññaṃ uppādenti. Attano pana ekantadukkhaṃvā ekantadukkhajanakaṃvā te najānanti. Tasmā te attano dukkhamuttiyā yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ āyūhanti. Taṃ taṃ attano dukkhavaḍḍhiyāeva sampajjati. Kiṃ pana ekantadukkhaṃ, kiṃca ekanta dukkhajanakanti. Atītānāgatapaccuppannabhūtā attano attano attahāvapariyāpannā tebhūmakadhammāeva attano attano ekantadukkhānāma. Kasmā, tehi mutteeva sabbadukkhehi muccanato, amutteca amuccanatoti. Attano taṇhāeva attano ekantadukkhajanakaṃnāma. Kasmā, tāya pahīnāyaeva ekanta dukkhehi muccanato, apahīnāyaca amuccanatoti.

The path leading to the cessation of suffering: here, it is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering because it leads to and accomplishes the cessation of suffering. It is the practice to be undertaken for the sake of making it arise in one's own continuum. The analysis is: it is both that which leads to the cessation of suffering and the practice. It should be understood that the Noble Eightfold Path is the path to the cessation of suffering through four aspects: as deliverance, as cause, as vision, and as governing principle. Herein, 'as deliverance' means the aspect of going forth towards the reverse stream of cessation—which begins with 'with the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of formations'—by turning back the stream of the cycle, which begins with 'ignorance as condition for formations,' and so on. 'As cause' means the aspect of accomplishing the well-established state of all noble qualities. 'As vision' means the aspect of penetrating the Dhamma of the Four Truths by abandoning the delusion known as non-knowledge and non-seeing. 'As governing principle' means the aspect of shining forth by becoming one's own master, by attaining the state of being a free man through liberation from the slavery of craving. For worldly paths, standing in the state of being an object for craving, do not transcend the slavery of craving. Here, these beings are exclusively averse to suffering and fearful of suffering. And towards that which generates suffering in them, they produce a perception of hostility. Yet, they do not recognize what is exclusively their own suffering, or what exclusively causes their suffering. Therefore, whatever actions they undertake for their own liberation from suffering, all that results only in increasing their suffering. But what is exclusively suffering, and what is exclusively the cause of suffering? Past, future, and present phenomena, included in one's own existence and belonging to the three realms—these themselves are called exclusively suffering. Why? Because only by being freed from them is one freed from all suffering; and by not being freed from them, one is not freed. One's own craving is called exclusively the cause of suffering. Why? Because only by its abandonment is one freed from what is exclusively suffering; and by its non-abandonment, one is not freed.

Tathā ime sattā ekantena sukhakāmā honti sukhābhinandino. Yeca attani sukhaṃ janenti. Tesu piyamittasaññaṃ uppādenti. Attanopana ekantasukhaṃvā ekantasukhamaggaṃvāte najānanti. Tasmā te attano sukhavaḍḍhiyā yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ āyūhanti. Taṃ taṃ attano dukkhavaḍḍhiyāeva sampajjati. Kiṃ pana ekantasukhaṃ koca ekanta sukhamaggoti. Ekantadukkhadhammassa abhāvoeva attano ekanta sukhaṃnāma. Ekantadukkhajanakassa pahānamaggoeva attano ekanta sukhamaggonāmāti imamatthaṃ dassento imāni catusaccapadāni kathesīti veditabbaṃ.

Likewise, these beings are entirely desirous of happiness and delight in happiness. And towards that which generates happiness in them, they produce a perception of a dear friend. But they do not know either what is exclusively happiness or the path to exclusive happiness for themselves. Therefore, whatever actions they undertake for the increase of their own happiness, those very actions lead only to the increase of their own suffering. But what then is exclusive happiness, and what is the path to exclusive happiness? The very absence of phenomena that are exclusively suffering is called exclusive happiness for oneself. The path of abandoning what generates exclusive suffering is called the path to exclusive happiness for oneself. To show this meaning, he taught these four truths—this should be understood.

[223] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

[223] Now, that which is to be explained:

“Dukkhassa anuppādanirodho ettha etenātivā dukkhanirodho”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha etenāti idaṃ nayujjati.

It is said: 'The non-arising and cessation of suffering here, by this, or thus, is the cessation of suffering.' Herein, this 'by this' is not appropriate.

Na hi nibbānaṃ dukkhassa anuppādanirodha kriyāsādhane dukkhena sahakārī kāraṇaṃ hotīti. Sesacetasikāti vedanā saññāhi sesā paññāsa cetasikā. Atītādivasena tividha bhinnānaṃ [M 0.0372] ajjhattādi oḷārikādi hīnādi dūrādivasena duvidhabhinnānañca dhammānaṃ rāsaṭṭhena khandhavohāro hoti. Nibbānassa pana tādi so bhedo natthīti vuttaṃ bhedābhāvenātiādi. Tañhi atītādike tividhabhede ekaṃpi na hoti. Kasmā. Aniddisitabba dhammattā. Tañhi tekālikadhammānaṃ khayavirāganirodhabhūto animitta dhammoyeva hoti. Tasmā idaṃ atīte asukabuddhakāle nibbānaṃ. Idaṃ anāgate. Idaṃ etarahīti evaṃ kālabhedena niddisitabbaṃ nahoti. Tathā disā desaṭhānabhedena parinibbutapuggalabhedena ca. Kevalaṃ pana anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe yattakāni anattha padāni dissanti. Tappaṭipakkhasiddhehi guṇapadehieva taṃ kathe tabbanti. Dukesu pana ajjhattadukaṃ patvā taṃ bahiddhāeva hoti. Na ajjhattaṃ. Oḷārikadukaṃ patvā sukhumameva hoti, na oḷārikaṃ. Hīnadukaṃ patvā paṇītameva hoti, na hīnaṃ. Dūre dukaṃ patvā dūreeva hoti, na santiketi. Khandhasaṅgahanissaṭanti khandhasaṅgahato vimuttaṃ.

For Nibbāna is not a co-operative cause with suffering in the accomplishment of the non-arising and cessation of suffering. 'The remaining mental factors' refers to the fifty mental factors apart from feeling and perception. The aggregates are designated by the characteristic of accumulation, being threefold by way of past, etc., and twofold by way of internal, etc., gross, etc., inferior, etc., and distant, etc. But Nibbāna has no such divisions, hence it is said to be 'without division,' etc. For it does not exist even as one in the threefold division of past, etc. Why? Because it is a phenomenon that cannot be indicated. For it is merely the signless phenomenon that is the destruction, fading away, and cessation of phenomena related to the three times. Therefore, it cannot be indicated by divisions of time, such as 'This is Nibbāna in the time of such-and-such a Buddha in the past; this is in the future; this is now.' Likewise, it cannot be indicated by divisions of direction, location, or differences in individuals who have attained final Nibbāna. Only in the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, where as many unwholesome states are seen, can it be discussed by means of qualities that are the accomplishment of counteracting them. However, with respect to the internal pair, it is external only, not internal. With respect to the gross pair, it is subtle only, not gross. With respect to the inferior pair, it is excellent only, not inferior. With respect to the distant pair, it is distant only, not near. 'Khandhasaṅgahanissaṭanti' means freed from the inclusion of aggregates.

Dvārālambaṇabhedenāti dvārachakka ārammaṇachakkānaṃ bhedena. Āyatanāni dvādasa bhavantīti yojanā. Etthaca dvārachakkaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃevāti sesadhammālambaṇaṃ sandhāya ārammaṇachakkaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dvārā.La. Pariyāyenāti channaṃ dvārānaṃ channaṃ ālambaṇānaṃ tesu dvārālambaṇesu uppannānaṃ viññāṇānañca kamena dhātuyo aṭṭhārasa bhavantīti yojanā. Etthapi dvārachakke manodvāraṃ viññāṇekadesameva hoti. Dvārachakkaṃ viññāṇasattakañca dhammā lambaṇekadesamevāti. Maggo lokuttaro maggonāma matoti yojanā. Maggayuttā ekūnatiṃsadhammā phalabhūtāca sattatiṃsa dhammā catusacca vinissaṭā catūhi ariyasaccehi vinissaṭā vimuttā. Yamettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttamevāti.

“By the distinction of doors and objects” means by the distinction of the six doors and the six objects. “The twelve sense bases come to be” is the connection. And here, it should be understood that the six doors are only the mind-object, and the six objects are stated with reference to the remaining dhamma-objects. By the method of doors, etc., it is connected that the eighteen elements come to be in sequence from the six doors, the six objects, and the consciousnesses arisen in those doors and objects. Here too, in the six doors, the mind-door is only a part of consciousness. And the six doors and the sevenfold consciousness are only a part of the dhamma-object. “The supramundane path is called the path” is the connection. The twenty-nine phenomena associated with the path, and the thirty-seven phenomena that are the fruit, are disjoined from the four truths, freed from the four noble truths. Whatever should be stated here has already been stated below.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus, of the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, the Paramatthadīpanī.

Catutthavaṇṇanāya samuccaya saṅgahassa

The fourth exposition, of the Compendium of Miscellaneous Items.

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The Paramatthadīpanā is completed.

Paccaya saṅgaha paramatthadīpanī

Paramatthadīpanī on the Compendium of Conditions.

166. Evaṃ [M 0.0373] sattahi paricchedehi pathamassa nāmarūpapariccheda ñāṇassa vidhānaṃ dassetvā idāni dutīyassa paccayapariggahañāṇassa vidhānaṃ dassento yesaṃsaṅkhatadhammānantiādi māha. Idāni yesaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ saṅkhatāsaṅkhatabhūtā yedhammā yathā yehi hetādīhi paccayākārehi paccayā upakārakā honti. Taṃ vibhāgaṃ tesaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ paccayuppannabhūtānaṃ vibhāgañca tesaṃ paccayadhammānaṃ vibhāgañca tesaṃpaccayākārānaṃ iha vibhāgañca imasmiṃ vuccamāne paccayasaṅgahe yathārahaṃ pavakkhāmīti yojanā.

166. Having thus shown the method of the first knowledge, the discernment of name-and-form, through seven sections, now, in order to show the method of the second knowledge, the comprehension of conditions, he says, “of those conditioned phenomena,” and so on. Now, whatever phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned entities, are supportive as conditions to those conditioned phenomena, in what manner, by what modes of conditions such as causes, etc.—that classification, and the classification of those conditioned phenomena that have arisen from conditions, and the classification of those conditioning phenomena, and here the classification of those modes of conditions—all this I shall explain appropriately in this Compendium of Conditions that is being spoken of. Thus is the connection.

[224] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[224] But what is to be explained?

“Paccaye dassetu”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ taṃ vibhāganti iminā na sameti.

It is said, “Show the conditions.” This does not agree with “that classification.”

[225] Yañca tattha

[225] And whatever there

“Iha imasmiṃ samuccaya saṅgahānantare ṭhāne”ti iha saddassa atthavibhāvanaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃpi na yujjati.

It is said that the meaning of the word “here” (iha) is explained as “here, in this place immediately following the Compendium of Miscellaneous Items.” That too is not appropriate.

Etasmiñhi atthe sati idāni saddo niratthako hotīti, paṭicca phalaṃ samuppajjati etasmāti paṭiccasamuppādo. Tattha paṭiccāti avinā, amuñcitvāti attho. Avijjādiko paccayadhammoti vaṇṇenti. Athavā, samuppajjanaṃ samuppādo. Sahajātadhammehi saheva kalāpavasena abhinibbatti pātubhāvoti attho. Yathāsakaṃ paccayaṃ paṭicca tena avinābhāvīhutvā samuppādo paṭicca samuppādo, atthato pana sabbesaṃ paccayapaccayuppannabhūtānaṃ saṅkhata dhammānaṃ paccayāyattavuttitāsaṅkhātaṃ sabbasaṅkhatasādhāraṇaṃ ekaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ. Yaṃ idappaccayatātica vuccati. Tatthaca idappaccaya tāti ayaṃ imassa paccayo ayaṃ imassa paccayoti evaṃ niddisitabbo ayaṃ paccayo etesanti idappaccayā. Saṅkhatadhammā. Idappaccayānaṃ bhāvo idappaccayatā. Yathāvutta sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ evāti [M 0.0374] attho veditabbo, na paṭicca phalaṃ samuppajjati etasmāti paṭiccasamuppādo. Avijjādiko paccayadhammotica imesaṃ paccayā idappaccayā. Idappaccayāeva idappaccayatātica. Visuddhimagge pana samuppajjanaṃ samuppādoti ayamattho paṭikkhitto. Pāḷiyaṃ pana ayameva adhippeto viya dissati. Yathāha –

For if this meaning holds, the word “now” (idāni) becomes meaningless. “Dependent origination” (paṭiccasamuppāda) means “a result arises dependent on this.” Herein, “dependent” (paṭicca) means “not without,” “not letting go”—this is the meaning. They explain conditioning phenomena as beginning with ignorance. Alternatively, “origination” (samuppāda) is “arising.” The meaning is manifestation, coming into being, together with co-arisen phenomena in a cluster. Dependent origination is the arising dependent on its respective condition, being inseparable from it. In essence, however, it is a single universal characteristic common to all conditioned things—namely, the mode of existence of all conditioned phenomena, which are the results of conditions, as dependent on conditions—which is also called “this-conditionality.” And therein, “this-conditionality” (idappaccayatā) should be indicated thus: “This is the condition for this, this is the condition for these”—these are “this-conditions.” Conditioned phenomena. The state of these “this-conditions” is “this-conditionality.” The meaning should be understood as the universal characteristic as stated, not “dependent origination” (paṭiccasamuppāda) means “a result arises dependent on this.” And “conditioning phenomena beginning with ignorance”—these conditions are “this-conditions.” “This-conditions” themselves are “this-conditionality.” In the Visuddhimagga, however, this meaning—“arising is origination”—is rejected. But in the Pali, this very meaning seems intended. As it is said—

Katamoca bhikkhave paṭiccasamuppādo. Jātipaccayā bhikkhave jarāmaraṇaṃ, uppādāvā tathāgatānaṃ anuppādāvā tathāgatānaṃ ṭhitāva sā dhātu, dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā idappaccayatāti.La. Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā uppādāvā.La. Idappaccayatā. Iti kho bhikkhave tatra tathatā avitathatā anaññathatā idappaccayatā. Ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhave paṭiccasamuppādoti.

“And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? With birth as condition, bhikkhus, aging and death arise. Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, that element stands firm, namely, the stability of the Dhamma, the fixedness of the Dhamma, specific conditionality. With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, that element stands firm, namely, the stability of the Dhamma, the fixedness of the Dhamma, specific conditionality. Thus, bhikkhus, concerning this, there is suchness, not-otherwise-ness, invariance, specific conditionality. This, bhikkhus, is called dependent origination.”

Ettha hi ṭhitāva sā dhātūtiādinā tatra tathatā avitathatātiādināca yathāvuttaṃ idappaccayatā saṅkhātaṃ sāmañña lakkhaṇameva paṭiccasamuppādonāmāti dasseti. Na cettha bhāvasādhane kate sati paṭiccasaddena saha samuppādasaddassa asamānakattutāsaṅkhāto byañjanayuttivirodho atthi. Yo paṭicca kriyāya kattā, tasseva samuppādakriyāyapi kattutā sambhavato. Na hi kriyānāma katturahitāsambhavatīti. Saṅkhatadhammesuca gambhīresu sati aniccatādilakkhaṇaṃ viya idaṃpi saṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ gambhīrameva hotīti nayidha gambhīravacanavirodho sambhavati. Athakho saṅkhatadhammato saṅkhatalakkhaṇameva gambhīrataraṃ hotīti. Tādisena pana sāmaññalakkhaṇena sampannā yathāvuttā avijjādayo saṅkhatadhammā paṭiccasamuppannānāma. Yathāha-katameca bhikkhave paṭiccasamuppannādhammā jarāmaraṇaṃ bhikkhave paṭiccasamuppannaṃ.La. Avijjā bhikkhave paṭiccasamuppannāti. Iti sabbesaṃ paccayapaccayuppanna bhūtānaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ paccayā satta vuttitāsaṅkhāto paṭiccasamuppādoca so nīyati ñāyati paṭivijjhīyatīti katvā nayocāti paṭiccasamuppādanayo. Paṭhapeti saṅkhatadhamme nānāpakārehi paccayabhedehi [M 0.0375] pavatteti deseti etthāti paṭṭhānaṃ. Mahāpakaraṇaṃ. Paṭṭhāne desito nayo paṭṭhānanayo.

Here, indeed, by “that element stands firm,” etc., and by “suchness therein, not-otherwise-ness,” etc., it is shown that the universal characteristic called “specific conditionality,” as stated, is itself dependent origination. And here, when the agentive sense is made, there is no contradiction in the grammatical usage, namely, the dissimilarity of agency between the word “dependent” (paṭicca) and the word “origination” (samuppāda). For the agent of the action of “depending” can also be the agent of the action of “arising.” Indeed, no action can occur without an agent. And when conditioned phenomena are profound, this characteristic of being conditioned is also profound, just like the characteristics of impermanence, etc. Hence, no contradiction arises here in calling it profound. Indeed, the characteristic of being conditioned is even more profound than conditioned phenomena themselves. Now, the conditioned phenomena, such as ignorance, etc., endowed with such a universal characteristic as described, are called “dependently arisen.” As it is said: “And what, bhikkhus, are the dependently arisen phenomena? Aging-and-death, bhikkhus, is dependently arisen… Ignorance, bhikkhus, is dependently arisen.” Thus, dependent origination is the characteristic of the existence of all conditioned phenomena, which are the results of conditions, as dependent on conditions. And because this method (naya) leads, is known, and is penetrated, it is called the method of dependent origination. The “Foundation” (Paṭṭhāna) is that which establishes, sets forth, and teaches conditioned phenomena in various ways through the distinctions of conditions. It is the Great Treatise. The method taught in the Paṭṭhāna is the Paṭṭhāna method.

Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ paccayadhamme bhāve vijjamāne sati te te bhavanti sīlenāti tabbhāvabhāvino. Saṅkhatadhammā. Tesaṃ bhāvo tabbhāvabhāvibhāvo, imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti. Imassa uppādā idaṃ uppajjatīti evaṃ pavatto saṅkhatadhammaniyāmo. Tabbhāvabhāvibhāvoeva ākāro tabbhāvabhāvibhāvākāro. So eva tabbhāvabhāvibhāvākāramattaṃ. Mattasaddena hetādipaccaya sattiniyamaṃ nivatteti. Tena upalakkhito nayo paṭiccasamuppāda nayo. Āhaccapaccayaṭṭhitiṃ ārabbhāti ettha hetu ārammaṇā divasena tathātathā upakārakatāsaṅkhāto paccayasatti viseso āhaccapaccayaṭṭhitināma. So hi avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārātiādīsu viya paccayadhammuddhāramatte aṭṭhatvā hetupaccayo ārammaṇapaccahotiādinā paccayasatti visesuddhāravasena āhacca matthakaṃ pāpetvā desitattā āhaccapaccayaṭṭhitīti vuccati. Paccayadhammā tiṭṭhanti attano paccayuppannābhisaṅkharaṇa kiccaṃ patvā anosakkamānā hutvā pavattanti etāyāti katvā. Ārabbhāti paṭicca. Vuccatīti bhagavatā kathīyati.

When this or that conditioning factor exists, those states arise by their nature; thus, they are conditioned by that nature. Conditioned phenomena. Their mode of being is a mode of being conditioned by that nature: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises—thus proceeds the order of conditioned phenomena. The mode of being conditioned by that nature is precisely the characteristic of being conditioned by that nature; that is, it is merely the characteristic of being conditioned by that nature. By the word 'mere,' the fixedness of the efficacy of causes and other conditions is excluded. The method indicated by this is the method of dependent origination. Here, concerning the establishment of specific conditions (āhaccapaccayaṭṭhiti), the particular efficacy of conditions, reckoned as helpfulness in such and such a way by way of cause, object, etc., is called 'establishment of specific conditions.' For it is called 'establishment of specific conditions' because, unlike in 'with ignorance as condition, formations arise' and so on, where it merely stands as the mention of a conditioning factor, here it is taught having been brought to its summit by way of distinguishing the particular efficacy of conditions, such as 'it is a cause-condition,' 'it is an object-condition,' and so on. By this, conditioning factors, having reached their function of conditioning their own conditioned results, proceed without retreating, and thus they 'stand' (tiṭṭhanti). 'Ārabbha' means 'dependent on.' 'It is said' means it is spoken by the Blessed One.

Ubhayaṃ pana vomissitvā papañcenti ācariyāti idaṃ paṭicca samuppādaṃ papañcente sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tehi taṃ papañcayantā paṭṭhāna nayaṃpi āharitvā papañcentīti. Yathā sūriyo udayanto andhakāre vidhametvā dabbasambhāre mahājanassa pākaṭe karoti. Evamevaṃ uppannaṃ catusaccañāṇaṃ avijjandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā catusacca dhammaṃ vidati pākaṭaṃ karotīti vijjā. Tappaṭipakkhattā moho avijjānāma. So hi uppajjamāno dhammesu aññāṇaadassana saṅkhātaṃ andhakāraṃ janetvāva uppajjati. Paṭicca phalaṃ eti āgacchati etasmā etenāti vā paccayo. Avijjāca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo. Tasmā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantīti sambandho. Saṅkhataṃ kāyavacīmanokammaṃ abhisaṅkharonti sattā etehīti saṅkhārā. Vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ. Vijānanti sattā etenāti [M 0.0376] vā viññāṇaṃ. Ārammaṇe namatīti nāmaṃ. Ruppati vikāraṃ āpajjatīti rūpaṃ. Adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanaṃ. Devānaṃ devāyatanamiva. Phusatīti phasso. Phusanti sampayuttakā dhammā etenāti vā phasso. Vedayatīti vedanā. Vedayanti paccanubhavanti sattā etāyātivā vedanā. Tassati paritassatīti taṇhā. Niccapipāsavasena ārammaṇahetu niccaṃ cañcalati pattheti vāti attho. Tassanti paritassanti cañcalanti sattā etāyāti vā taṇhā. Upādiyatīti upādānaṃ. Amuñcagāhaṃ gaṇhātīti attho. Upādiyanti sattā etenāti vā upādānaṃ.

Moreover, the teachers elaborate by combining both; this is said with reference to those who elaborate on dependent origination. For in elaborating it, they also bring forth the method of the Paṭṭhāna and elaborate on it. Just as the rising sun dispels darkness and makes material things clearly visible to the people, so too does the arisen knowledge of the Four Noble Truths dispel the darkness of ignorance and make the Four Noble Truths clearly known—this is knowledge (vijjā). Opposed to it is delusion, called ignorance (avijjā). For when it arises, it does so only after generating a darkness in phenomena characterized by unknowing and non-seeing. 'Paccaya' (condition) is that from which or through which a result comes or arrives in dependence. Ignorance, and that is the condition, thus 'ignorance-condition.' Therefore, formations arise dependent on ignorance—this is the connection. Beings construct conditioned bodily, verbal, and mental kamma through these, hence they are called formations (saṅkhārā). 'It discerns' (vijānāti)—this is consciousness (viññāṇa). Or, beings discern through this, hence consciousness. 'It bends' (namati) toward the object—this is name (nāma). 'It is afflicted' (ruppati) or undergoes change—this is form (rūpa). In the sense of a basis, it is a sphere (āyatana)—like the abode of the gods for the gods. 'It contacts' (phusati)—this is contact (phasso). Or, associated phenomena contact through this, hence contact. 'It feels' (vedayati)—this is feeling (vedanā). Or, beings experience through this, hence feeling. 'It thirsts' (tassati) or 'is agitated' (paritassati)—this is craving (taṇhā). The meaning is that due to constant thirst, it constantly wavers and yearns for its object. Or, beings thirst, are agitated, and waver through this, hence craving. 'It grasps' (upādiyati)—this is clinging (upādāna). It means taking a hold that is not released. Or, beings grasp through this, hence clinging.

Bhavati vaḍḍhatīti bhavo. Bhavanti jāyanti vaḍḍhanti sukhadukkhāni etenāti vā bhavo. Jananaṃ jāti. Jāyanti pātubhavanti saṅkhata dhammā etāyāti vā jāti. Jīraṇaṃ jarā. Jīranti jiṇṇabhāvaṃ gacchanti etāyāti vā jarā. Socanaṃ soko. Socanti cittapariḷāhaṃ gacchanti etenāti vā soko. Paridevanaṃ paridevo. Taṃ taṃ pavattiṃ parikittetvā devanti kandanti etenāti vā paridevo. Khamituṃ sahituṃ dukkaranti dukkhaṃ. Dummanassa virūpacittassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Bhuso āyāsanaṃ upāyāso. Āyāsananti anassāsanaṃ. Visīdananti attho. Evanti iminā yathāvuttena. Avijjādi saṅkhārādipaccayapaccayuppanna paraṃparavidhinā samudayo hotīti sambandho. Etassakevalassadukkhakkhandhassāti avijjādikassa etassa sakalassa dukkharāsissa kenaci sukhena asaṃmissassa vā dukkharāsissa abhinibbatti hotīti attho. Etthaca duvidho paṭiccasamuppādanayo suttantikanayo abhidhammanayoti. Tattha suttantikanayena tāva avijjā catubbidhā dukkhapaṭicchādikā samudayapaṭicchādikā nirodhapaṭicchādikā maggapaṭicchādikācāti. Abhidhammanayena pana pubbantapaṭicchādikā aparanta paṭicchādikā pubbantāparantapaṭicchādikā paṭiccasamuppādapaṭicchādikāti catūhi saddhiṃ aṭṭha vidhāti veditabbā.

It comes to be or grows, thus 'existence' (bhava). Or, because through it pleasures and pains come to be, arise, and grow, thus 'existence.' Generating, thus birth (jāti). Or, because conditioned phenomena are born and become manifest through it, thus birth. Decaying, thus aging (jarā). Or, because through it beings decay and go to a state of decay, thus aging. Sorrowing, thus sorrow (soka). Or, because through it beings sorrow and go to mental burning, thus sorrow. Lamenting, thus lamentation (parideva). Or, because having recounted this or that occurrence, they wail and cry through it, thus lamentation. It is difficult to bear, difficult to endure, thus suffering (dukkha). The state of an afflicted mind, of a distorted mind, thus mental pain (domanassa). Intense vexation, thus despair (upāyāsa). Vexation means lack of comfort. The meaning is sinking down. 'Thus' means in this way, as stated. The connection is that the origin occurs by the sequential method of conditions and conditioned results, beginning with ignorance, formations, and so on. The meaning of 'of this entire mass of suffering' is that there is the arising of this entire heap of suffering beginning with ignorance, or of this heap of suffering unmixed with any happiness. Here, there are two methods of dependent origination: the Suttanta method and the Abhidhamma method. Among them, according to the Suttanta method, ignorance is fourfold: concealing suffering, concealing the origin, concealing cessation, and concealing the path. But according to the Abhidhamma method, it should be understood as eightfold, together with four more: concealing the past, concealing the future, concealing both past and future, and concealing dependent origination.

Saṅkhārā suttantikanayena sāsavā kusalākusalacetanā apuññābhisaṅkhāro puññābhisaṅkhāro āneñjā bhisaṅkhāroti pana [M 0.0377] tividhā honti. Tattha dvādasa akusalacetanā apuññāti saṅkhāronāma. Kāmarūpa kusalacetanā puññābhisaṅkhāronāma. Arūpakusalacetanā āneñjātisaṅkhāronāma. Abhidhammanayena pana sabbāpi lokiyalokuttarabhūtā kusalākusalacetanā saṅkhārānāma. Kiriyacetanā pana sabbāpi vibhaṅge nagahitā. Aṭṭhakathāyañca kiriyadhammānaṃ pana yasmā neva avijjā na kusalā kusalamūlāni upanissayapaccayattaṃ labhanti. Tasmā kiriyavasena paccayākāro navuttoti vuttaṃ. Avijjāca kusalākusalamūlā nica kiriyadhammānaṃ upanissaya paccayā na honti. Tasmā kiriyadhammā paṭiccasamuppādadesanāyaṃ nagahitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṃyuttepi yato kho bhikkhave bhikkhuno avijjā pahīnā hoti. Vijjāuppannā. So avijjā virāgā vijjuppādā neva puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti. Na apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ. Na āneñjābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotīti vuttaṃ. Attano anurūpapaccayavasena pana tesaṃpi paṭicca samuppādo avāritoyeva. Nahi koci paṭiccasamuppādarahito saṅkhatadhammonāma atthīti. Esa nayo viññāṇādīsupīti. Viññāṇanti bāttiṃsavidhaṃ lokiyavipākaviññāṇaṃ suttantikanayena. Abhidhammanayena pana kiriyacittavajjitaṃ ekūnasattatividhaṃ lokiyalokuttaraviññāṇaṃ. Nāmarūpanti lokiya viññāṇa sahajātaṃ vedanādikhandhattayaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ kammajarūpaṃ pavattiyaṃ cittaja rūpañca suttantikanayena. Abhidhammanayena pana sabbaṃ kusalākusala vipākasampayuttaṃ khandhattayaṃ vuttappakārarūpañca. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana laddhapacchājātapaccayaṃ sabbaṃpi catusamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ gahitameva.

According to the Suttanta method, formations are threefold: the unmeritorious formation (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), the meritorious formation (puññābhisaṅkhāra), and the imperturbable formation (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), which are tainted wholesome and unwholesome volitions. Herein, the twelve unwholesome volitions are called the unmeritorious formation. The wholesome volitions of the desire and form spheres are called the meritorious formation. The wholesome volitions of the formless sphere are called the imperturbable formation. According to the Abhidhamma method, however, all volitions, whether mundane or supramundane, wholesome or unwholesome, are called formations. Functional volitions, however, are not included in the Vibhaṅga. And in the commentary, it is said that since functional states do not obtain the condition of decisive support, being neither ignorance nor wholesome or unwholesome roots, therefore the mode of condition is not stated in terms of functional states. Ignorance and the wholesome and unwholesome roots do not serve as decisive support conditions for functional states. Hence, functional states are not included in the teaching of dependent origination. In the Saṃyutta as well, it is said: 'When, monks, a monk has abandoned ignorance and knowledge has arisen, due to the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge, he does not generate the meritorious formation, the unmeritorious formation, or the imperturbable formation.' However, dependent origination is not prevented for them in accordance with their own suitable conditions, for there is no conditioned phenomenon whatsoever that is devoid of dependent origination. This is the method regarding consciousness and the rest as well. Consciousness refers to the thirty-two types of mundane resultant consciousness according to the Suttanta method. According to the Abhidhamma method, however, it is sixty-nine types of mundane and supramundane consciousness, excluding functional consciousness. Name-and-form refers to the three aggregates—feeling, etc.—arisen together with mundane consciousness, kamma-originated materiality at rebirth-linking, and mind-originated materiality during the course of existence according to the Suttanta method. According to the Abhidhamma method, however, it includes all three aggregates associated with wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant states, as well as materiality of the stated kinds. In the commentary, however, all materiality of the four origins is included, having obtained the condition of post-nascence.

[226] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the exposition,

“Tadubhayaṃpi idha paṭisandhiviññāṇasahagata”nti vuttaṃ. Taṃ anupapannaṃ.

It is said, “Both of those are accompanied by rebirth-linking consciousness here.” That is untenable.

Saḷāyatananti cha ajjhattikāyatanāni eva sabbattha pāḷiyaṃ vibhattāni. Ekacce pana ācariyā bāhirāyatanāni phassassa paccayā hontīti katvā tānipi idha gaṇhanti. Taṃpi nidānavagga pāḷiyā sametiyeva. Yathāha –

The six sense bases (saḷāyatana) are classified everywhere in the Pāli as just the six internal sense bases. However, some teachers, considering that the external sense bases are conditions for contact, include them here as well. This agrees with the Pāli text of the Nidāna section. As it is said:

Katamoca [M 0.0378] bhikkhave lokassa samudayo. Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpeca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā. Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā.La. Domanassupāyāsā sambhavantīti ayaṃ lokassa samudayo. Sotañca.La. Manañca paṭicca dhammeca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso.La. Lokassa samudayoti.

“What, monks, is the origin of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. From contact as condition, feeling arises. From feeling as condition, craving arises… sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. This is the origin of the world. Dependent on the ear… Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact… This is the origin of the world.”

Phassavedanādayopi nayadvaye taṃ taṃ viññāṇasampayuttā veditabbā. Taṇhupādānāni pākaṭāni. Bhavo duvidho kammabhavo upapattibhavoca. Lokiyakusalākusalabhūtā cetanāca. Cetanāsampayuttā abhijjhādayo anabhijjhādayoca kammabhavo. Yathāha-sabbaṃpi bhavagāmikammaṃ kammabhavoti. Kammanibbattā pana sabbepi lokiyavipākakkhandhā sabbānica kammajarūpāni upapattibhavo suttantikanayena. Abhidhammanayena pana lokuttara khandhāpi vibhaṅge āgatāeva. Jātijarāmaraṇāni sabbesaṃ saṅkhata dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇapattāni. Sokādīsu ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa socanākārena pavattā domanassavedanā sokonāma. Rodanākārena pavatto aniṭṭho cittajasaddo paridevonāma. Kāyikā dukkhavedanā dukkhaṃnāma. Cetasikā dukkhavedanā domanassaṃnāma. Ñātibyasanādinimittaṃ saṃsīdanavisīdanākārapavatto doso upāyāsonāma. Ayamettha vibhāgo. Yesaṃ pana khandhadukkhe avijjā appahīnā hoti. Tesaṃ itarasaccesupi sā appahīnāeva hotīti te khandhapavattiyaṃeva sukhasaññaṃ labhanti. Khandhanirodhe dukkhasaññaṃ. Khandhapavattimaggeeva sukhamaggasaññaṃ labhanti. Khandhanirodhamagge dukkhamaggasaññaṃ. Tasmā khandhapavattipaccayabhūtā puññā puññāneñjābhisaṅkhāradhammāeva tesaṃ avijjānivuṭānaṃ sukhakāmānaṃ dukkhapaṭikūlānaṃ sattānaṃ paṭisaraṇā hontīti vuttaṃ avijjāpacca yāsaṅkhārāti. Etthaca visesato paccuppannakhandhapaṭicchādikāya avijjāya duccaritabhūtā apuññābhisaṅkhārā sambhavanti. Anāgata khandhapaṭicchādikāya avijjāya sucaritabhūtā puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārā sambhavantīti [M 0.0379] veditabbā. Saṅkhāresu sati appahīnabhavataṇhānaṃ sattānaṃ cutianantaraṃ punabhavābhinibbattiyā koci vibandho nāma natthi. Tasmā saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ nāmarūpaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ phasso vedanāti ime attabhāvasaññitā pañcadhammā bhavantare pātu bhavanti. Tattha pana viññāṇameva padhānaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ. Saṅkhārapaccayāviññāṇanti viññāṇeca sati tassa udayabhūtānaṃ nāmarūpānaṃ uppattiyā vibandhonāma natthīti vuttaṃ. Viññāṇapaccayānāma rūpanti. Ettāvatā sāmaññato paripuṇṇonāma kāyo rūpa kāyoca vutto hoti. Evaṃsantepi tesu dvīsu kāyesu yedhammā sattapaññattiyā padhānaṅgabhūtā honti. Yehica phassā dīni upari aṅgāni āgatāni honti. Yesuca sattā attagāhaṃ daḷhataraṃ gaṇhanti. Te visuṃ nīharitvā dassetuṃ nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatananti vuttaṃ. Nāmarūpe sati tesaṃpi uppattiyā vibandho natthiyeva. Saḷāyatanasamuṭṭhitoca phasso saḷāyatane sati ekantena sambhavatīti vuttaṃ saḷāyatanapaccayāphassoti. Phassasamuṭṭhitāca vedanā phasse sati ekantena sambhavatiyevāti vuttaṃ phassapaccayāvedanāti. Sukhavedanāsadiso taṇhāya avassayonāma natthīti vuttaṃ vedanāpaccayātaṇhāti. Kāmupādānañcanāma ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe punappunaṃ samudācaritvā daḷhattappattā taṇhāeva, diṭṭhiyoca attanica attano ārammaṇesuca assādana khamana rocana bhūtāya taṇhāya vasena daḷhattaṃ āpajjantīti vuttaṃ taṇhāpaccayāupādānanti. Upādiyantāca tassa tassa upādāniyassa atthassa hitavuḍḍhisaññitaṃ taṃtaṃ kammabhavaṃ āyūhantiyevāti vuttaṃ upādānapaccayābhavoti. Bhavasaddo hettha vaḍḍhipariyāyo. Yathā –

Contact, feeling, and the rest should be understood as associated with their respective consciousnesses in both methods. Craving and clinging are evident. Existence is twofold: kamma-existence and rebirth-existence. Worldly wholesome and unwholesome volitions are also included. Kamma-existence consists of volitions associated with covetousness and the like, and non-covetousness and the like, as it is said: "All kamma leading to existence is kamma-existence." However, all mundane resultant aggregates and all kamma-produced material phenomena are rebirth-existence, according to the Suttanta method. According to the Abhidhamma method, the supramundane aggregates are also included, as stated in the Vibhaṅga. Birth, aging, and death are characteristics common to all conditioned phenomena. Among sorrow and the rest, sorrow is mental painful feeling that occurs in the mode of grieving when one is afflicted by misfortunes such as the loss of relatives. Lamentation is the undesired sound produced by the mind in the mode of wailing. Bodily painful feeling is called suffering, while mental painful feeling is called grief. Despair is the aversion arising in the mode of dejection and despair due to the loss of relatives and the like. This is the distinction here. For those whose ignorance regarding the suffering of the aggregates is not abandoned, that ignorance remains unabandoned in the other truths as well. Thus, they perceive pleasure in the continuation of the aggregates and suffering in their cessation. They perceive the path leading to the continuation of the aggregates as a pleasant path and the path leading to their cessation as a painful path. Therefore, for beings shrouded in ignorance, desiring pleasure and averse to suffering, the meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations that are the conditions for the continuation of the aggregates are their refuge, as it is said: "Volitional formations conditioned by ignorance." Here, specifically, unwholesome volitional formations, which are evil conduct, arise due to ignorance concealing the present aggregates. Meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations, which are good conduct, arise due to ignorance concealing future aggregates. This should be understood. As long as formations exist and craving for existence is not abandoned, there is no hindrance for beings to be reborn again immediately after death. Thus, conditioned by formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—these five phenomena, designated as personal existence—manifest in a new existence. Among them, consciousness is said to be the chief and foremost; thus it is said, 'formations condition consciousness.' And when consciousness exists, there is no hindrance to the arising of name-and-form, which arise from it; thus it is said, 'consciousness conditions name-and-form.' At this point, the complete body in general, both the mental body and the physical body, is described. Even so, among these two bodies, to show distinctly those phenomena that are primary factors in the designation of beings, by which contact and the subsequent factors come to be, and in which beings hold a very firm attachment to self, it is said, 'name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.' When name-and-form exists, there is no hindrance to their arising. And contact, which is originated by the six sense bases, certainly arises when the six sense bases exist; thus it is said, 'the six sense bases condition contact.' And feeling, which is originated by contact, certainly arises when contact exists; thus it is said, 'contact conditions feeling.' Because there is no support for craving like pleasant feeling, it is said, 'feeling conditions craving.' Clinging to sensual pleasures is merely craving that has become firm by repeatedly engaging with a single object. Views, too, become firm due to craving, which finds enjoyment, acceptance, and delight in itself and in its objects. Thus, it is said: 'Craving conditions clinging.' Those who cling generate kamma-existence, perceiving it as for the welfare and growth of the objects of clinging. Thus, it is said: 'Clinging conditions existence.' Here, the word 'existence' is a synonym for growth, as in:

Suvijāno bhavaṃ hoti, duvijāno parābhavoti.

Prosperity is easily known; decline is difficult to know.

Kammabhave sati ekantena punabhavopi sambhavatīti vuttaṃ bhavapaccayājātīti. Jātiyāca sati ekantena jarāmaraṇaṃ hotiyevāti vuttaṃ jātipaccayājarāmaraṇanti. Ayamettha tabbhāvabhāvibhāvavidhi. [M 0.0380] Sokādivacanañcettha īdisena tabbhāva bhāvibhāvena pavattassa sakalassa vaṭṭadhammassa ādīnavarāsidassa natthaṃ vuttanti. Etthāti imasmiṃ paccayasaṅgahe. Tatthāti tasmiṃ paṭiccasamuppādanaye. Addhānavante dhamme bhuso dhāretīti addhā. Kālo. So hi tekālike dhamme santānānupabandhavasena kappaparaṃparā vassa utu māsa pakkha ratti diva paraṃparāca hutvā apatamāne dhārento viya upaṭṭhātīti. Athavā, bhuso dahanti tiṭṭhanti pavattanti tekālikā dhammā etthāti addhā. Kāloyeva. So pana sayaṃ abhinnopi bhedavante dhamme upādāya bhinno viya upacarituṃ yuttoti vuttaṃ tayoaddhāti.

When there is kamma-existence, rebirth inevitably follows—this is stated as 'birth conditioned by existence.' And when there is birth, aging and death inevitably occur—this is stated as 'aging and death conditioned by birth.' This is the method of the arising of that from that. The mention of sorrow and the like here is made to show the mass of drawbacks of the entire cycle of existence, which unfolds in this manner, by way of this principle of the arising of that from that. Here—in this collection of conditions. There—in that doctrine of dependent origination. 'Addhā' is so called because it strongly sustains long-lasting phenomena. It is time. For it appears as though it holds together the succession of phenomena over the three times—whether eons, years, seasons, months, fortnights, days, and nights—in an unbroken flow, without ceasing. Alternatively, 'addhā' is where phenomena of the three times intensely persist, endure, and proceed. It is time itself. Though it is itself indivisible, it is conventionally spoken of as divided with regard to phenomena having distinctions. Thus, it is said to be 'threefold time.'

[227] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

But whatever is to be explained,

“Atati satataṃ gacchati pavattatīti addhāti vuttaṃ”. Taṃ na sundaraṃ.

'That which constantly goes and continues is called 'addhā'.' That is not suitable.

Evañhi sati addhānanti nasijjhati. Yathā addhānamaggapaṭipannoti. Aṅgānīti avayavapadhānaṅgāni. Padhānasambhārāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ākārāti avayavakoṭṭhāsā. Koṭṭhāsattho hettha ākārasaddo. Yathā dvattiṃsākārāti. Ākiranti tattha tattha pakiritvā thapitā viya hontīti ākārātipi vadanti. Sandhīti dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ saṅkhepānaṃ saṅghaṭanaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṅkhepāti padhānadhammasaṅgahā. Vaṭṭanti punappunaṃ āvaṭṭantīti vaṭṭāni. Mūlayanti sabbepi vaṭṭadhammā ettha tiṭṭhanti tadāyattavuttitāyāti mūlāni. Patiṭṭhā. Pabhavāti attho. Yasmā eko puriso ekāya aṅguliyā samuddo dakaṃ gahetvā mahājanassa mukhe pakkhipitvā catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakassa loṇabhāvaṃ saññāpento viya bhagavāpi avijjā paccayā saṅkhārātiādinā ekameva paccuppannabhavaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ desetvā anamataggassa sakalassa saṃsāravaṭṭassa pavattiṃ ñāpesi. Paripuṇṇaṃ desentenaca nāma tassa ekassa bhavassa hetuca desetabbo hoti. Phalañca desetabbaṃ hoti. Tattha hetū nāma purimabhave siddhā avijjā saṅkhārā. Phalaṃnāma anāgatabhave jāti. [M 0.0381] Iti ekabhavavisayāpi ayaṃ desanā ekadesena atītānāgata sādhāraṇāca hotīti vuttaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārāatītoaddhātiādi. Etthaca addhuno addhāvantānañca abhedaṃ viya katvā vacanaṃ dhammato visuṃ addhāsaṅkhātassa kālassa abhāvaṃ dasseti. Kāloyeva lokaṃ pavatteti nivattetīti pavattaṃ micchāvādañca nīvāreti. Na hi sayaṃ abhāvabhūto kālo kassaci pavattako nivattakoca bhavituṃ yuttoti. Kasmā panettha ekamekassa paccuppannassa attabhāvassa pavattiṃ dassento bhagavā atītabhave hetuñca anāgatabhave phalañca dassetīti. Ahetuvisamahetudiṭṭhīnaṃ nīvāraṇatthaṃ atītahetu dassanaṃ. Ucchedadiṭṭhi nīvāraṇatthaṃ anāgataphaladassanaṃ. Sassata diṭṭhinīvāraṇatthaṃ ubhayadassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha ahetu apaccayā sattā pavattanti nivattanti saṃkilissanti visujjhantīti pavattā diṭṭhi ahetudiṭṭhināma. Brahmā pajāpati issaranimmānādivasena abhūta hetudassanaṃ visamahetudiṭṭhināma. Sattā maraṇe ucchijjanti, anāgate jātināma natthīti pavattā diṭṭhi ucchedadiṭṭhināma. Attānicco dhuvo, sova bhavato bhavaṃ sandhāvati saṃsaratīti pavattā diṭṭhi sassatadiṭṭhināma. Evaṃ nicco hutvā sandhāvantopana avijjādīhi sādhetabbo nahoti. Tasmā avijjāsaṅkhārehi bhavantare puna viññāṇuppattiṃ vadantena sassatadiṭṭhi nīvāritā hotīti.

Indeed, if this were so, the term 'addhāna' would not be established, as in 'one who has entered the path of the journey.' The limbs—these are the component principal factors. It is said to be the collection of principal requisites. The modes—these are divisions of parts. Here, the term 'mode' has the sense of division, as in 'the thirty-two modes.' They also say 'ākārā' because they are scattered and placed here and there as if spread out. The joints—these are the places of connection for pairs of summaries. The summaries—this is the collection of principal phenomena. The cycles—they revolve again and again, thus they are called cycles. The roots—all cyclical phenomena stand here, because their function depends on these—thus they are called roots. They are the foundation. This is the meaning of 'source.' Just as a single man, taking a drop of water from the ocean with one finger and placing it in the mouths of many people, might make them perceive the saltiness of the water in the four great oceans, so too the Blessed One, teaching the full present existence through 'ignorance as condition for formations,' etc., revealed the entire endless cycle of saṃsāra. When teaching fully, the cause of that single existence must also be taught, and the result must be taught. Here, the causes are the ignorance and formations established in the past existence. The result is birth in the future existence. Thus, even this teaching, though concerning a single existence, partially pertains to the past and future and is common to both—hence it is said, 'ignorance and formations belong to the past,' etc. Here, by treating time and those who pass through it as if undifferentiated, the statement shows the absence of time as a distinct entity apart from phenomena. It also refutes the false view that time itself drives the world forward and backward. For how could time, being itself nonexistent, be the agent of anyone's movement or cessation? But why, while showing the arising of each present existence, does the Blessed One also show the cause in the past existence and the result in the future existence? To prevent the views of no-cause and wrong-cause, the past cause is shown. To prevent the view of annihilation, the future result is shown. To prevent the view of eternalism, both are shown. This should be understood. Here, the view that beings arise, cease, become defiled, or become purified without cause or condition is called the no-cause view. The false attribution of cause to Brahmā, Prajāpati, or a supreme being as creator, and so on, is called the wrong-cause view. The view that beings are annihilated at death and that there is no future birth is called the annihilation view. The view that the self is permanent, stable, and merely transmigrates from existence to existence is called the eternalist view. However, if it were permanent and transmigrating, it would not need to be established by ignorance and the like. Therefore, by stating that consciousness arises again in another existence due to ignorance and formations, the eternalist view is prevented.

Kasmā panettha sokādayo aṅgesu nagahitāti. Jātiyā sati sokādayo ekantena sambhavantīti evaṃ tabbhāva bhāvibhāva lakkhaṇassa abhāvato. Satipi hi jātiyā rūpa loke arūpalokeca te na sambhavanti. Kāmalokepi kesañci na sambhavantiyevāti. Yadievaṃ kimatthaṃ tesaṃ vacananti. Jātiyāvā avijjādikassavā vuttappakārassa sakalassa vaṭṭapavattassa mahāādīnavarāsidassanatthanti dassetuṃ sokādivacanaṃ panettha nissanda phalanidassananti vuttaṃ. Tattha nissandaphalanidassananti jātiyā mahāādīnava rāsisaṅkhātassa udayaphalassa nidassananti attho. [M 0.0382] Kasmā pana imassa paccuppanna bhavassa atītapaccayā dve avijjā saṅkhārā eva pāḷiyaṃ vuttā. Kiṃ pana te eva dve imassa paccayā hontīti. Aññepi hontiyeva. Atha kasmā te pāḷiyaṃ na vuttāti. Avuttānaṃpi tesaṃ atthato laddhattāti. Kathañca te avuttāpi laddhāti. Tabbhāva bhāvibhāvalakkhaṇena tadavinābhāvibhāvalakkhaṇenaca laddhāti dassento avijjāsaṅkhāraggahaṇenātiādi māha. Esa nayo paratthapi. Tattha avijjā saṅkhāraggahaṇenāti pāḷiyaṃ ādito vuttena avijjāsaṅkhāra vacanena. Taṇhupādānabhavāpi gahitā bhavantīti avijjābhāve bhāvato, abhāveca abhāvato avijjāgahaṇena taṇhupādānānipi gahitāni bhavanti. Saṅkhārabhāveca bhāvato, abhāveca abhāvato saṅkhāraggahaṇena kammabhavopi gahito bhavatīti attho.

Why are sorrow and the like not included among the factors here? Because they lack the characteristic of being a necessary consequence, namely, that when birth exists, sorrow and the like inevitably arise. For even when there is birth, they do not arise in the form realm or the formless realm. In the desire realm too, they do not arise for some beings. If that is so, what is the purpose of mentioning them? To show the great mass of dangers in the entire round of existence, beginning with ignorance, as described; thus, the mention of sorrow and the like here is said to indicate the resultant consequence. Herein, 'indicating the resultant consequence' means showing the resultant arising from birth, which is designated as a great mass of dangers. But why are only ignorance and formations, the past conditions for this present existence, mentioned in the Pāli text? Are only these two conditions for this? Others certainly are as well. Then why are they not mentioned in the Pāli text? Because even though unmentioned, they are understood in meaning. And how are they understood though unmentioned? By the characteristic of necessary connection and by the characteristic of inseparability; thus, to show this, it is said, 'by the inclusion of ignorance and formations,' and so on. This method applies elsewhere as well. Here, 'by the inclusion of ignorance and formations' means that through the mention of ignorance and formations from the beginning in the Pāli text, craving, clinging, and becoming are also included. For when ignorance exists, they exist, and when it does not exist, they do not exist; thus, by including ignorance, craving and clinging are also included. Similarly, when formations exist, they exist, and when they do not exist, they do not exist; thus, by including formations, karmic becoming is also included. This is the meaning.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

However, it is to be explained.

Kilesabhāvasāmaññato avijjāgahaṇena taṇhupādānāni. Kammabhāva sāmaññato saṅkhāraggahaṇena kammabhavo gahitoti vuttaṃ. Taṃpi yujjati.

By the general nature of defilements, craving and clinging are included through the inclusion of ignorance. By the general nature of kamma, karmic becoming is included through the inclusion of formations—so it is said. That too is fitting.

Tathā avijjā saṅkhārā gahitā bhavantīti sambandho. Tadavinā bhāvibhāvena taṇhupādānavacanena avijjāca bhavavacanena saṅkhārāca gahitāti attho. Lakkhaṇadhammānaṃ lakkhitabbadhammehi avinābhāvibhāvato tadavinābhāvibhāvena jātijarā.La. Gahitanti vuttaṃ. Itikatvāti iminā kāraṇena. Vīsatākārā bhavantīti sambandho. Pathamaṃ hetupañcakaṃ eko saṅkhepo. Dutīyaṃ phalapañcakaṃ eko. Tatīyaṃ hetupañcakaṃ eko. Catutthaṃ phalapañcakaṃ eko saṅkhepoti catusaṅkhepā honti. Cattāro saṅgahā hontīti attho. Catūsu pana saṅkhepesu siddhesu pathamena dutīyassa dutīyena tatīyassa tatīyena catutthassāti evaṃ tisso sandhiyopi sijjhantiyevāti vuttaṃ tisandhi catusaṅkhepāca bhavantīti. Etthaca hetupañcakaṃ phalapañcakanti etaṃ lokassa [M 0.0383] pākaṭavohāravasena vuttaṃ. Hetuphala saddā pana paccayapaccayuppannapariyāyā eva hontīti dutīyapañcakassa pathamaṃ upādāya phalapañcakatā tatīyaṃ upādāya hetupañcakatāca na na sambhavati. Tathā tatīyassapi catutthaṃ upādāya hetupañcakatā dutīyaṃ upādāya phalapañcakatācāti. Evañhi sati hetuto phalameva siyā. Na phalato hetūti codanā anokāsāeva hotīti. Dvīsu pana hetupañcakesu saṅkhārakammabhavānaṃ viseso aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttoyeva. Yathāha-dānaṃ dassāmīti cittaṃ uppādetvā māsaṃpi saṃvaccharaṃpi dānupakaraṇāni sajjantassa uppannā purimacetanāyo āyūhanasaṅkhārānāma. Paṭiggāhakānaṃ pana hatthe dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpayato uppannā cetanā bhavoti vuccati. Ekāvajjanesuvā chasu javanesu cetanā āyūhana saṅkhārānāma. Sattamajavanacetanā bhavo. Yākācivā pana cetanā bhavo. Taṃsampayuttā āyūhana saṅkhārānāmāti. Kammabhavo upapattibhavoti dve bhavā dvādasasu aṅgesu ekasseva bhava aṅgassa avayavānāma hontīti vuttaṃ kammabhavasaṅkhātobhave kadesotiādi. Etthaca saṅkhārakammabhavānaṃ viseso vutta nayeneva veditabbo.

Thus, the connection is that ignorance and formations are included. The meaning is that by their inseparable nature, ignorance is included through the mention of craving and clinging, and formations are included through the mention of becoming. Due to the inseparable nature of characteristics from the phenomena they characterize, it is said that birth, aging, etc., are included by that inseparable nature. For this reason, the connection is that there are twenty aspects. The first pentad of causes is one summary. The second pentad of results is one. The third pentad of causes is one. The fourth pentad of results is one summary. Thus, there are four summaries, meaning there are four collections. When these four summaries are established, the first connects with the second, the second with the third, and the third with the fourth. Thus, three connections are also accomplished. Hence, it is said there are three connections and four summaries. Here, the 'pentad of causes' and the 'pentad of results' are spoken of according to worldly convention. However, the terms 'cause' and 'result' are merely synonyms for 'condition' and 'conditionally arisen phenomenon.' Thus, it is not impossible for the second pentad to be the pentad of results with respect to the first, and the pentad of causes with respect to the third. Similarly, the third can be the pentad of causes with respect to the fourth, and the pentad of results with respect to the second. This being so, the objection that only a result would arise from a cause, and not a cause from a result, has no basis. In the two pentads of causes, the distinction between formations and kamma-becoming is stated in the commentary. As it is said: 'Having aroused the thought, "I will give a gift," and for a month or even a year preparing the requisites for giving—the initial volitions that arise are called "accumulating formations." The volition that arises when placing the offering in the hands of the recipients is called "becoming." Or, in a single adverting and the six javanas, the volition is called "accumulating formations." The volition of the seventh javana is "becoming." Or, any volition whatsoever is "becoming"; the states associated with it are called "accumulating formations."' Kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming are two types of becoming. It is said that in the twelve links, they are subdivisions of the single link of becoming, as in "a portion of becoming designated as kamma-becoming," etc. Here, the distinction between formations and kamma-becoming should be understood in the manner explained.

[228] Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

But in the Vibhāvanī, it is said:

“Kammabhavasaṅkhāto bhavekadesoti ettha āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayacetanā saṅkhārāti veditabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ idha na yujjati.

It is said: 'Here, in the part of becoming designated as kamma-becoming, the volition that is a condition for future rebirth-linking is to be understood as formations.' But this does not apply here.

Tesaṃ dvinnaṃpi dvīsu hetupañcakesu saṅgahitattāti. Yathā rutapāḷinayenavā etaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avasesācāti idaṃ jātijarāmaraṇehi saddhiṃ viññāṇādiphalapañcakaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Etthaca yadetaṃ pubbe jātijarāmaraṇaggahaṇena viññāṇādi phala pañcakaṃ gahitaṃ. Taṃ atthato upapattibhavoeva. Nahi phalapañcakato añño upapattibhavonāma atthīti. Evaṃ santepi dhammavibhāga rakkhaṇatthaṃ upapattibhavasaddena catutthapañcakaṃ gahitanti yuttaṃ. Dvādasasu [M 0.0384] aṅgesu avijjānāma moho. Soca akusalamūlaṃ. Taṇhānāma lobho. Soca akusala mūlanti vuttaṃ avijjā taṇhāvasena dve mūlānīti. Athavā, mūlanti sīsaṃ. Dve vaṭṭasīsānīti attho. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana purimaṃ pañcakadvayaṃ ekaṃ bhavacakkaṃ pacchimaṃ pañcakadvayaṃ ekaṃ bhavacakkanti katvā purimaṃ avijjāmūlaṃ. Tañca diṭṭhicaritānaṃvā apāyagāmīnaṃvā cakkaṃ. Pacchimaṃ taṇhāmūlaṃ. Tañca rāgacaritānaṃvā sugatigāmīnaṃvā cakkanti dassitaṃ. Cakkanti pana yato paṭṭhāya vaṭṭasantānassa ārabbho hoti. Tasmiṃ puna āgateeva cakkaṃnāma siyā. Tasmā idha dutīyena hetuphala yugaḷena saddhiṃ sabbaṃ ekameva cakkanti yuttaṃ.

Because both of them are included in the two pentads of causes. Or it should be understood that this is stated according to the method of the Pāli text as heard. And 'the rest' is said with reference to the pentad of results beginning with consciousness, together with birth, aging, and death. Here, that which was previously included as the pentad of results beginning with consciousness by the inclusion of birth, aging, and death, is in essence rebirth-becoming. For there is no rebirth-becoming apart from the pentad of results. Even so, to preserve the classification of phenomena, it is appropriate that the fourth pentad is included by the term 'rebirth-becoming.' Among the twelve links, ignorance is delusion, and it is an unwholesome root. Craving is greed, and it is an unwholesome root. Thus, it is said that there are two roots by way of ignorance and craving. Alternatively, 'root' means 'head.' The meaning is that there are two heads of the round of existence. In the commentary, however, the first pair of pentads is treated as one cycle of existence, and the latter pair of pentads as another cycle of existence. The first is rooted in ignorance, and that is a cycle for those of speculative temperament or those bound for the lower realms. The latter is rooted in craving, and that is a cycle for those of lustful temperament or those bound for happy destinies. But a 'cycle' is that from which the continuity of the round of existence begins. Only when that point is reached again can it be called a cycle. Therefore, here it is fitting that everything, along with the second pair of cause and result, is a single cycle.

Kasmā panettha āgamanasambhāresu avijjāeva sīsaṃ katvā vuttā. Gamanasambhāresuca taṇhāeva. Nanu ubhayattha ubhayaṃpi sīsaṃ katvā vattabbanti. Vuccate, sukhavedanāsadiso hi taṇhāya āhāronāma natthi. Tasmā vedanaṅgato paraṃ vaṭṭaṅgaṃ ghaṭentena vedanā nurūpātaṇhāeva vattabbā. Na avijjāti gamanasambhāresu tāva avijjāya okāso natthi. Sabbapathamaṃ ārabbhaṭṭhāneca sabbapadhānā avijjāeva vattabbā hoti. Sāca saṅkhāruppādane avirajjhanakaṅgabhūtāti na tesaṃ antare ekassa aṅgassa atthāya kiñci vattabbaṃ atthīti āgamanasambhāresu taṇhāya okāso natthīti. Ayañhi paṭiccasamuppādadesanānāma padhānaṅgapariggaha vasena pavattā. Na labbhamāna sabbadhamma pariggaha vasenāti.

Why is it that, in the factors for coming into existence, only ignorance is stated as the head, while in the factors for future existence, only craving? Should not each be stated as the head in both cases? It is said: Indeed, there is no nutriment for craving comparable to pleasant feeling. Therefore, when connecting the link of feeling to the next link of the round of existence, craving, which is appropriate to feeling, should be stated, not ignorance. Thus, in the factors for future existence, there is no place for ignorance. And in the very first instance, at the starting point, ignorance is to be stated as the most principal. And since that is the indispensable factor in the arising of formations, there is no need to say anything for the sake of a single link between them; thus, in the factors for coming into existence, there is no opportunity for craving. Indeed, this teaching of dependent origination proceeds by way of taking up the principal links, not by way of taking up all obtainable phenomena.

Yaṃ pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

But in the Vibhāvanī, it is said:

Pubbantassa avijjāmūlaṃ. Aparantassa taṇhāmūlanti vuttaṃ.

The past has ignorance as its root; the future has craving as its root, it is said.

Tattha pubbantassāti pubbassa hetuphalakoṭṭhāsassa. Aparantassāti pacchimassa hetuphala koṭṭhāsassāti atthoti. Kasmā panetāni dvemūlānināma hontīti āha –

Here, 'of the past' means of the former section of cause and result. 'Of the future' means of the latter section of cause and result—this is the meaning. Why then are these called the two roots? He explains:

Tesamevaca mūlānaṃ, nirodhena nirujjhatīti.

And with the cessation of these very roots, it ceases.

Tesaṃ samudayena sakalavaṭṭaṃ samudeti. Nirodhenaca nirujjhati. Tasmā tāni dvemūlānināmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Keci pana paṭiloma [M 0.0385] paṭiccasamuppāda dassanametanti vadanti. Paṭiloma paṭicca samuppādonāma avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodhotiādiko nirodhavāro. Idāni sokādi vacanaṃ na kevalaṃ nissandaphala nidassanatthameva hoti. Athakho jarāmaraṇena saddhiṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ hutvā upari vaṭṭamūladhammapaṭipādakānaṃ dukkhadhammānaṃ nidassanatthaṃpi hotīti dassento jarāmaraṇa mucchāyātiādi māha. Tattha mucchāsaddena sokādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tepi hi sayaṃ āsavasambhūtā hutvā puna āsavuppādāya paccayā hontīti etena tesaṃ jarāmaraṇaṅge gahaṇaṃ siddhaṃ bhavati. Jarāmaraṇamucchāya abhiṇhaso pīḷitānaṃ bālānaṃ āsavā abhiṇhaso samuppajjanti. Āsavānaṃsamuppādāavijjāca pavaḍḍhati. Āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayoti hi vuttaṃ. Evañca sati avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti puna ābandhameva vaṭṭanti attho. Etthaca –

With their arising, the entire round arises. With their cessation, it ceases. Therefore, it is said, they are called the two roots. Some, however, say this is a presentation of dependent origination in reverse. Dependent origination in reverse is the cessation section: 'With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases,' and so on. Now, the mention of sorrow and so on is not merely for the purpose of showing the resultant fruit. Rather, forming a single link together with aging and death, it is also for the purpose of showing the phenomena of suffering that produce the root-phenomena of the subsequent round. To show this, he said, 'aging, death, and infatuation,' etc. Here, by the word 'infatuation' (mucchā), sorrow and the like are included. For these, having arisen from the taints themselves, in turn become conditions for the arising of taints. By this, their inclusion in the link of aging and death is established. For fools who are constantly oppressed by aging, death, and infatuation, the taints arise again and again. With the arising of the taints, ignorance also increases. For it is said: 'With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance.' This being so, the meaning is that the round turns, being bound again by 'with ignorance as condition, formations.' And in this connection:

Nānā byasanaphuṭṭhassa, sokādīnaṃ pavattito;

Avijjā taṇhā vaḍḍhanti, yato vaṭṭaṃ pavattatī tipi.

For one afflicted by various misfortunes, from the occurrence of sorrow and the like, ignorance and craving increase, from which the round of existence revolves.

Vattabbaṃ. Yathāha-katamoca bhikkhave dukkhassa vipāko. Sammohavepakkaṃ vāhaṃ bhikkhave dukkhaṃ vadāmi. Pariyeṭṭhivepakkaṃvāti tattha sammoho avijjā. Pariyeṭṭhi taṇhā. Tadubhayaṃ vipākaṃ etassāti katvājarāmaraṇasokādikaṃ dukkhaṃ sammohavepakkaṃ pariyeṭṭhivepakkantica vuccatīti. Tattha sammohonāma ñātibyasanā dinā phuṭṭhosocati paridevati uratāḷi kandati, sammohaṃ āpajjatīti evaṃ āgato sammoho. Pariyiṭṭhināma yathā jigacchāti pīḷito. Bhojanaṃ pattheti pariyesati pipāsābhipīḷito. Pāṇiyaṃ pattheti pariyesati, evaṃ kenaci dukkhena phuṭṭho sukhaṃ pattheti pariyesatīti evaṃ pavattā pariyiṭṭhitaṇhā. Ettha pana yasmā jarāmaraṇasadisaṃ mahantaṃ visaṭaṃ niyatañca imassa lokassa dukkhaṭṭhānaṃnāma natthi. Dukkhanissaraṇatthañca satthusāsanaṃ. Tasmā ayaṃ paṭiccasamuppādadesanā jarāmaraṇanidānā hoti. Yathāha-kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno jāyatica jiyyatica [M 0.0386] miyyatica cavatica upapajjatica. Athaca panimassaṃ dukkhassa nissaraṇaṃ nappajānāti jarāmaraṇassātiādi. Yesu pana aṅgesu ādito paṭṭhāya ñātesu jarāmaraṇaṃ samūlaṃ khanitvā tato attānaṃ mocetuṃ sakkoti. Tāni dassetuṃ jātiādīni purimāni aṅgāni desitāni. Apica. Ekasmiṃ bhave ṭhatvā āgamanasambhārehica gamanasambhārehica āgatiyāca gatiyāca saddhiṃ attabhāvanibbattiyā dassitāya atīte anāgateca sakalasaṃsāre tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave tassa tassa attabhāvassa nibbatti dassitāeva hoti. Sabbānica diṭṭhigatāni nivattitāni. Bhavacakkañca anādimantaṃ hutvā ābandhatiyeva. Tasmā jarāmaraṇavacanenavā sokādivacanenavā avijjaṃ acintetvā vaṭṭapavattassa mahāādīnavarāsidassanameva paccetabbanti. Iccevantiādi nigamanaṃ. Iccevaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārātiādinā nayena paṭhapesīti sambandho. Iccevaṃ ābandhaṃ anādikaṃ tebhūmakaṃ vaṭṭantipi yojenti.

It should be said. As it has been said: 'What, monks, is the ripening of suffering?' I say, monks, that suffering has infatuation as its ripening, or searching as its ripening. Herein, infatuation is ignorance; searching is craving. Considering both as its ripening, suffering such as aging, death, sorrow, and so on, is called having infatuation as its ripening and searching as its ripening. Herein, 'infatuation' (sammoha) means that one who is struck by the loss of relatives, etc., grieves, laments, beats the breast, weeps, and falls into infatuation—thus infatuation arises. 'Searching' means, as when one is oppressed by hunger, one longs for food and searches for it; when oppressed by thirst, one longs for water and searches for it. Thus, when struck by any suffering, one longs for happiness and searches for it—thus craving as searching proceeds. Here, however, since there is no state of suffering in this world that is greater, more extensive, and more certain than aging and death, and because the Teacher's dispensation is for the escape from suffering, therefore this teaching of dependent origination has aging and death as its foundation. As it has been said: 'Hard indeed is this world fallen into—it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn. And yet, one does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging and death,' and so on. But when the links from the beginning are understood, one can uproot aging and death along with its root and then free oneself. To show those, the former links beginning with birth have been taught. Moreover, by showing the production of individual existence while abiding in one existence, along with the constituents of coming and the constituents of going, with coming and going, the production of each individual existence in each existence throughout the entire cycle of existence in the past and in the future is shown. And all wrong views are abandoned. And the wheel of existence, being without beginning, continues to bind indeed. Therefore, whether by the term aging and death, or by the term sorrow and so on, without considering ignorance, one should understand that one is perceiving only the great mass of dangers from the continuation of the round. Thus, and so on—this is the conclusion. Thus, the connection is made by teaching in the manner beginning with 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise.' Thus, in this way, they also apply this to the binding, beginningless, three-planed round.

Tattha iccevaṃ ābandhanti jarāmaraṇamucchāyātiādinā vutta nayena punappunaṃ ābandhaṃ. Anādikanti kasmā vuttaṃ. Nanu avijjā ādimhi vuttāti. Vuccate, vaṭṭassa ādibhūtattā sā ādimhi vuttā na hoti. Vaṭṭakathāya sīsa bhūtattāeva sā ādimhi vuttā. Evaṃ vuttāya pana tāya vaṭṭassa anādikabhāvopi dassito. Avijjā hi nāma bahiddhā na labbhati. Sattasantāne eva labbhatīti paccakkhatova siddhametaṃ.
