Ettha siyā, kasmā ārammaṇamattaṃpi.La. Na gacchatīti vuttaṃ. Nanu kammārammaṇāpi paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutiyo hontīti. Saccaṃ. Ettha pana mūlaṭīkāyaṃ kammaṃ pana tasmiṃ kate pavattamānānaṃ katūpacita bhāvena kammapaccayo hoti. Na ārammaṇākārena. Visaya mattatāvasenaca ārammaṇapaccayo hoti. Na santānavisesanaṃ katvā phaluppādanasaṅkhātena kammapaccayākārena. Tasmā te paccayākāravisabhāgattā saha ghaṭanaṃ nagacchantīti visajjitanti. Sahajātādhipati pana atthipaccaye. Nissayapaccayo tividho sahajāto vatthupurejāto vatthārammaṇapurejātoti. Tattha purimā dve atthipaccaye, pacchimo pana dvīsu ārammaṇatthi paccayesu. So ce garukato hoti upanissayepīti. Purejātapaccayo tividho ārammaṇapurejāto vatthupure jāto vatthārammaṇapurejātoti. Tattha vatthupurejāto atthipaccaye. Itare dve dvīsu ārammaṇatthipaccayesu. Tece garukatā honti. Upanissayepīti. Kammapaccayo duvidho sahajāto nānākkhaṇikoti. Tattha sahajāto atthipaccaye. Nānākkhaṇiko pana duvidho balavā dubbaloca. Tatthaca balavā duvidho akāliko kālikoca, tadubhayāpi upanissaye. Dubbalo pana visuṃ kammapaccayoyeva. Sabbo āhārapaccayo sabboca indriyapaccayo atthipaccaye.

Here it may be asked, why is it said that it does not consolidate even as a mere object? But do not rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death consciousness also have kamma as their object? True. However, in the Mūlaṭīkā, it is explained that kamma, when performed, becomes a kamma-condition by way of being done and accumulated for those who are continuing, not by way of being an object. It becomes an object-condition merely by way of being a sense-object, not in the manner of a kamma-condition, which is described as qualifying the continuum and producing results. Therefore, because these modes of condition are dissimilar in nature, they do not combine—thus the matter is resolved. The co-arisen predominance condition, however, consolidates into the presence condition. The dependence condition is threefold: co-arisen, pre-arisen physical base, and pre-arisen object-physical base. Among these, the first two consolidate into the presence condition, while the latter consolidates into the two conditions of object and presence. If this is weighty, it is also a decisive support condition. The pre-arisen condition is threefold: pre-arisen object, pre-arisen physical base, and pre-arisen object-physical base. Among these, the pre-arisen physical base consolidates into the presence condition. The other two consolidate into the two conditions of object and presence. If these are weighty, they are also decisive support conditions. The kamma condition is twofold: co-arisen and asynchronous. Among these, the co-arisen consolidates into the presence condition. The asynchronous is further divided into strong and weak. Among these, the strong is twofold: immediate and delayed—both of these consolidate into the decisive support condition. The weak, however, is solely the kamma condition itself. All nutriment conditions and all faculty conditions consolidate into the presence condition.

Vippayuttapaccayo catubbidho sahajāto vatthupurejāto vatthārammaṇapurejāto pacchājātoti. Tattha purimā dve pacchimoca atthipaccaye. Tatīyo pana dvīsu ārammaṇatthi paccayesu. [M 0.0406] So ce garukato hoti, upanissayepīti. Sesesu pana sattarasapaccayesu hetu, sahajāta, aññamañña, vipāka, jhāna, magga, sampayutta, avigatavasena aṭṭhapaccayā pacchā jātoca atthipaccaye. Anantara samanantara āsevana natthi vigata vasena pañcapaccayā upanissayeti. Iti sabbepi catuvīsatipaccayā sabhāgasaṅgahavasena saṃkhippamānā ārammaṇādīsu catūsu paccayesu samodhānaṃ gacchantīti.

The dissociation condition is fourfold: co-arisen, pre-arisen physical base, pre-arisen object-physical base, and post-arisen. Among these, the first two and the last are included in the presence condition. The third, however, is in the two conditions of object and presence. If it is made weighty, it is also in the decisive support condition. However, among the remaining seventeen conditions, the eight conditions—namely, root, co-arisen, mutual, result, jhāna, path, associated, and non-disappearance—as well as the post-arisen condition, are included in the presence condition. The five conditions—namely, contiguity, proximity, repetition, absence, and disappearance—are included in the decisive support condition. Thus, all twenty-four conditions, when summarized by way of inclusion in the same class, are consolidated in the four conditions beginning with the object condition.

[236] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[236] However, in the detailed explanation:

Tesu catūsu ekekasmiṃpi sabbe catuvīsatipaccayā samodhānaṃ gacchantīti iminā adhippāyena yaṃ vuttaṃ “nahi so kocipaccayoti”ādi. Taṃ sabbaṃpi ācariyassa matimattameva.

That in each of these four all twenty-four conditions are consolidated—with this intention, what was said, 'There is no condition whatsoever,' etc., all of that is merely the teacher's opinion.

[237] Yañhi tattha

[237] For what is stated there:

“Nahi so kocipaccayo atthi. Yo cittacetasi kānaṃ ārammaṇabhāvaṃ nagaccheyyāti” vuttaṃ, taṃ tāva na yujjati. Nahi idha dhammasarūpamattena samodhānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Paccayaṭṭhena saheva adhippetaṃ. Naca hetādipaccayaṭṭho ārammaṇādipaccayaṭṭho hotīti. Esanayo “saka sakapaccayuppannassaca upanissayabhāvaṃ nagacchatīti” etthāpi.

'There is no condition whatsoever that would not become an object for the mind and mental factors'—this statement is not tenable. For here, consolidation by the mere nature of phenomena is not intended; rather, what is intended is consolidation together with the meaning of condition. And the meaning of condition as root, etc., is not the meaning of condition as object, etc. This same principle applies also to this: 'and does not become a decisive support for what arises from its own condition.'

Ettha pana yo sakasakapaccayuppannassa upanissayabhāvaṃ nagacchati. Nahi so koci paccayo atthīti yojanā.

Here, however, the construction is: 'There is no condition whatsoever that does not become a decisive support for what arises from its own respective condition.'

[238] Yañca tattha

[238] And what is stated therein:

“Kammahetukattāca lokappavattiyā phalahetūpacāra vasena sabbepi kammasabhāvaṃ nātivattantīti” vuttaṃ.

'Because the world's continuity has kamma as its cause, and by way of the figurative expression of the cause of the result, all do not transcend the nature of kamma,' it is said.

[239] Yañca

[239] And that which:

“Teca paramatthato lokasammutivasenaca vijjamānā yevāti” vuttaṃ. Tadubhayaṃ pana sabbaso sāsanayutti yāpi viruddhamevāti.

'And these exist both in an ultimate sense and by way of worldly convention,' it is said. However, both of these are entirely contradictory to the Teaching and its reasoning.

Etthāti [M 0.0407] etasmiṃ paṭṭhānanaye. Sabbatthāpīti sabbesu saha jātasabhāgesu paccayesu. Yasmā pana paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃnāma nāmarūpānaṃ aññamaññapaṭibaddhaokāse cutiparicchinnassa sakalassa tassa tassa bhavassa sīsabhūtaṃ bījabhūtañca hoti. Yato sakalakāyabhūtassa nānārūpārūpasantānassa nibbatti hoti. Bījato viya mahārukkhassa. Yathāha –

Herein: in this system of the Paṭṭhāna. Everywhere too: in all conditions of the same class as co-arisen. For rebirth-linking consciousness is the head and seed of each and every entire existence, which is bounded by death and occurs in the sphere of mutually-bound name-and-form. From this occurs the arising of the continuum of diverse material and immaterial phenomena that constitutes the entire body, like a great tree from a seed. As it is said:

Viññāṇañca hi ānanda mātukucchismiṃ na okkamissatha. Apinukho nāmarūpaṃ mātukucchismiṃ samuccissathāti. No hetaṃ bhante. Viññāṇañca hi ānanda mātukucchismiṃ okkamitvā vokkamissatha. Apinukho nāmarūpaṃ itthattāya abhinibbattissathāti. Nohetaṃ bhante. Viññāṇañca hi ānanda daharasseva sato vocchijjissatha kumārassavā kumārikāyavā. Apinukho nāmarūpaṃ vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjissathāti. Nohetaṃ bhante. Tasmā hi ānanda eseva hetu esa nidānaṃ esa samudayo esa paccayo nāmarūpassa. Yadidaṃ viññāṇanti.

'Ānanda, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb, would name-and-form be constituted in the mother's womb?' 'Certainly not, venerable sir.' 'Ānanda, if consciousness, having descended into the mother's womb, were to depart, would name-and-form be produced for this state of being?' 'Certainly not, venerable sir.' 'Ānanda, if the consciousness of a young boy or girl were to be cut off, would name-and-form attain growth, increase, and abundance?' 'Certainly not, venerable sir.' 'Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for name-and-form—that is to say, consciousness.'

Tattha samuccissathāti vaḍḍhissatha. Nāmarūpañhi viññāṇassa vaḍḍhiyevāti. Vokkamissathāti bhijjissatha. Itthatthāyāti īdisassa attabhāvassa atthāyāti attho. Vuddhiṃ viruḷhiṃ vepullanti pathamavayavasena vuddhiṃ. Majjhimavayavasena viruḷhiṃ. Pacchimavayavasena vepullanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā paṭisandhikkhaṇe rūpuppattiyā ekantena viññāṇapaccayatā veditabbā. Evaṃ uppannañca panetaṃ paṭisandhirūpaṃ puna sayaṃ tasmiṃ bhave yāva cutiyā pavattamānānaṃ sabbāsaṃ catusamuṭṭhānikarūpasantatīnaṃ sita bhūtaṃ bījabhūtañca hoti. Atibalavantaṃpi hi cittaṃ purimuppannāya rūpapaveṇiyā asati rūpaṃ janetuṃ nasakkoti. Evaṃ utu āhārāpīti. Tatoyeva hi arūpabhave kāmāvacarādīni rūpajanakacittānipi tattha rūpaṃ najanentīti. Asaññasattepi utu samuṭṭhānarūpasantatiyo pathamuppannāya kammajarūpasantatiyā vijja mānattāeva uppajjantīti. Vuttañhi vibhaṅgaṭīkāyaṃ arūpaṃ pana rūpassa okāso [M 0.0408] na hotīti yasmiṃ rūpe sati cittaṃ aññaṃ rūpaṃ uppādeyya. Tadeva tattha natthīti attho. Purimarūpassāpi hi paccayabhāvo atthi puttassa pitisadisatādassanatoti. Etthaca puttassa pitisadisatādassanatoti etena imamatthaṃ dasseti. Yathā tiṇarukkhānaṃ bījabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ niyāmarūpaṃnāma atthi. Yassa ānubhāvena tannibbattātiṇarukkhā vaḍḍhantā yathāvā tathāvā avaḍḍhitvāattanā samānabījehieva tiṇarukkhehi sabbaso sadisā kāraṃ gahetvā vaḍḍhanti. Evamevaṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ sattānaṃ yoni bhāvasaṅkhātaṃ niyāma rūpaṃnāma atthi. Yassānubhāvena te samāna jātikehieva kulehi visesato mātāpitūhi eva sabbaso sadisarūpasaṇṭhānā honti. Iti bījaniyāmo viya yoniniyāmopi hoti. Soca paṭisandhirūpasseva ānubhāvoti veditabbo.

Therein, 'would be constituted' means 'would grow'. For name-and-form is indeed the growth of consciousness. 'Would depart' means 'would break apart'. 'For this state of being' means for the sake of such an existence—this is the meaning. Growth, increase, and abundance: growth by way of the first stage of life, increase by way of the middle stage, and abundance by way of the final stage—so it is said in the commentary. Therefore, at the moment of rebirth-linking, the fact that the arising of form has consciousness as its condition should be understood as certain. Moreover, this rebirth-linking form, once arisen, becomes the foundation and seed for all continuities of form with fourfold origination that persist in that existence until death. For even an extremely powerful consciousness cannot produce form when the previously arisen lineage of form is absent. The same applies to temperature and nutriment. For that very reason, in the formless realm, even consciousnesses of the sense-sphere and so on that are capable of producing form do not generate form there. Likewise, in non-percipient beings, material continuities originating from temperature arise only because of the presence of the initial material continuity produced by kamma. As stated in the Vibhaṅga subcommentary: 'The formless, however, is not a sphere for form,' meaning that the very form, in the presence of which consciousness could produce another form, is not present there. For the prior form also has the state of being a condition—from the observation of a son's resemblance to his father. Here, 'from the observation of a son's resemblance to his father' illustrates this point: Just as there is a determined form in grasses and trees, called 'seed-nature', by whose power the grasses and trees produced from it do not grow haphazardly, but grow taking on a form entirely similar to grasses and trees from seeds of their own kind. So too is there a determined form, called 'womb-nature', in beings lying in the womb. By its power, they come to have forms and features entirely similar to those of their kin of the same birth, especially their parents. Thus, just as there is a seed-determination, so too is there a womb-determination. And this power should be understood as belonging to the rebirth-linking form itself.

Apica, ayaṃ yoniniyāmonāma kalalakālādīsu puttānaṃ sarīresu mātāpitūhi samudāgataṃ utujarūpasantānaṃeva. Yassa ānubhāvena taṃsantānaṃ samānajātikasattasaṇṭhānasadisaṃ attano ñātikulasadisañca hoti. Yathāhiitthibhāvādirūpaṃ sattānaṃ itthiliṅgādīni bījarūpañca tiṇarukkhānaṃ taṃtaṃvaṇṇasaṇṭhānā dīni niyāmeti. Evaṃ yonirūpaṃ nānājātivasena sattānaṃ niyāmakaṃ vavatthāpakaṃ hotīti. Ettāvatā pavattiyaṃ thapetvā cittajarūpaṃ sabbesaṃ tisamuṭṭhānikarūpānaṃ uppattiyā cittanirapekkhatā purimuppanna rūpapaveṇi paṭibaddhatāca sādhitā hoti. Tenevaca tesaṃ cittassa ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesupi cittarahite nirodhasamāpatti kālepi uppatti hotīti. Tena vuttaṃ sahajātarūpanti panetthātiādi. Itītiādi nigamanaṃ. Tattha sambhavaṃti yathā sambhavaṃ. Sambhavātivā sambhūtā. Ajjhattañcāti ajjhattabhūtāca. Bahiddhācāti bahiddhābhūtāca. Saṅkhatāti saṅkhatabhūtā. Asaṅkhatāti asaṅkhatabhūtā. Evaṃ tekālikāca kālamuttāca ajjhattabahiddhā sambhūtāca. Tathā saṅkhatāsaṅkhatabhūtāca paññatti nāmarūpānaṃ vasena tividhā ṭhitā dhammā paṭṭhāne sabbathā catuvīsati paccayānāma [M 0.0409] hontīti yojanā. Etthaca tividhā ṭhitānaṃ dhammānaṃ tekālikādibhāve sati catuvīsatipaccayānaṃpi yathāsambhavaṃ tekālikādibhedo siddho hoti. Tattha ārammaṇaadhipati upanissayapaccayā tekālikā kālamuttāca honti.

Moreover, this principle of the womb is merely the continuity of temperature-produced matter that arises from the parents in the bodies of offspring from the kalala stage onwards. By its influence, that continuity becomes similar in appearance to beings of the same species and resembling one's own family lineage. Just as the form of femaleness, etc., determines the female gender, etc., in beings, and the seed-form determines the respective color and form, etc., in grasses and trees, so too does the womb-form determine and establish beings in various species. Thus far, in the course of existence, setting aside mind-produced matter, the independence of all threefold-originated matter from the mind for its arising, as well as its dependence on the previously arisen stream of matter, is established. Therefore, their arising occurs even at the moments of the mind's persistence and dissolution, and even during the attainment of cessation, which is devoid of mind. Therefore, it is said here 'co-nascent form' and so on. The conclusion is as follows. Here, 'sambhavaṃ' means 'according to possibility'. 'Sambhūtā' means 'arisen'. 'Ajjhattañca' means 'and internal'. 'Bahiddhāca' means 'and external'. 'Saṅkhatā' means 'conditioned'. 'Asaṅkhatā' means 'unconditioned'. Thus, phenomena that are threefold in time, and timeless, internal and external, and arisen, and likewise conditioned and unconditioned, established as threefold by way of designation, name, and form, become in the Paṭṭhāna the twenty-four conditions in every way—this is the connection. Herein, when the threefold established phenomena exist in terms of the threefold division of time and so on, the division of the twenty-four conditions into the threefold division of time, and so on, is also accordingly established. Among them, the object condition, dominance condition, and decisive support condition are threefold in time and timeless.

[240] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[240] But in the explanation:

“Ārammaṇaadhipatiupanissayapaccayānaṃ tikālikānanti” vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

It is said: “The object, dominance, and decisive support conditions are related to the three times.” That is not fitting.

Paññattinibbānānaṃpi kālamuttānaṃ tesu paviṭṭhattāti. Tattha imasmiṃ bhave abhinavānaṃ dhanadhaññabhogānaṃvā vijjāsippasutapari yattīnaṃvā sīlasamādhipaññānaṃvā bhavantare bhavasampattibhoga sampatti maggaphalasampattīnaṃvā paṭilābhatthāya pubbayogaṃ karontassa anāgatānaṃ tāsaṃ upanissayapaccayatā veditabbā. Paṭṭhāne pana anāgataṃ cakkhusampadaṃ patthayamāno sota, ghāna, jivhā, kāyasampadaṃ, vaṇṇasampadaṃ, sadda, gandha, rasa, phoṭṭhabbasampadaṃ patthayamāno anāgate khandhe patthayamāno dānaṃ deti sīlaṃ samādiyatītiādinā bhavantarapariyāpannāeva sampattiyo vuttā. Tā pana dānādīnaṃ kammānaṃ anurūpavasena vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Kammapaccayo pana paccuppannātītavasena dvikāliko. Anantara samanantara āsevana natthi vigata paccayā atītakālikā. Sesā pannarasa paccayā paccuppannakālikāti. Ajjhattabahiddhāduke ārammaṇā dhipati sahajāta aññamañña nissaya upanissaya purejāta āhāra atthi avigatā ajjhattabahiddhā honti. Sesā cuddasa paccayā ajjhattāva. Ārammaṇa adhipati upanissayā saṅkhatā asaṅkhatāca honti. Sesā saṅkhatāvāti. Pañcavidhaṃpiarūpanti pavuccati. Kasmā, kadācipi rūpasaṅkhātaṃ saṇṭhānatthaṃ anupagamanato nāmantica pavuccati. Kasmā, adhivacanasaṅkhātanāmābhidhānavaseneva suṇantehi gahetabbabhāvupagamanatoti.

Because designations and Nibbāna, being timeless, are also included among them. Herein, for one who in this existence makes preliminary effort for the attainment of newly acquired wealth, grains, and possessions, or for knowledge, skills, and learning, or for virtue, concentration, and wisdom, or for the attainment of prosperity in existence, prosperity in wealth, and the prosperity of the path and fruition in a future existence, the decisive support condition of those future attainments should be understood. In the Paṭṭhāna, however, it is said: “Aspiring to future excellence of the eye… aspiring to excellence of the ear, nose, tongue, body… aspiring to excellence of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles… aspiring to future aggregates, one gives a gift, undertakes the moral precepts,” and so on. By this, excellences pertaining to a future existence are spoken of. But these should be understood as being spoken of in accordance with the kamma of giving, etc. The kamma condition, however, is twofold, by way of the present and the past. The contiguity, immediacy, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions are related to the past. The remaining fifteen conditions are related to the present. In the pair of internal and external, the object, dominance, conascence, mutuality, support, decisive support, prenascence, nutriment, presence, and non-disappearance conditions are internal and external. The remaining fourteen conditions are only internal. The object, dominance, and decisive support conditions are conditioned and unconditioned. The rest are only conditioned. The immaterial is also spoken of as fivefold. Why? Because it never assumes the state of having a shape, which is designated as form. It is also called ‘name.’ Why? Because it is to be grasped by listeners only by means of names, which are designations called conventions.

169. Paññapīyatīti paññatti. Ayaṃpi eko vacanatthoti lokiyamahājanehi thapīyati. Voharīyati ceva sampaṭicchī yaticāti [M 0.0410] attho. Yokoci sammutisaccabhūto byañjanattho. Tathā paññāpetabbā atthā paññapīyanti etāyāti paññatti. Byañjanatthajotako paññattisaddoti evaṃ duvidhā paññattīti vuttaṃ tatoavasesā.La. Duvidhāhotīti. Tattha paññāpīyattā paññattīti attha paññattimāha. Paññāpanatopaññattīti saddapaññattiṃ. Taṃtaṃbhūtavipariṇāmākāranti pathaviyādīnaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ adhimattabhāvappakārasaṅkhātaṃ tathā tathā pariṇā mākāraṃ. Pavattivisesākāranti attho. Upādāyāti paṭicca. Nissāya. Pathamaṃ cittena gahetvāti attho. Tathātathā paññattāti ayaṃ pathavīnāma ayaṃ pabbatonāmāti evamādi nayena mahājanena paññattā, kathitā, voharitāti attho. Pathavipabbatādikātiādisaddena nadi samuddādikāyo saṅgaṇhati. Ayaṃ samūhapaññattināma.

169. “It is made known,” thus it is a designation (paññatti). This too is one meaning of the word, as established by worldly people. The meaning is that it is both used in convention and accepted. It is any meaning of expression that is a conventional truth. Likewise, “meanings to be made known are made known by this,” thus it is a designation. The word “paññatti” illuminates the meaning of expression. Thus, it is said that designation is of two kinds. Here, “because it is made known, it is a designation” refers to designation as meaning (attha-paññatti). “Because it makes known, it is a designation” refers to designation as a term (sadda-paññatti). “The mode of transformation of the various elements” refers to the mode of transformation in this or that way, which is reckoned as the mode of the predominant state of each of the great elements, such as earth. It means the mode of a distinct occurrence. “Depending on” means “in dependence on,” “relying on.” The meaning is “having first been grasped by the mind.” “Designated in such and such a way” means that it is designated, spoken of, and used by the general populace in ways such as “this is earth,” “this is a mountain,” and so on. “Earth, mountains, etc.”: by the word “etc.”, rivers, oceans, and the like are included. This is called designation of a collection (samūha-paññatti).

[241] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[241] But in the explanation:

“Saṇṭhānapaññattīti” vuttā. Sā yuttā viya nadissati.

It is said: “Designation of shape.” That does not seem fitting.

Nahi idha saṇṭhānaṃ padhānaṃ hotīti. Sambhārasannivesākāranti kaṭṭhādīnaṃ sambhārānaṃ tathā tathā sannivesākāraṃ. Etthāpi ādisaddena nāvādayo saṅgaṇhati. Ayaṃ saṇṭhāna paññatti. Kaṭṭhādayo eva hi gehākārena saṇṭhitā gehanti rathākārena saṇṭhitā rathoti vuccantīti.

For here, the shape is not primary. “The mode of arrangement of components” refers to the mode of arrangement in this and that way of components such as wood. Here too, the term “and so on” includes boats and the like. This is the designation of shape. For indeed, it is wood and the like which, arranged in the shape of a house, are called a house; arranged in the shape of a chariot, are called a chariot.

[242] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[242] But in the explanation:

“Samūhapaññattīti” vuttaṃ. Taṃ na yujjati.

It is said: “Designation of a collection.” That is not fitting.

Nahi idha samūho padhānanti. Purisapuggalādikā sattapaññatti upādāpaññattītipi vuccati. Candāvaṭṭanādikanti candasūriyādīnaṃ sineruṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā āvaṭṭanādikaṃ. Yato candimasūriyā udenti, sā pubbadisānāma. Pubbataraṃ laddhappakāsattā. Yattha pana atthaṃ gacchanti, sā pacchimadisānāma. Pacchāladdhapakāsattā. Tāsaṃ dakkhiṇapassā disā vuḍḍhiatthena dakkhiṇadisānāma. Itarā pana uccataraṭṭhena uttarādisāti vuccati. Yadā sūriyo udeti, tadā sakalassa [M 0.0411] ahassa pubbabhāgattā pubbanhoti vuccatīti. Evamādikā disā paññatti kālapaññattiyonāma. Ādisaddena thalaninnādikā desapaññatti saṅgahitāti. Asamphuṭṭhākāranti mahābhūtānaṃ aññamaññaṃ asamphusanākāraṃ. Ayaṃ ākāsapaññattināma. Taṃ taṃ bhūtanimittanti pathavīkasiṇādikaṃ uddhumātakādikañca bhūtanimittaṃ. Nīlakasiṇādikaṃ vaṇṇanimittañca ettheva saṅgayhati. Bhāvanā visesanti parikammādikaṃ bhāvanāvisesaṃca. Etena parikammanimitta uggahanimitta paṭibhāganimittānaṃ siddhakāraṇaṃ vadati. Ayaṃ nimittapaññattināma.

For here, the collection is not primary. The designation of a being, such as a person or an individual, is also called the designation by appropriation. “The circling of the moon, etc.” refers to the moon, sun, and so on circling Mount Sineru clockwise. The direction from which the moon and sun rise is called the eastern direction, because it receives light earlier. The direction where they set is called the western direction, because it receives light later. The direction on their right side is called the southern direction because of its meaning of growth, while the other, being higher, is called the northern direction. When the sun rises, it is called the forenoon because it is the earlier part of the whole day. Such designations of direction and designations of time are so named. By the term “and so on,” designations of place, such as high and low ground, are included. “The uncontacted state” refers to the state of non-contact among the great elements. This is called the designation of space. “The sign of such and such an element” refers to the earth kasiṇa, the bloated corpse, and other signs of elements. The blue kasiṇa and other color signs are also included here. “A distinction in meditation” refers to preparatory work and other distinctions in meditation. By this, the cause for the accomplishment of the preparatory sign, the acquired sign, and the counterpart sign is stated. This is called the designation of a sign.

Evamādibhedāti ettha ādisaddena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatā upādāpaññatti upanidhāpaññattiādayo saṅgahitā. Paramatthato avijjamānāpīti etena sammutito laddhabhāvaṃ dasseti. Teneva hi tāsaṃ vijjamānabhāvaṃ gahetvā tathā tathā voharantānaṃ musāvādonāma nahotīti. Atthacchāyākārenāti taṃ taṃ bhūtādīnaṃ paramatthānaṃ samūhasaṇṭhānādichāyākārena. Atthacchā yākārenātivā saddābhidheyyasaṅkhātena dabbapaṭibimbākārena saviggahākārenāti attho, taṃtaṃupādāyāti paramatthadhammānaṃ taṃtaṃpavattivisesaṃ upādāya. Upanidhāyāti olumbiya. Parikappiyamānāti parikappabuddhiyā parikappetvā gayhamānā. Ettha pana evamādipabhedā ālambaṇabhūtā parikappiyamānā sabbā paññatti paññāpīyatīti atthena paññattīti yojanā. Saṅkhāyatīti gaṇīyati. Gaṇanupagaṃ katvā thapīyatīti attho. Samaññāyatīti sammannīyati. Nāmaṃ, nāmakammaṃ, nāmadheyyaṃ, nirutti, byañjanaṃ, abhilāpoti ime cha nāma nāmakammā. Tattha atthe namatīti nāmaṃ. Atthavisayaṃ eva hutvā pavattatīti attho. Attanica atthaṃ nāmetīti nāmaṃ. Piṭakattayasaṅkhāte hi nāme sati taduggaṇhantānaṃ sabbe tadatthā padepade vākyevākye āgacchanti yevāti.

Here, in 'of such kinds and so forth,' by the word 'and so forth,' designations such as 'derived designation' (upādāpaññatti) and 'metaphorical designation' (upanidhāpaññatti) mentioned in the commentary are included. 'Though they do not exist in an ultimate sense'—this indicates that they are established only conventionally. For this very reason, for those who speak accordingly, having taken their existence as real, there is no false speech. 'In the manner of a shadow of the meaning'—this means in the form of a shadow, such as the collection or shape of this or that ultimate reality. Or, 'in the manner of a shadow of the meaning' refers to the form of an image of a substance, which is understood through the designation of sound, having a distinct form. 'Depending on this or that' means depending on the particular occurrence of ultimate phenomena. 'By comparison'—this means 'relying on.' 'Conceptualized'—this means being grasped through conceptual thought. Here, however, the connection is that all such designations, being objects and being conceptualized, are called 'paññatti' (designation) in the sense that they are 'made known' (paññāpīyati). 'It is reckoned'—it is counted. The meaning is that it is established by being brought into calculation. 'It is termed'—it is designated. There are six terms related to naming: 'nāma' (name), 'nāmakamma' (the act of naming), 'nāmadheyya' (appellation), 'nirutti' (expression), 'byañjana' (term), and 'abhilāpa' (utterance). Among these, 'nāma' (name) is so called because 'it inclines toward the meaning.' The meaning is that it functions solely within the sphere of meaning. It is also called 'nāma' because 'it inclines the meaning toward itself.' For when the Three Piṭakas, which are designated as 'nāma,' exist, all who study them encounter all those meanings in every word and every sentence.

Apica suṇantānaṃ ñāṇaṃ taṃtaṃatthābhimukhaṃ nāmetīti nāmaṃ nāmagahaṇavasena kattabbattā nāmameva kammanti nāmakammaṃ. Dhīyati dhārīyatīti [M 0.0412] dheyyaṃ. Nāmameva dheyyanti nāmadheyyaṃ. Aviditapakkhe ṭhito attho etāya tato nīharitvā vuccati kathīyatīti nirutti. Atthassa byañjanato pākaṭakaraṇato byañjanaṃ. Abhibyattaṃ katvā lapīyati kathīyati attho etenāti abhilāpo. Etthaca vaṇṇapaññatti, akkharapaññatti, sarapaññatti, dīghapaññatti, rassa paññatti. Byañjanavaggaghosāghosapaññatti, liṅgapaññatti. Padapaññatti, vākyapaññattiyopi etasseva pabhedāti daṭṭhabbā. Paramatthato vijjamānesu atthesu pavattā paññatti vijjamānapaññatti nāma. Avijja mānesu bhūmipabbatādīsu pavattā paññatti avijjamānapaññatti nāma. Etā eva samāsaṭṭhānaṃ patvā dvipadasaṃyogavasena itarā catassopi hontīti dassetuṃ tatthātiādi vuttaṃ. Etāya paññāpentīti etena vijjamānaṃ atthaṃ paññapenti etāyāti vijjamānapaññattīti imamatthaṃ vadati. Esanayo paratthapi. Cha abhiññā assāti chaḷabhiññoti katvā visesanabhūtānaṃ channaṃ abhiññānaṃ vijjamānattā visesitabbabhūtassa puggalassa avijjamānattā chaḷa bhiññoti vijjamānenaavijjamānapaññatti nāma. Itthī avijjamānā saddo vijjamānoti itthiyāsaddo itthisaddoti avijjamānena vijjamāna paññatti nāma. Cakkhuca cakkhuviññāṇañca ubhayaṃpi vijjāmānanti cakkhusmiṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhuviññāṇanti vijjamānenavijjamānapaññatti nāma. Rājāca puttoca dvepi avijjamānāevāti rañño putto rājaputtoti avijjamānenaavijjamānapaññattināmāti imamatthaṃ dassento ubhinnantiādimāha.

Furthermore, 'nāma' (name) is that which inclines the knowledge of those who listen towards its respective meaning. Because it is to be done by way of grasping the name, the name itself is the action; hence, 'nāmakamma' (the act of naming). What is thought of, what is borne in mind, is called 'dheyya.' The name itself is the 'dheyya'; hence, 'nāmadheyya' (appellation). A meaning, standing on the side of the unknown, is brought out from there and spoken by this; thus, it is called 'nirutti' (expression). By making the meaning clear through manifestation, it is called 'byañjana' (term). Because the meaning is spoken and explained by making it evident, it is called 'abhilāpa' (utterance). And here, designation of letters, designation of syllables, designation of vowels, designation of long vowels, designation of short vowels, designation of voiced and unvoiced consonants, designation of gender, designation of words, and designation of sentences should be seen as subdivisions of this same thing. A designation that occurs in respect to things that exist in an ultimate sense is called an 'existing designation.' A designation that occurs in respect to things that do not exist in an ultimate sense, such as land and mountains, is called a 'non-existing designation.' To show that these same designations, upon reaching a state of composition, also become the other four types through the combination of two terms, 'there' and so on was said. 'By this, they make known'—thus, it states the meaning that 'they make known an existing meaning by this,' hence it is called an 'existing designation.' This method applies elsewhere as well. One who possesses six higher knowledges is called 'chaḷabhiñño' (one with sixfold higher knowledge). Because the six higher knowledges, which are the qualifiers, exist, but the person to be qualified does not exist, 'chaḷabhiñño' is a 'designation of a non-existing thing by means of an existing thing' (vijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti). The woman is non-existent, but the sound is existent; thus, 'the sound of a woman,' or 'itthisaddo' (woman-sound), is a 'designation of an existing thing by means of a non-existing thing' (avijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti). Both the eye and eye-consciousness are existent; thus, 'consciousness in the eye,' or 'cakkhuviññāṇa' (eye-consciousness), is a 'designation of an existing thing by means of an existing thing' (vijjamānena vijjamānapaññatti). Both the king and the son are non-existent; thus, 'the king's son,' or 'rājaputto' (prince), is a 'designation of a non-existing thing by means of a non-existing thing' (avijjamānena avijjamānapaññatti). To show this meaning, he said 'of both,' and so on.

Ettha pana vacanato ca vacanatthatoca vinimuttā saddasabhāvā nāmapaññattināma visuṃ natthīti vadanti. Taṃ na yujjati. Atthajotaka bhāvena visuṃ siddhattā. Saddo hi nāma akkharapadabyañjanabhāvaṃ upagatoyeva atthajotane samattho hoti. Paramattha saddoca khaṇiko cuṇṇavicuṇṇabhūto tabbhāvaṃ upagato nahotīti. Tasmā saddasabhāvānāma paññattināma visuṃ atthiyeva. Atthibhāvocassā vacanasaddaṃ sutvā anantare akkhara pada byañjanagocaracittassa tadanantareca tadatthavijānanacittassa pavattiyā pākaṭoti [M 0.0413] dassento gāthādvayaṃ āha. Tattha vacīghosā nusārenāti uccāriyamānasaddasaṅkhātassa vacīghosassa ārammaṇakaraṇasaṅkhātena anusārena uppannāya sotaviññāṇa vīthiyā pavattiyā anantare uppannassa manodvārassa gocara bhūtā sāyaṃ paññattīti sambandho. Kīdisī pana sāyaṃ paññattīti āha atthāyassā.La. Tatoparanti. Tattha tatoparanti tato nāmapaññattārammaṇassa manodvārassa uppattito paraṃ atthā viññāyantīti sambandho. Yassā nāmapaññattiyā anusārena paramatthapaññattibhūtā atthā viññāyanti. Sā ayaṃ paññatti lokasaṅketanimmitāti viññeyyāti yojanā.

Here, however, some say that a name-designation is not something that exists separately from the nature of sound, freed from speech and the meaning of speech. That is not correct, because it is distinctly established by its nature of illuminating the meaning. For sound, having assumed the nature of letters, words, and syllables, is indeed capable of illuminating meaning. Ultimate sound, being momentary and pulverized, does not attain that nature. Therefore, a name-designation separate from the nature of sound indeed exists. Its existence is made evident by the arising of the mind-door consciousness, whose object is the letters, words, and syllables, immediately after hearing the speech-sound, and then by the subsequent arising of the consciousness that knows the meaning. To show this, two verses are stated. There, 'following the speech-sound' means that this designation is the object of the mind-door, which arises immediately after the ear-consciousness process that occurs by following the speech-sound—that is, by taking the uttered sound as its object. What, then, is this designation like? It is said, 'whose meanings...' and so on. 'Beyond that' means that after the arising of the mind-door, which takes the name-designation as its object, the meanings are understood. The meanings, which consist of ultimate realities and concepts, are understood by following that name-designation. This designation should be understood as created by worldly convention.

Etthaca sotaviññāṇavīthiyāti ettha atītasaddamattā rammaṇā tadanuvattikānāma manoviññāṇavīthipi saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Vuttañhi sāratthadīpaniyaṃ-tena vuttavacane yattakāni akkharāni honti. Tesu ekamekaṃ paccuppannaṃ atītañca gahetvā sota viññāṇavīthiyā manoviññāṇavīthiyāca uppajjitvā niruddhāya avasāne tāni akkharāni sampiṇḍetvā akkharasamūhaṃ gahetvā ekā manoviññāṇavīthi uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Tadanantaraṃ ayaṃ akkharasamūho etassa nāmanti nāmapaññattigahaṇavasena aparāya manoviññāṇa vīthiyā uppajjitvā niruddhāya tadanantaraṃ uppannāya manoviññāṇa vīthiyā ayametassa atthoti pakatiyā tadatthavijānanaṃ sambhavatīti. Maṇisāramañjūsāyaṃ pana tadanuvattikavīthito paraṃ ekaṃ vinicchayavīthiṃ viññattigahaṇavīthiñca vadati. Tato paraṃ ekakkhare sadde ekatthajotikāya nāmapaññattiyā gahaṇaṃ hoti. Yā vadantassa pubbabhāge manasā vavatthāpito paññattisaddonāma vuccati. Tatoparaṃ tadatthagahaṇanti. Īdisesu pana ṭhānesu tattha tattha javanavīthivārānaṃ paṭipāṭikathanaṃnāma padhānapākaṭagahaṇavasenevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ekaccharakkhaṇe aneka koṭisatasahassāni cittāni uppajjantīti hi vuttaṃ. Tathā –

And here, in the phrase 'ear-consciousness process,' it should be understood that the mind-consciousness process, which follows and takes the past sound as its object, is also included. For it is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī: 'In that spoken utterance, however many syllables there are, each one is taken as present and past, and after the ear-consciousness process and the mind-consciousness process have arisen and ceased, at the end those syllables are combined, and having taken the cluster of syllables, one mind-consciousness process arises and ceases. Following that, after another mind-consciousness process has arisen and ceased by way of grasping the name-designation as “this cluster of syllables is its name,” then, in the subsequent mind-consciousness process that arises, the understanding of its meaning as “this is its meaning” naturally occurs.' However, in the Maṇisāramañjūsā, it is said that after the process that follows, there is one decisive process and one process of grasping the expression. After that, in a single-syllable sound, the grasping of the name-designation that illuminates a single meaning occurs. That which is mentally determined by the speaker beforehand is called the 'designation-sound.' Following that, the meaning is grasped. In such cases, it should be understood that the description of the sequence of impulsion processes in various places is primarily by way of grasping what is primary and evident. For it is said that in a single finger-snap, many hundreds of thousands of crores of cittas arise. Similarly—

Ekamatto bhave rasso, dvimatto dīghamuccate;

Timattotupluto ñeyyo, byañjanaṃ addhamattikanticaṃ.

A short vowel is of one mora; a long vowel is said to be of two moras. A prolated vowel should be known as of three moras, and a consonant is of half a mora.

Na ca paramatthasaddasaṅghāṭānaṃ satasahassaṃpi ekakkharaṃnāma bhavituṃ pahoti. Tasmā idha bahuṃ vicāraṇā amhehi nakatāti.

And not even a hundred thousand combinations of ultimate sounds are able to become a single syllable. Therefore, much investigation has not been done by us here.

Iti paramatthadīpaniyānāma abhidhammatthasaṅgahassa

Thus, in the Paramatthadīpanī, the commentary on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,

Catutthavaṇṇanāya aṭṭhamassa paccayasaṅgahassa

in the fourth explanation of the eighth, the Compendium of Conditions,

Paramatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The Paramatthadīpanā is completed.

Kammaṭṭhāna saṅgaha paramatthadīpanī

The Compendium of Meditation Subjects: Illuminating the Ultimate Meaning

170. Evaṃ [M 0.0415] aṭṭhahi paricchedehi sapaccayapabhedaṃ nāmarūpa vibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni viditanāmarūpa vibhāgassa kammaṭṭhānavidhānaṃ dassento samathavipassanānantiādi māha. Ito paccaya saṅgahato paraṃ samathavipassanānaṃ bhāvanānaṃ duvidhaṃpi kammaṭṭhānaṃ yathākkamaṃ pavakkhāmīti yojanā. Tattha kilese aññepivā vitakkādayo oḷārikadhamme sametīti samatho. Tathā pavatto ekaggatāsaṅkhāto samādhi. Visesena passanti etāyāti vipassanā. Aniccānupassanādikā bhāvanāpaññā. Tāya hi yogino khandhesu lokiyamahājanena passitaṃ itthipurisādikaṃ niccasukhādikañca atikkamitvā visesena aniccādikameva passantīti. Bhāvetabbāti bhāvanā. Bhāventivā cittasantānaṃ etāhīti bhāvanā. Kiriyā kammaṃ. Tiṭṭhati etthāti ṭhānaṃ. Kammassa ṭhānanti kammaṭṭhānaṃ. Vīriyārabbhasaṅkhātassa yogakammassa pavattiṭṭhānanti attho. Kasiṇamaṇḍalādikaṃ kasiṇabhāvanādikañca. Ādimajjha pariyosānānañhi samudāyabhūkaṃ ekametaṃ pathavīkasiṇa bhāvanādikaṃ bhāvanākammaṃpi attano avayavabhūtassa yoga kammassa pavattiṭṭhānaṃ sambhavatīti.

170. Having thus shown in eight sections the division of name-and-form with its varieties of conditions, now, in order to explain the method of meditation subjects for one who has understood the division of name-and-form, he says 'calm and insight,' and so forth. The connection is: 'After this Compendium of Conditions, I shall explain in due order the two kinds of meditation subjects, namely, the development of calm and insight.' Herein, 'calm' (samatha) is so called because it calms (sameti) defilements and other coarse states such as initial thought. Similarly, the concentration (samādhi) that has arisen, characterized by one-pointedness, is also called calm. 'Insight' (vipassanā) is so called because one sees (passanti) specially (visesena) by means of it. It is the wisdom of development, such as the contemplation of impermanence. For by this, yogis, transcending what is seen by ordinary worldly people in the aggregates—such as male and female, permanence and pleasure—see only impermanence, etc., in a special way. That which is to be developed is 'development' (bhāvanā). Or, it is 'development' because they develop the continuity of mind by means of it. Action is 'kamma.' That in which one stands (tiṭṭhati) is a 'place' (ṭhāna). The place of kamma is 'meditation subject' (kammaṭṭhāna). The meaning is the place of occurrence for the yogic action, characterized by the arousal of energy. The kasiṇa circle, etc., and the kasiṇa development, etc. For this single earth kasiṇa development, etc., which is the work of development, being a collection of beginning, middle, and end, can also be the place of occurrence for its own component yogic action.

Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

But in the Vibhāvanī,

Uttaruttara yogakammassa padaṭṭhānatāya kammaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ bhāvanāvidhiñcātipi vuttaṃ. Tampi yujjatiyeva.

it is also said to be the method of development that has become a meditation subject by being the proximate cause for progressively higher yogic actions. That too is indeed fitting.

Yogakammamevavā sukhavisesānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhenaṭhānanti kammaṭṭhānaṃ. Tatthāti tasmiṃ duvidhepi kammaṭṭhāne. Samathasaṅgaheti samatha kammaṭṭhānasaṅgahe. Dasakasiṇānīti dasakasiṇamaṇḍalāni kasiṇajjhānānica. Tadubhayānipi hi yogānuyogasaṅkhātassa samatha kammassa pavattiṭṭhānattā samathakammaṭṭhānānināma hontīti. Dasaasubhāti dasaasubhavatthūni asubhajjhānānica. Dasaanussati yoti [M 0.0416] buddhaguṇādīni dasaanussatiṭṭhānāni anussaraṇasati yoca. Sesānipi yathānurūpaṃ vattabbānīti. Caraṇaṃ cariyā. Samudācaraṇanti attho. Pavattibahulatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rāgassa cariyā rāgacariyā. Rāgacaritāti pāṭho, so aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi, puggalaṭṭhāneeva so yuttoti. Esanayo sesesupi.

Or, 'meditation subject' (kammaṭṭhāna) is so called because yogic action itself is a 'place' (ṭhāna) in the sense of being a basis (adhiṭṭhāna) for special kinds of happiness. 'Therein' (tattha) means in those two kinds of meditation subjects. 'In the Compendium of Calm' (samathasaṅgahe) means in the compendium of calm meditation subjects. 'The ten kasiṇas' means the ten kasiṇa circles and the kasiṇa jhānas. For both of these are indeed called calm meditation subjects because they are the place of occurrence for the calm work, known as application to practice. 'The ten impurities' means the ten impure objects and the impurity jhānas. 'The ten recollections' means the ten bases of recollection, such as the qualities of the Buddha, and the mindfulness of recollection. The remainder should also be stated accordingly. 'Conduct' (caraṇa) is 'practice' (cariyā). The meaning is 'conduct.' It is said to be 'frequency of occurrence.' The practice of lust is 'lustful conduct' (rāgacariyā). The reading 'lustful temperament' (rāgacaritā) is not found in the commentary; it is only suitable in the section on individuals. This method applies to the remainder as well.

[243] Yo pana vibhāvaniyaṃ

But as for that which is in the Vibhāvanī [on page 243],

Cariyānaṃ saṃsaggabhedo vutto. So idha nādhippeto.

the distinction of the mixture of temperaments has been stated. That is not intended here.

Nahi kammaṭṭhānānaṃnāma saṃsaggacaritassapi ekassa dve tīṇi dātabbāni hotīti. Teneva hi so bhedo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ nagarukatoti. Sabbāpi appanāya pubbabhāgapavattā kāmāvacara bhāvanā parikammabhāvanānāma. Sā pana appanāya āsanne dūreti duvidhā hoti. Tattha yā āsanne, sā appanaṃ upecca samīpe ṭhatvā pavattattā upacārabhāvanāti vuccati. Itarā pana parikamma bhāvanāevanāma. Iti parikammabhāvanāpi samānā pubbāparavisesa pākaṭabhāvatthaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu dvīhi nāmehi gahitāti vuttaṃ parikammabhāvanā.La. Tissobhāvanāti tāsaṃ pana viseso parato āgamissati. Parikammanimittanti parikammabhāvanāya ārammaṇabhūtaṃ kasiṇamaṇḍalādinimittaṃ. Tañca tassā ārammaṇa bhāvena ekaṃpi samānaṃ pubbāparavisesapākaṭabhāvatthaṃ parikammanimittaṃ uggahanimittanti dvidhā bhinditvā vuttaṃ. Tesaṃpi viseso āgamissati. Vidatthicaturaṅgulasaṅkhātena parittapamāṇenavā khala maṇḍalādisaṅkhātena mahantapamāṇenavā kataṃ akataṃvā pathavī maṇḍalatalameva asesapharitabbaṭṭhena kasiṇanti pathavīkasiṇaṃ. Sakalasaddapariyāyo hi kasiṇasaddo. Yathā kasiṇena jambudīpassāti. Tasmā yattake pathavītale nimittaṃ gaṇhāti, tattakaṃ cittena asesaṃ pharitvā eva gahetabbaṃ hoti. Na pana tassa ekadese ṭhatvāti, tena vuttaṃ pathavīmaṇḍalatalameva asesapharitabbaṭṭhena kasiṇanti pathavīkasiṇanti. Esanayo sesakasiṇesupīti. Etthaca, avibhūtavaṇṇāya pathaviyā eka talabhāvenasanniviṭṭhāsaṇṭhānapaññattiidhapathavīkasiṇaṃnāma[M 0.0417]. Tathā āpokasiṇaṃ tejokasiṇañca. Phuṭṭhaṭṭhāne cittena saṇṭhānaṃ katvā gahitā vāyuvaṭṭi vāyokasiṇaṃnāma. Nīlavaṇṇavisiṭṭhāekā saṇṭhānapaññatti nīlakasiṇaṃnāma. Tathā pītalohito dātakasiṇānipi. Candasūriyaaggobhāsavisiṭṭhā katthaci dissamānā saṇṭhānapaññatti ālokakasiṇaṃnāma. Tittichiddavāta pānachiddādīsu dissamānā ākāsavisiṭṭhā saṇṭhānapaññatti ākāsakasiṇaṃnāmāti. Ativiya dhumātaṃ sunabhāvaṃ gatanti uddhumātaṃ. Tadeva kucchitattā uddhumātakaṃ. Tathābhūtassa chavasarīrassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tadeva pūtibhāvaṃ gatakāle purimavaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā puna nīlabhāvaṃ pattaṃ vinīlakaṃ. Tadeva puna paccitvā tato tato visandamānapubbayuttaṃ vipubbakaṃ. Yuddhabhūmiyādīsu satthena majjhe chinditvā thapitaṃ virūpachinnasarīraṃ vicchinnakaṃnāma. Soṇa siṅgālādīhi vividhākārena khāyitapadesayuttaṃ sarīraṃ vikkhāyitakaṃnāma. Soṇasiṅgālādīhi eva khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ katvā apakaḍḍhitvā tato tato khittaaṅgapaccaṅgayuttaṃ sarīraṃ vittakkhikaṃ nāma. Aṅgapaccaṅgesu satthena hanitvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ katvā tato tato khittaaṅgapaccaṅgayuttaṃ sarīraṃ hatavikkhittakaṃnāma. Paggharita lohitasarīraṃ lohitakaṃ nāma. Puḷuvaparipūraṃ sarīraṃ puḷuvakaṃ. Sakalo aṭṭhisaṅghāṭovā ekamekaṃvā aṭṭhi aṭṭhikaṃ nāma. Punappunaṃ nirantaraṃ saraṇaṃ anussati. Buddhaguṇassa anussati buddhānussati. Esa nayo sesāsupīti. Tattha arahatādiguṇo buddhaguṇonāma. Svakkhātatādiguṇo dhammaguṇonāma. Suppaṭipannatādiguṇo saṅghaguṇo nāma. Attano sīlassa akhaṇḍatādi guṇo sīlaguṇonāma. Attano dānassa vigatamalamaccheratādi guṇo cāgaguṇonāma. Attānaṃ devattaṃvā sakkattaṃvā brahmattaṃvā vahituṃ samatthā attano saddhādiguṇā devatāguṇānāma. Vatta paṭipattivasenavā dhutaṅgasamādānavasenavā jhānasamāpattivasenavā vipassanāvasenavā attano santāne ciraṃvikālaṃ vikkhambhitānaṃ kāmarāgādīnaṃ vūpasamo attanāadhigatanibbānañca upasamonāma. Ekabhavapariyāpannassa [M 0.0418] attano khandhasantānassa bhedo maraṇaṃ nāma. Kesakāyādīnaṃ nānākāyānaṃ samūhabhūto ayaṃ kāyo kāyonāma. Attani nirantaraṃ pavattamānā assāsa passāsā ānāpāṇaṃnāma. Mijjati siniyhatīti mettā. Yaṃ ārabbha uppajjati. Tassa hitasukhaṃ avippakiṇṇaṃ katvā saṅgaṇhatīti attho. Mittassavā esā mittesuvā bhavāti mettā. Atthato pana parasattānaṃ hitūpasaṃhāravasena pavatto adosoeva. Parasattānaṃ hitūpasaṃhāra hitamodana ahitāpanayanasaṅkhātaṃ byāpārattayaṃ pahāya tesaṃ kammasakatānubrūhanavasena upapattito yuttito pekkhatīti upekkhā. Tathā pavattā tatramajjhattatāeva. Appamāṇesusattesu bhavāti appamaññā. Na hi ettakesu eva sattesu etā pavattetabbā. Na tato aññesūti evaṃ etāsaṃ visayaparicchedonāma atthīti. Evaṃsantepi ādikammi kena ādito ekasmiṃ puggale attano bhāvanācittaṃ laddhāsevanaṃ laddhavisesañca katvā pacchā dvīsu tīsūtiādinā vaḍḍhitvā sīmasambhedoca odhisopharaṇa anodhisopharaṇa disāpharaṇāniva kattabbānīti. Yaṃ pana vibhaṅge mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatītiādinā paṭisambhidāmaggeca sabbesattā averā hontūtiādinā mettāvidhānaṃ nāma vuttaṃ. Taṃ mettājhāne vasībhāvappattānaṃ vasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etā pana visesena dosapakkhikānaṃ kilesānaṃ ujupaṭipakkhabhūtā hontīti taṃsamaṅginoca niccaṃ sommahadayabhāvena brahmasadi sattā brahmānonāma. Tesaṃ vihāroti brahmavihāro. Seṭṭhānaṃvā seṭṭhabhūtovā vihāroti brahmavihāroti. Āhāreti asita pīta khāyita sāyita vasena catuppabhede ajjhohaṭāhāre. Paṭikūlasaññāti āhārahetu anubhavitabbānaṃ dukkhadhammānaṃ paccavekkhanavasena sarasapaṭikūlatā paccavekkhanavasena āsayanidhāna pakkāpakkaphalanissandapaccavekkhana vasena ca tattha nikanti pahānasaññā. Catudhātuvavatthānanti sarīragatānaṃ pathaviādīnaṃ catunnaṃ mahādhātūnaṃ salakkhaṇā divasena [M 0.0419] visuṃ visuṃ paricchinditvā samanupassanaṃ. Tañhi catasso dhātuyo vavatthapiyanti vinicchiyanti sallakkhiyanti etenāti catudhātuvavatthānanti vuccatīti. Asubhasaññā bhāvetabbā rāgassapahānāyāti vacanato dasaasubhā.La. Rāgacaritassa sappāyāti vuttaṃ. Tattha rāgena caratīti rāgacarito. So hi kāmaṃ kadāci dosena carati. Kadāci mohena. Kadāci saddhādīsupi aññatarena. Rāgo panassa ussanno. Tasmā ussannena rāgena so rāgacaritoti saṅkhyaṃ gacchatīti. Esanayo sesesupi. Mettā bhāvetabbā byāpādassa pahānāyāti vacanato mettādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ brahmavihārānaṃ yathākkamaṃ byāpādavihiṃsā aratīnaṃ nissaraṇatāvacanato suparisuddhānañca vaṇṇakasiṇānaṃ dosavatthuttābhāvato catassoappamaññāyo.La. Dosacaritassāti vuttaṃ. Etthaca ādikammikassevāyaṃ cariyavibhāgo. Upekkhāca ādikammikassa nasambhavati. Vakkhatihi upekkhāpañcamajjhānikāti. Tasmā yassa purimā tisso sappāyā. Tassa tadanugatikā upekkhāpi sappāyānāma hotīti katvā catasso appamaññāyoti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Itarathā nissaraṇañhetaṃ rāgassa. Yadidaṃ upekkhā ceto vimuttīti vacanato upekkhā rāgacaritassāti vattabbaṃ siyāti. Nīlādīnica cattāri kasiṇānīti idañca manāpiyarūpāni nīlādīni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Amanāpiyāni pana tāni rāgacaritasseva sappāyānīti. Ānāpāṇasati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāyāti vacanato ānāpāṇaṃvitakkacaritassāti vuttaṃ. Mohacarito pana pakatiyā pamādabahulo hoti vikkhittacittoca. Ānāpāṇañcanāma nirantaraṃ pavattamānaṃ tassa satiṃ uppādentaṃ viya pavattatīti taṃ mohacaritassasappāyanti vuttaṃ siyā.

It is not the case that two or three meditation subjects should be given to one person of mixed temperament. For this reason, that distinction is not made prominent in the commentary. All mundane meditation that precedes absorption is called preparatory meditation (parikammabhāvanā). That, however, is of two kinds, near or far from absorption. There, what is near, having approached absorption and standing close, is called access meditation (upacārabhāvanā). The other is simply called preparatory meditation. Thus, preparatory meditation, though one, is referred to by two names in the commentaries to clarify the distinction between earlier and later stages—this is called preparatory meditation. As for the three meditations, their distinctions will be explained later. The preliminary sign (parikammanimitta) is the object of preparatory meditation, such as a kasiṇa disk. Though it is one in being the object, it is divided into two—the preliminary sign and the acquired sign (uggahanimitta)—to clarify the distinction between earlier and later stages. Their distinctions will also be explained later. The earth kasiṇa is the surface of an earthen disk, made either with a measured size of a span and four fingers or a large size like a threshing floor, whether prepared or unprepared, and must be fully pervaded in the sense of covering the entire earth disk. The term “kasiṇa” is indeed a synonym for “whole,” as in “the kasiṇa of Jambudīpa.” Therefore, one must mentally pervade the entire area where the sign is grasped, not just a part of it. Hence, it is said: “The earth kasiṇa is the surface of an earthen disk fully pervaded.” This method applies to the remaining kasiṇas as well. Here, the earth kasiṇa is the shape concept of the earth’s undifferentiated color and unified surface. Similarly, the water kasiṇa and fire kasiṇa. The air kasiṇa is the vortex of air, the shape of which is perceived by the mind in the place of contact. The blue kasiṇa is a distinct shape concept of blue color. Likewise, the yellow, red, and white kasiṇas. The light kasiṇa is the shape concept of light seen in places like the moon, sun, or fire. The space kasiṇa is the shape concept of space seen in holes like keyholes or window-holes. “Bloated” (uddhumātaṃ) refers to a corpse extremely bloated and gone to a state of being swollen. That very corpse, being repulsive, is called uddhumātaka. That is the name for such a corpse. “Discolored” (vinīlaka) is when it loses its original color and turns blue after having gone to a state of putrefaction. “Festering” (vipubbaka) is when it has putrefied and is endowed with pus oozing from here and there. “Slashed” (vicchinnaka) is a body cut in the middle by a weapon on a battlefield or the like and left deformed. “Gnawed” (vikkhāyitaka) is a body with parts eaten in various ways by dogs or jackals. “Scattered” (vittakkhika) is a body with limbs scattered here and there, having been torn to pieces and dragged away by dogs, jackals, or the like. “Hacked and scattered” (hatavikkhittaka) is a body with limbs scattered here and there, having been struck with a weapon and cut to pieces. “Bleeding” (lohitaka) is a body oozing blood. “Worm-infested” (puḷuvaka) is a body full of maggots. “Skeletal” (aṭṭhika) is a complete heap of bones or individual bones. Recollection (anussati) is remembering again and again without interval. Recollection of the Buddha’s qualities is “buddhānussati.” The same applies to the rest. Here, the qualities of the Buddha are the qualities beginning with being an Arahant, etc. The qualities of the Dhamma are its well-expounded nature, etc. The qualities of the Saṅgha are its virtuous practice, etc. The qualities of one’s own virtue are its unbroken nature, etc. The qualities of one’s generosity are its freedom from stain and stinginess, etc. One’s own qualities of faith, etc., capable of leading oneself to the state of a deity, Sakka, or Brahmā, are called the qualities of deities. “Tranquility” (upasamo) is the suppression of sensual lust, etc., which has long been suppressed in one’s continuum through moral practice, undertaking ascetic practices, meditative absorption, or insight, and the Nibbāna personally achieved. “Death” (maraṇa) is the breakup of one’s own continuum of aggregates limited to a single life. “Body” (kāyo) is this body, which is an aggregate of various collections, such as the collection of head-hairs. “Breath” (ānāpāṇa) refers to the in-and-out breath continuously occurring in oneself. “Loving-kindness” (mettā) is affection; it is what arises in relation to another. It means to embrace the welfare and happiness of that being undividedly. It is called “mettā” because it is of a friend or is found among friends. In essence, it is non-ill-will that proceeds by way of bringing about the welfare of other beings. “Equanimity” (upekkhā) is viewing other beings from the perspective of their being owners of their own karma, appropriately and reasonably, having abandoned the three activities of bringing about welfare, rejoicing in welfare, and removing harm. It is simply neutrality that arises in that way. “Immeasurable” (appamaññā) is what pertains to boundless beings. For these are not to be developed only in a certain number of beings, nor in others beyond that; thus, there is no limitation of their scope. Even when this is so, a beginner, having first developed his meditation mind on a single person, and having gained proficiency and special attainment, should then expand the practice to two, three, etc., and also break through boundaries by means of limited pervasion, unlimited pervasion, and directional pervasion. That which is stated in the Vibhaṅga, such as “Dwelling with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, one pervades one direction…” and in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, such as “May all beings be free from enmity…”, this instruction on loving-kindness should be understood as being spoken with reference to those who have attained mastery in the jhāna of loving-kindness. These [meditations], moreover, are specifically direct antidotes to defilements belonging to the side of hatred. And those endowed with them, by always having a gentle heart, are beings similar to Brahmās, and are called Brahmās. Their dwelling is therefore a “divine abode” (brahmavihāra). Or, it is a “divine abode” (brahmavihāra) because it is the dwelling of the best or is itself the best dwelling. “Food” refers to the four kinds of food taken in: eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. “Repulsive perception” (paṭikūlasaññā) is the perception of abandoning delight in food by reflecting on the suffering states to be experienced due to food, by reflecting on its inherent repulsiveness, and by reflecting on its receptacle, storage, digested and undigested state, result, and discharge. “Analysis of the four elements” (catudhātuvavatthāna) is the thorough discernment of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—within the body, distinguishing their characteristics individually. It is called catudhātuvavatthāna because by it the four elements are established, discerned, and noted. “Perception of foulness” (asubhasaññā) is to be developed for abandoning lust—thus, the ten foulness meditations are said to be suitable for one of lustful temperament. Here, one who behaves with lust is “rāgacarito” (one of lustful temperament). Indeed, such a person may sometimes behave with hatred, sometimes with delusion, sometimes with one of faith, etc. But lust is dominant in that person. Therefore, because of that dominant lust, that person is reckoned as one of lustful temperament. The same method applies to the rest. Based on the saying, 'Loving-kindness is to be developed for abandoning ill-will,' and on the statement that the three divine abodes beginning with loving-kindness are, respectively, an escape from ill-will, cruelty, and discontent, and also because the very pure color kasiṇas are not a basis for hatred, the four immeasurables are said to be suitable for one of hateful temperament. And here, this division of temperaments is for the beginner only. And equanimity is not possible for a beginner, for it will be said that equanimity belongs to the fifth jhāna. Therefore, it should be understood that the four immeasurables are spoken of because if the first three are suitable for someone, then the equanimity that follows them is also suitable. Otherwise, since this equanimity is a release from lust—namely, equanimity as liberation of mind—it should be said to be suitable for one of lustful temperament. And the four kasiṇas beginning with blue—this is said with reference to pleasing forms like blue. But unpleasing forms are suitable for one of lustful temperament. “Mindfulness of breathing is to be developed for cutting off discursive thought”—thus, mindfulness of breathing is said to be suitable for one of discursive temperament. One of deluded temperament, however, is naturally prone to heedlessness and has a scattered mind. And mindfulness of breathing, being continuously present, proceeds as if generating mindfulness for that person, so it is said to be suitable for one of deluded temperament.

[244] Vibhāvaniyaṃ pana

[244] But it is to be made clear.

Buddhivisayabhāvena mohapaṭipakkhattāti kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ yuttaṃ viya na dissati.

The reason has been given that, by being the object of wisdom, it is the antidote to delusion. That reason does not appear to be fitting.

Evañhi [M 0.0420] sati so buddhicaritena saha vattabbo siyāti. Kāmañca buddhaguṇādayopi ekantena buddhivisayāeva honti. Te pana visesato saddhaṃ upabrūhayantīti vuttaṃ buddhānussati ādayo.La. Saddhācaritassāti. Paramatthato sukhumatarāni maraṇādīni vipulabuddhīnaṃ eva visayānāma hontīti vuttaṃ maraṇa. La. Buddhicaritassāti. Sesānipanasabbānipīti cattāri bhūta kasiṇāni dve ālokākāsakasiṇāni cattāro āruppācāti dasavidhāni kammaṭṭhānāni. Tatthāpīti tesu dasasu sesa kammaṭṭhānesupi. Puthulaṃ khalamaṇḍalādipamāṇaṃ mohacaritassa sappāyaṃ. Sambādhasmiñhi okāse cittaṃ bhiyyo saṃmohaṃ āpajjatīti. Khuddakaṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulapamāṇaṃ vitakkacaritasseva sappāyaṃ. Mahantañhi vitakkasandhāvanassa paccayo hotīti. Tatthaca vitakkacaritassevāti ettha evasaddo khuddakantipade yujjati. Vitakkacaritassa khuddakameva sappāyaṃ. Na puthulanti. Sabbañcetaṃ ujuvipaccanikavasenaceva atisappāyatāyaca vuttaṃ. Rāgādīnaṃ pana avikkhambhikā saddhādīnañca anupakārikā kusalabhāvanānāma natthītipi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbatthāpīti sabbesupi cattālīsa kammaṭṭhānesu. Parikammabhāvanā labbhateva parikammena vinā ekassapi kammaṭṭhānassa asampajjanato. Dasasukammaṭṭhānesuupacārabhāvanāva sampajjati natthi appanā. Kasmā iti ce. Buddha dhamma saṅgha sīla cāga devatā upasama guṇānaṃ tāva gambhīratāya nānāppakāraguṇā nussaraṇādhimuttatāyagāti hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha gambhīra tāyāti etena ekekassapi guṇapadassa gambhīrattā tabbisayo samādhi mahāsamudde sasako viya tattha appanaṃ patvā niccalabhāvena patiṭṭhātuṃ nasakkotīti dasseti. Nānāppakāra guṇānussaraṇādhimuttatāyavāti etena tesaṃ guṇānaṃ atappa niyasabhāvattā ettakeeva guṇapade ṭhatvā appanaṃ pāpessāmīti attano cittaṃ sandhāretuṃpi nasakkotīti dassetīti. Sesesu pana maraṇasaññāvavatthānesu maraṇaṃ tāva sabhāva dhammattā saṃvejanīyadhammattāca itarānica dve sabhāvadhammatāya gambhīrattā [M 0.0421] appanāya patiṭṭhā nahontīti. Yadievaṃ kasmā lokuttarajjhānāni atigambhīre nibbānasaṅkhāte sabhāvadhamme appanaṃ pāpuṇanti. Dutīyacatutthāruppajjhānānica pathamatatīyāruppa saṅkhāte sabhāvadhammeti. Vuccate, lokuttarajjhānāni tāva visuddhito sammasanañāṇatoca paṭṭhāya anukkamena uparuparipavattānaṃ visuddhibhāvanānaṃ balena atigambhīrepi nibbānasaṅkhāte sabhāvadhamme appanābhāvena patiṭṭhātuṃ sakkonti. Āruppajjhānānica appanāpattasseva pañcamajjhānasamādhissa udayamattāni hontīti ārammaṇasamatikkamanamattakaraṇena sabhāvadhammepi ārammaṇe appanābhāvena patiṭṭhātuṃ sakkontīti. Tatthāpīti tesu samatiṃsaappanākammaṭṭhānesupi. Pañcakajjhāne niyuttāni pañcakajjhāni kāni. Jhānapañcakassa ārammaṇabhāvayogyānīti vuttaṃhoti. Paṭikūlārammaṇānināma atianiṭṭhāni lūkhāni cittarabhijanane paridubbalāni hontīti na tāni attani cittaṃ rocetvā thapetuṃ sakkonti. Tasmā vitakkena vinā cittaṃ tattha ekaggaṃ hutvā na tiṭṭhati. Vitakkabaleneva tiṭṭhatīti vuttaṃ dasaasubhā.La. Pathamajjhānikāti. Yadievaṃ kathaṃ tesu somanassajjhānaṃ hotīti nīvaraṇasantāpaṃ pahānabalenaceva taṃ taṃ ānisaṃsadassana ñāṇabalenaca. Byādhidukkhapīḷitassa rogino vamanavirecanapavattiyaṃ viya bahuṃ dāni vettanaṃ labhissāmīti ānisaṃsadassāvino pupphacchaṭṭakassa gūtharāsidassane viya cāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mettādayo tayo brahmavihārā domanassasamuṭṭhitānaṃ byāpādavihiṃ sāaratīnaṃ nissaraṇabhūtā hontīti na te kadāci somanassena vinā appanaṃ pāpuṇantīti vuttaṃ mettādayo tayo catukkajjhānikāti. Upekkhā pana sattesu sabbaso udāsinapakkhe ṭhatvā bhāvitabbattā kadācipi upekkhāvedanāya vinā appanaṃ napāpuṇātīti vuttaṃ upekkhāpañcamajjhānikāti. Cattāropanaāruppāti kasiṇugghāṭimākāsādīni cattāri āruppārammaṇāni. Sabbatthāpīti sabbesupi cattālīsakammaṭṭhānesu. Yathārahanti taṃtaṃārammaṇānurūpaṃ. Ārammaṇena vinā parikammaṃnāma na sijjhati. Ārammaṇassa suṭṭhu [M 0.0422] daḷhavibhūtagahaṇasaṅkhātena uggahena vinā ārammaṇasampatti nāma natthi. Asatica ārammaṇasampattiyā upacārajjhānaṃpi tāva na sampajjati. Pageva appanājhānanti vuttaṃ parikammanimittaṃ.La. Labbhantevāti. Tattha sabbatthāpīti sabbesupi cattālīsakammaṭṭhānesu. Yathārahanti taṃtaṃkammaṭṭhānānurūpaṃ. Pariyāyenāti idaṃ pana kassaci ārammaṇassa cakkhunā passantasseva avibhūtatarattā vuttaṃ. Yattha pana pathamaṃ sabhāvadhammaṃ gaṇhitvā pacchā tādise tadākāre taṃsaṇṭhāne paññattārammaṇe upacārovā appanāvā pavattati. Tattheva paṭibhāganimittaṃnāma labbhatīti vuttaṃ paṭibhāga nimittaṃpanātiādi. Vuttamevatthaṃ daḷhaṃ karonto tatthahītiādimāha. Evaṃ samathakamme pathamaṃ uggahakosallaṃ dassetvā idāni ādito paṭṭhāya bhāvanāvidhānaṃ dassento kathantiādi māha. Nimittaṃ uggaṇhantassāti ārammaṇassa yathā saṇṭhitaṃ ākāraṃ citte uparupari vibhūtaṃ katvā gaṇhantassa samanupassantassa. Sācabhāvanāti uggahaṇākārena pavatta javanavīthiparaṃparasaṅkhātā sā cittabhāvanā parikammabhāvanā nāma. Punappunaṃ karaṇavasena vaḍḍhanākārasaṇṭhitattā. Samuggahitaṃ hotīti vatvā yathā suṭṭhu uggahitaṃ samuggahitaṃnāma hoti taṃ dassetuṃ cakkhunāpassantassevamanodvārassa āpātamāgatanti vuttaṃ. Tattha manodvārassaāpātamāgatanti cakkhūni nimmilitvāvā aññasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhatvāvā āvajjantassa cakkhunā diṭṭhasadisaṃ manodvāre paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti. Uggahanimittaṃnāma. Suṭṭhu avinassamānaṃ katvā gahitattā. Sāca bhāvanā samādhiyati. Na tāva bhāvanantarabhāvaṃ pāpuṇātīti adhippāyo. Tathā samāhitassāti tena matthakapattena parikammasamādhinā samāhitassa etassa yogino. Tatoparanti uggahanimittuppatti to paraṃ. Bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa citte sannisinnanti sambandho. Tattha anuyuñjanthassāti nirantaraṃ padahantassa. Tappaṭibhāganti sabhāva dhammabhūtena tena uggahanimittena sadisaṃ. Vatthudhammavimuccitanti meghavalāhakantaratovā rāhumukhatovā nikkhantacandamaṇḍalaṃ viya [M 0.0423] sabhāvadhammabhūtā uggahanimittato vimuccitvā visuṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ. Tatoyeva paññattisaṅkhātaṃ nimittapaññattiiti kathitaṃ. Bhāvanā mayanti kevalaṃ bhāvanācittabalena pasiddhaṃ. Ālambaṇanti tadeva samuggahitaṃ nimittālambaṇaṃ cittesannisannaṃsamappitaṃhotīti manodvārikacittasantāne sannisinnaṃ niccalabhāvena saṇṭhitaṃ hutvā suṭṭhu appitaṃ pavesitaṃ hoti. Tanti nimittālambaṇaṃ pavuccatīti sambandho. Yasmā candamaṇḍalādikassa viya tassa nimittālambaṇassa parisuddhapariyodātabhāvena upaṭṭhitatānāma kilesamalavikkhambhanena parisuddhapariyodātabhāvaṃ patvā obhāsajātassa cittassa vaseneva hoti. Na tassa ālambaṇassa vasena. Nahi paññatti dhamme tādiso guṇonāma upalabbhatīti. Tasmā paṭibhāga nimitte samuppanne nīvaraṇasaṅkhātānaṃ paṭibandhakadhammānaṃ vikkhambhitatā siddhā hotīti vuttaṃ tatopaṭṭhāyātiādi. Paṭibandhanti nīvārenti nissaraṇapakkhikaṃ cittaṃ pātentīti paṭibandhā. Nīvaraṇa dhammā. Visesena pahīnā paṭibandhā etāyāti paṭibandhavippahīnā. Samāsevantassāti suṭṭhu āsevantassa. Sattavidhaṃ nimitta rakkhaṇavidhānaṃ sampādetvā cakkavattigabbhaṃ viya suṭṭhu rakkhitvā punappunaṃ bhāvanāvasena sevantassāti attho.

Thus, when this is the case, one should address a person of intellectual temperament. Indeed, the qualities of the Buddha and others are exclusively objects for the intellectual temperament. But it is said that these specifically strengthen faith—hence, the recollections of the Buddha and so forth are mentioned for one of faithful temperament. From the ultimate standpoint, subtle phenomena such as death are indeed the domain only of those with vast intellect—thus, the meditation on death is mentioned for one of intellectual temperament. The remaining ones, all of them, are the four primary-element kasiṇas, the two light and space kasiṇas, and the four formless attainments, making ten meditation subjects. Even among these ten remaining meditation subjects, a large object, of the measure of a threshing floor or a circle, is suitable for one of deluded temperament, for in a constricted space, the mind becomes even more deluded. A small object, of the measure of a span or four fingers, is suitable only for one of speculative temperament, for a large object is a cause for the wandering of thoughts. Here, the word 'only' in 'only for one of speculative temperament' applies to the term 'small.' For one of speculative temperament, only a small object is suitable, not a large one. All this is stated both by way of direct opposition and by way of excessive suitability. Moreover, it is said in the commentary that there is no wholesome development that does not suppress defilements such as lust and does not assist factors such as faith. In all cases, that is, in all forty meditation subjects, preliminary meditation is indeed attainable, for without preliminary work, not even a single meditation subject can be accomplished. Among the ten recollections, only access concentration is attained; absorption is not. Why? Because the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, deities, and peace are profound, and because the mind is inclined to recollect diverse kinds of qualities—so it is said in the commentary. Here, by 'due to their profundity,' it is shown that because each quality-term is profound, the concentration pertaining to it, like a hare in the great ocean, cannot, having reached absorption there, remain steadily established. And by 'due to the inclination to recollect diverse kinds of qualities,' it is shown that because these qualities are of an insatiable nature, one's mind cannot even restrain itself, thinking, 'I will attain absorption by remaining on just this much of a quality-term.' But among the remaining subjects, death, for its part, being a natural phenomenon and a phenomenon that inspires urgency, and the other two, being natural phenomena, are profound and thus do not become a basis for absorption. If this is so, why do the supramundane jhānas attain absorption in the extremely profound natural phenomenon called Nibbāna? And why do the second and fourth formless jhānas attain absorption in the natural phenomena called the first and third formless states? It is said: The supramundane jhānas, by the power of purification meditations that proceed successively higher, starting from purification and comprehension-knowledge, are able to become established in the mode of absorption even in the extremely profound natural phenomenon called Nibbāna. And the formless jhānas, being merely the arising of the fifth jhāna concentration that has attained absorption, are able to become established in the mode of absorption even in a natural phenomenon as an object, by merely transcending the object. Even among these thirty absorption meditation subjects, those connected to the fivefold jhāna system are said to be of the fivefold jhāna. This means they are suitable to be objects for the fivefold jhāna. Repulsive objects, being extremely disagreeable, coarse, and very weak in generating delight in the mind, are unable to establish the mind in themselves with delight. Therefore, without initial application, the mind does not become one-pointed and remain there. It remains only by the power of initial application—thus, the ten foulness meditations are said to be of the first jhāna. If this is so, how is a jhāna with joy possible in them? By the power of abandoning the affliction of hindrances and by the power of the knowledge of seeing their respective benefits. It should be understood as in the case of a sick person afflicted by the suffering of disease, who, during vomiting and purging, rejoices thinking, 'Now I will gain much relief,' or as in the case of a scavenger who, anticipating a reward, rejoices upon seeing a heap of dung. The three divine abodes, loving-kindness and so forth, are the escape from ill will, cruelty, and discontent arising from displeasure, and thus they never attain absorption without joy—hence, it is said that the three, loving-kindness and so forth, are of the fourfold jhāna system. Equanimity, however, must be developed by taking a completely neutral stance toward beings, and thus it never attains absorption without the feeling of equanimity—hence, it is said that equanimity is of the fifth jhāna. And the four formless states are the four formless objects, such as the sphere of infinite space derived from the removal of the kasiṇa. In all cases, that is, in all forty meditation subjects, according to suitability, that is, in accordance with each respective object. Without an object, preliminary work is not accomplished. Without the thorough, firm, and clear grasping of the object, called the learning sign, there is no success in the object. And without success in the object, even access jhāna is not accomplished, let alone absorption jhāna—thus, the preliminary sign is mentioned. They are indeed attainable. Here, 'in all cases,' i.e., in all forty meditation subjects, according to suitability, i.e., in accordance with each respective meditation subject. 'By method,' however, this is said because for someone seeing an object with the eye, it is not very clear. Where, however, one first grasps a natural phenomenon and afterwards access or absorption occurs in a conceptual object of that form and appearance, there alone is the counterpart sign attained—thus, 'the counterpart sign, however,' and so forth, is said. Making firm the meaning already stated, he then says, 'For in that case,' and so forth. Having thus first shown skill in learning in serenity meditation, he now, showing the method of cultivation from the beginning, says, 'How?' and so forth. 'For one learning the sign' means for one grasping and observing the object's established appearance, making it clearer and clearer in the mind. And that cultivation, that is, that mental cultivation which is a succession of thought-moments occurring in the mode of learning, is called preliminary cultivation, because it is established in the mode of increasing by repeated doing. Having said, 'It is well learned,' to show how that which is well learned is called 'well learned,' it is said, 'It has come into the range of the mind-door as if seen with the eye.' Here, 'it has come into the range of the mind-door' means that for one attending, whether with eyes closed or while staying in another place, it appears in the mind-door as if seen with the eye. This is called the learning sign, because it is grasped without being lost. And that cultivation becomes concentrated, but it does not yet reach the stage of another cultivation—this is the meaning. 'For one thus concentrated' means for this meditator who is concentrated with the preliminary concentration that has reached its peak. 'Thereafter' means after the arising of the learning sign. The connection is that for one applying himself to cultivation, it becomes settled in the mind. Here, 'applying himself' means striving without interruption. 'Its counterpart' means similar to that learning sign which is a natural phenomenon. 'Freed from the physical object' means appearing separately, freed from the learning sign which is a natural phenomenon, like the moon's disk emerging from between clouds or from Rahu's mouth. Therefore, it is called a conceptual sign, being a concept. 'Produced by meditation' means accomplished solely by the power of the meditative mind. 'The object' means that very well-learned sign-object becomes settled and fixed in the mind; that is, having become settled and steadily established in the mind-door thought-process, it is well-entered and inserted. The connection is that it is called the sign-object. Because the appearance of purity and clarity of that sign-object, like that of the moon's disk and so forth, occurs solely by the power of the mind that has attained purity and clarity through the suppression of defilement-stains and has generated radiance. It does not occur by the power of that object, for such a quality is not found in conceptual phenomena. Therefore, when the counterpart sign arises, the suppression of the obstructive phenomena called hindrances is accomplished—thus, 'from then on,' and so forth, is said. Obstructions, that is, hindrances, are those that obstruct, that is, they cause the mind inclined to liberation to fall. 'Freed from obstructions' means that by this, obstructions are especially abandoned. 'For one cultivating it well' means for one cultivating it thoroughly. The meaning is, for one cultivating it repeatedly through meditation, having fulfilled the sevenfold method of protecting the sign, guarding it thoroughly like the embryo of a wheel-turning monarch.

Āvāso gocaro bhassaṃ, puggalo bhojanaṃ utu;

Iriyāpathoti satte te, asappāye vivajjaye.

Dwelling, resort, speech, person, food, season, and posture—these seven, one should avoid if they are unsuitable.

Sappāye satta sevetha, evañhi paṭipajjato;

Nacireneva kālena, hoti kassaci appanāti hi vuttaṃ.

The seven suitable things one should resort to. For one who practices thus, in no long time, absorption occurs for someone—so it is said.

Rūpāvacarapathamajjhānaṃappetīti kāmataṇhāya visayabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā sātisayaṃ saṇhasukhumabhāvappattaṃ upacārajjhānato sataguṇenavā sahassaguṇenavā thiratarajjhānaṅgayuttaṃ rūpāvacara saṅkhātaṃ pathamajjhānaṃ tasmiṃ nimitte anupavisitvā viya vattatīti attho. Tameva pathamajjhānaṃ vasībhūtaṃ katvāti sambandho. Pañcasu vasītāsu pana pathamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya pathamaṃ vitakkaṃ āvajjati. Tato vicāraṃ. Tato pītiṃ. Tato sukhaṃ. Tato samādhiṃ. Tato [M 0.0424] puna vitakkaṃ. Tato vicāranti evaṃ punappunaṃ jhānaṅgāni āvajjantassa yadā taṃtaṃjhānaṅgālambaṇā cittavārā antarantarā katipayabhavaṅgehi antaritā hutvā nirantarabhūtā viya pavattanti. Tadā āvajjana paccavekkhana vasitāyo vasībhūtānāma honti. Etā pana sabbaññubuddhānaṃ matthakappattā honti. Tesañhi yamakapāṭi hāriyādikālesu lahukapavattiṃ icchantānaṃ taṃtaṃjhānaṅgā rammaṇācittavārāpi catupañcajavanikāeva pavattanti. Antarabhavaṅgānipi pacchimavārassa upacāra bhūtāni bhavaṅga calana saṅkhātāni dveeva pavattanti. Yattha aparaṃ jhānaṅgaṃ āpāta māgacchati. Nahi ārammaṇe āpātaṃ anāgate bhavaṅgaṃ calati. Naca vinā bhavaṅgacalanena āvajjanuppattināma atthīti. Thapetvā sabbaññubuddhe aññesaṃ vasibhāvapattānaṃpi antarantarā bhavaṅgacāre gaṇanānāma natthīti paṭisambhidāmaggaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Visuddhimagge pana ayaṃ pana matthakappattāvasī bhagavato yamakapāṭihāriyakāle labbhati. Aññesaṃvā evarūpe kāleti vuttaṃ. Jhānassa sīghataraṃ samāpajjanasamatthatā samāpajjanavasīnāma. Teneva hi pāḷiyaṃ samāpajjane dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ. Esanayo sesāsupīti. Tathā samāpajjitaṃ jhānaṃ accharāmattādivasena atiparittakaṃpi khaṇaṃ thapetuṃ samatthatā adhiṭṭhānavasīnāma. Samāpajjitajjhānato sīghataraṃ vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthatā vuṭṭhānavasīnāma. Paccavekkhanavasī pana āvajjanavasiyā siddhāya siddhāeva hotīti.

“One establishes the first jhāna of the form realm” means: having transcended the sphere of sensual craving, one abides as if having entered into that sign, the first jhāna, known as of the form realm, which has reached a state of excellent subtlety and refinement, and is endowed with jhāna factors a hundred or a thousand times more stable than those of access concentration. The connection is: “having brought that very first jhāna to a state of mastery.” Among the five masteries, however, upon emerging from the first jhāna, one first adverts to initial application (vitakka). Then, to sustained application (vicāra). Then, to rapture (pīti). Then, to pleasure (sukha). Then, to unification of mind (samādhi). Then again, to initial application, then to sustained application—thus repeatedly adverting to the jhāna factors. When the cognitive series with those respective jhāna factors as object, though interrupted by a few moments of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in between, occur as if uninterrupted, at that time the masteries of adverting and reviewing are considered mastered. These, however, are masteries that have reached their pinnacle only for the Omniscient Buddhas. For them, on occasions such as the Twin Miracle (yamakapāṭihāriya), when they wish for a swift process, the cognitive series with those respective jhāna factors as object proceed with just four or five impulsions (javana). Even the intervening life-continuum moments—the two known as “life-continuum vibration” (bhavaṅga-calana) that are preparatory to the final cognitive series—are all that occur. Where another jhāna factor is about to come into range, the life-continuum does not vibrate before the object has arrived. And without the vibration of the life-continuum, there is no arising of adverting. Except for the Omniscient Buddhas, even for others who have attained mastery, there is no counting of the intervening flow of the life-continuum—so it is stated in the commentary to the Paṭisambhidāmagga. In the Visuddhimagga, however, it is said: “This mastery that has reached its pinnacle is found in the Blessed One at the time of the Twin Miracle, or in others on such an occasion.” The ability to attain jhāna more swiftly is called mastery in attainment (samāpajjanavasī). For this reason, it is said in the Pāli canon that there is no slowness in attainment. This is the method for the remaining masteries as well. The ability to sustain the attained jhāna for even an extremely short time, such as the snap of a finger, is called mastery in resolution (adhiṭṭhānavasī).
